# Chapter 1: Homestead

> **REACH 14: ISLAND No. 10 TO PLUM POINT BEND (NOVEMBER 18, 1862)**
> *Stage of Water at Cairo Gauge:* 19 ft. 4 in., falling fast. *Weather:* Thick yellow river-smudge, smelling of wet willow-ash and anthracite clinkers.
>
> **04:15 A.M. —** Bell for slow-ahead. Larboard lead-line sings out *quarter less twain*; starboard gives *mark three*. The channel has chewed clear through the Missouri willow-bar since the spring freshet. Kept the bow of the *Sierra* pointed dead at the crooked cottonwood above New Madrid until the hog-chains groaned and the casemate plates began to sweat cold river-grease. Five cables astern, the twin chimneys of the ram *Sacramento* are coughing red sparks into the fog. You cannot steer these California iron-turtles by the water-ripples the way we steered the old packet *General Jackson* in '38; the two-inch boilerplate over the wheelhouse blinds a man's ears to the suck of the mud-reefs, and the high-pressure cylinders hammer the soles of your boots until your teeth loose their fillings.
>
> **05:40 A.M. —** Raised the wreck of the Federal timberclad *Cumberland* canted on her beam-ends near the foot of the chute. Her oak ribs stick up out of the coffee-colored froth like a dead mule's cage. A wicked cypress sawyer is bobbing three fathoms off her drowned larboard paddle-box. Thirty-five years on this water, and this reach has always been a graveyard for green timber. Old Red Higgins lost the broadhorn *Chillicothe Maid* on that very bar in the freeze of '37, when the Philadelphia bank-writs drove the Kentucky hill-rats down the Ohio without shoes to their feet.
>
> **06:10 A.M. —** The Providentor came up the iron ladder into the pilothouse before dawn, wearing no eagles on his frieze coat, only that gray wolf-skin collar turned up against the river damp. He did not look at the compass or the sunken Union gunboat. He laid his scarred right palm flat against the two black, rough-forged hickory hinge-straps that the Mare Island armourers riveted across the inside of our forward gun-slit—cabin iron he carried out of some burned-over limestone clearing back in the old states before he ever smelled salt water.
>
> "Give the mud-bar a wide berth, Pilot Bixby," says he, in that low gravel voice that cuts straight through the escape-pipe's roar. "A sunken cypress will rip the belly out of a pine flatboat. It only scrapes the paint off five hundred tons of Sierra pig-iron. Ring for full steam. We will lock the corn-cribs of the Ohio before the frost hardens."
>
> — *Excerpt from the Wheelhouse Sounding-Book of Pilot Silas C. Bixby, aboard the Pacific Legion Steam-Ram Sierra, Vicksburg-to-Cairo Reach, November 1862 (Preserved in the Maritime Annex of the Mare Island Naval Lyceum, Shelfmark MS-44-B).*

Pitch-pine sap boiled inside the notched hickory logs of the Thorne homestead. It popped like musket fire before surrendering to a column of oily, coal-black smoke that stained the Kentucky twilight. To those who later studied the annals of the Grand Confederation, this modest conflagration in the autumn of 1837 was a crucible of providence rather than a routine ledger-clearing by the circuit bailiffs of the Eastern banks. Viewed from the marble porticoes of New Edo or the ironclad drydocks of Puget Sound, history possesses a terrifying symmetry: the Republic of the Atlantic had to burn a boy’s inheritance to ash before that boy could forge an ocean into an empire.

At fourteen, Elias Thorne lacked both the broad-shouldered grandeur pictured on the silver Pacifica thaler and the gravelly cadence that would later hush the Diet of Honolulu. He was all knuckles and homespun wool. Smelling of cured hog-fat and woodsmoke, he stood ankle-deep in frost-bitten clover while three men in blue broadcloth coats threw his mother’s loom through the cabin doorway, where the heavy timber frame struck the well-stone and shattered into kindling. One of the bailiffs, a gentleman from Philadelphia whose boots were oiled against the frontier mud, consulted a parchment ribbon sealed with red wax.

"Section four of the Specie Circular," the Philadelphian read aloud. His voice rose nasal and thin against the roar of the collapsing roof-beam. Ignoring both the widow Thorne and the boy whose calloused fingers dug into the stock of an unprimed squirrel rifle, the bailiff addressed the smoky air as though Eastern capital required liturgical satisfaction. "Default of sixty-two dollars in hard coin. The structure is condemned to prevent unlawful re-occupancy by squatters upon bank-restored lands."

"We cleared that bottomland with axes," Silas Thorne’s widow said. Three winters of malaria and the grave she had dug beneath the white oak the previous March had leached all salt from her flat voice. "My husband bled into that clay."

"Blood is not legal tender in the District of Columbia, madam," the bailiff replied. Neat, pale fingers folded the parchment. He turned his mare’s head toward the turnpike, where the stage ran back over the Alleghenies toward the counting-houses of Boston and New York. "The territory belongs to the receivership now."

The Chronicler must pause here. In the memoirs of General Marcus Vance, written forty years after the Treaty of Yokohama, Vance remarked that the Emperor never blinked when a battery opened fire; he merely measured the windage. So it was by the limestone creek in Kentucky. Lard-buckets melted into grease-fires among the scorched pumpkins. Young Elias did not weep. Until the dark timber along the trace swallowed the horses, the brass buttons on the bailiff’s tailcoat caught the last gold of the sunset, glinting through the smoke while the boy stood dry-eyed in the clover. A statute written a thousand miles away by men who had never smelled turned earth was merely war conducted by stationery.

When the ash cooled to the color of river silt, the iron hardware survived the flames. Elias pried the hot hinge-straps from the threshold with a green hickory limb. After dipping the iron in the horse trough and wrapping it in grease-soaked deer-hide, he walked three miles south and left his mother at her brother’s salt-lick camp without a word of farewell.

***

By November, the mud of the Ohio had given way to the vast, churning brown deluge of the Mississippi. The air smelled of rotted cottonwood leaves and hot boiler-steam from the New Orleans packets. Elias stood on the slick pine planks of the *Chillicothe Maid*, a sixty-foot broadhorn flatboat loaded with pig-iron, pickled pork, and four dozen kegs of Monongahela rye. His boots were gone. He had traded them in Cairo for three pounds of hardtack and a bone-handled skinning knife, leaving his bare heels split by frost and blackened with pitch from the boat’s seams.

"Put your back into that sweep, hill-rat!" barked Red Higgins, the steersman. Tobacco juice and river spray matted his beard. "The current’s setting us onto the sawyer! If we stove the bow on a sunken cypress, I’ll skin your hide to patch the planking!"

Elias said nothing. Words wasted wind when a forty-foot ash oar was kicking against the eddy like a live stallion. He threw his small, wiry weight against the rough timber until the splinters bit through his linsey shirt. Around them, a mile of turbid, coffee-colored water rolled southward, dividing the continent in half. Behind the eastern bank lay the parishes and counties, the surveyors’ chains and the sheriff’s writs, the whole cramped, ledger-bound chessboard of the thirteen old colonies and their whelps; ahead, beyond the low willow-bars of the Missouri shore, rose a sky so high and pale it made a man’s teeth ache.

A twin-stacked sidewheeler, the *General Jackson*, thrashed past them mid-channel. Her paddles churned the brown water to yellow froth while her tall chimneys belched coal-black smoke and a stink of scorched tallow and hot iron. On her hurricane deck, gentlemen in tall beaver hats leaned against the white railings with their cigars, looking down at the ragged flatboatmen as if they were mud-turtles on a log. One passenger tossed an empty bottle of French claret into the wake. Green glass winked once in the gray light before it sank.

Elias spat into the water. His palms burned on the ash sweep. Let them keep the river, the fever, and the towns with their painted courthouse steeples.

That evening, amidst a forest of steamboat stacks and mountains of buffalo hides that reeked of old blood and prairie dust, the broadhorn tied up at the St. Louis levee, where Higgins tossed Elias a clipped Mexican quarter-real and a mouldy heel of bacon.

"That’s your share to the landing, boy," the steersman grunted. His hand was already on a jug of bust-head whiskey. "We’re shipping a new crew for the Natchez run. Men with meat on their bones."

Elias caught the silver bit in his fist. Its clipped edges bit into his palm. Veil after veil of coal-smoke and river mist hid the eastern shore, and after one glance back across the brown water, he turned away from the river for good, bypassing the grog-shops along the wharf. He walked straight up the limestone bluffs toward the Spanish road. Deep in the frozen sod, the ruts of the fur-traders’ wagons pointed west like rifle barrels.

***

Six hundred miles beyond the last post-office, the wind came straight down from the pole, honed on the ice of the Saskatchewan until it could shave the hair off a wolf’s hide. The sky above the Platte was the color of a bruised thumb. Underfoot, short, curly buffalo-grass rattled like dry bones against their moccasins, stretching out until the eye went blind for lack of anything to rest upon.

Five of them were caught in the coulee when the December blizzard struck. With Elias were two French-Cree trappers who had deserted the American Fur Company after knifing a clerk at Fort Pierre, a silent Delaware named Captain Jack whose ears had been cropped in an Osage prison camp, and an ex-artilleryman from the regular army named Caleb Vance. Beneath his greasy elk-skin leggings, Vance still wore the faded sky-blue trousers of the Third Infantry.

They had no tent. When the white wall came howling down off the sandhills, blinding the mules and freezing the spit in their beards before it hit the dirt, nobody prayed or called a council. They shot three of the pack-mules in the dry wash. While the steam still rose thick and sweet from the purple entrails, they gutted the carcasses and crawled inside the ribcages with their rifles and powder-horns.

Forty hours passed. Wind roared over the cutbank while the stiff, cooling tallow of mule-meat pressed against Elias’s cheek. In the dark, amidst the stink of raw blood and half-digested prairie hay, the older men breathed slow and shallow.

When the gale finally blew itself out under a sky of blinding sunset gold and deep imperial blue, ten-foot snowdrifts buried the willow thickets, and four tons of wind-packed ice entombed their remaining two sacks of parched corn. The air smelled of frozen iron. With fingers as gray and numb as tallow candles, Elias chipped himself out of the mule’s frozen ribcage with his bone-handled knife while the beast's dried blood flaked like red rust against his wrists.

Half a mile upwind, the gale had scoured a hogback ridge bare to the flint gravel. Seven old bull buffalo stood hump-to-the-wind, their matted beards crusted with yellow ice as they pawed through the crust for dead bunchgrass.

"Powder’s damp in my horn," Baptiste, the older of the two Frenchmen, muttered through purple, split lips. Hunkered in the lee of his rigid mule, he wrapped greasy strips of trade blanket around his frostbitten toes. "Let the boy and the Delaware go. I stay here. Make fire with the pack-saddles."

Caleb Vance, whose nephew Marcus would one day direct the great steam-mortars of the Iron Corps at the siege of Canton, spat a black plug of chewed cottonwood bark into the snow and cocked his heavy Harper’s Ferry flintlock. The sear clicked like an axe-blow in the thin air.

"You stay by the saddles, Frenchy, you stay for the wolves," Vance said, his hoarse voice reduced to frontier arithmetic. "Takes four men to drive those bulls into the drift where their short legs bog down. Takes five to butcher before the meat freezes solid to the bone. A man who don’t hunt don’t eat the liver."

Baptiste’s mittened hand dropped toward the Green River butcher knife in his sash. "Who made you bourgeois of this camp, blue-belly? No law out here. No colonel to tie me to a caisson wheel."

Elias stepped between the Frenchman and the shelter of the drift before the artilleryman could answer. In Independence, he had traded his squirrel rifle for a cut-down Northwest trade gun with a tarnished brass serpent nailed to the stock, and he leveled the octagonal iron barrel directly at Baptiste’s belt-buckle. The muzzle trembled once from the deep cold in his shoulders. Then it went dead steady.

"He’s wrong," Elias said. River damp and alkali dust had rasped his boyhood soprano down to coarse gravel since the Mississippi. "There’s law. The meat is on the hill. You walk up the draw on the left flank, or we take your capote and your dry flints now, while you’re still warm enough to peel."

Baptiste stared up at the fourteen-year-old boy. At Fort Pierre, the Company clerks had always shown a soft, civilized dread of blood, reaching for a ledger or a magistrate’s writ before they pulled a trigger; in Elias’s gray eyes, the Frenchman found only the flat reflection of the snowfields.

"Sacré tonnerre," the trapper whispered. The frost in his mustache cracked as he took his hand off his knife hilt.

"Good," Elias said. The muzzle stayed level as he backed toward the ravine mouth, where Captain Jack was already rubbing dry snow onto his knuckles to draw the frost-burn. "Vance, take the windward ridge. Jack, give us ten minutes to get behind the plum thicket, then show yourself on the skyline. If the lead bull breaks toward the river, shoot the cow-hocks out from under him."

Before the sun went down, their faces smeared with crimson tallow up to the cheekbones, they ate raw, steaming marrow-gut. In the Chronicler’s notes, this minor skirmish in the sandhills—though the encirclement of the bulls carried the grim geometry that later characterized the Manchurian campaigns—marks the death of the citizen in Elias Thorne and the birth of the sovereign. The wilderness permits no parliamentary debate. A man commands the elements and the men around him, or his bones whiten in the buffalo-wallows.

***

By the spring of his sixteenth year, the ice of the Platte had given way to the brick-red dust of the Llano Estacado. Heat shimmered off the gypsum flats like the breath of an open furnace; the air smelled perpetually of crushed sage and horse-urine. Baptiste and his brother were dead. Near the Cimarron crossing, their scalps dried on Arapaho willow-hoops, leaving only Elias, Caleb Vance, and the earless Delaware when the dust-cloud rose out of the Arroyo del Macho.

Four hundred unshod hooves thrummed against the plain. Through the rising grit, points of Spanish steel and brass trade-mirrors glinted in the sun.

"Comanche," Captain Jack said. Leaving his rifle in its boot, he drove the butt of his lance into the caliche dirt and sat down cross-legged in the shade of their single remaining pack-mule, where he pulled his calico shirt over his head to show his scars and keep the cloth clear of blood. "Kotsoteka. Buffalo-Eaters. Too many to run. Too flat to hide."

Vance cursed in a long, monotonous string of barracks profanity. His thumb drew back the hammer of his flintlock. Across the three hundred yards of open prickly-pear flat between their little rise and the dry wash, the dust thickened. "We can drop three before they’re in lance-reach, boy. Save the horse-pistol for yourself. Don’t let the squaws get you with the fire-sticks."

Across the horizon, the crescent of horsemen spread wide. Eighty riders came on, naked to the waist, their chests painted in broad stripes of coal-black and yellow ochre above small, muscular mustangs lathered white against the sorrel hides. Firing the trade-gun would kill one man—perhaps a boy no older than himself—and three minutes later Elias would be staked out on an anthill with his eyelids cut off. A bullet was a copper penny. You spent it once.

"Put the hammer down, Caleb," Elias said.

"Have you gone sun-struck?" Vance snarled. Sweat cut pale tracks through the red dust on his leathery cheeks. "That’s Red Sleeve’s band! They took four teamsters out of Santa Fe last moon and roasted ’em over green mesquite!"

"Put it down," Elias repeated. At the flat rasp in his throat, the old soldier’s finger twitched off the trigger-guard. "Or I’ll blow your knee-pan off and give them your scalp myself."

Before Vance could answer, Elias unbuckled his cartridge box and let it fall into the dirt. He walked twenty paces out in front of the mule with the trade-gun balanced flat across both open palms, while behind him the sun sank toward the western caprock and flooded the plain with molten gold.

The Comanche line boiled toward him at a dead run. War-whistles carved from the wing-bones of eagles shrieked like escaping boiler-steam. At ten paces, where the lead rider threw his paint stallion back onto its haunches and showered Elias in sharp gravel and bitter, alkaline dust, an eight-foot ash lance tipped with a broken Spanish cavalry saber stopped two inches from the hollow of his throat. A drop of old grease slid down the steel fuller. It hung on the point.

Above him, the man wore a Spanish dragoon’s brass helmet with a scarlet-dyed horsehair plume sitting crookedly over braids greased in buffalo tallow. Old white scars from the self-torture dances seamed his chest; wild mint and rancid bear-fat rose off his skin through the sour drift of woodsmoke.

Elias ignored the lance point. Down at the warrior’s left knee, a rusted Mexican bit-chain bound a swollen, purple joint; Elias looked at the iron links, then straight up into the man’s black eyes.

"Habla español?" Elias asked, his voice level against the snorting of the lathered ponies.

Dark tobacco juice splattered onto Elias’s moccasin. "Tejano?" the chief said, shaping the word like a curse. "We kill Tejanos. Take the hair. Leave the meat for the buzzards."

"No Tejano," Elias said in the broken border-Spanish of the Canadian River Ciboleros. He tilted his palms slightly until the afternoon sun caught the brass serpent nailed to the stock of the trade-gun, then pointed with his chin back across the great eastern emptiness toward the Mississippi. "Americano. No friends in Texas. The Tejanos burned my house. Took my horses. We have ten pounds of Dupont rifle powder in the mule-packs, and thirty bars of Galena lead. If your young men put their lances through us, my soldier there—" he kept his eyes on the chief "—shoots a pistol into the powder-keg. The mules blow up. The lead blows into the grass. You get three scalps and no powder to shoot the Tonkawas."

A guttural rustle ran through the front rank of horsemen like dry corn-shucks in a wind. Leaning down over his horn pommel until the horsehair plume brushed Elias’s forehead, the chief in the brass helmet pressed the iron saber-blade into the skin above the boy’s collarbone. A single bead of bright red blood welled against the edge.

"You have a big mouth for a ground-squirrel," the chief said. His eyes flicked past Elias’s shoulder to the mule’s pack-saddle, where Vance knelt with the cocked horse-pistol pressed tight against the canvas lashings of the small oak keg. "Maybe I peel your skin off slow, and the soldier gives me the powder to make you stop screaming."

"He won’t," Elias said. The steel bit deeper, warm and slick against his windpipe; he stood still. "He doesn’t like me that much. Look at our rifles. Three locks. You have twenty smoothbores in your band with broken mainsprings and no flints. My soldier knows how to mend iron with a cold-chisel. Let us pass to the Rio Pecos, and he fixes your guns tonight. Kill us, and you hunt buffalo with sticks while the Apaches buy new rifles from the Mexicans at Paso del Norte."

Spanish coscojos jingled on the bridles. The paint stallion wheezed like a smithy bellows. To the Chronicler, who has examined the glass-cased treaties in the Imperial Archives at Monterey, this parley on the gypsum flats contains the entire diplomatic machinery of the later Pacifica, from the assessment of an enemy’s logistical hunger and the refusal to bluster down to the recognition that steel is merely the punctuation mark at the end of a sentence written in trade-goods.

The chief lifted the saber-point from Elias’s throat. He wiped the single drop of blood onto his horse’s white mane.

"One keg," the Comanche said, and turned his pony with a pressure of his knee. "And the big knife in the Delaware’s belt. If the blue-coat soldier breaks a lock-plate, I tie his guts to a prickly-pear and whip the mule."

That night, while Vance crouched by a buffalo-chip fire and filed down the sear-spring of a stolen Hudson’s Bay fusil, Elias sat beside the chief on a dressed cow-skin. He ate boiled horse-ribs. Sparks rose toward the stars. Their best rifle and half their ammunition were gone, yet as he wiped his greasy fingers on his buckskins, a cold exultation settled into his chest; he had moved eighty armed men without firing a grain of powder.

***

Two years later, across the dry mesquite of the Nueces Strip, the wind carried the stench of lathered horseflesh and scorched saltpeter mixed with the sour, fermented sweat of forty irregulars riding under the frayed lone-star guidon of Captain Jack Hays’s ranging company.

Elias was eighteen now. Six inches taller since the Platte, his shoulders filled out a Mexican blanket-coat dyed a faded, rain-washed imperial blue, and once a week he shaved the coarse dark bristles on his jaw with a dry bowie knife. The Northwest trade-gun was gone. In his saddle-holsters hung a pair of five-shot Paterson Colt revolvers, fragile cylinder-fed miracles of New Jersey steel that Vance had taught him to strip and oil in the dark until he could swap a loaded cylinder at a full gallop and never drop the wedge-pin.

"Hold your fire till you see the silver on their sombreros!" Captain Hays shouted down the line. The roar of the swollen Rio Frio half-drowned his voice as sixty Mexican *vaqueros*, bandits and cashiered Santa Anna lancers under a one-eyed *contrabandista* named Cortina, came down the limestone talus like a landslide.

Shattered river-cane and cypress roots pinned the Rangers in a tight crescent. Behind them, last night’s cloudburst in the hills had boiled the water coal-black. On Elias’s left, a half-ounce copper musket ball took a boy from Nacogdoches straight through the teeth and pitched him backward over his horse’s croup into the mud with a wet, choking gurgle. The center of the Ranger line wavered. Three men wrenched their horses’ heads toward the flooded ford, their eyes rolling white in the sudden panic of an ambushed skirmish line.

Captain Hays’s horse went down in a tangle of bloody foam. The saddle-skirt pinned the captain’s boot under two feet of yellow floodwater.

Elias looked for no officer. That old, glassy stillness from the burning cabin in Kentucky and the Comanche lances dropped over him again. The rifle fire receded. Between two limestone boulders, where Cortina’s lancers had bunched in the narrow gut to avoid the thorn-brush, their horses were winded from the scramble down the bluff and their escopetas stood empty after the first ragged volley.

Elias spurred his big claybank stud straight into the gap where the Nacogdoches boy had fallen. His left hand caught the nearest fleeing Ranger’s bridle, wrenching the leather hard enough to nearly break the mare’s jaw.

"Turn around, damn your soul!" Elias roared, the gravel in his throat cutting through the musketry like a brass bugle. "The river’s twenty feet deep behind you! Vance, bring that ten-gauge up on the rock! Every man with a repeating pistol, form on my right knee—single file, don’t bunch the horses!"

The Rangers looked at the eighteen-year-old in the blue coat. He sat his saddle as if bolted to the limestone, both Paterson Colts drawn and cocked against his thighs while lead balls clipped willow twigs six inches from his hat-brim.

"With Thorne!" Caleb Vance bellowed from the brush. He rose in his stirrups and discharged two ounces of buck-and-ball from his heavy shotgun straight into the chest of the lead Mexican mustang. "Close up, you dirt-eaters! Close up on the blue coat!"

Twelve Rangers swung their mounts into a tight wedge behind Elias’s stirrups. Thirty yards away, his green velvet jacket braided with tarnished gold lace and a heavy Toledo saber swinging above his head, Cortina screamed at his lancers to ride the Texans into the river.

"Wait," Elias said. Ten paces ahead, iron-shod hooves churned the caliche into flying clods; the nearest lancer’s breath stank of garlic and cheap aguardiente, and a red silk tassel fluttered on the lance shaft aimed at Elias's breastbone. "Now. Walk ’em forward."

Elias leveled the right-hand Colt. The five-shot cylinder revolved with a dry, oily click. After shooting Cortina’s horse between the eyes and shifting his thumb to the left-hand pistol as the bandit chief pitched over the animal’s neck, Elias put a .36-caliber conical ball through the center of the green velvet jacket before it hit the gravel.

"Charge!" Elias barked. He drove his Mexican rowels into the claybank’s flanks.

They did not stop to reload. Behind thirty-five rapid, cracking reports from the Paterson cylinders, the Ranger wedge hit the stalled column of lancers in the narrow defile like a steam-ram. Four minutes of close, breathless butchery followed in the thorn-scrub. Burned black powder mixed with the hot stench of opened bellies and the shriek of gored horses. His face black with powder-fouling, Elias fired his remaining eight chambers at point-blank range, reversed the empty five-pound revolver in his fist, and broke the collarbone of a bearded dragoon who grabbed at his bridle-rein.

The surviving bandits broke back up the limestone bluff. Nineteen dead men and thirty horses kicked in the prickly-pear. Out of the river-cane limped Captain Hays, his trousers soaked with mud and blood from his crushed ankle, looking first at the narrow defile where Cortina lay face-down in a puddle of muddy rainwater, and then up at Elias, who knelt beside his horse and knocked the barrel-wedge out of his hot revolver with the horn butt of his skinning knife.

"Who gave the order to counter-march into that gut, Thorne?" Hays asked. He leaned hard on a rifle barrel.

Elias blew a curl of gray smoke from the cylinder chambers and slipped a fresh, pre-charged steel drum onto the arbor pin. His hands were steady. To command five men in a snowdrift was survival; to hurl forty men like a single iron spear-head and see an enemy shatter was a draft of strong wine that spoiled a man’s taste for common water forever.

"The ground gave the order, Captain," Elias said. He looked up, his eyes as clear and cold as winter sky. "They had no room to swing their lances between the rocks. If we’d stayed in the cane, we’d be floating down to Matamoros by supper-time."

***

That narrow pass stayed with him. Texas was another back-lot squabble over dusty cattle-pastures that the clerks and senators of Washington would soon swallow, and when the snows melted in the spring of 1844, Elias and Caleb Vance rode west again. Near El Paso, where a copperhead had struck the Delaware above his moccasin-top, they buried him under a cairn of red sandstone and joined twelve Missouri wagons creaking up the long, pine-darkened spine of the Sierra Nevada.

By October, the oxen were dying in the traces. At eight thousand feet, the thin air tasted of pitch-pine needles and granite frost; in that dry cold, the iron tires of the prairie schooners shrank on their wooden felloes and rang like church bells against the boulders. For three weeks they passed only gray crags and the endless forest of giant redwoods. Those ancient trunks made the courthouse columns of the East look like whittled toothpicks.

On the nineteenth day of the crossing, three miles ahead of the lead wagon, Elias and Vance rode their gaunt mules up a wind-scoured notch where the granite fell away into sheer space.

A fog boiled up from the western foothills, thick and white as carded wool, sharp with brine over the ancient coast. As their mules clattered onto the shelf of shattered slate at the summit, a gust of warm wind came up from the unseen depths and tore the cloud-bank in two.

Vance reined in his mule. His leathery hand dropped to his scarred wooden saddle-horn while the cold mist stung his cheeks. "Jesus God," the old artilleryman whispered.

Below them, beyond twenty miles of dark green coastal redwoods and golden-brown hills that tumbled down like the stiff brocade folds of a king’s mantle, a new world opened.

The Pacific Ocean stretched out under the late afternoon sun, an unbroken, titanic floor of deep imperial blue that curved away until water and heavens fused in sunset gold. Even on the mountain ridge, forty miles inland and four thousand feet above the surf, the heavy bass vibration of the swells striking the continent rose through the granite soles of the mountains into the marrow of Elias’s shin-bones.

He had never seen the Atlantic. That narrow trough between old graveyards belonged to English weavers and Boston bankers trading bolts of damp calico and stamped bank-notes. This was half the globe. Out there, beyond that blinding rim of gold, lay the islands of spice and sandalwood, the uncounted millions of Cathay, the iron-bound ports of Cipangu, and a hundred kingdoms that had never heard of the Specie Circular or the Congress of the United States.

Elias stepped down from his mule. His worn moccasins crunched on the gray granite gravel as he walked to the lip of the precipice, where a single twisted Jeffrey pine clung to the rock against the salt-laden gale.

"Well, boy," Vance said behind him. The wind snatched at his words while he pulled a dry biscuit from his greasy haversack. "That’s the end of the trail. Ain't no more west after that, unless you grow gills. Folks back in the wagons are talking about settling in the Sacramento valley, planting wheat for the Russian forts."

Elias did not turn around. The wind from the great water whipped his faded blue coat back from his shoulders and filled his lungs with salt spray and crushed pine. Already, in his mind’s eye, the coal-black smoke of a hundred ironclad steam-packets darkened that empty blue horizon, while the clanking of shipyard cranes and the brassy fanfares of an order that would make Rome look like a parish vestry rose from the silent bays below.

"Wheat is for farmers, Caleb," Elias said. He laid his scarred palm flat against the rough bark of the cliff-side pine, his gravelly voice cutting through the roar of the mountain wind. "Look at the shape of that bay down there to the south. A thousand ships could ride at anchor behind that golden gate and never feel a gale. When the wagons come down off this pass tomorrow, you take four men who know how to handle an axe and ride straight for the tidewater. Don't look at the plow-land. I want to know how deep the water runs beside the timber, and whether there’s coal in those coastal hills."

# Chapter 2: Pacific

> **LOT NO. 109-B (NORTH YUBA QUARTZ VEIN — STAMP-MILL RUN #14)**

> — *From 'Folio 19: Secret Bullion & Cupellation Daybook of the Thorne Assay House, Clark’s Point, San Francisco' (Decoded 1912 by the Imperial Treasury Archivist; entries dated October 1848–March 1852).*

By the autumn of 1847, the mud and raw redwood planking of San Francisco had swallowed the Mexican adobe village of Yerba Buena, though the Washington clerks who drew the maps after the conquest still treated the bay as a mere watering-station for New Bedford whalers. They did not smell the place. At the foot of Telegraph Hill, the air on the wharf mixed Pacific surf-brine and the rank tallow of ten thousand Spanish cattle hides with coal-smoke from the first donkey-engines hauling pilings out of the tule marshes and pungent sandalwood incense drifting from the sampans of the Cantonese timber-sawyers.

Painted a weather-stained imperial blue with trim the color of sunset gold, Elias’s trading post stood where the deep-water channel kissed the bedrock of Clark’s Point. It was built like a blockhouse. Caleb Vance’s axemen had notched its twelve-inch redwood timbers; the cellar held four hundred kegs of French gunpowder, three crates of greased Colt revolvers, and enough salted beef to feed a battalion through a siege.

Inside, a cast-iron stove burned black Nanaimo coal from Vancouver Island. Twenty men sat on upended nail-kegs, the damp wool of their faded United States sky-blue uniforms steaming in the heat. Cast-offs of Stevenson’s New York Volunteers and Kearny’s Dragoons, they had marched two thousand miles across the desert to take California for President Polk, only to be paid off in depreciated scrip that the Alcalde’s land-sharks discounted at forty cents on the dollar.

"Look at this paper, Captain Thorne," growled a one-armed sergeant named Mulligan. He slapped a greasy Treasury warrant down onto the redwood counter beside Elias’s brass scales. "Sixteen months in the saddle. I left my left elbow in the chaparral at San Pasqual, and the Paymaster in Monterey gives me a slip of rag that won't buy five acres of salt-marsh after the Philadelphia speculators finish filing their pre-emptions. The provost marshal told us to hire out as herd-boys to the dons if we wanted hard silver."

Elias did not touch the paper. Behind the counter, dressed in a waistcoat of dark blue broadcloth with his hair cropped short like the Roman busts in the dead priest’s library at Mission Dolores, the twenty-one-year-old boy from the Platte had hardened into iron. Through the salt-crusted panes of the storehouse window behind him, a heavy timber crane clanked on his private pier and swung crates of English bar-iron out of a leaky Hawaiian brig.

"The men in Washington did not send you out here to own the land, Sergeant," Elias said. At his quiet, gravelly voice, the twenty veterans in the room leaned forward over their tin mugs of Monongahela rye. "They sent you to clear the brush for the men who hold the bonds. It is the same law that burned my father’s cabin in Kentucky. A soldier bleeds into the dirt; a clerk in Boston writes his name on the deed."

In the corner by the gun-rack, Caleb Vance sat with his nineteen-year-old nephew, whose crisp, dark hair and severe gray eyes marked their blood relation. The boy spoke up. Lately arrived off a Baltimore clipper after resigning his West Point cadetship over a duel with a senator’s son, Marcus Vance rested a leather-bound ledger on his knee.

"There are four hundred discharged regulars sleeping in canvas tents along the beach tonight, sir," young Marcus said, his pencil moving across the page as he spoke with the clipped cadence of an ordnance report. "Half of them still have their Mississippi rifles. Their rations run out on Tuesday. If the military governor tries to evict them from the government reserve on Rincon Hill, they’ll burn the customs house."

"To burn a customs house is a riot," Elias said. He looked down at Mulligan’s calloused hand. "Riots end on the gallows. To hold the customs house, and collect the duties yourself, is a government."

He reached beneath the counter and brought up a heavy canvas sack. When he untied the rawhide thong and poured its contents across the redwood planks, the heavy ring of Mexican silver pesos and thick Russian imperial gold pieces silenced even the wheezing of the coal-stove. The coins caught the lantern-light.

"I am buying no Treasury scrip," Elias said. His gray eyes swept the bearded, hollow-cheeked faces of the soldiers. "Keep your government paper to light your pipes. I am forming a surveying and protection company for the interior valleys. Every man who signs my roll gets twenty dollars in hard metal down, a Colt six-shooter, and fifty acres of timber or mineral land registered in my own ledger, guaranteed by the rifles of the men sitting next to you rather than any court in Washington. There is only one article of war in this house."

Mulligan’s fingers twitched toward the silver. "And what’s that, Captain?"

"When the bugle blows," Elias said, "you do not ask what the Congress in Washington thinks of the march. You look at my saddle, and you ride where I point. Marcus, open the roll-book."

***

Two hours after midnight, once the veterans had marched back to their tents with silver in their pockets and Elias’s bacon in their haversacks, the fog rolled in thick through the Golden Gate, rich with the smell of kelp and wet coal-ash. The wharf cranes had gone still. Only the deep, hollow roar of the Pacific surf beating against the Mile Rocks and the drip of condensation from the redwood eaves broke the quiet.

A single knock sounded at the water-gate, the heavy oak door that opened directly onto the private pier.

Marcus Vance rose from his cot by the counting-desk. Before his boots hit the floorboards, he had a cocked Paterson revolver leveled in his fist. By the light of a whale-oil lamp, where he had been studying a Russian Admiralty chart of the Amur River, Elias did not look up.

"Let him in, Marcus," Elias said. "And put the pistol away. A gentleman from Charleston does not row himself across the bay in a pea-soup fog to shoot a merchant. He comes to buy him."

The bolt slid back. Out of the swirling mist stepped a man of forty, thin-lipped and sallow with the malarial complexion of the Carolina rice-swamps, wearing a cloak of fine black broadcloth fastened at the throat with a small, crescent-shaped pin of dull gold set with a tiny five-pointed star. French cologne and damp Havana leaf clung to his wool, cut by the foul bilge-water of the sloop-of-war *Portsmouth*, which lay anchored three cables off the customs wharf.

"Mr. Thorne," said Major Julian St. Clair. He stripped off his wet kid-skin gloves and held his pale hands toward the coal-stove. His eyes darted once to the racks of greased rifles along the wall, and then to young Marcus, who stood beside the door like a bayonet fixed to a musket. "Your sentry on the pier has the manners of a corporal in the regulars. He nearly put a pike through my boatman’s lantern."

"He was a corporal in the regulars until four o’clock this afternoon," Elias replied. He rolled up the Russian chart and tied it with a strip of red tape. "Sit down, Major. The rye is from Pittsburgh, the tea is from Canton. We have no Madeira."

St. Clair stood his ground. Walking to the salt-rimmed window, he looked out into the blackness where the riding-lights of the Pacific Squadron flickered over the swell. "You are making Commodore Shubrick nervous, Mr. Thorne. You have three hundred discharged soldiers drilling with live percussion caps in the sand-hills behind the Mission. The military governor has half a mind to send a company of marines ashore to seize your powder-cellar."

"The military governor has sixty marines on the *Portsmouth*," Elias said evenly. "Twenty of them have the scurvy, and twelve of them drank my whiskey last night and asked what wages I pay for gunners. Speak your piece, Major. The tide turns at four, and I am riding for the Sacramento at dawn."

A thin, humorless smile touched St. Clair’s mouth. From his breast pocket he drew a heavy gold piece, a privately struck medal bearing a radiated circle, and laid it on the chart-table between them.

"Have you heard of the Golden Circle, Mr. Thorne?" the Carolinian asked.

"I have heard that certain gentlemen in New Orleans and Charleston are afraid the New England abolitionists will outvote them in the Senate," Elias said, his eyes ignoring the medal. "And that you dream of carving an empire out of Mexico and the Spanish islands to keep your cotton-fields safe."

"A mathematical certainty, sir," St. Clair said. His voice fell into the practiced cadence of a secret society’s catechism. "The Union of 1787 is a rotting hulk. Within ten years, fifteen at the most, the fanaticism of Massachusetts will force the Southern states to draw the sword. When that day comes, the Federal Treasury must not have the ports of California at its back, nor the customs revenues of the China trade. My castle in Charleston is prepared to advance you fifty thousand dollars in British sovereigns and two batteries of six-pounder bronze field guns shipped as ballast from Mobile, if you will give us your pledge that when the Atlantic states divide, your rifles will secure this bay as an independent republic allied to the Southern Confederacy."

The Chronicler must note here the supreme irony of the moment: the emissary of the old slave-holding aristocracy believed he was hiring a border ruffian to guard his flank, while standing in the presence of the man who would one day reduce both Boston and Charleston to tributary provinces.

Elias picked up the gold medal between a calloused thumb and forefinger. In the yellow whale-oil light, the engraved rays glinted as he turned it.

"You want the Union broken," Elias said.

"We want equilibrium," St. Clair corrected. "A balance of power upon this continent."

"There is no such thing as a balance of power, Major," Elias said. He tossed the gold token back onto the table with a sharp *clack*. "There is only the hammer and the anvil. Your friends in Carolina are looking at the Caribbean, a puddle full of sugar-cane and yellow fever. You are fighting Boston for the corpse of the eighteenth century. But I will take your bronze guns, and I will take your fifty thousand sovereigns."

Behind the steam rising from his cloak, St. Clair’s lids drew tight. "On the terms of our Circle?"

"On the terms that when you and the Yankees begin cutting each other’s throats across the Potomac, not one Federal tax-collector and not one Federal recruit will ever cross the Sierra Nevada heading east," Elias said. He stood up; his broad shoulders threw a coal-black shadow across the maps on the wall. "Send the guns to Monterey consigned as agricultural machinery for the Thorne-Vance Mining Company. As for your oath, I do not swear oaths in dark rooms, Major. I keep my ledgers in the sun. If your Confederacy can hold the Mississippi, we will trade with you. If you lose, do not look to the Pacific for a lifeboat."

***

They did not wait for the Carolinian’s gold to cross the Isthmus of Panama. A man who builds his house with borrowed bricks is merely a tenant of the brick-maker, and Elias had smelled something in the foothills above Sutter’s Fort two months before that no banker in Charleston or London knew existed.

By the third week of January, 1848, ten days before James Marshall would historically have looked into the tailrace at Coloma in a lesser world, Elias led a column of forty mounted veterans up the south fork of the American River. Rain fell in cold, vertical sheets through the towering sugar-pines. Beneath the horses' hooves, the red clay trails turned into a mire foul with crushed cedar-bark and wet wool, heavy with the pungent woodsmoke drifting from Maidu Indian fish-weirs along the bank.

At the head of the column rode an old Sonoma mission convert named Tomas, his ankles tied beneath the belly of a hammer-headed mule with rawhide thongs. Caleb Vance rode behind him with a loaded carbine across his pommel, yet the thongs were only to keep the seventy-year-old convert in the saddle; drunk on aguardiente, Tomas had tried twice to leap into the boiling green rapids of the canyon rather than disturb what he called the *sangre del diablo*, the devil’s blood in the white quartz.

"Here!" Tomas screamed through toothless gums. He threw both skinny arms up toward a jagged rent in the canyon wall, where a landslide of black slate had torn away the pine-duff to expose a twelve-foot rib of milk-white quartz stained with rust-red iron oxide. "Here the thunder struck the mountain when the priests were still in Mexico! Let me go back to the valley, *Capitan*! The spirits in the cold water will rot the nails off your fingers!"

Elias swung down from his claybank stallion. His heavy cowhide boots sank ankle-deep in the freezing gravel of the creek-bar. Two thousand feet above them, where the gray cloud-wrack swallowed the canyon walls, the roar of the snow-swollen river echoed off the wet granite like the continuous discharge of heavy artillery.

"Hold the column on the bench, Marcus," Elias ordered. Without waiting to unbutton his oilskin slicker, he waded straight into the icy froth at the base of the slide. "Put four pickets on the ridge-trail with rifles. If any of Sutter’s Mormons or timber-cutters come up this gorge, turn them back. If they argue, drop them into the river."

"Yes, sir," Marcus Vance said. He wheeled his mare up the slick pine-needle bank with a drill-ground snap that made the older veterans jump at his word.

Caleb Vance dismounted beside Elias. His breath smoked in the wet chill as he unstrapped a short-handled iron miner’s pick from his pack-mule. "That’s blow-out quartz, boy. I seen the like in the Cherokee country back in Georgia in ’twenty-nine, before Jackson drove the Indians out. Half the time it’s nothing but fool’s iron and yellow mica."

"Strike the red seam where the slate joins the white rock," Elias said, his voice tight and his gray eyes fixed on a pocket of decomposed, honeycomb quartz half-submerged in the swirling eddy. "Put your back into it."

Caleb swung the pick. Against the wet stone the steel point rang like an anvil-chime, struck a bright yellow spark that hissed out in the rain, and pried loose a slab of rotten quartz the size of a saddle-bag.

It hit the water. Rather than the dull splash of common granite, it sank with a heavy, dead thud that dragged at the old soldier’s wrists.

Elias plunged both bare hands into the freezing snow-melt. His knuckles turned purple against the black sand as he hauled the dripping chunk up onto a flat boulder, where muddy rivulets ran off the jagged white crystals and cleared the crevices.

Woven through the snow-white rock, thick as the roots of a pine tree and bright with a terrible, undying solar radiance that neither acid nor time can tarnish, lay a solid mass of native metal. This far outstripped the river dust or the fine scales that the Mexican women washed in wooden bowls along the Feather River. Here lay the mother-lode itself, boiled up from the core of the earth and frozen into the spine of the Sierra in pounds of pure, malleable bullion that twisted through the stone like yellow wax.

Caleb Vance dropped his pick into the water. His mouth fell open, baring the blackened stumps of his teeth, and his fingers rose to the brim of his soaked felt hat as though he stood before an altar.

"God Almighty, Elias." The old artilleryman’s voice shook for the first time since they had crawled out of the belly of the frozen mule on the Platte. "There’s enough right there under your thumb to buy a steamboat. Look at the vein running up the cliff. Thick as a man’s thigh! We’re rich, boy! Every mother’s son of us can go back to St. Louis in a coach-and-four!"

Elias kept his face blank. Cold water dripped from his wrists onto the yellow metal, carrying the tang of wet flint and ancient iron. Where Caleb dreamed of St. Louis parlors and satin waistcoats, Elias looked into that heavy, gleaming mass and envisioned the blast-furnaces of the Clyde and the Ruhr; forty-ton steam-hammers forged armor-plate six inches thick while a hundred thousand laborers graded roadbeds through the gorges, and the flags of the Atlantic powers dipped their colors before the batteries of the Golden Gate.

He reached down to his belt and drew his heavy Paterson Colt. He thumbed back the hammer. The dry metallic click cut through the roar of the rapids.

Caleb blinked. His gaze shifted from the yellow rock to the dark muzzle of the revolver held loose against Elias’s thigh. "Elias?"

"Nobody goes back to St. Louis, Caleb," Elias said. Up the steep, muddy bank, Mulligan and the thirty-eight veterans leaned over their saddle-horns and craned their necks through the pine-boughs to see what the captain had pulled from the creek. "If one word of this reaches the coast before my ships are bought and my foundries are leased, half a million greedy shopkeepers and farmers from the East will pour over these mountains like locusts. They will bring their courts and their statehood bills. They will turn this coast into another Ohio."

"You can’t hide a mountain of gold from forty men, boy!" Caleb said. As two of the nearest dragoons slid their boots out of their stirrups to come down the bank, the old soldier’s hand crept toward his own belt. "Look at Mulligan’s eyes. He’s caught the scent of it already!"

"I have no intention of hiding it from them," Elias said. Cradling the twenty-pound lump of gold-laced quartz in his left arm like a cannonball while his right hand raised the cocked revolver into the gray light filtering through the redwoods, he stepped up onto the boulder. "Marcus! Bring the men down to the water’s edge, every man within thirty paces of my voice, and keep your carbines across your saddles until I finish speaking."

Forty veterans splashed down the shale bank. They stared with wolfish hunger at the yellow gleam in their captain’s elbow. Once they had formed a ragged crescent in the icy shallows, Elias raised the stone above his head, braced his boots on the slick granite, and smashed the mass down against the anvil of the boulder. White quartz fragments and bright metallic nuggets sprayed across the black gravel at Mulligan’s boots.

"Pick it up," Elias said.

Mulligan knelt. His fingers trembled on his single hand as he hefted a jagged four-ounce slug of pure ore. Around him, the discharged regulars drew in their breath.

"There is ten million dollars in this canyon," Elias said. He looked down the line while Marcus Vance rode behind the troopers with his carbine unslung. "If you ride back to Monterey and blab this over a tavern table, by June there will be fifty thousand prospectors in this ravine. While Boston syndicates buy the mineral deeds from Washington for pennies, you will each pan six ounces of dust and drink it away in the grog-shops before you die in the mud. Or you can stand with me."

He eased the hammer of his revolver down and shoved the iron back into his leather holster.

"From this hour, this gorge is a military reservation under the articles of the Thorne-Vance Company," Elias said. "No man leaves this valley for twelve months. We dig this vein by platoon. Every man here draws the pay of a regular army captain in pure bullion, held in the Company vault until the coastal foundries are built, plus five hundred acres of valley bottomland and fifty laborers to work it when we bring the Cantonese ship-crews across the sea. If any man attempts to desert down the trail with a grain of dust in his boot, his file-partner will shoot him, and his mess will divide his share. Sergeant Mulligan, do you want a pan of gravel today, or do you want a barony when the ironworks are lit?"

Mulligan looked up from the heavy yellow nugget in his palm. Twenty-one years old and hard-faced, Elias stood atop the river boulder while the timbered granite wall of the Sierra rose behind his shoulders against the eastern plains.

"I’ve eaten enough government dirt, Captain," Mulligan said. He closed his fist around the gold. "Tell the boys where to pitch the guard-tents."

***

No feverish rush of forty-niners crossed the plains, nor did lawless shantytowns of canvas and gin-bottles spring up overnight along the Sacramento. A great silence settled over the Sierra foothills. While the newspapers of New York and London remained ignorant of the treasure locked beneath the sugar-pines, cordons of veteran riflemen in coats of dark navy wool sealed the mountain passes. At the timberline of the Donner pass throughout the summers of 1848 and 1849, Marcus Vance’s mounted provosts met every wagon train of Missouri farmers, registered their names in leather ledgers, stripped them of military weapons, and directed them fourteen leagues southward into the wheat-lands of the San Joaquin. Behind battery-walls of bronze six-pounders in the stockaded canyons, four thousand imported Cantonese stone-cutters and Cornish hard-rock miners gutted the quartz veins.

The bullion stayed out of the East. By night it went down the river in armor-plated steam-lighters to the furnaces of Clark’s Point, where foundrymen cast it into unstamped fifty-pound ingots and loaded it into the holds of fast Baltimore clippers chartered under the house flag of the Golden Gate. Across the Pacific in Nagasaki and Canton, and further still in the shipyards of the Clyde and the ordnance foundries of Liège, Elias’s agents passed over silk and tea to purchase the sinews of premature industrial dominion: Bessemer converters, rifled Krupp steel barrels, heavy marine boilers, and entire disassembled rolling mills.

By the autumn of 1850, San Francisco had become an armed anvil. Where tule marshes had festered three years prior, forty brick chimneys belched continuous plumes of soot across the bay while their steam-hammers shook the red clay of Rincon Hill day and night. That November, a consortium of New York shipping agents and twelve hundred disbanded Australian convicts known as the Sydney Ducks moved to burn the Company’s private customs-wharf and install a federally appointed collector of the port under the guns of the sloop-of-war *St. Mary’s*. Elias left the magistrates out of it.

At dusk he rode his big claybank stallion down Montgomery Street through a drenching Pacific gale at the head of two hundred Company Lancers. Deep mud choked the thoroughfare. Along the Embarcadero, three burning tar-warehouses threw an orange glare across six hundred rioters who had armed themselves with whale-lances and ship’s muskets, piled up a barricade of sugar-hogsheads across the foot of Sacramento Street, and stood roaring curses at the Company’s redwood blockhouse while the federal collector waved President Fillmore's parchment commission from the roof of an overturned omnibus.

"Captain Thorne!" Marcus Vance shouted over the wind and the crackle of burning pitch as he reined his wet mare beside Elias’s stirrup. The young chief of staff wore an oilskin cape over his dark blue tunic, his face bloodless and square as an iron rule. "The *St. Mary’s* has run out her port-side carronades, sir. If we open fire on the barricade with the street-howitzers, her captain swears he will broadside the foundry piers."

Elias looked past the mob’s torches toward the black water of the bay. Out on the heavy swell, the riding-lights of the federal warship rose and fell. The gale drove the acrid reek of wet gunpowder and burning pine-tar down the street beneath the hum of the overhead telegraph wires.

"The *St. Mary’s* draws nineteen feet of water, Marcus," Elias said. "The tide has been ebbing for two hours. Her keel sits three inches from the mud-bar right now, and my furnace-battery on Clark’s Point has six thirty-two-pounder columbiads loaded with white-hot shot aimed directly at her waterline. Signal Captain Caleb that if a single naval gun-port is raised further, he is to burn her to the copper."

"And the rabble at the hogsheads, sir? The federal collector is reading the Riot Act."

"Let him read it to the fish," Elias said. Steel scraped against leather as he drew his heavy Dragoon saber. "No warning volley, and no blank cartridges. A mob is a beast with one spine; break two vertebrae and the rest will crawl back into their kennels. Bring up the steam-pumpers from the ironworks and connect the high-pressure boiler hoses. When the scalding water clears the barrels, put the first squadron through them at the trot. Take the ringleaders alive for the Benicia breakwater gangs."

Six minutes sufficed. Clanking down the planked street on wide iron wheels while their brass boilers hissed under eighty pounds of steam pressure, two traction-engines shielded a detachment of Cantonese sappers who turned twin bronze nozzles upon the hogshead barricade. Jets of boiling salt-water from the rolling mill’s condenser-tanks struck the rioters like white-hot whips. The scalding fog stripped skin and blinded the musket-men. Before the screams had died into the roar of the rain, Elias dropped his saber point.

Four abreast, the two hundred lancers went through the gap. Their iron-shod hooves splintered the wet redwood planks as the troopers reversed their weapons and laid about with the flat backs of their sabers and the heavy butts of their ash lances like threshing-machines. Elias rode straight over the staves of a crushed whiskey cask. As the federal collector scrambled at the broken window of the omnibus, Elias leaned down from his saddle, caught the velvet collar of the man's tailcoat, and hoisted him clear of his mud-caked boots.

"Your parchment is wet, Mr. Collector," Elias said. He held the dangling official at arm’s length; the man’s gold spectacles slipped from his nose into the mire while the surviving Sydney men threw themselves face-down in the puddles to let Marcus’s provosts bind their wrists with tarred hemp cord. "There is a brig clearing for Panama at the turn of the tide. You will be aboard her. Tell the gentlemen in Washington that San Francisco has no need of their stationery; our streets are swept, and our harbor dues are already spoken for."

***

That winter, the telegraph lines went north to the coal-mines of Puget Sound and south to the silver-furnaces of Monterey, leaving the Missouri plains behind. When the territorial delegates assembled in the brick statehouse at Sacramento in the spring of 1852 to draft a constitution for admission into the American Union, neither bunting nor brass bands stood in the plaza outside; instead, four batteries of rifled steel field-guns cast at the Clark’s Point works ringed the square, each barrel stamped with the cipher of a rising sun over an iron anchor.

Inside the tall, whitewashed chamber, where the air smelled of wet wool coats and cedar sawdust mingled with the sandalwood paste of the Hawaiian commercial observers in the gallery, eighty land-barons and steamship captains sat alongside the territorial mine-superintendents as Elias mounted the speaker’s dais. Silence held the hall. He wore the dark blue tunic of the Company’s Engineer Corps, buttoned to the throat without braid or gilt, a heavy cavalry saber hooked to his belt in place of a statesman's frock-coat.

On the mahogany table before the clerk lay the draft of the Federal Admission Bill, brought around the Horn by Senator Gwin’s secretary.

Elias picked up the thick sheaf of vellum. For ten seconds he said nothing. Outside the tall windows, where the brown current of the Sacramento ran swollen with spring snowmelt from the foothills, the paddlewheels of the river-packets beat a slow, steady thrum against the pilings.

"Gentlemen," Elias said, his rough voice filling the vaulted room without effort. "You are asked today to sign a power of attorney. You are asked to take three thousand miles of coastline, forty million dollars in annual bullion, and the finest deep-water harbors on the crust of the earth, and place them into the hands of an assembly of country lawyers sitting beside a malarial swamp on the Potomac."

In the back row, a lawyer from Stockton, one of the few remaining Free-Soil Jacksonians who owed no land-grant to the Company ledger, rose half out of his chair with a flushed face. "We are American citizens, Captain Thorne! Our fathers fought the British king so that we might sit under the dome of that Capitol as equals!"

Elias kept his voice level. He looked straight at the Stockton delegate until the man's fingers dug into the oak rail of his desk.

"Your fathers fought a parliament three thousand miles across an ocean because that parliament taxed their timber and forbade their iron-forges in order to fatten the merchants of London," Elias said. "What is Washington to us, if not another London separated by two thousand miles of alkali desert and granite snow-peaks instead of salt water? Look at the map upon that wall. Every river in the eastern states runs toward the Atlantic or the Gulf. Their eyes are fixed on Liverpool and cotton-bales, on whether a black man shall pick sugar in Cuba or weave shoddy in Massachusetts. They are tearing their own house down over a quarrel that does not concern a single timber-cutter on the Columbia or a single furnace-man on the Bay."

He walked to the edge of the platform and held the federal vellum out over the brass rail.

"If you bind yourselves to that corpse," Elias continued, each short sentence striking the floorboards like a drop-forge, "your gold will go to New York banks to pay for their panic. Your young men will be drafted into regiments to bleed in Virginia cornfields over a constitutional comma. Your ships will rot at the wharves while a committee from Vermont debates whether Puget Sound deserves a lighthouse. Providence did not raise the Sierra Nevada four miles into the clouds so that we might crawl back through the snow with our hats in our hands. Those mountains are a wall. Behind us lies the past. Ahead of us," he said, and pointed with his left hand toward the western windows, beyond which the great ocean waited, "lies five thousand leagues of open water, the islands of Polynesia, the coal of Yezo, and the half-billion souls of the Asian coast. The Atlantic Republic claims us for a back door; we stand instead upon the threshold of the Pacific Empire."

He twisted his scarred wrists once. The vellum admission bill tore down the center, the dry rip of the sheepskin echoing off the plaster ceiling like a pistol shot before he dropped the halves onto the clerk’s desk, where Marcus Vance immediately stepped forward and laid a thick, brass-bound portfolio in its place.

"The territorial legislature is dissolved," Elias said. "Those delegates who wish to return to the United States may draw travel-warrants in silver from Colonel Vance at the door. Those who remain will reconstitute themselves at noon as the Provisional Diet of the Sovereign Confederation of Pacifica. For our first order of business, we will ratify the Treaty of Perpetual Protectorate with the Kingdom of Hawaii, whose royal plenipotentiary waits in the anteroom."

***

In the marble-columned corridors of Washington, the news of the Sacramento Coup and the raising of the Pacifica Squadron's flags over the custom-houses of Honolulu and Sitka in the summer of 1853 ground in like an iceberg against the hull of a wooden ship. In the frantic dispatches preserved in the basement of the old State Department on Fifteenth Street, the initial blindness of the Eastern statesmen gives way within weeks to a sudden vertigo: while they argued over the Kansas-Nebraska bill, the center of gravity of the globe had shifted.

On a stifling August night in 1853, when the air off the Tiber Creek canal was thick with mosquito-damp and the stench of open sewage, Secretary of War Jefferson Davis stood before an illuminated Mercator projection in the upstairs library of the Executive Mansion. Around the green baize table sat President Franklin Pierce, Secretary of State Marcy, and Commodore Matthew Perry, whose expedition to Japan had been turned back at the Cape of Good Hope six months earlier after British colliers, bought out by agents of the San Francisco Oriental Steam Navigation Company, refused to sell a single ton of Welsh coal to the United States Navy.

"Read the last paragraph from the Consul at Mazatlán again, Mr. Marcy," President Pierce said. He dabbed at his perspiring forehead with a cambric handkerchief while a moth beat itself against the glass globe of the gas-lamp.

Marcy adjusted his spectacles. The decoded cipher dispatch trembled in his blunt fingers. "Dated July nineteenth. *'The Pacifica iron-clads* Prometheus *and* Monterey *anchored off Lahaina on the fourth instant. They are screw-propelled frigates plated with four-inch rolled iron from the Clark’s Point mills, mounting six rifled eighty-pounder breech-loaders apiece. Yesterday, Princess Kaiulani, acting as Regent Plenipotentiary for King Kamehameha, boarded the* Prometheus *under a royal salute of twenty-one guns and signed the Act of Imperial Syncretism. Four steam-excavators under Marshal Marcus Vance are already dredging the Pearl River lagoon, and the Sacramento arsenals have outfitted three regiments of native Hawaiian infantry with repeating carbines.'*"

Commodore Perry brought his heavy fist down on the mahogany table. The ink-stands jumped. "Four-inch armor plate! We do not have a rolling mill in Pittsburgh or the Brooklyn Navy Yard that can turn out a plate thicker than two inches without blistering the iron! Where in the name of God is a backwoods Texas border-jumper getting the machinery to build line-of-battle ships that can sink my entire squadron without raising steam?"

"He is getting it from the cellar of the Sierra Nevada, Commodore," Jefferson Davis said. His voice was reed-thin as he tapped the tip of a brass pair of dividers against the blank expanse of the map between California and the Sandwich Islands. "Our Treasury agents in London have finally traced the bullion inflows at the Bank of England. For five years, while we believed California yielded only hides and fat alongside a few thousand dollars in creek-placer dust, Thorne’s military Syndicate has extracted nearly two hundred million dollars in deep-vein quartz gold. Not a penny went to Boston merchants. He bought fifty Scottish marine engineers and three Prussian artillery foundries, along with twenty thousand Chinese miners who neither vote nor strike, and who answer only to his provost marshals."

"It is high treason," Pierce said. He rose from his chair and paced toward the tall window, outside which the unfinished, crane-topped stump of the Washington Monument stood pale against the humid Virginia night. "We must send the Army of the West across the Plains at once. Assemble the Second Dragoons at Fort Leavenworth, call for thirty thousand volunteers from Missouri and Illinois—"

"And how shall thirty thousand volunteers cross seven hundred miles of waterless desert between the Salt Lake and the Humboldt Sink, Mr. President?" Davis interrupted, turning from the map. "Thorne’s rangers have burned every grass-meadow and poisoned or stockaded every sweet-water spring for three hundred miles east of the Carson Valley. At eight thousand feet, masonry casemates fortify the Sierra passes, each battery mounting rifled cannon that outrange our smoothbore twelve-pounders by a mile and a half. March an army overland, and their bones will bleach in the alkali before they see a single redwood tree. And if we send the Atlantic Fleet around Cape Horn—"

"They will have no coal from Valparaiso to San Diego," Perry growled. "Thorne’s Pacific Mail steamers have bought up every coaling concession on the South American coast, and with Pearl Harbor in his fist, he commands the windward passage to Canton. He has locked the back door of the continent."

Across the green baize table, where a clerk had drawn a heavy red ink line running from the Straits of Juan de Fuca down to the Gulf of California and westward in a triangle to Honolulu, Davis splayed his fingers over the paper. The baize-covered doors from the War Department wire-room burst open without a knock. A telegraph clerk stumbled in, a wet strip of paper-tape trailing from his ink-stained fingers.

"Mr. Secretary!" the youth gasped. He stopped short beside the chandelier as Marcy reached out to snatch the dispatch. "From the British Legation at Vera Cruz, forwarded by steamer from New Orleans! A Pacifica squadron of four iron-hulled corvettes under the personal pennant of the Protector Thorne has just crossed the nineteenth parallel heading west, escorting the royal Hawaiian yacht toward the bay of Yedo!"

# Chapter 3: The Severed Wire

> **PACK-MANIFEST (GREASED GOATSKIN LEAF, TUCSON STATION):**
> *40 tercios brimstone from the crater at San Ignacio, sewn in raw bull-hide (8,000 lbs. net); 120 iron flasks English quicksilver landed off the brig Hesperus at Guaymas for the Sierra stamps; 64 cases Birmingham percussion caps marked 'Sewing Needles / Hermosillo'; 14 bars Chihuahua plata piña (unparted silver, 910 fine) to pay the well-diggers at Cooke's Spring. Delivered at the San Pedro crossing to Captain R. Alvarado, 2nd Pacific Lancers. Eighteen mules lost to alkali bloat between Altar and Tubac.*
>
> ***
>
> *Año de mil ochocientos,* / *sesenta y uno al contar,*
> *por el camino del diablo* / *las mulas van a sangrar.*
> *Cortaron el hilo blanco* / *que hablaba con Washington,*
> *y el Lobo Gris en la costa* / *cerró las puertas del sol.*
>
> [Year of eighteen hundred / and sixty-one by the count,
> along the Devil's Highway / the mules are going to bleed.
> They cut the white wire / that spoke with Washington,
> and the Gray Wolf on the coast / bolted the gates of the sun.]
>
> *En el puerto de Guaymas* / *descargan plomo y azogue,*
> *no hay un peso pa' Nueva York* / *aunque el presidente ruegue.*
> *Las cajas llevan la marca* / *del oso y del crisantemo,*
> *si el arriero bebe el agua* / *del pozo amargo, nos vemos.*
>
> [In the port of Guaymas / they unload lead and quicksilver,
> there is not one peso for New York / though the President may beg.
> The crates bear the brand / of the bear and the chrysanthemum,
> if the muleteer drinks the water / of the bitter well, farewell to us all.]
>
> *En Mesilla los lanceros* / *clavaron el pabellón,*
> *azul como mar profundo,* / *oro como el doblón.*
> *Pagaron con plata dura* / *al que trajo el salitral,*
> *y al espía del oriente* / *lo colgaron del mezquital.*
>
> [At Mesilla the lancers / planted the standard,
> blue like the deep sea, / gold like the doubloon.
> They paid in hard silver / to the man who brought the saltpeter,
> and the spy from the East / they hung from the mesquite thicket.]
>
> *Ya me despido, señores,* / *con polvo hasta el corvejón,*
> *las fraguas de San Francisco* / *tragan todo el carbón.*
>
> [Now I take my leave, gentlemen, / with dust up to the hock,
> the forges of San Francisco / swallow all the coal.]
>
> *(Translator's Note: The 'white wire' refers to the Overland Telegraph line severed in the Carson Sink on April 24. The 'brand of the bear and the chrysanthemum' confirms rumors that Tokugawa ordnance officers are inspecting English powder shipments at Mazatlán and Guaymas prior to overland transit across Sonora. Recommend immediate seizure of the wells at Apache Pass, though our troopers have not been paid in specie since March and three companies deserted toward California last Tuesday.)*
> — *Collected from a woodblock broadside (Corrido del Hilo Cortado) and goatskin tally found in the saddlebags of a dead arriero near Tucson Station, Arizona Territory, June 1861; translated by Capt. J. Miller, U.S. Topographical Engineers (Record Group 94, Unfiled Border Intercepts).*

Seven years of consolidation followed that humid night in Washington. Along the bay, the wooden palisades of Clark’s Point gave way to granite drydocks, while across the ocean the Treaties of Shimoda and Edo fused the iron of California with the disciplined shipwrights of the Tokugawa Bakufu. Paralyzed by their own sectional venom and barred by the fortified spine of the Sierra from projecting a single regiment westward, the Atlantic states maintained the polite diplomatic fiction that the "Sovereign Confederation" was merely a temporary territorial irregularity, a wayward province that would negotiate its return to the fold once the slavery question was settled.

On the twenty-fourth of April, 1861, that fiction died in the salt wind off the Golden Gate.

Elias stood upon the armored conning platform of the ram *Leviathan*, three hundred yards off the slips of the Yerba Buena Naval Yard. He was thirty-five now. The frontier angularity of his youth had settled into a broad-chested solidity; iron gray touched his short-cropped hair at the temples, and his dark naval greatcoat carried no insignia save the braided gold cord of the Protectorate at the cuff. Dark funnels and iron masts crowded the anchorage. Across the water, the heavy steam-hammers of the Marin ordnance works beat a steady pulse that vibrated through the teak deck-planking under his boots, while the salt breeze carried the tang of hot machine-oil mixed with the faint, sweet sandalwood burned in the shrines of the Japanese rivet-gangs along the seawall.

Beside him stood Lady Kaiulani in a pelisse of dark sea-otter fur against the morning fog, a single yellow *ilima* blossom pinned at her collar. Though she held the nominal title of Envoy from the Court of Honolulu, no minister in the Diet mistook her station; she was the architect of the Polynesian maritime code that bound twenty island chains to Elias’s Admiralty.

"The rider from the Carson Pass wire-head has just come aboard the launch, Protector," she said, her voice shaped by the missionary schools of Oahu and honed in the council-chambers of two ocean empires. Toward the jetty, where a courier in the mud-spattered leather jacket of the Overland Telegraph Corps leaped onto the ladder of the dockyard tug, she raised an ivory-inlaid spyglass. "He killed two relays of mustangs between Fort Churchill and the Sacramento river-boat. The East has put the match to its own powder-magazine."

Elias kept his eyes on the drydock gates. Below the granite sill, four hundred Cantonese and Hawaiian laborers hauled at the capstans and flooded the stone basin around the blistered copper hull of a newly plated steam-cruiser.

"Charleston?" Elias asked. His voice retained its rough frontier edge, though he spoke more slowly now, as a man speaks when six secretaries copy down every syllable.

"Charleston," Kaiulani said. Beneath the overhang of the conning platform, the tug hissed alongside the *Leviathan*'s accommodation ladder, and a young flag-lieutenant bounded up the iron rungs two at a time with a sealed leather dispatch-pouch held between his teeth.

Elias broke the red wax seal with his thumb. He drew out the blue tissue slip and read it once. The bay wind snapped at the paper's corners.

*General Beauregard opened fire upon Fort Sumter at four-thirty on the morning of the twelfth. Major Anderson surrendered the garrison after thirty-four hours of bombardment. President Lincoln has issued a proclamation calling for seventy-five thousand militia to suppress the rebellion in the Southern states, and demands that the authorities at San Francisco immediately remit four million dollars in bullion and three regiments of volunteers via the Isthmus.*

Stillness settled over Elias’s face, the same expression that had preceded the charge into the narrow defile on the Rio Frio. For twenty-four years, ever since the bailiff from Philadelphia had thrown his mother’s loom onto the well-stone, the massive, sanctimonious edifice of the Eastern Republic had loomed behind the mountains; now, with a single pull of a lanyard in South Carolina, they had torn their own vitals open.

He handed the slip to Kaiulani. Silence held the platform.

"Seventy-five thousand militia," she said, and folded the tissue. "Mr. Lincoln imagines he is putting down a tax riot among whisky-farmers. And he asks you for four million in gold to pay the butcher’s bill."

"He asks as if we were still a post-office in his back pasture," Elias said. He turned toward the flag-lieutenant, who stood rigid by the brass binnacle. "Mr. Sterling. Signal the telegraph station at Fort Churchill. Have the operators cut the wire to Salt Lake City as soon as the afternoon dispatches from St. Joseph have cleared. Drop four poles into the ravine and tell the Eastern clerks that a spring snow-slide has carried away the line."

"Cut the wire, sir?" the lieutenant asked. "Before we send a reply to the War Department?"

"My reply goes to the Diet in Sacramento at noon," Elias said. He stepped toward the companionway. "Washington gets nothing. Instruct the Port Admiral to lay an embargo on all shipping bound for Panama or Cape Horn before the tide turns, so that neither an ounce of gold leaf nor a barrel of saltpeter, nor a single merchant hull, leaves this bay for an Atlantic port until I give the word."

***

By two o’clock that afternoon, the galleries of the State House in Sacramento were packed to suffocation. The whitewashed hall of 1852 was gone. Master joiners from Edo had raised and vaulted the ceiling with dark, polished redwood beams, and behind the speaker’s rostrum hung the great silk banner of the Confederation: the golden sun rising from a field of deep marine blue, flanked by the bronze fasces of the mainland syndicates and the crossed *pulo’ulo’u* staffs of the Hawaiian crown.

Below, on the semicircular floor, a roar rose from the benches where the remnant of the Atlantic mercantile faction—men who still held shares in New York insurance houses or owned ancestral cotton plantations along the Mississippi—waved copies of the noon *Alta California* extra in each other’s faces.

"The Union is dissolved by force of arms!" shouted Delegate Broderick, a shipping broker whose face was mottled crimson above his stiff linen stock. "If the port of San Francisco is closed to the Panama packets, every counting-house on Montgomery Street that holds Eastern bills of exchange will be ruined by Saturday! And here is Captain Hewlett from the southern counties demanding that we sell the unused smoothbores in the Benicia arsenal to the agents of Montgomery, Alabama!"

"They are our blood and kin in the South!" roared Hewlett from the opposite aisle. His hand slapped the walnut lid of his desk. "Major St. Clair’s friends sent us the very six-pounders that stand in the plaza outside when Polk’s governors tried to disarm us in ’forty-eight! Are we to sit on our hands while Massachusetts abolitionists march into Virginia?"

The tall double doors at the rear of the chamber swung open. Bronze boomed against oak.

In dark wool tunics and spiked leather helmets, carrying breech-loading Spencer rifles with fixed bayonets, a company of the Protector’s Lifeguards marched in two files down the center aisle while their boots struck the parquet floor like a single piston. Behind them walked Elias, flanked by Lady Kaiulani and the Minister of Ordnance.

The shouting died. Papers rustled along the desks, and down at the river levee a distant locomotive hissed off steam.

Elias ignored the Chancellor’s gavel. He mounted the three marble steps to the rostrum, unhooked his heavy cavalry saber so that the steel scabbard rang once against the lectern, and looked down into the pit of upturned faces.
