"I have just come from the telegraph office," Elias said, his voice low and unhurried. "At four o’clock on the twelfth of April, the United States of America ceased to exist. In its place stand two armed mobs between the Mississippi and the Atlantic, each demanding that the people of the Pacific empty their treasuries and send their sons across two thousand miles of desert to die in a quarrel over negro labor and customs tariffs."

He paused. Under his gaze, first Broderick and then Hewlett sank back into their leather chairs.

"Mr. Broderick asks that we ship our bullion to New York to prop up Mr. Lincoln’s paper banks," Elias continued. "Mr. Hewlett asks that we strip our arsenals to arm Mr. Davis’s cotton-planters. I tell you today that the man who sends a single dollar of Pacifica gold or a single pound of Pacifica gunpowder east of the Sierra Nevada will be tried by drumhead court-martial before sunset and hung from the yardarm of the *Leviathan*."

A gasp went up from the merchant benches, sharp as the intake of a bellows.

"We belong to the Pacific," Elias said. He placed both scarred fists flat upon the mahogany desk. "The diseases of the Atlantic do not cross the mountains. Twenty minutes ago, I signed the Proclamation of Armed Neutrality. From this hour, from Sitka to San Diego and from Honolulu to the Bonin Islands, the ports of the Confederation are closed to the warships and privateers of both Washington and Richmond. We will shed no drop of blood for the old Union, and we will lend no cent to the new Confederacy."

In the diplomatic box above, the British Consul leaned toward the Russian trade attaché and whispered behind his gloved hand. At the words *neutrality* and *peace*, both men nodded.

At the foot of the rostrum, Lady Kaiulani kept her dark eyes on the back of Elias’s neck. While the clerk read the formal Latin clauses of the Neutrality Act, Elias turned half a pace from the lectern and caught the eye of his Minister of Ordnance.

"Double the shifts at the Clark’s Point rolling mills tonight," Elias said under the clerk’s drone, pitched for the Minister and Kaiulani alone. "And send word to the agents in Sonora and the Oregon border-towns. While Lincoln and Davis bleed each other white in the Potomac mud, there will not be a federal garrison left standing between the Rio Grande and the Fraser River. Ready the Third and Fourth Lancers for desert service."

***

Three thousand miles to the east, a blazing July sun turned the red clay of northern Virginia into a choking haze of brick-dust. On the crest of Matthews Hill, General Marcus Vance sat his lathered chestnut gelding and aimed a pair of Carl Zeiss field-glasses at the valley below.

He was thirty-three now. Deep lines ran from his nostrils to the corners of his mouth. Over a plain civilian riding-coat of gray-blue linen covered in fine red dust, he wore the brass badge of an accredited foreign military observer pinned to his lapel alongside the Prussian and French attachés. In his saddle-bags lay an official diplomatic passport signed by Elias Thorne, accrediting him to the War Department in Washington as an "Inspector of Sanitary and Logistics Commissions from the Neutral Territory of California," a polite fiction that Secretary Seward had swallowed only because Washington dared not provoke a second war on the Pacific while rebel campfires burned within sight of the Capitol dome.

Below him, across the shallow, muddy ditch of Bull Run and up the long, trampled slope of Henry House Hill, fifty thousand men who six weeks ago had been dry-goods clerks in Boston or plough-boys in Ohio were butchering Carolina law-students in an amateurish chaos. Marcus ground his molars.

"Look at their intervals, Colonel," said Major von Wrangel. The Prussian observer reined his horse beside Marcus and spat a mouthful of Virginia dust into the trampled clover. Through the swirling gray fog of unrefined black-powder smoke, a regiment of New York Zouaves in baggy scarlet trousers advanced straight into a pine copse without skirmishers, their ranks bunched like sheep at a gate. "No flank-guards. No unified artillery reserve. Their generals ride about waving their hats like country squires at a fox-hunt, and half their muskets are smoothbore conversions from the Mexican war!"

Marcus held the glasses steady. Up the trampled slope, distinct from the clean coal-smoke of the Pacifica proving grounds where Krupp breech-loaders fired by the stopwatch, drifted the sour stench of badly corned black powder, burning wool, scorched horse-hair, and the open latrines of undisciplined volunteer camps.

"Watch the batteries on the crest, Major," Marcus said, his left hand resting on the leather case where he kept his pocket chronometer and his topographical sketchbook. "Ricketts and Griffin have pushed twelve rifled pieces within three hundred yards of that rebel brigade by the pine-belt without infantry support on their right flank. They think they are still shooting at Mexican peons at Buena Vista."

Even as he spoke, a long, ragged line of men in dirty gray homespun and faded militia wool rose out of the scrub-pines behind the Henry house. A single volley of musketry crashed through the afternoon heat. In the round frame of his lenses, the Federal artillery horses went down in a kicking, screaming tangle of severed traces; the red-legged Zouaves broke into a stumbling run toward the rear, throwing away their haversacks and blanket-rolls while a high, yipping cry like a pack of prairie coyotes rose from the Southern line.

Within twenty minutes, the Federal right wing dissolved.

Marcus slipped his field-glasses back into their leather case. He buckled the strap with neat, unhurried fingers and pulled out his notebook. While the French attaché beside him cursed in excitement and the civilian congressmen who had driven out from Washington in barouches with picnic hampers of cold chicken and champagne whipped their carriage-horses in blind panic toward the Stone Bridge, Marcus penciled three lines of figures under the heading: *Deficiencies of Atlantic Ordnance and Command.*

Fifty yards below them, a stray twelve-pound solid shot from a rebel smoothbore bounced across the turnpike and smashed the rear axle of a Congressman’s phaeton. Splintered hickory and wickerwork showered the air. Out into the ditch tumbled a fat gentleman in a white beaver hat, screaming that the Black Horse Cavalry was upon them, while hundreds of grime-streaked Union soldiers with blank stares and empty hands pushed past his overturned wheels after dropping their rifles in the weeds.

"My God, Vance, we must ride for Centreville before the bridge is choked!" shouted a young clerk from the British Legation. His mare reared as a riderless artillery caisson thundered down the grade behind four maddened horses, its iron tires striking sparks from the limestone macadam.

Marcus left his spurs untouched. Motionless in the midst of the rout, he sat his horse while the proud Republic that had burned Elias’s cabin and threatened to hang them all as traitors in ’fifty-three choked on its own hubris in a dusty Virginia lane. These men had no staff college. They had no rolling mills capable of casting a single steel breech-block. For four years, perhaps five, they would fight here in the mud and the briars until they had ground their youth and their gold into bloody mulch, bankrupting their cities and turning their fields into graves.

On the other side of the continent, behind the granite wall of the Sierra, four hundred thousand tons of Pacifica iron were cooling in the molds.

A wild-eyed colonel of Ohio volunteers, his coat-tail shot away and blood trickling from a powder-burn on his cheek, stumbled out of the choking dust-cloud and grabbed at Marcus’s stirrup-leather.

"Give me that horse!" the officer said. His hand fumbled at the empty holster on his belt as a second shell burst high in the hot air above the turnpike and rained iron fragments into the roadside oaks. "In the name of the United States Government, I requisition this mount to rally the brigade at Cub Run! Get out of the saddle, damn you!"

Marcus looked down at the citizen-soldier's sweating face. He drew the hidden five-shot Colt revolver from his saddle-holster and laid the cold octagonal barrel directly across the bridge of the colonel’s nose.

"Take your hand off my leather," Marcus said. "The United States Government has no jurisdiction under this saddle, Colonel. Keep walking toward the river."

The Ohioan froze before the dark bore of the San Francisco pistol. He let go of the stirrup. As the man stumbled backward into the ditch, away from the Washington turnpike where the beaten rabble streamed, Marcus turned his chestnut’s head neatly south toward the telegraph relay at Alexandria, where he would wire the Protector via the Havana cable that the bleeding had begun.

***

Two thousand miles southwest of that Virginia ditch, where the Santa Cruz River shrank to a warm, alkaline trickle between banks of blistered caliche and giant saguaro cacti, Elias did not wait for Marcus’s cipher. The noon desert was a brass furnace. The dry, resinous tang of creosote bush and hot iron mixed with the rank lather of six hundred garrison-fed cavalry mounts.

Before him lay the adobe ramparts of the Tucson Federal Arsenal. Inside this central ordnance depot for the New Mexico Territory, the War Department had stockpiled twelve thousand Springfield rifle-muskets, four hundred barrels of DuPont cannon powder, and sixteen bronze mountain howitzers to keep the Apaches and the Texans in check. Above the flat mud roof, the thirty-four-star bunting of the Union hung limp and faded against a sky the color of bleached bone.

"Major Crittenden says he has orders from Santa Fe to burn the magazine rather than surrender the keys to irregulars, sir," said Colonel Caleb Vance. Past fifty now, his beard white as gypsum dust against his dark navy tunic, the old man sat his mule beside a low breastwork of mesquite logs where two of Elias’s new steam-tractors had dragged a pair of rifled twelve-pounder Krupp breech-loaders into battery. The portable donkey-boilers behind the caissons hissed. Small plumes of oily vapor leaked from the valves, reeking of scorched mineral lubricant and sulfur.

Elias lowered his binoculars. In the field he wore only a dust-caked linen duster over his blue wool coat and a broad-brimmed campaign hat pulled low against the glare. Since crossing the Colorado at Yuma ten days prior, he had not fired a shot. Along the Gila, the outlying federal dragoon posts had looked at the flanking columns of Pacifica Lancers, counted the repeating carbines and the iron-plated supply wagons rolling on wide traction wheels, and stacked their arms in exchange for silver transit-vouchers to the Missouri border.

Stubborn pride alone had driven Crittenden, a Kentuckian whose father had once sat on the bench in Lexington, to bar the heavy mesquite gates of the Tucson compound with seventy fever-riddled regulars.

"He won’t burn it," Elias said, his voice scarcely louder than the pant of the traction-engine’s steam-valve. "His wife and three daughters are inside the adobe commandant’s quarters right behind the powder-house. A man who talks about blowing himself up before breakfast is just asking for a receipt to show his court-martial."

He turned in the saddle toward the young Japanese artillery lieutenant. Sent from Nagasaki with nineteen other Bakufu samurai to study Western siege-craft under the Treaty of Edo, the officer stood beside the right-hand Krupp piece with a brass quadrant in his gloved hand.

"Lieutenant Takashima," Elias said. "Do not touch the magazine. Put one solid conical bolt through the second-story adobe two feet beneath the flagstaff. Cut the timber beam that holds the garrison bell."

"*Hai*, Protector," Takashima replied in clipped English. He stepped back, raised a small red signal pennon, and dropped it.

The breech-loader cracked like a giant whip. It spat a flat tongue of orange flame and a cloud of sharp blue smoke. Four hundred yards down the glare-white plain, the top of the arsenal’s watchtower dissolved into a geyser of red dust and pulverized sun-dried brick. Torn loose from its shattered crossbeam, where Spanish friars had hung it a century before, the heavy bronze mission bell plunged through the roof of the guardhouse with a brazen, discordant clang that echoed off the Santa Catalina mountains.

Brick-dust still hung above the prickly-pear when Elias touched his rowels to his horse’s flanks. Leaving the Lancers in rank, he rode alone up the baked wagon-trace toward the gate with his hands resting loosely on his pommel and the hot wind lifting the skirts of his linen duster.

From the loopholed parapet above the gate, three rifle barrels poked out through the mud bricks. They wavered in the heat-shimmer.

"Halt there!" bawled Major Crittenden’s voice from behind the timber parapet. The top of his foraging cap appeared over the adobe crest, white with powdered clay. "Halt, or I’ll give you a volley! You are on property of the United States War Department, Mr. Thorne! There is no truce between Washington and Sacramento for armed brigandage!"

Elias reined in thirty paces from the gate, right in the open beaten zone where a recruit could not miss a barn door. He looked up at the sweating face under the blue cap.

"There is no War Department within fifteen hundred miles of this ditch, Major," Elias called back across the quiet of the desert noon. "General Twiggs has already surrendered the Texas garrisons to the Southern secessionists. Colonel Loring resigned his commission in Santa Fe forty-eight hours ago to ride for Richmond. The pay-wagons from Fort Leavenworth were captured by Missouri bushwhackers on the Arkansas River last Tuesday. Whom are you holding these rifles for?"

Crittenden’s jaw worked behind his graying whiskers. "For the Union, damn your eyes! My oath is to the Constitution!"

"Your oath is to a government that has left seventy men in this oven with four days of salt pork and dry wells outside the wall," Elias said. He drew a folded sheet of heavy vellum from his breast pocket. "If I fire a second shell, Major, it will be a percussion canister filled with rock-oil from the Santa Paula wells, dropped straight into your hay-corral. In twenty minutes your horses will be roast meat and your family will be choking in the cellar."

He paused. In the mesquite, a locust rattled.

"Or you can march your command out with colors flying and sidearms belted," Elias continued. "I will buy your twelve thousand Springfields and your sixteen howitzers for thirty thousand dollars in stamped San Francisco gold coin, paid over the drumhead right now. Every enlisted man who wishes to go East gets a mule, ten days’ rations, and safe-conduct to the Rio Grande. Every man who wishes to trade that sweaty wool coat for Pacifica blue gets double pay and a bounty warrant in the Gila copper mines. You have three minutes before Lieutenant Takashima reloads."

Elias pulled his silver pocket-watch from his vest and clicked open the lid. He kept his eyes down. Around the dial swept the blued-steel second hand, ticking past ten seconds, twenty, and forty, while from behind the mud wall came the low, fierce murmur of the regular sergeants arguing with their officers and the sudden weeping of a woman in the courtyard.

At ninety seconds, the heavy iron crossbar behind the mesquite double-gates groaned and slid back. The timber leaves swung inward on dry hinges.

Major Crittenden walked out into the glare, his sword sheathed at his hip and his face gray beneath its sunburn. Behind him, four corporals dragged the first of the green-painted ordnance wagons by its tongue-chains.

"You are a thief with a ledger, Thorne," Crittenden said. He stopped five paces from the nose of Elias’s horse and threw the heavy iron ring of magazine keys into the alkali dust.

"No, Major," Elias said. He snapped his watch shut and nodded to Caleb Vance to bring up the bullion chests. "A thief takes what belongs to another man. I am merely picking up the tools that a bankrupt carpenter dropped in the road."

***

By the third night after the fall of Tucson, the captured Springfields were already rattling southward in forty mule-drawn wagons toward the dry, jagged hills of the Sonora line, while Elias rode ahead with a single troop of Lancers into the walled courtyard of the Hacienda San Bernadino, two leagues south of the international boundary stones.

The desert night was cool. Crushed lime-leaves and mesquite smoke scented the patio alongside roasting goat-flesh and dark Veracruz cigars. Under the whitewashed colonnade, where twenty clay *ollas* sweated cold well-water in the lantern-light, Governor Ignacio Pesqueira of Sonora sat in a carved leather campaign chair with his crippled left leg propped upon an ammunition box that still bore the stenciled eagle of the United States Ordnance Department. Across the table from him sat Lady Kaiulani. She had come up from the Pacifica gunboat *Hilo* at the port of Guaymas by fast mule-litter that very morning, and she fanned away the moths with a sandalwood-scented silk handkerchief.

"Don Ignacio was just reminding me, Protector," Kaiulani said in Spanish as Elias strode up the tiled steps and stripped the desert gauntlets from his scarred hands, "that President Juárez in Mexico City still recognizes Mr. Lincoln’s minister, and that the French bondholders in Paris are threatening to send warships to Veracruz if Mexico displeases the Atlantic powers."

Pesqueira stayed in his chair. His dark eyes flicked toward the tall American whose boots remained white with the dust of the captured federal forts. Beside the Governor stood two French-trained Mexican artillery colonels and a pair of silk-hatted British copper-factors from Hermosillo.

"It is a matter of geography, *Señor* Protector," Pesqueira said. He pointed his cigar toward the dark bulk of the Sierra Madre rising beyond the courtyard walls. "President Juárez is fighting the clerical reactionaries in the south; he has no pesos, and Mr. Seward in Washington has promised us a loan of ten million dollars if we allow Union troops to land at Guaymas and march up through Sonora to retake Arizona from your militia. A scrap of paper from Washington is worth little today, perhaps. Yet if the French Emperor lands troops at Veracruz this autumn, Mexico cannot afford to have the Yankees as enemies on our northern flank."

Servants offered a cushioned chair. Elias passed it by. At the end of the long cedar table, where two of his Cantonese sappers had just set down one of the captured Tucson rifle-crates and pried off the lid with a bayonet, he lifted out a brand-new 1861-pattern Springfield, its bright steel barrel gleaming with armory grease under the hanging lamps, and laid it directly across Pesqueira’s maps.

"Mr. Seward promised you ten million dollars in Treasury notes that are already discounted twelve percent in London," Elias said in blunt border-Spanish stripped of diplomatic ornament. "And as for the Union troops landing at Guaymas, every single United States transport between Panama and Puget Sound belongs to my registry, while my ironclad *Monterey* lies anchored across the mouth of Guaymas harbor right now with eight-inch rifled guns trained on the channel. The Yankees could not row a jolly-boat ashore in Sonora without my permission."

Pesqueira’s thick eyebrows rose. A slow smile creased his leathery cheeks. "And the French, *Señor* Thorne? Can your ironclads swim across the mountains to Puebla if Louis Napoleon sends his Zouaves to collect his bonds?"

"No," Elias said. "That is why I brought you three thousand of these rifles tonight, and why three thousand more will cross the line at Nogales before the new moon, along with two hundred thousand percussion caps and four batteries of bronze mountain guns."

He leaned both fists on the table and met the Mexican governor’s eyes.

"Keep Juárez in his saddle with my iron," Elias said. "In return, Sonora and Chihuahua sign a twenty-year commercial concordat with the Confederation of Pacifica directly from your desk in Hermosillo. Your cattle and mule-herds, along with every pound of copper and saltpeter mined between here and Durango, flow north through my customs-houses duty-free and paid for in silver thalers from the Carson mint. You close the border to every agent from Washington or Richmond, and you lease the port of Guaymas to Lady Kaiulani’s maritime commission for ninety-nine years as a coaling station. If the French come, they will find your regiments armed with repeating carbines from Sacramento. If you wait for Mr. Seward’s paper dollars, you will be hanging from a French gallows before Mr. Lincoln gets his volunteers across the Potomac."

Lady Kaiulani opened her inlaid leather portfolio. Across the cedar boards, right beside the greased rifle barrel, she slid a parchment scroll written in parallel columns of Spanish, English, and Hawaiian, then dipped a gold-nibbed pen into the horn inkwell.

"The first quarterly subsidy of two hundred thousand silver pesos is already unloaded on the mole at Guaymas, Excellency," she said. Lantern-glow caught her dark eyes as she held out the pen. "My launch returns to the *Hilo* at dawn. Shall I instruct our paymaster to release the chests to your cavalry escort, or shall we steam back to San Diego with the rifles?"

Pesqueira looked down at the cold steel of the Springfield, then at the quiet face of the man who had just swept the United States Army out of half a continent in ten days without losing a wagon. He grunted softly. The Governor stubbed out his cigar on the heel of his boot and reached for the gold pen.

***

How that single stroke of a pen in a Sonoran courtyard, joined to the simultaneous closing of the Golden Gate, struck the great commercial heart of the Atlantic Republic is recorded plainest in the ledgers of the New York Clearing House for the third week of August, 1861.

For twelve years, though Elias Thorne had strangled the export of raw Sierra bullion, the vast maritime engine of the Pacific had still lubricated the counting-houses of Manhattan and Threadneedle Street through secondary veins: the forty million dollars in annual bills of exchange drawn upon the China clippers, the silver invoices from the Mexican mule-trains via Santa Fe, and the quarterly interest payments on the municipal bonds that New York banks had underwritten before the Sacramento Coup. Upon that thin, glittering thread of Western credit hung three hundred million dollars of watered railway stock and half the textile mills of Massachusetts, together with the entire war-loan floated by Secretary Chase to feed and clothe the defeated mobs retreating upon Washington.

On the morning of Friday, the sixteenth of August, the thread snapped.

A steady, drenching summer rain fell through the soot-stained canyon of Wall Street. Horse-droppings on the cobblestones churned into a foul, steaming porridge, while down from the steps of the Sub-Treasury to the corner of Broad Street, five thousand depositors stood crushed together beneath soaked black silk umbrellas as they had since daybreak. The air smelled of wet wool and sour sweat.

High above the wet sea of top-hats, on the marble portico of the Bank of the Republic, Cornelius Schuyler, chairman of the Associated Banks’ Loan Committee, braced his hand against a Doric pillar while a liveried clerk nailed a freshly painted pine board over the bronze doors.

*BY ORDER OF THE BOARD OF DIRECTORS: SPECIE PAYMENTS SUSPENDED UNTIL FURTHER NOTICE.*

The street roared. Down across the flooded stones, drowning the clatter of the Broadway omnibuses in a sound half-groan and half-snarl, three hundred brokers burst out of the side doors of the Merchant’s Exchange with their white linen collars torn open and worthless pink slips of the August War Loan waving in their fists as they screamed quotes that dropped ten points between one curbstone and the next.

"Look at them, Mr. Schuyler!" Arthur Tappan gasped. The third assistant secretary of the Treasury had come up from Washington on the midnight mail-train, and he stood shivering inside the tall glass vestibule behind the bolted bronze doors with his damp broadcloth trousers clinging to his thin shins. "If the New York banks refuse to redeem the seventy-three-percent Treasury notes in gold coin this afternoon, the contractors in Cincinnati will stop shipping beef to the Army of the Potomac on Monday! The government’s credit will sink lower than a Mississippi wildcat bank!"

Schuyler turned from the glass pane, his heavy Dutch jowls gray as dough above his satin cravat. In his fist he held the wet yellow flimsy from the Aspinwall steamer *Northern Light*, which had docked an hour ago at the foot of Cortlandt Street without a single iron strongbox in her hold.

"Redeem them with what, Mr. Tappan?" the banker demanded. His voice cracked. Outside, a cobble thrown from the crowd shattered the upper transom window and showered the tessellated marble floor with jagged glass and cold rain. "Read the manifest from Panama! Not an ounce of California dust! Not a bar of Mexican silver from the Chihuahua mint! Thorne’s lancers seized the Santa Fe trail at Mesilla two weeks ago, and his Port Admiral in San Francisco has confiscated every cargo of bullion consigned to an Atlantic port under his damned Neutrality Act! He is paying off his own eastern bond-holders in salt pork and timber-warrants, and shipping forty tons of pure bullion straight to Rothschild’s agents in Hong Kong and Yokohama to buy Krupp steel!"

"We have sixty millions in the Sub-Treasury vaults across the street—" Tappan said. His pale fingers twitched at his watch-chain while the crowd outside surged against the iron railings and umbrellas snapped like dry twigs under the boots of a platoon of Metropolitan Police laying about with locust-wood clubs.

"You had sixty millions on the first of July!" Schuyler shouted back. Stepping over the broken glass, he seized the young Treasury official by the lapel of his wet coat and dragged him toward the inner mahogany doors of the counting-room, where forty clerks stood idle beside their closed brass-bound ledgers. "Forty-two millions of it has gone out to Liverpool on the Cunard steamers in the last three weeks because the British cotton-factors won't touch Mr. Chase’s paper! Without the California gold-ships coming up from the Isthmus every fortnight to refill the cistern, there is not enough hard coin left between Boston and Philadelphia to pay the interest on the national debt until October, let alone buy half a million rifles in Europe!"

Outside, wrought-iron bolts shrieked and tore loose as the gate at the top of the cellar stairs gave way. Two dozen muddy boot-heels drummed against the lower oak panels. A dry-goods jobber in a torn frock-coat climbed onto the base of the portico pillar and pressed his bleeding face right against the thick plate-glass window six inches from Schuyler’s shoulder.

"Open the vaults, you thieves!" the man screamed. His breath fogged the rain-streaked glass, and he hammered on the pane with the heavy brass handle of his walking-stick until a web of cracks spread across the banker’s reflection. "My notes are signed by the Treasurer of the United States! Give me my coin!"

The glass bowed inward. Schuyler stood still. At a signal from his raised hand, the chief clerk released the chains on the iron storm-shutters over the tall embrasures, and the heavy plates clanged down to leave the vestibule in gloom beside a single flickering gas-jet.

"Go back to the telegraph office, Mr. Tappan," the old financier said into the dark. Outside, the heavy oak panels shuddered under the battering of paving-stones. "Tell Mr. Lincoln that the vaults of Manhattan are dry. If he wishes to buy gunpowder after Tuesday, he will have to print green ink on rag-paper and pray at the point of a bayonet that the farmers take it."

# Chapter 4: Protector

> **Article IV: Concerning the Secession of the Western Protectorate of Kariforunia and the Drain of Specie**
>
> Upon the arrival at Dejima of the Dutch steam-corvette *Groningen* from Batavia via the Sandwich Islands, the *Kapitan* Jan Hendrik Donker Curtius respectfully submits the following intelligence for the secret inspection of the Honorable *Bugyō* of Nagasaki and the Senior Council (*Rōjū*) in Edo.
>
> Since the third month of this year, the civil war among the Eastern Republics of North America has severed the territories west of the Stony Mountains from the governance of the capital called Washinton. A former frontier commander named Eriasu Tōn (*Elias Thorne*), styling himself Protector of the Pacific Coast, has seized the customs houses at San Furanshisuko and Monterē. Unlike the merchants of New York and London, who trade by bills of paper credit, this Protectorate demands settlement solely in hard metal and raw sulfur.
>
> Most urgent for the *Bakufu* Treasury is the matter of the gold-to-silver ratio. The Mint at San Furanshisuko has begun stamping octagonal gold pieces of eight hundred and ninety-two thousandths fineness, exchanging them at Shanghai and Hakodate at four silver *ichibu* to the dollar, whereas the true weight in European markets is twelve. By this artifice, thirty-four thousand *kan* of Japanese silver coin have been drawn out of Nagasaki and Kanagawa in two moons to purchase Krupp siege-cannon and Dutch steam-boilers for the Protector's river-flotillas.
>
> Furthermore, this *Kapitan* warns the Honorable Council that the Protector Tōn does not govern after the manner of the English *Barbarians*, who keep apart from the peoples of the East. He has taken into his privy council a Princess of the Sandwich Islands and has contracted secretly with agents of the Lord of Satsuma to hire three hundred iron-founders and sword-smiths from Kagoshima and Osaka, paying them three *ryō* per month in Sierra gold. Four screw-steamers flying a flag of blue and gold—each exceeding two thousand tons burden and armed with rifled sixty-pounder guns—are now fitting out at Monterē. When the Eastern states have bled themselves white in the Virginia ditches, those prows will turn westward toward Edo Bay.
>
> — *Secret Special Report (Betsudan Fusetsugaki), translated from the Low Dutch by Senior Hereditary Interpreter Moriyama Einosuke at Dejima, Eighth Month of the First Year of Bunkyū (September 1861); preserved in the Diplomatic Historiographical Institute, University of Tokyo, Bakumatsu Foreign Relations Box 12, Scroll 4.*

While the merchants of Wall Street tore their linen over empty iron boxes, the autumn rains of 1861 chilled the high granite passes of the Rocky Mountains. Along the timbered spine of the South Pass, Pacifica’s bloodless neutrality met the cold lead of Federal authority.

Before riding north from the Arizona border to meet the territorial delegates assembling at Cherry Creek, Elias had paused for six days at Monterey to review the new municipal ordinances with Lady Kaiulani. Even there, beside the curve of the bay where the bells of the old Spanish mission rang out the quarter-hours alongside the bronze gongs of a newly erected Shinto shrine for the Edo shipwrights, the friction of his design showed through the varnish.

They had walked together along the high timber seawall above the customs wharf. Up on the scaffoldings, Cantonese masons laid courses of gray Sierra granite beneath a curved, copper-sheathed roof modeled after the audience halls of Honolulu and Osaka. Down on the slips, while three hundred Bakufu iron-workers in dark indigo tunics marched to their barracks with wooden practice-swords thrust through their sashes, a company of discharged Missouri dragoons in the high-collared navy wool of the Pacific Legion lounged against a pile of Krupp gun-crates. They spat tobacco juice onto the swept flagstones and cursed the heathen idol-house rising above the anchorage. They did not lower their voices.

"Your Americans have strong backs for the pickaxe, Protector," Kaiulani had said. She drew her sea-otter pelisse closer against the salt wind as a sergeant of the Legion jostled a Japanese master-carpenter off the dry plankwalk into the ankle-deep mud. "And they die well enough when you point them at a Mexican battery. Yet they still carry the parish vestry inside their skulls. Yesterday, two of Colonel Mulligan’s veterans broke the porcelain lanterns outside the Cantonese guild-hall because the laborers worked through the Christian Sabbath. And in Honolulu last month, your provost marshal tried to billet horse-artillery in the sacred taro terraces of Nu’uanu without asking the *Ali’i* council."

Elias had stopped by the parapet. He set his scarred palms flat against the wet timber of the rail. Down in the mire, the Japanese carpenter rose with his hand frozen on the lacquered hilt of his short-sword while two Legion corporals fingered the butts of their Colt revolvers.

"Sergeant Croker," Elias had called down from the wall. He spoke at an unhurried, gravelly pitch, yet every man on the wharf stiffened like a pine mast. "Take off your belt."

The Missouri veteran looked up. The blood drained from his ruddy cheeks beneath his beard. "Protector? That yellow devil wouldn't yield the crown of the walk to a white soldier."

"That man is a third-class artificer of the Naval Foundry," Elias said, descending the stone steps two at a time. "He draws a lieutenant's ledger-pay. He cast the trunnions on the cannon that kept your spine whole at Tucson. Unbuckle that belt. Or the provost will take the hide off your back and spike you to the chain-gang on the Benicia breakwater before the dinner-bell rings."

When the disgraced sergeant had been marched away to the guardhouse under the custody of his own squad, Elias had turned back to Kaiulani, his gray eyes glassy and unblinking as river-ice. "They will learn."

"By the lash?" she asked. Beneath the brim of her feathered bonnet, her dark gaze remained steady, and she lowered her voice to a private register. "You can bolt boiler-plates together with hot rivets, Elias, because iron has no memory. Flesh is not ore. My cousins in the islands gave you Pearl Lagoon because I promised them the Kamehameha line would sit as kings beside an emperor, not crouch like tailoring clerks beneath a board of San Francisco syndicate directors. If your frontier captains treat the princes of Oahu and the sword-gentry of Satsuma like conquered peons, your patchwork quilt will tear along every seam the morning after your heart stops beating."

"Then I will not die until the new timber is seasoned," Elias had answered. Out beyond the anchorage, a heavy gray fog-bank rolled through the Gate toward the inner harbor. "I do not ask them to love each other, Kaiulani. The Roman legionary from Gaul had no love for the Greek ship-master from Alexandria. They obeyed the same standard because the road was graded, the pirate was hung, and the coin carried the same stamp on both sides. You stitch the code for the courts. I will break the jaw of the first man who spits on the ledger."

Now, three weeks later, that same necessity had brought him seven thousand feet above the sea, where the wind off the Wind River Range carried the bitter scent of juniper smoke and wet gunpowder.

Along the narrow defile of Willow Creek, where the stage-road from Fort Laramie dipped down toward the headwaters of the Colorado, Colonel Philip St. George Cooke, a Virginian who had refused to follow his state into the Southern rebellion and still commanded four squadrons of the United States Second Dragoons in the Utah Territory, had thrown a line of dismounted skirmishers across the frozen gravel bar. In his pocket Cooke carried an unsealed warrant from Secretary of War Cameron, which commanded him to arrest "Elias Thorne, calling himself Protector of California, and sundry other traitors in arms," and to escort them in irons to Fort Leavenworth.

Elias sat his claybank stallion behind a granite outcrop four hundred yards down the gorge. Around him, four hundred Missourians and Texans on the right flank of the Pacific Legion, along with three hundred riflemen of the First Hawaiian Royal Guard on the left whose dark Polynesian faces remained impassive beneath fleece-lined shakos, lay flat in the snow-crusted sagebrush with the blued steel barrels of their seven-shot Spencer repeating carbines resting across the stones.

Down in the creek-bottom, a Federal trumpeter blew a single, brassy parley call that rang off the red sandstone cliffs. Cooke himself rode fifty paces out in front of his blue-coated line. Frost stiffened his gray mustache as he waved a folded parchment above his gauntleted fist.

"Disperse to your homes, you deluded rascals!" the old regular colonel roared, his voice cracking in the thin mountain air. "You stand in open treason against the colors of the United States! Deliver up the usurper Thorne, and every enlisted man who grounds his musket shall have the President’s sovereign amnesty!"

Beside Elias’s stirrup, Caleb Vance spat a brown stream of tobacco juice into the crusted snow. His broad thumb rubbed the brass elevation screw of a mountain howitzer that two mules had packed up the timber trail. "That’s old Cooke, sir. I eat government dirt under him at Fort Riley in ’thirty-four. He’s got three hundred blue-bellies behind them cottonwoods with Sharps single-shot carbines. If we open with canister at this yardage, there won't be enough meat left of the Second Dragoons to grease a caisson wheel."

Elias looked down at the faded stars and stripes fluttering above the creek. His right hand slipped into his coat pocket and thumbed the smooth, clipped edge of his Mexican quarter-real. Until this morning, every post he had taken had surrendered to silver coin or empty flour barrels. His balance-sheet held no regular army blood. Once the lead flew in this gulch, any parchment treaty from a bankrupt Congress in Washington would be settled by iron alone.

"He has his warrant, Caleb," Elias said, his voice flat and low against the whistle of the gorge wind. "We have the high ground. Tell the Hawaiians on the left bench to shoot the horse-holders behind the grove. When the herd breaks, give the skirmish line two volleys from the Spencers and drop a shell into the road-cut."

"God forgive us," Caleb rasped. His weathered hand remained steady as he pulled the friction-primer lanyard.

The bronze howitzer barked once. The report rolled down the granite walls like a rockslide. Three seconds later, the case-shot burst ten feet above the Federal horse-lines in the cottonwoods in a dirty puff of white smoke and shrieking lead balls, and eighty riderless cavalry mounts plunged screaming through the frozen brush. Before the sound died, the left ridge erupted in the mechanical clatter of three hundred lever-action Spencers firing fourteen rounds a minute, a continuous roar that drowned the slow, measured rhythm of the single-shot locks below.

Through his field-glasses, the blue skirmish line along the gravel bar melted into the snow. Veterans who had fought the Sioux and the Cheyenne stood up in bewilderment to ram cartridges, only to take three balls in the chest before their iron ramrods touched the bore. Blood spouted from the nostrils of Colonel Cooke’s charger; the animal reared straight up and crashed backward onto the ice, where its bulk pinned the old Virginian beneath his saddle-bags while his surviving troopers scrambled up the opposite talus in a rout.

"Cease fire!" Elias barked, and raised his gloved hand.

The carbines stopped on the instant. Down on the white drift stained crimson by forty groaning regulars, gutted horses whinnied in the hush. Elias rode down the shale slope onto the creek-ice, the iron shoes of his claybank ringing against the blood-splashed stones, until he halted above Colonel Cooke. The old officer was struggling to draw his heavy dragoon revolver from beneath his dead horse’s flank.

"Leave it in the leather, Colonel," Elias said. "My surgeons will splint your leg. Keep your saber. When the snow melts in the spring, take your cripples back to the Missouri. Tell Mr. Cameron his paper warrants do not run west of this ridge."

***

Five days after the snow reddened at Willow Creek, cold November rain sluiced down the muddy clay ruts of Alexandria, Virginia, where the grand cantonments of the Army of the Potomac stretched for twelve miles of leaking Sibley tents and typhoid hospitals beside the overflowing mule-corrals.

Inside a commandeered brick tavern near the wharf, General Marcus Vance stood before a smoky pine-knot fire. With the brass poker, he fed his preliminary rough drafts into the flames. Having discarded the civilian linen of the summer’s battle, he wore a heavy rubberized poncho over a plain traveling suit, and his saddle-bags lay packed and strapped beside the door. Across the deal table sat three men in the dark blue frock-coats of the United States Corps of Topographical Engineers and the Ordnance Bureau. Their names had stood near the top of the West Point register ten years before; now they looked out at the mud of McClellan’s camp like craftsmen forced to work for an asylum.

"You have the cipher key for the Cincinnati foundry agents, Major Sterling?" Marcus asked. He kept his eyes on the grate as a curl of tracing-paper blackened and rose up the chimney.

"Sewn into the lining of my valise, General," said Sterling, a lean Pennsylvanian in spectacles who had spent the last four months trying in vain to convince Secretary Cameron’s political brother-in-law to refuse five thousand condemned Belgian muskets at twenty dollars a stand. "Captain Mordecai carries the complete blueprint folios for the ten-pounder Parrott rifled guns and the fifteen-inch Rodman coastal columbiads, plus the time-tables and pay-rosters of all forty-two master machinists at the Watervliet Arsenal who have gone unpaid since the August bank suspension."

"And the cavalry pickets along the Leesburg pike?" asked the third officer, a regular dragoon captain named Custer whose damp yellow hair hung over his collar. "McClellan’s provost-guard seized two Maryland legislators at the ferry landing at six this morning. If Baker’s detectives suspect four regular officers are boarding the Baltimore packet without War Department passes, we will be locked in the Old Capitol Prison before the midnight relief."

Marcus turned from the hearth. His face was as bloodless as an iron casting, his molars grinding once against the stench of wet wool and unburied offal drifting from the camp outside. During the four months since Bull Run, while dining with Northern senators, auditing the chaotic supply depots along the Chesapeake, and watching Lincoln appoint Tammany Hall ward-heelers and abolitionist newspaper editors to command brigades, Marcus had sounded out thirty-six of the finest young engineers and ordnance officers in the regular establishment. They were men sickened by the Washington contractors' corruption and convinced that the Republic was bleeding itself into insolvency. He had foreclosed on the Union’s brains.

"Baker’s detectives are auditing the south bank for Rebel couriers," Marcus said. He consulted his heavy Geneva pocket chronometer, noting the exact minute-hand angle against the muffled Alexandria church bell tolling the hour across the wet roofs. "My steam-launch from the British mail-tender lies at the coal-wharf two hundred andforty yards below the arsenal wall. By zero-five-hundred, gentlemen, after clearing the river batteries on the ebb tide, we board a Clyde-built screw steamer making fourteen knots under the Hawaiian ensign. Beyond the three-mile marine league, no blockading hull in the Atlantic Squadron has the boiler pressure to overhaul us."

He walked to the table, where a leather dispatch-case stamped with the gilt eagle of the War Department lay open, and drew out a single sheet of tissue-paper that had come through the Havana cable two hours before.

"Protector Thorne engaged the Second Dragoons at South Pass on the nineteenth," Marcus said. Tallow-light flickered across their faces. "Cooke’s command broke in twelve minutes and forty seconds. With the mountain passes closed, delegates from Colorado, Utah, Nevada, and the Oregon country are assembling at Denver this week to sign the Act of Confederation. When you step into that launch tonight, you close your accounts with the United States Army on this table. The East is an insolvent ledger. In San Francisco, a major of engineers draws three hundred dollars a month in minted gold specie and commands a regiment of three thousand graded laborers under a single executive rather than a committee of country pettifoggers. If any one of you prefers to stay here and rot in the Virginia mud while Mr. McClellan polishes his boots at a deficit oftwo million dollars a day, speak now."

Major Sterling stood up. He unpinned the tarnished gilt shoulder-straps from his blue coat and dropped them onto the scarred pine table beside the empty ink-bottle. One by one, the others did the same.

"The tide is at the flood, General," Sterling said. "The launch will lose the ebb in eighteen minutes. Let us go to the wharf."

***

By the first week of December, deep snow buried the raw pine-log shanties and canvas saloons of Denver City to the eaves, while sixty miles to the west the jagged wall of the Front Range stood against the sky like a line of white-hot iron teeth.

Inside the Broadwell House, the largest brick hotel between St. Joseph and Salt Lake, the long dining room had been stripped of its gaming tables and billiard cloths to accommodate the fifty-two men who claimed to speak for two million square miles of mountain and desert. The room was stifling. Four cast-iron stoves roared against the frost, baking the wet buffalo-skin coats, cheap cherry-wood tobacco, smoky coal-oil lamps, and sour tallow of mountain boots into a thick stench.

They were a harder breed than the silk-stockinged planters of Charleston or the maritime grandees of Sacramento. Mormon bishops from the Salt Lake valley with square, shovel-trimmed beards and flinty eyes sat beside silver-prospectors from the Washoe lodes in velveteen waistcoats hung with gold watch-chains, rugged wheat-factors from the Willamette, and half-wild territorial judges from the Santa Fe ring whose pockets bulged with hidden derringers.

At the center of the floor stood William Gilpin. President Lincoln had sent him out in the spring as Territorial Governor of Colorado with an empty treasury and a bundle of unsigned promissory notes, and now his tall frame shook with fury as he brandished a handful of green-tinted Federal demand notes in the face of the delegation from the Pike’s Peak mining districts.

"I tell you that to sign articles of confederation with San Francisco is to put a hemp rope around every neck in this room!" Gilpin shouted, his voice hoarse from three days of losing debate. "By virtue of the statutory authority vested in my office, the Congress in Washington has appropriated five hundred thousand dollars for the defense of this territory! My drafts upon the Treasury carry the sovereign seal of—"

"Your drafts ain't worth the tallow grease it takes to fry a side of sow-belly, Governor!" Old Judge Slaughter roared from the Auraria bench. He slammed his hickory cane down on the floorboards while a dozen miners in the gallery jeered. "The stage from Omaha hasn't brought a sack of hard mail in three weeks because the Cheyenne have burned the relay stations along the Platte, and your blue-belly friends in Washington pulled every regular soldier out of Fort Wise to go fight Beauregard in Virginia! Who’s going to buy our quartz-crushers when the New York wildcatters won't pay gold? Who’s going to keep the Arapaho out of the gulches this winter, Abe Lincoln’s postmaster with a bundle of green rag-paper?"

At the rear of the dining hall, four troopers of the Pacific Legion in wolf-skin pelisses over their navy tunics swung back the heavy double doors on oiled hinges and held their Spencer carbines at the carry.

Elias walked down the narrow aisle between the benches. Three hours earlier he had ridden down from the Cheyenne pass at the head of eight hundred cavalry and two batteries of rifled Krupp field-pieces, whose brass muzzles now pointed down Larimer Street from the high bank of Cherry Creek. Frozen alkali and red mountain mud crusted his heavy cavalry boots; frost silvered the short-cropped hair at his temples. Behind him walked Caleb Vance, spitting a dark streak of tobacco juice near the stove-box, and Elder Kimball of the Salt Lake delegation, with whom Elias had concluded a private concordat at Fort Bridger four days prior.

The clamor died. Snow melted off the troopers’ boots and hissed against the hot stove-plates.

Elias stepped up onto the low pine platform beside Governor Gilpin. Ignoring the federal appointee, he turned to face the fifty-two delegates, unbuttoned his heavy wool greatcoat, and laid his scarred right palm flat upon the raw pine lectern.

"Three weeks ago," Elias said, his rough, low voice filling the timbered room without effort, "Colonel Cooke tried to plug the South Pass with four squadrons of regular dragoons. His men are in my field-hospitals at Green River. His rifles are in my wagons outside."

Gilpin took a step forward. His trembling hand dropped toward the breast of his frock-coat. "Mr. Thorne, by virtue of the commission I hold from the President of the United States, I command you to lay down your—"

Elias turned his head half an inch. Under that pale, unblinking stare, the Governor’s mouth clicked shut in the middle of the syllable.

"You hold a scrap of stationery from a town that cannot pay its own clerks in silver, Mr. Gilpin," Elias said. "Look out that window. On the grade beside the creek, forty freight-wagons sit hitched to steam-traction engines from the Sacramento iron-works. We brought ten thousand repeating rifles, four hundred tons of San Joaquin flour, and two hundred thousand silver thalers minted at Carson City. Tomorrow morning, my surveyors drive the first stakes for a broad-gauge iron track from the Salt Lake through the Wasatch granite to the Golden Gate."

He turned back to the benches. In the yellow lamp-light, the Mormon elders and the mining captains leaned forward over their knees.

"The East is a bankrupt carpenter's shop," Elias said. Each word fell like a drop-forge on cold boiler-plate. "Between this creek and the Missouri River lie six hundred miles of burned grass and broken wildcat banks. Hostile tribes hold the fords. Look toward Washington, and you starve in the snow while two gangs of Eastern lawyers butcher half a million farm-boys over a parchment ledger they tore in half themselves. Look west toward the tidewater. Sign the Act of Union today, and by noon my paymasters will buy every dollar of Governor Gilpin’s rag-paper in hard Pacifica silver at par. Every territory in this hall keeps its local courts, its church tithes, and its own militia captains, so long as your bullion goes into the San Francisco crucibles and your timber braces our rails while the iron of my Legion bolts your outer door."

From the center bench, Elder Kimball rose, his broad-brimmed black hat held across his chest. "And the federal circuit judges that Washington sent to the valleys of Ephraim to cast our elders into prison, Captain Thorne? What becomes of their warrants under your covenant?"

"They ride in the same eastbound stagecoach that leaves with Governor Gilpin in twenty minutes," Elias said. He drew the heavy vellum roll of the Western Compact from his belt and slapped it down across the pine table so hard the ink-horn jumped. He took the brass-handled dip-pen from Gilpin’s motionless fingers and held it out toward Judge Slaughter at the head of the Colorado bench. "Step up and put your names to the iron, gentlemen. The horses are freezing in the traces."

***

By the break of spring in 1862, the ink on the Denver parchment had dried into a line of fire stretching from the Black Hills of Dakota to the red-dirt crossings of the Red River. If the mountain territories were to remain an impregnable citadel while the great railways were bolted to the granite of the Sierra and the Rockies, the vast oceanic glacis of the Great Plains had to be swept clean of anything that could feed a marching regiment or draw an ordnance wagon.

On the nineteenth of May, Elias stood on the high cedar gallery of the burned stage-station at Fort Kearny. Below the bluffs, the Platte spread out into a mile of braided, muddy channels through the newly sprouted buffalo-grass. Twenty-four years had passed since he had crawled out of the frozen mule’s ribs sixty miles upriver; now, down the valley toward the Missouri border, seven distinct columns of greasy black smoke rose straight into the windless spring sky.

"The telegraph relay at Plum Creek was severed at zero-four-thirty, Protector," said General Marcus Vance. He climbed the charred timber stairs with a sheaf of wet dispatch-flimsies in his gauntlet and his leather calculation-book tucked beneath his arm. He had returned from the Atlantic coast in February via the Panama steamer with forty-two former regular officers who now wore the plain navy wool of the Pacifica General Staff. "Major Custer’s lancers intercepted the last four federal supply trains three miles east of the Little Blue at dawn. The audit tallies two hundred and twelve wagons of salt pork and hardbread bound for Fort Riley. We shot the four hundred draft-oxen in the yokes and fired the oil-soaked spokes and canvas. Not a single axle turns between this meridian and Topeka."

Elias kept the brass spyglass to his eye, his left thumb rubbing the smooth Mexican quarter-real in his coat pocket. Down on the river-flat below the ruined fort, three hundred Cantonese sappers and two companies of Hawaiian pioneers sledged the iron tires off a captured park of Union commissary wagons; they loaded the scrap metal onto flat-bedded steam-lorries while the traction boilers hissed and panted in the damp grass, reeking of sulfur and hot cylinder-oil. Beside the road-bed, where a band of Kotsoteka Comanches and Cheyenne auxiliaries wore heavy silver peace-medals stamped with Elias’s profile and carried breech-loading carbines from the Benicia arsenals, four thousand head of requisitioned Missouri beef-cattle lumbered westward at the point of the lance.

"The wells along the Smoky Hill grade?" Elias asked.

"Contaminated with three hundredweight of arsenic and bloated mule carcasses from Fort Wallace to Salina," Marcus answered, consulting his calfskin ledger with a cadence as dry as a quartermaster’s receipt for winter forage. "Given the current evaporation rate, the buffalo-grass will be dry enough by the tenth of July to burn the entire quadrangle from the Republican Fork to the Arkansas. General Halleck in St. Louis wired the War Department yesterday that crossing the hundredth meridian will require forty thousand cavalry and ten million dollars in wagon-tonnage. His depots hold neither."

From the courtyard below rose a shrill clatter of tongues. A detail of Missouri Legionnaires had dragged a captured federal quartermaster, a stout, red-faced captain of Illinois volunteers, out of the sod cellar where he had been hiding among broken pickle-barrels. The prisoner stumbled into the sunlight and spat at the boots of a Japanese artillery surveyor who was measuring the brick foundations of the magazine with a brass theodolite.

"You Christian turncoats!" the Illinois captain bawled. He wrenched against the hemp cord binding his wrists, his face purple above his torn blue collar as he glared up at the gallery where Elias stood. "You’re burning the Christian bread of your own countrymen and turning painted red savages loose on the settlements while white men bleed for the old flag in Tennessee! Is this your Western law, Thorne, handing free American soil over to yellow heathens and Kanakas?"

Beside Elias at the rail, Lady Kaiulani rested her gloved fingertips on the scorched cedar balustrade, drawing her dark green broadcloth pelisse closer against the river wind. Having ridden up from the Denver rail-head in an armored stagecoach to codify the Indian boundary treaties, she wore a traveling habit cut in the European fashion, though her throat was clasped with a collar of braided human hair and whale-ivory, the ancient *lei niho palaoa* of the island chiefs.

"The commissary from Illinois dislikes the stitching of your new quilt, Protector," she said, her voice measured and clear above the hiss of the steam-lorries. "He forgets that when a house is framed with iron rivets, the carpenter does not ask the timber which forest it grew in." In the yard below, the guards forced the prisoner to his knees in the churned mud.

"He is bawling because his trough is empty," Elias said. He walked to the head of the stairs, laid his hands flat on the charred cedar rail, and looked down into the yard. "Captain."

The Illinois officer jerked his chin up, spitting mud from his lip. "I demand the rights of a commissioned officer under the Geneva usage! You have no lawful warrant to burn private homesteads and poison public wells!"

"A well in the desert is a rung on a ladder for a thief," Elias said. His voice dropped into the yard like lead shot into water. "You hauled six hundred wagons out here to fatten regiments that Mr. Lincoln meant to drive through South Pass once he finished with Virginia. Take a hard look at this river, Captain. Across the three hundred miles of dirt between this post and the Missouri, by August there will not be a blade of green grass, a standing telegraph pole, or a dipper of sweet water. Any man who steps across the ninety-eighth parallel carrying a Washington musket dies of thirst before he smells the smoke of my forges. Marcus, put his boots in his saddle-bags and turn him loose on foot toward Omaha. Let him walk back and show General Halleck the grade to California."

Down in the mire, the provosts sliced the captain’s bonds with a skinning knife and stripped off his riding-boots. By the scorched cedar rail, while the wind off the burned prairie lifted the black veil at her hat-brim, Kaiulani drew her sea-otter pelisse closer against the ash-laden gust and turned her shoulder so that Marcus, standing three paces behind them, could not catch her words. "A moat of ash seven hundred miles wide," she said. "It is effective, Elias. No army will cross this waste in our lifetime. Yet when we rode through the camps at Cheyenne last week, the Texas lancers were singing around the grease-fires. Do you know what they sang? That when they had finished burning the Yankees off the plains, they would ride back to San Francisco and throw the bronze Buddha out of the Monterey temple into the bay."

Elias turned his head and met her gaze. "Men who live by the saddle talk big when their bellies are full of salt beef."

"Men who burn churches on the Platte today will burn shrines on the Sacramento tomorrow unless they know the shrine belongs to the crown," she replied. Her voice dropped to a private, measured register, cold as iron drawn from silk. "You stitch a great quilt out of ten different cloths, Elias. You use the Cheyenne to strip the plains and my islanders to hold your mountain passes; you use the Shogun’s samurai to cast your cannon. To your Missourians, they are merely iron rivets and spare timber like those steam-tractors down in the mud, to be scrapped when the fort is built. Iron rivets do not hold human flesh together; memory and law hold it. If this empire is to outlast the general who pitched its tents, the chief’s club must sit higher than the camp-fire. Give my council the provost-courts in the coast cities this summer, or by autumn you will be fighting a mutiny in your own shipyards."

Below the gallery, while two sullen Missouri troopers looked on with folded arms, the Japanese surveyor bent again to his brass level and sighted across the smoking brickwork of the federal bakery.

"Draw the commission tonight," Elias said. He laid his scarred palm flat against the charred cedar of the rail. "Appoint an American, a Hawaiian, and an Edo magistrate to every maritime bench. And tell the *Ali'i* that any soldier of the Legion who lays a finger on an imperial shrine or a guild-house gets twenty lashes at the cart’s tail and five years in the quicksilver mines at New Almaden. Order is a hammer, Kaiulani. It hits both ways."

***

To the chronicler who studies the diplomatic archives of the short-lived Southern Confederacy, the summer of 1862 presents a spectacle of tragic delusion unmatched since the ambassadors of Athens begged the Persian satraps for gold while Spartan spears already ringed the Long Walls. In Richmond, where the church bells tolled for the seven days’ slaughter before the Chickahominy and the hospitals stank of gangrene and raw turpentine, President Jefferson Davis and Secretary of State Judah Benjamin clung with the desperation of drowning men to a single strategic chimera: that the iron tyrant of San Francisco, having broken the Union’s western flank and ruined the banks of New York, was their natural brother-in-arms.

They chose in their extremity to forget that the man who now ruled from Sitka to the Rio Grande had begun his march beside the smoking ashes of a Kentucky squatter’s cabin.

In the first week of August, the heat lay thick and wet as a poultice over the brick tobacco-warehouses of the Virginia capital. Major Julian St. Clair, wearing the buff-and-gray frock coat of a Confederate State Department commissioner, sat in the high, shuttered library of the Brockenbrough mansion with his leather dispatch-case open upon his knees. Fifteen years had passed since that foggy midnight on Clark’s Point when he had tossed the gold medal of the Golden Circle onto a redwood table and offered a twenty-one-year-old frontier captain fifty thousand British sovereigns to guard the Southern flank. Now St. Clair’s hair was white. His left sleeve was pinned empty to his breast from a federal shell-fragment at Shiloh, and his remaining hand shook with tertian fever as he held out the cipher telegram that had arrived from Matamoros via the Havana blockade-runner.

"Read it yourself, Mr. Benjamin," St. Clair said, his voice a dry, feverish rattle in the dim room while blowflies buzzed against the Venetian blinds. "I rode three hundred miles by mule from San Antonio to the Pecos crossing in June to re-establish the equilibrium of forty-seven. His provosts barred my escort from crossing the river into New Mexico. For four days in an adobe sheep-pen at Presidio del Norte, they penned a commissioner of the Sovereign South like a Mexican horse-thief until General Vance arrived on an armored railway flatcar from El Paso."

Judah Benjamin took the tissue slip. His plump, olive-skinned face lost its habitual courtly smile as he scanned the decoded lines. Across the mahogany table, President Davis leaned back in his horsehair armchair, a cold vinegar compress pressed to his neuralgic eye.

"What does he say to the Treaty of Mutual Guaranty, Judah?" Davis asked. "We offered him permanent recognition of the Rocky Mountain line and a twenty-percent reduction on all cotton shipped through Guaymas to the Cantonese looms, provided his ironclad squadron steams around the Horn to break Farragut’s blockade at the mouth of the Mississippi and his cavalry marches from the Red River into Missouri."

Benjamin did not read the dispatch aloud at first. He laid it beside the brass inkstand, as if the paper itself would blister his fingers.

"Mr. Thorne sends an invoice, Mr. President," the Secretary of State said.

Davis pulled the damp cloth from his temple, his gaunt cheek flushing dark red. "An invoice?"

"From Marshal Vance at El Paso," Benjamin read in a flat, clinical monotone. *"'The Protector of the Grand Confederation acknowledges receipt of the memorandum from the belligerent authorities at Richmond. The Confederation of Pacifica recognizes no government east of the hundredth meridian save that of force in being. The fifty thousand sovereigns advanced by the Charleston syndicate in the year 1847, together with six percent compound interest, were discharged in full by the shipment of salt pork and lead to Matamoros in January last. Should the Richmond authorities desire the passage of cotton through the port of Guaymas, the tariff is forty percent ad valorem, payable exclusively in pig-iron, locomotive boilers, or skilled negro mechanics who shall upon crossing the Rio Grande become free indentured artificers of the Pacifica Crown. As for the Mississippi River, the Protector bids Major St. Clair inform Mr. Davis that when the guns of Pacifica appear upon the father of waters, they will come to collect the mortgage on the continent.'"*

Outside on Clay Street, an iron-tired ambulance-wagon clattered over the cobblestones. Inside the library, neither man spoke.

"Free indentured artificers," Davis whispered, his thin knuckles whitening as he gripped the horsehair arms of his chair. "He asks us to sell him our own slaves to build his railroads across Texas, and calls us *belligerent authorities*, as if we were a band of Nicaraguan filibusters! Does this Kentucky dirt-scratcher imagine that because he has stolen a few alkali cellars and bribed a Polynesian princess, he can audit the books of the sovereign states of the South?"

"It is a mathematical certainty, Mr. President," St. Clair rattled. He rose from his chair and walked to the tall wall-map where the War Department clerks had shaded the vast western half of North America in heavy blue pencil. "You have not seen his camps. I saw them at the Pecos. Our Confederacy is a dismasted hulk fighting with flintlocks converted to percussion and locomotives held together with baling-wire, while Vance’s troopers ride behind steam-wagons that lay their own iron track across the sandhills at four miles a day, backed by cast-steel artillery from Essen and Nagasaki and infantry carrying seven-shot repeaters that empty a saddle at six hundred yards. When I reminded General Vance of the compact Thorne gave me in forty-seven, do you know what he did? He pulled out a Geneva pocket-chronometer. My pass expired in twenty-two minutes, he said, and if General Sibley’s Texas brigade ever set foot west of the Brazos again, they would hang every gentleman officer from the telegraph poles."

Benjamin folded the tissue telegram into a neat square and creased the edge with his thumb. He stared up at the plaster rosette on the ceiling. "He waited until McClellan’s cannon were within five miles of this house, and until Grant had split our line in Tennessee. A restored Union and a victorious Confederacy suit him equally little. Once we strangle each other in the ditch, once the last dollar is spent and the last regiment buried, he will walk down the eastern slope of the mountains and buy the ruins for the price of a meal."

***

Thorne left the last regiment unburied. When dry-rot eats two-thirds through the main beam of an old barn, a master carpenter takes an axe to the king-post before the timber falls upon his head.

Throughout the winter of 1862 and the bloody, inconclusive spring of 1863, while Lee and Hooker mauled each other in the Virginia wilderness and Grant’s battered army rotted in the mud canals before Vicksburg, fourteen thousand laborers worked behind a triple cordon of cavalry in the dry bed of the Tehuantepec Isthmus and the ship-slips of Guaymas. New York and London newspapers remained blind to what the gangs bolted together from the modular iron sections coming down the coast out of the Clark’s Point rolling mills. Instead of deep-sea frigates, the slips launched broad-beamed, turret-mounted river monitors of shallow draft. Their hulls comprised twenty-four numbered steel compartments: sections built to ride across the Mexican divide on double-track railway cradles, take pneumatic rivets in the Gulf Coast lagoons within twelve days, and turn twin high-pressure screw propellers on crude rock-oil from the southern California wells.

On the fourth of July, 1863, while Rear Admiral Porter’s gunboats and General Pemberton’s starving garrison stared at each other through the heat-haze of the Mississippi bends, the river darkened three miles below Natchez.

Elias stood on the armored bridge-house of the flagship *Sacramento*. The twin-turreted monitor’s sloped six-inch casemates of rolled nickel-steel rose scarcely four feet above the turbid brown flood. Twenty-six years had passed since he had stood barefoot on the pine planks of Red Higgins’s broadhorn flatboat, his heels split by frost and his palm clutching a clipped Mexican quarter-real while the *General Jackson* thrashed past him in a cloud of scorched grease. Twelve iron sisters steamed in line ahead behind his wake now. Their telescopic funnels trailed thin, colorless plumes of superheated petroleum vapor, and forty armor-plated troop-barges towed alongside carried twenty thousand veterans of the Pacific Legion: Missouri riflemen and Hawaiian guards alongside three regiments of Bakufu marine infantry under the rising-sun pennon of the Confederation.

"*Hai*, Protector. Federal tin-clad picket boat rounding the point. Range six hundred yards, bearing zero-one-five," Captain Takashima reported from the conning-slit below. Beneath the bridge, where the monitor's twin screws churned the muddy current into yellow yeast, his clipped voice rang up the brass speaking-tube. "Vessel is the *Baron DeKalb*. Hoisting United States identification signal. Running out two bow Dahlgrens."

Beside Elias on the narrow iron grating, General Marcus Vance consulted his Geneva pocket chronometer against the mileage chart of the lower river. After the clean dry winds of the Sierra, the Mississippi bottomlands steamed like a cauldron. The humid air carried the reek of rotted cypress knees and mud-flats, thick with the rank, sweetish stench of dead mules floating down from Grant’s siege-lines above.

"Both belligerent ledgers are in default, sir," Marcus said, his eyes fixed on the neat figures in his leather field-book. "Pemberton’s garrison inside Vicksburg has subsisted on twelve ounces of pea-meal and mule-meat per man for forty-two days. Grant’s regiments in the trenches show a forty-one-percent morbidity rate from malaria, with their sole logistical artery restricted to the single river channel north to Memphis. At our current steaming rate of eight knots, if we sink the picket boat and pass the batteries before eighteen hundred hours, neither army possesses ordnance with the muzzle velocity to indent our six-inch glacis."

Elias looked across the mile-wide expanse of brown water toward the eastern bluffs. Among the live-oaks, the white columns of a burned Louisiana sugar-plantation stood like broken teeth. In his pocket, his thumb found the smooth, clipped Mexican quarter-real Red Higgins had thrown at him on the St. Louis levee a quarter-century ago, the eagle rubbed nearly flat into the silver.

"Save your shell," Elias said. The deep, steady thrum of the oil-burners beneath the deckplates vibrated in his chest. "We brought these guns two thousand miles for bigger game than river-scows. Takashima, give the *Sacramento* full steam ahead. Put our ram-bow straight through her midships, and let the current carry the wreck down to New Orleans so Admiral Farragut can see what kind of iron cuts wood. Marcus, hoist the blue-and-gold standard at the main-truck and tell the buglers on the barges to sound the general assembly."

On the Federal gunboat ahead, orange flame flashed and dirty white smoke burst from the bow-ports. Two nine-inch round-shot struck the sloped steel prow of the *Sacramento* like a sledgehammer on an anvil. Flattened into ragged lead-colored saucers, the iron skipped fifty feet into the air and splashed into the muddy wake.

Iron splinters whined overhead. Elias stood fast. He braced his gauntleted hands against the armored coaming of the bridge while the massive steel ram beneath his boots surged forward at twelve knots, boiling the water white over her submerged snout as the wooden side-paddles of the Union vessel beat astern to escape the oncoming mountain of steel.

"Hai, Protector. Range two hundred yards," Takashima called through the brass speaking-tube, his gloved fingers steady on the rim. Behind the thin boiler-iron bulwarks of the gunboat, Federal gun-crews dropped their rammers and scrambled toward the stern-rail. "Range one hundred yards. Collision stations on the main deck."

"Hold your course," Elias said. He looked past the doomed vessel toward the smoke-shrouded bluffs of Vicksburg rising in the northern haze. "Run the signal to the second division. Drop anchor-chains across the Yazoo mouth the moment we clear the bend. Before the moon rises tonight, not a skiff crosses this ditch from Minnesota to the Gulf without a pass stamped by my Provost-General."

The steel beak of the *Sacramento* struck the *Baron DeKalb* just abaft the port paddle-box. It sounded like a dry pine forest snapping in a hurricane. Twelve feet of solid, forged San Francisco iron sheared straight through oak frames, iron boiler-plate, and coal-bunkers. The impact lifted the Union gunboat’s bow six feet out of the yellow flood and rolled her over on her beam-ends in a roaring geyser of escaping steam and boiling river-mud.

The steam cleared from the Mississippi by evening. Down from their rifle-pits, Grant’s starving besiegers and Pemberton’s hollow-eyed garrison looked out upon twelve silent steel monsters moored bow-to-stern across the channel, their twin eight-inch rifled turrets trained equally upon the stars-and-stripes on the right bank and the stars-and-bars on the left.

***

Seizing the Mississippi spine merely transferred the war from the battlefield to the council-chamber. Before the final eastward march to the Atlantic could begin, Elias returned to Monterey in the winter of 1863 to weld together the disparate halves of the colossus he had conjured from the sea.

The capital of the Confederation had outgrown its Spanish adobe bones. Along the curving granite esplanade above the bay, a new imperial architecture rose from the coastal fog: vast administrative ministries built with the heavy, pillared porticoes of Virginia, yet crowned with the sweeping, upturned cedar eaves of Kyoto and flanked by the basalt *ahu* altars of the Hawaiian islands. On the morning of the Winter Solstice, a cold drizzle blew in off the Pacific surf. It brought the sharp tang of kelp and wet coal-ash from the naval foundries, mingled with heavy aromatic aloeswood smoke drifting down from the great syncretic cathedral of St. Michael and the Sun Goddess on the hill.

Inside the Hall of the Council, forty-foot columns of polished redwood met a ceiling coffered in beaten copper. Elias sat at the head of the semicircular table. He had refused the title of King when the Diet offered it in October, leaving his brow bare, though clasps of raw California quartz-gold fastened his high-collared tunic of dark navy wool. Before him stood three men and one woman: Lady Kaiulani, Lord Shimazu of the Satsuma naval mission, and Judge Jeremiah Black, spokesman for the newly annexed Mississippi Valley territories.

"The freeholders of Missouri and Iowa will not endure it, Protector!" Judge Black said. Sweat slicked his broad red face as he struck a vellum scroll against the redwood table. "Your Marshal Vance has quartered two regiments of Japanese infantry in the circuit courthouse at St. Louis, and yesterday a magistrate sent from Honolulu fined a Christian minister fifty silver thalers for preaching against the Shinto shrine erected at the Arsenal! We entered this Confederation to escape the abolitionist fanatics of New England and preserve our property from ruin. Now the common law of our Anglo-Saxon fathers is subordinated to the decrees of Polynesian royalty and pagan sword-men!"

Across the table, Lord Shimazu's narrow, bronze-cast face remained still. His left thumb rested upon the gold-lacquered guard of the long sword thrust through his silk sash. Behind him, through the tall arched windows, the cranes of the naval yard swung sixteen-inch steel gun-barrels into the holds of the transport fleet.

Lady Kaiulani drew the royal feather cape of Kamehameha closer across the shoulders of her severe, Victorian-cut gown of deep forest-green velvet, its ten thousand tiny crimson and yellow *mamo* feathers catching the gray winter light like living fire.

"Judge Black forgets whose rifles cleared the Cheyenne from the Platte so that his Missouri wagons might reach the river," Kaiulani said, her diction clear and cold as mountain snow-melt. "And he forgets that three thousand subjects of the Hawaiian Crown and four thousand samurai of the Western Clans lie buried in the passes of the Rockies and the mud of Vicksburg to purchase the safety of his cornfields. The Compact of Denver bound you to an oceanic empire, sir, not a county parish."

"All lawful government must have its foundation in nature and the established stations of life!" Black said. He turned back toward Elias, his chest heaving beneath his broadcloth waistcoat. "In the old states, a white man knew his rightful station under God! Here, my own nephew, a captain in the Missouri militia, was ordered yesterday to salute a Cantonese commissary officer at the Sacramento rail-depot! If you force this unnatural mingling of the races upon the Valley, Protector, you will have fifty thousand rifles in rebellion from Dubuque to Memphis before the snow melts!"

Elias leaned forward and set both rough, weather-beaten palms flat upon the polished redwood. He said nothing. Below the cliff, Pacific swells boomed against the granite sea-wall.

"When I was fourteen years old, Judge," Elias said, and along the wall the clerks stopped whispering, "a gentleman of pure Anglo-Saxon blood rode out from Philadelphia with a parchment writ and burned my mother’s roof over her head for sixty-two dollars. When I was fifteen, I would have frozen to death in a mule’s belly on the Platte if a Delaware Indian with cropped ears had not shown me how to drop a buffalo bull in the drift. I care nothing for the color of a man’s skin. I care less for what name he gives the Almighty on Sunday morning."

He rose. Though he stood a head shorter than the Missouri judge, the chamber went dead still around the broad, square-set bulk of his shoulders.

"Look out that window, Mr. Black," Elias said. He pointed a blunt finger toward the gray expanse of the harbor. "Fifty leagues west of that fog-bank, the water runs clear to Asia. There are four hundred million souls on the far side of this trough, and less than thirty million on this side. The Atlantic states tried to build a house on the notion that one race of shopkeepers could sit in a parlor and argue over parchment rights while their timber rotted.
