Tonight, in the Virginia ditches, their sons are paying the bill."

He walked around the curve of the table and halted between the Missouri judge and the Japanese lord.

"In Pacifica, there is only one race: the men who pull the weight of the state," Elias said. Under his pale, unblinking stare, Black shrank into the tufted leather of his chair. "And there is only one blasphemy: mutiny. Your nephew will salute the Cantonese commissary because that commissary holds my iron, and if your nephew refuses, Marshal Vance will spike him against the depot wall. On the other hand." Elias turned his head toward Kaiulani and Lord Shimazu. "No Shinto priest and no Hawaiian provost will meddle with a Christian congregation west of the Mississippi so long as the ledger is squared in silver and the conscripts report to the muster-rolls on the hour. Lady Kaiulani, you will amend the Maritime Code before tonight’s sitting. Local parish courts in the Valley keep the marriage books, the church timber, and the Sabbath. Imperial Provost Courts keep treason, commerce, and the articles of war."

Kaiulani inclined her head half an inch. The yellow feathers of her lei rustled against the dark velvet of her collar. "It is a wise distinction, Protector. Render unto Caesar the iron rivets, and leave the villagers their prayer-books, so long as the prayer-books are printed on imperial presses."

"Wait outside, Judge Black," Elias said. He flicked his wrist toward the doorway. "Sign the sheet with the Chancellor."

The heavy bronze doors swung shut behind the judge and the Japanese envoys, and the iron latch dropped into its socket. Only Kaiulani remained beside the great terrestrial globe in the center of the floor. Elias let his shoulders drop an inch, walked to the tall casement, and rested his forehead and one scarred palm flat against the cold glass. Below the cliff, through the gray sheets of rain, a column of Hawaiian recruits in sodden blue greatcoats marched over the cobblestones toward the eastern troop-trains.

"You yield to the Missourians today so that your railways will not be torn up behind you while you march on Washington," Kaiulani said, lowering her voice to a private register as she stepped up beside his shoulder. Her gaze stayed fixed not on the wet troops below, but on the silver threads multiplying in the coarse hair at his temples. "But you know as well as I do, Elias, that a patchwork quilt holds together only while the tailor’s needle is in the cloth. What happens when we have swallowed the Atlantic coast? A hundred million people who hate our laws, bankrupt and starving, chained to an ocean they have never seen."

"We will work them as provinces," Elias said. His breath fogged the cold pane. "We will take their young men and put them in garrisons on the Amur River and the islands of the South Sea, and we will put Lord Shimazu’s samurai on the ramparts of Fort Monroe. By the time their grandsons come home, they will not remember whether their fathers wore blue or gray."

# Chapter 5: The Articles of Dissolution

> [Written in watered-down iron-gall ink and carpenter's lead across the uncut verso of six unissued $500 Seven-Thirty Treasury Bond proofs, stitched together with waxed cartridge-twine; the margins are translucent with mutton-tallow and charred along the lower fold.] November 12, 1864. Casemate No. 4, Fort Runyon, Southern Approach to the Long Bridge. My Dearest Clara, If the Provost-Marshal's boat reaches the Chesapeake before the Western rams close the river mouth, you must take this packet to Mr. Riggs at the bank and sell the silverware your father gave us at Saratoga. Do not wait for my pay-warrants; the Treasury clerks downstairs are burning the unissued fractional notes in the cellar stoves to keep the damp out of the powder-magazines, and a sack of mouldy Baltimore cornmeal costs four hundred dollars in green paper this morning. We boiled the headquarters orderly's bay mare in a copper wash-kettle behind the parapet at daybreak. Her hide had the taste of harness-oil and canal mud, yet the men of the 4th Artillery licked the grease from their thumbnails and thanked God for the salt. Across the water, the lights of Alexandria burn all night like an iron-foundry. We can hear the steam-whistles of their armored trains shunting flatcars along the Orange & Alexandria tracks, and when the wind shifts out of the Virginia oaks, it brings the smell of frying bacon and coal-tar straight into our rifle-pits. Half the invalid regiment deserted across the Eastern Branch at dusk; their boots had rotted off their feet in the yellow mire along Maryland Avenue, and the provost guard had no heart left to shoot them. November 13, Four o'clock in the afternoon. The flag of truce has just gone back from the toll-gate. Clara, I looked through the brass telescope in the embrasure and saw Marcus Vance sitting his horse beside the barricade on the southern bank. He wore a heavy blue pelisse trimmed with sea-otter fur and the gold-braided collar of the Pacific Legion, and behind him stood two iron land-engines forty feet long with steam hissing from their condenser-cocks. He is the same Marcus who shared my blankets at West Point in the winter of fifty-three, the boy who stood beside me in the chapel at Cold Spring when we swore our oath to the United States and held your mother's shawl at the landing. I took my class ring from my little finger and wedged it into the muzzle-groove of a three-inch Parrott shell so that if God is merciful and our gunners find his range, he might have his own gold back in his breastbone. My left thumb is frostbitten so that I can scarce hold the cedar pencil. The iron rams have begun to grind across the southern planking of the bridge, and the timbers are screaming under their wheels. Tell little Henry his father kept his coat buttoned to the chin and did not take the California silver. Your affectionate husband, H. Halloran, Maj., 4th U.S. Art. > — *Item #809-B, Impounded Sack 14, U.S. Post Office Department Dead Letter Archive (Recovered from the lining of a forage cap beside the overturned caisson at the Seventh Street Wharf following the Capitol Steps Tribunals, November 1864).*

Ten months later, in the freezing twilight of November 1864, that imperial standard stood above the muddy bluffs of the Potomac.

The campaign from Vicksburg eastward had been an engineering foreclosure. Behind armored rail-cruisers that swept the countryside with rifled Krupp shell at four miles’ range along the parallel tracks of the Baltimore & Ohio and the Pennsylvania Central, the hundred thousand veterans of the Pacific Legion had rolled up the ragged remnants of the Union and Confederate armies like wet carpet. Richmond had fallen in September without a siege after Marcus Vance’s flying columns severed its last rail-line to the Carolinas; at Appomattox Court House, Lee’s starving regiments had stacked their rusted muskets for three hundred wagon-loads of California flour.

Now only the Federal District remained. Fifty-eight earthen forts and a ten-mile belt of red mud and felled abatis ringed the capital, manned by invalid home-guards, armed treasury clerks, and the stubborn skeleton of the Sixth Corps.

Elias sat his aging claybank stallion on the heights of Arlington before the Doric columns of Robert Lee’s abandoned mansion. The wind carried the stench of wet woodsmoke and rotted horse-carcasses from the canal below, thick with sulfurous coal-fumes from twenty siege-locomotives parked on the Alexandria siding. Across half a mile of leaden water, Washington lay under a low bank of sleet.

Since his boyhood by the burning logs in Kentucky, Elias had pictured the seat of Eastern power as a capital of white marble. Through the ground-glass lenses of his binoculars, a half-built village drowned in yellow mire. The white dome of the Capitol stood finished above the leafless trees, yet around its base sprawled acres of rotting slaughter-pens and boarded-up brick rooming houses. Halfway between the Capitol and the river rose the flat-topped stump of the Washington Monument, abandoned at a hundred and fifty feet with its wooden derrick rotting against the gray sky like a broken gallows.

"General Meigs refuses the summons to surrender the river bridges, Protector," Marcus Vance said as he rode up the muddy carriage-drive through the dripping oaks. Virginia clay splattered his dark blue greatcoat to the waist, and a fresh white bandage wrapped his left hand where a sniper’s Minié ball had grazed his knuckles at the Chain Bridge that morning. "He sent the flag of truce back from the Long Bridge five minutes ago. He says President Lincoln and a quorum of the rump Congress are still sitting in the Capitol basement, and that they will blow the aqueduct and fight from street to street until the spring thaw."

Elias lowered his glasses. Beside his stirrup stood his old comrade Caleb Vance, now a brigadier of the reserve with his white beard tucked into the collar of a wolf-skin pelisse, and Colonel Takashima of the First Edo Artillery.

"A man who has eaten salted horse-meat for six weeks does not fight from street to street, Marcus," Elias said. Sleet whistled through the bare oak boughs above them. "He sits behind a pile of cobblestones until someone gives him an excuse to drop his rifle without being shot by his own provost. How many shells do we have in the armored cars at the bridge-head?"

"Four thousand rounds of eight-inch percussion, sir, and twelve hundred incendiary canisters," Marcus said. He flipped open his damp leather field-book. "The wind is from the northwest. If we drop forty canisters into the timber yards along the Seventh Street wharf, the whole lower town from the canal to Pennsylvania Avenue will be afire in an hour."

"No fire," Elias said. "I am not burning a house I have already bought. Those departments are full of tax rolls and coast-charts that took seventy years to draw. We will need the clerks on Monday morning to audit the Eastern debt."

He turned his horse a fraction toward the steep mud bank. Down on the planking of the Long Bridge, two giant steam-traction rams—iron-plated behemoths forty feet long, driven by four-cylinder oil engines and armed with revolving Gatling batteries in their prows—hissed and clanked in the wet gloom.

"Break the barricade at the southern end of the bridge with the rams," Elias ordered. He pulled on his heavy leather gauntlets. "Do not fire a single large shell into the residential squares. Put the First Hawaiian Guard and the Missouri Lancers straight up Maryland Avenue at the double-quick, and sweep the Mall to the foot of Capitol Hill. Use the Gatlings on any earthwork that shows a flag, and throw a cordon around the Executive Mansion before their cabinet can burn the cipher-books. Marcus, you have the vanguard. I want the doors of the Capitol open in forty minutes."

***

Twenty minutes later, General Marcus Vance stood in the armored conning-cupola of the lead traction-ram *Tahoe*. Its eight-foot iron cleaver-wheels ground over the splintered timbers of the Federal toll-gate on the Washington side of the river.

Below the quiet geometry of the Arlington heights, the dying capital was a slaughterhouse. Laid out seventy years before by French engineers to be a broad avenue of republics, Maryland Avenue had dissolved into a knee-deep quagmire of frozen mud and raw sewage, choked with overturned omnibus-bodies and breastworks of cordwood torn from the government fuel-yards.

From the second-story windows of a brick row-house on Seventh Street, a ragged volley of musketry cracked out; a dozen lead balls flattened with sharp *spangs* against the *Tahoe*'s half-inch boiler-plate skirt. Behind the ram, a corporal of the Hawaiian Guard pitched face-down into the slush. Dark blood pooled against the gray sleet.

"Battery left, second story brick!" Marcus barked down the hatchway. He held his open pocket watch in his bandaged left palm.

In the forward casemate, the twin six-barrel Gatling guns swung forty degrees on their greased bronze trunnions. The gunner cranked the handle. With a mechanical roar like sheets of corrugated iron ripping in half, four hundred .58-caliber bullets a minute chewed straight through the brick mullions and shattered the window-sashes, collapsing the interior lath-and-plaster walls and shredding the blue-coated marksmen inside before they could draw a second ramrod.

"Forward!" Marcus ordered. He snapped his watch shut. The column debouched from the avenue onto the open, sleet-swept pastures of the Mall.

Ahead of them, through driving snow-squalls and drifting clouds of black powder smoke, rose the white marble tiers of the United States Capitol. Across the gravel plaza at the western base of the hill, behind a redoubt of granite blocks hauled from the unfinished Treasury extension and reinforced with overturned army baggage-wagons, two thousand veterans of the Iron Brigade and the regular artillery stood shoulder-to-shoulder in tattered coats and powder-blackened faces behind six brass Napoleon twelve-pounders. Nailed to a splintered lance-staff in the paving-stones above them, a torn silk regimental flag flapped in the freezing gale.

"Halt the infantry at the canal bridge!" Marcus shouted through his brass speaking-trumpet as the four Napoleon guns on the slope flashed simultaneously in a long sheet of red flame.

Four solid twelve-pound shot came howling across the dead grass of the Mall. One struck the cast-steel glacis of the *Tahoe* with an ear-splitting *boom* that filled the conning-tower with hot iron-scale; a second tore through the wheel-house of the flanking traction-engine, severed a steam-pipe in a shrieking cloud of scalding white vapor, and hurled two Cantonese engineers broken into the mud.

Shrapnel screamed past the vision-slit. Marcus did not duck. Between the iron palings of the Botanical Garden fence and the piled granite of the barricade, three hundred yards of frozen turf sloped upward toward the smoking brass muzzles. If he sent the Missouri infantry up that icy hill with bayonets, those starving regulars behind the stones would kill four hundred of his men before the breastwork was carried, and dead soldiers wasted rolling-stock capacity.

"Bring up the two railway-mortars on the B&O spur!" Marcus commanded. Behind the ram's rear fender, Major Sterling crouched over an oilskin box where a portable field-telegraph key clicked furiously. "Keep the shells off the building. The Protector wants the marble whole. Elevation twelve degrees, fuse cut to one and one-half seconds. Drop six hundred-pound Krupp air-bursts directly over the gun-emplacements behind the granite wall, then advance the three rams abreast at full throttle and crush the wagons!"

Back by the river-tracks, two monstrous short-barreled steel mortars mounted on eight-wheeled iron flatcars elevated their snouts toward the gray sky. They fired. Along Pennsylvania Avenue for half a mile, the concussion shattered every unbroken pane of glass.

Six seconds later, the air fifty feet above the Capitol barricade turned into a furnace of jagged steel. With the blinding yellow-white flash of picric acid, the Krupp high-explosive shells detonated overhead and scythed downward like an iron flail. The wind tore the smoke-cloud apart. Four of the six brass Napoleons lay dismounted on broken axles amidst a writhing heap of disemboweled artillery horses and mangled gunners.

Before the dazed survivors behind the granite blocks could stagger to their feet, Marcus dropped his gloved hand.

"Sound the charge!" he said.

Steam-whistles shrieked. Drowning out the faint cheers of the dying defenders, the three forty-ton traction rams surged up the slope of Capitol Hill with their wide iron cleats chewing the frozen turf into red mire, while two thousand Pacifica riflemen came behind them at a dead run and fired their seven-shot Spencers from the hip. The steel prows crashed straight through the granite-and-wagon barricade in a roar of splintered oak.

***

While Marcus Vance’s iron rams ground the last barricade below the Capitol dome into kindling, Elias rode at a walk up the deserted width of Pennsylvania Avenue toward the Executive Mansion with Caleb Vance, Lady Kaiulani in an armored carriage, and fifty troopers of the Life Guard.

Paper choked the street. From the broken windows of the Treasury Building on the corner of Fifteenth Street, fleeing clerks had tossed thousands of unissued greenback dollar bills and pension ledgers into the wind; they blew across the frozen cobbles like dirty snow, stuck to the wet fetlocks of the horses, and swirled around the abandoned boots of deserters. The great iron gates of the White House stood wide open. One leaf hung crookedly from a broken hinge where a six-mule baggage wagon had struck it during the midnight flight of the Cabinet toward the Baltimore turnpike.

Elias reined in beneath the tall white columns of the north portico. No sentries stood post. Under a dusting of sleet in the circular driveway lay a frozen artillery mule with a bloated belly, and on the marble steps a half-starved hound dog licked at a spilled sack of oats.

He swung down from his saddle. His stiff knees popped in the cold. He handed the reins to Caleb.

"Keep the troopers in the yard, Caleb," Elias said, looking up at the tall, soot-streaked windows of the mansion, where a single torn lace curtain fluttered through a broken pane. "No looting. If a soldier pockets so much as a silver spoon from the pantry, shoot him on the lawn."

He walked up the steps alone, his heavy cavalry boots ringing against the stone, and pushed open the tall oak front doors.

The entrance hall was cold as a vault. It smelled of stale tobacco smoke and the sour tallow of extinguished chandeliers. Across the black-and-white marble tiles, two deep gouges marked where someone had dragged a heavy iron safe before abandoning it beside the foot of the grand staircase. Down the corridor, in the East Room where soldiers had cut down the velvet draperies for blankets, a squad of invalid Union veterans from the Veteran Reserve Corps sat around a dying fire built directly on the parquet floor out of broken gilded chairs and boiled coffee in tin cups. When the tall figure in the navy wool greatcoat with the four-pointed gold star at the collar stepped across the threshold, the veterans left their muskets leaning against the wallpaper. They stared up with dull, sunken eyes. After lifting their forage caps from their heads, they went back to warming their blue fingers over the burning chair-legs.

Elias said nothing to them. He climbed the wide mahogany staircase to the second floor, his palm sliding up the banister that Jackson and Lincoln had gripped. Charred telegraph flimsies and torn maps of Virginia lay ankle-deep in the upstairs hallway.

At the southeast corner of the passage, the white-painted door to the President’s office stood ajar. Elias pushed it open with the toe of his boot.

The oval-ended library was empty. In the marble grate, a coal fire still radiated a faint, dry heat that smelled of burned sealing-wax and old leather. On the long oak cabinet table in the center of the carpet lay an unfinished meal: a plate of hardtack biscuits, a half-empty glass of buttermilk with a skin of ice forming at the rim, and a pair of steel-rimmed spectacles resting beside an unsigned proclamation calling for three hundred thousand more men to save the Union. Through the tall south windows, beyond the sleet-whitened expanse of the lawn and the stinking mud-flats of the Tiber canal, the gray waters of the Potomac rolled down toward the sea.

Twenty-seven years ago, a bailiff from Philadelphia had stood in the smoke of a Kentucky cabin and told a fourteen-year-old boy that blood was not legal tender in the District of Columbia.

Spurs clinking on the worn Brussels carpet, Elias walked to the head of the table. He stood behind the high-backed leather armchair where the green baize was stained with ink and scarred by the pen-knives of twenty-five presidents. He touched the cold leather of the backrest with one weather-chapped hand. Then he sat down.

For a full minute he did not move. From the brass inkwell and the spectacles left behind by a tired lawyer from Illinois, his gaze rose to the tarnished gilt eagle painted on the plaster ceiling above the chandelier.

Heavy boots and the rustle of silk sounded in the corridor outside. Lady Kaiulani stepped through the doorway in a dark sea-otter pelisse sparkling with melted sleet, followed closely by General Marcus Vance, whose right hand still held his drawn saber while his left carried a wet sheaf of telegraphic dispatches.

"The Capitol has surrendered, Protector," Marcus said. He came to attention before the oak table, his boots leaving tracks of red Maryland clay across the presidential carpet. "General Meigs delivered his sword at the foot of the eastern steps ten minutes ago. Mr. Lincoln and Secretary Stanton escaped northward toward Philadelphia on a hand-car before the B&O tracks were severed at Bladensburg, but eighty-four members of the Senate and House are under guard in the old Supreme Court chamber awaiting your pleasure."

Elias picked up the steel-rimmed spectacles from the green baize. He folded their thin wire temples with a *click* and laid them inside the open drawer of the desk.

"Let Mr. Lincoln run to Boston if he likes," Elias said, his rough voice loud in the low-ceilinged room. "A president without a treasury or an army is just a country lawyer on a hand-car. We will not make a martyr of him."

Kaiulani walked to the south window. Her dark fur mantle gleamed with melted sleet as she looked out through the falling snow toward the broken stump of the Washington Monument, then turned back toward Elias where he sat framed between the velvet curtains.

"And the eighty-four gentlemen in the basement across the avenue, Elias?" she asked. "They still believe they are the Roman Senate waiting in their curule chairs for the Gauls. If you march them out in irons, every newspaper in London and Paris will call it the murder of liberty."

"I am not going to put them in irons," Elias said. He leaned back into the deep leather of the chair, rested his elbows on the arms, and looked up at his general. "Marcus, take two wagons of hard silver coin from the pay-train, minted with the sun and anchor, and drive them up to the Capitol steps. Pay every senator and every representative his back mileage from the day the banks suspended in sixty-one, provided he signs a receipt acknowledging the Articles of Dissolution and the transfer of the Atlantic Debt to the Imperial Receivership at San Francisco. Any man who signs goes home on the evening train with his pockets full. Any man who refuses stays in the cellar without coal until he changes his mind."

The corner of Marcus's mouth twitched. From his breast pocket he drew out a fresh dispatch printed on the blue paper of the trans-continental wire. "It will cost less than a regiment’s rations for a week, sir. Before I go back to the hill, this just came through the Fort Churchill relay from Nagasaki, forwarded by Admiral Farragut at New Orleans. The British China Squadron and four French ironclads have anchored off Shimonoseki to demand that the Shogunate repudiate the exclusive coaling monopoly with Pacifica or face bombardment before the new moon."

Elias’s fingers tightened on the mahogany arms of Lincoln’s chair. Across the brick walls of the White House and three thousand miles of conquered prairie and mountain, his gaze fixed on the western ocean.

"So London thinks our hands are full in this mud-hole," Elias said. As Marcus stepped forward to unroll the Pacific chart across the unsigned Union proclamation, Elias rose from the chair and took his wet campaign hat from the table. "They think because we marched twenty thousand men to the Potomac, the slips at Yerba Buena are empty. Let us finish the funeral of this Republic before sundown, Marcus. I have no time to waste on eastern bailiffs when the British fleet is knocking at the gates of Edo."

***

To the Chronicler who has examined the original parchment of the Articles of Dissolution, preserved today under thick crystal in the Rotunda of the Diet at Monterey, nothing instructs so clearly on the fall of the first American Republic as the ledger-bound banality of its final hour. Great empires are supposed to expire in the glare of burning palaces or beneath the shields of dying legions; the Union of Washington and Jefferson ended at four o’clock in the afternoon in the damp, gas-lit basement of the old Supreme Court chamber, amidst the scratching of steel nibs and the heavy clinking of Mexican-milled silver.

Eighty steaming wool overcoats and the sour reek of unwashed bandages from the temporary hospital in the crypt next door choked the semicircular cellar beneath Latrobe’s low Etruscan vaults. At the center of the floor, directly beneath the plaster figure of Justice whose scales had been chipped by a stray rifle ball during the morning’s assault, Marshal Marcus Vance had ordered two green-painted commissary chests placed upon the clerk’s mahogany table. Twelve troopers of the First Hawaiian Guard stood behind him. Rainwater dripped from their dark blue capes onto the worn carpet while they held their repeating carbines at rest.

"The terms of the Receivership are non-negotiable, gentlemen," Marcus said. He turned a page of his roster, his flat voice echoing off the low stone arches. "By signing the instrument before you, you attest that the compact of 1787 is void by reason of insolvency and civil war; that the federal custom-houses upon the Atlantic seaboard are mortgaged in perpetuity to the Treasury of Pacifica to satisfy eighty-two million thalers in war claims; and that the sovereign states east of the Mississippi are hereby reconstituted as autonomous protectorates. As the Clerk calls your state, step to the baize and sign the parchment. Captain Takashima will weigh out your back allowances in silver coin."

From the rear bench, where a cluster of New England radicals sat huddled in their shawls like wet crows, Senator Charles Sumner of Massachusetts rose to his full height. His face was pale above his black cravat, his temple discolored by a bruise from a fallen plaster cornice.

"This is a ransom—the ransom of Brennus, sir!" Sumner’s baritone boomed through the vault, trembling at the edge with exhaustion. "You bring armed Polynesians and Japanese mercenaries into the sanctuary of the Constitution, you throw a butcher’s ledger upon the altar of the law, and you ask the representatives of a free people to sell their birthright for thirty pieces of silver!"

Marcus did not look up from his list. "Thirty-four hundred pieces of silver in your case, Mr. Sumner, calculating mileage to Boston at forty cents the league since the August suspension. And I must remind you that the furnace boilers in the cellar were extinguished at noon to conserve coal for our locomotives. Those gentlemen who decline to sign the Articles will remain in this chamber until the Provost-General convenes the military commission for the trial of belligerent debtors on Monday."

He nodded to the clerk. "Call the roll. State of Maine."

For twenty seconds no man moved. Melting sleet dripped from the broken basement casements; outside on the plaza, the parked traction-rams hissed. Then a representative from the Portland shipping district, whose three merchant brigs were currently rotting at the wharf for want of clearance papers, slowly unbuttoned his coat, walked down the narrow steps with his gaze fixed upon the toes of his boots, and took the pen from Captain Takashima’s gloved fingers.

The steel nib scratched across the vellum like a saw. Immediately afterward, hard Pacifica thalers poured from a brass scoop into a canvas sack.

A shudder ran through the benches. Men who had lived for three years on depreciated green paper that would hardly buy a pair of boots in a Washington tavern craned their necks toward the chests. When New Hampshire was called, two congressmen jostled each other in the aisle; by the time the clerk reached Pennsylvania and Ohio, forty politicians were lined up three deep before the mahogany table, blowing on their chilled fingers and signing away the Continental Congress’s inheritance with the haste of country passengers scrambling for the last stagecoach before a flood.

Only nineteen men remained seated in the darkening alcove behind Sumner when the last canvas bag was tied.

"Clear the hall of the signatories, Captain," Marcus ordered. He snapped his roster shut and looked toward the silent nineteen in the shadows. "Give them passes for the six o’clock train to Baltimore. As for Senator Sumner and his companions, lock the iron grilles on the corridor and post four sentries with bayonets. The Protector will deal with the irreconcilables after the ceremony on the portico."

***

Outside, the sleet had ceased. Long, ragged bands of amber light tore the sky above the Potomac, catching the wet marble of the Capitol’s eastern front and turning the puddles in the gravel plaza into pools of liquid brass.

Elias stood alone on the central platform of the grand steps, where nine presidents had taken their oaths beneath the Corinthian columns. Below him, across the broad expanse between the portico and the iron fences of the green, twelve thousand soldiers stood drawn up in hollow squares: the Missouri Lancers on the right with their red pennons drooping in the damp wind, the dark-skinned battalions of the Hawaiian Royal Guard in the center, and on the left, four regiments of liberated negro railway-pioneers and Bakufu artillerymen beside the smoking boilers of the forty-ton traction-rams.

Directly at the foot of the stairs, on a temporary pine dais covered in wet bunting, sat sixty men in civilian broadcloth. While the ragged congressmen crept out the back basement doors with their sacks of silver, these Peace Commissioners from New York, Philadelphia, and Richmond—mayors of bankrupt port cities, railway presidents whose tracks were held by Pacifica garrisons, and the surviving Peace Democrats of the midwestern legislatures—waited where Marcus’s provosts had placed them after bringing them up by special train that morning.

"In the name of the Provisional Diet of the Atlantic Municipalities," read Horatio Seymour of New York, his voice thin and trembling as the cold wind off the river whipped the parchment in his red-knuckled hands, "and to prevent the utter desolation of industry, commerce, and Christian society between the Alleghenies and the sea, we do hereby constitute these sovereign commonwealths as the American Free States, under the perpetual protection, customs-union, and military suzerainty of Elias Thorne, Protector of the Grand Confederation of Pacifica and Providentor of the Atlantic Realm."

Seymour held the scroll up the steps. Elias did not take it. One step below him in her green velvet gown, the crimson-and-yellow feather cape of the island kings blazing against the white marble, Lady Kaiulani received the vellum and passed it to the Chancellor.

Elias stepped to the stone balustrade. His rough hands gripped the cold marble. Across the plaza, eighty cornets and great bronze siege-horns of the Legion brass bands sounded the three slow, crashing chords of the Imperial Fanfare, a metallic blast that shook the loose glass in the Capitol dome overhead.

"You have called these territories the Free States," Elias said when the echoes had died away down the muddy valley of the Tiber. He spoke in the short, blunt sentences of the frontier, yet in the quiet plaza every word carried to the gun-crews sitting on the caissons by the gate. "Understand what you are free from. You are free from the speculators who turned your treasuries into paper rags. You are free from the lawyers who sent six hundred thousand of your sons into the ditches for a tariff bill and an abolition tract. From this evening, no state between Maine and Florida will coin money, build a warship, or raise a regiment of militia beyond its municipal police."

He looked out over the heads of the shivering mayors toward the eastern horizon, where night was rising out of the Chesapeake and where, ten thousand miles across the curve of the earth, British guns trained on the straits of Japan.

"Your coastal forts will be garrisoned by my troops," Elias continued. "Your customs houses will pay thirty percent of their gross receipts into the railway and naval chests at Monterey. In return, my granaries in the San Joaquin and the Mississippi will feed your cities through the winter, and the iron of the Pacific will guard your harbors. Go back to your counting-houses. Beat your muskets into plowshares and boiler-plate. The war on this continent is finished; the work of the ocean has begun."

Before the commissioners could raise their hats in a ragged cheer, he turned his back on the newly christened Free States and walked straight toward the bronze doors of the Rotunda, where Marcus Vance waited in the shadow of the portico with a lantern in his hand.

"How many refused the silver, Marcus?" Elias asked, crossing the threshold into the echoing gloom of the Capitol without breaking his stride.

"Nineteen in the cellar, sir," Marcus answered. He fell into step beside him while their boot-heels rang across the sandstone flags beneath Trumbull’s paintings of the Revolution. "Sumner of Massachusetts, Thaddeus Stevens of Pennsylvania, Wade of Ohio, and sixteen others. And we took Secretary Stanton’s chief provost-marshal, Colonel Baker, trying to burn the War Department cipher-archive on Seventeenth Street with a squad of six partisan rangers. They killed two of our Cantonese sappers with pistol-shot before we took them."

Elias stopped beneath the great dome. High overhead, in the freezing twilight filtering through the oculus, Brumidi’s fresco of Washington sitting in the clouds looked down from another world. Behind Elias, Lady Kaiulani paused by the marble pillar, her dark eyes fixed on the lines of fatigue around his mouth.

"We cannot leave eighty thousand troops on the Potomac through the spring, Marcus," Elias said, low enough that only his general and Kaiulani could hear. "If the British and the French bombard Shimonoseki before our cruisers arrive, the Satsuma clans will think our alliance is a paper shield, and the whole western basin will slip from our grasp while we police bread-riots in Baltimore. I need four divisions of the Legion on the troop-trains for San Francisco before Wednesday noon."

"If we pull four divisions out of the eastern provinces this week, Protector," Marcus said, "Sumner and Stevens will have a rebel congress sitting in Boston before Christmas, and every bushwhacker from Virginia to Pennsylvania will be shooting our tax-collectors from the woodlots."

"Not if we pack the governing machinery into boxcars and take it with us," Elias said.

Kaiulani took half a step forward. The feathers of her cloak rustled in the cold draft of the rotunda. "Elias. A senator in a cellar is an old man with a dry tongue. A senator on a scaffold is an immortal spirit. My ancestors knew when to break a chief’s bones with a club, and when to bring his household gods into the king’s own compound. Leave no martyrs in this swamp, and leave no seat of authority for a mob to rally around."

Elias looked up at the great dome overhead, then down toward the dark doorway of the crypt. "She is right, Marcus. Mr. Stevens stays off the monument. A gallows only makes a shrine for Boston preachers. Hang Colonel Baker and his six bushwhackers from the burnt rafters of the Seventeenth Street archive where they killed our sappers; do it quietly, as common arsonists, before the street-lamps are lit. Put Stevens, Sumner, and the seventeen irreconcilables in a locked Pullman car behind my own engine tonight."

Marcus paused. His pencil hovered over his leather field-book. "You are bringing them to the Coast, sir?"

"I am bringing the entire carcass of their government to the Coast," Elias said. Beyond the eastern portico, the cold rain turned to sleet. "Strip the Treasury of its plates and dies. Empty the Patent Office and the War Department vaults, clean out the Coast Survey, unbolt the printing presses, pack the original parchments of their laws into zinc-lined crates, and take down the bronze doors of this building. By Saturday night, I want Washington reduced to a country turnpike junction between the tobacco fields. When a man in New York or Richmond wants a land-patent or a pension-warrant or a customs-clearance, he will face west."

# Chapter 6: The Currency of Iron

Moving an empire’s center of gravity required an exhausting, mud-choked migration of iron and paper across two thousand miles of winter mountain and alkali flat. For six weeks in the opening months of 1865, the single completed broad-gauge track of the Central Pacific groaned beneath forty-two special convoys that crept westward through the snow-sheds of the Sierra Nevada. While the Provisional Diet sat in Monterey to adjudicate the ancient ceremonial privileges of the Polynesian and Bakufu missions, Elias decreed that the realm's mints and archives, along with its high courts of receivership, should sit directly upon the granite jaws of the Golden Gate.

On the nineteenth of February, Elias stood beneath the dripping redwood scaffolding of the new Citadel on Rincon Hill. Up the mud-slick plankway from the Embarcadero, a double-team of steam-winches hauled a twelve-ton crate of cast-iron Treasury plates. Coal-soot from the donkey-engines and the rank brine of the low-tide mud-flats thickened the morning bay fog, mingling with the sweet, heavy smoke of camphor-wood that burned in the braziers of the Cantonese stone-masons.

The grand design already creaked at the joints. Half a mile down the hill, where the wooden shanties of the newly arrived Baltimore and Philadelphia treasury clerks pressed against the brick walls of the Edo naval barracks, four hundred Eastern copyists who had been uprooted from their Maryland brick row-houses at the point of a bayonet and shipped across the continent in unheated passenger coaches gathered in the ankle-deep mire outside the commissary depot. A dull, angry murmur rose through the mist. They waved soggy ration-tickets at a line of Hawaiian provost-guards.

"The axle-boxes on the third archive train gave out at Truckee yesterday, Protector," Major Sterling said, and limped up the wet timber ramp with a manifest clipped to a cedar board. Seventy hours without sleep had left the former Union engineer's eyes bloodshot, aging him ten years since that night in Alexandria; locomotive grease stained his navy tunic. "We have six hundred boxes of Eastern land-deeds and the entire registry of the Philadelphia Mint sitting on a siding in twelve feet of snow because the Sacramento rolling-mills diverted our spare wheel-castings to the naval yard. And these Washington clerks down on First Street refuse to open the customs ledgers unless they get brick quarters with coal-grates and silver pay instead of quartermaster vouchers."

Elias ignored the shouting clerks. He rested his rough palm against a freshly dressed block of Sierra granite. Cold and wet, the stone bore the combined mason-marks of a Cornish quarryman and an Osaka castle-builder.

"Why were the wheel-castings diverted without my counter-signature?" Elias asked over the wheeze of the winch-boilers.

"Marshal Vance’s requisition, sir," Sterling said. Behind them, Lady Kaiulani stepped from the arched doorway of the temporary Chancery with a dark wool shawl drawn over her high-collared silk dress, and the major lowered his voice. "And Lord Shimazu’s naval board. They claim the British China Squadron at Hong Kong has taken on four thousand tons of Welsh steam-coal and twelve hundred Royal Marines. If the drydocks at Hunters Point are not finished before the spring typhoons clear, Shimonoseki will stand alone."

"If the customs ledgers are not opened by Monday, Major," Kaiulani said, her voice cool and sharp as she looked down the muddy slope toward the simmering riot at the commissary, "neither Marshal Vance nor Lord Shimazu will have the silver to pay the rivet-gangs by April. You have swallowed a whale, Elias, and it is kicking in your belly. Soft-handed and full of Eastern spite as those small men down there are, they remain the only men on this continent who can read the cipher-codes of the Boston and New York tariff-houses. Put them on the breakwater with a pickaxe, and the Atlantic revenues stop tomorrow."

Below them, a grey-haired clerk from the Sixth Auditor’s Office tried to push past the rope. A corporal of the Hawaiian Guard dropped the butt of his carbine onto the man's toes. Out of a neighboring tea-house strolled twenty off-duty Japanese sword-gentry from the foundry, who rested their hands on their hilts and looked on at the loud-mouthed Americans with open contempt.

A desert skirmish line allowed a volley of repeaters to settle the arithmetic. Here, three worlds ground together on a single narrow peninsula of rock and mud.

"Take twenty wagons of seasoned oak cordwood from the military reserve at the Presidio, Sterling," Elias said, and turned from the parapet. "Issue every married clerk from the Washington departments two cords of wood and a sack of white San Joaquin flour, plus ten silver thalers against his March salary. Tell them that at noon tomorrow, the Providentor will inspect the counting-rooms in person. Every ledger that is balanced and open on the desk by twelve o’clock carries a warrant for a freehold house-lot on the Mission slopes, while every desk still empty at five minutes past twelve will have its occupant shipped to the Sitka timber-camps on the evening packet. As for the wheel-castings, come with me to the boat-slip. Marshal Vance must remember that a fleet without a treasury is only scrap-iron floating on salt water."

***

Three miles south of the muddy chaos on Rincon Hill, the volcanic serpentine rock of Potrero Point jutted into the deep-water channel of the bay. General Marcus Vance stood upon a vibrating catwalk of bolted iron grating fifty feet above the floor of Graving Dock Number Two.

To the Chronicler, the Imperial Shipyards of San Francisco in that winter of 1865 resembled the forge of Hephaestus roofed over with corrugated Birmingham iron and timbered with the primeval forests of Oregon. Beneath Marcus’s mud-caked boots lay the cavernous stone trough of the basin, pumped dry by four giant Cornish beam-engines whose walking-beams rose and fell through the roof-steam like the elbows of titans. In the pit sat the skeleton of the *Kamehameha*. Her massive cellular double-bottom was forged from Sacramento pig-iron, her five-thousand-ton ocean-going hull plated with six-inch compound armor rolled at the Nagasaki and Clark’s Point works.

The din inside the shed pressed against the eardrums until a man had to shout to hear his own thoughts. Four hundred pneumatic and hand-swung riveting hammers beat against red-hot boiler plate, circular steel saws shrieked through teak backing-timbers, leaking steam-pipes hissed, and six hundred Cantonese coolies chanted hoarsely as they hauled a forty-ton Krupp stern-post along greased iron skids to the strike of a bronze gong.

Through all the terrifying grandeur of the spectacle, Marcus Vance’s gray eyes tracked the flaws in the iron.

"Look at that starboard strake below the water-line, Takashima," Marcus said. With his brass-tipped walking-stick, he pointed toward a chalk-marked plate near the bilge-keel, where a gang of Scottish boilermakers and Satsuma shipwrights argued fiercely through an interpreter with their hammers lowered while the red-hot rivets cooled to a dull purple in the tongs. "The edges have blistered three-eighths of an inch on the bend. That is the third plate from the Benicia furnaces we have had to condemn since Tuesday."

Colonel—now Rear-Admiral of Ordnance—Takashima wiped a smear of black coal-grease from his cheek with a white cotton handkerchief. Fatigue darkened his narrow eyes. "The pig-iron from the new Oregon mines carries too much phosphorus, Marshal. And the rolling-mill crews have worked eighteen-hour shifts since the Protector telegraphed from Washington. Yesterday, after the Shinto priest had purified the new steam-hammer and an Irish foreman from Pittsburgh spat tobacco into the quenching-trough, two of my master-smiths from Kagoshima drew their blades on him. We lost four hours on the main shaft while the provosts separated the guilds."

Marcus opened his damp leather ledger and rested it against the iron railing of the catwalk. Three feet above their heads, a traveling overhead gantry-crane rumbled past. Fine black flakes of soot and hot lubricating oil showered down over their shoulders. The numbers on the page were merciless.

In the field, an army lived on momentum; you took the enemy’s corn or burned his bridges, and if a hundred horses died in the traces, you requisitioned mules from the next county. Geography at the edge of the great water refused to be bullied. Steaming six thousand miles across the western ocean to meet the Royal Navy in the Straits of Shimonoseki required three tons of anthracitic coal for every mile, drydocks at Honolulu and Midway that remained half-dredged coral lagoons, and armor plate that held when an Armstrong three-hundred-pounder struck it at point-blank range.

"We cannot wait for the Benicia chemists to sweeten the Oregon ore," Marcus said, his pencil scratching a rapid calculation in the margin of his book. "If Lord Palmerston’s cabinet in London learns that we have stripped our Eastern garrisons before the *Kamehameha* and the *Satsuma* are ready for sea, the British squadron at Esquimalt will steam down from Vancouver Island and blockade the Puget Sound coal-colliers inside a week. Strip the four river-monitors we left at Cairo and Memphis. Have their six-inch turret-plates unbolted and loaded onto flatcars, then rushed through the South Pass before the March blizzards close the grade."

"Unbolt the river-monitors?" Takashima asked, a rare note of alarm breaking through his samurai reserve. "Marshal, if you disarm the Mississippi flotilla now, the Illinois and Tennessee partisans will cross the river in flatboats before the month is out! General Caleb Vance wired from St. Louis this morning that he has barely enough riflemen to guard the railway bridges against disbanded Confederate bushwhackers!"

"Let them burn a bridge in Illinois," Marcus said. He snapped his ledger shut as the shrill whistle of the Protector’s steam-launch sounded from the fitting-out basin outside the shed. "We can hang bushwhackers at our leisure next autumn. If the British and French burn the Shogun’s forts at Shimonoseki in May, we lose the Western Ocean forever. Come down the ladder, Admiral; the Protector has just rounded the mole, and by the look of Major Sterling behind him, the civilian departments are already crying for our iron."

***

By the third week of March, the struggle between the demands of the dockyard and the collapse of the Eastern counting-houses had reached a pitch that no provost’s bayonet could quiet.

Across the cities of the Atlantic protectorates, from the silent textile towns of Massachusetts down to the weed-choked wharves of Charleston, worthless paper swirled through the gutters: the bloated greenbacks of Mr. Lincoln’s fugitive congress, the dead grey notes of Richmond, and the temporary grain-vouchers of the Pacifica military governors. Farmers in Ohio refused to bring their winter wheat to the rail-depots for scrip. In New York, bakers shuttered their ovens while ten thousand unemployed dock-wallopers marched down Broadway behind black flags and smashed the windows of the municipal customs-receivers.

On the twenty-fourth of March, Elias summoned the Joint Council of the Realm and the captive commissioners of the Eastern banks to the great vault-hall of the new Imperial Mint on Market Street.

The building was a fortress of rusticated blue basalt and brick. From twenty assaying furnaces in the cellar, its tall chimney-stacks poured continuous heat into the damp spring sky. Inside the central weighing-room, nitric-acid fumes from the parting-vats and the smell of hot beeswax sharpened the scorching air, thick with the heavy, greasy odor of six steam-powered coining presses that stood in a row along the north wall like iron guillotines.

At the center of the granite floor, stacked upon low oak pallets until they formed a solid breastwork four feet high and thirty feet long, lay four thousand unstamped bars of pure Sierra quartz-gold and Washoe silver, the accumulated hoard that Elias had locked behind the mountain passes while the East bled itself white.

Around this gleaming rampart stood an uneasy congregation: Lord Shimazu and two Tokugawa treasury officials in dark silk *hakama*; Lady Kaiulani flanked by the merchant-princes of Oahu; Cornelius Schuyler of the New York Clearing House, brought overland under military escort; and rising from a wooden bench near the iron doors, his wrists free of chains though two Hawaiian guards stood behind his shoulders, Senator Charles Sumner of Massachusetts.

Elias walked out from the assaying office in his plain dark wool tunic. Between his thumb and forefinger he held a single newly struck coin. Stepping directly onto the lowest tier of the bullion-pallets rather than mounting a platform, he rested his heavy military boot upon five hundredweight of dull yellow metal.

"Mr. Schuyler," Elias said. His rough voice carried over the low hiss of the steam-presses. "You told my Treasury Secretary yesterday that the merchants of New York and Boston cannot collect the thirty-percent customs tribute because no man between Maine and the Mississippi knows what a dollar is worth."

Schuyler swallowed hard. He wiped the acid-sweat from his bald crown with a crumpled silk handkerchief, his gaze fixed on the mountain of gold beneath the Protector’s boots. "It is a matter of commercial faith, sir! There are nine hundred millions of Federal greenbacks and national bank-notes in the hands of the eastern public! If you repudiate them entirely, every savings-bank and widow’s annuity and insurance company from Portland to Baltimore will crash before noon! Yet if you leave them in circulation without specie redemption, no cargo will move on the Erie Canal this spring!"

"And by what right," said Charles Sumner, who rose from his bench against the heavy hand of the Hawaiian sergeant pressing down on his broadcloth shoulder, "does a military usurper in a frontier mint presume to annul the public faith of the United States? Those notes bear the sacred pledge of a free Congress, issued to preserve the Union and strike the shackles from four million bondsmen! If you turn them into ashes to build your pagan ironclads, history will curse your name alongside Alaric and Attila!"

Elias looked across the yellow bars at the tall Massachusetts senator. His face held the flat, weathered patience of a man who had watched a prairie fire burn itself out against a river.

"Your Congress printed nine hundred million dollars of promises on rag-paper because you lacked the stomach to tax your own shopkeepers for the blood you were spilling," Elias said. "A piece of paper is a lie signed by a clerk who hopes he will be out of office before the note comes due, Mr. Sumner."

He tossed the heavy gold coin across the width of the bullion-pile. Schuyler caught it clumsily against his waistcoat. Broader and thicker than the old American double-eagle, the disk was stamped on the obverse with the rising sun over an anchor and the legend *IMPERIUM PACIFICUM*; on the reverse, in English, Japanese *kanji*, and Hawaiian, stood its weight in pure grains.

"At six o’clock this morning," Elias said, looking from the New York banker to the foreign envoys along the wall, "I signed the Currency Decree. From the first of April, there is only one legal tender between the Atlantic Ocean and the China Sea: the Pacifica gold thaler and its silver tenth. Every furnace in this cellar and every press in Carson City and Osaka is running day and night to coin eighty million thalers before the summer solstice."

Schuyler’s fingers trembled as he turned the heavy disk in the gas-light. "And the nine hundred millions in Federal greenbacks, Protector? At what discount will your customs-houses receive them?"

"At one hundred cents on the dollar, for ashes." Elias stepped down from the bullion pallet and walked toward the nearest of the great brick assaying-furnaces, where a Cantonese stoker stood with his long iron slice-bar before the roaring white-hot grate. "Bring up the first crate from the Washington train, Marcus."

Four sappers wheeled an iron hand-truck across the granite flags and tipped a zinc-lined box of unissued hundred-dollar Treasury notes beside the furnace door.

"Hear the law," Elias said. His hand rested on the warm brickwork of the flue while the orange glare of the coals lit the deep lines around his jaw. "For ninety days, every holder of a Federal greenback or an Atlantic bank-note may bring his paper to the provost-marshals in New York, Chicago, or New Orleans. We will redeem the old Union paper at twenty cents on the dollar in twenty-year Pacifica Railway and Dockyard bonds bearing four percent interest in gold, redeemable only upon the completion of the Shimonoseki and Honolulu fortifications, since coin would flee to London on the next packet. As for the paper of the Southern rebellion, it is waste-rag. And every Federal note handed in across the counter will come here."

He nodded to the stoker. The Cantonese laborer swung open the heavy cast-iron furnace door. A blast of dry, roaring heat swept the room and drove Sumner and Schuyler a step backward.

"You are chaining every bank in New York to the wheels of your war-chariot in Asia!" Schuyler cried out. He took a half-step forward as the stoker pitched the first bundle of green-tinted Washington bank-notes onto the white-hot coals, where the copper-oxide ink flared into a blinding sheet of yellow-green flame.

"I am giving your banks a foundation of rock instead of swamp-mud," Elias replied over the roar of the draft. On the grate, the engraved portraits of Hamilton and Lincoln curled into black cinders and vanished up the chimney just as Marcus Vance stepped through the side door from the telegraph room with a wet blue cipher-strip held tight in his bandaged hand.

"Protector," Marcus said, coming straight to Elias’s elbow without waiting for the banker to answer, the heat of the burning millions beating against their faces, "a fast dispatch-steamer from Hakodate just made the Cape Flattery wire-station. Admiral Kuper has rejected the Shogun’s mediation and cleared his gun-decks in the Inland Sea. Our lead cruiser off Midway has just blown her starboard high-pressure cylinder."

Elias kept his face still. Green flames reflected across his brass buttons. If Schuyler or the Japanese envoys caught him flinching now, the twenty-year dockyard bonds would be worth no more than the cinders going up the flue.

"Keep your voice down, Marshal," Elias said under the roar of the furnace blower. "Let the stokers finish the crate. Tonight we dance with their wives and daughters on Nob Hill, and if the patricians of Manhattan and Boston are to pay for a second fleet across the Pacific, they must first believe the first one has already won."

***

By nine o’clock that evening, the warm beeswax and bruised tuberose of the Protectorate Palace on the crest of Mason Street had replaced the nitric fumes of the Market Street Mint. Where wind-scoured chaparral had stood fifteen years before, a vast quadrangle of pale Sierra granite and gilded cast-iron conservatory domes rose above the fog-line. Corinthian pilasters carved from white marble met sweeping, copper-tiled roofs modeled after the shogunal audience halls of Nijo, and the ballroom floor was laid in alternating strips of dark Hawaiian koa and California redwood polished with pumice until it reflected the three hundred gas-chandeliers like black water.

Elias stood near the raised dais beneath the great silk banner of the rising sun. His plain dress coat of dark navy wool bore no medals. Around him moved five hundred prisoners disguised as guests: the Schuylers and Livingstons of New York, the Cabots of Boston, the Biddles of Philadelphia, and the surviving rice-grandees of the Carolina low-country, whom Marcus Vance’s railway commissioners had politely invited to winter in San Francisco while their eastern estates were assessed for the Imperial Receivership.

In the center of the floor, a string orchestra from the Vienna Conservatory played a Strauss waltz. Every thirty seconds, the deep subterranean thud of the fifty-ton drop-forges down at the Potrero Point armor-works punctuated the music and set the Venetian crystal prisms on the candelabra shivering and chiming.

"You see how quickly the thoroughbred takes to the new harness, Elias," Lady Kaiulani said beside his elbow. She wore a gown of amber Lyons silk draped with the royal crimson feather-work of Oahu across the bodice, a tiara of raw Washoe diamonds and black pearls binding her dark hair. Toward the refreshment tables she tilted her ivory fan: there Cornelius Schuyler’s nineteen-year-old daughter laughed behind her gloved hand at a compliment from young Captain Takashima, whose Satsuma clan crest was embroidered in gold thread upon the high collar of his naval tunic, while three paces away Judge Biddle of Chestnut Street inquired of Lord Shimazu’s factor regarding the dividend yields on the Nagasaki coal-mines.

"A horse takes the harness when the whip is in the driver’s boot," Elias replied. Under the swell of the violins, his low voice was rough as unplaned timber. "Judge Biddle is asking about Nagasaki coal because we burned his Pennsylvania railway bonds at noon. He wants to know which way the trough is tilting before he puts his snout back in."

"Do not despise their greed, Protector; it is the mortar that will save you ten regiments of garrison troops east of the mountains," Kaiulani said. She smiled as Mrs. Livingston, whose grandfather had signed the Declaration of Independence, swept past them and dropped a stiff, reluctant curtsy to the Polynesian envoy. "If you leave these families sitting in their cold parlors on Beacon Hill and Gramercy Park, nursing their humiliation like old wine, they will finance every partisan bushwhacker from Maine to Georgia. Marry their daughters to your frontier colonels and your samurai admirals. Give their younger sons clerkships in the Amur fur-monopoly and seats on the Honolulu Sugar Board. Within twenty years, a Cabot will draw a sword against Boston to protect his wharf-shares in Yokohama."

Cornelius Schuyler detached himself from a knot of Baltimore shipping merchants and approached the dais. Under the gas-jets his bald head gleamed with perspiration; a glass of Sonoma champagne shook in his plump fingers. He had the deference of a broker who has examined the bailiff’s books at noon and decided by nightfall to join the syndicate.

"A magnificent house, Protector," the New York financier said. He bowed low enough that his white cravat brushed his watch-seal. "My wife was just remarking to Lady Kaiulani’s chamberlain that the Tuileries itself has no finer glass-work than your winter garden. Though, if a man of business may speak plainly among friends, the news from the Western Ocean has caused some tightness among our underwriters tonight. A rumor reached the Exchange Room at the Palace Hotel an hour ago that the *Midway* has put back into Honolulu with a cracked cylinder-head, and that the British fleet at Hong Kong outnumbers Lord Shimazu’s steam-sloops two to one."

Elias looked down at the banker. His gray eyes were still, reflecting only the twin pinpoints of the chandelier overhead.

"The *Midway* is a scout-corvette of twelve hundred tons, Mr. Schuyler," Elias said. Six neighboring gentlemen from Philadelphia and Charleston stopped their conversation and turned their ears toward the dais at the volume of his voice. "When a wheel breaks on one of your Broadway omnibuses, do you close the clearing-house?"

"No, sir, certainly not, only—"

"The *Kamehameha* and the *Monterey* carry twelve inches of rolled compound iron on their water-lines, Mr. Schuyler, and they do not steam alone," Elias said. He stepped down from the dais; the old-money patricians gave way before his broad shoulders. "Since you gentlemen are now the principal bond-holders of the Imperial Dockyards, it is right that you should see how your four-percent interest is secured. Tomorrow morning at eight, my launch will take you across the bay to the Marin magazines. As for the union of our two coasts, I have decided tonight to establish the Order of the Golden Gate: fifty hereditary baronies of the Pacific Realm, each carrying ten thousand acres of prime timber and coal land on Vancouver Island and the Amur estuary, free of the Eastern war-tax."

Silk gowns and black tailcoats rustled across the floor. Judge Biddle’s austere Quaker jaw dropped half an inch.

"The first twelve patents," Elias said, as his gaze passed slowly over Schuyler’s daughter and rested upon the pale young scions of the Boston and Carolina houses standing by the pillars, "will be conferred on the first of June upon those eastern houses whose sons accept commissions in the Pacific Marine Corps for the Asian station, or whose daughters wed officers of the General Staff roster. Enjoy the music, gentlemen. The lists open in the Chancellor’s office at ten."

***

It is the custom of the beaten provinces along the Atlantic to portray the great migration of the late eighteen-sixties as a Babylonian captivity, a forced transplanting of mechanics and gentlefolk driven at the point of Marshal Vance’s lances to build the pyramids of a Western Pharaoh. Yet the Chronicler, who has stood upon the stone viaducts of the Humboldt River and examined the parish registers from the Willamette to the Straits of Juan de Fuca, must record a stranger and more majestic truth. Once the tumor of parliamentary faction had been excised by the sword of Sacramento, the pent-up energies of the continent burst westward like a mountain river when the ice-jam is dynamited in the spring.

History provides few spectacles to match what the court philosophers of Monterey termed *The Salutary Effects of Order*. For thirty years prior to the Coup, the settlement of the interior had been paralyzed by the endless wrangling of Washington lawyers over whether a territory should be slave or free, whether a railroad should run through Chicago or New Orleans, and whether a squatter’s pre-emption took precedence over a speculator’s scrip. Under the iron hand of the Providentor, these questions vanished overnight.

Where four months of creaking ox-wagon misery had once separated the Missouri from the Pacific tidewater, double-tracked broad-gauge railways now spanned the alkali sinks and pierced the granite heart of the Sierra through tunnels illuminated by coal-gas and ventilated by giant steam-fans. Every week through the summers of 1865 and 1866, down the western slopes into the valleys of the Sacramento and the Columbia, thirty-six immigrant trains rolled behind twin ten-wheeled Baldwin-Nagasaki locomotives whose brass cow-catchers bore the rising sun. No ballot-boxes or land-lawyers rode those cars. Disbanded soldiers from the armies of Grant and Lee who had found their eastern homesteads mortgaged to the chimney-tops filled the benches alongside Lancashire cotton-spinners starved out by the blockade, Cornish tin-miners, Bavarian iron-founders, and ten thousand emancipated negroes from the Mississippi delta. Each passenger held a brass-stamped Imperial Freehold Warrant guaranteeing forty acres of irrigated ditch-land or three silver thalers a day in the timber-mills in exchange for seven years’ liability in the Territorial Reserve.

To travel the Great Trunk Road from Salt Lake to Monterey in those years was to witness the birth of a new race under an older, sterner sky. Imperial engineering had replaced the mud-walling individualism of the old frontier with geometric grandeur. At every fifty-mile division point rose a standardized stone depot, a grain-elevator sheathed in galvanized iron, and a syncretic garrison-chapel where the bronze cross of the Christians and the polished mirror of the Sun Goddess stood side by side beneath a roof of red redwood shingles. In the mining towns of the Washoe and the Idaho gulches, where six years earlier drunken prospectors had shot one another over disputed claim-stakes in the mud, the great quartz-stamps now thundered day and night with the regularity of cathedral clocks, while masonry aqueducts built by Cantonese sappers channeled the waste-waters across five hundred thousand acres of sagebrush desert to water orchards of peach and olive.

The transformation reached beyond iron and wheat. In the new port cities springing up around the deep waters of Puget Sound, at New Osaka on the Elliott Bay and Port Vance below the snow-dome of Mount Rainier, the narrow, puritanical horizon of the old American republic dissolved into the salt-scented immensity of the Great Arena. Here the grandson of a Connecticut ship-carpenter worked at the same drafting-table with a naval architect from Edo; here the ordinances of the harbor were cried in three tongues from the steps of basalt customs-houses; and the children of Illinois ploughmen grew up by the wharves as four-masted iron tea-clippers and armored depot-ships came home from Canton and the Kuriles with the weeds of the western ocean trailing from their copper hulls.

Men forgot how to vote for a county sheriff. The granaries were full, the silver coin never varied by the tenth of a grain, and a woman could walk from the Rio Grande to the Fraser River without seeing a highwayman who was not hanging in chains from an iron telegraph pole. If this was servitude, as Senator Sumner continued to write from his walled villa above the Santa Cruz redwoods, it was a servitude that paved the wilderness with gold and taught a fractured nation to march to the beat of a single drum.

***

On a sleet-driven afternoon in November of 1866, eighteen months after the British demonstration at Shimonoseki had ended in an armed truce along the thirty-second parallel, Elias stood at the northern rail of the headland battery above Cape Flattery, where the black basalt cliffs of the Washington Territory met the unbroken winter Pacific.

Two hundred feet straight down below the gun-parapet, gray swells charged out of the northwest fog-bank like ranks of white-maned horses and smashed against the jagged sea-stacks; the boom shook the wet turf beneath Elias’s boots and flung plumes of freezing spindrift high over the muzzles of the ten-inch Rodman columbiads. Behind him, along the timbered shore of the Strait, four colliers from the Nanaimo mines battled the head-wind. Their screw-propellers thrashed out of the troughs as they crept toward the coaling-hulks at Port Angeles.

Elias was forty now. Campaigning from the Kentucky ashes to the steps of the Capitol in Washington had left him lean and weathered, with dry, tightened sinew instead of the fat of hereditary kings; the wind off the North Pacific whipped his iron-gray hair flat against his skull, and a deep vertical furrow cut between his eyebrows.

Beside him stood General Marcus Vance. Water streamed down his oilskin cape as he held open a weighted zinc map-cylinder to shield a Russian Admiralty chart from the freezing drizzle.

"Admiral Takashima’s squadron cannot hold the Kurile passage through another winter without a windward base, Protector," Marcus shouted over the surf. He was gaunt and hollow-cheeked; the logistics of keeping twelve ocean-going ironclads supplied with coal and boiler-tubes four thousand miles across the northern steamer-lane via Midway had aged him five years in eighteen months. "We lost two coal-barques in the October gales south of the Aleutians, and the *Satsuma* had to burn her own teak cabin-bulkheads to make Hakodate with her bunkers empty. If the British reinforce Esquimalt in the spring and the Royal Navy closes the southern belt from Singapore to Hong Kong, our ships in the Sea of Japan will be trapped in a bottle."

Elias left the chart unread. Across twenty miles of white-capped gray water, where the mountainous, pine-blackened spine of Vancouver Island loomed through the squall under the Union Jack, and beyond that toward the fog-shrouded curve of the globe where the continent bent westward like a drawn bow toward Asia, he kept his eyes fixed north.

"A man does not cross a canyon on a single rope when there is a stone bridge three miles upstream, Marcus," Elias said. His low, rough voice cut through the hiss of the sleet against their oilskins. "How many miles is it from Honolulu to Yokohama against the winter westerlies?"

"Thirty-four hundred marine leagues, sir," Marcus answered at once. His cold-stiffened finger traced the long, empty southern curve across the chart. "And two thousand miles of it without a single sheltered anchorage or a seam of coal between Midway and the Bonins."

"And by the Great Circle?" Elias raised his gloved hand and pointed straight into the teeth of the northwest gale, up the coast past the British forts at Victoria, toward the fifty-fourth parallel. "Up the inside passage to Sitka, along the stepping-stones of the Aleutian chain, and straight down to the Kuriles and the mouth of the Amur?"

Marcus looked down at the top of the zinc cylinder, where the Russian characters of the Imperial Fur Company marked the indented, island-choked coastline of Russian America. "Twenty-five hundred miles from Puget Sound to the Japanese straits, Protector. With land-locked harbors every hundred leagues, timber to spar ten fleets at Sitka, and outcrop coal at Cook Inlet and Unalaska. You could steam torpedo-rams and shallow-draft monitors all the way from Seattle to Kamchatka without ever being more than forty hours from a drydock or a telegraph cable."

"Baron Stoeckl is at New Osaka this week," Elias said. He turned from the stone parapet, and the wind flattened his heavy wool greatcoat against his boots. "He came over from St. Petersburg via the Siberian post-road and the Nikolayevsk packet. The Tsar’s treasury is empty from the Polish rebellion and the emancipated serf-loans, and the Grand Duke Constantine knows that if war breaks out between Russia and England this winter, the British squadron at Esquimalt will sail up and seize Novo-Arkhangelsk before a single Russian frigate can clear Kronstadt."

"Stoeckl has been hinting at a sale of the fur-posts since fifty-nine," Marcus said. He let the zinc map-cover snap shut. "Before the war, he offered the territory to Buchanan’s cabinet for five million dollars, and the eastern senators laughed him out of the room because they said it was nothing but icebergs and walrus-blubber."

"The eastern senators never looked at a globe," Elias said. Down the wet granite steps of the battery, past the cliff-edge where three Hawaiian signalmen worked the semaphore arms above them, he walked toward the timber guard-house and the cedar shed where their horses stood steaming. "They looked at flat maps on a parlor wall and thought the top of the world was an edge you fell off. Look at the curve of that coast, Marcus. With the Aleutians under our thumb, the North Pacific becomes a roofed lake, and the British station at Vancouver is caught in the nutcracker between Puget Sound and Sitka."

Marcus fell into step beside him on the muddy corduroy road and dropped his hand to the hilt of his saber to keep it from banging against his wet boot. "If we buy Russian America, Lord Stanley in London will read it as an act of encirclement against British Columbia. The Hudson’s Bay factors are already arming the steamer-crews at Victoria, and our ironworks at Clark’s Point are six months behind on the heavy turret-castings for the third division."

"Let London read it how they please," Elias said. Beside the stirrup of his big bay gelding, he stopped and took the wet leather reins from the orderly’s hand. "Our payment will bypass the London gold markets entirely, Marcus. Tell Lady Kaiulani to have the Chancellor meet me at the telegraph car at four. We will offer Baron Stoeckl seven million two hundred thousand thalers: half in silver bullion delivered at Vladivostok, and half in four armored coastal monitors built on the slips at San Francisco to guard the mouth of the Amur for the Tsar. If the British want to stop the deed, they will have to fight the Russian bear and the Pacific eagle in the same pass."

He swung his boot into the iron stirrup and pulled himself into the wet saddle. The leather creaked. Off the gray rollers below, a fresh squall of hail came howling up the bluff, stinging the cheeks of the horses and rattling like buckshot against the corrugated roof of the telegraph shed.

"And Marcus," Elias added, leaning down from the saddle as his general reached for the bridle of the second mount and the semaphore paddles above them clacked wildly in the mist with an incoming priority cipher from the south—

The heavy cedar door of the telegraph shanty burst open. Major Sterling stumbled out into the sleet without his cap, the wet blue paper ribbon of the Port Townsend submarine cable trailing from his fingers.

"Protector!" Sterling shouted over the roar of the breakers below the cliff. "From the harbour-master at Port Angeles, relayed from our picket-corvette off the San Juan channel! Rear-Admiral Denman has just warped the British ironclad *Zealous* and two screw-frigates out of Esquimalt harbour under full steam! They are heading north through the Georgia Strait with two battalions of Royal Marines aboard, and the British Governor at Victoria has issued a proclamation placing the Russian American Company’s coal-seams at Cook Inlet under the temporary protection of Her Majesty’s fleet to prevent foreign piracy!"

Marcus Vance’s boot froze in his stirrup. Across the twenty miles of churning gray water, low-hanging cloud-wrack swallowed the dark smudge of coal-smoke from the British dockyards. "Denman knows Stoeckl is with us. Someone in the St. Petersburg Foreign Ministry sold the draft treaty to the British ambassador. If the *Zealous* drops anchor in Sitka sound before the cession is signed and our garrison is ashore, Denman will raise the Union Jack over the Russian governor’s house and call it a preventative occupation. We have nothing in the Strait tonight heavier than two wooden torpedo-launches and the monitor *Shasta*."

Elias stayed in the saddle. He reined his bay gelding hard around on the wet logs of the road until the animal’s iron shoes bit into the bark right beside the doorway of the telegraph hut.

"How many knots can the *Zealous* make against a northern gale, Marcus?" Elias asked, his voice low beneath the shriek of the wind.

"Eight, perhaps nine if she burns her prime Welsh coal," Marcus answered at once. "It is seven hundred miles up the outside passage to Sitka. With the winter rollers running off Queen Charlotte Sound, Denman will take the inside channel behind Vancouver Island, which gives us ninety hours before his marines can row ashore at Baronov Castle."

"And the Russian overland wire through Nikolayevsk and Irkutsk?" Elias looked down at Sterling.

"Open all the way to the Winter Palace, sir!" Sterling wiped the sleet from his spectacles. "We laid the last splice across the Amur mouth three weeks ago, and Baron Stoeckl is waiting in your railway car at the Port Angeles siding right now with the St. Petersburg cipher-clerks!"

"Good," Elias said. He dismounted in a single heavy drop, tossed the reins to the orderly, and strode into the cramped, kerosene-heated belly of the telegraph shed. "Marcus, wire the naval yard at New Osaka. Put the First and Second Regiments of the Atlantic Free States Volunteer Rifles, the old Pennsylvania and Virginia veterans, aboard the fast paddle-transports *Oregon* and *Constitution* tonight. Tow the monitor *Shasta* behind them with double hawsers. You will leave the Strait before midnight, steam outside Vancouver Island through the open sea regardless of the gale, and beat Denman to Sitka by six hours."

"The *Shasta* has only eighteen inches of freeboard, Protector," Marcus said from the doorway. On the pine table, the brass sounder chattered like an angry squirrel. "If we tow a flat-bottomed river monitor into the open North Pacific in November, the swells will bury her turret before we clear Nootka Sound."

"Batten her hatches with tarred canvas and lash two coal-barges alongside her beam to break the wave-slap," Elias said. He stripped off his wet leather gauntlets and threw them onto the operator’s table beside the humming galvanic batteries. "If the sea takes her, she sinks. If she reaches Sitka, her fifteen-inch Dahlgren will punch through the *Zealous*'s four-inch armor like wet pasteboard. Get to the boats, Marshal."

# Chapter 7: Department of the North

Four hours later, the mahogany-paneled saloon of the armored command-car beside the Port Angeles coaling-pier smelled of Turkish cigarettes and hot sealing-wax, thick with the damp wool of six men who had ridden twenty miles through a coastal hurricane. Outside the double-paned windows, the locomotive’s boiler panted to keep the steam-radiators hot against the freezing rain. Two hundred yards down the jetty, the red torches of the dock-gangs flared through the sleet as three thousand veterans of the old Army of the Potomac and the Army of Northern Virginia, wearing the slate-gray greatcoats of the Atlantic Auxiliary Corps with the rising sun brassard on their sleeves, marched up the gangplanks of the troop-steamers.

Baron Eduard de Stoeckl sat at the center of the saloon table. He was sixty and bald-headed, his deeply pouched eyes trained by thirty years in the courts of Europe and America. Two strips of blue telegraph tape lay before him. They had just come off the trans-Siberian wire from the Ministry of Finance in St. Petersburg, six thousand miles of copper cable strung across the frozen birch-forests of the Amur and the snows of the Urals.

Beside Stoeckl stood Lady Kaiulani, her dark hair still damp from the ride down the mountain trail, her fingers resting on the back of the Chancellor’s chair as she translated the French cipher-groups aloud.

"Prince Gorchakov is hesitant, Protector," Stoeckl said in his heavily accented English. He tapped his gold snuff-box against the green baize. "He wires from the Winter Palace that the British Ambassador, Sir Andrew Buchanan, called upon him at midnight Petersburg time.
