London warns that if His Imperial Majesty transfers the ports of Russian America to a belligerent maritime power that holds the American Atlantic states in receivership, Great Britain will consider the Treaty of Paris void and will move her Baltic squadron to Revel in the spring. The Grand Duke Constantine urges caution. He asks for a thirty-day armistice in the negotiations while a joint commission meets in Berlin."

Elias stood at the head of the narrow car in his mud-spattered boots, his broad shoulders nearly filling the space between the polished redwood bulkheads. He picked up the brass telegraph key connected to the repeater-line and looked down at the Russian envoy.

"In thirty days, Baron," Elias said, "Rear-Admiral Denman’s marines will be drinking rum in your governor’s cellar at Sitka, and the Union Jack will be flying from Mount Edgecumbe. Do you think Lord Stanley will pay the Tsar seven million thalers for a house he has already taken with a squad of sailors?"

"The British claim they are merely policing the waters against filibusters," Stoeckl said. A bead of sweat rolled down his powdered cheek. "And Prince Gorchakov objects to the medium of payment. St. Petersburg requires gold coin in London to meet the Rothschild railway coupons in January. Your offer of four monitors and silver bars at Vladivostok does not satisfy the Tsar’s bankers."

"The Tsar’s bankers in London are Englishmen," Elias replied. He leaned both calloused palms flat upon the table until the brass lamp-brackets rattled. "If I send seven million in gold sovereigns to Threadneedle Street tomorrow, the Bank of England will attach every penny of it before noon to satisfy the defaulted cotton-bonds of the old Southern states, or lend it to their own Admiralty to build ironclads for the Baltic. Tell Prince Gorchakov to wipe the sleep out of his eyes and look at the map."

He turned to the telegraph operator hunched in the corner cubicle. "Clear the Siberian line to the Winter Palace. Tell the relay clerks at Irkutsk and Omsk that if a single key drops out of circuit before I finish speaking, I will cut the subsidy to the Amur Telegraph Company at midnight. Take this down in plain English, and let the Russian clerks translate it for the Tsar’s cabinet as it comes off the wire."

The operator’s fingers closed on the vulcanite knob. The metallic clatter of the armature filled the railway car.

"From Thorne, Protector of Pacifica, to Alexander Imperator and Prince Gorchakov at St. Petersburg," Elias dictated. He kept his gaze fixed on Stoeckl’s face. "The British ironclad *Zealous* cleared Esquimalt four hours ago to seize Russian America by force of arms. My fleet is already at sea to intercept her. If His Imperial Majesty signs the Act of Cession before four o’clock this morning Pacific time, back-dated to the first of November, the soil of Sitka is Pacifica territory, and I will blow Admiral Denman out of the water as a trespasser upon my realm. If the treaty is not signed within the hour, I will recall my troop-ships to Puget Sound, open the Straits of Juan de Fuca to the Royal Navy, and inform London that Pacifica has no objection to a British annexation of both Sitka and the mouth of the Amur River."

Baron Stoeckl half-rose from his velvet seat. His snuff-box spilled brown powder across his white waistcoat. "Monsieur le Protecteur! That is an ultimatum to the Autocrat of All the Russias! You cannot speak to the Winter Palace as if you were dealing with a Mexican customs-collector!"

"A bankrupt is a bankrupt, whether he wears a sheepskin coat or a diamond crown," Elias said. "And I will sweeten the iron for him, Baron. Tell Gorchakov that in addition to the seven million two hundred thousand in silver and monitors, I will hand over the complete working drawings of the Clark’s Point compound marine engines and send fifty Edo and Scottish master-machinists to the shipyards at Kronstadt before the spring thaw. Russia needs steam and steel to keep the British out of the Black Sea, and London’s gold will not buy them. Send the wire."

Rain lashed the glass. From the harbor mouth, the deep whistle of the transport *Oregon* sounded three long blasts as Marcus Vance’s flotilla cast off into the dark. For twenty-two minutes, no one spoke inside the car. Lady Kaiulani poured a small porcelain cup of hot green tea and set it beside Elias’s elbow; he left it untouched. Right, left, right swung the brass pendulum of the bulkhead clock while the electric spark leapt across the frozen roof of the world, racing through the log stations of Kamchatka, under the ice of the Okhotsk sea-margins, and past the convict-mines of Nerchinsk into the gilded telegraph room where the Tsar’s ministers stood in their embroidered coats.

At eighteen minutes to four, the receiving magnet clicked once, twice, and broke into a steady stream of dots and dashes.

The operator tore the blue slip from the brass spool with trembling hands and laid it before Baron Stoeckl.

Stoeckl adjusted his gold-rimmed pince-nez. As he read the French groups, his shoulders sagged inside his coat.

"His Imperial Majesty accepts the terms of the Port Angeles convention in full," Stoeckl whispered, looking up from the cipher. "I am instructed to affix my seal to the parchment immediately, and to wire Captain Pestchouroff at Sitka that the territory, forts, timber, and ice of Russian America are transferred to the sovereign crown of Pacifica from the stroke of noon yesterday."

"Give the Baron the pen, Kaiulani," Elias said. He reached for his wet cavalry cloak on the brass hook behind the door. "And have the operator forward the Tsar’s order to the Sitka semaphore station ahead of the fleet. Marcus will need the paper dry before his guns clear the headland."

***

Five days later, at the gray dawn of November twenty-fourth, General Marcus Vance stood upon the ice-sheathed hurricane deck of the paddle-transport *Oregon* as she rolled through the mountainous, lead-colored swells off Sitka Sound.

The voyage up the outside passage had tested every timber in the squadron. For ninety hours, a sixty-knot sub-arctic gale had screamed down from the Gulf of Alaska; six inches of solid blue ice coated the walking-beams and wire rigging of the steamers, and off Queen Charlotte Island the port towing-hawser of the monitor *Shasta* had parted like pack-thread. Three times the flat-bottomed ironclad had disappeared beneath forty-foot green rollers. Her single smoke-pipe belched black brine and steam while her Cantonese stokers worked knee-deep in freezing bilge-water to keep the oil-burners lit, and only the two timber-laden coal-barges lashed tight against her armored sponsons kept the hull from turning turtle in the trough.

Ahead, the snow-squall parted. Out of the black water rose the jagged volcanic cone of Mount Edgecumbe, and beyond the spray-lashed granite reefs of the channel huddled the Russian settlement of Novo-Arkhangelsk: heavy spruce-log blockhouses and red-painted shingled roofs clustered around the green-copper onion dome of the Cathedral of St. Michael beneath the sheer timber ramparts of Baranov’s rock.

"Look to starboard, General!" Captain Takashima shouted from the ice-crusted wheelhouse. He pointed his brass glass toward the southern entrance of the sound, where the timbered islets met the open sea.

Three miles off the Biorka channel, through the driving veil of snow, a three-masted black hull with twin yellow funnels thrashed through the kelp-beds under both steam and reefed topsails. Twin curtains of white foam boiled from her bow as she raced for the inner anchorage. Her Britannic Majesty’s armored frigate *Zealous* had come up the inside passage four hours behind them.

Marcus leaned over the bridge-rail, his cheekbones blue-white with frostbite and his eyelashes crusted in rime.

"Cast off the towing-cables on the *Shasta*!" Marcus roared through his speaking-trumpet to the deck-crews below, where forty former Virginia infantrymen hacked at the frozen hemp hawsers with boarding-axes. "Signal Lieutenant Mordecai in the turret to clear his fifteen-inch guns and lay his hull directly across the four-fathom channel between Japonski Island and the town! If the Englishman attempts to force the inner harbor, put a solid cored shot through his rudder-post!"

He turned to Colonel Mulligan. The one-armed veteran of San Pasqual commanded the First Atlantic Free States Regiment, twelve hundred lean survivors of Gettysburg and Chancellorsville who stood packed in the waist of the steamer with slate-gray coats buttoned over buffalo-wool vests, their breath smoking from their beards as they greased the breech-blocks of their Spencer repeaters.

"Get the whaleboats into the water, Colonel," Marcus ordered. He checked his silver watch and tucked it back beneath his wool scarf. "Do not wait for the ships to anchor. Row the first four companies straight to the Russian timber-wharf, march up the steps to the Governor’s castle at the double-quick, and put twenty riflemen in each of the log blockhouses overlooking the beach. I want the sun-and-anchor flying above that flagpole before Admiral Denman’s gig touches the kelp."

Twenty minutes later, Marcus’s boots crunched onto the frozen gravel of the Sitka parade-ground at the summit of the rock. The wind carried the reek of wet spruce-bark and rancid seal-oil from the Tlingit canoes drawn up along the stockade wall, mixed with the sour grease of the garrison’s tallow candles.

Before the tall spruce flagstaff stood two hundred soldiers of the Siberian Line Battalion in ankle-length drab overcoats and flat forage caps, their cheeks sunken with scurvy. Beside the halyards waited Captain Pestchouroff and Prince Maksutov, the last Governor of the Russian American Company, in full gold-laced uniform. Down in the harbor below the log parapet, the flat iron turtle-back of the *Shasta* swung broadside across the narrow channel; her twin fifteen-inch muzzles gaped at less than four hundred yards’ range while the towering black bow of the British *Zealous* shuddered to a halt against her backed screw-propellers and her anchor-chains roared down into the mud to avoid the monitor’s ram.

"You have the dispatch from Baron Stoeckl, General Vance?" Prince Maksutov asked in stiff French. His breath puffed white in the freezing drizzle. On the timber gallery behind him, his Princess wept into her sable muff.

"I have the Tsar’s own cipher, Excellency, and two hundred thousand silver thalers in the purser’s strongbox below to pay the arrears of your garrison," Marcus replied. He drew the oilskin packet from his breast and handed it over as four hundred of Mulligan’s veterans clattered up the wooden stairs from the wharf, their bayonets dull gray through the snow, and filed into the casemates behind the rusted Russian thirty-two-pounders.

Maksutov glanced down at the harbor. A British twelve-oared cutter had just dropped from the davits of the *Zealous*, a red-faced Royal Navy post-captain standing in the stern-sheets and waving a white boat-cloak toward the wharf. The Russian prince’s mouth twitched.

"It appears our English friends have arrived too late for the christening," Maksutov said, turning to his sergeant at the flagstaff. "Lower the eagles."

The Russian drums beat a slow ruffle. Down the spruce mast jerked the double-headed imperial eagle. Halfway down, the wet hemp fouled on a resinous knot in the wood, and the yellow silk flapped damply against the bark until, at a nod from Maksutov, a Russian sailor climbed the icy shrouds, freed the line, and dropped the standard into the waiting arms of the Siberian guard.

Marcus did not wait for the British boat to reach the landing-stage. He stepped forward, hooked the brass grommets of the Pacifica ensign, heavy blue wool embroidered with the golden rising sun and the iron anchor, onto the halyard, and nodded to Colonel Mulligan.

"Haul away, Sergeant," Mulligan barked.

Up into the arctic snow-squall rose the blue-and-gold banner. It snapped taut in the gale from the Gulf. Below the parapet, the fifteen-inch gun in the turret of the *Shasta* roared out the first blank charge of a twenty-one-gun salute; the concussion of fifty pounds of mammoth powder shook the icicles from the eaves of St. Michael’s Cathedral and stopped the British cutter dead in the water fifty yards off the piles.

Ten minutes later, the British post-captain climbed the slippery timber steps to the castle gate with his cocked hat white with snow and two armed Royal Marines at his heels. No Russian governor waited to receive his proclamation. Beneath the dripping spruce arch stood General Marcus Vance, flanked by a rank of former Pennsylvanian and Virginian riflemen with repeating carbines held across their chests.

"I am Captain Hewett of Her Majesty’s Ship *Zealous*!" the Englishman snapped. He clapped a hand to his sword-hilt and glared up at the blue-and-gold banner whipping overhead. "Rear-Admiral Denman demands to know by what authority an armed force of American irregulars has occupied the fortification of a friendly European power in time of peace!"

"You are standing on the soil of the Northern Province of the Grand Confederation of Pacifica, Captain," Marcus said. "Purchased by treaty from His Imperial Majesty Alexander the Second on the nineteenth of November. Admiral Denman may water his ships at the outer anchorage for twenty-four hours if his boilers are dry; after noon tomorrow, any British warship entering these waters without a clearance-pass from the Port Admiral at New Osaka will be treated as an enemy vessel. Good morning, sir."

While the diplomatic salons of London and Paris rang with angry denunciations of the "Port Angeles Fraud" and Lord Stanley rushed two regiments of Canadian militia overland toward the Red River, Elias left the warm marble council-rooms of Monterey behind. A treaty was merely ink until a road was cut through the timber. On the twelfth of January, 1867, in the dead, black heart of the sub-arctic winter when the sun rose scarcely four hours above the southern horizon, Elias stood inside the great log trading-hall of Baronov Castle at Sitka among the steam-radiators that his engineers had bolted into the old Russian porcelain stoves.

Geological surveys and rough birch-bark maps drawn by Russian creole fur-traders covered the long spruce table beside coal-samples from the Kenai Peninsula. Outside the frost-feathered panes, where a hundred Tlingit laborers and Cantonese railway-graders cleared snow from the foundation-trenches of the new naval foundry by the glare of pine-tar cressets, the mercury stood at twelve degrees below zero. Inside, the hall smelled of wet dog-sled harnesses, seal-blubber, hot machine-oil, and the strong black brick-tea that Baronov’s old clerks brewed in brass samovars.

"The coal at Cook Inlet is lignite, Protector," Marcus Vance said. His finger tapped a chunk of dull, flaky black stone on the edge of the chart. "It will serve for the stationary donkey-engines at the timber-mills and the domestic stoves, but it clinkers the grates of the high-pressure cruisers. Until we sink deep shafts into the Matanuska valley behind the mountains, our northern squadron will still have to haul thirty thousand tons of Nanaimo or Welsh steam-coal a month up the inside passage, right past the muzzles of the British batteries at Victoria."

Beside the stove, Lady Kaiulani sat wrapped in a heavy mantle of silver fox-fur that Prince Maksutov had presented to her before sailing for Vladivostok. Despite the stifling heat of the iron pipes, her slender fingers were stiff with the northern chill as she turned the pages of the native census ledger.

"And your Tlingit chiefs along the Lynn Canal are a different breed from the plains Comanches, Elias," she said, her voice clear and low against the howling of the williwaw wind coming down off the glaciers behind the town. "The Russians stayed inside their log stockades for sixty years because four thousand Sitka and Chilkat warriors hold the mountain passes to the interior. They carry British Hudson’s Bay muskets and trade with Victoria by canoe, and their shamans told my interpreter this morning that if your Cantonese pioneers cut a single cedar tree on their burial islands for your drydock pilings, they will burn every fishing-station from here to Wrangell."

"Give the Chilkat chiefs fifty repeating carbines apiece and ten barrels of Sacramento valley flour for every village, and commission their headmen as Imperial Wardens of the Passes with the pay of cavalry captains," Elias said. With his hands clasped behind the small of his back, he paced down the length of the spruce table. "Let them tax the British Hudson’s Bay trappers fifty percent on every beaver-pelt that comes down the Stikine River, and keep half the silver for their own lodges. A chief who draws a government salary to rob his old friends forgets his shaman."

Before Marcus could enter the order in his ledger, a heavy commotion broke out in the timber guard-room at the foot of the stairs. A creole sentry barked a guttural Russian challenge; a hoarse, frost-cracked American oath answered him, and snow-shoes thudded against the log wall.

The double spruce doors swung open. Lantern held high, Major Sterling stepped inside with a man who looked as if he had been dug out of a glacier.

It was Luke Harmon, a former Washoe silver-prospector and scout of the Pacific Legion whom Elias had sent north across the Chilkat divide with two Russian half-breeds in October, three weeks before the treaty was even signed, to trace the rumors of yellow gravel that old Hudson’s Bay factors had whispered about at Fort Yukon.

Harmon could scarcely stand. His wolf-skin parka was charred down the left sleeve from sleeping too close to a spruce-fire; greasy rags black with dry gangrene from frostbite wrapped the tip of his nose and two fingers of his left hand; his beard was a solid mass of yellow icicles and dried caribou blood. As two Hawaiian orderlies caught him by the elbows to keep him from pitching face-first onto the floor, he wrenched his right arm free and clutched a heavy, greasy moose-hide poke against his breastbone.

"Clear the door, Sterling," Elias said. He stepped around the table and pulled a heavy wooden armchair up to the stove with one hand. "Sit down, Harmon. Give him a mug of rye."

Harmon ignored the whiskey when Sterling held the tin rim to his split, purple lips. Sinking into the oak chair, he squinted his snow-blinded, bloodshot eyes against the lamp-glare until they found Elias’s face.

"Is the paper signed, Captain Thorne?" the scout asked, his voice like two pieces of dry sandstone rubbed together. "Did you buy the ice from the Rooshians?"

"Every foot of it from the Portland Canal to the Frozen Ocean," Elias said. He stood over the chair while the rime in the scout’s wolf-fur melted and dripped onto the spruce planks with a rapid *pat-pat-pat*. "Where are the two creoles I sent with you?"

"Left the young one under a pile of stones at the White Horse rapids when our canoe stove in the November freeze," Harmon wheezed. His good hand fumbled with the stiff rawhide strings of the moose-skin bag. "The old one’s down on the sled with his feet froze black to the ankles. We came four hundred miles down the ice of the big river, what the Indians call the Kwikpak, and back over the Chilkat pass in the dark with the thermometer forty below and the mercury froze solid in the bulb. The Hudson’s Bay men at Fort Selkirk tried to bushwhack us on the Pelly when they seen where we was panning. I put a Spencer ball through their factor’s brisket and took his dogs."

With his teeth and his remaining thumb, Harmon tore the rawhide knot loose and upended the moose-hide poke directly over the geological charts of Cook Inlet.

Dull, heavy, butter-yellow metal rattled across the paper. It rolled over the ink lines of the Russian forts and knocked Baronov’s brass inkwell onto its side. In place of the sharp, white-quartz crystals of the Sierra mother-lode that Elias had pulled from the American River nineteen years before, these water-worn nuggets were smooth as horse-beans and pigeon-eggs, mixed with two pounds of coarse, greasy flakes that shone in the kerosene light like the scales of a golden carp.

Marcus Vance drew in a sharp breath. Beside the stove, Lady Kaiulani rose from her chair, the silver fox-furs slipping from her shoulders as she looked down at the table.

"We didn't even have a pickaxe to reach bed-rock, Protector," Harmon whispered. Leaning forward over his knees, he pushed a three-ounce slug of pure gold across the map toward Elias’s thumb with his trembling, frost-blackened fingers. "The ground up on those feeder-creeks by the Klondike and the Sixty-Mile is froze harder than cast iron twenty feet down. We had to build spruce-fires on the gravel at night to thaw six inches of muck, and scoop it out with a frying-pan in the dark. Every pan we washed carried ten thalers to the dirt! There’s three hundred miles of creeks up behind that mountain wall where the gold’s laying in the frozen gravel thicker than cheese in a sandwich, hundreds of millions of it, Elias, laying right across the British line!"

Elias picked up the largest nugget. Still bitter cold from the scout’s coat, heavy and greasy between his calloused fingers, the gold bore the dark red stain of the Hudson’s Bay factor’s blood in its crevices. After a glance at the metal, Elias turned his eyes to the faint dotted line on Stoeckl’s map, where the hundred and forty-first meridian ran straight up through the blank white paper toward the polar sea.

"The creek where you shot the Englishman," Elias said, his voice flat in the overheated log hall. "Which side of the Russian line does it lie on?"

Harmon spat bloody saliva onto the floorplates. "Ten leagues east of the stake, Captain, up the Pelly fork. In Queen Victoria’s pasture. Though there ain't a white man within five hundred miles of it now that the factor’s under the ice."

"There is no line where there are no surveyors," Elias said. At the window, he looked down through the black sub-arctic noon toward the harbor, where the twin funnels of the *Oregon* were already raising steam for the return run to San Francisco. "Marcus. Have the surgeon take Harmon’s fingers off in the cellar and lock him and the creole in the inner ward of the castle with two Hawaiian sentries at the door. If a single sailor on the transports hears the word *Klondike* before my clerks in San Francisco have drawn the boundary statutes, we will have fifty thousand deserters streaming over the passes in canoes, and the British cabinet will send the Channel Fleet to Vancouver before the ice breaks."

***

Three weeks later, on the fourteenth of February, 1867, the fog off the Golden Gate pressed cold and salt-heavy against the tall arched windows of the Old Custom House on Battery Street, though inside the newly partitioned third floor the dry air smelled of fresh pine shelving, hot red sealing-wax, and the iron-gall ink of sixty steel pens scratching in unison.

Elias walked down the central aisle between the double rows of high mahogany standing-desks. Sixty men perched upon the tall iron stools. They wore identical coats of plain slate-colored wool with black linen sleeve-protectors tied at the elbows; half of them were former auditors of the United States Treasury from Philadelphia and Baltimore, and the other half were clerks of the Tokugawa rice-magistracies from Osaka, their hair cropped in the Western fashion as they worked side by side over massive leather-bound folios stamped in gold leaf with the cipher of the *Department of the North*.

Behind Elias walked Lady Kaiulani, her dark green velvet skirts brushing the oiled redwood floorboards, and Cornelius Schuyler, whom Elias had appointed three days prior as Chief Comptroller of the Northern Bullion Reserve.

"You see the beauty of the double-entry system when applied to wilderness, Protector," Schuyler said. His plump hand gestured toward a long wall of pigeon-holes where thousands of brass-tagged zinc cylinders were racked according to latitude and stream-bed. Given a monopoly to administer, the New York banker had lost his hunted look and now glowed with the quiet zeal of an archbishop inspecting a cathedral. "Unlike the chaos of forty-nine, when every roughneck who stumbled into a creek in the foothills claimed freehold over the mineral, no private foot touches the Yukon basin. Under the Organic Statute you signed on Monday, the entire watershed north of the fifty-eighth parallel is declared Crown Ordnance Domain."

Elias stopped beside the drafting table of a young Japanese topographer who was laying down red ink contour lines across a blank chart of the Chilkat and White Pass trails to translate Harmon’s rough grease-paper sketches into the rigid geometry of military engineering.

"How many tons of provisions are staged at the Lynn Canal depot, Mr. Schuyler?" Elias asked, his rough voice low enough to leave the rhythm of the scratching pens unbroken.

"Fourteen thousand barrels of salt pork, six thousand sacks of dried beans, and two hundred miles of portable narrow-gauge iron rail," Schuyler said, his thumb hooked over an ivory memorandum tablet. "Every laborer who embarks from Puget Sound or Canton signs a five-year indenture with the Department before he steps onto the gangplank. In exchange for his mark, he receives a brass neck-tag stamped with his battalion and creek-number, four pounds of bacon a week, and two silver thalers a day credited to his book in this room, payable only upon his return to San Francisco. The gold never enters a miner’s pocket. From the riffles of the sluice-box, under the eye of a departmental assay-clerk and two armed Hawaiian guards, the amalgam goes straight into locked iron retorts."

"And the boundary with the British possessions?" Kaiulani asked. She stopped before the great wall-map where the fresh crimson paint of the Pacifica border bulged two hundred miles eastward of the old Russian meridian and swallowed the entire headwaters of the Yukon and the Pelly down to the Cassiar range. "Lord Stanley’s minister in Washington sent a formal protest through the Montreal wire yesterday. The Hudson’s Bay Company claims their factor at Fort Selkirk has been missing since November, and that our surveyors have moved the Russian boundary-cairns five degrees east into Rupert’s Land."

Elias looked up at the wet red paint on the wall. Years ago in Pennsylvania, a county bailiff had condemned his father’s cabin with a ribbon of parchment; now Elias had the clerks, the rulers, and the ten-inch cannon behind them.

"The treaty of St. Petersburg states that the boundary follows the summit of the mountains parallel to the coast," Elias said. "When those summits happen to lie two hundred miles inland around the headwaters of the Pelly, the error belongs to the Almighty’s geography rather than my surveyors. Write to the British Commissioner at Victoria, Kaiulani. Tell him that the Department of the North has established six meteorological and police posts along the upper river to protect the native tribes from unlicensed whiskey-peddlers, and that we will be happy to appoint a joint boundary commission to examine the cairns in the summer of eighteen-seventy. By the time their surveyors walk up those canyons with a transit, we will have washed the gravel clean to the bedrock."

***

To the Chronicler who has traveled the great iron road of the Northern Department in later, gentler decades, when heated Pullman cars carry imperial magistrates from the wharves of Skagway to the electric-lit boulevards of Dawson in fourteen hours, the records of that first terrible spring of 1867 read like a descent into the circles of Dante’s ice. History, in its grand balance-sheet, records the two hundred and forty million thalers of hyperborean bullion that flowed into the vaults of Market Street between the signing of the Sitka treaty and the outbreak of the British war; yet providence demands that we examine the furnace in which that key was forged.

No singing prospectors stampeded up the Klondike. No dance-halls or gaming-tents rose along the riverbars. Instead, as the March gales howled down the funnel of the Lynn Canal, blackened iron troop-transports landed thirty thousand men on the boulders of Dyea beach. They were the sweepings of two continents and an ocean: disbanded Confederate infantrymen from the prisoner-of-war stockades at Rock Island who had traded their shackles for a five-year northern pickaxe, starving Irish navvies from the bankrupt Erie railway towns, Cantonese coolies from the Pearl River delta, and four battalions of stony-faced Satsuma pioneers who marched up the ice-steps with wooden numbering-tallies hanging from their belts.

Above the beach rose the Chilkoot, a thirty-five-degree chute of blue glacier-ice and granite talus climbing three thousand feet straight into a sky the color of wet slate.

At the foot of the ice-wall stood the stone blockhouse of the Department of the North. Beneath a giant painted board bearing the words *ORDER IS PROVIDENCE*, where twelve clerks in wolf-skin coats sat behind pine trestles heated by sheet-iron charcoal braziers, every man’s pack went onto the brass steelyards before the provost-guards unlocked the timber turnstile. Each bearer carried at least seventy pounds of Departmental pig-iron, boiler-plate, or salt-pork upon his spine. No one broke his place in the human chain that stretched like a black, wriggling ant-column up the white face of the mountain.

Blizzards swept down from the summit. Four feet of dry, suffocating powder buried the notched ice-steps, froze eyelashes together, and crusted men's throats with blue rime, yet at the Crater Lake station above, the whistle of the steam-winch blew on without pause. When a Virginia veteran or a Cantonese bearer slipped from the hemp guide-rope, his lungs burning in the thin air and his knees buckling beneath a cast-iron sluice-gate, the file behind him stepped past. A ten-minute halt on the upper chute would freeze two hundred men solid in their tracks before the line could move again. Wearing iron crampons on their boots and carrying stout hickory alpenstocks, the provost-corporals rolled the fallen man and his pack out of the trough into the drift beside the trail, chalked the four-digit number from his brass neck-tag onto a slate, and waved the next bearer up the step.

Beyond the summit lay the flat, timberless marshes of the Klondike and the Bonanza creeks. There, where the April sun rolled like a cold brass disk along the southern hills before plunging back into twenty hours of violet darkness, the earth itself turned the pickaxe.

For ten thousand years the auriferous gravel had lain locked in forty feet of permafrost, a cement of black muck, mammoth bones, and blue ice that blunted the steel point of a Cornish pick like an anvil. To reach the yellow scales lying upon the rotten slate bedrock, the legions of the Department turned the sub-arctic valleys into a smoky, sulfurous pit. For twenty miles along the winding trenches of the Eldorado, work gangs stripped every dwarfish spruce and stunted birch from the hillsides to feed ten thousand night-fires at the bottom of narrow, timber-shored shafts.

All through the arctic night, a low roof of yellow woodsmoke choked the canyon over the stench of thawing Pleistocene carrion and tallow-dip candles flickering in the mud. Half-naked men worked in twelve-hour relays beneath the earth. With their wool shirts stiff with frozen sweat at the shoulders and their boots ankle-deep in boiling black slush, they scooped the thawed six inches of gravel into iron buckets before the frost could bite the dirt hard again. Above them, on the lip of the drifts, the high-pressure donkey-boilers brought over the pass in numbered pieces panted and wheezed in the forty-below air. Jets of scalding steam shot through iron pipes to thaw the dump-heaps before the summer sun could melt the snow.

Scurvy blackened the gums of the Irishmen. Pneumonia carried off the Cantonese by platoons when they came dripping out of the steam-drifts into the arctic wind, and the graveyard on the frozen bench above the river grew faster than the log barracks. Yet every morning at six, when the bronze gong sounded from the Assay Stockade, the armed mule-sleds drove down the creek-bed to collect the iron amalgam-cans. Clerks entered every man’s tally in the great ledgers in duplicate; the assay staff weighed every ounce of coarse yellow metal, sealed the bars with the red wax of the Protectorate, and stacked them like cordwood in the log magazine to await the breaking of the river-ice. By stopwatch and bugle-call, the Department gutted the continent’s cellar to buy the sinews of a fleet six thousand miles away.

***

On the nineteenth of June, 1867, the northern harvest came home to the Golden Gate.

A stiff afternoon wind blew in from the Farallones. It drove whitecaps across the bay and whipped the smoke from the seventy foundry chimneys of Potrero Point and Clark’s Point into a long, gray canopy reaching all the way to the Oakland mud-flats. Down on the private granite mole of the Naval Citadel, the low-tide brine mingled with the smell of hot valve-oil from the dockside hydraulic cranes and damp, tarry hemp hawsers drying in the sun.

Elias stood near the edge of the stone quay, his hands thrust deep into the pockets of his navy wool greatcoat. Beside him stood General Marcus Vance, Cornelius Schuyler, and Rear-Admiral Takashima. Twenty paces behind them, a double rank of the Life Guard held the dock-gates against four hundred foreign consuls, shipping underwriters, and reporters from the London *Times* and the Paris *Débats* whom Elias had permitted to stand upon the upper timber gallery overlooking the slip.

Out in the main channel, her black iron hull streaked with white salt-crust to the tops of her paddle-boxes and her bow-plates dented by the pack-ice of the Bering Sea, the armed treasure-steamer *Sitka* warped slowly against the stone pilings behind two wheezing harbor tugs. The dock-crane's chains clanked as the steamer's iron gangway swung out from her bulwarks.

"Seven hundred and forty days since we closed the eastern banks, Protector," Cornelius Schuyler said, a tremor in his voice. "Lord Rothschild’s agent in San Francisco told me at breakfast that the Bank of England has raised its discount rate to nine percent on the rumor that your northern mines were nothing but iron pyrites and frozen mud. Look at the British Consul up there on the gallery. He has his spyglass trained right on the main hatch."

"Let him look," Elias said. Gulls screamed overhead, and the *Sitka*’s waste-steam pipe hissed as it roared off pressure. "A man with a spyglass saves me the cost of a telegram to Downing Street. Marcus, how many chests are in this first run?"

"Two hundred and forty iron-bound boxes, sir," Marcus answered, his eyes on the manifest that the harbor-master’s launch had brought ashore twenty minutes earlier. "Eleven tons of retorted Klondike bar-gold and coarse nuggets from the April washings. Enough to plate four first-rate battleships and buy every ton of saltpeter in Chile for three years."

On the deck of the *Sitka*, the boatswain’s pipe trilled. By the mainmast, the heavy steam-winch clattered into gear, its wire cable singing taut until a rope net rose four feet above the deck holding a rectangular chest of polished oak bound with thick straps of blued San Francisco steel.

The crane-boom swung the chest out over the granite quay and lowered it onto a flat-bedded iron hand-truck. Four burly Cornishmen strained at the handle-bars while the solid cast-iron wheels groaned and shrieked against the stone flags under five hundred pounds of dead weight.

Elias stepped forward. He raised one gloved hand. Three paces from the foot of the gallery stairs, right below the redwood railing where the foreign consuls leaned so far out that their top-hats threatened to tumble into the slip, the Cornishmen halted the truck.

"Open the first box, Mr. Schuyler," Elias said, pitching his tone to carry up to the timber gallery. "The damp air of the northern sea sometimes rusts the locks. Let us see if the metal has spoiled on the voyage."

Schuyler stepped forward with a heavy brass key, unlocked the double padlocks on the steel hasps, and threw back the oak lid.

Dropping toward the Marin headlands in a clear sunset blaze, the late afternoon sun struck directly into the open chest. Inside, packed without sawdust or shavings, lay twenty-four rough, unstamped bricks of dull, buttery yellow bullion, each the size of a mason’s hod-stone, covered to the brim with ten-pound drifts of coarse, water-worn Klondike nuggets that spilled over the oak lip and rattled down onto the granite flagstones at Elias’s boots.

Up on the gallery, the British Consul’s spyglass clicked shut. Forty European observers stood quiet along the rail above. Down on the deck of the *Sitka*, the steam-winch clanked and hissed, hauling the second chest, the third, and the tenth up out of the dark hold in a steady column of yellow iron.

Elias did not look up at the gallery. He bent down and picked up a single jagged nugget the size of a walnut from the stone by his toe. Across his palm he rolled the metal once; then he tossed it back into the chest with a heavy thud.

"Admiral Takashima," Elias said. He turned his head slightly toward the Japanese officer while the second iron truck came rumbling down the granite pier behind them.

"Protector," Takashima answered, his hand gripping the hilt of his naval dirk.

"The British Ambassador in St. Petersburg warned Baron Stoeckl in November that Her Majesty’s Government would never permit a single power to hold both sides of the North Pacific," Elias said. His pale eyes lifted toward the western sky, where the hulls of the First Armored Squadron rode at anchor off Alcatraz. "You will take the *Kamehameha*, the *Satsuma*, and the four new turret-ships out with the morning tide. Do not steam by the northern circle yet. Before we force the gates of Yedo, we must bolt down our own threshold in the mid-ocean."

Down at the end of the mole, the door of the dockyard signal-tower flew open. Major Sterling came running down the granite steps with his coat-tails flying in the salt wind. Before he had even reached the guard-line, he waved a wet yellow cable-dispatch from the Honolulu-Midway relay.

"Protector!" Sterling shouted. His boots skidded on the wet kelp by the crane-base as Marcus Vance stepped sharply forward to intercept him. "From the Consulate at Honolulu, relayed via the French packet! King Lot Kamehameha the Fifth has refused to renew the Pearl Lagoon dockyard lease without a vote of his Privy Council, the British frigate *Curaçoa* has dropped anchor inside the reef with four hundred Royal Marines, and the native royalists have seized the water-batteries at Punchbowl Hill to bar our colliers from the harbor!"

Elias took the damp slip from Sterling’s fingers without haste. For fourteen years, the Treaty of 1853 had left the Hawaiian monarchy an ornamental crown, a polite fiction of dual sovereignty designed to flatter the island chiefs while Pacifica’s engineers dredged their lagoons and conscripted their youth. Now the British China Squadron was probing the western approaches.

"Marshal Vance," Elias said. He folded the cablegram into a neat square. "Divert the *Kamehameha* and the First Atlantic Auxiliary Division from the northern run. Embark four batteries of street-artillery tonight. Since King Lot has forgotten whose iron keeps the French and the English out of his palace, you will sail to Oahu and remind him."

# Chapter 8: The Insular Act

Twelve days later, the morning trade wind coming down off the emerald ridges of the Ko’olau range carried the sweet, heavy fragrance of crushed ginger-blossom and drying copra over the warm coral brine of the reef, until before noon a greasy, low-hanging pall of Nanaimo coal-smoke fouled the air and stained the turquoise waters of Mamala Bay.

Lady Kaiulani stood alone upon the high stone *lanai* of the old harbour-customs house. Her hands rested motionless upon the sun-bleached teak rail. Five days ahead of the main battle-squadron, she had come home aboard the fast dispatch-steamer *Hilo* in the hope that she might persuade her royal cousin at Iolani Palace to open the lagoon gates before Marcus Vance’s turret-ships cleared Molokai channel. She had failed. Behind her, in the dusty palm-shaded streets of Honolulu, three thousand native retainers from the outer islands, men armed with old whaling-muskets and wooden shark-tooth clubs, were piling coral blocks across the intersections of King and Nu’uanu streets while they sang the ancient war-chants of Kamehameha the Great.

Out beyond the white line of the surf, where Cantonese divers had blasted the deep-water channel thirty feet through the living coral ten years before, the ironclads came in.

Seven monitors crept through the boiling foam of the reef-gap like iron sea-turtles. Painted a dull, leaden imperial blue from waterline to funnel-top, they carried decks stripped clear of bulwarks so that nothing showed above the Pacific swell save the massive, sloped cylinders of their twin gun-turrets and the armored conning-towers spitting jets of white waste-steam.

At the head of the column steamed the *Kamehameha*. Five thousand tons of California steel bore the stolen name of her own dynasty upon the stern in letters of cast brass. Behind the monitors steamed four immense, black-hulled screw-transports, their upper decks dark with the slate-gray uniforms of the Atlantic Free States Regiments, veteran troops from the slaughter-pens of Fredericksburg and Vicksburg who looked up at the green volcanic cliffs of Oahu as a redoubt to be carried by the bayonet.

"The British frigate is slipping her cable, Your Highness," said Keoni, her aged chamberlain. He stepped out onto the gallery with a brass telescope trembling in his spotted hands. "Captain Bowden-Smith signaled the Palace twenty minutes ago that he has no instructions from London to engage six-inch armor inside a closed reef. He is standing out to sea and leaving the King’s batteries to face the Marshal alone."

Kaiulani did not reach for the glass. Under the broad brim of her woven *lauhala* hat, the British warship scurried past Diamond Head under full steam and topsails like a gull fleeing a squall. For fourteen years she had walked the marble halls of Monterey and Sacramento; after writing the syncretic codes and dining with Elias’s generals, she had told herself that by bending like the reed before the mainland gale, she was preserving the blood and the sceptre of her people inside the belly of the whale.

At three hundred yards’ range, the lead monitor swung its twin fifteen-inch guns directly toward the coral parapet of Fort Kekuanohu.

"They call it protection in the dispatches, Keoni," she said. The trade wind lifted the black silk scarf at her throat as the first longboat dropped from the davits of the transport *Constitution*, packed gunwale-to-gunwale with Missouri and Pennsylvania riflemen whose bayonets flashed like needles in the tropical sun. "When we signed the first alliance in fifty-three, Elias promised my uncle that our flag would fly beside the rising sun on every masthead. Look at the main-truck of the *Kamehameha*."

The chamberlain raised his glass. Slowly he lowered it, his leathery brown cheek sagging. The eight stripes of the Hawaiian kingdom were gone from the yardarm; in their place flew only the solitary blue-and-gold standard of the Protectorate, and beneath it, the blood-red battle-pennant of the Provost-General.

"Go to the Palace by the back taro-paths, Keoni," Kaiulani commanded. She turned from the rail while the deep, brazen roar of the *Kamehameha*’s steam-siren echoed off the walls of Punchbowl crater and drowned the drums of the royalist militia in the square below. "Tell King Lot that if his gunners on the hill pull a single lanyard when those boats touch the wharf, there will not be a stone of his throne-room left standing by sunset. I am going down to the quay to meet General Vance before his Virginians set the thatch on fire."

***

Two thousand miles northeast of that smoking reef, in the high, cedar-vaulted cabinet room of the Citadel on Rincon Hill, heavy crimson curtains shut out the afternoon fog off the Golden Gate while anthracite coal crackled in a grate of polished Sierra black marble.

Elias stood before the great table of inlaid Hawaiian koa-wood. His broad back was turned to the four men sitting in the leather armchairs behind him: Chancellor Gwin, Cornelius Schuyler, and the two frightened envoys of the Honolulu Privy Council who had been detained at the Palace Hotel since the arrival of the first cipher. On the wall above the mantelpiece hung a newly finished hydrostatic chart of the Pacific Basin, ten feet square, upon which the draftsmen of the Naval Bureau had drawn thick crimson lines radiating outward from San Francisco like the web of an iron spider to Sitka and the Kuriles in the north, down to Guaymas and the Galapagos in the south, and dead center through the Sandwich Islands to the gates of Canton and Yedo.

"The treaty of fifty-three was a solemn compact between two sovereign crowns, Protector!" protested Judge Varigny, the French-born minister to King Lot. His pale forehead gleamed with sweat as he half-rose from his chair. "His Majesty merely asserted his ancient royal prerogative to audit the harbour-dues of Honolulu and regulate the quartering of foreign sailors! To declare the Kingdom an Imperial Prefecture by unilateral decree is an act of naked annexation that will outrage every court in Europe!"

Elias did not turn around. Up in the center of the chart, the small, ink-blackened cluster of the Hawaiian chain sat alone in two thousand leagues of blue paper.

"What is a sovereign crown, Monsieur Varigny?" Elias asked. His rough, low voice filled the quiet room without rising half a tone. "Can King Lot cast a twelve-inch gun? Can he roll a single plate of two-inch iron, or mine a ton of steam-coal to fill the bunkers of the ships that keep the French and the British from dividing his beaches like a melon?"

"He has the law of nations—" Varigny said.

"The law of nations is written by the men who hold the coaling-stations," Elias said. Turning from the hearth, he walked to the head of the koa table, where a single sheet of heavy vellum lay engrossed in the three imperial scripts with a broad cake of unpressed scarlet wax at its foot. "For fourteen years I have allowed Honolulu to play at being a court because Lady Kaiulani kept the lagoon open and the native regiments full. Last week, while my northern fleet was preparing to sail for Japan, your King listened to the British consul over a glass of port and closed my drydocks."

He placed both wide, weather-roughened palms flat upon the table and leaned forward until the Frenchman sank back into the leather cushions.

"A bridge across a chasm cannot have a toll-gate in the middle of the span where a drunken gatekeeper can drop the bar whenever London whistles," Elias said. "From this noon, the Polynesian Protectorate Act is the supreme statute of the sea. Every island and reef between the Tropic of Cancer and the Marquesas, from Kauai to Tutuila and the mid-ocean shoals, is incorporated forever into the Maritime Domain of Pacifica. Provided he signs the abdication of his military and customs prerogatives before Marshal Vance’s forty-eight hours expire, the King at Honolulu will retain his palace and his feather-cloaks, along with an annuity of one hundred thousand silver thalers from the sugar-tax. If he refuses, Thursday will find a provost-marshal in a stone fort on Oahu in place of a king."

Chancellor Gwin dipped the heavy gold pen into the inkwell and held it out. "And Lady Kaiulani, Protector? Her signature is absent from the draft, and her cousins sit in the house of nobles that you are abolishing."

Elias took the pen. His thumb paused on the engraved gold shaft. Beneath the wet spruce boughs at Sitka, her dark eyes had stayed fixed on him once, and she had warned him that men were no iron ore to be bolted together with hot rivets.

"Lady Kaiulani is a Princess of the Realm and High Commissioner of the Insular Courts," Elias said. Across the heavy vellum, down through the broad cake of red wax waiting at the foot of the three imperial scripts, he drove the steel nib in a firm, scratching stroke that left a wide black track of ink before he sank his heavy signet ring into the tallow. "She knows better than any man in this room that an empire has only one head. Wire the text to the Midway relay, Mr. Gwin. Tell Marshal Vance the Act is law; he has my leave to clear the streets."

***

In Honolulu, twenty minutes remained of the forty-eight hours. Pulverized coral dust choked Queen Street, mixed with the stink of hot whale-oil lubricant from the traction-engines and the sour sweat of men trapped between the mountain and the sea.

Fifty paces behind a barricade of overturned sugar-carts and coral blocks that the royalist retainers had thrown up across the entrance to the Palace square, General Marcus Vance sat his tall bay charger at the junction of the harbour road and Fort Street. His high-collared navy wool tunic was buttoned to the chin under the ninety-degree tropical glare. A white linen havelock hung from his peaked cap over his neck. All the way back to the stone wharves, where two six-barrel Gatling batteries on wide-tired iron carriages were trundled forward by Cantonese artillerymen, sixteen hundred lean, sun-blackened veterans of the First Atlantic Auxiliary from the Shenandoah and the Susquehanna stood in double files with their gray tunics dark at the armpits and their seven-shot Spencer carbines held at the hip.

Down from the banyan trees by the custom-house rode Lady Kaiulani on a lathered white mare. Coral-powder coated her green riding-habit to the knees. She reined in beside Marcus’s stirrup and seized the brass bit-rein of his bridle before his orderly could interpose.

"General Vance!" she cried. Down at the pier, the *Kamehameha*’s steam-pumps thumped a steady rhythm, while ahead of the horses three thousand islanders massed behind the coral wall beat their shark-tooth clubs against sheet-iron shields. "Hold your artillery for one hour! I have just come from the Palace basement. King Lot is weeping over his father’s bones, and the British consul has fled to the hills! The *Ali’i* will sign the customs lease if you will only march your white regiments back to the wharf and let my own Royal Guard police the square!"

Marcus looked at her with weary gray eyes. In his left gauntlet he held the decoded slip that had arrived off the *Hilo*’s wire-boat ten minutes before with Elias’s signature to the Pacific Island Act.

"It is no longer a question of a customs lease, Your Highness," Marcus said. His flat cadence cut right across the howling of the conch-shells from the native barricade. "The Protector signed the Insular Incorporation statute at San Francisco yesterday. There is no Kingdom of Hawaii. And I cannot wait an hour; the tide turns at four, and I have three colliers waiting outside the reef to coal the *Satsuma* for the Yokohama run. Every hour these streets are blocked costs the fleet forty tons of steam-coal."

"Those men behind the carts are my blood!" Kaiulani dug her fingers into his sleeve. Out in front of the lead Gatling piece stepped Colonel Mulligan, his single arm raising a brass speaking-trumpet toward the barricade. "They have old flintlocks and wooden spears, Marcus! If you open on them with machine-guns in this narrow lane, you will butcher five hundred men in three minutes and turn every island from here to Hawaii into a charnel-house of hate!"

"If I spend three minutes now, Your Highness, I save six months of bushwhacking in the sugar-canes later," Marcus replied. He lifted her gloved hand from his forearm and turned in his saddle toward the battery commander. "Amputation requires speed. Sergeant, take Her Highness’s bridle and lead her mount behind the custom-house wall."

Before the two Missouri troopers could close on her mare’s head, a tall warrior in a yellow feather helmet leaped onto the crest of the coral barricade eighty yards away. He brandished a brass-bound whaling lance and screamed a curse in the old tongue. Beside him, twenty rusty muskets poked through the sugar-cart wheels and belched a ragged cloud of dirty white smoke. Past Marcus’s ear hummed a lead ball that smashed a clay flowerpot on the veranda behind him; a second struck a Pennsylvania corporal in the throat and pitched him backward onto the crushed coral in a bright spray of arterial blood.

Marcus left his saber in its scabbard. Two fingers of his right hand rose, then dropped toward the barricade.

"Battery," Marcus said. "Clear the street. Two hundred rounds per piece, traverse from flank to flank, then advance the first battalion with the bayonet."

"Marcus, no—!"

Kaiulani spurred her rearing mare straight against the chests of the provost-guards. Colonel Mulligan dropped his arm. The two gun-captains threw their weight onto the iron cranks of the Gatlings. As the twin bronze clusters revolved and the first clattering roar of twelve hundred .58-caliber lead slugs tore down the palm-lined tunnel of Fort Street, splintering the wooden carts into flying toothpicks and scything the feathered line of islanders down like dry cane before a brush-hook, Marcus Vance consulted his timepiece by its gold chain. His thumb pressed the stem to measure the advance. Ahead of him, Colonel Mulligan’s veterans leveled their bayonets and stepped into the drifting smoke.

Three minutes. On the bronze trunnions, the whale-oil boiled. Behind the coral masonry of the custom-house, two Missouri privates hung onto the foaming bit of Kaiulani's mare until the mechanical clatter ceased and the single, ragged cheers of the Shenandoah and Susquehanna veterans rose over the splintered carts as they went in with eighteen inches of cold steel. Under the banyan trees, the tropical noon grew wet and heavy. Then came the cries. High, bubbling shrieks rose from boys from the Kona fishing-villages whose bellies had been opened by half-inch lead, answered by the sharp *pop-pop* of Spencer carbines settling the wounded in the hibiscus ditches.

Twenty minutes later, they led her between two files of bayonets across the trampled grass of the Palace yard. Blood from the Fort Street dust stiffened her green riding-skirt to the hem. On the wide stone steps of Iolani Palace, where a young chief from Maui whom she had danced with at the autumn *luau* lay doubled over an overturned brass spittoon with his yellow *mamo* feather cape soaked black between the shoulder-blades, a Virginia corporal calmly stripped the gold signet ring from the boy's stiffening finger.

Inside the throne room, rifle-butts had smashed open the tall Venetian shutters to let out the powder-reek. King Lot sat slumped in the carved koa-wood chair upon the dais. His broad Polynesian face was gray as pumice, his hands trembling upon his knees while four American engineers in muddy boots hammered a portable telegraph repeater directly into the mahogany wainscoting beside the royal coat of arms. On the center table, where the kahili standards of crimson bird-plumes had been thrown down like dirty brooms to clear the wood, lay the vellum sheet of the Insular Incorporation Act.

Marcus Vance stood at the foot of the dais. He had taken off his peaked cap. A dark line of sweat stained the band of his forehead, and dried white coral-lime spotted his right cuff.

"The King’s hand is too unsteady for the pen, Your Highness," Marcus said as Kaiulani walked across the blood-tracked matting. Leaving her to stand, he held out a steel-nibbed dip-pen whose brass barrel was still warm from the clerk’s fingers. "And since His Majesty’s signature alone might be contested by the outer island chiefs as given under duress, the Protector’s instructions from San Francisco are explicit. Your name goes beneath the royal seal as Regent-Guarantor of the Insular Courts. When the people of Kauai and Hawaii see the daughter of the Oahu line upon the proclamation, they will lay down their muskets."

Kaiulani stopped two paces from the table. Through the shattered louver of the eastern window came the rhythmic *chug-hiss* of the steam-excavators down at the reef-channel, dredging coral without pause through the three minutes of the slaughter, while closer at hand corpses thudded onto the beds of the military bullock-carts in the square.

"And if I break that pen across your face, Marshal Vance?" she asked. Her voice was dry and brittle as burned palm-thatch.

"Then Colonel Mulligan hangs the forty royalist nobles we took in the cellar from the breadfruit trees along King Street before the four o’clock tide," Marcus answered without a blink, his gray eyes steady as a balance-scale. "And tomorrow morning I send two regiments of the Atlantic Auxiliary over the Pali to burn every taro-patch and every fishing-canoe on the windward coast until the survivors come into the stockades to beg for salt pork. Do not mistake me for a cruel man, Your Highness. I have four thousand tons of coal to load before dark, and Rear-Admiral Takashima’s squadron clears for the Western Ocean in ten days. I have neither the time nor the rifle-cartridges to leave an unpacified island behind my rudder."

On the dais, King Lot raised his heavy, tear-streaked face.

"Sign it, cousin," the King whispered in the native tongue. His chin sank onto his gold-braided chest. "The gods of the volcano are dead. Their iron is too heavy for our bones."

Kaiulani looked down at the parchment. For fourteen years she had believed she sat at the bridle of the beast to guide its iron hooves away from her garden; now hot tallow reeked on its hide, and her own blood wet its teeth. Her fingers were cold as the arctic slush of Sitka. She took the brass pen from Marcus’s gauntlet. Skipping the Latin and the English clauses, she drove the steel point into the horn inkwell and wrote *Kaiulani* across the vellum in letters so sharp they tore the fibers of the sheepskin and scattered black droplets like buckshot across the seal of the rising sun.

"There is your coal, butcher," she said. She dropped the pen onto the table; it rolled off the edge and stuck point-first into the matting at Marcus’s boot. "May it choke your furnaces when you meet the English guns."

***

Nine days later, paint-blistered and reeking of scorched cylinder-tallow from a forced run against the northeast trades, the fast paddle-frigate *Hilo* backed her paddles inside the Golden Gate and ran out her gangplank at the private stairs of the Citadel wharf.

Elias waited for her alone in the high, glass-domed conservatory of the Palace on Mason Street. Outside, a cold, salt-heavy summer fog poured over the Marin hills like dirty wool across the late June afternoon, blotting out the sun until only the distant, booming groan of the steam-foghorns on Alcatraz and the iron *clink-clank* of the dockyard hammers down at Potrero Point reached the hill. Inside the glass dome, four furnace-flues kept the air at the wet, stifling heat of the tropics. Giant tree-ferns brought from the valleys of Hilo and orchids from the Mindanao jungles dripped condensation onto the tessellated marble pavement. The vault smelled of warm loam and wet leaves.

When the bronze doors at the end of the palm-walk opened and Kaiulani stepped across the threshold, she had left behind the green velvet of the Monterey court and the diamonds of the Washoe mines. She wore a plain, high-necked mourning gown of dull black bombazine, salt-stained at the hem from the deck of the steamer, and around her shoulders the crimson-and-yellow feather cape of the Kamehamehas. Down the left breast of the plumage ran a six-inch crust of dried, blackened blood from the palace steps where she had knelt beside the dying Maui boy.

Elias stood beside a granite basin. Gold-spotted carp from the Shogun’s gardens swam in the dark water. He wore his severe blue naval coat with his hands clasped behind his back, his short-cropped hair showing more iron than brown in the gray light filtering through the glass roof.

"You made the crossing in two hundred and ten hours," Elias said as the guards closed the doors behind her and left them alone among the dripping ferns. "Captain Sterling tells me the *Hilo* burned her spare main-topmast to keep the steam-gauge at forty pounds. I am glad you are here, Kaiulani. The Diet convenes at noon tomorrow to ratify the Insular Prefectures, and your chair beside the rostrum has been empty too long."

She walked down the marble flagway until only the stone rim of the carp-basin separated them. Beneath the hollow violet rings under her dark eyes, her spine was stiffer than the bayonet on a sentry’s rifle.

"Do you know whose blood this is upon the *mamo* feathers, Elias?" she asked, her low voice trembling like a taut wire. "It is Kalanimoku’s son. He was seventeen years old. He had an old whaling-lance with a wooden shaft in his hand, and your Virginians blew his chest open with a machine-gun on Fort Street while General Vance held his timepiece in his palm to see how long it took the carts to splinter."

Elias looked down at the dark stain on the yellow feathers. His weathered cheek remained still; his gray eyes were as flat and bottomless as the winter water of the Platte.

"He had a lance in his hand against my colors while a British frigate lay inside the reef waiting to seize my coal-bunkers," Elias said, his tone low and rough as quarry-stone. "If a boy of seventeen points a weapon at the column when the fleet is clearing for action, he dies like a man of forty. I told you on the Platte five years ago, Kaiulani: order is not a bargain. When King Lot closed the gates of Pearl Lagoon to please an English post-captain, he ceased to be a king and became a mutineer."

"He was a king before your grandfather built a log hut in Kentucky!" she cried. She struck the granite rim of the basin with her bare palm. "We gave you the islands when you had nothing but four leaky steamers and a wooden fort on the mud-flats! I wrote your laws! In Sacramento and Sitka I stood beside you and lied to my own blood, telling them that if we gave the American Caesar our harbors and our young men, he would shield our crown beneath his eagle! And the moment your vaults were full of Klondike gold and the Eastern states were in chains, you sent a pack of pardoned Rebel convicts to butcher my cousins in the dust and turn my homeland into a coal-bin!"

"Look at me, Kaiulani," Elias commanded.

He stepped around the stone basin and closed the distance between them until his broad naval shoulders blotted out the light from the conservatory dome. He stood within arm's reach, his tall shadow falling across her mourning bombazine in the wet heat.

"Do you think I brought you back from Oahu in nine days to hear a woman weep over a barricade?" he said. "In three weeks, Admiral Takashima and I meet the combined squadrons of Great Britain and France in the Straits of Shimonoseki. If we lose that battle, Lord Palmerston’s cruisers will be anchored off Honolulu before September, and they will not leave you a feather-cloak or a court-house. They will turn your islands into a sugar-plantation worked by coolies under an English factor’s whip, just as they did in Jamaica and Mauritius."

From the breast of his tunic he drew a heavy gold collar set with the Imperial seal of the Grand Council and held it between his rough, square-nailed hands.

"There can be no little kingdoms inside the hull of an ironclad," Elias said. "The Kingdom of Hawaii is dead because the world is too small for canoes. In its place stands the First Naval Prefecture of the Empire, and you are its High Imperial Advisor and Chancellor of the Insular Diet, second only to myself from the California coast to the China Sea. Four hundred royalist prisoners are sitting in the coral quarry at Oahu tonight under sentence of treason. Put this collar around your neck, walk into the Diet with me tomorrow noon to proclaim the Incorporation, and those four hundred men go back to their valleys with free pardons. Refuse me, and I will send instructions by the midnight cable for Colonel Mulligan to clear the quarry with the Gatlings at sunrise."

Kaiulani stared up at the iron-cast lines of his face. Behind him, through the misted glass of the dome, the Pacific surf beat against the Mile Rocks, and a brassy bugle called the evening watch at the Presidio. In their leather books, the court chroniclers called this providence: a steam-hammer that made you either the face of the die or the iron crushed beneath it.

Her chin lifted half an inch. Her dark eyes were as cold as the volcanic glass of Mauna Loa.

"Give me the collar, Protector," she said, her voice ringing like hollow steel. "And wire your butcher in Honolulu to unlock the quarry gates tonight. I will sit beside your throne tomorrow, and I will live long enough to see what happens when your boiler bursts."

***

To the Chronicler who sails into the great land-locked basin of Pu’uloa, which the Americans call Pearl Lagoon, in the summers following the Act of Incorporation, the ancient pastoral paradise described by Captain Cook and the early Boston missionaries is as remote as the gardens of the Hesperides. Where the outrigger canoes of the *Ali’i* once glided over clear coral shallows in pursuit of the mullet, and the green taro-terraces stepped gently down from the mist-veiled clefts of the Waianae mountains, the great harbor now smokes at the hub of the Great Arena.

Geography, when wedded to the steam-engine of Imperial necessity, permits no sentiment. Because the islands of Oahu and Maui sit at the exact mathematical focus of the northern ocean, two thousand miles from the Golden Gate and four thousand from the gates of Canton, the garden was paved with iron. By the autumn of the Incorporation year, Cantonese helmet-divers had lowered forty-ton charges of nitro-glycerine into the surf and shattered the coral reef that had barred the entrance to the inner lagoons for ten millennia. Through a straight, vertical-walled canal forty feet deep and three hundred yards wide, lined on either side with casemated batteries of fifteen-inch Rodman and Krupp guns cast at the San Francisco works, the largest armored battleships of the Pacifica Navy now steam at full speed in any weather to lie secure behind the volcanic ramparts of the island.

From the red-earth heights of Punchbowl Hill at noon, the syncretic machinery of Elias Thorne’s dominion operates at full pressure. Below, along six miles of newly dredged stone quays where the coco-palms have been felled to make room for traveling hydraulic gantry-cranes, thirty colliers from Vancouver and the Kenai mines unload mountains of gleaming black anthracite into iron hopper-cars drawn by small, whistling geared locomotives. Salt spray, hot cylinder-tallow, wet coal-dust, and the biting sulfur of the vulcanizing sheds sting the nostrils. Down in the three vast graving-docks hewn out of the living basalt at Waipio Peninsula, four thousand laborers work in three eight-hour relays under the glare of calcium lime-lights that turn the tropical night into a ghastly, shadowless noon: Hawaiian royal guardsmen in navy-blue tunics stand sentry on the catwalks above gangs of former Confederate prisoners of war from Georgia and Alabama, who swing twenty-pound sledges alongside bare-chested Cantonese riveters and taciturn Satsuma master-machinists. Even the hills above the harbor have been recast in the image of the

new order. Upon the upper slopes of Nu’uanu, where the wind roars down through the Pali gap, geometric rows of corrugated-iron barracks and brick ordnance magazines have replaced the thatched grass houses of the native villagers. Over them all presides the four-story bulk of the Insular Admiralty: its lower colonnades are hewn from grey Honolulu coral block in the severe American style, while its upper stories rise in the sweeping, red-lacquered timber galleries of a Japanese castle, surmounted by tall semaphore-masts and humming copper telegraph wires that carry the Protector’s will from the submarine cable-house at Waikiki to the uttermost shoals of Midway and the Bonins. Here, in the mid-ocean clearing-house of empire, a regiment of Missouri cavalrymen disembarks from a San Francisco paddle-steamer to stretch their horses’ legs on the parade-ground beside a battalion of Bakufu samurai infantry drilling with seven-shot Spencer rifles; here, the silver thaler with the sun and anchor buys rice from Saigon and salt beef from the Illinois protectorate Alongside casks of whale-oil from the Okhotsk sea. Five hundred square miles in beam, the stationary ironclad sits anchored at the center of the globe to coal the squadrons that rule the water.

# Chapter 9: Manila

Before the British and French admirals off Shimonoseki could even test that northern lock, thirty-six thousand tons of Pacifica armor steamed westward from Pearl Lagoon. Six thousand leagues from Portsmouth, the European commanders weighed the cost of an ocean war against that mathematical certainty and quietly hauled down their battle-pennants to sign the Convention of Nagasaki. The Royal Navy yielded the northern passage without firing a broadside. Still, the southern buttress of the arch rested in foreign hands.

On the twelfth of October, inside the high press-room of the *Imperial Gazette* on Montgomery Street in San Francisco, the air was hot and thick with the reek of boiled linseed-oil ink, damp rag-paper, and the sour tallow of the four-cylinder Hoe rotary presses thumping beneath the floorboards.

Elias stood beside the composing-stone in his plain dark wool tunic, his hands clasped behind his spine. Beside him, a hunchbacked former printer from the *New York Tribune* named Horace held a pair of brass tweezers poised above the lead formes. Across the zinc-topped table, where Lady Kaiulani stood in the black bombazine mourning-dress she had sworn to wear so long as a single Virginia soldier walked the streets of Honolulu, Cornelius Schuyler gripped a wet, freshly pulled proof-sheet between his plump fingers.

"Read the headline again, Mr. Schuyler," Elias said.

Schuyler cleared his throat. Outside the tall ink-stained windows, where chalked bulletin-boards stood in the afternoon drizzle along Market Street, three thousand dock-workers and discharged soldiers were already gathering. "*'SPANISH TREACHERY IN THE MARIANAS! The Pacifica Survey-Corvette* San Joaquin *Blown Up at Anchor in Apra Harbor! Two Hundred American and Hawaiian Seamen Murdered by a Submarine Mine Laid by Order of the Captain-General at Manila!'*"

Schuyler lowered the damp paper. He wiped a smear of black printer’s ink from his thumb with his cambric handkerchief. "Protector, the cable from Captain Takashima on the *Hilo* reached my marine insurance desk in cipher two hours ago. The *San Joaquin* was a thirty-year-old wooden collier that we condemned for dry-rot in August. Her forward boiler burst because her chief engineer had been instructed to tie down the safety-valve after the crew was rowed ashore in the dark. Four Cantonese stokers failed to reach the jolly-boat in time, leaving only them and a cargo of condemned mule-harness aboard. The Spanish Governor at Guam lacked a single pound of blasting-powder in his magazine; he sent his own launch out to pick our swimmers off the reef!"

"A boiler explosion in an old wooden tub is an insurance claim, Mr. Schuyler." Walking to the edge of the composing-stone, Elias picked up a heavy three-inch lead woodcut engraved with a lurid scene of Spanish priests and musketeers firing from a stone fort upon drowning sailors in the surf. "A submarine mine is an act of war."

From the shadow of the tall type-racks, Lady Kaiulani spoke. Since the day she had put on the gold collar of the Insular Diet, she had administered his maritime courts from the bench beside him.

"And why must we have an act of war against Madrid this week, Elias?" she asked. At the sound of her clear voice, the typesetter stepped back from the stone. "The Queen of Spain is a bankrupt woman sitting in a palace of dusty velvet. Her garrison at Guam consists of sixty half-caste militiamen whose muskets have no flints, and her frigates at Cavite have not been careened since the year fifty-eight. If you want the Philippines and the Ladrones for coaling-stations to flank the British at Hong Kong, why not send Marshal Vance to take them as you took Honolulu? Why play the theater-manager for the San Francisco rabble with four dead Chinamen and a lie printed in two-inch type?"

Elias turned his head toward her. The gas-jet above the stone lit the deep, weathered lines around his mouth and the heavy iron-gray at his temples.

"Because the fifty thousand men I am shipping across the ocean on Monday are the sweepings of the Atlantic Free States, Kaiulani, rather than your islanders or my old Texas rangers," Elias said. "After spending four years trying to bayonet each other across a stone wall, those men from Pennsylvania and Massachusetts and Georgia still spit in the street when my Hawaiian provosts walk past. If I order them to board a transport to conquer a coal-harbor for the Crown of Pacifica, half of them will mutiny at the gangplank. Give them a Christian atrocity committed by a Catholic king, tell them that Spanish dons have blown up the flag in the night, and those same Yankees and Rebels will fight each other for the privilege of carrying the first scaling-ladder up the walls of Manila."

He set the woodcut down squarely in the center of the lead page-frame. It struck with a sharp *clack*.

"Lock the forme, Horace," Elias ordered the printer. "Run off a hundred thousand extras on yellow paper so the ink shows through the rain, and give them to the boys to cry through the Irish wards and the military barracks free of charge. At eight o’clock tonight, when the bonfires are lit in Portsmouth Square, I will go down to the balcony of the Customs House and sign the Declaration of Maritime Reprisal against the Crown of Spain."

***

Eighteen days after the yellow sheets went flying through the wet streets of San Francisco, the sun rose out of the Philippine Sea like a cannonball heated white in a forge. Outside the coral barrier of Apra Harbor, the long, oily swells gleamed like blinding sheets of molten brass.

General Marcus Vance stood in the armored conning-tower of the fast fleet-ram *Monterey*, his field-glasses braced against the salted iron rim of the vision-slit. Inside the turret-house, the brass thermometer bolted to the bulkhead read ninety-eight degrees. The air was thick with the stench of hot mineral oil from the hydraulic turret-gears and bilge-water, soured by the sweat of six signalmen crammed around the speaking-tubes.

Ahead of the squadron’s bows, across half a mile of emerald-green lagoon where the charred, half-submerged ribs of the scuttled *San Joaquin* still poked above the coral heads like the backbone of a dead whale, lay the Spanish citadel of Santa Cruz and the low, whitewashed stone ramparts of Piti landing. The tropical dawn steamed. Above the coconut palms, the red-and-gold banner of Castile hung motionless.

"The Spanish battery at Point Orote stands empty, Marshal," said Rear-Admiral Takashima. He lowered his glass as the *Monterey*'s twin screws slowed to dead-slow, her wake washing in milky foam over the sunken coral shelf. "Four artillerymen in straw hats are leading a yoke of water-buffalo down to the beach with water-casks, and an officer in white linen is sitting under an umbrella on the quay. Our scouts cut their submarine cable from Manila on Tuesday; they are still ignorant that Madrid and San Francisco are at war."

"They will know it in four minutes," Marcus replied. Opening his waterproofed leather notebook, he checked the tide-tables for the inner lagoon. "We are here to test whether three regiments of the Atlantic Auxiliary Corps can be put ashore from self-propelled iron landing-barges under covering fire in less than twenty-two minutes, Admiral, rather than fight a duel with sixty sleep-walking Spaniards. If the timetable fails here, it will fail before the Krupp batteries that the British have secretly sold to the Captain-General at Cavite. Signal the *Oregon* to drop her bow-ramps."

Behind the *Monterey*, two immense, flat-bottomed iron troop-ships built on the slips of New Osaka for Elias’s insular doctrine swung their square, box-like bows directly toward the coral shoals. Wooden whaleboats stayed on their davits. Instead, while the troop-ships' stern-wheels churned the turquoise water into boiling froth, four forty-foot steel lighters slid out of flooded well-decks in their bellies, each barge driven by a high-pressure donkey-engine burning rock-oil and shielded in front by a sloped, half-inch steel breastwork loopholed for twin Gatling guns.

Inside the first two barges stood the Second Virginia Regiment of the Atlantic Auxiliary; in the third and fourth stood the Fourteenth Massachusetts. Thirty months ago, these men had torn each other’s throats out in the Bloody Angle at Spotsylvania. Now they wore the identical blue-and-slate canvas fatigue jackets of the Pacifica Marine Line, their faces greased against the tropical sun and their thumbs hooked over the hammers of seven-shot Spencer repeaters.

Down on the stone mole at Piti, the Spanish captain under the umbrella stood up. He shaded his eyes with his hand as the four smoking iron boxes came chugging across the reef-flat at eight knots. From the courtyard of the fort, where a brass bugle warbled a cracked alarm, ten barefoot native *artilleros* came running out of the guardhouse to pry the wooden tompions from the muzzles of two ancient bronze twenty-four-pounders cast in Seville in the reign of Charles the Third.

"Range seven hundred yards to the masonry parapet," Marcus said into the brass tube by his chin. "One round of picric-acid shell from the forward eight-inch rifles. Hold the second volley; let the barges take the wharf on the smoke."

The twin rifles in the *Monterey*'s bow-turret slammed back on their hydraulic recoil-slides. The double thunderclap flattened the sea into white rings for fifty yards around the hull and sent ten thousand white sea-birds screaming up from the mangroves of the Orote cliffs.

Three seconds later, the center of the Spanish water-battery vanished in a towering, dirty-yellow pillar of pulverized coral limestone and shattered coconut logs, tossing the bronze gun-barrels end over end. Stones splashed back into the lagoon. Twenty yards below the smoking breach, the iron prows of the four self-propelled barges grounded with a harsh screech upon the gravel beach.
