Steam-winches hissed; the armored bow-ramps dropped flat into the three-foot surf like drawbridges; and six hundred Virginians and New Englanders poured out into the warm, waist-deep water in a single disciplined wave, their rifles silent and their eighteen-inch trowel-bayonets leveled at the hip as they raced up the shattered masonry slope side by side.

The blue-and-slate line crested the ruined parapet and hauled down the red-and-gold rag of Spain while the black smoke of the picric shell still hung in the palm-tops.

"Seventeen minutes and forty seconds from the drop of the well-gates," Marcus said. He closed his ledger and handed his field-glasses to his orderly. "The Virginia battalion was thirty seconds slow clearing the starboard ramp because their colonel stopped to form company fronts on the wet sand. Have Colonel Armistead report to my cabin when we re-embark at noon; tell him that in the Pacifica service, a man who halts on a beach to dress his ranks will be reduced to the commissary wagons. Admiral, leave two companies of Hawaiian garrison police to hold the coal-hulks, and set course for the Bernardino Strait at four. The timetable for Luzon begins on the first of November."

***

By the twenty-second of November, the winter rains had come early to the coast of northern California. A weeping curtain of cold gray mist wrapped the high granite towers of the Citadel on Rincon Hill, carrying the smell of wet redwood bark and the bitter coal-smoke beaten downward from the foundry stacks of the Mission.

Inside the high-arched Map Room on the fourth floor of the Chancery, coal grates kept the air dry and warm. Across the entire thirty-foot length of the western wall, from Monterey to Honolulu, from Honolulu to Midway and Guam, and from Sitka down the volcanic chain of the Kuriles to the locked gates of Edo and the mouth of the Pearl River, stretched a newly completed relief-chart of the Great Arena, cast in solid plates of bronze and inlaid with silver wire to mark the submarine cables beneath the sea.

Elias stood on the narrow iron gallery before the bronze wall, a brass-mounted magnifying glass in his left hand. At forty-one, the years since he had ridden out from the ashes of his father’s cabin in Kentucky had hollowed out the flesh beneath his cheekbones. His jaw sat like an axe-head wedged into the high collar of his dark wool coat.

Below him, around the green baize council-table, sat his ministers: Cornelius Schuyler with his portfolio of Eastern customs receipts; Lord Shimazu of the Satsuma mission; Major Sterling, now Director of the Imperial Telegraphs; and at the far end of the mahogany, sitting upright and motionless in her black bombazine mourning-gown beneath the gas-chandelier, Lady Kaiulani.

The side door from the wire-room clicked open. A young Japanese signal-lieutenant in the dark blue uniform of the Cable Corps marched across the parquet floor, bowed twice from the waist before the gallery stairs, and handed a decoded blue tissue slip up to Major Sterling.

Sterling adjusted his spectacles. A flush crept up his lean Pennsylvanian cheeks. He read the lines aloud into the hush of the vaulted room.

"From Marshal Vance, headquarters aboard the flagship *Kamehameha*, anchored off the Pasig River mouth, Manila Bay, relayed via the Guam cable and Honolulu at six o’clock this evening!" Sterling’s voice rang against the bronze plates of the map. "*'The Spanish squadron of Rear-Admiral Montojo, seven wooden screw-frigates and two iron gunboats, was destroyed at anchor behind the Cavite arsenal at daybreak on the twentieth by our armored division without the loss of a single life aboard the Protectorate fleet. Our ten-inch rifles opened at four thousand yards, firing over the sand-spit; within ninety minutes the Spanish flagship* Reina Cristina *was burned to the water-line and the shore batteries silenced. At noon yesterday, the First and Second Divisions of the Atlantic Auxiliary Corps, supported by the Satsuma Marine Brigade, carried the southern walls of the Intramuros by storm after the railway-mortars breached the Real Gate. Captain-General Jaudenes signed the unconditional capitulation of the Philippine Archipelago at four this afternoon. The sun-and-anchor flies over Fort Santiago, and four thousand Spanish regulars are marching into the stockades.'*"

Around the long table, the American and Japanese councillors rose to their feet with a deep-throated murmur. Cornelius Schuyler slapped his fat palm down upon his leather ledger.

"God be praised, Protector!" Schuyler cried, looking up at the iron gallery. "Six hundred miles from the coast of China, and ten million new subjects added to the poll-tax rolls in a single morning! With Manila in our fist and Sitka on the north, the British at Hong Kong are caught between the jaws of a vise! There is not an ocean on this planet that can show a sail to match us!"

Elias’s mouth remained flat. He walked slowly along the iron grating of the gallery until he stood before the lower left quadrant of the bronze map, where the sculpted brass islands of Luzon and Mindanao jutted down toward Borneo and the Malay Strait at the outer rim of the seven-thousand-mile basin he had first surveyed from the snowy crest of the Sierra Nevada twenty-three years before.

From the tray beside the rail, he took a small magnetic marker of gilded iron shaped like the rising sun over an anchor and clapped it down upon the bronze indentation of Manila Bay. The magnet bit against the metal wall with a sharp *clink*.

Down at the end of the table, Lady Kaiulani kept her seat. Her dark eyes stayed on the small gold token gleaming on the bronze coast of Asia, and when the murmur of the councillors subsided, her voice rose clear and low through the room.

"The wheel is full circle, Elias," she said. Her slender, ivory-ringed fingers rested upon the edge of the mahogany. "Twenty-three years ago you rode over the mountains with two mules and a rusty rifle because the men in Washington tried to rule a country three thousand miles away with a piece of parchment and a bailiff’s horse. Look at your wall tonight. From the customs-house in Boston to the gates of Manila is ten thousand miles of salt water and iron rail. You have three hundred regiments standing guard over sixty million souls who speak twelve tongues and pray to six different gods, and every one of them waits for a wire from this room before he dares to bake a loaf of bread."

Elias looked down from the gallery rail. The yellow light of the gas-globes gleamed off the silver threads in his short-cropped hair and the deep crease between his brows.

"The men in Washington ruled with lawyers’ ink and fifty-page speeches, Kaiulani," Elias said, his words dropping into the quiet room like blocks of dressed granite. "I rule with six-inch compound armor and a silver coin that weighs the same in Manila as it does in Baltimore. Width never breaks an empire; softness at the center breaks it, when the men at the table let the provinces argue with the axle."

He turned from the bronze map and descended the narrow spiral of the iron gallery stairs. His heavy cavalry boots rang *clang, clang* against the cast-iron treads while the councillors below bowed their heads.

"Mr. Schuyler," Elias said as his boot touched the parquet floor, walking without a pause toward the head of the table where the blank vellum sheets of the winter decrees lay beside the red wax taper, "you will draft the Organic Act for the Prefecture of Luzon before you sleep tonight. The Spanish friars’ lands are confiscated to the Crown Naval Reserve; the customs tariff at Manila is fixed at twenty percent in silver thalers, with a complete drawback for goods carried in Pacifica bottoms; and you will notify the British governor at Hong Kong through our consul at Canton that from the first of January, all foreign warships entering the South China Sea north of the tenth parallel will register their coal-manifests with Admiral Takashima’s flag-captain at Cavite—"

His square, weather-beaten hand had just touched the heavy gold dip-pen in its stand when the double mahogany doors at the rear of the Map Room flew open without a knock. Colonel Caleb Vance strode straight past the startled Hawaiian sentries. November rain soaked his white beard; mud from a hard gallop up the hill from the Oakland ferry-slip splashed his dark blue reserve uniform to the belt; a drawn Colt revolver filled his left fist and a blood-stained leather dispatch-bag swung from his right.

"Clear the room of the clerks, Elias!" the old frontier veteran barked. He slammed the bloody leather pouch down directly on top of the wet Manila cablegram. "The Spanish minister from Washington didn't wait for the winter packet. He came over the Sierra on the mail-car with two French priests and a trunk full of royal seals, and some bushwhacking son of a bitch from the Sacramento Irish wards tried to put a knife in his ribs on the ferry-apron!"

Elias left his own pistol in its holster. He looked down at the dark crimson smear drying on the salted calfskin of the pouch, and then up at Caleb’s heaving chest.

"Did the Spaniard live?" Elias asked.

"Live? He’s sitting in your anteroom downstairs drinking brandy out of a tin dipper and shaking like a wet dog," Caleb grunted. He holstered his revolver and wiped the rain from his forehead with the back of his sleeve. "He says the Queen in Madrid has dismissed her cabinet, the mob is tearing up the cobbles in the Puerta del Sol, and he has full powers from the Escorial to buy back the friars’ estates before Marshal Vance hangs the Archbishop of Manila."

***

To the Chronicler who contemplates the demise of the older maritime thrones of Europe, a melancholy grandeur attends the spectacle of Madrid during that black December of 1867. Three centuries had elapsed since the galleons of Philip the Second had turned the Pacific into a Castilian lake and carried the silver of Potosí to the counting-houses of Acapulco and Manila under the shadow of the True Cross. Yet an empire built upon bullion-fleets and papal bulls is merely a crustacean shell. Two hundred years of sloth had shriveled the living meat inside.

The news of Cavite bypassed the slow courier-ships of the old Indies Council. Relayed from Hong Kong through the British wires at Suez and Malta in twelve hours, the dispatch leaped out of the brass telegraph instruments at the Ministry of Marine like an electric viper.

Outside the gray granite facade of the Royal Palace, a bitter Guadarrama wind swept down across the treeless plateau of New Castile, rattled the bare chestnuts of the Prado, and drove sleet into the faces of ten thousand citizens packed around the iron railings of the Plaza de Oriente. The drums stayed silent. The railway stations stood empty of the volunteers who had marched when Napoleon’s marshals crossed the Pyrenees. A vast stupor held the crowd, like the numbness of an ancient gentleman who wakes at midnight to find that a creditor he had considered a barbarian herdsman has kicked down his garden gate and seized his ancestral tapestries.

Inside the Hall of Mirrors, where the portraits of Charles the Fifth and Velázquez’s captains looked down through a blue haze of brazier-smoke and damp wool, Queen Isabella the Second wept into a lace handkerchief while the aged Duke of Valencia, Marshal Narváez, stood beside the gilded console table with the British Ambassador’s note of refusal open in his crippled fingers.

"Lord Stanley will not move a single gunboat from Singapore, Your Majesty," Narváez said. An asthmatic wheeze rattled beneath his gold-embroidered fleece. "And the Emperor Napoleon in Paris sends his regrets through the wire. With the Prussian armies massed upon the Rhine and four hundred thousand American veterans drilling under the rising-sun standard from Boston to New Orleans, France cannot risk a war in the Pacific to save the Augustinian monasteries of Luzon."

"They are pirates!" The Queen's fat, jeweled hands struck the velvet arms of the throne. "Heretics and savages who have armed the heathens of Japan with rifled cannon! We have forty thousand troops in Cuba! We have the *Numancia* at Cádiz! Let Admiral Méndez Núñez steam around the Horn and burn this San Francisco to the water!"

The Minister of Marine, an old sailor who had inspected the compound-engine monitors of the Protectorate during his embassy to Vera Cruz, bowed his silver head until his chin touched his stock.

"Majesty," the Admiral said, "if the *Numancia* steamed around Cape Horn tomorrow, there is not a Spanish port between Valparaiso and Manila where she could buy a basket of coal that is not guarded by Thorne’s lancers or leased to his Honolulu syndicate. Her boilers would go cold before she reached the equator, and the ironclads that Marshal Vance has anchored off the Pasig carry fifteen-inch steel rifles that can pierce our wrought-iron plates at two miles’ distance. The ocean is closed to us. The eighteenth century ended on the twentieth of November; if we do not instruct the Marquis de la Habana at San Francisco to sign whatever parchment the Providentor lays before him this week, Vance’s cruisers will be off Havana before Easter, and we shall lose the Antilles as well."

***

Seven thousand miles from the gilded mirrors of Madrid, the twentieth of November had given way to the steaming, rot-heavy December of the Luzon lowlands. Sinking seven wooden frigates, General Marcus Vance had found, was a simpler matter than governing a jungle.

He rode at the head of a column of the Second Virginia Auxiliary along the flooded dike-road five miles south of Cavite, where the deep green wall of the bamboo brakes and nipa palms pressed in upon the narrow causeway. Rain had ceased an hour after dawn. The ninety-five-degree air hung in a wet, blinding greenhouse mist that reeked of stagnant paddy-mud, rotting water-buffalo hides, crushed betel-nut, and the pungent woodsmoke of burning thatch.

Two hundred yards ahead, at the stone bridge crossing the Imus River, a company of Satsuma Marine pioneers dragged the bloated corpses of four Missouri telegraph-linemen out of the ditch where they had been ambushed the night before. Spanish regulars sat quietly behind the barbed-wire stockades on the Luneta, eating Pacifica hardtack and playing cards. Heavy *bolo* knives had hacked these four linemen to pieces. Their killers were the native Tagalog *insurrectos* of Emilio Aguinaldo’s grandfather, men who had risen against the Spanish friars the moment the *Kamehameha*’s guns broke the walls of Intramuros, and who had imagined that the dark-blue soldiers from California had come across the sea to hand them a republic.

"They cut down two miles of copper wire between the convent and the river-landing, Marshal," reported Colonel Armistead. He reined his sweating Philippine pony beside Marcus’s stirrup. Mud and green slime stained the old Virginian’s slate-gray tunic to the pockets, and a fresh bolo-slash had taken the tip off his left ear during the night’s skirmish in the cane-fields. "And when my patrols went into the *barrio* behind the church to look for the wire-spools, the village headman swore by the Virgin that every man in the huts was a peaceful fisherman, while our boots stood in fresh cartridge-paper and three of my corporals took buckshot from a bamboo thicket fifty yards away. You can’t tell a soldier from a farmer in this brush, sir. They wear no uniforms; they throw their knives in the mud-puddle and pick up a hoe the minute our bugles sound."

Four mutilated linemen lay on the wet stone parapet of the bridge. Beyond them, across the emerald expanse of the rice-paddies, a hundred native women and barefoot men in white cotton shirts stood in the shade of the mango trees beside the tin roof of the village church half a mile away.

Marcus’s gaunt, malaria-yellowed face remained still. Anger belonged to amateurs who treated war as a passion play. To Marcus, guerrilla warfare in the tropics was an algebraic equation in which an enemy hid a small fraction of rifles inside a large denominator of population. One simply reduced the denominator.

"How many yards of wire are missing, Colonel?" Marcus pulled his damp leather field-ledger from his saddle-holster and rested it on his pommel.

"Eight hundred yards of number-nine galvanized, sir," Armistead answered.

"That is sixteen hundred minutes of interrupted communication between the fleet anchorage and the southern outposts," Marcus said, his pencil moving across the page. "We will not chase men with big knives through bamboo swamps in ninety-degree heat, Colonel. A Virginian or a Pennsylvanian costs the Treasury four hundred thalers to train and transport six thousand miles; a Tagalog bushwhacker costs nothing. Unlimber the two twelve-pounder mountain howitzers on the bridge, and bring up the rock-oil wagons from the rear guard."

Armistead glanced toward the mango grove. "The women and young ones are still in the *barrio*, General."

"They have legs." Marcus did not look up from his ledger. "Give the church bell three strokes with a rifle-butt. Every soul who walks out onto the stone road between here and the bridge within ten minutes with empty hands will be marched down to the Cavite drydocks and indentured to the coaling-gangs for five years to pay for the wire. At the eleventh minute, put four rounds of canister through the bamboo huts, pump two hundred gallons of Santa Paula rock-oil over the thatch, and burn every structure and rice-granary and fishing-proa within one league of the broken poles. Then take ten men from the village roster, one for every eighty yards of stolen copper, and hang them from the cross-arms of the new telegraph posts before noon."

He slapped the ledger shut and tucked the pencil into its loop.

"Publish the order in Spanish and Tagalog on every church door between Manila and Batangas tonight," Marcus said. He turned his horse’s head back toward the smoking funnels of the fleet above the palms of the bay. "For every imperial soldier killed from the brush, the nearest village within two miles of the body ceases to exist, its rice-lands go to the Satsuma military colonists, and its adult males go to the Mindanao sulfur-mines for life. The Spaniards took three hundred years to convert a parish, Colonel. I have orders from the Protector to release four regiments from this island by February for the Canton demonstration, and by the first of January a child will carry a sack of silver from Cavite to Aparri without losing a thaler."

***

On the twenty-ninth of December, while a solid wall of Pacific rain beat against the western casements and hid the winter sun, four massive chandeliers of polished brass burned refined whale-oil in the great oval Council Chamber on the second floor of the San Francisco Citadel, shedding a hard, shadowless yellow light over the green baize table.

At the center of the table, flanked by two trembling secretaries from the Madrid Foreign Office and a pair of black-robed Dominican procurators who had come up from Manila under parole, sat Don José Gutiérrez de la Concha, Marquis of Havana and Plenipotentiary of Her Catholic Majesty. Six days on the trans-continental snow-trains had wrinkled his court uniform of dark blue cloth and scarlet cuffs. The bandage where the Irish assassin’s knife had grazed his ribs beneath his shoulder-blade held him stiffly upright, like a wooden saint carried in a Good Friday procession.

Opposite him, Elias stood before the roaring redwood fire on the hearth, his broad shoulders framed against the carved stone mantel where the fasces of the Confederation were chiseled into the gray Sierra granite. To his right sat Lady Kaiulani in her black mourning silk, a stack of Pacific hydrographic charts open before her; to his left sat Cornelius Schuyler, his gold-rimmed spectacles perched upon his nose as he totaled a column of figures on a sheet of blue foolscap.

"Two million silver thalers in cash, Señor Protector?" The Marquis of Havana looked down at the draft treaty that Schuyler had pushed across the baize, his thin nostrils flaring. "You ask the Crown of Spain to cede the entire Philippine Archipelago, the Carolines, the Pelew Islands, and the Marianas, the patrimony of Magellan and Legazpi, containing nine million Christian souls and the richest tobacco and hemp lands in the Orient, for the price of a single sugar-plantation in Matanzas? Why, the stone forts of Cavite and the cathedral plate of Manila alone are worth twenty millions!"

"The forts of Cavite are piles of rubble, Marquis," Elias said. He kept his voice level. "And the nine million souls were cutting the throats of your priests before my marines landed on the beach. My soldiers have already taken the islands from Her Catholic Majesty with blood and iron. The two million thalers is a charitable contribution to pay the passage of your four thousand captive soldiers back to Cádiz so they do not starve in my stockades."

The older of the two Dominican friars leaned forward. His tonsured skull gleamed wetly under the lamps, and his rosary rattled against the edge of the table. "And the endowments of the Religious Orders, Excellency! For three hundred years the Augustinians and the Dominicans have held the titles to the estates of Cavite and Laguna under the royal seal! By the law of Christendom, private property cannot be confiscated by a conqueror!"

"Your orders held those lands on the condition that you kept the peace for Madrid," Elias replied. He stepped away from the fire and walked to the edge of the table. "You failed. A landlord who cannot keep his tenants from shooting my telegraph-linemen has forfeited his deed. Every acre of church land in the islands goes into the Imperial Naval Reserve to pay for the dredging of Subic Bay and the settlement of my veterans. Your friars may remain in their parish churches and say their Latin masses so long as they preach obedience to the Provost-General at Manila. The first priest who reads a pastoral letter from Rome or Madrid without my censor’s stamp on the margin will be put aboard a timber-brig for Sitka in his cassock."

The Marquis of Havana’s pale hand shook as he picked up the last page of the protocol. "There is an error in the sixth clause, sir. Your clerks have included the harbor of Pago Pago and the eastern islands of the Samoan group, what your whalers call the Navigators’ Islands, together with the German and British copra-stations at Apia. Spain has no garrison in Samoa. Our seventeenth-century claim to those reefs has been dormant for two hundred years! If I sign a quit-claim ceding the Samoan littoral to Pacifica, Lord Stanley in London and Count Bismarck in Berlin will protest that Madrid is giving away what she does not own!"

Beside the charts, Lady Kaiulani raised her dark eyes. For the first time in three months, a faint smile touched her mouth as she tapped the southern triangle of the map with her ivory pencil.

"Spain discovered the islands under Queirós in the year sixteen hundred and six, Excellency," Kaiulani said, her voice as smooth as oiled steel. "The fact that your navigators were too lazy to build a lighthouse at Pago Pago does not extinguish the prior right of the Iberian Crown when transferred to a successor who has the ironclads to enforce it. With Honolulu in the north and Manila in the west, the land-locked crater of Tutuila in the south closes the triangle of the ocean. The British packets from Sydney to Panama will steam through a Pacifica canal, or they will not steam at all."

Elias reached down. He took the heavy gold pen from beside Schuyler’s inkwell and held it out across the green baize toward the Spanish ambassador’s bandaged chest.

"Let Count Bismarck send his protest to my harbour-master at Apia when the *Satsuma* drops anchor there next month," Elias said. Rain hammered the tall glass behind them while he held the Spaniard’s watering gaze. "You have until the clock on that mantel strikes five, Marquis. Sign the parchment, and Mr. Schuyler will hand you a draft on the Bank of Amsterdam for two million thalers before you leave this room. Refuse, and I will wire Admiral Takashima at Cavite to embark ten thousand Satsuma infantry for the Canary Islands; by March, while your cortical ministers are still drafting notes for London, you will be negotiating for the suburbs of Cádiz."

The Marquis’s fingers closed around the warm gold barrel. Behind the Chancellor’s desk, the small mahogany door clicked open; Major Sterling stepped onto the carpet with a fresh ribbon of blue telegraph paper, but Elias raised two fingers without turning his head and halted the officer in the shadow of the bookcase. The telegraph could wait.

The steel nib scratched across the vellum. It tore slightly on the rough parchment and left a blot of black ink beside the scarlet wax. Across the green baize, as Schuyler slid the Amsterdam bank-draft toward the Spanish chair, the Marquis dropped the pen, sank back against the leather, and covered his eyes with a trembling palm.

When the Spaniards and the weeping Dominicans had been ushered out into the rain-darkened corridor, Elias looked at Sterling. "What is it, Major?"

"Routine acknowledgment from the Nagasaki relay, Protector," Sterling said. He laid the paper on the corner of the desk. "The Tokugawa regency council has died of its own divisions. The young Boy-Emperor at Kyoto has declared the restoration of direct imperial rule, and the French military mission at Yokohama is arming the northern daimyos to contest the decree. Lord Shimazu asks when your flag will appear off Uraga."

Elias looked down at the wet ink of the Spanish cession. He had bought and battered every rim of the basin from the ice of the Yukon to the swamps of Luzon. Yet as he pressed his thumb against his left ribs, where a dull ache had lived beneath his breastbone since the winter crossing of the Rockies, the sheer span of the roof he had raised bore down on him. He had no son. If his heart stopped before the western anchor of the arch was mortared into place, Marcus Vance would rule by the camp-kettle and Schuyler by the counting-house, while Kaiulani watched the whole iron edifice rust into rival kingdoms within a decade.

"Tell Lord Shimazu to have his pilots waiting off Cape Sagami on the first of March," Elias said. He walked toward the tall, rain-lashed window. "I am not sending a squadron this time. I am bringing the line of battle myself."

# Chapter 10: Edo

On the fourth of March, 1868, twenty-four compound marine engines turned their twin screws at eighty revolutions to the minute, and their concussion beat the morning mist over the Uraga Channel flat against the dark green waters of Edo Bay.

Elias stood alone upon the open flying-bridge of the *Prometheus*. The three-thousand-ton frigate of the fifties had been broken up for scrap to feed the furnaces of Clark’s Point; in her place rode a nine-thousand-ton casemate battleship, her hull painted the deep imperial blue that the Japanese coast-watchers still called coal-black in their dispatches. Fifteen years earlier, when Commodore Matthew Perry was turned back at the Cape of Good Hope for want of Welsh coal, Elias’s merchant-captains and four light corvettes had negotiated the treaties of Shimoda. Those early conventions had been the polite bargains of equals who needed iron and shipwrights. The fleet had returned in force.

Behind the *Prometheus*, two parallel columns stretched four miles down the strait toward the smoking volcanic cone of Oshima. Sixteen ocean-going ironclads and eight monstrous troop-liners steamed in line: the *Leviathan*, the *Kamehameha*, the *Monterey*, the *Sitka*, and their sisters, their armored sides rising like sheer cliffs of riveted Pittsburgh and Sacramento steel above the frail cedar hulls of the local fishing-junks. The sunset-gold sun over the iron anchor snapped from every masthead. Twenty-eight telescopic funnels poured a continuous canopy of black Nanaimo coal-smoke across the snowy peak of Mount Fuji in the western sky.

"The Tokugawa fort on Sarushima Island is manning its barbette batteries, Protector," said Rear-Admiral Takashima. With his binoculars slung across his gold-laced breast, the Satsuma officer mounted the iron ladder to the bridge; though he had served Pacifica for seven years, his bronze cheeks pulled tight as drum-skin before the pine-clad headlands of his native realm. "And the French dispatch-corvette *Dupleix* is anchored off the Yokohama bund with her boarding-nets triced up. The Shogun’s harbor-commissioner has just put off from the Shinagawa mole in a twelve-oared barge waving the red banner of parley. They are signaling us to drop anchor below the treaty-line at Kanagawa."

Elias rested his gloved hands upon the cold brass rail. Salt spray kicked up from the battleship’s submerged ram-bow, carrying the taste of kelp and the pine-smoke drifting from the shore villages, where it mixed with the hot tallow and scorched mineral oil rising through the engine-room gratings beneath his boots. In his chest, that small knot beneath the breastbone pulsed once against his wool waistcoat. A man of forty-one who had lived on hardtack and telegraph tape could not afford three years of oriental ceremony.

"The treaty-line of fifty-four was drawn for wooden ships that feared the shoals, Admiral," Elias said. His rough voice carried no farther than the wheelhouse behind him. "How much water do we have under the keel off the Shinagawa batteries?"

"Six fathoms at the flood, sir," Takashima answered. "Within two thousand yards of the Shogun’s own castle ditches."

"Hold your speed at ten knots," Elias ordered. "Do not slow for the commissioner’s barge. Let our wake roll him back to the beach. If the French corvette off Yokohama does not dip her tricolor before our beam passes her anchorage, clear the port sixteen-inch turret and train the muzzles on her water-line until she finds her halyards. We will drop anchor where the people on the castle walls can smell our fires."

***

To the Chronicler who conversed in later years with the aged councillors of the Bakufu, the men who watched that armada round the headland of Kanonzaki on the third day of the third moon, no words in the courtly vocabulary of Kyoto or Edo could compass the vertigo of the realm. For a decade, the Japanese had seen the merchant-steamers of San Francisco and the isolated cruisers that brought machinery to Nagasaki; by sending five hundred samurai youth to work in the foundries of Clark’s Point and Monterey, the Shogun's ministers had flattered themselves that they were learning the barbarian’s trick of fire and iron so that they might one day close the gates again.

They had mistaken a bucket of water for the sea.

The sixteen steel leviathans steamed straight past the treaty-buoys of Kanagawa without furling a yard or answering the frantic gongs of the guard-boats. The tide of the bay surged against the sea-walls of the capital. Along the five miles of timber wharves and stone bastions at Shinagawa, two hundred thousand citizens and two-sworded retainers of the northern clans stood beside shaven-pated priests in the cold spring wind. Before them, floating mountains of black and blue iron moved against a head-tide without a rag of canvas, driven by a subterranean thunder that rattled the paper sliding-doors in the tea-houses along the Tokaido road three miles inland.

Inside the pentagonal earthworks of the First Daiba, the island battery that the Shogun’s Dutch engineers had built to bar the inner harbor, the gun-captains stood beside their bronze eighty-pounder smoothbores with smoking match-ropes in their hands. At four hundred yards’ distance, the towering armored flank of the *Prometheus* glided past the embrasures.

"Look at the thickness of the casemate around the gun-ports," whispered Matsudaira, the Commander of the River Guard. His lacquered war-fan dropped into the wet sand at his sandals. "A thirty-two-pound round-shot would shatter against that curve like a clay teacup thrown at a temple bell. And look upon the aft deck of the second vessel. Those are the red-lacquered helmets of the Satsuma and Choshu clans standing beside the giant hairy artillerymen from the American river!"

He spoke the truth. The Protector had returned with foreign monsters of iron manned by Japan’s own children, re-forged in the furnaces of California. Off the mouth of the Sumida River, the fleet dropped its thirty-ton bower anchors in unison with a roar like a hundred iron bridges collapsing into the sea at a single whistle-blast. No clumsy black powder smoked from the gun-ports. Instead, from the fighting-tops of the *Leviathan* and the *Kamehameha*, great parabolic mirrors of polished silver caught the glare of electric carbon-arc lamps powered by the ships’ dynamos and swept long beams of white noon-light across the gray battlements of Edo Castle through the afternoon haze.

Upon the twelve quarterdecks, the brass bands struck up the Imperial Anthem. Heavy European tubas and cornets blared across the anchorage, answered by the deep boom of giant *taiko* war-drums and the shrill wail of Polynesian conch-horns, while across four hundred yards of oily water the samurai beneath their silk banners stared out from the castle walls at the iron turrets.

Three days later, the scene shifted from the salt-stung parapets of the harbor to the inner sanctuary of the Nijo audience-halls. By Elias’s express demand, the young Emperor Mutsuhito and his regency council had been brought down from the ancient, land-locked seclusion of Kyoto by forced litter-march to meet the Lord of the Pacific within sight of the fleet’s guns.

Afternoon rain fell through the twisted black pines of the inner garden and dripped from the green bronze gargoyles of the upturned eaves onto beds of raked white river-gravel. Inside the Great Hall of the Pine, the cold air smelled of aged hinoki cypress and damp straw *tatami* mats, heavy with the resinous smoke of aloeswood burning in bronze tortoises at the four corners of the chamber.

At the northern end of the room, upon a raised dais hung with split bamboo curtains through which the outlines of silk-robed courtiers glimmered like ghosts in a pond, sat the sixteen-year-old Son of Heaven. Two paces below the curtain knelt Prince Sanjo and the leaders of the Western Clans, Lord Shimazu among them, with their foreheads touching the matting.

Elias did not kneel. He had not removed his heavy cavalry boots at the lacquer threshold. Down the center of the priceless cypress floor, flanked by General Marcus Vance in full blue-and-gold staff uniform and Lady Kaiulani wearing the royal feather mantle of the islands over her black silk, he walked while the steel rowels of his spurs tore tiny, regular crescent-scars into soft straw matting that had never before borne the leather of a foreign shoe. Behind them marched twelve troopers of the Life Guard: six six-foot Missourians and six giant Hawaiians carrying seven-shot repeating rifles with bayonets fixed.

Ten paces from the bamboo screen, where a low table of red lacquer marked the limit of approach, Elias halted.

"Tell the Regent," Elias said to Rear-Admiral Takashima, who stood half a pace to his right as interpreter, "that I cannot speak to a sovereign through a basket. Raise the screen."

A hiss like wind through dry reeds ran along the ranks of the kneeling *kuge* nobles in their tall black gauze hats. Prince Sanjo raised his shaved head from the mat, his face white as rice-paper.

"The person of the Heavenly Sovereign has not been looked upon by unanointed eyes since the age of the gods, Excellency!" Sanjo said through Takashima, his voice trembling. "Even the Shogun spoke to the throne from the lower floor!"

Elias kept his voice level. Past the kneeling prince, he looked toward the shadow behind the bamboo slats, while three miles out in the bay the sixteen-inch gun of the *Prometheus* fired its noon time-signal with a dull *thump* that rattled the paper screens along the garden veranda in their frames.

"The age of the gods ended when my ships dropped anchor off Shinagawa, Prince Sanjo," Elias said. "I am a ruler from the Atlantic Ocean to the China Sea, come neither as a Dutch merchant crawling on his belly for a cargo of copper nor as a Tokugawa clerk. If the Emperor of Japan wishes to sit beside me as a brother-monarch when we divide the western coast of this ocean, he will look me in the face. If he prefers to hide behind split cane like a woman in a harem, I will go back to my flagship, recognize the Tokugawa rebels in the north, and turn Edo into another Manila before the cherry-trees bloom."

For ten seconds no man breathed in the hall. Rain pattered on the gravel outside, and from the rear of the chamber came the dry, metallic click of Marcus Vance opening the lid of his pocket watch.

Then, from behind the bamboo blind, a young, high-pitched voice spoke three sharp words in the court dialect of Kyoto.

Two chamberlains in white silk crept forward on their knees. They grasped the braided crimson tassels and drew the bamboo screen up to the cedar lintel.

Upon the lacquer throne chair sat a slight, narrow-shouldered boy in stiff robes of white and purple brocade too heavy for his frame; yet as the light from the garden fell across his painted eyebrows and dark, almond-shaped eyes, he refused the floor and stared straight past his trembling ministers at the tall, broad-chested American in the plain navy wool coat whose hair had the gray cast of forged iron.

Elias inclined his head two inches, the exact salute he gave to his own fleet admirals, and stepped forward until his boot touched the red lacquer table.

"Your Majesty," Elias said. His deep, rough voice filled the cypress vault as Takashima translated sentence by sentence. "Three hundred years ago, the Spaniards and the Portuguese came to your islands with wooden ships and iron crosses to turn your people into subjects of Madrid. Twenty years ago, the English came to Canton with opium and smoothbore cannon to turn the Emperor of China into a tax-collector for London cotton-mills. Today, the British sit at Hong Kong and Singapore, the French are landing soldiers in Cochin-China, and the Russians are building forts at Vladivostok. If Japan stands alone with her wooden junks and her clan-swords, within ten years your ports will be British treaty-ports and your samurai will be pulling rickshaws for Liverpool clerks."

The boy on the dais did not blink. His small, pale hand tightened on the ivory sceptre across his knee. "And the Protector of the Eastern Ocean?" the Emperor asked, his voice thin and steady as Takashima rendered the words. "You come with sixteen ships of iron and ten thousand foreign soldiers into my inner sea. How is the eagle of San Francisco different from the lion of London?"

"Because London wants a market of beggars, and I want an ally of iron," Elias answered. He stepped around the low lacquer table; Prince Sanjo gasped and half-reached for a ceremonial dirk, then froze as Lady Kaiulani took a single step forward and laid a heavy parchment scroll bound in blue velvet directly upon the steps of the dais.

"I have eighty million people on my side of the water, and too many miles of prairie to police with American farmers alone," Elias continued, his pale gaze holding the boy-emperor’s eyes as he pointed toward the scroll. "You have thirty million subjects who know how to obey an order and die without asking a parliament why, sitting on barren rocks without iron ore or rock-oil or wheat. Sign the Grand Pacific Alliance today, and I will give your throne the monopoly of the Asian mainland from the Yalu River to the gates of Canton. My rolling-mills at Sacramento and Nagasaki will plate your ships; my granaries in California will feed your armies; and for every regiment of Japanese infantry that serves under my Marshal in the Atlantic provinces to keep the Eastern cities quiet, my fleet will put two regiments of your samurai ashore in Korea and Manchuria under the joint standard of the Sun and the Anchor."

Mutsuhito looked down at the velvet-bound treaty on the black lacquer steps, then out through the open screen toward the wet pines, beyond which the grey smoke of the Pacifica battleships stained the afternoon sky. Slowly, the boy extended his hand and touched the blue velvet.

***

By the third week of April, the boots of twelve thousand recruits had beaten the cherry blossoms along the bluff above Yokohama into the red mud, while the spring wind off the bay carried the stench of cosmoline grease, scorched wool, and the pungent sulfur of forty thousand brass cartridges expended every morning on the Kanagawa rifle-butts.

General Marcus Vance stood upon a raw pine reviewing-stand erected over the ruins of the old Dutch factor’s warehouse. Cold drizzle ran down the collar of his oilskin cape while he held his binoculars to his eyes. Below him, across two miles of drained rice-paddy that his Cantonese engineers had graded and rolled with crushed volcanic cinders into a level parade-plain, the first four brigades of the New Imperial Japanese Army wheeled by battalion at the double-quick.

Behind the quartermaster sheds lay the two-handed swords, the lacquered bamboo breastplates, and the flowing silk *hakama* of the Tokugawa wars, stacked in huge, rusting heaps to be melted down for scrap-ballast in the Nagasaki cupolas. In their place, every man from the proudest Satsuma lance-corporal to the humblest Choshu peasant-conscript wore the standardized, high-collared tunic of dark imperial blue wool woven in the conquered mills of Lowell, Massachusetts, topped by a visored cap bearing the brass chrysanthemum above the Pacifica anchor. They carried the new model 1867 Sacramento needle-rifle, a breech-loading steel weapon that fired a paper-patched metallic cartridge at nine rounds to the minute. It was a grim hybrid.

"The third battalion of the Sendai regiment is still bunching at the pivot, Colonel Armistead," Marcus said, his glasses still raised as he spoke to the scarred Virginian beside him. Armistead, along with two hundred former officers of the Army of Northern Virginia and the Union Sixth Corps, had come up from Manila on the March transports to serve as drill-masters for the new levies.

"It’s the clan-pride in ’em, General," Armistead replied. He shifted a plug of damp Virginia leaf in his cheek and pointed with his hickory rattan stick toward the left flank, where a young samurai captain was beating a slow pivot-man across the shoulders with the flat of a steel saber. "The Satsuma boys on the right wing march like clockwork because Admiral Takashima’s cousins command the companies, but those northern men from Aizu and Sendai still think it’s a dishonor to take their dressing from a peasant corporal who carried night-soil buckets last winter. Yesterday evening in the barracks, one of the Aizu lieutenants cut his own belly open with a sharpened bayonet because my sergeant major from Pennsylvania dressed him down in front of the privates for having rust on his firing-pin."

Marcus lowered his binoculars. He drew his damp memorandum book from his breast pocket. The malaria from the Luzon swamps still lived in his marrow; it gave his gaunt cheeks the tint of old tallow and left a persistent, ringing hum behind his temples that no dose of quinine could silence.

"A soldier who kills himself over a rusty firing-pin wastes twenty-four hundred grains of government powder and six months of rations," Marcus said, and noted the regiment’s number in pencil on the wet page. "Issue a general order to the division commanders before evening mess: the ancient custom of *seppuku* is hereby classified as self-mutilation to avoid duty in time of war. Any officer who takes his own life without the written warrant of a Provost Court will have his corpse hung in chains over the regimental latrine, his family’s rice-pension forfeited to the Crown, and his clan-name erased from the rolls. If they wish to die for their Emperor, Colonel, let them do it in front of a British battery at Hong Kong where their bodies will at least soak up lead meant for my artillery horses."

Down on the cinder-plain, a bugler of the First Maryland Auxiliary blew a long, brassy blast. Twelve thousand blue-coated figures dropped to one knee in the wet gravel; twelve thousand steel breech-blocks clicked open like a locust-swarm descending on a cornfield; and at the drop of Rear-Admiral Takashima’s saber, a continuous sheet of orange flame and grey smoke tore across the front as four brigades poured three volleys in twenty seconds into the plank targets eight hundred yards away against the sea-wall.

Through the drifting smoke-bank, six four-gun batteries of light Krupp mountain pieces bounded through the intervals of the infantry line. Teams of twenty bare-legged Japanese artillery-coolies trotted in rope harnesses where scarce island horses would have failed, and the crews unlimbered their steel trails in the mud in forty seconds flat.

Down by the beach, the wooden targets dissolved into flying splinters under the high-explosive shells. The lash that kept Irish and Confederate conscripts moving on the Chilkoot ice had no use here, nor did the silver bribes that bought Washington politicians. Eight hundred years in a closed furnace had tempered these men into iron; they had lacked only the die-stamp of modern logistics.

Up on the bluff behind them, the Union Jack drooped over the brick compound of the British Legation, and four hundred sullen Royal Marines of the 9th Foot gripped the iron palings to stare down at the drill, until a sudden spasm of coughing shook Marcus's narrow chest. Bright pink foam flecked his gray wool gauntlet.

He wiped the glove clean against his hip before Armistead could look.

***

Two months later, on the sixteenth of June, 1868, the summer sun hung high and blinding above the cold gray fog-banks rolling through the Golden Gate. Twenty miles out at sea, lookouts could spot the gilded copper roofs of the Citadel on Rincon Hill.

Elias bypassed the small oval cabinet room where he had dictated the humiliation of Madrid. For the ratification of the Treaty of Edo, the instrument that closed the Western Ocean forever to European merchant flags, he had thrown open the great Rotunda of the Chancery to three hundred delegates of the Diet, the marshals of the Atlantic Protectorates, and the captive diplomatic corps.

The chamber measured eighty feet across. Green serpentine marble from the coast ranges faced the lower walls beneath captured regimental battle-flags of the old Union, Confederate, and Spanish armies, while overhead, suspended from the coffered dome, hung a massive bronze chandelier cast from the melted cannon of Fort Sumter and Cavite. Beeswax and damp broadcloth thickened the air, cut by sharp brine blowing up from the naval slips below the cliff and the bitter camphor of the ceremonial robes worn by Prince Sanjo’s retinue.

Elias sat upon the raised chair of state, a severe curule seat cast from solid, dull-gray Washoe silver and upholstered in plain navy leather, having long despised the velvet and gilt of bankrupt Bourbons. He wore his unadorned blue wool tunic buttoned to the throat. Though his shoulders remained broad as an ox-yoke, the skin around his temples stretched tight and dry as drum-parchment over the bone; his right hand rested open upon his knee, while his left thumb hooked inside his breast-button and pressed against the dull, hot weight that had settled behind his ribs on the voyage home from Yokohama. That ache never left.

At the center of the porphyry table below the dais, Prince Sanjo wore the gold-braided court coat of a Pacifica Privy Councillor over his silk trousers. He affixed the great vermilion seal of the Chrysanthemum Throne to the vellum scroll. Chancellor Gwin and Cornelius Schuyler countersigned for the Maritime Board.

"By the seventh and eighth articles of this perpetual concordat," Chancellor Gwin read aloud, his voice booming toward the diplomatic gallery where Sir Edward Thornton, the British Minister, stood rigid as a poker beside the French envoy, "His Imperial Majesty the Tenno of Japan and the Providentor of the Grand Confederation of Pacifica declare the waters of the Western Sea, from the Kurile Straits to the Formosa Channel, to be an exclusive customs-preserve of the Two Crowns. From the first day of August next, all extra-territorial concessions heretofore granted to European powers at Yokohama, Kobe, and Nagasaki are annulled. No foreign vessel not registered upon the rolls of San Francisco, Honolulu, or Edo shall discharge cargo within the Empire of Japan save upon payment of a sixty-percent differential duty in gold thalers; and the policing of the treaty-ports is hereby transferred in perpetuity to the Joint Imperial Admiralty."

Up in the gallery, Sir Edward Thornton did not wait for the conclusion. His face purple beneath his gray side-whiskers, and his secretary hurrying behind him with his portfolio, the British Minister clapped his tall beaver hat onto his head inside the chamber, turned on his heel, and strode out.

The Englishman’s back vanished through the mahogany arch. Around the floor below, the syndics of San Francisco and the railway barons of Sacramento broke into a deep, rumbling cheer and struck their canes against the marble tiles. Schuyler beamed like a man just handed the keys to the Bank of England.

Only Lady Kaiulani sat still. In her high-backed chair to the left of the silver seat, the heavy gold collar of the Insular Diet rested upon her black mourning silk as Elias rose to take the gold pen and add the final *E. Thorne, Providentor* beneath the red wax, and under cover of the cheering she leaned toward him.

"You have locked the shop door in the lion’s face, Elias," she said. She ignored the Japanese prince and stared at the beads of cold sweat along Elias’s hairline as he bent over the porphyry table to write. "And your hand is shaking on the nib."

Elias did not look up. He drove the steel point through the last letter of his title with crushing force, laid the pen upon the silver tray without a click, and straightened his spine against the cold ache in his chest.

"My hand is steady enough to sign the sailing-orders for the China Squadron, Kaiulani," he said, his voice rough as river-gravel and pitched for her ear alone while Prince Sanjo bowed three times before the dais. "Let Sir Edward run to his telegraph wire. We have forty-two ironclads in commission between Sitka and Cavite, and sixty million thalers of Klondike bullion in the Mint cellar. If London wants to open the gates of Edo again, they will have to send their fleet sixteen thousand miles around the world without a coaling-station between the Falklands and Hong Kong."

"London’s fleet does not concern me, Protector," she said. Her gaze dropped to the left breast of his tunic, where his thumb had slipped back between the brass buttons. "A roof that rests upon a single pillar does not need a cannonball to bring it down. It only needs the winter rot inside the oak. Look at your floor below: Schuyler is already whispering with the Boston railway factors about who shall control the Treasury when you are gone, and Admiral Takashima’s samurai do not even look at General Vance’s officers when they pass in the corridor. Who holds the hammer when your arm grows cold?"

Out across the floor spread a sea of upturned faces: the florid jowls of the American syndicate directors, the stony masks of the Satsuma lords, and the scarred veterans of the conquered East standing guard beneath the captured banners. For forty years he had never looked backward or imagined a morning when the sun would rise over the Pacific without his boot on the deck. Now the hall tilted. Beneath his heels, the Rincon Hill granite shifted like the plank of a flatboat riding a brown, bottomless flood.

"The hammer does not leave my hand while I draw breath," Elias said. He turned from her to face the cheering Diet and raised his right arm for silence.

***

The true origin of the First Contest with Great Britain lies in the ledger-books of the Manchester Cotton Exchange and the smoking chimneys of Sheffield during that black summer of 1868, far more than in the naval estimates of Whitehall or the proud traditions of Trafalgar.

For a hundred years, ever since the sails of Lord Clive and Captain Cook had whitened the eastern seas, the island kingdom of the North Atlantic had rested upon an unchallenged axiom of providence: the oceans of the earth formed a continuous highway paved by the Royal Navy so that raw cotton, tea, and bullion from the outer continents might flow into the looms of Lancashire and the vaults of Threadneedle Street, returning outward as Birmingham hardware and six-percent loans. Now a backwoods surveyor from the American wilderness, a man whose name had not even appeared in the *Almanach de Gotha* fifteen years prior, had torn the United States in half, reduced New York and Boston to tax-farms, swallowed the Russian ice and the Spanish islands in a single winter, and bolted the doors of Japan and the northern China coast with a stroke of a pen. To the Victorian mind, this was a blasphemy against the order of nature.

On the night of the twenty-eighth of June, twelve days after Sir Edward Thornton’s cipher had passed beneath the Atlantic cable from Halifax to Ireland, a thick, yellow coal-fog mixed with summer drizzle hung over the wet cobblestones of Whitehall. Inside the high, oak-paneled Cabinet Room at Number Ten Downing Street, the gaselier hissed above the long green cloth. Prime Minister Benjamin Disraeli sat with his chin sunk into his black satin cravat, his hooded eyes fixed upon the First Lord of the Admiralty and the Governor of the Bank of England.

"Fourteen textile mills in Oldham and Blackburn shut their gates on Saturday, Prime Minister," Lord Stanley, the Foreign Secretary, said as he laid a sheaf of consular dispatches beside the silver inkstand. "Since Thorne’s Customs Decree went into force at Manila and Yokohama, sixteen British tea-clippers and eight P&O steam-packets have been turned back from the Japanese straits with their cargoes of Manchester shirting unbroken in their holds. Worse, the Bank of Rotterdam notified us this morning that the San Francisco Mint is dumping thirty million thalers of pure Yukon gold onto the Frankfurt market exclusively to buy up the Krupp ordnance patents and the entire nitrate output of Peru. If we permit this Pacifica monopoly to stand through the autumn, the pound sterling will be driven out of every counting-house east of Singapore before Christmas."

At the foot of the table, Admiral Sir Sydney Dacres, First Sea Lord of the Admiralty, struck the edge of his brass-bound Pacific chart with a heavy, sun-freckled fist. He was sixty-four. The Crimean veteran had grown grey in a world where a single British gunboat could bring an oriental kingdom to its knees before breakfast.

"The fellow is a blown-up land-pirate playing at Bonaparte with river-scows!" Dacres said. His bushy white whiskers bristled over the map. "Give the word to the telegraph office tonight, Mr. Disraeli. We have seven first-rate ironclads of the Channel Fleet lying with banked fires at Spithead: the *Warrior*, the *Black Prince*, the *Hercules*, and the *Monarch*. Order them to Gibraltar and around the Cape to join Admiral Kuper’s squadron at Hong Kong, while we send four armored rams through the Straits of Magellan to reinforce Esquimalt. Between Vancouver Island and the China Sea, where his wooden docks at Puget Sound sit exposed and his Japanese allies crowd their coastal rice-swamps, our squadrons will catch this San Francisco upstart and blow his fleet to pieces before the November gales!"

Disraeli did not move his head. Only his long, sallow fingers, set with a single emerald ring, rose an inch from the green baize.

"And how much Welsh coal does the *Hercules* burn in twenty-four hours at ten knots, Sir Sydney?" the Prime Minister asked. His smooth voice carried an ancient irony that belonged to an older sea than the Atlantic.

"Eighty tons a day, sir, when the grates are clean," Dacres answered.

"Eighty tons," Disraeli said. At the far end of the cloth, the Governor of the Bank wiped his spectacles with a trembling hand. "From the Cape of Good Hope to Hong Kong is six thousand miles; from the Falkland Islands to Vancouver is seven thousand. Since this 'land-pirate' seized Honolulu, Guam, Manila, and the Samoan craters in December, and since he has leased every coaling-mole in Chile and Sonora with his Yukon silver, pray tell the Cabinet, Admiral: in what harbor between Valparaiso and Puget Sound will your four iron rams fill their bunkers when their coal-sacks are empty off the equator?"

Dacres opened his mouth. His ruddy face darkened to the color of old port. He hesitated. Across the five thousand miles of blue paper that marked the eastern Pacific, where every deep-water anchorage bore a red dot and every dot now carried the penciled cross of a Pacifica battery, his stubby finger traced the empty water.

"We will send colliers under convoy from Cardiff and Sydney—"

"Slow sailing-barques towed behind steam-battleships across the roaring forties," Disraeli said. He rose. With his stooped, dandyish gait, he walked to the tall window and pulled back an inch of the heavy crimson drapery to look out at the wet gas-lamps shining on the policemen’s capes in Whitehall. "Meanwhile Mr. Thorne sits at the center of the circle. He moves his squadrons along interior lines from Sitka to Yedo with coal dug at the water’s edge, and holds four million Irish and American riflemen at the border of Canada ready to march into Montreal the morning our first shot is fired at Esquimalt."

The curtain fell back into place. Disraeli turned to the room and hooked his thumbs into the armholes of his embroidered waistcoat.

"Do not deceive yourselves, my lords," he said. Every minister at the board leaned forward to catch the quiet words. "The Tsar at Sebastopol and the Emperor of China at the Peiho forts ruled medieval states rotting from the inside. What has risen on the far side of the American mountains is Rome with a steam-engine in its belly. This new empire has strangled its own senate, married its iron to the thirty million sword-men of Japan, and turned the greatest ocean on the globe into a private mill-pond. We cannot fight Mr. Thorne across twelve thousand miles of empty water with colliers this autumn. Before the lion springs, across the border in Canada, throughout the discontented cities of New England, and among the proud island princes whom Marshal Vance has just trampled in the mud of Honolulu, we must first cut the tendons behind his knees."

He walked back to his seat and rested his slender hand upon a locked red morocco dispatch-box stamped with the royal cipher of the Secret Service.

"Lord Stanley," Disraeli said. He turned the small gold key in the brass lock and lifted the lid an inch. "You will instruct Sir Rutherford Alcock at Peking to release fifty thousand sovereigns from the Hong Kong secret service fund to the anti-foreign secret societies in Shantung and Chihli, the Militia of Righteous and Harmonious Fists, as the mandarins call them. Let them burn the railway sleepers that Mr. Thorne’s engineers are laying from Tientsin, and let them besiege the foreign legations. If the American Caesar wishes to own the Asian littoral, let him try to digest four hundred million starving peasants while his own heart-valves are failing in the fog of San Francisco."

# Chapter 11: The Thornean Mandate

Three months later, the autumn equinox of 1868 churned the shallow, silt-choked Yellow Sea into ochre foam.

Fifty miles off the low mud-flats of the Peiho River mouth, where the turbid discharge of the northern Chinese plains stained the salt water the color of rusted iron for twenty leagues out to sea, the First Armored Battle Squadron of Pacifica rode the long, greasy ground-swell in double column. The flagship *Prometheus* steamed at the head of the windward line. Her nine-thousand-ton hull rolled ten degrees to port and starboard while the north wind whipped the coal-black smoke from her twin telescopic funnels flat across the yellow wave-tops.

Inside the armored chart-house beneath the flying bridge, the steam-radiators and the sharp tang of camphor-spirits stifled the air. Elias sat upon a bolted oak locker beside the brass binnacle. He had unbuttoned his navy wool tunic at the throat to ease the constriction around his windpipe. On the mahogany chart-table before him, weighted down by lead bars against the roll of the ship, lay the hydrographic survey of the Taku forts; beside the chart stood a small blue glass phial of digitalis that his chief surgeon had left by the water-carafe that morning.

Elias did not touch the medicine. His broad, square-nailed thumb rested upon the inked soundings of the river bar, though every fourth beat of his pulse sent a dull, irregular thud up into the base of his carotid artery, like an engine-piston knocking against a worn cylinder-head.

"The water on the Taku bar is scarce eleven feet at low tide, Protector," said Rear-Admiral Takashima. He braced his sea-boots against the pitch of the deck and leaned over the chart with a pair of brass dividers. "The *Prometheus* and the *Leviathan* draw twenty-four. Even at the spring flood tonight, our heavy battleships cannot cross the mud-spit to reach the inner anchorage. And the smoke from the shore shows that the Boxers have already fired the Russian and French timber-concessions at Tientsin."

Across the narrow cabin, Lady Kaiulani sat wrapped in her dark sea-otter mantle, her back straight against the iron bulkhead. Though she had accompanied the flagship from Nagasaki as High Commissioner of the Maritime Courts to adjudicate the seized customs-houses of the northern treaty ports, she kept her dark eyes fixed upon the gray ring around Elias’s lips.

"They are burning more than timber, Admiral," Kaiulani said. Beneath the deck, the iron rudder-chains groaned against the swell. "Before the lines were cut, the British consul at Chefoo wired that the Empress Dowager’s guard regiments have joined the Righteous Fists, torn up forty miles of the new Pacifica railway grade between Taku and Peking, crucified eight of our Cantonese survey-clerks upon the telegraph poles, and surrounded the legation quarter. How convenient for Mr. Disraeli that a peasant uprising in Shantung should strike exclusively at the wharves and rail-depots mortgaged to San Francisco."

Elias lifted his head. Beyond the thick, salt-crusted bull's-eye glass of the forward port, the smoke of burning coal-yards and missionary compounds drifted out over the Bohai Gulf and smudged the western horizon with a dirty, copper-colored pall.

"Convenient for London in September," Elias said. Despite the tightness in his chest, his rough voice held steady; he closed his fist over the blue glass phial and slipped it unseen into his coat pocket. "Fatal for London by Christmas. For twenty years the European ministers at Peking have kept us out of the northern provinces by claiming that their treaties with the Manchu court guaranteed the peace of the coast. Now the Manchus have broken the lock themselves, and the British have only four wooden sloops in the river."

He rose from the oak locker and braced his wide shoulders against the brass stanchion. A heavy yellow sea broke over the *Prometheus*'s turtle-back bow. Muddy spray rattled like gravel against the armor-plate.

"A merchant who cannot protect his warehouse forfeits his lease to the man who brings the fire-engine," Elias said. "We do not need the battleships inside the bar, Takashima. Transfer my pennant to the shallow-draft monitor *Sacramento* and bring up the twelve armored river-barges we towed from Nagasaki. When the tide makes at four o'clock, cross the mud-flats and lay our fifteen-inch turrets three hundred yards off the South Fort. Do not summon the Mandarin to parley. Until the mud walls slide into the ditch, open with high-explosive picric shell upon the water-gates, and put Marshal Vance’s vanguard ashore on the wet silt before the smoke clears. We are going to rescue the European ambassadors whether they wish to be rescued or not. When the fire is out, the keys to the river stay in my pocket."

***

Nine days after the fifteen-inch guns of the *Sacramento* reduced the mud-brick casemates of Taku to a smoking vitrified slag-heap, the autumn wind from the Mongolian steppe struck the high, serrated ridges of the Yan Mountains like a blade of polished ice.

Forty miles north of the burning plains around Peking, the ancient stone rampart of the Great Wall twisted across the granite hogbacks like the petrified spine of a dragon that had died before Rome was pupped. The air at two thousand feet was bone-dry. Pulverized yellow loess-dust and wild wormwood blew on the wind, thick with the rank, ammoniac reek of two thousand Manchurian pack-mules straining up the paved military road toward the Nankou Pass.

General Marcus Vance sat his gaunt, raw-boned California mare in the shadow of a crumbling Ming watchtower. Three centuries ago, the iron arrows of the Tartars had chipped its crenelated brickwork; three hours ago, the four-inch rifled shells of the Pacifica Mountain Artillery had shattered the parapet anew.

Though the northern gale swept down the gorge, the Luzon malaria that recurred every third afternoon flushed Marcus’s sunken cheeks with dry fire, and beneath his heavy navy-blue greatcoat his ribs ached with the pleurisy he had taken during the crossing of the Yellow Sea. His coat remained buttoned to the chin. Down by the mule-lines, the hospital ambulance waited, ignored. Bracing his Carl Zeiss binoculars against the stone parapet of the wall, he looked down the long, boulder-strewn defile toward the south.

In the entire history of warfare since Alexander marched his Macedonians and Persians across the Hindu Kush, the sun had never looked down upon such an army as the column now winding through the broken gates of the Chinese Empire.

At the head of the pass marched the First and Third Regiments of the Atlantic Free States Auxiliary. Five years earlier these three thousand sun-blackened veterans had worn the faded blue of the Army of the Potomac or the ragged butternut of Lee’s Virginians; now they stepped in four-deep cadence beneath the Sunset Gold and Imperial Blue standard of the Protectorate. Ancient Cathay dust coated their bearded Anglo-Saxon faces grey. Across their shoulders they carried seven-shot Sacramento repeating carbines. Behind their company guidons, six armored steam-traction engines from the Clark’s Point works dragged heavy steel siege-mortars up the grade, and their wide iron cleaver-wheels crushed the two-thousand-year-old granite flagstones of the Chin Dynasty into white powder.

Flank-to-flank with the Americans, occupying the left half of the stone road in silent, lock-stepped battalions, came the Second Imperial Division of Satsuma and Choshu infantry.

The old veterans of Gettysburg and Shiloh no longer spat tobacco at the smaller, bronze-skinned men beside them. Four days prior, during the bloody night-assault through the burning sorghum-fields of Tientsin, thirty thousand screaming Boxers in red turbans and Prince Tuan’s Manchu Bannermen had charged the railway embankment through a blinding dust-storm; when a Virginia regiment’s ammunition-mules stampeded, two battalions of Choshu riflemen wheeled into the gap without a bugle-call, poured nine aimed rounds a minute into the massed lances, and went in with eighteen-inch steel bayonets in dead silence.

"The Boxers have thrown up a barricade of carts and stone blocks across the southern mouth of the pass, Marshal," reported Colonel Armistead. He rode up the rubble slope where a squad of Cantonese sappers was bolting a porcelain telegraph-insulator directly into the masonry of the Great Wall. "And their flankers are rolling powder-barrels down the cliffs from that Buddhist monastery on the left spur. If we send the infantry down the gut in column, we’ll lose two hundred men before we reach the plain."

Marcus lowered his glasses. He coughed into his wool gauntlet, tight and dry, hiding the red fleck on the cloth from the staff officers behind him. Fever dulled his eyes, yet his brain worked like a cold, unhurried adding-machine.

"We will not send the infantry down the gut, Colonel," Marcus said. His voice scraped like dry sand against his windpipe. Turning in the saddle, he looked back down the northern slope, where the flanking fire of his Japanese mountain-guns had just driven four thousand Manchu cavalry from the Kalgan garrison into a box-canyon. "How many prisoners did General Saigo’s brigade take at the upper gate this morning?"

"Twelve hundred, sir," Armistead answered, squinting through the yellow dust. "Mostly Red Fist militia and Shantung sword-men."

"Have the Satsuma provosts wire their wrists together in ranks of twenty and drive them down the stone road three hundred yards ahead of our lead traction-engine," Marcus ordered. He drew his field-book from his coat and rested it on his saddle-horn. "If the monks on the cliff roll their powder-barrels, they will blow up their own brethren. Meanwhile, put two batteries of the four-inch Krupp rifles onto this watchtower parapet. Elevation four degrees. Leave the barricade alone, and put forty rounds of white-phosphorus incendiary shell straight through the tiled roofs of that monastery on the spur. When the timber catches, the draft from the gorge will roast every marksman on the cliff inside ten minutes."

Armistead’s weathered hand rose to his cap-brim. "And when we clear the pass, General? The road to Peking is open across the flat for thirty miles. The British and Russian commanders down at Tientsin sent a courier this morning asking that we halt outside the Tartar Wall so that the European detachments can come up and enter the Forbidden City at the head of the column."

Marcus’s fever-cracked lips pulled back against his teeth. Past the ancient grey battlements of the Ming emperors, out in the southern haze, the yellow roofs of the northern capital waited like ripe grain for the sickle.

"The European detachments are still sitting in the mud at Yangtsun waiting for their bullock-carts," Marcus said. He closed his book. "We have steam-traction and they have mules. March the Virginia and Satsuma brigades through the night in two-hour relays. By dawn tomorrow, before the first British marine sees the smoke of the city, I want our mortars unlimbered before the Chienmen Gate and the Sun-and-Anchor flying over the Temple of Heaven. If Sir Rutherford Alcock wishes to enter Peking, he will present his pass to a Pacifica corporal at the gate."

***

While Marcus Vance’s iron wheels ground the flagstones before the Forbidden City into dust, Elias stayed away from the dry, medieval furnace of Peking. A carpenter who knows where the main rafters of a house are joined leaves the garret alone; he sits down at the front threshold where all the grain and silver of the household must pass in and out.

Three hundred miles south of the Yellow Sea, where the Whangpoo River joins the vast, chocolate-colored deluge of the Yangtze Kiang, the arterial highway draining the wealth of two hundred million souls from the tea-hills of Hankow to the silk-looms of Soochow, lay the mud-flat port of Shanghai.

On the twelfth of November, 1868, a cold autumn rain fell vertically into the river. It pitted the brown current and wrapped the stone banking-houses of the British and French Bund in a sodden, coal-stained twilight. Yet along the two miles of river-front north of the Soochow Creek, where the old American missionary settlement of Hongkew had stood six weeks earlier, two hundred electric arc-lamps on tall iron lattice-poles banished the gloom.

Two companies of the First Hawaiian Guard occupied the yamen of the Taotai of Shanghai, and the birth of the Pacifica Concession proceeded by the pile-driver and the steam-dredge. Down in the liquid mud of the foreshore, while twenty floating donkey-engines hissed overhead, three thousand Cantonese coolies and twelve hundred conscripted Shantung prisoners worked knee-deep in the cold slime to drive sixty-foot trunks of Oregon Douglas fir into the silt, supporting a continuous quay of Sierra granite blocks brought over as ballast in the holds of the San Francisco grain-fleet. The air was a thick, suffocating soup. River-sewage and wet coal-soot mingled with the sharp nitric tang of blasting-gelatine, while the sweet, heavy smoke of opium and sandalwood drifted from the crowded native sampans corralled behind a boom of chained timber spars across the creek.

Inside the upper gallery of the newly erected Admiralty House, a gaunt, three-story fortress of red brick and cast-iron columns bolted together from prefabricated Sacramento sections in twenty-eight days, Elias stood before the open casement window with his heavy wool boat-cloak draped loosely over his shoulders.

He had not slept in forty hours. Below his left collarbone, the dull iron weight had sharpened since the morning. With every third breath, a slow, rhythmic vice squeezed his ribs and drove a cold, tingling numbness down the inside of his left arm all the way to the ring-finger. His fingers were the color of tallow. He kept his left hand buried deep in his coat pocket, hidden from both Cornelius Schuyler and Sir Harry Parkes, Her Britannic Majesty’s Minister Plenipotentiary, who had steamed up from Hong Kong in a furious haste the night before.

"This is no mere violation of the Treaty of Tientsin, Mr. Thorne!" Sir Harry Parkes said. His small, wiry frame trembled with indignation. Beside the mahogany table where Lady Kaiulani sat sorting the stamped customs-manifests of forty detained British tea-clippers, he struck his wet umbrella against the parquet floor. "Marshal Vance has occupied the Imperial Ministry of Revenue in Peking with Japanese infantry! He has forced Prince Kung at the point of a bayonet to sign a decree transferring the entire Maritime Customs Service of the Yangtze Valley to a board of San Francisco syndics, and now your harbor-master informs the captain of the P&O steamer *Ganges* that he may not warp into the British Bund without paying tonnage dues to a Hawaiian port-warden!"

Elias stayed at the window. Down on the wet granite apron of the new pier, a traveling steam-crane swung a forty-ton locomotive boiler bearing the brass plate of the *Central China & Pacifica Railway* out of the hold of the transport *Oregon* and lowered it directly onto the broad-gauge iron rails that already stretched five miles inland across the leveled graves of the suburban rice-fields.

"Mr. Robert Hart and your British inspectors collected the customs for the Manchu court on the condition that you kept the river open and the rebels down, Sir Harry," Elias said. He turned slowly from the casement. Though he had to pause for a fraction of a second between his phrases to let the spasm under his breastbone subside, his rough, low voice carried the same flat, immovable weight it had held in the snows of the Platte thirty years before. "Last month, while your gunboats were anchored right out there off the Bund, the Boxers burned the silk-filatures at Soochow and murdered thirty foreign factors within ten miles of your consulate flagstaff. Your roof leaked. I have put a new one on."

"You have erected a fortified colony in the throat of the Yangtze!" Parkes shot back. His whiskers bristled. Through the rain-streaked glass, out toward the mouth of the Woosung river, the twin sixteen-inch turrets of the *Leviathan* lay moored in mid-channel to block the fairway to every merchantman in the East China Sea, and Parkes pointed straight at them. "Look at the boundary stones your engineers have driven into the mud along the Defense Creek! You have annexed twelve square miles of the richest alluvial delta in Asia, declared it sovereign territory of the Sacramento Diet under the laws of the Insular Code, and placed a twenty-percent transit tax on every chest of tea and bale of raw silk that passes down the river from the interior to the British godowns!"

"Twenty-five percent, Sir Harry, if the cargo is insured in London rather than at Mr. Schuyler’s desk on Montgomery Street," corrected Lady Kaiulani. She kept her eyes on her register, dipped her steel pen into the inkwell, and affixed the red stamp of the Insular Court to a clearance warrant. "Though any British merchant house in the old settlement is free to remove its offices three hundred yards north across the Soochow Creek into the Pacifica Concession, where it may enjoy the protection of our provost-courts, our electric telegraph, and our five-percent preferential tariff, provided fifty-one percent of its stock is registered in San Francisco gold thalers."

Parkes stared from the dark-eyed Polynesian princess in her black mourning silk to the plump, smiling face of Cornelius Schuyler, who stood warming his coattails before the coal-grate like a cat in a dairy. The blood drained from the Englishman’s ruddy face.

"You do not intend to fight us at Hong Kong at all," Parkes whispered. His fingers tightened on the ivory handle of his umbrella. "You intend to starve Hong Kong to death without firing a gun. By holding the mouth of the Yangtze here and the railway at Peking, you drain the whole trade of the Chinese Empire into your own paved compound and leave our concessions downriver as empty mud-banks!"

"A man does not batter down a stone fort when he can turn the river into a new channel upstream, Sir Harry," Elias said. From the tall casement window to the head of the mahogany table he walked slowly, his right hand sliding along the leather armchair backs to steady his knees against a sudden wave of vertigo that spun the gas-lamps into yellow rings. "The Concession of Shanghai is open to all nations that acknowledge the Maritime Code. Your merchants may come across the bridge and trade in my silver, or they may sit behind your consular palings and watch the grass grow between the cobbles."

He stopped at the head of the mahogany table. Beneath him lay the great map of the Yangtze basin, where the fresh red ink of the new Imperial Concession sat like a steel padlock upon the commercial heart of Asia; from Sitka to Tutuila, from the ruined Capitol on the Potomac to the mud of the Whangpoo, the circle was welded shut. No west remained.

Sir Harry Parkes bowed stiffly and stalked toward the double doors. As Cornelius Schuyler stepped forward with a bundle of newly printed Shanghai Municipal Bonds, the iron band around Elias’s chest twisted like a cold bayonet between his ribs, and when his right hand reached for the gold pen in Kaiulani’s fingers, the dark room tilted forty degrees to starboard and the inkwell slid into blackness.
