The Protector struck the parquet floor like a felled redwood.

***

For eleven days during that rain-swept November of 1868, while Elias Thorne lay behind the triple-bolted oak doors of the Shanghai Admiralty’s upper bedchamber with mustard plasters upon his chest and the smell of camphor and digitalis thick in the curtains, the world remained ignorant that the heart of the colossus had missed its stroke. Lady Kaiulani took the keys to the submarine cable-room before the surgeon had even risen from his knees. Every cipher going out under the sea to Monterey or London passed beneath her black sleeve. Down in the guardrooms and among the restless captains of the Satsuma and American divisions, the word went out that the Providentor was secluded with the Ch’ing variance rolls to draft the new provincial tax-codes in his own hand. He remained unseen.

Yet along the muddy alleys of Chihli and the stone quays of the Yangtze during that suspended fortnight, an extraordinary contagion took hold of the conquered populations. Neither Cornelius Schuyler’s clerks nor Rear-Admiral Takashima’s provosts had foreseen this religious and political fever, which history has since termed *The Thornean Mandate*.

For twenty years the peasantry of the Middle Kingdom had endured the slow death-throes of the Manchu dynasty: the twenty million corpses of the Taiping rebellion, the burning of the Summer Palace by the Anglo-French armies, the flooding of the Yellow River, and the final madness of the Righteous Fists. In the mind of the Chinese tiller of the soil and the scholar-gentry of the river towns alike, the *T’ien-ming*, the Mandate of Heaven, belonged to a cosmic lease held only so long as the sovereign kept the dikes repaired and the grain-barges moving on the Grand Canal, with the bandits hung along the post-roads. Corrupt dynasties lost their grip on the elements. Then Heaven sent a scourge from beyond the mountains to sweep the threshold clean.

And what scourge had ever arrived with such unmistakable providence as the iron fleets of the Eastern Sea?

The British and the French had merely nibbled at the treaty-ports like wharf-rats to sell Indian opium and Lancaster calico before sailing away. This new Lord of the Ocean arrived with the geometry of an ancient founder of dynasties. Within three weeks of the fall of Taku, while Elias still lay gray-faced against his pillows and rain beat on the Whangpoo, sixty thousand conscripted coolies under the supervision of Satsuma engineers and Virginia quartermasters were already dredging the silted bends of the Peiho with giant steam-shovels that did the work of ten thousand baskets. Stone depots rose at twenty-li intervals along the ruined post-roads where the Boxers had burned the granaries. From these standardized storehouses, the Pacifica Commissariat distributed white San Joaquin wheat and stamped silver coins whose weight never varied by a barleycorn.

In the tea-houses of Soochow and the ruined temples of Tientsin, where the Taoist fortune-tellers and wandering Buddhist mendicants gathered around the charcoal-pans, the whispered myth took shape with the speed of a prairie fire. The foreign Protector held a mandate far grander than that of the red-haired English merchant-barbarians. Had he not brought the warriors of the Eastern Dwarfs and the dark kings of the Southern Isles kneeling at his stirrup, broken the White Tribes of the Atlantic first, and bound the Dragon of the Ocean in chains of black iron?

Before November was out, the woodblock printers along the Bund were secretly striking off thousands of cheap vermilion broadsheets that found their way into the ancestral shrines of five provinces. Upon them, Elias sat in the stiff iconography of the Ming martial gods: enthroned upon riveted boiler-plate beneath the Rising Sun and the Iron Anchor, his brow furrowed with the celestial thunderbolt, his left hand holding a scroll of the Universal Land-Tax and his right a seven-shot repeating carbine. The Confucian magistrates returned. Having fled Peking before Marcus Vance’s railway-mortars, they now rode quietly back to the yamen gates in their mule-litters, brushed the dust from their ceremonial robes, and petitioned the Hawaiian and American provost-courts for new seals of office under what the literati gravely styled *The Ta-P’ing-Yang Ch’ao*, the Dynasty of the Great Peace of the Ocean. No one asked whether the new Emperor in the brick house by the river could stand without his surgeon’s arm.

***

Two months later, the winter fog of January 1869 rolled through the Golden Gate so thick and yellow with the smoke of a hundred foundry chimneys that the gas-lamps along the Embarcadero had to be kept burning at high noon.

Lady Kaiulani stood upon the high, covered timber bridge that connected the second story of the Imperial Custom House with the great brick Immigration Barracoons on the Pacific Mail wharf. Below her, through the tall, salt-rimmed casements, the deck of the five-thousand-ton paddle-transport *Canton* discharged its human cargo down four broad gangways into the sleet-chilled drizzle, while the heavy donkey-winches aft swung crate after crate of raw Kiangsu silk and Hankow brick-tea, along with pigs of Yunnan tin, onto the waiting flatcars of the Trans-Continental Railway.

Inside the glass-walled gallery, the steam-pipes warmed the air. It smelled heavily of wet wool and carbolic disinfectant from the quarantine pens below, mixed with the garlic and tobacco of the four thousand Shantung and Kwangtung laborers filing past the registration desks on the concrete floor underneath.

"Fourteen thousand landed at this pier since the first of the month, Your Highness," said Cornelius Schuyler. He bustled up the gallery stairs with a thick leather portfolio tucked beneath his velvet-collared overcoat; since the two weeks in Shanghai when he and Rear-Admiral Takashima had stood outside Elias’s locked bedroom door, eyeing each other like two wolves over a sick stag while Kaiulani held the cipher-key in her palm, the New York financier had grown markedly deferential toward the dark-robed woman beside him. "Three thousand go to the Washoe silver drifts and four thousand to the Puget Sound timber-gangs. The remainder board the boxcars at Oakland to double-track the Pennsylvania Central through the Alleghenies. Yet the Municipal Board in Philadelphia wired my desk again this morning. They protest that our bringing Chinese coolies and Japanese garrison regiments into the eastern towns is driving the native mechanics into the woods to join the Fenian bushwhackers."

Kaiulani kept her face to the window. She wore her habitual black bombazine, the gold collar of the Insular Diet gleaming dully against her collarbone in the yellow fog-light. Beneath the glass, a squad of Hawaiian provosts stamped the brass neck-tags of a newly arrived company of northern Chinese stone-masons while her hands, encased in tight gloves of black kidskin, rested motionless upon the redwood rail.

"Let the Philadelphia mechanics go into the woods if they prefer acorns to silver, Mr. Schuyler," Kaiulani said, her voice low and cold. "For every Irish bricklayer in Pennsylvania who throws down his trowel to listen to a rebel preacher, I have ten men from the Yellow River down on that wharf who will lay twice the brick for half the rice, and who do not care whether Mr. Lincoln is hiding in Montreal or in hell."

"It is the cost of the garrison transports that troubles the syndicate directors, Your Highness," Schuyler said. He lowered his tone and glanced toward the end of the gallery, where two Satsuma staff-captains from Admiral Takashima’s naval board stood over the unloading of the tin-ingots with cold, proprietary eyes. "While the Protector remains in Peking with Marshal Vance, the Admirals here are demanding another six million thalers for the Cavite drydocks, and General Caleb Vance insists that we cannot spare a single locomotive from the Missouri military district to haul Boston coal. Every department pulls the blanket toward its own side of the bed. If, God forbid, the Protector’s winter cough should worsen in that northern ice—"

Kaiulani turned her head slowly. Her dark, deep-set eyes fixed upon the plump banker until Schuyler’s tongue clicked dry against his teeth.

"The Protector’s cough is entirely mended, Mr. Schuyler," she said, each syllable cut as cleanly as a diamond scratching glass. "He walked the walls of the Tartar City yesterday for three hours without his cloak. And while he remains across the water, the blanket remains pinned where I have nailed it."

She picked up a stamped parchment schedule from the clerk’s desk beside the pillar and held it out toward him.

"You will inform the Philadelphia and Boston boards that the Pacific Arc is a single cistern," Kaiulani continued. Below the iron turnstiles, the long line of blue-bloused Chinese laborers marched out toward the waiting ferry-boats, their breath rising in a single cloud of white steam under the lamps of the wharf. "Pennsylvania iron goes to Nagasaki to plate the fleet, Nevada silver goes to Shanghai to buy the silk, and Shantung muscle goes to the Potomac and the Hudson to rebuild the roads the Yankees tore up. If any syndicate director on Montgomery Street or Wall Street withholds a single carload of rolling-stock from my labor-trains this month, I will act before the Protector’s cable arrives. At noon I will sit in the High Court of Receivership to annul his bank’s charter under the Insular Emergency Statute, and divide his wharf-shares among Lord Shimazu’s factors. Do we understand one another, Comptroller?"

Schuyler bowed so low that his gold pince-nez swung free from his waistcoat ribbon. "Perfectly, Your Highness. The locomotives will be at the Oakland mole before the six o’clock tide."

Silk hat held tight against his chest, the banker retreated down the timber stairs. Kaiulani remained alone above the roaring human river of the barracoons. In her pocket lay the private cipher that had come from Peking three hours ago: Marcus Vance’s chief surgeon reported that the Protector had suffered a second, milder spasm on the steps of the Temple of Heaven and was hiding the digitalis phials in his saddle-holsters.

Beyond the dirty glass, out on the gray water of the bay, a Hawaiian war-corvette saluted a Japanese troop-transport with three blasts of her steam-whistle. Copper wire and iron rail bound the two halves of the earth together now, with empires reduced to labor-gangs and kings to customs-clerks; yet as the cold fog seeped through the casement joints against her cheek, the overstrained timbers creaked beneath the paint.

***

Peking lay under the blinding, crystalline winter sky of the northern plain. Beneath that dome of pale imperial blue, so cold and dry that the breath of the sentry-horses froze into white powder on their bits before it could form icicles, spread the vast, silent sea of yellow glazed tiles roofing the Forbidden City.

On the afternoon of the nineteenth of January, 1869, Elias walked alone up the central marble ramp of the Hall of Supreme Harmony, treading the carved dragon-stone pavement over which, for five hundred years, only the bearers of the Son of Heaven’s palanquin had passed.

Thirty-two years had gone by since the autumn twilight when he pried the hot iron hinge-straps from the threshold of his father’s burning cabin in Kentucky with a green hickory limb. His mud-stained cavalry boots met the razor-edged wind coming down from Mongolia. Having left behind both the gold-braided uniform and the heavy silver collar sent across the sea by the Monterey Diet for his investiture as Sovereign of the Realm, he wore the same severe, high-collared dark blue wool greatcoat he had worn at Vicksburg and Washington, its skirt whipping around his legs.

Fifty paces below him, at the foot of the triple white marble terrace where the gilded bronze cranes and incense-burners stood cold and smokeless in the sun, General Marcus Vance leaned heavily upon his saber-scabbard beside Rear-Admiral Takashima and a silent, fur-hatted delegation of the Grand Secretariat under Prince Kung. Marcus’s dry, rattling cough echoed off the vermilion pillars behind him like a worn-out bellows pumping air through cracked leather.

Elias did not look back. He climbed the last ten marble steps. Two thousand soldiers of the Virginia Auxiliary and the Satsuma Guard stood drawn up across the immense flagged courtyard below, so he measured his stride to keep the treacherous, fluttering monster behind his breastbone from betraying a stumble. At the top platform, he rested his scarred right palm against one of the massive, red-lacquered cedar columns supporting the double-eaved roof, and looked southward.

Before him, gate beyond gate, court beyond court, stretched the geometric heart of the oldest empire on the globe: the Meridian Gate, the bridges of white jade arching over the frozen Golden Water, and beyond the towering outer bastions, the brown, smoke-hazed immensity of the Chinese plain rolling away toward the ocean he had made his own.

The sun caught the ten thousand yellow tiles below him and turned them into a floor of solid sunset gold. A strange, intoxicating lightness filled his skull, sharper than the thin winter air and sweeter than the strong wine of the Rio Frio.

At twenty, reading the dog-eared Latin histories in the dead priest’s library at Mission Dolores while the rain beat on the adobe roof, he had paused over the pages where Arrian described the Macedonian standing upon the banks of the Hyphasis to weep because the world had run out of horizons before his sword was dull. Alexander had been a boy with a bronze spear who conquered a strip of desert from Greece to the Indus; his empire shattered into four pieces before his corpse was cold in Babylon because he had only horse-flesh and parchment to bind it.

*I have gone farther than the Greek,* Elias thought. His lips moved soundlessly in the cold wind as he walked out from the shadow of the eaves into the open doorway of the great throne-hall. *He stopped at the edge of the eastern mountains. Having taken the mountains in my stride and bridged the great water he never knew existed, I have bolted the two ends of the earth together with steel rails and copper wire so tight that not a sparrow falls between Boston and Canton without its weight being entered in my books.*

Inside the cavernous gloom of the Hall of Supreme Harmony, the air was twenty degrees colder than the terrace outside. It smelled of ancient dry dust and cedar-rot, mingled with the cold tallow of ceremonial candles extinguished when the Empress Dowager fled westward toward Shensi two months before. Felled in the forests of Szechuan three centuries ago and covered in flaking gold leaf, seventy-two giant pillars of *nanmu* timber rose into the dark coffered ceiling where carved wooden dragons coiled around the pearl of heaven.

*Clink-clank, clink-clank.* Elias’s spurs rang across the black, polished bricks of the floor, baked in the kilns of Soochow and soaked in boiling tung-oil until they shone like dark ice. He climbed the seven steps of the high lacquer dais at the center of the hall and stood before the Dragon Throne.

Footsteps scraped against the marble sill of the wide southern doors behind him. While Prince Kung halted outside on the terrace and refused to cross the sill where the barbarian’s boots had profaned the sanctuary, Marcus Vance and Rear-Admiral Takashima stepped into the slant of pale winter sunlight, their breath smoking white in the freezing vault.

"Protector," Marcus said. Hoarse and thin, his voice echoed among the seventy-two golden columns as he held out a portfolio just brought up from the Tientsin wire-head. "The plenipotentiaries of the northern provinces are waiting in the Board of Ceremonies to hear the terms of the salt-gabelle mortgage. And the surgeon asks—"

"Damn the surgeon," Elias said. Without turning around, he reached out with his bare, weather-chapped right hand and laid his fingers upon the carved gold dragon-head of the throne’s armrest. The wood was colder than the ice on the Platte. "Come up here to the steps, Marcus. Both of you. Look out through those doors."

Slowly, Marcus and the Japanese admiral walked across the black bricks. They stood at the base of the lacquer platform and looked up at the tall, gray-haired figure framed against the gilded screen of the Ming emperors.

"Twenty-two years ago, Marcus," Elias said, turning to face them as his rough, low voice filled the silent throne-room, his left hand slipping beneath the breast-flap of his coat while his pale gaze burned unblinking in the half-dark, "your uncle Caleb and I stood on a rock in the Sierra snow and looked down at an empty sea. In Washington they told us that the continent belonged to the lawyers, and in London they told us that the ocean belonged to the Queen’s ships. Look at the map in your hand today. Washington is gone. Borders are gone. From the ice of the Yukon to the gates of this palace, three hundred million men eat bread from my granaries and march when my bugle blows, coining my silver."

He took half a step down the lacquer stair. His right hand rose to point straight through the open red doors toward the blinding blue sky above the southern gates.

"Alexander died in a fever-swamp at thirty-two because he thought the world ended at the Indian sea," Elias said, his voice rising until the old dust sifted down from the dragon-beams overhead. "We have no edge to stop at. By the spring thaw, our broad-gauge rails will run from this gate through the Kalgan pass straight across the Gobi to Irkutsk, and when the Russian Tsar cannot pay the interest on the Sitka monitors next winter, we will foreclose on Siberia all the way to the Urals and look down into Europe from the back door! Takashima, tell your Emperor at Edo that the title of Protector belongs to a republic’s nursery. On the first of May, when the fleet assembles at Honolulu, the Diet will proclaim the—"

A sudden, terrible cough from Marcus Vance broke across the words. The Marshal doubled over at the foot of the stairs, handkerchief pressed to his mouth; as Elias stepped down the second lacquer tread to catch his general’s shoulder, his own boot-heel slipped on the frozen tung-oil brick, his left hand tore at his collar as if an unseen wire had just been drawn tight around his windpipe, and the seventy-two golden pillars spun into a single blinding whirlpool of dark red lacquer.

His knees never touched the Ming bricks. Blackness crept in at the edges of his sight, and a cold iron vice beneath his sternum squeezed the breath from his lungs in a ragged wheeze, yet Elias locked his right elbow around the carved wooden tail of the dragon balustrade to hold his two hundred pounds upright by the stubborn refusal of his wrist-bones to yield before a Satsuma admiral. For six weeks they hid that second stumble behind the high walls of the northern capital. They fed the Protector digitalis in porcelain teacups while Takashima and Cornelius Schuyler’s cable-agents circled the sickroom and measured the breadth of his coffin with their eyes.

# Chapter 12: The Bering Caissons

By June, when the sub-arctic summer finally broke the pack-ice of the sixty-sixth parallel, Elias Thorne stood upon the basalt headlands of Cape Prince of Wales, where the uttermost western horn of the American continent thrusts its black volcanic chin out toward the bleak, snow-streaked cliffs of East Cape in Asia.

Between the two worlds ran fifty-three miles of racing, lead-colored water, split dead in the center by the twin granite tables of the Diomede Islands.

Out of the Chukchi Sea came a wind heavy with green glacier-melt and crushed granite, soured by the coal-smoke of six armored ice-breakers ramming their reinforced steel prows into the rotting floes two hundred yards offshore. On the gravel beach below the cliff, where the whale-rib huts of the Eskimo had stood the previous autumn, four thousand Cantonese and Irish convicts from the Yukon camps dragged massive timber caissons toward the surf behind wheezing steam-winches. Overhead, seagulls screamed around the tall, raw pine derricks of the Imperial Engineering Corps.

Inside a glass-enclosed wind-shelter bolted directly to the bedrock of the cape, Elias sat wrapped to the chin in a heavy sea-otter pelisse. He had lost thirty pounds since the winter in Peking. The skin of his cheeks hung slack and gray as wet buckskin around his jaw, and a brazier of glowing Nanaimo anthracite burned between his boots to keep the arctic damp out of his congested lungs. Pressed shoulder to shoulder in a closeness that smelled of wet wool and mutiny, the four pillars of his realm stood around the cramped, cedar-planked shelter: Marcus Vance, his sunken eyes burning with the dry hectic flush of consumption; Rear-Admiral Takashima; Cornelius Schuyler, shivering in three fur waistcoats; and Lady Kaiulani, positioned behind Elias’s chair in her black robes.

"The soundings across the channel never exceed thirty fathoms, Mr. Schuyler," Elias said. The resonant bugle that had once rallied the rangers on the Rio Frio had dried to a gravelly wheeze, requiring a sharp pull of breath after every fifth word, yet no man in the glass box looked away from his face. "Twenty-seven miles from this rock to the Big Diomede. Twenty-six miles from the Little Diomede to the Siberian shore. A mud-bottom overlaid with gravel, and two granite islands placed by providence in the middle of the ditch for central piers."

Schuyler adjusted his fogged spectacles. Across the drafting-trestle, Major Sterling had pinned a six-foot blueprint roll, and the banker stared down at the measurements in open horror. "Protector, the syndicate boards in San Francisco and New York have examined Major Sterling’s estimates with the utmost care. Sinking four hundred pneumatic cast-iron caissons into a tide-race where the winter pack-ice moves at six knots with the weight of ten million tons, and spanning fifty miles of sub-arctic sea with tubular steel trusses high enough to clear a whaler's masts, will consume eight hundred thousand tons of Bessemer plate and two hundred million gold thalers! The Market Street Mint is already overdrawn by the Yangtze railway bonds. The Boston banks threaten to suspend the quarterly tribute if we float another forced loan this autumn. Why build a bridge at the top of the world where nothing lives but walruses and ice-bears, when our steamers cross from Puget Sound to Vladivostok in twelve days?"

"Because a British cruiser can sink a steamer in a fog, and a typhoon can close a sea-lane." From beneath the sea-otter fur, Elias lifted his gaunt right hand and tapped a blunt, bluish fingernail against the inked span of the Bering Bridge. "When my heart missed its beat in Shanghai last November, Mr. Schuyler, how long did it take you and Lord Shimazu’s factors to whisper in the telegraph room about dividing the shipping monopolies between Edo and San Francisco?"

Schuyler’s pudgy cheeks went the color of lard. Beside him, Rear-Admiral Takashima’s hand stiffened on the hilt of his dirk.

"You think I did not hear you through the oak door?" Elias asked. A grim smile pulled at the corner of his mouth as he looked from the banker to the samurai. "You think because a man lies on a mattress with mustard on his chest, he is already under the sod? Leave this empire held together only by wooden ships and copper wires under the salt water, and the morning after you bury me at Monterey, Takashima’s admirals will cut the cable at Midway to take Asia for the Tenno, while Schuyler’s friends in New York call back the Montreal lawyers and sell the Atlantic provinces to London."

Behind his chair, Lady Kaiulani rested her gloved fingers on the high wooden back of the seat. "The Providentor knows his heirs well, gentlemen," she said. "Water divides. Iron holds."

"We are going to bolt the two continents together so tight that ten generations of traitors will lack the chisels to pry them apart," Elias said. He leaned forward over the blueprint until the heat of the charcoal brazier reddened his hollow chin. "Double-track broad-gauge steel from the Oakland depot, up the Fraser and the Yukon, straight across the Bering piers on tubular trusses eighty feet above the ice-pack, and down through the Stanovoy mountains to the Amur and Peking. When a locomotive can roll from the piers of Manhattan to the gates of the Forbidden City in fourteen days without wetting a wheel in salt water, East and West will vanish. Only the road will remain."

"And the Tsar’s charter for the western abutment, Protector?" Across the strait, the Siberian shore showed dimly through the lifting sea-smoke; Takashima kept his narrow eyes fixed on that gray coast. "Baron Stoeckl sold us the American ice in sixty-six because he believed the water between these capes was an eternal moat. According to our survey-parties on the Chukotka peninsula, the Governor-General at Irkutsk has refused to countersign the land-grants for the western bridge-head, and four sotnias of Amur Cossacks are riding north from Anadyrsk to drive our engineers into the sea."

Elias coughed once into his fur collar. His eyes watered from the iron stab in his breast. He looked at Marcus Vance.

"The Tsar owes the San Francisco Treasury four million thalers in unpaid interest on the Kronstadt engine-patents," Elias said. "If Alexander refuses to sign the right-of-way for the western piers at his desk in St. Petersburg, Marshal Vance will take three regiments across the strait on the ice-breakers this afternoon and sign it on the ground. Put the first caisson into the water, Major Sterling. I intend to ride the pilot-engine across that channel before I die."

***

In the secret archives of the Winter Palace for the sixty-ninth year of the century, the design of the Bering Bridge marks the shift of modern power from the maritime rim to the continental heartland. For three hundred years, ever since Yermak the Cossack crossed the Urals with his matchlock-men, the Empire of the Tsars had pushed eastward through birch-forests and tundra like a glacier moving in the dark, guarded at its back by the polar ice and before it by an empty ocean that no European army could cross.

Now came the pale, sleepless midsummer nights of St. Petersburg. Outside, the granite embankments of the Neva shone with a mother-of-pearl twilight at midnight; inside the Malachite Room of the Winter Palace, where General Milyutin had pinned the intercepted lithographs of Major Sterling’s tubular bridge across a green military map of Eastern Siberia, Emperor Alexander the Second paced beneath the gilded ceiling through the drifting smoke of his papiros.

Russian memory had been bred on the Tartar hordes and the Grande Armée crossing the Niemen. A bridge was a spear-shaft.

"Baron Stoeckl assured the Imperial Council that we were selling a frozen wilderness to a maritime syndicate that looked southward toward Canton," the Tsar said. He halted beside the malachite pilasters, his tall, heavy-shouldered frame rigid inside his Chevalier Guard tunic. Through the tall windows, the golden spire of the Peter and Paul Fortress pricked the white night sky like a bayonet. "We took his seven million thalers to build railways to Odessa and Sebastopol, believing the Strait of Behring was fifty miles of pack-ice that no steam-engine could ever cross. Now you tell me this San Francisco dictator is driving four hundred cast-iron piers into the sea-floor at the Diomedes, and that his Japanese vassals are already grading a double-track bed up the valley of the Anadyr!"

General Milyutin dispensed with the soothing platitudes of the diplomatic corps. Having studied the campaigns of Vicksburg and the Nankou Pass, the War Minister understood what a broad-gauge rail-line meant with Marcus Vance at the throttle.

"Sire, eighty-pound steel rails and stone blockhouses every ten versts across the tundra are built for war," Milyutin answered. He tapped the blank, unmapped expanse between the Stanovoy Range and Lake Baikal. "We have scarce twelve thousand line-infantry and six regiments of irregular Cossacks scattered across four thousand miles of wilderness between Irkutsk and the sea. East of Perm, we have no railroad. In winter, a courier takes eighty days by sleigh to carry an order from this room to the mouth of the Amur. Let Thorne’s engineers link their Yukon track to the Siberian shore, and San Francisco will sit fourteen days by locomotive from the heart of Asia while our own reinforcements trudge through the mud of Tomsk."

Beside the cold porcelain stove, Prince Gorchakov adjusted his spectacles in his armchair with a dry, papery sigh. "And yet, Your Majesty, how are we to forbid him? The British Cabinet has washed its hands of the northern sea since the fall of Shanghai, and Mr. Schuyler’s agents in Frankfurt hold forty million rubles of our state railway obligations. Yesterday, when I reminded the Pacifica envoy that Chukotka is the sovereign soil of the Russian Crown, that Polynesian princess who signs their maritime decrees in red ink sent back a note claiming that since the Ministry of Finance is six months in arrears on the Vladivostok dockyard bonds, the Confederation is exercising the right of a mortgage-holder to improve the bailiwick."

"A mortgage-holder!" Alexander brought his fist down upon the malachite table. The bronze inkwells leaped. The Romanov autocracy had survived Charles of Sweden and Bonaparte of France, yet this American border-ruffian and his cabinet of Japanese and island ministers treated the Crown like a bankrupt squire, a humiliation that burned like raw vitriol. "Today he claims the right to lay iron rails across Chukotka to collect four million thalers. Tomorrow, when his tracks reach the Lena and the Amur, he will claim the gold-washings of Nerchinsk and the forests of Baikal to pay for the coal his engines burned on the road!"

The Tsar walked to the map. With the back of his gloved hand, he swept the lithograph of the Bering Bridge onto the parquet floor.

"Send a priority wire to Governor-General Korsakov at Irkutsk before the sun rises," Alexander said, his pale, protuberant eyes fixed upon his War Minister. "Tell him to mobilize the Trans-Baikal Cossack Host and move every battery of bronze field-guns on the Amur northward toward the Anadyr divide. They will not wait for a formal declaration from St. Petersburg. Tear up the American survey-stakes, burn their timber-trestles, and drive their Chinese digging-gangs back into the sea. If the whale wishes to crawl out upon the land, the bear’s claws will be waiting in the moss."

***

Four thousand miles east of the Neva’s marble quays, twenty-two hours of blinding, brassy sun hung low along the northern rim of the tundra. Black arctic mosquitoes bred in the heat, thickening the air into a humming gray fog that choked the horses' nostrils through their net-veils.

Three leagues inland from the western shore of the Bering Strait, General Marcus Vance sat upon an upturned barrel of tallow-grease beside the open door of an armored flatcar. Beneath the wheels of the construction train, two thousand Cantonese graders had stripped the spongy Siberian sphagnum moss down to the blue permafrost, laying a mattress of felled larch-trunks and crushed volcanic basalt to take the seven-foot cross-ties of the Asian Trunk Line. Sour swamp-water, creosote oil, and wet horse-blankets fouled the damp air, mixed with the green alder-bark smudge-fires that the Virginia infantrymen kept burning around their rifle-pits against the flies.

Marcus had laid aside his coat. Though the July afternoon stood at a damp sixty degrees, night-sweat soaked his linen shirt dark between the shoulder-blades; in his left hand he held a tin cup of boiled willow-bark and quinine, while his right thumb marked his place in a calfskin calculation-book.

Wait-times were lengthening. In an over-extended campaign, that lag was the first symptom of decay, and Marcus recorded it with the displeasure of a watchmaker listening to a rusted mainspring. Along the Platte or the Potomac in the old days, when he had signed a requisition for ten thousand kegs of track-spikes or four hundred mules, the iron had arrived on the flatcars within the hour; now, before a single bolt or fish-plate ever reached the ships at Puget Sound, it had to be pried loose from the jealous fingers of three rival ministries.

"Look at these priming-tubes from the Market Street arsenal, Marshal," Colonel Armistead said. He limped up the gravel embankment with a handful of corroded brass friction-primers in his scarred palm, his face swollen with mosquito-bites beneath smeared axle-grease. "Half of ’em are filled with sweepings and brick-dust instead of fulminate. Mr. Schuyler’s new civilian contractors in Philadelphia are shaving two cents a hundred off the ordnance contracts and splitting the silver with the Treasury clerks, while Admiral Takashima’s quartermasters down at the beach refused to unload our spare repeating-carbine cases this morning until the ice-breakers had finished landing twelve hundred tons of cut granite for the Satsuma war-memorial on the Diomede rock! If the Protector stays in his sick-bed at San Francisco another month, the bankers and the samurai will have stolen the tires off our caissons before we see a single Russian."

Marcus took a slow sip of the bitter quinine. Above the western ridge, the dwarf-willows gave way to barren ridges of shattered slate. Since the eleven days in Shanghai when Elias had lain behind the locked doors of the Admiralty, the iron unity of the Confederation had hair-cracked along every joint. To Schuyler’s syndicate directors in San Francisco, who wanted capital for their Yangtze cotton-mills, the Bering Bridge was a bottomless sinkhole; to Takashima’s admirals, any land-road into Asia threatened the Japanese Navy’s monopoly over the northern sea-lanes. Both factions were quietly starving Marcus’s vanguard of coal and brass. They hoped the Siberian winter would freeze the survey-parties in their tracks and force the old man in the Citadel to abandon the work.

"We do not need the Philadelphia primers for the mortars today, Colonel," Marcus said. His dry whisper barely carried over the clang of the Chinese spike-mauls behind the car. "And as for Admiral Takashima’s granite, I had Major Sterling’s sappers dump four hundred blocks of it into the soft bog at the second culvert an hour ago for trestle ballast. When the Admiral comes ashore to unveil his monument, he can look for it under my locomotive wheels."

He rose stiffly from the tallow-barrel. A familiar bubbling rattle caught in his left lung. Unsloshing his field-glasses, he aimed them a mile ahead where a solitary horseman in the buckskin shirt of the Nez Perce scouts came galloping hard down the shale ridge, his pony’s hooves kicking up splashes of black peat-water from the bogs.

Behind the scout, crowning the skyline where the trail dipped down toward the Anadyr river-basin, a long bristle of eight-foot steel-tipped lances rose out of the willow-scrub.

"There is your Russian answer to the mortgage-note, Armistead," Marcus said. He braced his elbows against the iron side of the flatcar and focused the lenses. "Six sotnias of the Amur Cossacks, about seven hundred saddles. And they have dragged two batteries of bronze nine-pounders up the river-bed on sledges. They are forming line for a charge against the Chinese grading-gangs at the end of the track."

Down at the rail-head four hundred yards away, the unarmed Cantonese coolies raised a shrill cry. While a Russian bugler sounded the gallop, the wild, long-coated horsemen in their tall sheepskin caps came trotting down the slope with the flat blades of their curved *shashka* sabers flashing in the low arctic sun. Several hundred laborers dropped their shovels. Bolting backward down the wooden sleepers toward the beach, they threatened to swamp the two companies of the First Pennsylvania Auxiliary who knelt behind a breastwork of stacked iron rails.

"Shall I pull the coolies back behind the flatcars, General?" Armistead asked. His hand dropped to the holster of his Colt. Across the spongy turf the Cossack line broke into a dead run, their shrill, wolfish *Hourrah!* echoing off the basalt hills as the two Russian bronze guns on the ridge opened fire in a dirty puff of white black-powder smoke.

A nine-pound round-shot buried itself with a *thuck* in the frozen peat fifty yards short of the embankment.

"If you let two thousand coolies run through the Pennsylvania line, they will carry the riflemen into the ditch with them," Marcus said. He reached into his coat for his pocket chronometer and clicked open the case. "Tell Captain Rafferty to drop the first ten labourers who cross the ditch with the bayonet; that will turn the rest back to their picks. Then run the locomotive forward fifty yards and open with the two steam-Gatlings from the cupola at four hundred yards’ range. Aim low into the chests of the horses, leaving the riders alone. Three hundred miles from his base, a dismounted Cossack in high boots is a corpse."

***

Six days after the Amur Cossacks left three hundred dead ponies and two bronze cannon in the black moss of the Anadyr trail, the mid-July fog lay cold and motionless against the glass dome of the Citadel conservatory in San Francisco.

Inside the steaming, fern-choked vault, the eighty-five-degree air smelled of decaying orchid-bark and wet marble, thick with the bitter herbal smoke of the stramonium leaves that the physicians burned in a silver dish beside Elias’s wicker chair to ease his breathing spasms.

The Protector had stayed out of the Council Room since the fleet returned from the north in late June. Propped upright among dark blue horsehair cushions beside the carp-basin, he kept a heavy woolen lap-robe tucked tightly around his shrunken thighs over the watery swelling that had crept from his ankles to his knees over the past fortnight. On a low redwood table at his right elbow lay the bronze-mounted telegraph repeater connected directly to the St. Petersburg and Irkutsk cable; at his left sat Lady Kaiulani, her black mourning-gown rustling as she sorted the afternoon dispatches from the four quarters of the basin.

Before the carp-pool stood Cornelius Schuyler and Rear-Admiral Takashima, summoned from a stormy session of the Joint Supply Board downstairs.

"It is sheer madness to push the rail-head another mile into Chukotka, Protector!" Schuyler said. Wet conservatory heat shone on his plump face as he mopped his neck with a silk handkerchief; though he spoke to Elias, his eyes flicked toward Kaiulani’s calm profile to gauge how many weeks of life remained in the grey-faced shell in the wicker chair. "The Rothschilds in Paris and Frankfurt have just refused our new issue of Siberian Bridge debentures following the skirmish on the Anadyr! The Tsar has ordered six army corps from Moscow and Poland to march toward the Urals, and the Russian cruisers at Vladivostok have seized three of our timber-brigs off Sakhalin! If we fight a continental war across five thousand miles of frozen desert to build a road nobody wants, the silver reserve on Market Street will fall below the twenty-percent statutory limit before October!"

"And the Imperial Navy cannot spare another ton of compound armor-plate for Major Sterling’s bridge-caissons, Excellency," Takashima added. His voice was stiff with the formal courtesy of Edo, yet it carried an edge of iron defiance never heard in that room while Elias stood on two good legs. "Lord Shimazu wires from Nagasaki that the Russian Baltic Squadron has passed Gibraltar heading for the Cape of Good Hope. My board has therefore suspended the shipment of the forty girder-spans from the Sacramento rolling-mills and diverted the steel to complete the two new turret-rams at Yokosuka. The sea is our wall; let General Vance hold the beach at Cape Prince of Wales with his rifles and leave the Siberian marshes to the wolves."

For ten seconds Elias sat still. Only his broad, bluish-nailed hands upon the wicker arms of the chair closed slowly until the woven rattan cracked under his knuckles. As the stramonium smoke curled past his hollow cheek, his enlarged heart beat beneath his navy wool coat with a heavy, laboring thud—*one, two, pause, three*—like a crippled donkey-engine hauling a forty-ton boiler up a wet grade.

"You diverted my bridge-steel, Admiral?" Elias asked. His voice was a dry, gravelly scrape at the bottom of his throat, scarce louder than the drip of the tree-ferns into the pool.

"By vote of the Joint Naval Commission this morning, Protector," Takashima replied. He lifted his chin slightly and exchanged a swift, sidelong glance with Schuyler. "In view of Your Excellency’s... temporary indisposition, the Commission deemed it necessary to prioritize the defense of the Western Sea."

Elias turned his head half an inch toward Kaiulani. "Give me the wire from Irkutsk."

She lifted the blue slip from her lap and placed it between his fingers. Her dark hand brushed his cold knuckle. Pitiless and clear as volcanic glass, her eyes met his; she had promised him in this very room that she would sit beside his throne and watch his boiler burst, yet looking at the banker and the samurai standing like impatient buzzards on the marble flags, she hated the jackals more than the lion.

"General Korsakov at Irkutsk wires in the Tsar’s name," Elias said. He ignored the paper he already knew by heart and locked his pale, sunken eyes upon Takashima’s throat. "He offers an armistice along the coast if we dismantle the Diomede caissons before August and pay two million thalers indemnity for the Cossacks Marcus shot in the moss."

"A most reasonable basis for negotiation!" Schuyler cried, taking half a step forward. "With two million thalers we can stabilize the Frankfurt exchange by Monday, and—"

Elias kicked the woolen lap-robe from his swollen knees. He seized the heavy iron walking-stick leaning against the basin and hauled himself upright. Schuyler staggered back. His plump heel caught against a glazed terracotta fern-pot, and muddy water slopped over his patent-leather shoes. Even Takashima’s hand dropped to the gold-wrapped hilt of his naval dirk as the tall, skeletal figure towered over the carp-pool and swayed on pillar-like legs, a dark flush of blood surging up into his weathered cheekbones. For three weeks down on Montgomery Street, inside the cedar-paneled smoking room of the Union Club, the Comptroller and the Admiral had divided the post-Thorne world over glasses of dry Madeira: the Eastern banking syndicate would take back the Atlantic customs-houses and sell the Yukon mines to a London joint-stock company, while the Satsuma Navy severed the northern bridge-head to keep the Yellow Sea as a private fief of the Tenno. They had measured his digitalis; they had bribed his body-servant to count the wet handkerchiefs in his laundry-basket and gauged the water in his ankles to the eighth of an inch.

"If a single girder-span is missing from the Sitka freight-steamer when the tide turns at six o’clock tonight, Takashima," Elias roared, the old frontier thunder breaking through the fluid in his chest like a twelve-pounder bursting a plank door, "I will have Marshal Vance march a battalion of Virginia riflemen into the Japanese compound on Rincon Hill and hang every member of your Naval Board from the telegraph poles by their own silk sashes! And if you mention the Frankfurt exchange in my hearing again before the bridge is bolted to the Siberian rock, Mr. Schuyler, I will strip your coat off your back and send you up the Chilkoot chute with seventy pounds of pig-iron chained to your spine!"

He struck the tessellated marble floor with the ferrule of his iron stick. The blow cracked a square of green serpentine in half and drove the golden carp into the dark weeds at the bottom of the pool. His trembling left hand pointed at the bronze telegraph key on the table.

"Sit down at that key, Kaiulani," Elias said. His breath whistled through his teeth like wind through a keyhole while he leaned his weight hard upon the stick to keep from sinking back into the cushions under their eyes. "Clear the line through the Bering cable to Irkutsk and the Winter Palace. Tell the Russian operators to take this down in plain French so every clerk from Lake Baikal to the Neva can read it before supper."

Kaiulani slid onto the velvet stool before the repeater. Without hurrying or looking at the two men beside the ferns, she closed her black-gloved fingers over the vulcanite knob, and the circuit opened with a metallic click.

"From Thorne, Providentor of the Grand Confederation, to Alexander Romanov at St. Petersburg," Elias dictated. The armature chattered in the damp heat of the conservatory as his gaze swept from the blanched, sweating jowls of the New York banker to the Satsuma admiral's rigid brow. "You sold me the threshold of the North, and no man locks the door in my face after I have paid the silver. My engineers are laying two miles of broad-gauge iron a day toward the valley of the Lena. If the gates of Siberia are not opened to my surveyors from the Strait to Lake Baikal before the first snow falls on the Stanovoy mountains, I will cross before your six corps walk the Urals. I will put two hundred thousand American and Japanese rifles across the Bering piers before the ice breaks and water my horses in the Obi over the ashes of Irkutsk. Send that first, Kaiulani. Then keep the circuit open to the northern fleet."

***

To the Chronicler standing upon the basalt heights of East Cape during that sun-bleached August of 1869, the mobilization of the Pacifica Armada in the waters of the Bering Strait belonged to the nightmare of a mechanized Titan. For ten thousand years, those fifty-three miles of racing green water between the continents had carried only the skin-covered kayaks of the Chukchi hunters and the occasional grease-stained topsails of a New Bedford whaling-bark dodging the summer pack-ice. Now the roof of the world was black with iron. A hundred furnaces soured the air. In the arithmetic of his own failing arteries, the Providentor had calculated that his empire would fracture into three warring succession-states the morning after his funeral unless the army and the fleet were locked together in the vise of an irreversible foreign campaign; he had therefore emptied every slip from Puget Sound to Nagasaki into the northern funnel. Between the granite tables of the Diomede Islands and the gravel beaches of Chukotka rode forty-six ocean-going vessels of war beside eighty-two iron-hulled colliers, cable-layers, and troop-transports, all moored in six parallel lines five miles long against the six-knot tide-race. The August air hung low and suffocating over the strait in a greasy yellow-gray canopy of burned Nanaimo coal-soot, boiled whale-oil lubricant, and sulfurous fumes from the floating foundry-hulks. Day and night, beneath a sun that never dipped more than four degrees below the northern horizon, the sea vibrated with the sub-aqueous thrum of steam-condensers and pneumatic air-pumps.

Along the three-mile line of the eastern bridge-way, twenty-eight cylindrical caissons of bolted San Francisco boiler-plate, each forty feet in diameter and filled with two thousand tons of Sierra granite rubble and Portland cement, already rose like a row of decapitated black towers out of the churning white water. Between them, monster floating sheer-legs mounted on double-hulled iron pontoons groaned as their wire cables hoisted three-hundred-foot spans of lattice-steel girder into the freezing mist, while swarms of Cantonese and Irish riveters clung like black beetles to the swinging iron sixty feet above the waves and dropped showers of orange sparks from their red-hot portable forges to hiss out in the frigid swells below. The vanguard steamed through the narrow channels. Twenty-two shallow-draft armored rams and turret-monitors of the *Sacramento* and *Kamehameha* classes pushed past the piers, their low steel decks piled high with bags of Welsh and Vancouver anthracite to save bunker-space, their sixteen-inch Krupp and Rodman gun-barrels coated thick with white tallow-lead against the arctic salt-rime. Aboard the eighty troop-liners, sixty thousand men sat packed between the iron bulkheads: veterans of the Potomac and the Shenandoah who had grown grey in the Pacifica blue; divisions of Choshu and Satsuma infantry whose regimental priests burned aloeswood before brass mirrors bolted to the ships’ mainmasts; and regiments of Hawaiian pioneers who sang the canoe-chants of Oahu while sharpening eighteen-inch trowel-bayonets on steam-driven grindstones. On the ice-slicked bridge-wings, officers walked with their collars turned up against the sleet and listened to the rattle of the anchor-chains, dreading the hour when the old man in the glass house three thousand miles to the south might stop breathing before the first gun fired and leave sixty thousand armed men of four races trapped together in an iron cage at the end of the world.

***

In San Francisco, Elias had refused his bedchamber. For four days and nights following the scene by the carp-pool, he had lived inside the high-arched Map Room on the fourth floor of the Chancery. He had ordered his iron camp-cot, the narrow frame of bolted gas-pipe he had slept upon before the walls of Vicksburg, set up directly beneath the thirty-foot bronze relief-chart of the Pacific Basin. The room smelled of a dying sickroom, thick and sour with camphor-liniment, burnt stramonium weed, cold mutton-broth, and the sharp ammonia the surgeons used when the fluid in his pleura choked him at three in the morning. Yet he wore his dark blue Engineer’s tunic buttoned to the third hook. His heavy cavalry boots remained laced over his swollen calves; once the boots were cut off his feet, he would never get them on again, and a Caesar in bedroom slippers was already half a corpse to his marshals.

On the afternoon of the twelfth of August, the yellow summer fog pressed blind against the tall western casements. Around the green baize table sat the four heirs of the realm, summoned to watch him move the iron across the board: Kaiulani at the telegraph desk, her black bombazine skirts hiding the small Derringer pistol she carried in her reticule against the afternoon when Takashima’s marines or Schuyler’s provosts might try to seize the wire-room; Cornelius Schuyler at the foot, his ledger-books open while his pale eyes tracked the purple, distended vein pulsing in Elias’s neck; Rear-Admiral Takashima standing rigid beside the Japanese coast-charts; and Major Sterling at the speaking-tube. Elias sat on the edge of the iron camp-cot. His scarred hands rested upon the cross-piece of his iron walking-stick between his knees. Every breath sounded in the quiet room like a dry brush dragged across sandpaper.

"General Korsakov has burned the timber-depots at Anadyrsk and pulled his Cossacks back behind the Kolyma range," Elias said. He spoke slowly, rationing his wind as a desert scout rations water from a canteen, though his pale gaze remained sharp as flint. "He thinks because the tundra is five hundred miles wide and the frost begins in twenty days, he can draw Marshal Vance’s locomotives into the bogs and let January fight his battle for him, the way his grandfather did to Bonaparte at Moscow."

"It is the traditional strategy of the Russian War Ministry, Protector," Takashima said. He stepped half a pace toward the bronze wall. "And General Vance’s own medical chief wired from the Strait yesterday that the Marshal is coughing blood twice a day and has to be lifted onto his flatcar by two orderlies. If our columns march inland from the Bering beach into forty-below cold while their commander is dying on a stretcher, the Siberian winter will swallow forty thousand men without Korsakov firing a cannon."

"We are not going to march five hundred miles across the moss after Cossack ponies, Admiral," Elias said. A grey smile twitched at the corner of his mouth. "You and Mr. Schuyler have been hoping for three weeks that I had gone soft in the head with the dropsy and would bury the Legion in the Chukotka snow so you could divide the treasury at your leisure in December. Stand up to the map, Sterling."

Major Sterling stepped onto the low iron stool before the left-hand plates of the bronze wall and held a long brass pointer tipped with a magnet.

"Bonaparte walked into Russia by the front door across the Niemen because he had no ships," Elias said. He lifted his iron stick two inches from the parquet floor and pointed it fifteen hundred miles south of the Bering Strait, down the jagged, fog-bound coast of the Sea of Okhotsk and the Tartar Strait to the long, narrow horn of rock that curved around the Golden Horn Bay at the forty-third parallel. "The Tsar’s back door has only one hinge. Move the fourth and fifth divisions from the Strait to Hakodate, Sterling. Put the *Prometheus* and the twelve heavy turret-ships through the Tsugaru channel at full steam."

Takashima’s bronze cheek twitched. "Vladivostok, Protector? The Russian batteries on Cape Egersheld and Gold Horn Bay mount sixty-four rifled steel Krupp guns that they sledged down the Amur last winter! And if you place a Pacifica garrison at the mouth of the Ussuri, sixty leagues from the Korean border, the Privy Council at Edo will view it as an infringement upon the northern sphere promised to the Tenno in the treaty of March!"

"The Tenno will take what I give him after my guns have broken the gate," Elias said. He leaned forward on his stick until the Satsuma officer dropped his eyes. "And as for Marshal Vance, if Marcus has only thirty days of breath left in his lungs, he will not spend them sitting in a tent on the Anadyr watching Cantonese coolies shovel mud. I have wired him to leave Colonel Armistead with ten thousand men to bolt the bridge-spans together through the winter, and to take the main battle-fleet south himself. If we take Vladivostok and the Amur mouth before September, Korsakov’s army in Siberia is cut off from the sea, and the whole Russian Pacific coast falls into our lap like a rotten plum. Kaiulani, read the Marshal’s acknowledgment from the *Prometheus*."

Beside the repeater, Lady Kaiulani lifted a strip of blue paper from the brass basket. She looked across the green baize at Takashima and Schuyler. By sending Marcus Vance two thousand miles south into the cannon’s mouth at Vladivostok, Elias was stripping himself of the only loyal sword that could keep these two jackals from his throat if his heart stopped before the equinox; yet her voice rang clear and cold as a temple bell:

"*'From Vance, Commanding Expeditionary Force aboard flagship Prometheus off Kurile Islands, twelfth August: Fleet cleared Tsugaru Strait at four this morning in dense fog. My lungs are sufficient for the tonnage required. We shall be off the Golden Horn at daybreak on the fifteenth, and I will place the keys of the Russian citadel on the Protector’s desk before the first frost.'*"

# Chapter 13: Frozen Hell

Seventy-two hours later, at five o’clock on the morning of the fifteenth of August, a wet sea-fog lay rolled like greasy sheepskin wool across the Peter the Great Gulf. It hid the steep, oak-forested hills of the Muravyov-Amursky Peninsula and the green-painted iron roofs of Vladivostok inside a gray twilight that smelled of rotting sea-kelp and cold mud. Four miles southwest of the rocky promontory of Cape Egersheld, outside the waters of the Eastern Bosphorus in the open sea beyond the stony spine of Russky Island, eight flat-decked iron vessels rode like floating brick-kilns in a curved, two-mile arc, anchored bow-and-stern with heavy kedge-cables so the current could not swing their hulls a single degree off the compass-mark. These were the new *Vulcan*-class steam-bombardment monitors, built in secret behind the high board fences of the Mare Island yard during the winter after the Manila campaign and brought across the northern circle under tow. They carried neither masts nor broadside casemates. Amidships of each vessel’s four-thousand-ton cellular hull rose a single, fixed oval citadel of fourteen-inch compound steel armor, out of whose slotted roof protruded the stubby, gaping muzzles of twin twenty-inch rifled breech-loading steam-mortars; cast at the Potrero Point works around an inner tube of compressed Essen steel, these weapons were loaded by telescopic hydraulic rams driven directly from the ships’ main boilers at three hundred pounds of pressure to the square inch, lifting twelve-hundred-pound conical shells that no human muscle could ever have heaved.

Inside the armored conning-tower of the flagship *Prometheus*, anchored five hundred yards to the rear of the mortar-line, General Marcus Vance sat propped in a high wooden barber’s chair. The ship’s carpenters had bolted it directly to the steel deck-plates around the periscope-slit so the Marshal could observe the range-buoys without standing on his trembling legs. The narrow iron chamber was ninety degrees from the heat of the engine-room uptakes directly aft, and reeked of carbolic acid, hot cylinder-oil, and the dark, sweetish smell of blood. Marcus wore his navy wool coat buttoned over a flannel chest-protector soaked in turpentine. Across his knees lay his waterproofed calculation-book and his Geneva chronometer, while beside his right boot stood a porcelain spittoon half-filled with crimson-streaked sawdust. He had not slept since passing the La Pérouse Strait two nights ago. In the yellow light of the binnacle-lamp, with his bleached-bone skin stretched tight over his cheekbones and the bridge of his nose like a skull beneath a peaked military cap, his gray eyes squinted through the brass binocular-tubes bolted to the vision-slit as steady and pitiless as a surveyor’s transit.

"The tethered balloon from the tender *Shasta* has reached twelve hundred feet above the fog-bank, Marshal," Major Sterling said. He stood beside the speaking-tubes with a pair of electric ear-phones strapped over his temples, connected by an insulated copper wire that ran up through the conning-tower roof to the silk observation-gasbag floating in the clear sunlight above the mist. "Lieutenant Mordecai in the basket reports the Russian coastal batteries on Cape Goldobina and the Egersheld point have their gun-crews sleeping beside their pieces under tarpaulins. Admiral Erdmann’s four wooden corvettes are moored bow-to-stern inside the Golden Horn right below the Governor’s magazine. They cannot see a yard through the sea-smoke on the water, and their lookouts are facing the eastern channel—they have no idea

an enemy ship is within twenty leagues of the coast, let alone anchored behind the island with two miles of rock between us and their guns."

Marcus lifted a folded white linen handkerchief to his lips. He coughed once. The wet, tearing convulsion deep in his chest jerked his lean shoulders against the leather straps of the barber’s chair, and he dropped the stained cloth into the spittoon at his feet before his fingers closed upon his pencil. "They fortified the narrows on the assumption that a fleet must see a fort in order to shoot at it, Sterling," Marcus said. Tubercular ulcers in his throat reduced his voice to a metallic scrape that barely carried to the speaking-tube six inches from his chin. "That is the error of gentlemen who learned their mathematics before the telegraph was married to the mortar. A gun does not need eyes when a man in a silk bag twelve hundred feet in the air has a copper wire and a triangulation table. What is the wind-drift at a thousand feet?"

"Four knots from the south-southeast, sir," Sterling answered from the needle on the brass dial before him. "And the barometric pressure is thirty point one-two."

Across the damp page of his book, where the invisible target beyond the forested hills of Russky Island, the balloon in the sky, and the anchored monitors formed a blind geometric triangle, Marcus’s pencil scratched three rapid logarithms into degrees of arc and pounds of nitro-cellulose powder. He leaned his forehead against the cold iron brow-pad of the vision-slit. His bony thumb pressed the stem of his chronometer. "Signal the mortar flotilla by the underwater cable," he ordered. "Ships one through four: azimuth thirty-four degrees twelve minutes east, elevation fifty-two degrees. Ships five through eight: azimuth thirty-six degrees four minutes, elevation fifty-one and one-half. Charge: one hundred and eighty pounds of prismatic cocoa-powder; fuse: delayed percussion with four hundred pounds of wet guncotton bursting-charge in the core. Leave the water-batteries on the cape alone so the Russian gunners can sit by their cannon while the sky falls on their backs. Put the first salvo straight over the mountain ridge into the main powder-magazine and the foundry slips at the head of the Golden Horn, four miles inland."

Down on the wet steel decks of the eight *Vulcan* monitors, red electric lamps blinked once inside the armored turrets. Steam-valves hissed. After the massive bronze hydraulic rams shoved eight six-foot cones of forged steel taller than a man into the rifled chambers of the twenty-inch monsters, the heavy screw-breeches swung shut with the dull, greasy *thud* of a bank-vault closing; at the drop of the Marshal’s thin white hand in the conning-tower of the *Prometheus*, Major Sterling pressed the brass firing-key on the bulkhead. A single galvanic spark from the flagship’s battery fired all eight mortars as one volcano.

***

Three weeks after that southern hammer-stroke at the mouth of the Golden Horn, in the freezing dawn of September, the fifty-three miles of racing green water at the sixty-sixth parallel remained the true testing-ground of Elias Thorne’s providence. He had refused the warm conservatory on Mason Street while other men bolted his monument together. To the factions in the Diet who believed him a dying invalid propped on horsehair pillows, he would give an answer written in five-inch rivets above the Arctic tide.

At the tip of the Cape Prince of Wales masonry abutment, Elias stepped down from the platform of the armored inspection-car and leaned his weight upon the heavy iron walking-stick from San Francisco. His valet had slit his wide-soled boots twice down the leather seams that morning to accommodate the bruised, watery swelling of his ankles. Beneath them stretched the first completed mile of the Bering Bridge.

A colossal rectangular tunnel of black-painted Bessemer plate and open lattice-girders, thirty feet wide and twenty-four feet high, rested eighty feet above the white-maned rollers of the strait upon twin rows of forty-foot cylindrical piers filled with Sierra granite and Portland cement. Four-inch gaps separated the creosoted Oregon fir cross-ties. Straight down through the timber slots boiled the emerald vortex where the waters of the Pacific met the Polar Sea. Out of the Chukchi fog, striking the four-thousand-ton steel trusses like a continuous battery of solid shot, the gale set the entire mile-long cantilever humming with a deep, subterranean bass note that vibrated up through the ferrule of his stick into his congested ribs.

They followed him. Huddled together on the narrow timber catwalk bolted between the broad-gauge tracks came the three predators waiting for his boots to empty: Cornelius Schuyler in a triple-caped sealskin ulster with a fur muffler tied over his ears; Rear-Admiral Takashima, his Satsuma face pinched blue-gray by the twenty-degree gale; and Lady Kaiulani, her black mourning-cloak snapping behind her shoulders like the wings of a raven against the low, grease-colored sky.

"Fourteen piers set into the bedrock since the July thaw, Protector," Schuyler shouted against the wind and the ear-splitting *rat-tat-tat-tat* of the pneumatic riveting-guns working inside the smoky iron womb of the fifth span ahead. His teeth chattered. Fifty feet below, as a sheet of freezing salt-spume broke over the lower caisson-skirts and showered the track with sleet, the banker's plump hands gripped the vibrating wire guide-rope. "And every pier has cost the Treasury four hundred thousand thalers and thirty dead coolies! The diver-crews in the pneumatic bells below the mud-line are coming up paralyzed with the caisson-sickness six at a time! If we do not suspend the riveting before the October pack-ice comes down from Wrangell Land, the floes will shear our floating derricks from their anchors and sink two million thalers of machinery in thirty fathoms!"

Elias ignored the wire guide-rope. He walked forward down the center of the six-foot gauge. Every third cross-tie took the square plant of his iron stick to mask the heavy, dragging numbness in his left leg. Inside the lattice-truss, where Irish boys heated nine-inch steel rivets to cherry-red in portable coke-forges, the acrid smoke mixed with the reek of hot whale-oil lubricant and the sharp, salty breath of the sea below.

He paused beside a gang of Cantonese riveters. They dropped to their knees on the icy ties as his shadow fell across their forge. "When the floating derricks are crushed by the ice, Mr. Schuyler," Elias said, his rough, low voice cutting through the metallic hum of the girders around them, "we will lay the rails out to the end of the twelfth span, roll the fifty-ton travelling cranes out upon the completed iron itself, and swing the next girders straight forward into the air from the nose of the track. A bridge that waits for summer weather in this latitude will never reach the Diomedes."

Takashima stepped abreast of Schuyler on the narrow planking. He fixed his dark eyes upon the purple, laboring pulse in the hollow of Elias’s throat. "And who will pay the iron-founders at Sacramento when the spring comes, Excellency?" he asked. "Marshal Vance has taken Vladivostok, yes, at the cost of six thousand shells and two burned-out mortar tubes. Yet General Korsakov did not surrender when the port fell. He has retreated westward up the valley of the Amur and the Shilka toward Lake Baikal, tearing up the post-roads and burning every village behind him. Now the Marshal demands that we ship twenty locomotives and forty thousand tons of coal up the frozen Tartar Strait to Nikolayevsk so he can chase the Russians into the heart of Asia before December! My naval board has voted this morning that the fleet cannot risk its screws in the Okhotsk ice-pack to feed a winter land-campaign two thousand miles from salt water."

Elias stopped dead at the extreme seaward lip of the fifth span. Ten paces ahead of his boots, where the wooden cross-ties ended over sheer emptiness and a pitching barge waited below with the floor-plates, two naked sixty-foot steel I-beams projected out into the swirling gray mist like the jaws of an open vise.

He turned around on the wet timber. The narrow iron cage hung suspended between the sky and the water. Behind his breastbone, a dull, red-hot bar of pig-iron pressed against his spine, and every fourth heartbeat missed its stroke to leave a black hollow in his chest that made the sleet on his face warm by comparison. Takashima and Schuyler huddled against the wind while he stood unbraced at the edge of the drop.

"Your naval board voted," Elias said softly.

"In consultation with the Treasury Committee, Protector," Schuyler put in quickly. He took half a step backward along the catwalk, his heel striking a bucket of cold bolts. "The interest on the Eastern Receivership bonds falls due on the first of November. If we pour another thirty millions into Marshal Vance’s Siberian adventure while the winter closes the rivers, the counting-houses in New York and Osaka will refuse our paper! We must consolidate! We must digest what we have taken—"

"You are buzzards waiting on a fence-rail, Mr. Schuyler," Elias said. The howling wind off the Diomedes carried his unraised voice back down the iron tunnel of the bridge. "Because my legs are swollen with water and Marcus is spitting his lungs into a bucket, you think you can starve his regiments in the Siberian snow this winter, let the Russians cut his throat at Baikal, and then come home to San Francisco to divide the carcass between the counting-house and the quarterdeck."

Beside the girders, Lady Kaiulani shifted her dark eyes from Elias’s gray face to the Satsuma admiral’s hand. Her right hand rested inside her warm fur muff, her fingers on the cold steel trigger of her Derringer. "Be careful, Admiral," she said. "A bridge has no bulwarks, and the water below is very deep for a man in heavy boots."

Elias took one step back from the open gulf. His iron cane struck the eighty-pound steel rail at his feet.

"Hear me, both of you," Elias said, his gaze locking them to the planks. "I built this empire out of Kentucky ash and Sierra quartz before Mr. Schuyler ever saw a gold thaler or Admiral Takashima ever looked through the breech of a rifled gun. This iron under your shoes is my bone. The wire running through that lead pipe is my nerve. So long as I sit in the chair, with boots on my feet or propped in a glass-fronted coffin, every bolt goes into this bridge, and every ton of coal Marcus asks for goes up the Amur before the ice locks the bar. Hold back a single collier at Nagasaki this week, and I will skip the council to appoint Lady Kaiulani Sole Regent of the Treasury and the Fleet with power of drumhead execution, while her Hawaiian guards drop both of you through that tie-gap into the strait before the tide turns. Walk back to the car, gentlemen. Sign the Nikolayevsk coal-warrants while my hand is still warm enough to hold the seal."

***

To the Chronicler who measures the hubris of mortal princes against the ancient hostility of the earth, the winter march of the Pacifica Expeditionary Force from the waters of the Amur to the frozen inland sea of Baikal stands as the supreme tragedy of the mechanical age. Xerxes whipped the Hellespont with iron chains. The Corsican drove his half-million Europeans across the Niemen into the summer dust of Lithuania. Yet when those captains contended against distance with only the muscles of horses and the leather soles of marching men, Marshal Marcus Vance attempted a thing far more unnatural, dragging the entire roaring, coal-eating industrial carcass of the nineteenth century across two thousand miles of sub-arctic wilderness at forty degrees below zero.

Through October and November, before the black frost sealed the rivers to the bedrock, sixty shallow-draft stern-wheelers and iron barges from the Sacramento and the Yangtze fought their way up the turbid, snag-choked current of the Amur and its tributary the Shilka. They landed thirty-five thousand veterans of the Atlantic Auxiliary and the Satsuma Infantry at the old Russian convict-depot of Stretensk. Westward from that point, across the Yablonoi Mountains to Chita and the shores of Lake Baikal, where neither navigable stream nor iron rail had ever been laid through the dark timber, stretched only the Great Siberian Post-Track, a rutted swath of frozen mud and birch-forest beaten down by the Tsar’s couriers over two centuries.

Upon that frozen mire, Marcus Vance let loose the iron monsters of Clark’s Point.

The war-museums of Monterey still preserve the surviving specimens of the thirty *Mammoth*-class steam-traction locomotives that led the vanguard over the Yablonoi pass. Forty-ton behemoths encased in half-inch boiler-plate, they ran upon eight-foot-wide iron wheels fitted with spiked steel cleats and pushed revolving steam-plows designed to chew through six-foot snowdrifts. Behind each machine, where four-inch Krupp field-guns rode alongside portable telegraph dynamos, barrels of Santa Paula rock-oil, and the standardized rations of dried San Joaquin beef and compressed bean-cake, clanked a train of twelve iron-wheeled wagons.

For the first hundred leagues, the mercury hovered near zero. The geometry of San Francisco triumphed over the steppe. At three miles an hour, while tall smokestacks belched pillars of greasy black petroleum-soot across the virgin snows of the taiga and Cantonese linemen unreeled bare copper telegraph wire directly onto the dry, bone-hard ice that required neither poles nor glass insulators to carry the Protector’s spark unbroken back to the sea, the great traction-engines ground steadily over the frozen ruts.

And then, in the second week of December, the sky cleared to a dome of dark imperial blue, the wind died altogether, and the real cold came down out of the pole.

Thirty-two years earlier on the Platte, Elias and Caleb Vance had survived a blustering snow-gale inside a dead mule’s ribs. Siberia brought a vast, crystalline stillness. The spirit of the thermometer shrank down into the bulb at fifty-two degrees below zero, and the frost attacked the chemistry of iron.

Under that soundless pressure, the molecular structure of forged steel changed. The eighty-pound Krupp gun-barrels and the solid wrought-iron axles of the traction-engines grew brittle as Venetian glass. Metal shattered. When an artillery wheel struck a frozen boulder in the road, or a sapper struck a steel crowbar with a sledgehammer to clear a trench, the iron broke into three pieces with a sharp report like a pistol shot. In the feed-pipes of the traction-locomotives, hot water froze solid between the tender-tank and the injector-valve within three feet of the roaring firebox. If a stoker stopped the donkey-pump for ninety seconds to clear a clinker from the grate, the cast-iron cylinder-head split from end to end with the boom of a bomb, and the cloud of scalding vapor that enveloped the crew fell back upon their coats ten seconds later as a crust of solid white ice.

The air burned the lungs of men bred by the Chesapeake or the warm lagoons of Kyushu. A breath drawn too deeply through the open mouth seared the bronchial tubes like a draft of boiling vinegar, while the moisture of the eyeballs froze the lashes together and the brass breech-block of a Sacramento needle-rifle welded a square inch of living skin from any bare thumb that touched it.

Along three hundred miles of white forest between Chita and the Selenga valley, the mechanical march slowed to a crawl. Mineral lubricating-oil in the wheel-hubs congealed into hard tallow against the steam-jets. Wrapped in four layers of tattered wool blankets, raw sheepskins stripped from dead Russian cattle, and straw bound around their boots with telegraph wire, entire battalions of Virginia and Pennsylvania veterans were harnessed by fifties to drag the stalled artillery-sledges through the drifts by main strength. Behind them trailed a two-mile wake of blackened snow and spilled coal-cinders. Rigid, frost-whitened carcasses of draft-mules marked the road alongside the crouching figures of Cantonese coolies and Japanese infantrymen who had sat down beside the track for three minutes to adjust a boot-strap and frozen into statues of blue marble before the rear-guard ambulances reached them.

***

On the afternoon of the twenty-first of December, the winter solstice, when the sun above the fifty-second parallel barely lifted its dull, copper-red rim over the snow-choked pines of the Khamar-Daban range before sinking back into the violet twilight, the head of that bleeding iron snake reached the eastern shore of Lake Baikal.

The forest ended against a sheer rampart of black granite cliffs. Before the column stretched the Sacred Sea of the Tartars: four hundred miles of fresh water frozen six feet deep into a single floor of greenish-black mirror-ice, where jagged pressure-ridges ten feet high groaned and boomed through the twilight like subterranean artillery as the deep water shifted beneath the frost.

General Marcus Vance had no horse. His last California mount had died of frozen lungs at Verkhne-Udinsk four days prior. He lay propped at a forty-five-degree angle inside a narrow box-sledge mounted on steel runners and towed directly behind the surviving flagship of his land-fleet, the forty-ton armored traction-engine *Sierra*. Roofed with bolted boiler-plate and heated by a flexible copper steam-pipe bled off the locomotive’s main dome, the cramped three-by-six coffin stank at ninety degrees of leaking cylinder-tallow and carbolic acid, thick with the rot of the Marshal’s own left lung.

Every two minutes, Major Sterling scraped the rime from the three-inch slot in the front iron plate with a bone-handled knife. Through that gap lay the twilight-purple plain of the frozen lake and the western shore forty miles away, where the road to Irkutsk climbed the timbered gorge of the Angara.

Two miles out from the gravel beach, directly astride the sled-track that the Russian tea-caravans had used for a hundred years, General Korsakov had built his wall.

Fifty-below frost forbade earthworks or brick. Sawing ten thousand three-foot blocks of solid blue lake-ice from the pressure-cracks and stacking them into a continuous crenellated rampart twelve feet high and a mile long between two rocky ice-bound islets, the Russians had poured water over the joints until the whole barrier froze into a seamless monolith of living glacier that turned four-inch rifled shells like snowballs. Behind that crystal breastwork waited eighteen thousand Siberian Riflemen in white sheepskin *tulups* and forty heavy bronze siege-cannon dragged out from the Irkutsk arsenals.

"Colonel Armistead reports the Second Virginia and the Choshu Brigade are deployed behind the first pressure-ridge at eight hundred yards, Marshal," Major Sterling said. He crouched on his heels beside the sledge-runner with the field-telegraph box between his frost-blackened mittens. The surgeon at Chita had amputated Sterling’s left ear after the November gale, and a dirty linen bandage was frozen stiff to the side of his skull. "The ice under the *Sierra*’s wheels is sixty-four inches thick by the auger-borings, sir, and ringing like a bell. If we bring the four remaining traction-rams out onto the lake abreast, the weight may hold. Still, the firing-pins on thirty percent of the men’s needle-rifles are snapping off at the first pull from the cold, and the glycerine in the recoil-cylinders of the Krupp guns has frozen solid since noon. We have to heat the gun-breeches with kerosene-torches before every shot."

Inside the iron box, Marcus kept his face to the vision-slit. Protruding from the sleeves of a wolf-skin coat three sizes too large for his wasted frame, his skeletal hands rested upon the waterproofed pages of his ledger, where dark brown circles of dried blood spotted the columns of figures. His breath came in shallow, whistling gasps. Forty-two to the minute, by the Geneva watch hanging from the bolt before his nose. Before the sun rose again over the Manchurian mountains behind him, the last usable air-sacs in his right lung would fill with fluid.
