Yet a halt here on the eastern beach until spring would send word of his repulse flashing back along the copper wire in the snow to the Bering Strait and San Francisco within four hours. By noon tomorrow, while Cornelius Schuyler closed the Market Street Mint and Takashima’s cruisers steamed out of the Golden Gate to seize Honolulu for the Tenno, Elias Thorne would die alone in a partitioned village with the vultures tearing his maps in half.

"A gun whose recoil-cylinder is frozen is simply a rigid mortar, Major," Marcus whispered. The words rattled like dry pebbles in a tin cup. Lifting his pencil with two blue-nailed fingers, he wrote a single three-digit number on the page. "And a rifle whose firing-pin snaps at eight hundred yards still has eighteen inches of cold San Francisco steel fixed to the muzzle. How many gallons of Santa Paula rock-oil remain in the tank-sledges behind the *Sierra* and the *Shasta*?"

"Twelve hundred gallons, General," Sterling answered. He squinted through the stinging ice-fog. Two miles away in the purple gloom, a battery of Russian twenty-four-pounders atop the glacier-wall flashed dull orange; four solid cast-iron balls howled and skipped across the polished black ice like monstrous curling-stones until one struck a pressure-hummock fifty yards ahead of the locomotive and exploded the four-foot ice-crest into a geyser of diamond-sharp splinters that rattled against the sledge’s armor-plate.

"Solid ice does not shatter under point-detonation because it yields and freezes again," Marcus said. In the reflection of the binnacle-lamp, he coughed a mouthful of bright scarlet onto the wolf-skin lap-robe and left it there. "Therefore we will not shoot at their ice-wall with shells, Sterling. We will melt the floor out from under their boots. Order the four traction-engines to disconnect their supply-trains and couple the oil-tankers directly behind their fireboxes. Turn the high-pressure steam-coils into the oil-vats to heat the petroleum to boiling, and advance the four machines in line abreast at full throttle straight across the open lake against the center of the Russian glacier. Behind each engine, put two battalions of the Virginia and Choshu infantry in column of platoons, unloaded rifles and bayonets fixed, without a single cheer, using the iron hulls as moving shields against their grape-shot."

Through the vision-slit, two miles of glass-smooth black ice stretched out, swept clean of snow by the wind and crisscrossed by the white tracks of bouncing Russian cannonballs. "Marshal, at three hundred yards their heavy bronze pieces will punch right through half-inch boiler-plate!" Sterling said. "And if we pump boiling rock-oil onto six-foot lake ice and set it afire with shell—"

"It will burn at two thousand degrees across ten acres of the ditch and crack the ice-sheet under the weight of their own cannon," Marcus said. His bony hand reached up and pulled the brass whistle-cord connecting his sledge to the cab of the *Sierra* above him. "It will drop General Korsakov’s center straight into three hundred fathoms of freezing water. And if the ice cracks beneath our own cleats as well, Major, then we shall see whether a Virginian or a Siberian sinks faster in fresh water. Pull the lanyard."

Fifty-below frost choked the brass throat of the whistle into a hoarse, strangling roar, swallowed at once by the grinding of the eight-foot spiked wheels as they bit into the dark mirror of the lake.

Inside the towed iron coffin, the vibration jarred the teeth. Every spike of the *Sierra*’s treads drove the deep, booming groan of the stressed lake-ice straight through the steel runners into Marcus’s rotting spine. Behind the four advancing behemoths, four thousand men walked in lock-step through the violet twilight, their faces wrapped in bloody sheepskin rags while their breath rose in four parallel walls of frozen white fog that blotted out the stars. Only the wheezing pant of the steam-cylinders and the continuous, ringing *spang-crunch* of four thousand pairs of iron-cramponed boots striking the black glass broke the stillness of the march.

At six hundred yards, the entire mile-long crest of Korsakov’s glacier-wall erupted in a single, rolling sheet of yellow black-powder flame.

Forty heavy bronze guns spoke together. To the right of the *Sierra*, a twenty-four-pound solid shot struck the forward boiler-casing of the traction-engine *Tahoe* dead center. In the brittle, sub-arctic cold, the wrought-iron plates burst inward like an eggshell struck with a spoon. Superheated steam and white-hot anthracite coals geysered fifty feet into the freezing air; before the fifty-below gale froze the wet steam on their tunics into solid white armor, the blast scalded the thirty Choshu infantrymen of the leading platoon into red, screaming meat.

"Hold the interval!" Colonel Armistead’s voice cracked across the ice. Behind the wrecked machine, the Virginians stepped straight over the steaming, rigid bodies of their Japanese comrades without breaking stride and closed up behind the remaining three engines while Russian grape-shot hissed across the ice like cast-iron hail, snapping off rifle-barrels and taking men’s legs clean off at the knee-joint.

A conical shell glanced off the sloped roof of the sledge three inches above Marcus’s head. The concussion burst both drums in Sterling’s ears and sent a trickle of dark blood down his soot- and grease-blackened jaw. "Four hundred yards, Marshal!" he shouted. "The *Shasta*’s steering-chains are shot away. She’s yawing into the pressure-ridge!"

In the red glare of the firebox, Marcus’s bloody lips formed the words: "Open the oil-cocks on all three vats. Elevate the brass nozzles. Pump."

From the prows of the *Sierra* and the *Sacramento*, twin rotary steam-pumps throbbed at two hundred strokes a minute. Two thick, arching black rainbows of boiling California petroleum burst from the brass-bound fire-hoses. Shooting a hundred yards ahead of the crunching wheels, the crude splashed in smoking, viscous floods across the base of the twelve-foot Russian ice-rampart until the stench of raw kerosene and scorched sulfur drowned out the blood and frost. Up on the crystal parapet, the Siberian Riflemen in their white sheepskins paused with their ramrods half-drawn. They stared down as the black, steaming grease soaked their boots and pooled around the timber sledges of their bronze cannon.

Marcus’s fingers locked like iron claws onto the edge of his calculation-book as the *Sierra*’s spiked cleats ground within eighty paces of the wall. With his last breath, he shaped the order: "One round of white-phosphorus canister from the bow-howitzer."

The short bronze piece in the locomotive’s nose barked once.

Where the phosphorus stars struck the boiling Santa Paula crude, the violet Siberian night vanished. A forty-foot wall of blinding, roaring orange-white flame leaped from the surface of the lake with the thunder of an exploding gas-works and sucked the freezing air out of the soldiers’ lungs for three hundred yards around. Fed by twelve hundred gallons of superheated oil, the fire ate downward into the blue crystal like nitric acid.

It held for ninety seconds. While the sheepskin coats of the Russian gunners caught fire like tallow-wicks and men leaped screaming from the melting parapet, the six-foot floor of Lake Baikal bore the load, until at last, beneath forty bronze siege-pieces, ten thousand tons of stacked ice-blocks, and the two-thousand-degree furnace blistering its skin, the ancient geological fault-line of the lake gave a single, thunderous report that echoed from the Khamar-Daban mountains to the gorges of the Angara.

A jagged black fissure, ten yards wide and steaming like the mouth of hell, zig-zagged straight under the center of Korsakov’s battery and backward beneath the wheels of the *Sacramento*.

The glacier-wall tilted slowly backward. Splitting into three colossal blue bergs, the parapet plunged into the black, bottomless water and dragged twelve Russian cannon and six hundred shrieking riflemen in white sheepskins under the boiling scum of burning oil. At the same instant, the ice beneath the forty-ton *Sacramento* gave way like wet rotten timber. Her iron prow reared straight up toward the stars; her boiler exploded as the freezing lake-water rushed into her white-hot flues; she slid backward into the abyss and took two full companies of the Fourteenth Pennsylvania with her before they could loose their hands from the guide-ropes.

"The center is gone!" Sterling screamed through his deafened ears. He clutched the side of the sledge while the *Sierra*’s locked brakes slid twenty yards along the tilting lip of the black water, where burning oil-patches floated among the bobbing heads of drowning Russians and Americans alike. "General! The road to the western shore is open around the crack!"

Marcus Vance did not answer. His chin had dropped forward onto his turpentine-soaked chest. Against his thumb, his Geneva chronometer ticked steadily on, while his open, unblinking gray eyes stared through the three-inch slit at the burning water.

***

Six thousand miles away, where the December rain fell warm and salt-heavy upon the granite paving-stones of San Francisco, the news of the Baikal furnace brought ten thousand wet, starving men and women into the mud of Plaza Square with iron cobbles and broken pickaxe-handles in their fists.

For four months, since Elias had ordered the autumn levies and the final sixty-million-thaler Siberian Bridge loan, the machinery of the home provinces had ground between the upper millstone of the war-tax and the lower millstone of the dockyard conscription. The thirty-percent customs tribute from Boston and New York had dried to a trickle as the eastern ports rotted in commercial paralysis. To feed the locomotives in Chukotka and the foundries at Potrero Point, Cornelius Schuyler’s tax-gatherers had raised the excise on San Joaquin flour to four silver tenths a barrel, while the provost-guards swept the Irish and American mechanics’ wards every Tuesday night to fill the replacement drafts for the northern ice.

Inside the high-arched Map Room of the Citadel on Rincon Hill, the winter dusk smelled of wet wool and coal-gas, thickened by the pungent stramonium-smoke that hung like a burial-shroud beneath the coffered ceiling.

Elias stood clear of his wicker chair. Propped on both elbows against the windowsill of the tall western casement, his swollen legs wrapped in flannel bandages from ankle to thigh beneath his unlaced cavalry boots, he looked down the steep, rain-swept slope of First Street toward the Embarcadero. Down there, through the yellow smear of the gas-lamps, a mile-long column of torches surged up the hill from the silent ironworks of the Mission. White-bearded veterans of the forty-nine mining camps filled the ranks alongside wives of the Pennsylvania and Virginia auxiliaries whose husbands had just gone down under the Baikal ice, joined by two thousand discharged dock-masons marching behind a black canvas banner painted with a single white skull and the words: *NO MORE BONES FOR THE STRAIT.*

Through the double-thick plate glass of the Chancery, the low, rhythmic roar of their chanting vibrated against Elias’s breastbone: *"Bread or blood! Bring home the Legion! Bread or blood!"*

"Marshal Vance is dead, Protector," Cornelius Schuyler said from the head of the baize table behind him. The news that the bloodless shadow who had held the whip over the army lay frozen in a Siberian box-sledge had put iron back into the banker's spine, stripping all deference from his voice as he stood flanked by Rear-Admiral Takashima and six directors of the California Steam Navigation Syndicate. "And four thousand men of the First and Second Divisions are either drowned in Lake Baikal or dying of gangrene in the burned huts along the Selenga! Look down that street, sir! The First California Reserve Battalion at the Presidio refused to draw ball-cartridge when the Provost-Major ordered them out an hour ago to clear Market Street! Their sergeants said they would not shoot down the mothers of the boys who took Vicksburg for you!"

Elias stayed at the glass. Down at the corner of Folsom Street, the mob had just overturned two of the Treasury’s armored bread-wagons; rioters set the soaked wood ablaze with coal-oil and hurled paving-stones through the stained-glass windows of the Syncretic Chapel on the corner.

"They are shouting because their bellies are pinched and they smell a funeral in this house, Mr. Schuyler," Elias said. His breath rattled wetly in his throat, and his scarred right hand gripped the mahogany window-mullion until the varnish cracked. "Who gave the casualty lists from the Selenga wire to the printers on Montgomery Street before they crossed my desk?"

Only the hiss of the gas-jets and the distant crash of a shop-front giving way down the hill broke the silence.

Beside the bronze telegraph repeater, Lady Kaiulani raised her head. Her face was pale and sharp as carved ivory above her black mourning-dress, her right hand motionless inside the folds of her skirt.

"Mr. Schuyler’s chief clerk carried the decode to the *Alta California* office at two o’clock, Elias," Kaiulani said, her clear voice cutting through the gloom like a lancet. "And Rear-Admiral Takashima gave orders at four that the marines aboard the *Kamehameha* are to remain at their moorings and take no part in civil disturbances among the American population. They wished you to see the torches from your window so that you would sign the Regency Act before midnight."

Takashima stepped forward into the yellow circle of the chandelier, his bronze face hard and expressionless. "The Satsuma Brigade lost twelve hundred men on the ice on Tuesday, Excellency, to buy twenty miles of Russian snow while the British China Squadron is reinforcing Singapore. With Marshal Vance dead, there is no general on the continent whom both the American auxiliaries and the Imperial Japanese divisions will obey. The Joint Board therefore requests that Your Excellency retire to the warm springs at Monterey, constitute a Council of Regency under Comptroller Schuyler and myself, and sign the immediate recall of the Siberian and Yukon armies."

Elias turned from the window. Ten seconds passed while he pivoted his water-logged boots across the parquet floor and dragged his iron cane inch by inch. Cold grey sweat coated his hollow cheeks; his lips had turned the color of a bruised plum. Below in the street, the orange glare of the burning bread-wagons framed his iron-gray head like the flames of that Kentucky cabin thirty-two years ago, and as he leaned his broad, skeletal shoulders back against the glass and fixed his sunken eyes on the table, Schuyler stepped behind his leather chair.

"Marcus is dead," Elias said, his voice a dry rattle. "He died eight thousand miles west of the river where we met, with his boots pointing toward the Urals. And you think because my best dog is cold in the snow, the wolves can come into the kitchen and divide the meat?"

"Be reasonable, Mr. Thorne!" Schuyler cried. His fat hands gripped the back of his chair while a fresh roar from the ten thousand rioters outside shook the window-panes. "They are three blocks from the Citadel gates! The California militia will not fire on them, and Takashima’s sailors will not land! With what soldiers do you propose to hold this hill tonight, let alone Siberia?"

"With the soldiers who have no mothers in San Francisco," Elias said.

He lifted his trembling left hand. A thick, blue-nailed finger pointed straight at Kaiulani.

"Open the local wire to the Presidio barracks, Kaiulani," Elias said, each short phrase torn from his failing lungs like a nail pulled from oak. "Pass over the California Reserve. Wire Colonel Kalakaua of the First and Second Hawaiian Royal Guard, and the three battalions of the Shantung Railway Pioneers quartered at the Mint. Tell them that the rabble on First Street has burned the Polynesian chapel and is marching to loot the Cantonese pay-vaults. Order Kalakaua to bring the four steam-rams up from the Embarcadero with the high-pressure boiler hoses coupled to the salt-pumps, and put two thousand Hawaiian and Chinese bayonets down the hill in column of companies. No parley. No blank powder. Clear the streets to the water’s edge, and hang the first twenty white mechanics taken with a torch in their hands from the iron lamp-posts outside Mr. Schuyler’s bank before the clock strikes eight!"

Schuyler’s mouth fell open. His face went grey as putty. "You are setting Asian coolies and Kanakas to bayonet American citizens in the streets of San Francisco?!"

"In my empire, Mr. Schuyler, there are only subjects who obey the law and traitors who feed the crows," Elias said. He took a single heavy, dragging step toward the table and raised his iron stick until the ferrule pointed straight between Takashima’s eyes. "And when Colonel Kalakaua has washed the cobbles clean outside, he will march two companies of his islanders up these stairs to stand behind your chairs while we draft the spring conscription for Lake Baikal. Sit down at that table, Admiral, before I have you shot on the carpet for desertion in the face of the enemy!"

***

To the Chronicler who writes in the quieter noon of the twentieth century, looking back across two decades from the marble libraries of New Edo upon the convulsions that remade the earth, the true corpse laid out upon the Siberian snow that winter was the three-hundred-year-old autocracy of the House of Romanov. Elias Thorne’s Grand Confederation of Pacifica bled gold and iron from every pore, and the dying Marshal came home across the sea in a lead-lined cask of spirits, yet the Confederation survived.

History is a balance of weights. Cast a ten-thousand-ton iron ball into the eastern scale, and the western beam kicks heavenward until the fulcrum snaps.

In the winter of 1869, Emperor Alexander the Second had imagined a frontier border-war against an over-extended maritime adventurer, a campaign to be settled, like the Crimea, by sacrificing a few regiments of serfs in the snow and signing a parchment in Paris. Instead, the iron jaws of the Pacifica vise closed upon the valley of the Yenisei and stayed shut. For eighteen years after the battle on the lake, while the tubular steel spans of the Bering Bridge were bolted one by one across the Diomede piers and the double-track iron road crept westward through Chita and Irkutsk like black gangrene eating up the continent, the Russian Empire bled its youth and treasure into an open grave four thousand miles from Moscow.

To keep the blue-coated legions of San Francisco and Edo from crossing the Obi, the Ministries of War and Finance in St. Petersburg stripped the European provinces bare. Every silver ruble wrung from the starving peasantry of the Volga and the Ukraine bought Krupp cannon and coal for the Siberian stockades. Every spring, two hundred thousand ploughboys were torn from the communal *mirs* of Great Russia and packed into unheated boxcars along the single military track from Perm. They went east into the taiga. Most died there; the rest returned five years later as legless, frost-bitten beggars who sat outside the tavern doors of Tula and Kharkov, telling of yellow-and-white soldiers who rode behind liquid-fire steam-fortresses and fired seven times without a ramrod.

An autocracy can survive poverty and tyranny, the familiar weather of the steppe. Eighteen years of unavenged, bankrupt humiliation at the hands of a creditor who treated the Tsar of All the Russias as a defaulting tenant broke its back.

By the winter of 1887, European Russia had been hollowed out like an oak whose heartwood has been eaten by white ants while the bark still stands painted with the double-headed eagle. The gold reserve in the Fortress of Peter and Paul had vanished into the vaults of Frankfurt and San Francisco to pay for the fruitless counter-offensives of seventy-four and eighty-one. In the Viborg quarter, paper assignats of the Imperial Bank could no longer buy a loaf of black rye bread. Down in the cellars of St. Petersburg and along the silent, coal-starved iron-mills of the Fontanka, a new and pitiless breed of men had grown up in the shadow of the eastern disaster.

The dreamy constitutional liberals of the fifties, who had read French novels and wept over the serfs, were gone. In their place stood men hardened in the same iron furnace that Elias Thorne had lit upon the Pacific: engineers and cashiered artillery officers from the Siberian front, joined by factory-committees who looked at the rotting gilded carriages of the Grand Dukes and asked why the Russian people should starve in the snow to preserve a German dynasty that had lost half of Asia to an American syndicate.

On the nineteenth of February, 1887, the twenty-sixth anniversary of the Emancipation that had given the peasants stones instead of bread, the boiler burst along the freezing quays of the Neva.

A dry, twenty-below gale blew across the ice from the Gulf of Finland. It drove gritty clouds of snow and coal-dust past the tall red granite columns of St. Isaac’s Cathedral and piled white drifts against the bronze hooves of Peter the Great’s horse on the Senate Square. For six days no flour-trains had reached the Nikolaevsky Station from the south because the railway-brigades had seized the locomotives at Ryazan to haul their own starving battalions home from the Urals; in the workingmen’s barracks of the Putilov ironworks, the grates lay dead cold.

At ten o’clock in the morning, the great alarm-bell of the Putilov foundry tolled. Its rapid, brazen clangor echoed across the frozen canals, bringing forty thousand iron-molders and dock-laborers, along with women in ragged shawls, pouring out across the river ice toward the Admiralty spire. Four thousand mutinous soldiers of the Pavlovsky and Volynsky Guard depots marched at their head. Ordered the night before to entrain for the Tomsk trenches, those men had shot their colonels in the barracks courtyard and tied strips of red bunting from the regimental target-flags to the muzzles of their Berdan rifles.

Inside the high, crimson-damask salon on the second floor of the Winter Palace, the aging Tsar stood with his hands behind his back beside the double-paned window. Below him lay the immense white expanse of the Palace Square, where the Alexander Column rose against the gray sky and a squadron of the Chevalier Guard in brass cuirasses and white horsehair plumes formed a thin, shivering line across the snow between the Arch of the General Staff and the palace gates.

"They are carrying the icons of the Virgin mixed with red flags from the machine-shops, Your Majesty," said Count Tolstoi, the Minister of the Interior. His voice shook at the adjacent casement as the dark, roaring human tide spilled out of the Nevsky Prospekt, filling the square from curb to curb with the stink of wet sheepskin and cheap *makhorka* tobacco. "And the Prefect of Police telephones that the Cossacks of the Don Guard at the Anichkov Bridge refused to use their *nagaikas* when the women walked under the horses’ necks! Sire, you must take the sledge to Tsarskoye Selo while the river-road to the Warsaw station is still open!"

"And leave St. Petersburg to a mob of blacksmiths and deserters because we lost a railway junction in Siberia?" Alexander asked. He turned from the glass. At sixty-eight, after two decades of unbroken defeat that had bowed his shoulders and stained the deep pouches beneath his eyes purple in the cold northern light, the stubborn fatalism of his father Nicholas still held his spine rigid. "General Vannovsky, have the artillery of the Guard unlimber the four bronze pieces at the corner of the Millionnaya. Give them one blank charge over the heads of the crowd to clear the base of the column. If they do not disperse to their workshops within five minutes, open with canister."

Down in the square, the Chevalier Guard drew their long straight palashes. Steel flashed in the frosty air. The forty thousand did not halt.

At the foot of the red granite monolith in the center of the snow, a young captain of the Siberian Sapper Corps, his left sleeve pinned empty to his grey greatcoat from a Pacifica shrapnel-burst on the Yenisei and his chest bearing the tarnished St. George’s Cross, climbed upon the shoulders of two bearded Putilov hammer-men and raised a battered brass speaking-trumpet to his lips.

"Brothers of the Guard!" the one-armed sapper’s voice rang out across the packed snow, clear and hard before the shivering horsemen at the palace railings. "Look at the coats on your backs! The cloth was mortgaged to the bankers in Berlin before you put it on! Look at the rifles in your mittens! There are ten cartridges apiece in the pouches because the Grand Dukes stole the powder-money to buy diamonds for their dancers while our brothers froze to death in front of the American ironclads at Baikal! Will you shoot down your own mothers in the snow of Petersburg so that the Romanovs can send you to rot in the Siberian marshes tomorrow?"

On the flank of the cavalry line, a nineteen-year-old cornet of the Chevalier Guard sat his mount with frost-pinked cheeks beneath his brass helmet. He raised his saber high in his gloved fist. "Close ranks! For the Tsar! Trot—*march!*"

The heavy bay horses took three steps forward into the snow. Fifty paces away beside the iron lamp-posts, the front rank of the mutinous Volynsky infantrymen brought twenty Berdan rifles to their shoulders in a single level line, schooled to a cold volley-discipline by eighteen winters of fighting the Pacifica legions along the eastern rivers.

"Aim at the officers' breastplates," the one-armed sapper called through his trumpet. Above them, the palace windows shook with the first dull boom of the Guard artillery wheeling into position by the arch. His arm dropped. "And fire!"

The volley tore through the freezing air. Twelve gilded saddles emptied at once, and dark blood stained the trampled snow of the Senate Square.

# Chapter 14: The Coral Sea

While the winter of 1887 brought the ancient house of Peter the Great crashing down into the embers of the Neva, a mechanized mummy presided over the three-thousand-mile iron road that had drained Russia’s veins.

Elias Thorne had refused to die. Eighteen years had passed since that December night in sixty-nine when Colonel Kalakaua’s Hawaiian bayonets washed the cobbles of First Street clean of rioters, and the Providentor’s long twilight upon Rincon Hill had grown into a strange, airless spectacle. The dropsy that had swollen his limbs during the laying of the Bering piers had never receded. By his fifty-ninth year, the lower half of his body had turned into two useless pillars of cold stone; every morning, attendants hoisted him from his iron bedstead to a rubber-tired wheeled chair with a brass chain-pulley bolted into the ceiling beams. Caleb Vance was dead. The first Marshal Marcus Vance lay in a lead-lined coffin in the crypt beneath the Monterey basilica, and the original generation of Virginia and Pennsylvania captains who had carried the eagles to the Potomac and the Great Wall had all gone into the earth before him.

The civil war that Cornelius Schuyler and Admiral Takashima had plotted over their Madeira in the sixties had never come. Instead, across the wheels of the old man’s bath-chair, the aged Schuyler’s banking syndicates, Prince Takashima’s Satsuma Admiralty, and Lady Kaiulani’s Insular Provostry balanced one another in a bureaucratic oligarchy of mutual suspicion, each terrified to pull the linchpin lest the others seize the axle. Now that permanent concrete casemates along the Yenisei walled off the Siberian frontier, the foundries at New Osaka and Nagasaki hungered for work. The Triumvirate required a new treasury to gut.

On the afternoon of the fourth of March, 1887, the high glass dome of the Citadel conservatory hummed with the dry warmth of naked Edison carbon-filament bulbs strung like yellow hornets among the giant tree-ferns. The old coal-flues were gone. The air smelled of carbolic soap and nitro-glycerine heart-lozenges, mingled with the oiled brass of the pneumatic message-tubes rising out of the marble floor beside the carp-basin.

Elias sat in his wheeled chair of dark koa-wood and nickeled steel. A heavy blanket of sea-otter fur covered his dead knees. Cropped close to a skull that showed every suture of the bone beneath the yellow skin, his hair was white as bleached salt, and although his left eyelid drooped permanently from a minor apoplexy suffered during the Canton rice-riots of eighty-two, his single wide, water-clear eye remained fixed upon the southern hemisphere of the great bronze globe before him with all the cold focus of the Kentucky creek-bed.

Behind his right wheel stood Lady Kaiulani. At fifty, the Princess-Chancellor had grown severe, her hair braided with threads of silver above the unchanging black bombazine of her dress as she held the silver spoon used to measure the Providentor’s afternoon digitalis. Across the basin, leaning upon ebony canes of their own, stood the seventy-year-old Comptroller Schuyler, his jowls hanging like empty saddle-bags over his stiff collar, beside Grand-Admiral Marquis Takashima, whose chest was a solid breastplate of Chrysanthemum and Pacifica stars.

"The Russian Republic that the mutineers proclaimed in St. Petersburg last month has signed the armistice at Tomsk, Protector," Schuyler wheezed. He tapped a ticker-tape ribbon that had just dropped from the pneumatic chute. "They cede everything east of the Yenisei in perpetuity in exchange for ten million sacks of California wheat to feed Moscow. The northern ledger is closed at last! The sixty thousand troops we have had sitting in the Siberian blockhouses for eighteen winters can be paid off, and the iron-rolling mills at Potrero Point can reduce their shifts to peacetime maintenance!"

Elias’s crooked, blue-nailed right forefinger did not lift from the bronze curve of the globe. Down the meridian from Manila it traced a slow, scratching arc, past the spice-straits of Macassar and the broad, green-enamelled belly of Dutch Java and Sumatra to the buff-colored continent of New Holland, where the British colonies of Victoria and New South Wales sat like fat, unguarded sheep-runs at the bottom of the world.

"Paid off?" In the hush of the fern-house, Elias’s voice was a dry rustle, like dead corn-shucks blown across a frozen barn floor. "If you turn sixty thousand men who have lived on army beef and bayonet-drill for twenty years loose into the streets of San Francisco and Osaka tomorrow, Mr. Schuyler, whose windows do you think they will break before Saturday?"

"The Treasury cannot carry four hundred thousand men under arms in time of peace, Excellency!" Takashima protested. The old samurai’s eyes flicked toward Kaiulani’s still face. "Our coal-bunkers at Manila and Cavite are choked to the roofs, and the twenty new *Leviathan*-class steel battleships have nothing to shoot at between the Kuriles and the Equator!"

"Look at the bottom of the ball, Takashima," Elias whispered. His heavy white head tilted half an inch toward the bronze southern ocean. "For forty years we have built a roof over the northern water. Yet every pound of gutta-percha that insulates our submarine cables, every barrel of tin for our canneries, and half the petroleum for our new turbine-cruisers sits in the Dutch islands between Borneo and Batavia. Below them sit Sydney and Melbourne, the last open harbors where a British squadron from the Cape can coal and refit to strike our southern flank."

Schuyler stared through his gold pince-nez. "The Dutch East Indies and Australia, Protector? Holland is under the protection of the German Emperor in Berlin, and Australia is flesh and blood of the British Crown! Since the panic of seventy-nine, London has transferred half the wealth of the old island to the banks of Melbourne and the gold-fields of Ballarat!"

"Then Melbourne is where the gold is," Elias said. A thread of clear saliva gleamed at the drooping corner of his mouth, and his hand closed over the carved bronze boss of Capricorn. "A circle with the bottom broken out is only a horseshoe, Mr. Schuyler. When the water runs out of the northern sluice, you tilt the pan south. We do not disband a single regiment from the Yenisei. Put them on the broad-gauge cars for Port Arthur and Manila this week, tell young Marcus Vance that his father’s memory requires the Dutch straits cleared before the monsoon turns, and have the first division of the Fleet steam for the Timor Sea. I will not go down into the granite at Monterey while an English governor collects customs-dues on the shores of my ocean."

***

Six weeks later, under the steaming, bruised-violet clouds of the April monsoon, the second General Marcus Vance stood upon the vibrating steel wing of an armored river-monitor as it pushed up the turbid brown flood of the Solo River in eastern Java.

He was twenty-nine, born in the year of the Sacramento Coup, the son of the man who had died in the iron box on Lake Baikal and grandson of old Caleb’s blood. Where his father had carried the weary memory of West Point and the old Republic in his bones, the younger Marcus had been shaped entirely by the Polytechnic Academy of New Edo and the Staff College of Monterey; he spoke Japanese, Cantonese, and English with the same clipped cadence, wore no saber, and carried a slide-rule in his breast pocket above a nickeled nine-shot self-loading pistol holstered over his khaki tropical tunic.

The jungle of the Dutch residency pressed in against the monitor’s low freeboard. It was a wet green wall of giant teak and weeping *waringin* trees, banana-fronds and tangled cane, where the ninety-eight-degree air stank of rotting river-silt and crushed cloves from the burned colonial godowns along the bank, cut through by the sharp, vinegary smoke of smokeless cordite powder.

"The Dutch Governor-General has concentrated four battalions of the Royal Netherlands East Indies Army and two regiments of British Sikh infantry from Singapore behind the railway embankment at Surakarta, General," reported Major Kuroda, his Satsuma chief of staff. He wiped the monsoon rain from the celluloid cover of his map-board. "They have dammed the irrigation canals to flood the rice-paddies in front of the rubber plantations, and their Krupp field-guns are registered on the stone bridge. If we deploy the Filipino and Californian brigades across the wet sawahs, the mud will bog our Maxim-gun carriages to the hubs."

Young Marcus left his binoculars on his chest. He looked at the brass pressure-gauge of the pneumatic tube-launcher bolted to the monitor’s foredeck, then down at his cuff, where a strapped radium-dialed chronometer ticked off the seconds to the noon barrage.

"My father used to say that mud is merely water that has not yet been boiled, Major," Marcus said, his voice thin and rapid. "The Dutch and the English are fighting to preserve their rubber-trees and their sugar-mills because their shareholders in Amsterdam and Penang expect a six-percent dividend in October. We do not care about the trees; the Treasury only wants the sap-tappers and the tin-dredges. How many drums of the new Baku-Santa Paula jellied naphtha do we have in the lighter-barges?"

"Four hundred drums, sir," Kuroda answered. "And the two squadrons of shallow-draft hydroplane-launches have already worked up the side-canals behind the British left flank."

"Do not shell the railway embankment with shrapnel," Marcus ordered. He slid the ivory cursor of his rule across the logarithmic scale and snapped it shut with a dry *click*. "Open the sluice-gates of the upper oil-barges and pump two thousand barrels of jellied naphtha directly onto the flooded surface of the irrigation canals. The current sets straight down against the foot of the Dutch breastworks at two knots. Give the slick fifteen minutes to coat the water-weeds around their barbed-wire stakes, then have the mortar-boats drop six thermite-shells into the ditch."

Half a mile ahead, where the red-tiled roofs of the Dutch colonial sugar-factory rose above the feathery tops of the bamboo, the twelve-pounder batteries of the Singapore garrison opened a rapid, barking fire through the rain. Two high-explosive shells burst in the mud-bank fifty yards to starboard. Black slime and shredded palm-fronds showered the monitor’s steel deck-canopy. A splinter hummed through the open bridge-screen and shattered the glass face of the engine-room telegraph.

Marcus did not turn his head toward the broken glass. Ahead of the bows, a black, iridescent film of jellied petroleum spread out across the flooded rice-terraces, smoothing the rain-pitted water into a greasy mirror that crept around the knees of the Javanese and Sikh skirmishers crouching in the inundated ditches.

"Range nineteen hundred meters," Marcus said into the telephone-mouthpiece wired to the mortar-barge astern. "Thermite canister. Fire."

The compressed-air mortars gave four deep, coughing *thumps*, like a giant clearing his throat in a cellar. Four dull aluminum cylinders tumbled through the grey monsoon curtain.

Where they struck the flooded paddies in front of the railway embankment, the tropical rain turned into a three-thousand-degree furnace of white-hot magnesium and liquid fire. The naphtha floating upon the irrigation water ignited with a single, hollow *whoomp* that shook the monitor’s hull against her anchor-chains. Within thirty seconds, across half a mile of inundated rice-terraces and up to a height of fifty feet, a solid sheet of greasy, black-edged flame rolled straight over the Dutch trenches, boiling the ditch-water around the legs of the screaming Sikh infantrymen and exploding the caissons of the Krupp batteries in showers of brass cartridges until a hundred acres of prime colonial rubber-trees stood as torches of blistering black resin. It burned everything.

"Advance the Filipino bicycle-battalions along the stone dike on the right as soon as the masonry cools," Marcus said. He dropped the telephone receiver onto its hook and pulled out his requisition pad before the screams from the burning cane-brakes had reached their pitch. "And wire the Comptroller’s agents at Batavia that the Surakarta district is cleared for receivership. Any Dutch planter who brings his coolie-rolls to my provost tent before sundown keeps ten percent of his crop-value in silver certificates; any plantation whose manager has fled to the hills goes to the Satsuma Veteran Colonization Board at par."

***

To the Chronicler who stood upon the sandstone heights of the South Head at the dawn of the twenty-fourth of May, 1887, on the very morning when the loyal municipalities of Sydney had hung out their crimson bunting and gilded pasteboard crowns to celebrate the Golden Jubilee of Her Britannic Majesty’s fifty years upon the throne of England, the sky to the eastward gave no warning of providence save a low bank of yellow-black coal-haze that stained the pale winter blue of the Tasman Sea against the rising sun.

For a hundred years since Captain Phillip had landed his first boatloads of chained English pickpockets and Irish rebels among the eucalyptus groves of Port Jackson, the colonies of the southern continent had grown fat in a pastoral dream at the uttermost antipodes of the earth. While the old United States was being ground into iron provinces behind the Sierra, and while the ancient empires of China and Russia were bleeding their lives out against the bayonets of the Pacific Legion, the sheep-barons of New South Wales and the gold-bankers of Melbourne had comforted themselves with two delusions: that six thousand miles of salt water was an impassable moat, and that the Royal Navy’s Australian Squadron, five aging iron-hulled corvettes anchored off Garden Island, remained the invincible trident of Trafalgar.

In the new geometry of steam and steel, the ocean had become a paved turnpike. Its proprietor had come to collect the rent.

At six-thirty in the morning, as the Jubilee bells of St. Andrew’s Cathedral pealed across the mist-wreathed coves of the harbor and the first holiday ferry-boats loaded with picnickers in white flannel put out from Circular Quay, the semaphore-telegraph atop the Macquarie Lighthouse jerked its wooden arms in spasmodic terror. Two minutes later, the six-inch Armstrong rifle in the casemate at Middle Head fired a single blank alarm-gun that sent ten thousand white cockatoos screaming out of the gum-trees along the North Shore.

Down George Street toward the Domain streamed the holiday crowds, passing the cellar stairs to pack the seawalls at Mrs. Macquarie’s Chair and the battlements of Fort Denison. They shaded their eyes with programmes of the Queen’s Regatta and peered eastward toward the mile-wide gap between the Heads.

Through the sandstone jaws of the harbor mouth, moving at a dead-slow eight knots against the ebbing tide without a single pilot-jack flying at their fore-trucks, came the First and Third Battle Squadrons of the Grand Confederation.

A generation had passed since low, turtle-backed monitors rammed the Union gunboats at Vicksburg and shelled the mud-forts of Taku. Entering the waters of Port Jackson that May morning were fourteen sixteen-thousand-ton barbette battleships of the *Imperator* and *Mutsuhito* classes: towering, castle-like citadels of Harveyized nickel-steel painted a dark imperial blue, their hulls sixty feet high from the submerged ram-snouts to the armored fighting-tops where the brass lenses of electric range-finders glinted in the morning sun. Each ship carried four eighteen-inch rifled breech-loaders mounted in twin pear-shaped turrets fore and aft, weapons whose fifty-foot barrels could hurl a two-thousand-pound shell packed with melinite twelve miles over the Blue Mountains. From their triple yellow-and-black funnels rose a continuous, oily thundercloud of burned Borneo petroleum that smelled of hot asphalt and sulfur. The stench blotted out the salt-water and the flowering wattle along the cliffs.

On Garden Island, Rear-Admiral Tryon of the Royal Navy stood upon the quarterdeck of his flagship, the composite screw-corvette *Nelson*, with his telescope held to his eye. Four hundred yards away, the lead battleship *Elias Thorne* glided past Pinchgut Island under the combined sun-and-chrysanthemum flag of Grand-Admiral Marquis Takashima, her upper batteries of rapid-fire six-pounders manned by bare-armed Japanese and American marine gunners standing motionless beside their brass ammunition-hoists.

"Shall we slip the moorings and clear for action, sir?" whispered the *Nelson*’s flag-captain, his face white as his tropical duck trousers as the colossal blue steel flank of the second battleship, the *Kamehameha II*, swung broadside across the mouth of Woolloomooloo Bay. Her shadow fell cold and black across the wooden decks of the British corvette until the sun vanished from the binnacle.

Tryon lowered his glass. He had served in the Mediterranean and the Channel, and he knew naval arithmetic. His five corvettes carried wrought-iron armor belts that would split like pine-shingles before a six-inch shell, while the shore batteries at Bradley’s Head held forty rounds of black powder apiece in their magazines. Behind the fourteen battleships, already rounding the South Head in double column toward Bondi, steamed thirty-two twin-screw iron troop-transports, their decks dark with the grey-and-blue ranks of forty thousand veterans from the Java and Vladivostok campaigns.

"If you pull a lanyard on this ship, Captain," Tryon said, his voice breaking in the stillness as the deep roar of the *Elias Thorne*’s steam-siren echoed off the sandstone cliffs of the harbor, "those floating foundries will blow half of Sydney into the brick-fields before our first round-shot reaches their water-line. Keep the men from the braces. Here comes their launch."

Down at the stone stairs of the Man-o'-War Jetty below the Botanical Gardens, where Lord Carington, the Royal Governor of New South Wales, had arrived ten minutes earlier in his state landau wearing his plumed cocked hat and the riband of St. Michael and St. George for the morning levee, a detachment of two hundred Hawaiian Royal Guards and Satsuma Marines leaped ashore from four self-propelled steel motor-barges. They bypassed the water-police. Drilling as they had at Honolulu and Shanghai, they fixed eighteen-inch bayonets to their magazine-rifles, wheeled into a hollow square across the quay, and pushed the silk-hatted Sydney aldermen and their weeping wives back against the iron palings of the garden.

Out of the stern-cabin of the lead barge stepped Lady Kaiulani’s nephew and Deputy-Commissioner for the Southern Ocean, Prince David Kalakaua, dressed in the white-and-gold tropical uniform of a Pacifica Privy Councillor. Beside him walked General Marcus Vance the younger, whose khaki boots still bore the red clay of Surakarta.

Lord Carington took two steps forward across the flagstones. His hand trembled upon his ceremonial court-sword as he confronted the tall Polynesian prince and the lean American general beneath the shadow of a Moreton Bay fig tree.

"By what outrageous piratical license," the British Governor demanded, his voice rising shrill and thin against the rumble of twenty-eight anchor-chains roaring down into the mud of Sydney Cove behind them, "do the warships of San Francisco and Edo violate the neutrality of a British self-governing colony upon Her Majesty’s Jubilee? There is no state of war between Whitehall and the Pacific Confederation!"

Young Marcus Vance ignored the plumed representative of Queen Victoria; he was already unstrapping his field-telephone case and handing the copper ground-spike to a Cantonese corporal to drive into the mortar between the quay-stones. Prince Kalakaua drew the heavy, brass-bound vellum scroll from beneath his arm. He broke the scarlet seal of the Insular Diet with a thumb that wore the ancient whale-ivory ring of Oahu.

"There is no neutrality inside the Great Arena, My Lord," Kalakaua said in the musical English of the Monterey court. He held the scroll open before the Governor’s blanched face while four companies of the First Virginia and Second Choshu Regiments marched up the stone ramp behind him, the steel wheels of their Maxim-guns rattling over the cobbles. "By the Decree of the Southern Circle, signed at the Citadel of San Francisco on the first of April by the Providentor Elias Thorne, it is declared that the safety of the Pacific Realm no longer permits the maintenance of European penal settlements or crown customs-houses south of the Equator. From the stroke of eight this morning, the colonies of New South Wales, Victoria, Queensland, and New Zealand are detached from the British Crown and constituted as the Southern Commonwealth of Pacifica."

"You are mad!" shouted Sir Henry Parkes, the white-bearded Premier of the colony. He pushed his bulky frame past the Governor’s shoulder and shook his fist at the blue steel battleships towering above the ferry-slips. "There are three million free-born British subjects on this continent! We have our own parliaments! We will tear up the railway tracks to Bathurst and fight you from every gum-tree in the bush before we pay a penny of tribute to a dying Yankee tyrant in a bath-chair and his yellow mercenaries!"

Young Marcus Vance looked up from his telephone-box. He pulled his slide-rule half an inch from his breast pocket, pushed it back with a click of his thumb, and studied the old white-bearded colonial politician with the same curiosity his father had turned upon the Zouaves at Bull Run twenty-six years ago.

"You have six hundred miles of mixed-gauge railway track that cannot even carry a freight-car from Sydney to Melbourne without unloading the boxes at the border, Mr. Parkes," Marcus said, his clipped voice cutting through the premier’s rhetoric as a squad of Satsuma telegraph-sappers ran past them toward the General Post Office on Martin Place with coils of insulated wire over their shoulders, "and forty percent of your wool-clip is already mortgaged to Mr. Schuyler’s banking-house in Hong Kong. Lift a single rail between here and Parramatta tonight, and I will leave your bush-rangers in the gum-trees. I will turn the eighteen-inch guns of the *Elias Thorne* upon the Sydney water-reservoir at Botany Swamps, burn the wool-warehouses at Circular Quay with thermite shell, and land thirty thousand Cantonese and Irish railway-navvies at Port Phillip tomorrow morning to re-lay your tracks to the Imperial six-foot gauge while your parliament sits in the coal-hulks. Corporal, take this gentleman’s watch and keys, and escort Lord Carington to the telegraph office; I require his signature on the railway-transfer order before the eight o’clock gun fires."

***

By the third week of July, the document which the court historians at Monterey gravely recorded as the *Australian Petition for Statehood* had arrived in the high conservatory on Rincon Hill, though the twelve colonial premiers, wool-factors, and Ballarat mine-owners who carried it up the marble stairs under the escort of Hawaiian bayonets looked less like petitioners than debtors walking behind a bailiff’s cart.

Inside the glass dome, the summer heat was thick with camphor-ice and the sour corruption of an aged body kept vertical by steel braces and digitalis. Elias remained mute. He had not spoken a full sentence aloud since the second apoplexy struck him on the morning the Java cable was spliced in June. The right half of his face might have been carved from gray Sierra granite, its pale eye staring wide from a sunken socket while the left corner of his mouth sagged into the white stubble of his jaw. Yet so long as the old man sat in his nickeled bath-chair beside the carp-pool with the seal-ring on his bloated, purple-nailed thumb, neither Grand-Admiral Takashima’s fleet-captains nor Comptroller Schuyler’s eastern directors could claim the regency without facing Lady Kaiulani’s provost-guards in the corridors below.

"The Delegates of the Southern Commonwealth have signed the Petition of Incorporation at Melbourne, Protector," Kaiulani said. She stood beside his right wheel. Three paces beyond the fern-pots, the twelve Australians halted in black broadcloth coats that smelled of sea-damp and bilge-water from the fast Honolulu packet. Ignoring the parchment that trembled in Schuyler’s spotted hands, Kaiulani kept her dark gaze beneath her silver-braided hair fixed upon the spasmodic twitching of Elias’s right forefinger against the sea-otter lap-robe. "They pray that the Crown of Pacifica will assume the forty-million-pound railway debt heretofore owed to the banking-houses of London, and that we unify the continental gauge from Brisbane to Adelaide while admitting the four provinces to the Imperial Customs Union upon the same footing as Oregon and Luzon."

Across the basin, Marquis Takashima’s hand closed hard upon the gold-lacquered hilt of his court sword. "A petition that drags our battleships two thousand leagues south of the Equator while the British Admiralty has stripped the Mediterranean and the Channel to send nineteen first-rate ironclads around the Cape of Good Hope!" the old Satsuma noble snapped. He had dropped all pretense of a lowered voice before the mute figure in the chair. "My cruisers off Timor intercepted the P&O mail-steamer from Colombo four days ago. Admiral Hornby has united the British Squadrons from the Cape, India, and China at Thursday Island: thirty-two armored ships of the line steaming down the Great Barrier Reef to retake Sydney! And my dockyards at Yokosuka are starved of nickel-steel because Mr. Schuyler’s board has diverted sixty thousand tons of rail-iron to Melbourne!"

"The Ballarat gold-escorts and the Broken Hill silver-mines have already yielded twelve million thalers to the Market Street reserve since June, Marquis!" Schuyler wheezed back. While the Australian delegates looked from one aging oligarch to the other like captives watching their jailers draw knives over the ransom-chest, the banker jabbed a shaking finger at the leather portfolio under his arm. "If we abandon the southern ports to Hornby’s fleet now, every bond we floated in Frankfurt and New York on the security of the Australian wool-clip will drop to ten cents before noon! General Vance’s land-batteries can hold Sydney—"

*Clang.*

The Providentor’s right arm had moved before either Schuyler or Takashima looked down. With a sudden jerk of his good shoulder, Elias swept the heavy brass inhaling-kettle from the side-table onto the tessellated marble pavement, where it spilled boiling stramonium-water and glowing charcoal across the polished boots of the Japanese admiral and the silk stockings of the New York banker.

From the sagging cavern of Elias’s throat came a low, rattling animal growl. The clot in his brain had locked the tongue that had once hushed the Diet of Sacramento. Raising his right hand, which was swollen like a bruised turnip, two inches from the fur blanket, he wrenched the thick parchment of the Australian Petition from Schuyler’s frozen fingers and crushed the vellum together with the wax seal directly against the hot, wet brass of the overturned kettle until the sheepskin scorched and smoked. The short hairs rose on the necks of the Australians by the door.

"The Providentor has ratified the Southern Act," Lady Kaiulani said into the hush. She stepped between the smoking parchment and the two men, her black skirt brushing the spilled coals. "And he bids me inform the Joint Board that Grand-Admiral Takashima will remain here in San Francisco to sit beside the Treasury desk where I can see his hands, while young General Vance takes the First and Third Battle Squadrons out of Port Jackson tonight to meet Admiral Hornby in the Coral Sea. Gentlemen of Melbourne, you are subjects of the Empire. Go down to the Comptroller’s office and count your iron."

***

On the ninth of August, four hundred miles east of the Queensland coast where the long, sapphire-blue rollers of the Coral Sea break into white foam over the sunken coral ramparts of the Saumarez Reefs, the nineteenth century met the twentieth across six miles of sunlit water.

No land was in sight. Under a sky of cloudless brass, the northeast trade-wind blew warm and steady at fourteen knots, heavy with tropical brine until the two greatest armadas since Lepanto fouled the Trade with eighty thousand horsepower of burning coal and Borneo residue.

To the north came the last throw of the British dice. Steaming in two stately, indented columns painted the traditional black-and-white buff of Nelson’s navy, nineteen ocean-going battleships and twelve armored cruisers bore down under Admiral Sir Geoffrey Hornby with the wind at their backs and white ensigns whipping from every peak to sweep the colonial usurpers from the southern ocean. Here came the pride of Portsmouth and the Clyde: the turret-rams *Inflexible*, *Devastation*, *Dreadnought*, and *Thunderer*, steaming alongside the new citadel-ships *Colossus* and *Edinburgh* behind twenty-four-inch wrought-iron belts and eighty-ton muzzle-loading Woolwich guns.

General Marcus Vance the younger stayed off the open bridge and wore no sword. Deep beneath the four-inch armored deck of the flagship *Elias Thorne*, fifteen feet below the waterline where the high, whining scream of the forced-draft steam-turbines and the constant *tick-clack-tick* of the brass range-calculators drowned the sea, he sat strapped into a revolving steel seat inside the electric fire-control central.

Before him stretched a ground-glass plotting-table under hooded green incandescent bulbs. Six Japanese and American midshipmen with vulcanite ear-phones stood over the glass, where they shifted small lead markers to match the bearings telephoned down every ten seconds from the thirty-foot coincidence range-finders in the armored mastheads eighty feet above.

"Range to the lead British division, the *Inflexible* and *Colossus*, eleven thousand four hundred meters, General," reported Major Kuroda. His gaze remained fixed on the spinning dials of the Dumaresq mechanical trig-computer bolted to the bulkhead. "Admiral Hornby has formed his heavy rams in double echelon on our port bow. He is closing at thirteen knots under full coal-draft to bring his eighty-ton muzzle-loaders inside three thousand yards, and his flagship is hoisting the signal for a general charge to ram."

Young Marcus adjusted the throat-microphone strapped over his khaki collar. Green light reflected off the celluloid cursor of his slide-rule. In the ninety-two-degree heat of the steel vault, the dry air smelled of warm gutta-percha insulation and lubricating-grease.

"Admiral Hornby thinks he is fighting the French at Lissa in sixty-six," Marcus said into the vulcanite mouthpiece. Armoured cable carried his clipped voice simultaneously to the conning-towers of all fourteen *Imperator*-class battleships as they steamed in a single, rigid line-ahead at eighteen knots. "His muzzle-loaders take four minutes to sponge and ram by hydraulic chain, and his gunners are sighting over open iron notches through their own coal-smoke. We will not close within eight thousand meters. Alter course twelve degrees to starboard together by flag-telegraph; keep the sun behind their smoke-stacks and hold the range at nine thousand yards. We will kill them with the math before their iron rams ever see our paint."

He flipped the brass switch on the master firing-board.

"All ships: main batteries load fifty-caliber armor-piercing capped shell with cast picric-acid filler. Elevation eleven degrees forty minutes; deflection left four knots. Fire by director-salvo on the flagship’s bell."

Up in the blinding tropical glare above the armored deck, electric endless-chain hoists fed two-thousand-pound projectiles from the magazines every thirty-eight seconds into fifty-six eighteen-inch rifled steel barrels, each fifty feet long, which swung in oiled unison toward the northern horizon.

Marcus closed the circuit. Free of the dirty white billow of old black powder, the fourteen battleships spat a mile-long, pale yellow flash of smokeless nitrocellulose cordite whose concussion stripped the white paint from their own waterways and flattened the trade-wind swells into dead, foaming milk for two hundred yards to leeward.

For twenty-one seconds the fifty-six one-ton cones of hardened San Francisco steel climbed through the upper stratosphere of the southern sky, whistling like fifty express-trains plunging into a tunnel before they dropped at a forty-five-degree angle straight onto the flat, two-inch wrought-iron decks of the British vanguard five miles away.

Down in the plotting-room of the *Elias Thorne*, the hulls gave no tremor of impact; only the observer in the fore-top shouted numbers into the wire:

*"Splash! Straddle on the lead turret-ship! Two, four, five direct hits abaft the funnel! Her central citadel has opened up—she’s blowing her magazines!"*

Across six miles of sparkling blue water, Her Majesty’s Ship *Inflexible*, ten thousand tons of British iron that had taken seven years to build at Portsmouth, took the blow from above like a turtle struck by a falling boulder, her thick side-armor untouched. Two eighteen-inch picric shells had punched clean through her thin teak-and-iron deck-plating to detonate inside her main boiler-rooms and hydraulic-loading chambers. A column of greasy black-and-orange smoke, thick with spinning iron deck-beams, life-boats, and human limbs, rose twelve hundred feet into the tropical sky; when the base of the pillar collapsed thirty seconds later, the water where the flagship of the Mediterranean had steamed was empty save for a spreading circle of boiling white foam and oil.

Before the second ship in the British line, the *Dreadnought*, could haul out of the blinding wreckage of her consort, the electric bells inside the Pacifica turrets rang a second time.

For ninety minutes under a sun that turned the steel decks into frying-pans, the Pacifica fleet executed a long-range industrial demolition. Four knots faster than the coal-choked British ironclads, the fourteen blue-hulled sisters held the outer arc of the circle like traction-engines plowing a furrow. Every forty seconds they poured fifty-six tons of high-explosive steel into a fleet whose short-barreled muzzle-loaders dropped their round-shot harmlessly into the swells two miles short of Marcus’s wake.

By two o’clock in the afternoon, the Coral Sea for ten miles leeward of the Saumarez Reefs was a floating abattoir of burning oil-slicks and shattered teak spars among listing, gutted iron hulks whose red-hot casemates hissed like laundry-irons as they rolled over into the two-thousand-fathom trough. Nine British battleships had gone to the bottom. Six more, the *Colossus* and the *Devastation* along with four armored cruisers, lay dead in the water with their rudders jammed and their funnels shot away to the deck-stubs; from the stumps of their signal-masts, surviving officers waved white bed-sheets while sharks tore at the hundreds of scorched, oil-blinded sailors clinging to the floating hammocks.

Down in the green-lit vault of the *Elias Thorne*, young Marcus Vance unstrapped his ear-phones, wiped a bead of sweat from his upper lip with a clean linen square, and studied the red ink tallies on the glass table.

"We have expended thirty-four percent of our eighteen-inch outfit to sink or disable fifteen capital units, Major Kuroda," Marcus said. He tapped a column of figures with his pencil. "That is twelve rounds per hull, which is three rounds higher than the Monterey proving-ground tables allowed for wrought-iron targets at nine thousand meters. Have the gunnery officers of the third division explain the variance in their evening reports. Signal the cruisers to pick up Admiral Hornby’s survivors and put prize-crews aboard the four hulks that can still float; their scrap-plate will pay for the cordite when we tow them into Sydney. Open the wireless-telegraph spark to the Noumea cable-head, and tell San Francisco the southern ocean is swept."

# Chapter 15: The Hundred and Twenty-Four States

On the nineteenth of August, the city of San Francisco lit its fires well before nightfall. From the granite quays of the Embarcadero to the high, wind-swept ridges of Twin Peaks, four hundred thousand electric arc-lamps and open barrels of blazing Santa Paula tar turned the afternoon fog into a roaring, brass-colored canopy. The air smelled of hot copper and scorched grease alongside tons of red Chinese firecrackers that exploded continuously along the balconies of Dupont and Market streets.

Down in the deep-water channel off Clark’s Point, where forty years earlier a twenty-one-year-old frontier captain had stood in front of a redwood log storehouse and bought twenty discharged soldiers with a canvas sack of Mexican pesos, the three-mile line of the Home Fleet fired a hundred-and-one-gun salute from twelve-inch breech-loaders. Each blank discharge shook the soot from the seventy foundry chimneys of Potrero Point. Up on Nob Hill, the bronze bells of the Syncretic Cathedral boomed in a discordant peal with the steam-sirens of sixty anchored grain-liners.

Inside the high-arched Map Room on the fourth floor of the Citadel, attendants had rolled Elias’s wheeled chair out onto the narrow iron gallery directly before the thirty-foot bronze relief-wall of the globe for the setting of the last magnet.

He was very small now inside the vast, dark wool folds of his old Engineer’s coat. Over the past ten days, the dropsical water that had swollen his legs for twenty years had risen into his pericardium; his skin had turned the color of wet wood-ash, and his chin tilted upward against the leather head-rest so that he could draw thin, whistling threads of air through his open mouth. The left side of his body was dead from shoulder to heel. Thin as a hickory ramrod inside the blue sleeve, his right arm was strapped lightly to the koa-wood armrest with a silk scarf to keep his trembling fingers on the brass rail.

Yet his right eye remained fixed in a wide, lidless stare as Major Sterling climbed the iron ladder with the gilded sun-and-anchor token in his hand.

Below the gallery, the grandees of the finished world packed the floor of the hall: white-haired Cornelius Schuyler on the arm of his secretary, Grand-Admiral Marquis Takashima in his blaze of Satsuma stars, the envoys of the tributary courts of Edo and Peking alongside Bangkok's legation, and sixty senators of the Diet in their blue-and-gold robes of state.

"Set it upon the barrier reef at the twentieth parallel, Major," Lady Kaiulani called up from her place beside the right wheel of Elias’s chair. She alone wore no gold braid. In her severe black mourning bombazine, with the heavy collar of the Insular Chancelleries resting upon her breast, she stood like the priestess of an iron idol before the mute stone. "And read the final paragraph of General Vance’s dispatch from Noumea so that the Comptroller’s clerks may enter it upon the Grand Ledger."

Sterling clapped the heavy gilded magnet onto the bronze indentation of the Coral Sea. A sharp *clink* rang through the hush of the room as the cannon-salutes outside momentarily paused. On the narrow grating, the one-eared veteran of Lake Baikal turned and held up the white paper ribbon from the southern cable.

"*'Admiral Sir Geoffrey Hornby died of his burns aboard our hospital-ship off Brisbane yesterday morning,'*" Sterling read, his old voice cracking against the bronze plates of the map. "*'Before his death, he signed the convention surrendering the remaining British naval stations at Esquimalt, Hong Kong, Singapore, and Auckland to our squadrons to prevent the bombardment of Melbourne. Not a single European warship remains afloat between the Cape of Good Hope and Cape Horn. From the eightieth parallel of the Arctic ice to the borders of the Antarctic pack, the ocean is one.'*"

A deep, ragged roar went up from the sixty senators and syndicate directors below. Canes hammered the parquet floor and silk hats flew toward the chandelier, while Cornelius Schuyler wept openly into his cambric handkerchief at the prospect of the Hong Kong and Singapore vaults opening their iron doors to his auditors.

Up on the iron gallery, Elias did not blink. In his ears roared the vast, rushing thunder of the brown Mississippi flood and the howling of the December gale over the dead mules in the Platte coulee, drowning out the cheers of the Diet and the twelve-inch cannon on the bay as he looked across the thirty feet of cast bronze.

It was all there. Forty-three years ago he had stood in his torn moccasins on the granite lip of the Sierra Nevada; now, every river-mouth and coal-seam, along with every deep-water harbor from his vision, bore the little gilded suns of his Mint. He had bought the Philadelphia bailiffs who once carried writs against his cabin, melted their law-books into boiler-plate, and fenced the half-world with steel rails.

His wide gray eye dropped from the bronze wall to the floor below, catching what the cheering senators missed.

Down at the foot of the spiral gallery-stairs, Marquis Takashima stood silent and unapplauding. Stepping quietly to the side of the door, the old samurai admiral whispered three rapid sentences in the Satsuma dialect to two of his naval aides-de-camp, whose hands rested on their sword-hilts while they measured the twelve Hawaiian guardsmen around the telegraph repeater. Ten paces to the left, before the echoes of Sterling’s voice had died in the dome, Cornelius Schuyler was already pulling two Boston railway directors into the shadow of the serpentine pillars. His plump, trembling fingers sketched percentages on the back of the Noumea dispatch to divide the spoils of the Hong Kong banks before the corpse above them was cold.

*They are waiting for the last wheeze,* Elias thought inside the locked, silent iron box of his skull. A cold, dark tide of salt water rose another inch around his laboring heart. *I bolted the continents together with eighty-pound rail, I washed their streets with canister, I gave them an ocean for a pasture, and the minute my eye shuts, the shopkeeper and the swordsman will tear the coat in half over my knees.*

He tried to lift his right hand to strike the iron railing. The silk scarf held his wrist fast to the koa-wood. Only his bloated thumb twitched once against the sea-otter fur, a dry scratch that went unheard below the gallery.

Kaiulani heard it.

She looked down at his purple fingernail on the pelt, then followed the line of his solitary gaze to the floor where Takashima’s aides edged toward the corridor door and Schuyler’s syndicate-men huddled by the pillars. For twenty years she had worn the black bombazine of Oahu’s dead independence. Through that long, eighteen-year twilight between the winter of the Baikal ice and the fall of the Romanovs, she had stood beside him while he ground the world into a single circular trough. Together they had built the Bering spans and starved St. Petersburg into revolution; they had boiled the Dutch canals of Java, yet the machine had grown so vast that its own creators now stood like thieves in the engine-room, eager to strip the copper pipes before the pressure-gauge dropped to zero.

From the dying Caesar in the chair, she looked down to the greedy, small-souled heirs who waited to butcher sixty million people in a war of succession over customs-books and clan-fiefs. Her dark face hardened.

Over the back of the wheeled chair she leaned until her lips brushed the white, cropped bristles above Elias’s right ear, her black mantle shielding his face from the room below.

"Do not spend your breath on their collars, Elias," she whispered, so low the air did not stir a hair on his temple. Reaching into the bosom of her black dress, she bypassed the phial of digitalis to draw out the small brass master-key to the Citadel’s palace guard-gates, together with the thick, wax-sealed cylinder of the Final Organic Statute that they had drafted in secret through the sleepless nights of his apoplexy. "If you leave them the old territories, if you leave Takashima an intact Japan and Schuyler a solid New York, they will have cannon firing across the bay before your body is in the Monterey vault. Let us break their fiefs into gravel while your eye is still open to watch them sign."

In the shadow of her black sleeve, Elias’s single gray eye shifted half an inch until it met hers. Inside the calcified cage of his ribs, where the fluid pressed like cold lead against his lungs, the old frontier arithmetic flared up in one final, triumphant blaze. Forty years had gone into bolting the plates together. Now he would shatter the hilt into fragments only the throne could hold.

Down by the mahogany doors, the four Hawaiian sentries outside in the corridor swung the heavy bronze leaves shut and dropped the iron bar into its sockets with a dull *thud*. Marquis Takashima spun around on his heel. His sword came six inches out of its scabbard as he looked up toward the gallery rail, where Lady Kaiulani stepped forward to the head of the iron stairs and raised her left hand to the four Maxim-gun detachments of the Insular Guard emerging from behind the velvet draperies of the upper loggia.

"My lords and gentlemen of the Diet," Kaiulani’s clear, musical voice rang out across the frozen hush of the rotunda, before the first man on the floor could reach the barred doors. "Do not trouble the sentries. The Providentor has observed your anxiety regarding the administration of our newly completed circumference, and before the Te Deum is sung in the cathedral, he has summoned you into executive session to witness the promulgation of the Statute of the Hundred and Twenty-Four States."

Up on the iron gallery, through the swimming mist of his failing vision, Elias stared down at the central balustrade, across which Major Sterling unrolled a second, smaller chart where the surveyor’s straight-edge had erased the old names of history. California, Japan, China, New England, and Australia were gone.

"Look upon the wall, Marquis Takashima," Kaiulani said. Behind her, the paralyzed figure’s crooked, swollen right forefinger tapped the brass rail like a death-watch beetle in the beams of an old house: *tap, tap, tap*. "Look upon the wall, Comptroller Schuyler. For thirty years the Confederation has tolerated the ancient borders of conquered kingdoms and rebel republics as temporary conveniences of the march. Now that the southern ocean is swept and the Siberian frontier rests upon the Yenisei, those provincial names have become nests for faction and treason."

Below the stairs, Cornelius Schuyler’s jaw sagged open. He squinted through his pince-nez at the red grid-lines bisecting the continents. "You have cut the State of New York into four separate prefectures! You have detached Manhattan from the Hudson valley and joined it to the maritime district of Nova Scotia, and the Sacramento mines are severed from the bay!"

"And the domains of Satsuma and Choshu are dissolved into numbered insular cantons!" Takashima roared. His bronze face mottled with apoplectic fury as he took two steps up the iron spiral stair, before the four brass water-jackets of the Maxim guns in the loggia swung downward with a synchronized, oiled *click* and trained their muzzles directly upon his starred breast. He halted. "This is the work of a woman’s cabal! The Tenno at Kyoto signed an alliance of crowns, not an incorporation into an American census-roll!"

Up in the koa-wood chair, the dark tide rose another inch inside Elias’s chest. It drowned the lower lobes of his lungs until the golden chandelier above the rotunda turned the color of dried blood; yet with a last spasm of the muscles in his right neck, he forced his chin off the leather pad. His lips parted. From the ruined cavern of his throat came two words, slurred and gravelly as a landslide in the Sierra:

*"Sign... it."*

The two syllables dropped into the rotunda like a two-thousand-pound shell from the *Elias Thorne*. Every senator on the floor flinched backward from the gallery rail. Even Takashima’s fingers froze upon his lacquered hilt as he stared up into that solitary, lidless gray eye burning down from the shadow of the bronze map.

"You hear the voice of your Sovereign," Kaiulani said. She descended three steps of the iron stair and held the open parchment roll out before her like a shield. "One hundred and twenty-four imperial states, drawn by watershed and coal-seam, each containing five million souls, each governed by a civil prefect appointed from Monterey and a military commandant drawn from the opposite shore of the ocean. No Japanese soldier will ever again garrison an Asian island; no American regiment will sit within two thousand miles of its native river; and no bank on Montgomery Street will clear a bill of exchange without the counter-stamp of the Bureau of Integration. Step to the porphyry table, Marquis. The Providentor’s eye is upon you, and the gunners have their thumbs upon the triggers."

***

Three weeks later, the old man’s eye was shut. Six inches of soldered sheet-lead and five tons of polished Sierra granite sealed him in the crypt of the Monterey Basilica, yet his iron geometry sat heavier upon the neck of the world than his living hand had ever done.

On an afternoon in middle September, when the scorching *diablo* wind blew down from the inner valleys across the bay and turned the sky above San Francisco into a brass dome dusted with red alkali and the soot of the Potrero smelters, Lady Kaiulani sat at the head of the long teakwood table in the Bureau of Integration.

The chamber occupied the entire third story of the old Mint building on Fifth Street. Wrought-iron grilles barred its tall windows against the street-mobs that still gathered weekly around the bread-depots. From the floorboards to the eighteen-foot ceiling, bypassing all silk banners or bronze maps of conquered oceans, galvanized iron pigeon-holes lined the walls with forty thousand sheepskin-bound digests of local law: the *Code Napoléon* of Quebec and Cochin-China, the *Great Qing Legal Code* of the Yangtze provinces, the Anglo-Saxon common law of Massachusetts and New South Wales, the feudal house-statutes of the Tokugawa clans, the *Adat* customary rolls of Java, and the oral *Kapu* genealogies of the Polynesian reefs. That was all.

The thermometer stood at ninety degrees. Locked in with the Regent-Chancellor since six in the morning to hammer the customs of half the human race into a single volume before the autumn assizes opened, twelve men soured the room with the stench of their bitter sweat and the reek of flour-paste and scorching blotting-paper.

"It cannot be reconciled without provoking a general rising along the Hwang-ho, Your Highness!" cried Magistrate Shen, the former President of the Peking Board of Punishments. Across the ink-stained teak, while his long fingernails clicked against the ivory beads of his abacus, he glared at Chief Justice Field of the California bench and Judge Hoshino of the Edo Cassation Court. "By the forty-second statute of the new Canton Six-Foot Code, your American clerks have written that a son who strikes his father in a dispute over railway wages shall be fined ten silver thalers or sentenced to thirty days on the county road-gang! In the Middle Kingdom, parricide or filial battery is an abomination that shakes the pillars of the sky! If the village elders of Shantung hear that a boy may strike his sire for the price of a pig and walk free, they will tear down the telegraph poles and burn your district magistrates in their beds! The penalty must remain the *Ling-ch'i*, the slicing of the flesh by a thousand cuts in the market-square!"

"And am I to instruct an Anglo-Saxon jury in Boston or Melbourne," thundered Justice Field, his white whiskers bristling as he slammed his copy of Blackstone’s *Commentaries* down upon the teak and sent a cloud of red pounce-dust into the hot air, "that a twenty-one-year-old mechanic who quarrels with his father over a pint of beer is to be tied to a post on Boston Common and carved into beef-steaks by a Cantonese executioner? And what of this clause inserted by Judge Hoshino from the Satsuma house-laws, that a military officer of the third rank may strike off the head of a civilian merchant who fails to dismount from his buggy when the imperial post-carriage passes? Try that on Broadway or in Sydney, madam, and all the Maxim guns in your arsenal will not keep the stones in the pavement!"

Judge Hoshino spoke without raising his voice. He sat with his small, dry hands tucked into the sleeves of his black alpaca judicial gown, his spectacles glinting.
