"In the seventy-ninth prefecture, which your surveyors formerly called Victoria, three Australian teamsters spat upon the sedan-chair of Colonel Kuroda’s wife last Tuesday and refused to yield the crown of the road. Because the local magistrate was an Englishman who applied your 'common law' of assault, the teamsters were released on five thalers' bail. That night, two companies of the Choshu garrison marched out of their barracks and burned the teamsters' suburb to the ground. If the law does not protect the honor of the sword, Your Highness, the sword will write its own docket in fire."

Kaiulani rested her temples against her ungloved fingertips. Beneath the heavy black bombazine of her dress, the whale-bone stays cut into her ribs with every breath, and her eyes burned from reading six-point legal proofs in three languages by the glare of the electric bulbs.

For twenty years Elias had cut through such knots with a single stroke of a cavalry saber or a threat to open the sluice-gates. Terror had served for jurisprudence while the conqueror lived; men obeyed contradictory decrees because the crippled Titan on Rincon Hill would send a monitor up their river if they argued. Now Elias was cold lead in Monterey. Though she had locked Schuyler and Takashima into the Council of Regency with bayonets at their backs, an ocean conquered with steam and nitro-glycerine still left eight hundred million souls at breakfast beyond the governance of an eighteen-inch gun.

Every concession she made to Justice Field’s Americans was telegraphed within the hour by Takashima’s spies to Edo as proof that the white syndicate was reducing the samurai to coolies; every sop she threw to Shen’s mandarins was printed on secret hand-presses in the cellars of Philadelphia to prove that a Polynesian witch had sold Christendom to the pagans.

"We will have neither the thousand cuts of Peking nor the twelve shopkeepers in a jury-box of Boston," Kaiulani said. Over the babble of the twelve jurists, beside the English steel pens arranged upon the ink-stained blotter, she dipped her brush into the red vermilion ink-stone. "You are still thinking like parish clerks of dead nations. Only the Forty-Second Agricultural Canton exists where Shantung stood, Magistrate Shen. Only the Ninth Atlantic Industrial District remains of Massachusetts, Justice Field."

She drew the master-proof of the *Codex Pacificus* across the teak and struck out three pages of Field’s habeas corpus clauses with a single diagonal slash of wet crimson.

"From the first of October," she dictated to the three stenographers behind her chair, "all trials by civilian jury between the Yenisei and the Atlantic are abolished as relics of parliamentary sedition. In their place, every canton court shall consist of a Tripartite Bench: one magistrate of American birth, one of Asian, and one of Insular blood, none of whom may sit within three thousand miles of the province where he was born. As for filial rebellion and insult to the uniform, the State is now the universal father of all subjects and the sole bearer of the sword. A son who strikes his parent or a teamster who obstructs an imperial officer commits *Sabotage of the Imperial Order*, punishable across all one hundred and twenty-four states by ten years’ penal servitude in the Bering tunnel-gangs. Write it down, gentlemen."

# Chapter 16: Examination Sheds

To the Chronicler who walks the broad, granite-paved esplanades of San Francisco or New Osaka in these closing years of the nineteenth century, the silence that falls over the cities during the third week of every October marks the final burial of the old American Republic.

In the barbarous decades before the Pivot, as the curious student may still read in the yellowing files of the *New York Herald* or the *Charleston Mercury* preserved in the locked stacks of the Chancery, the autumn season along the North American littoral was a time of drunken Saturnalia which the ancients called an Election. Every four years, the workshops were emptied and the counting-houses shuttered. Millions of unlettered ploughmen and newly landed European ditch-diggers marched with tavern-keepers through the mud behind brass bands and pine-tar torches, roaring the names of rival country lawyers and stuffing slips of printed rag-paper into wooden boxes to determine who should command the fleets and rob the post-offices for the next forty-eight months.

Today, the pine-tar torches are gone, and the wooden ballot-boxes have long since been split up to kindle the assay-furnaces of the Mint. In their stead stands the Examination Shed.

In the winter after the Providentor’s burial, when the old millionaire syndics of Montgomery Street and the clan-admirals of Satsuma believed they could turn their seats on the Joint Boards into hereditary baronies, Lady Kaiulani’s Regency delivered its supreme stroke: it borrowed the most ancient engine of Oriental despotism and welded it to the steel chassis of Western polytechnics. If the hundred and twenty-four fragmented states were to hold together against centrifugal force, they required a priesthood of clerks who owed their bread solely to the competitive stamp of the Imperial Seal, independent of any New York banker’s purse or Japanese daimyo’s pedigree.

The Grand Triennial Examination at the Berkeley compound across the bay from the Golden Gate is the true furnace in which the citizenry of the twentieth century is cast. Upon a leveled plateau above the oak-groves rise ten thousand identical, windowless cells of corrugated Birmingham iron and poured Portland cement. Numbered rows divide them like the honeycombs of a mechanical hive, enclosed within a double stockade of electrified barbed wire where the Hawaiian Guard walks its posts.

On the eighteenth of October, before the morning fog has lifted from the water, the steam-siren sounds. Ten thousand youths between their eighteenth and twenty-second years, the survivors of the rigorous prefectural eliminations held the previous spring in Melbourne, Hankow, Boston, Irkutsk, and Honolulu, file through the main iron turnstiles. Orderlies strip them to the skin in the carbolic disinfecting-sheds to ensure that no logarithmic table or political crib is sewn into a hem. Whether fair-haired grandson of a Virginia planter or spectacled heir of a Soochow silk-mandarin, whether bred on a Hankow wharf or born the broad-shouldered son of a Maori chief, each candidate receives an identical, coarse gray tunic of unbleached prison-duck stamped across the shoulder-blades with a five-digit cipher. He takes two dip-pens, a cake of India ink, a slide-rule of standardized boxwood, a tin bucket of boiled rice and salt beef, and a wooden board that serves for seat, bed, and writing-desk inside his four-by-six iron cubicle.

At the stroke of noon, the heavy steel drop-bars clang shut across the ends of the hundred alleys. Ten thousand youths remain sealed inside their iron tombs for seventy-two unbroken hours. Beneath the fog, the silence is so profound that the scratching of ten thousand steel nibs upon foolscap carries half a mile away like a million silkworms devouring a mulberry forest.

No question of rhetoric or natural rights, nor any chronicle of dead parliaments, ever sullies the white paper pushed through the food-slots by the silent, soft-shoed proctors. Under the *Curriculum of the Three Harmonies* drafted by the Bureau of Integration, the youth who aspires to wear the silver anchor of an Imperial Prefect must prove his orthodoxy in harder coin. During the first twenty-four hours, he renders an edict of the Monterey Chancery concurrently into classical literary Chinese, court Japanese, and English statute-prose without a single variance of legal meaning; during the second, he calculates the ballistic trajectory of an eighteen-inch melinite shell allowing for Coriolis drift and barometric pressure, together with the coal-tonnage and axle-grease required to move an army corps of thirty thousand men six hundred leagues by broad-gauge rail at thirty below zero. Then comes the final night. By the glare of the single naked electric bulb suspended above his head, drawing upon the commentaries of Thucydides and Confucius alongside the dispatches of Elias Thorne, he must compose a five-thousand-word dissertation upon the *Moral Necessity of the Pacific Pivot* to demonstrate that parliamentary liberty is merely the infancy of anarchy.

Every morning at six, Cantonese orderlies unlock the iron doors of those cubicles where the scratching has ceased. The casualties come out on canvas stretchers. Boys from the Ohio valleys go raving mad from seventy hours of logarithmic tables under a sixty-watt glare and try to dash their brains out against the corrugated iron; consumptive scholars from Kyoto cough their lungs onto the wet ink of their railway-schedules; and third-generation scions of the old Boston and Charleston patriciate, finding by the third afternoon that their family names carry no weight behind a five-digit number and that failure means seven years as a private conscript in the Sumatra rubber-swamps, open their own femoral arteries with the sharpened steel nibs of their government pens.

Down along the central elevated catwalk that bisects the ten thousand iron roofs, Chief Examiner Shen and General Marcus Vance the younger walked through the drizzling October dusk. Their rubberized capes gleamed under the arc-lamps above the wire-mesh ventilators of the lighted cells.

"Candidate Four-Four-Zero-Nine in the third Canton row has stopped writing, General," Shen said. He paused beside a ventilator stack and peered down through his thick horn-rimmed spectacles at the top of a cropped yellow head bowed motionless over a blotting-pad fifty feet below their boots. "That is the youngest grandson of Comptroller Schuyler. He has been staring at the third problem of the Siberian coal-modulus for four hours without moving his slide-rule, and his candle-ration is burned to the socket."

Young Marcus Vance ignored the wire grate. Pulling his radium-dialed chronometer from his wet cuff to check the forty-one minutes remaining before the final siren, he looked across the yard toward the eastern gate of the compound, where a closed black carriage bearing the private crest of the New York Banking Syndicate waited in the mud behind two steaming horses.

"The old Comptroller asked me at the Council table yesterday if the mathematics paper might be waived for a boy whose grandfather financed the Market Street Mint," Marcus said. He rested his gloved hand upon the master bell-switch bolted to the iron post beside them; his clipped voice matched the flat hum of the electric dynamos at the end of the yard. "He reminded me that when the Providentor was still alive, during that autumn before the stroke in the conservatory when the old man spent his last walking afternoon inside the State Archives, even Elias Thorne had allowed the syndicate directors to buy exemptions for their eldest sons."

Shen adjusted his spectacles against the cold mist off the bay. His narrow shoulders stiffened beneath his oiled silk cape. "And how did you answer him, General?"

"I told him that when the Providentor walked through the State Archives in the autumn of eighty-five to review the Great Triennial Census, I was the aide who carried his portfolio," Marcus replied, his gaze on the carriage lamps flickering through the rain. "We stood for three hours in the subterranean vaults beneath the Mint, where the Hollerith punch-card tabulators were sorting the tallies from the Yangtze and the Mississippi down to the Yukon. Three hundred million subjects, Magistrate. The old man ran his scarred thumb down the summary folios: eighty million in the American provinces, thirty-eight million in the Japanese archipelago, a hundred and seventy million in the Chinese prefectures, twelve million across the southern islands and the Siberian rail-corridors. Do you know what he said to me when the Chief Statistician showed him that the old white families of the Atlantic and California made up less than one-fifth of the military muster-rolls?"

Down in the cubicle beneath their boots, young Schuyler shoved his wooden board away. It scraped across the cement floor, loud through the wire mesh, and he dropped his face into his ink-stained palms.

"The Providentor did not record that observation in the official gazette," Shen said.

"He kept it from the syndicate directors," Marcus said. "He looked at the brass counting-dials clicking off the births in Hankow and Osaka, and he took me by the elbow. His grip could still bruise the bone through a wool tunic then. He said: *'Marcus, your father and I built the frame of this house with frontiersmen and Rebel veterans because they were the timber nearest the axe. Look at the numbers in that book. Three hundred million souls cannot be held by a handful of New York bankers’ nephews and Satsuma cousins sitting on velvet cushions. Within ten years, the blood that built this empire will be a drop of tallow in an ocean of brine. If you let Schuyler and Takashima turn the prefectures into family pastures after I am under the stone, the three hundred million will tear the fences down in a single night. Grind the names out of them, boy. Make the ledger the only father a magistrate has.'*"

Marcus checked the glowing green dial on his wrist. The second-hand swept across the twelve. Forty minutes still remained, yet down in Cell Four-Four-Zero-Nine the candidate had already upset his porcelain ink-pot across the blank pages of his Siberian coal calculation; black fluid soaked into the coarse gray duck of his sleeve while his shoulders shook with dry, silent sobs.

"A candidate who deliberately spoils his examination folio before the siren forfeits his remaining time under Article Nine," Marcus said, and he pulled the heavy iron lever of the sector-alarm down until the copper contacts bit.

Below them, along the wet concrete alley of the third Canton row, the electric gong over Cell Four-Four-Zero-Nine gave two short, strident clangs. Before the echo had died against the corrugated Birmingham iron, two Cantonese orderlies and a Hawaiian provost-corporal trotted down the narrow passage with a key-ring and a pair of canvas-webbing ankle-straps. The heavy drop-bar clattered up. The cell door swung outward into the drizzle.

"Let us go down to the turnstile, Magistrate Shen," Marcus said. Turning on his heel, he descended the cleated iron steps of the catwalk with the brisk, unhurried stride of the parade-ground at the Imperial Military Academy at Monterey. "Comptroller Schuyler has been sitting in his brougham since four o’clock with a hot-water brick at his feet, expecting to drive his grandson up to Nob Hill for supper. It would be discourteous to keep a member of the Regency Council waiting in the mud."

At the main eastern gate, where the double stockade of electrified barbed wire parted before a guardhouse of gray Sierra granite, the air smelled of wet horse-manure and the carbolic wash tracking off the boots of the guard-relief, sharp with the hot copper tang of the transformer-sheds.

Inside the fenced courtyard behind the guardhouse, a compound that served both as the processing-pen for failed candidates and as the primary coastal depot for the Cadet Corps of the Imperial Military Academy, four hundred eighteen-year-old youths stood drawn up in four hollow squares under the sizzling blue glare of the carbon-arc lamps. Marcus had spent the morning inspecting their drill before crossing the bay to the Examination Sheds. As his boots struck the wet gravel at the bottom of the catwalk stairs, the cadet-captains brought their squads to rigid attention. Leather rifle-slings slapped in unison against coarse blue wool.

Here stood the census ledger Elias Thorne had read in the subterranean vaults. In the first rank of the right-hand square, a six-foot youth from the Shensi hill-country flanked the dark-skinned son of a Samoan harbor-chief and a red-haired boy from the Pennsylvania iron-towns; in the second stood a samurai cadet from Hizen beside a Tagalog from Luzon and a boy from the Melbourne sheep-downs. Their brass collar-plates bore no surnames, stamped only with the Roman numeral of a birth-canton and the four digits of an Academy matriculation. Since their twelfth year, when the Triennial Assessors had taken them from their parish schools, they had spoken their mother-tongues only as tactical exercises, eating the same ration of pressed bean-curd and salted beef, sleeping on the same iron cots, and reciting the *Maxims of the Providentor* in unison every morning before the sun-and-anchor rose above the parade-ground.

"Present *arms!*" barked the cadet-adjutant, a youth born in the conquered ruins of Atlanta who spoke with the clipped, nasal accent of the New Edo staff schools.

Four hundred magazine-rifles snapped vertical before four hundred identical chests. In the drizzle, the bayonets gleamed like a row of wet icicles.

Marcus touched two fingers to his oilskin cap-brim. His gaze swept the line. Where his father had been forced to bribe Missouri bushwhackers with silver bags and threaten Hawaiian kings with Gatling guns just to keep the columns moving, these boys in the yard behind him knew nothing of the United States Constitution or a Tokugawa shogun; if an order came down the pneumatic tube bearing the Chancery stamp, they would shoot their own fathers upon the church steps of Boston or Kyoto.

Outside the iron turnstile, the door of the black syndicate carriage swung open. Old Cornelius Schuyler leaned upon his gold-headed ebony cane and the arm of a liveried footman as he stepped down onto the plank walk laid across the mud. Beside him walked Grand-Admiral Marquis Takashima in a heavy naval boat-cloak, having ridden up from the Oakland ferry-slip in an Admiralty steam-phaeton whose boiler still hissed behind the hedge.

"General Vance!" Schuyler called out. His wheezing voice rose through the iron bars of the gate as he peered past Marcus’s shoulder into the processing-yard. From the third alley, two Cantonese orderlies emerged with their hands clamped on the elbows of a stumbling, bare-headed boy in a stained gray prison-duck tunic. "Why is Arthur being brought out by the hospital-men before the six o’clock siren? Is the boy taken ill with the chill? Bring him to the carriage at once. My physician is inside with hot brandy!"

Marcus stopped three feet behind the locked iron turnstile and clasped his hands behind the small of his back. At his left elbow, Chief Examiner Shen held the wet, ink-blotted examination folio between two pairs of brass tongs as if it were a dead rat.

"There is no Arthur Schuyler in this compound, Comptroller," Marcus said. "If you refer to Candidate Four-Four-Zero-Nine of the Seventh Maritime District, his examination concluded nine minutes ago when he overturned his ink-horn upon the third sheet of the Siberian logistics problem. Under the Statute of the Hundred and Twenty-Four States, which you and the Marquis countersigned in the Rotunda two months ago, a candidate who fails the polytechnic minimum by reason of wilful defacement is automatically inducted into the Second Class Pioneer Reserve for seven years’ service on the southern frontier."

The arc-light struck the boy's cropped yellow hair and pale, tear-streaked face. "Grandfather!" he choked out. He wrenched against the Cantonese corporals’ grip as a Hawaiian blacksmith stepped from the induction-shed with a pair of heavy steel shears, clipped the candidate’s number-patch from his shoulder, and replaced it with the yellow canvas brassard of the Sumatra rubber-battalions. "Grandfather, don't let them put me in the steamer! The logarithms were for sixty-below temperatures. Nobody taught us the Siberian tables at the New York grammar school! They changed the questions on purpose!"

Old Schuyler’s face went the color of wet tallow, then swelled to a mottled purple beneath his white side-whiskers. He struck the iron bars with the ferrule of his cane.

"Unlock this gate, Major Shen!" the seventy-year-old financier roared. His voice cracked in the wet dusk. Inside the fence, two young Academy cadets took a half-step forward, their thumbs resting on the safety-catches of their magazine-rifles. "General Vance, have you lost your senses? That boy is the sole heir to the Schuyler-Livingston banking trust! His father underwrote forty million thalers of the Yukon Gold Reserve when you were in short trousers! You cannot ship the grandson of a Regent of the Realm to dig ditches in a malarial swamp alongside coolies and felons because he missed a sum in algebra!"

Beside Schuyler, Marquis Takashima stepped to the wet bars. The old Satsuma warlord looked from the weeping boy to the four hundred cadets standing like bronze statues in the yard behind Marcus’s back.

"My own grand-nephew, Shimazu Tadao, sits in the ninth row of that shed tonight, General Vance," Takashima said. "Am I to understand that if a clerk from Peking marks his Chinese syntax deficient at six o’clock, the heir of the Satsuma house is likewise to be sheared like a sheep by your Hawaiian turnkeys? While the Providentor breathed, there was respect for the blood that forged the sword."

"While the Providentor breathed, Marquis, he was forced to humor the pride of old men who remembered the world before the Pivot," answered a clear voice from the shadow of the granite guardhouse.

Lady Kaiulani stepped from beneath the stone arch onto the wet gravel beside Marcus Vance. Having crossed from San Francisco on the five-thirty launch in her high-collared black bombazine and a cloak of dark sea-otter fur, accompanied by Colonel Kalakaua and six Insular Guard troopers with holstered self-loading pistols at their belts, she walked straight to the iron bars until less than twelve inches of rainy air separated her pale face from the noses of her two fellow Regents. She looked directly at Takashima.

"The Providentor is in his granite box at Monterey, gentlemen," Kaiulani said. Behind them, the Hawaiian blacksmith forced young Schuyler to his knees on the wet concrete and closed the iron rivet of the Sumatra identification-collar around the boy’s neck with a sharp *clink* of his hammer. "Before he closed his eye on the gallery, he gave us the Statute of the Hundred and Twenty-Four States so that there would be no Schuyler banking trust and no Satsuma clan ten years from tonight. If I spare Mr. Schuyler’s grandson from the rubber-boats at six o’clock, how shall General Vance command those four hundred boys behind him to die at the Yenisei trenches at seven?"

"This is a coup d'état against the Council of Regency!" Schuyler gasped. He gripped the wet iron palings with his plump hands while the orderlies hauled his grandson to his feet and pushed him toward the covered gangway leading down to the quarantine wharf, where the green and red lights of the Batavia transport glowed through the fog. "Marquis, you have the Second Cruiser Squadron anchored off Goat Island! Order your captains to land six hundred marines at the ferry-slip before that transport clears the pier! And I will wire the Clearing House in New York and Osaka to stop payment on every garrison draft from here to Irkutsk at nine tomorrow morning! We will see how long Her Highness and this boy-general can play at being Caesar without a silver thaler in the chest or a ship in the bay!"

Takashima’s right hand dropped to the hilt of his sword. He turned half around toward his waiting steam-phaeton on the road. "My launch is at the foot of the hill, Comptroller. Once I am aboard the *Kamehameha II*—"

"Your launch was impounded by the cadets of the Third Maritime Company twenty minutes ago, Marquis," young Marcus Vance interrupted. Without raising his voice half a tone, he drew a folded white telegraph-form from his khaki breast pocket and held it up against the iron grate where the blue arc-light fell across the wet ink. "And as for the Second Cruiser Squadron off Goat Island, you are quite right that a divided fleet is a danger to the public peace. At four-fifteen this afternoon, acting under the Emergency Integration Warrant signed by the Chancellor, the newly commissioned cadet-officers of the Naval Polytechnic relieved every Satsuma post-captain in the bay of his command. Your cruisers are currently under the guns of the Alcatraz eighteen-inch batteries with mixed crews of Californian and Cantonese and Hawaiian artificers at the throttles."

Takashima froze. His boot hung an inch above the mud of the road, and his bronze cheek turned the color of old tallow under the lamp. "My captains... relieved by schoolboys?"

"By Imperial Citizens, Marquis," Kaiulani said. She rested her gloved hand upon the iron turnstile lock as the deep blast of the Batavia transport’s steam-whistle sounded from the wharf to announce the casting off of the conscript-barges. "And you need not trouble the telegraph operators in New York tonight, Mr. Schuyler. At noon today, the Bureau of Integration foreclosed upon the private shares of the Schuyler-Livingston Syndicate for arrears on the Siberian war-assessment. Your clerks on Montgomery Street are now civil servants of the Fifth Fiscal Grade, answering directly to Magistrate Shen."

She nodded once to Colonel Kalakaua. The iron gate remained locked. From the side sally-port, twenty cadets of the Imperial Academy marched out in double file with fixed bayonets and surrounded the black syndicate carriage and the Admiralty phaeton in the muddy lane.

"You will not be harmed, my lords," Kaiulani said. Across the ten thousand iron roofs of the Examination Sheds behind her, the driving rain drummed hard enough to drown young Schuyler's faint cries from the wharf below under a metallic roar like the marching of three hundred million feet. "The Empire does not make martyrs of its bookkeepers. You will drive back to the ferry under the escort of General Vance’s cadets, and tomorrow afternoon at four you will sit in your accustomed chairs upon the high balcony of the Chancery beside me to review the autumn parade. The people of San Francisco must see that the Triumvirate is united, even if only two of us still hold the pen."

***

By three o’clock the following afternoon, the October gale had blown itself clear out to sea. Above the Golden Gate, a hard dome of imperial blue curved unbroken from the redwoods of Marin to the smoking slag-heaps of the Contra Costa shore.

Seventy feet above the granite terrace, where the thirty-foot bronze statue of Elias Thorne cast from the melted cannon of Washington and London and St. Petersburg stood facing the sunset with his iron walking-stick planted upon the globe, the tall French doors of the Chancery balcony stood open to the salt wind on the western facade of the Citadel on Rincon Hill.

Inside the threshold, just out of sight of the half-million subjects who packed the stepped avenues and roof-tops down to the water’s edge, Cornelius Schuyler and Marquis Takashima sat side by side in two high-backed chairs of carved Hawaiian koa-wood. Through the binoculars of the foreign consuls down in the plaza, the two aged oligarchs sat in state beneath the silk canopy of the Rising Sun in their full gold-braided collars and the broad blue ribands of the Order of the Golden Gate. Heavy canvas webbing strapped their ankles to the chair-legs behind the velvet valance. Three paces from the balcony rail, directly behind the two men's headrests, a broad-faced youth from the Amur Cossack settlements and a dark-eyed boy from the Cantonese dock-guilds—both twenty-year-old cadet-lieutenants of the Academy—stood with cocked nine-shot pistols hidden beneath their dress capes.

Lady Kaiulani walked out past their knees to the stone balustrade. General Marcus Vance the younger stepped to her left elbow.

Below them stretched the City of the World, the monumental, smoking capital of the Great Arena. For twelve miles around the horseshoe of the bay, the straight-edge of the Imperial Engineers had swept away the wooden shanties of the gold-rush era. From the foot of Telegraph Hill to the southern slips of Hunters Point ran a continuous, three-tiered embankment of gray Sierra granite and red brick: on the lowest level, sixty ocean-going cargo-liners and armored depot-ships lay moored bow-to-stern beneath hydraulic gantry-cranes that clanked and hissed in unison as they swung bales of raw Kiangsu silk, ingots of Broken Hill silver, and crates of Lowell textiles onto the electric freight-cars of the Belt Line; on the second tier, elevated thirty feet above the mud upon cast-iron colonnades, thundered the broad-gauge express trains arriving from Boston and Irkutsk and Peking via the Bering Bridge without a single change of locomotive; and rising up the steep hills behind the smoke-canopy stood the geometric terraces of the ministries, their white marble Roman porticoes crowned with sweeping green copper roofs in the style of Kyoto and Peking above avenues shaded by alternating rows of Australian eucalyptus and California palms. It smoked to the sky.

Down the hundred-foot width of Market Street, between twin walls of dark blue-and-gold banners that snapped taut in the wind off the water, marched the autumn levy of the Hundred and Twenty-Four States.

No regimental colors bore the names of Virginia or Satsuma or New South Wales. At the head of each brigade, forty-piece brass bands crashed out the slow, metallic chords of the Imperial Anthem, their heavy European tubas answered by the deep boom of *taiko* drums and the wail of island conches, while ten thousand men in identical tunics of slate-gray and navy wool stepped across the granite paving-stones as a single machine. The sun dropped toward the Farallones in a blaze of clear sunset gold. It caught the forest of eighteen-inch bayonets and turned the avenue into a river of moving fire. Up to the balcony rose the mingled breath of the finished realm: salt spray from the Gate, the sharp spark-tang of the electric street-railways, burned Borneo fuel-oil from the battleships anchored off Alcatraz, and the heavy aloeswood smoke drifting from the great Cathedral of the Sun and St. Michael on the crest of Nob Hill.

"The transport from Batavia cleared the heads at dawn, Your Highness," young Marcus Vance said. He pitched his clipped voice just above the roar of the brass bands below and rested his gloved hand upon the cold stone balustrade beside hers. "And the new prefects from the Berkeley examination will take their oaths in the Rotunda at six. Of the ten thousand who entered the sheds on Monday, twelve hundred passed the third modulus. Not one of them bears a family name that appeared in the peerage rolls of sixty-five."

Behind them in the shadow of the canopy, Cornelius Schuyler’s head drooped forward onto his gold-laced breast. A thin trickle of saliva wetted his white cravat while he stared through blurred, watery eyes at the gray bayonets of the youths who had taken his bank and his grandson in the same night. Beside him, Marquis Takashima sat rigid as an idol of lacquered wood; across the sunlit paving-stones of the terrace, past the velvet valance and the armed cadets, his gaze remained fixed upon the thirty-foot bronze shoulders of Elias Thorne’s statue towering at the foot of the stairs. He did not blink.

Kaiulani looked out past the bronze head of the dead Titan, across the mile of sparkling blue water where the eighteen-inch turrets of the *Elias Thorne* and the *Kamehameha II* swung their fifty-foot barrels skyward to fire the sunset salute. She was fifty years old. Her youth lay buried under the coral blocks of Fort Street in Honolulu, and the man who had broken her kingdom and chained her to his chariot was rotting under five tons of stone at Monterey. Now the first blank charge from the fleet roared across the bay, and as the concussion rattled the glass in the conservatory dome overhead and turned a half-million faces in the plaza upward toward her black-robed figure on the balcony as if she were the sun itself, the cold, terrible exultation that Elias had known on the snowy lip of the Sierra forty-three years before rose in her chest.

"General Vance," Kaiulani said. She did not turn her head from the blinding gold of the western water. Reaching into her black bombazine sleeve, she drew out the small brass cylinder containing the winter mobilization tables for the Southern Isthmus and held it toward the young marshal while the second cannon-salute thundered off the hills. "When the parade has passed the Mint, you will have the surgeons certify that Comptroller Schuyler and Marquis Takashima have suffered a grave exhaustion from the afternoon’s ceremonies, and remove them to the sanatorium at Santa Cruz. And when you have locked their doors, order the special train for the Tehuantepec and Darien line. Before the old man took to his bed in eighty-four, he stood with your father’s engineers upon the red clay of Culebra and swore that the Atlantic ships would pass into our ocean through an iron trough of his own cutting. The northern bridge is bolted; you and I are going south to inspect the final ditch."

# Chapter 17: The City of the Cut

In the private diaries of the Providentor, which Lady Kaiulani carried southward in her velvet dispatch-box aboard the coastal packet *Culebra* during that first week of November, the entry for the nineteenth of March, 1884, written during the last journey Elias Thorne had ever made upon his own two feet before the dropsy chained him to the conservatory, remained blotted with the brown stains of Darien mud.

He had stood that afternoon upon the high, blasted ledge of Gold Hill, fifty miles south of the Caribbean surf, with both hands leaned upon his iron walking-stick under an equatorial sun that beat down through a yellow fog of dynamite fumes and pulverized red cucaracha shale. Below his boots, where the French canal syndicate of Monsieur de Lesseps had gone bankrupt in eighty-two before the Pacifica gunboats foreclosed upon the Colombian concessions, stretched a steaming, mile-wide wound torn straight through the green spine of the Americas.

It was an open-pit slaughterhouse of stone and steam. Three hundred feet down in the boiling red trough of the Cut, seventy ninety-ton Bucyrus-Nagasaki steam-shovels, monstrous iron crabs with dipper-buckets armed in forged manganese-steel teeth, chewed into the sliding clay terraces. With every biting swing of their crane-booms, the machines belched thick columns of coal-black smoke and white exhaust-steam; in the ninety-eight-degree humidity that vapour refused to rise, hanging instead between the raw red cliffs like the breath of a subterranean dragon. Mile-long dirt-trains crawled along seven tiers of narrow-gauge track notched into the mud walls. Geared Baldwin locomotives, their brass bells clanging in an endless chorus, hauled the disemboweled guts of the Cordilleras out toward the Pacific dump-heaps at Naos Island.

"The Frenchmen tried to dig a sea-level ditch with donkey-carts and Martinique spades, Protector," Major Sterling had shouted into Elias’s ear over the roar of forty pneumatic rock-drills hammering into the basalt shelf twenty yards below them. Even then, three years before his death, Elias’s breath had come in thick, whistling pulls against a wet heat foul with rotting jungle lianas and nitro-glycerine fumes and the sour tallow of the shovel-gears. "Their clay slides came down from Contractor’s Hill faster than their buckets could lift the muck! We have stepped the banks back at forty-five degrees, laid eighty-pound broad-gauge rail on every bench, and put sixty thousand Cantonese, Jamaican, and Georgian convict-navvies into the trench in three eight-hour relays under electric arc-lamps!"

Elias had wiped the hot red mud-spatter from his cheek with a rough thumb. His solitary clear eye squinted down through the sulfur-haze toward the southern end of the gorge, where the colossal twin concrete chambers of the Miraflores Locks rose like the unfinished temple-pylons of Karnak above the mangrove swamps.

"Do not talk to me of the Frenchmen, Sterling," Elias had said. He planted his stick deeper into the greasy red clay. Down at the bottom of the Bas Obispo reach, where a five-ton charge of blasting-gelatine detonated with a subterranean thump that drove up through the soles of his cavalry boots, splinters of blue trap-rock rained across the tin roofs of the guard-sheds. "De Lesseps was a stock-jobber digging a turnpike for Liverpool tramp-steamers. I am cutting a sally-port for the Battle Fleet. How wide are those lock-chambers at the sill?"

"One hundred and twenty feet clear between the concrete walls, sir, and a thousand feet from mitre-gate to mitre-gate," Sterling had answered, and he opened his oilskin plan-roll against the drizzle that fell every afternoon at three o’clock like warm soup from the Chagres hills. "Wide enough to pass the *Elias Thorne* or the *Imperator* with ten feet of water to spare on either beam, and fed by the artificial lake we have dammed behind the Gatun spillways. When the eighty-foot steel leaves of those gates swing shut, Protector, the Atlantic Ocean ceases to be an ocean. It becomes a back-canal of the San Francisco Admiralty. A squadron of our turret-ships can steam out of the Golden Gate, pass through this hill in nine hours without coaling, and lay their eighteen-inch guns off the mouth of the Thames or the Narrows of New York before the European cables know they have cleared Balboa."

Elias had looked down at the swarming floor of the Cut. There, a gang of two hundred bare-chested men in the striped duck trousers of the Atlantic draft-dodgers strained with iron crowbars to shift a section of muddy track before the next dirt-train backed down the switch. One of the men slipped in the red slime. Before the corporal’s whistle could blow, the flange of a loaded dump-car took him across the thighs; out of the steam-fog trotted two Cantonese stretcher-bearers with a canvas sack and a lime-bucket, who shoveled the red clay over the spot without halting the locomotive’s bell for a single stroke.

"Pour the concrete at night, Sterling," Elias had said, turning his heavy, failing frame back toward the armored inspection-car waiting on the upper spur. "My ankles are filling with water, and this heat rots a man’s liver. I will not live to see the first battleship pass the sill. Make sure the lock-walls are twelve feet thick at the base. When my stone is laid in Monterey, this ditch is the padlock on the eastern door; I want no Englishman with a bag of powder knocking the hinges off after I am gone."

***

Now, in the November of 1887, the old man’s diary lay closed upon the brass table of the *Culebra*’s deck-saloon, and as the steamer rounded the fortified volcanic bastion of Flamenco Island into the anchorage of Panama Bay, the Chronicler who accompanied the Regent’s suite looked out upon the monstrous realization of that afternoon’s command.

In the annals of the older empires, great public works like the wall of Hadrian or the Grand Canal of the Sui left behind them only the quiet bones of their builders buried under the turf. At the southern mouth of the Isthmian trench, however, the collision of forty million gold thalers in annual payroll with the human dregs of four continents had spawned a brick-and-corrugated-iron cancer that the engineers called the Fourth Naval Canton, and the sailors of the world called the *City of the Cut*.

Where the moss-grown Spanish battlements and tumbledown adobe convents of old Panama City had rotted beside the tidal mud-flats twenty years earlier, a geometric metropolis of two hundred thousand souls now festered under a canopy of yellow coal-smoke and crude petroleum vapor. The streets processed muscle and extracted silver. Along the three miles of newly blasted basalt quays at Balboa, where the giant floating caisson-gates of the Pacific entrance-locks loomed eighty feet above the low-tide slime like cliffs of grey cast iron, stood the monumental, windowless storehouses of the Isthmian Commissariat: cold-storage beef-vaults cooled by ammonia-engines from Chicago, quinine-distilleries, and the six-story red-brick barracks of the Satsuma and Hawaiian garrison regiments.

Behind that rigid frontage of Imperial Blue and Sunset Gold lay the *Boca*. Stretching back up the steaming red-clay slopes of Ancon Hill toward the mouth of the Culebra gorge, four square miles of two-story timber shanties roofed with flattened kerosene-tins sat eight feet above the black, bubbling sewage-ditches upon creosoted Oregon pilings, joined by narrow plank catwalks slick with fish-offal and spilled palm-gin.

To walk the elevated boardwalks of the Avenida Central at eight o’clock in the evening, when the six-o’clock shift-trains had vomited thirty thousand mud-caked laborers out of the Cut, was to descend into a polyglot furnace of commercialized delirium. The air under the sizzling blue carbon-arc lamps stood at ninety-two degrees, thick as wet flannel. It smelled of fried plantains, scorching human hair from the barber-stalls, the sharp carbolic-and-lime wash that the Chinese sanitary gangs pumped into the open gutters every four hours to kill the yellow-fever larvae, and the heavy, sickly-sweet fumes of Yunnan opium mixed with cheap Monongahela whiskey.

Here, beneath painted canvas signs written in English, Spanish, Japanese *katakana*, and Cantonese characters, every vice of the Great Arena was sold by the stopwatch and taxed at twenty percent by Magistrate Shen’s municipal excise-clerks. Inside the *Saloon of the Two Oceans*, five hundred negro shovel-men from the Mississippi protectorates and scar-faced Irish navvies from the Massachusetts levies drank green wormwood absinthe at zinc bars alongside bare-footed Tagalog dynamite-drillers and tattooed Marquesan boatmen; up on the sawdust stage, meanwhile, a troupe of bankrupt actresses from the New York theaters danced the can-can to a Bavarian brass tuba and a Cantonese two-stringed fiddle. Next door, beyond a quarter-inch redwood partition through which the swearing and the clink of silver tenths sounded without pause, stood the licensed bath-houses and brothels of the Yoshiwara Concession. Four hundred girls brought over on five-year treasury indentures from the starving fishing-villages of Kyushu and the orphanages of Charleston sat behind wooden lattices in kimonos of cheap Lowell cotton. Every Tuesday morning, a former surgeon of the Union Army wearing the brass armband of the Pacifica Sanitary Police stamped their health-tickets.

No man in the City of the Cut owned the roof over his bunk. Overhead wire-tramways carried the red rock of Culebra day and night across the housetops toward the breakwater dumps; no man walked three hundred yards without passing beneath the shadow of that endless, rumbling iron conveyor as it dropped flakes of wet shale into the soup-bowls of the eating-houses and shook the plank walls with the vibration of the ditch. At the foot of every street, where the boardwalks met the double-track railway embankment, stood the concrete pillbox of the Provost Guard. Its loopholed steel shutters hung half-open to show the brass water-jacket of a Maxim gun trained straight down the gutter.

***

On the morning of the fourteenth of November, lukewarm sheets of rain poured from the black clouds over the Chagres valley, flooding the carbolic ditches to the level of the boardwalks and washing three dead rats against the iron steps of the Sanitary Headquarters at Empire Station.

Inside the former French hospital, double envelopes of fine brass-and-copper screening enclosed the verandas against the *Stegomyia* mosquitoes. General Marcus Vance the younger stood in the high, whitewashed operating-hall before a long pine trestle-table covered in glass specimen-jars and wet yellow morning reports. He wore his khaki tunic buttoned to the chin over a rubberized apron. Stifling air filled the screened room; through the louvers drifted the reek of iodoform and boiling corrosive sublimate, mingled with the sour-sweet stench of the *vomito negro* from the quarantine-wards down the hill.

Across the table stood Colonel Gorgas, Chief Surgeon of the Isthmian Works, his white linen duck trousers splashed to the knees with yellow clay and crude petroleum, beside Major Kuroda of the Satsuma Garrison Brigade.

"Fourteen new cases in the Gorgona barracks since midnight, General, and twenty-two among the Italian and Georgian mason-gangs at the Pedro Miguel lock-pit," Colonel Gorgas said. His fingers trembled from exhaustion and forty grains of daily quinine as he laid a fever-chart stained with black spots before Marcus’s slide-rule. "The October slides in the Cut dammed the east diversion-channel and created forty acres of stagnant brush-swamp right behind the coolie-lines. My oil-gangs cannot spray the puddles because the three thousand Jamaican and Georgia shovel-men in Sector Four threw down their picks at daybreak. They have barricaded themselves inside the timber-shanties along the Las Cascadas ridge. They say the doctors are poisoning the well-water with carbolic to kill off the sick men and save their back-pay for the Mint, and they shot two of my Hawaiian hospital-orderlies who tried to bring the sulphur-pots into the street!"

Marcus left the stained fever-chart untouched. Picking up a pair of nickel-plated forceps, he lifted the corner of the paper to examine the daily mortality curve on the sheet beneath, then let it drop.

"How many cubic yards of rock did Sector Four send to the Naos dump yesterday, Major Kuroda?" Marcus asked. His clipped, metallic voice cut across the surgeon’s report as if the black vomit were an error in coal-consumption.

"Eleven thousand two hundred, sir," Kuroda answered from his pocket-book. "Sixteen thousand below the daily quota required to clear the lock-sills before the February fleet-maneuvers. And the strike is spreading down the line toward Balboa. The Irish mechanics at the Gorgona machine-shops have banked their forge-fires and are demanding that the quarantine-cordon be lifted so they can take the Friday steamer back to New Orleans before the yellow jack gets into the white quarters."

Marcus pulled his ivory slide-rule from his breast pocket. Rain drummed upon the corrugated tin roof. For ten seconds nothing else sounded in the copper-screened hall save the dry *slick-slap* of the celluloid cursor sliding between the young general’s steady fingers.

"A single skilled steam-shovel engineer from the Gorgona shops costs the Bureau twelve hundred thalers to train and six months to replace from Sacramento," Marcus said. He read the figure off the rule and slipped the instrument back into his pocket. "A Jamaican or Georgian pick-man in the Las Cascadas shanties costs thirty thalers in bounty-money, and we have twelve thousand fresh Shantung coolies waiting in the quarantine-hulks at Taboga Island whose resistance to the Chagres fever is eighteen percent higher by the August tables. We will not risk the machine-shop crews by letting the *Stegomyia* mosquitoes breed in the Las Cascadas thatch for another twenty-four hours."

Colonel Gorgas blinked through his rain-speckled spectacles, his gaunt face paling beneath his tropical tan. "General, there are four thousand men, plus three hundred women and children from the old French camp, huddled inside those timber tenements on the ridge. If my orderlies cannot go in with the sulphur-pans and the wire-screens because of the strikers’ rifles, it will take two weeks of house-to-house parley to segregate the infected cases!"

"We do not have two weeks, Doctor; Lady Kaiulani’s battle-squadron passes the locks on the tenth of February, and a mosquito does not listen to parley," Marcus replied. He turned to the wall-map of the Culebra reach, where the red pins of the fever-outbreak clustered thickest along the wooden shantytown of Las Cascadas. "When a gangrene appears in a toe, my father did not poultice the boot; he took the leg off below the knee so the trunk could march. Major Kuroda."

"General?" The Satsuma officer clicked his heels on the wet pine boards.

"Take the First and Second Battalions of the Choshu Infantry and the four armored oil-train flatcars up the east berm-track to the Las Cascadas switch," Marcus ordered. Unbuckling his rubberized apron, he tossed it onto the specimen-table and reached for his oilskin cap. "Do not send a single soldier into the boardwalks where a man with a shotgun can shoot him from a window, and do not arrest the strike-committee. Surround the entire four-hundred-yard perimeter of the Las Cascadas shantytown with two rows of portable barbed-wire hurdles and eight Maxim guns. Give the inhabitants fifteen minutes by the locomotive whistle to walk out naked through the carbolic dipping-troughs at the railway-cut. Every man who comes out through the trough goes into the iron boxcars for thirty days’ solitary quarantine on the Naos rock-pile at half-rations."

Colonel Gorgas stepped forward and caught the edge of the table, staring at the twenty-nine-year-old general’s bloodless profile. "And those who are too sick with the fever to crawl out of their bunks in fifteen minutes, General Vance? Or the strikers who refuse to leave the barricade?"

"At the sixteenth minute," Marcus said, already walking toward the double-screened door where his horse-holder waited in the pouring rain beside the railway-handcar, "Kuroda’s engineers will turn the high-pressure hoses from the four oil-cars onto the shingle roofs, soak the entire Las Cascadas quarter with ten thousand gallons of unrefined Borneo crude, and fire four thermite canisters into the center alley. Fire sterilizes both the mosquito-larvae and the mutiny in a single operation, Doctor, and the ashes will dry up the stagnant puddles in the diversion-ditch. Come along with your microscope; I want the ground inspected for live pupae as soon as the tin cools."

Twenty minutes later, the geared inspection-locomotive pushed Marcus’s armored flatcar up the four-percent grade of the Las Cascadas spur. Its brass driving-rods flashed through the grey curtain of the downpour while the wheels ground over red shale that slid like melted butter across the ties.

Ahead of the cow-catcher, perched upon the raw clay shelf between the three-hundred-foot abyss of the Cut on the left and the steaming green wall of the virgin jungle on the right, stood the shantytown of Sector Four: two hundred densely packed, two-story tenements of unpainted pine and corrugated iron, their upper galleries hung with soggy red blankets and hand-lettered boards reading *SILVER OR STEAMSHIPS—NO MORE LIME-PITS.*

Down on the main broad-gauge track below the plank-walks, four companies of Choshu infantry in dark blue oilskin capes had uncoiled six-foot concertinas of rusted barbed wire across the approaches. On the embankment opposite the town’s central market-shed, two eight-wheeled steel tank-cars bearing the yellow stencil of the *Imperial Sanitary & Petroleum Commission* hissed and throbbed as their steam-pumps built pressure to two hundred pounds on the dial.

Marcus remained above the mud. Beneath the bolted steel canopy of the flatcar, he rested his gloved hand beside the breech of the brass three-pounder Hotchkiss mountain-gun mounted on the forward pedestal. Fifty yards away, perched upon the corrugated tin roof of a grog-shop above a barricade of overturned dump-carts, a red-bearded Georgian mechanic in a faded Confederate forage cap, his left hand missing three fingers from a rock-drill at Bas Obispo, leveled a stolen Winchester repeating rifle across the rain-swept wire.

"You hear me down there in the iron car, General Vance!" the Georgian roared. His voice cracked over the hiss of the oil-pumps and the wailing of two hundred fever-stricken men and women whose yellow, blood-streaked faces pressed against the unscreened wooden shutters of the upper bunk-houses behind him. "We got eighty kegs of giant-powder stacked under the floor of this saloon, and we got four hundred white men and Jamaicans behind these carts with dynamite-sticks in their shirts! You turn those yellow devils loose on us with bayonets, or you try to lock us in the fever-cars for Naos, and we’ll blow this whole clay bank straight down into your ditch and bury ten of your steam-shovels fifty feet deep! Bring the pay-wagons up the track and give us clearance papers for the New Orleans packet, or by God—"

Marcus checked his wrist. Twelve minutes had elapsed since the locomotive’s first warning blast had echoed down the gorge; only forty-six men, mostly Cantonese water-carriers schooled in the ways of the Provostry, had crawled out through the mud to strip off their rags and plunge through the smoking vats of carbolic acid by the switch-tower. Up in the second-story windows of the shanties, dark swarms of mosquitoes rose like grey smoke from the rain-barrels under the eaves whenever a sick man’s arm struck at the air.

"He is standing directly over the main drainage-culvert of the upper bench, Major Kuroda," Marcus said. He did not raise his voice toward the Georgian on the roof. Reaching down, he turned the brass elevating-screw of the Hotchkiss three-pounder two turns to the left. "If he detonates eighty kegs of nitro-glycerine powder under that grog-shop, the concussion will shear the clay toe of the embankment and cost us three weeks of steam-shovel time to clear the slide before the Regent’s steamer arrives tomorrow. We will not wait for the fifteenth minute."

"The women are still on the lower porch, General," Colonel Gorgas said from the rear of the flatcar. His hand gripped the wet iron stanchion until the skin stretched taut over his finger-joints.

"They are carriers of the Stegomyia parasite, Doctor, and they are standing on eighty kegs of government blasting-powder," Marcus said. Down the wet brass barrel of the mountain-gun, across the fifty yards of rain-swept wire and overturned dump-carts, he brought the front blade to rest squarely upon the buckle of the Georgian mechanic’s belt. Before his right thumb could depress the firing-lanyard, the field-telegraph box bolted to the rear bulkhead of the flatcar clattered with the sharp, urgent triple-spark of the Regent’s personal launch.

Major Kuroda snatched the wet paper ribbon from the brass spool and stepped to Marcus’s elbow. "From Her Highness aboard the *Culebra* at the Balboa quarantine-buoy, General. You are to hold the thermite batteries. The Envoys of the Andean and Caribbean Republics are riding up the gorge on the noon observation-train with the Regent, and she refuses to have them choke on roasted Georgian meat while she is negotiating the Darien Hinterland Buffer."

Marcus took his thumb off the brass lanyard. The gun’s elevation remained fixed. Beneath the dripping steel canopy, where the hot grease of the breech-block smelled sour in the wet air, he straightened his spine and looked back toward the winding red-clay throat of the gorge, where the white plume of the Regent’s geared mountain-locomotive already rose above the wet banana-fronds.

"Turn off the steam-heaters in the oil-vats, Major," Marcus said. He pulled a clean square of linen from his pocket and wiped the rain from his slide-rule. "Pump the Borneo crude cold through the hoses at two hundred pounds pressure. Knock the Georgian off the tin with the water-stream, flood the cellar under the saloon until their giant-powder is wet porridge, and let the Choshu battalions go over the carts with clubs and pick-handles. If Her Highness wishes to show the South Americans a scrubbed camp instead of a furnace, we will give them cold iron."

***

It was during that same three-o’clock deluge of the previous autumn, six months before the final silence in the Monterey crypt, when Elias Thorne could still sit propped among his horsehair cushions before the bronze map in San Francisco, that the first spark had passed unbroken beneath the mud of the Isthmus from the Atlantic water to the Golden Gate.

In the annals of the Chancery, that October afternoon of 1886 stands recorded for the strange, suffocating quiet inside the fourth-floor Map Room when Major Sterling uncoiled the insulated gutta-percha lead that connected the Rincon Hill repeater directly to the newly submerged trans-isthmian cable at Colón. Outside, the San Francisco autumn had been clear and sharp with the smell of crushed wine-grapes coming down on the Sacramento barges and the coal-smoke of the Potrero rolling-mills. Inside, camphor and burnt stramonium thickened the air to keep the Providentor’s congested lungs drawing breath.

Elias sat in his wheeled chair of Hawaiian koa-wood. Gray flannel wrapped his swollen ankles beneath his unlaced cavalry boots. While Cornelius Schuyler and Marquis Takashima whispered beside the porphyry table over the autumn silver-tallies, Elias kept his solitary wide eye fixed upon the small brass sounder set upon a block of green serpentine marble beside his right elbow.

"The siphon-recorder at the Balboa lock-house is linked through the Culebra conduit to the Limon Bay breakwater on the Caribbean side, Protector," Major Sterling said, his one-eared head bent low over the galvanometer needle as it trembled under the first test-current from three thousand miles south. "General Vance’s sappers laid the last splice through the Gatun spillway trench twenty minutes ago. For the first time since the creation of the earth, the tide-gauges of the two oceans are beating on the same wire."

Across the room, old Cornelius Schuyler looked up from his discount-sheets. His gold pince-nez slipped down his nose as he peered at the little brass machine. "A triumph of engineering, Major, no doubt, though until the Culebra clay-slides are dredged to forty feet, a copper wire through the mud does not pay the four-percent coupon on the Isthmian Canal Debentures. The London underwriters are still betting at Lloyd’s that the Chagres river floods will wash our concrete lock-sills into the Caribbean before a single keel crosses the divide."

Elias ignored the banker. His right hand, the sole limb still obedient to the iron will locked behind his scarred brow, rested upon the leather arm of his chair, where his thick, yellowed fingernail tapped a slow, uneven measure against the wood. Beside his wheel, Lady Kaiulani stood in her rustling black bombazine. Upon the wall, the galvanometer mirror flashed a tiny spot of green light.

Then the armature clicked.

The signal bypassed the old relays that once stuttered round the Horn through Valparaiso or across the torn wires of the Eastern states. It struck the brass anvil with a sharp, metallic ring that filled the high-arched room like the cocking of a Paterson revolver.

*Clack-clack-clack. Clack-clack.*

Sterling left the clerk’s paper form blank. He read the dots directly off the brass tongue as they leaped from the Caribbean surf across the mountains of Mexico and up the granite spine of California:

"*'From Port-Captain, Atlantic Terminus, Cristóbal Mole, to the Providentor at San Francisco,'*" Sterling said, his voice trembling in the hush. "*'High water on the Limon Bay gauge stands at twenty-two inches above mean datum. The Pacifica gunboat* Culebra *passed through the temporary diversion-channel from the Pacific side at noon and has just dipped her ensign in salt water off the Toro Point lighthouse. The Atlantic Squadron salutes the Throne. There is no longer a Cape Horn.'*"

Marquis Takashima took a single step toward the bronze relief-map on the wall and stared at the thin silver wire inlaid across the waist of the Americas. "A gunboat in the Caribbean," the old samurai said in his stiff English. "Within six days’ steaming of Havana and the mouth of the Mississippi, without touching a British coaling-station."

Elias lifted his right hand from the koa-wood armrest. It was a heavy, dragging motion. With three ragged pulls of breath through his open teeth, he reached out and laid his scarred palm directly over the vibrating brass sounder on the marble block, where the electric pulse of the Atlantic Ocean beat like a captured bird against the callouses that had once worked Red Higgins’s ash sweep on the muddy Mississippi.

He had never seen the Atlantic. Forty-nine years ago, when the bailiff from Philadelphia had burned his mother’s loom in the Kentucky clover and ridden back across the Alleghenies toward the counting-houses of Boston and New York, that eastern sea had been the invisible throne of his enemies, the cold, arrogant water from which the laws and bank-writs of the old world came forth to master the wilderness. For half a century he had turned his back upon it. Around the vast, roaring bowl of the sunset he had built his house until the West grew too heavy for the East to bear.

Now the eastern sea was a mill-pond at the back door of his canal, and its water ticked under his thumb.

"Write the reply, Kaiulani," Elias whispered. His voice scraped like dry gravel from the bottom of his congested chest while his solitary clear eye burned across the baize at Schuyler and Takashima. "Tell the Port-Captain at Cristóbal to unlimber two sixteen-inch Krupp rifles on the Toro Point mole facing north toward Jamaica and New York. And tell the underwriters at Lloyd’s that the Grand Confederation is no longer a Pacific state. Where the water runs, the law is one."

***

Thirteen months after that spark had rattled the brass sounder under the dead Titan’s palm, the rain over the Las Cascadas ridge had slackened to a warm, dripping mist that smelled of wet Borneo petroleum and the sharp carbolic vapor rising from the quarantined shanties.

High above the smoking red trench of the Culebra Cut, upon the glass-enclosed observation veranda of the Regent’s armored salon-car parked on the Bishop’s Hill siding, Lady Kaiulani sat before a table of polished Nicaraguan mahogany. Around the curve of the brass rail below the windows, five hundred feet down through the swirling yellow steam of the Bucyrus shovels, the four Battalions of the Choshu Infantry marched the last of the stripped, oil-blackened Georgian and Jamaican strikers down the railway ties toward the iron boxcars at Empire Station. Not a shot had been fired. Only the rhythmic *thwack* of pick-handles and the hiss of the cold petroleum hoses rose through the wet afternoon.

Across the mahogany table from Kaiulani sat four gentlemen in faultless Parisian broadcloth whose high starched collars were wilting in the ninety-degree greenhouse air: Don Rafael Núñez, President of the Colombian Confederation at Bogotá; General Guzmán Blanco of Venezuela; and the plenipotentiaries of Costa Rica and the Nicaraguan lakes. They had been brought up from the Balboa wharf behind General Vance’s locomotive to see the ditch before they signed the parchment.

"You observe, Excellencies, that the Regency does not waste powder when water will serve," Kaiulani said. Her black bombazine mourning-sleeves brushed the corner of the map, right where the red boundary-line of the *Isthmian Neutrality Zone* swept in a two-hundred-mile arc from the Gulf of Urabá to the Chiriquí lagoon, while she poured dark Bogotá coffee from a silver pot into four tiny porcelain cups. "Had General Vance allowed that lunatic on the grog-shop roof to fire his Winchester, eighty kegs of nitro-glycerine would have slid half a million cubic yards of red clay back into the channel, and the commercial dividends of your republics would have been delayed until the spring equinox."

Don Rafael Núñez left his cup untouched.Thirty years of governing mountain caudillos with French philosophy had thinned his scholarly face, and the skin over his cheekbones went grey as he looked down through the plate glass at the long file of naked, shivering mechanics driven through the carbolic troughs by Japanese soldiers half their height.

"When the French company of Monsieur de Lesseps dug in this valley, Madame la Régente," Núñez said in Spanish, while ninety feet below the cliff a ninety-ton steam-shovel bit into the shale with a shriek of iron teeth that made the coffee-spoons chime against the saucers, "they leased a strip of ten kilometers along the Chagres River and paid the Treasury at Bogotá two hundred and fifty thousand gold francs a year in transit-dues. Now the Providentor is dead in California, and you lay before us the *Treaty of the Darien Hinterlands*. You demand ten kilometers no longer; you demand the sovereign police-administration of the entire watershed from the Atrato River to the Costa Rican frontier, the abolition of our municipal customs at Cartagena and Barranquilla, and the right to garrison the Andean passes with your Asian regiments! In Bogotá, madam, they will call this the extinction of Bolívar’s republic!"

"In Bogotá, Don Rafael, your treasury has not paid the interest on its London railway bonds since the year seventy-nine," Kaiulani replied. She rested her ungloved dark hands, unadorned save for the heavy whale-ivory ring of Oahu, upon the edge of the treaty scroll. "And last month, while your Liberal and Conservative generals were shooting each other in the plaza at Medellín over a church-tax, three British cruisers from the Jamaica station anchored off Cartagena and offered to buy the Atrato river-concession as a rival canal-route. Do you imagine that the empire which bridged the Bering Strait and sank Admiral Hornby in the Coral Sea will permit seven bankrupt republics to sit above the lock-chambers of our main arterial road, waiting to sell the high ground to London or Berlin whenever a local colonel needs silver to pay his ragged lancers?"

General Guzmán Blanco of Venezuela leaned forward; his heavily pomaded black beard brushed the gold braid on his chest. "We are sovereign states of the Latin race, Your Highness! Even when the old United States in Washington proclaimed their Monroe Doctrine, they did not ask us to put Hawaiian magistrates in our custom-houses or rebuild our mountain railways to a six-foot California gauge! If we refuse this protectorate and retire to the cordilleras, will you send your Choshu infantry to climb twelve thousand feet into the Andes after us, as your Marshal did in Siberia?"

Kaiulani’s mouth curved at the corners. Past the Venezuelan general’s shoulder, out on the rear platform where the rain blew under the iron canopy, young General Marcus Vance stepped aboard, stripped off his wet oilskin cape, and handed it to his orderly without a spot of mud upon his khaki tunic.

"General Vance does not climb mountains when he can close the beach, Excellency," Kaiulani said. "Look down at the bay behind us. Every sack of coffee that leaves Guayaquil or Maracaibo, every hide from the Orinoco, every bar of silver from the Cauca mines reaches the markets of the world in bottoms registered at San Francisco and Osaka. If you return to Bogotá and Caracas tonight without signing the Hinterland Concordat, not a single Pacifica rifle will march up your mule-trails. At noon tomorrow, the Bureau of Integration will place a one-hundred-percent quarantine tariff upon every port between Vera Cruz and Valparaiso that lacks the customs-pennant of the Triumvirate, and Mr. Schuyler’s banks will sell your defaulted European debt at auction to the coffee-planters of Java and Brazil."

She took a small leather case from beside the coffee-tray. The lid clicked open on four heavy gold stars of the *Imperial Order of the Two Oceans*, each set with a central nugget of unworked Yukon bullion.

"On the other hand," she continued in the quiet cadence she had learned thirty years ago in the candle-lit salas of Sonora and Monterey, "if the Presidents of the Hinterland Republics enter the Customs Union today as Hereditary Wardens of the Southern Approaches, the Market Street Mint will immediately assume your London debt at par, advance twelve million silver thalers for the completion of the Quito-Bogotá broad-gauge spur, and guarantee your present presidential administrations for life against all domestic insurgents by stationing two cruisers of the Insular Fleet permanently at Cartagena and La Guaira. Keep your flags, gentlemen. Keep your cathedrals and your Spanish courts; we ask only for the gauges of the track, the keys of the quarantine-stations, and five thousand of your mountain youth every spring to serve in the Amur garrisons where they cannot plot revolutions at home."

General Vance stepped through the mahogany sliding-door into the salon. Wet wool and raw Borneo petroleum cut through the fragrance of coffee and cigar-smoke. After a stiff bow from the neck to the four Latin envoys and a glance at the gold medals on the table, he laid a damp engineer’s report beside Kaiulani’s saucer.

"The Las Cascadas bench is cleared, Your Highness," Marcus said in his flat, rapid voice. "Four hundred and twelve laborers have been processed through the carbolic vats and entrained for the Naos rock-quarries; the steam-winches have pulled down the shanties to prevent mosquito-breeding in the timber, and the six-o’clock shift from the Shantung depot is already moving into the cut with fresh drill-steels. If these gentlemen have concluded their inspection of the earthworks, the pilot-engine is coupled to take us down to the Miraflores lock-sill before the tide turns."

Don Rafael Núñez looked up at the twenty-nine-year-old general whose father had burned the ice of Lake Baikal, and then back at the fifty-year-old Polynesian princess in her black dress, the gold pen poised between her fingers. Outside, the ninety-ton steam-shovels had resumed their iron-jawed chewing into the red clay of the continent. Every bite shook the floorplates of the car.

"Give me the parchment, Madame," the President of Colombia whispered. He reached for the pen.

***

Twelve years later, when Don Rafael Núñez and old Cornelius Schuyler and Marquis Takashima had all gone down into the quiet earth to join the first generation of the conquerors, and the nineteenth century itself was dying in the glare of ten thousand blast-furnaces, the great ditch was done.

On the morning of the first of January, 1900, the tropical sun rose out of the Caribbean and climbed over the drowned jungles of Gatun Lake to shine upon a straight, silent canyon of dressed Sierra granite and poured gray concrete fifty miles long, through whose hundred-foot channel the green waters of the two oceans mingled without a ripple.

At the Pacific entrance of the Balboa reach, where the twin eighty-foot steel mitre-gates of the lower Miraflores chamber stood open to the morning flood, rose the colossal Arch of the Pivot: two hundred feet of white California marble and green Japanese bronze spanning the lock-walls like the legs of the Rhodesian Colossus, with the three words from the Providentor’s Sacramento speech of fifty-two cast across its frieze in six-foot letters of gilded iron:

*BEHIND US LIES THE PAST.*

Upon the high stone reviewing-tribune built directly into the western abutment of the lock-wall, shaded from the blinding equatorial glare by an awning of imperial blue silk, stood the two survivors who kept the gauge of the completed world: Lady Kaiulani, now in her sixty-third year, her hair white as the foam on the Honolulu reef above her unchanging black bombazine and the gold collar of the Sole Regency; and beside her, General-in-Chief Marcus Vance, forty-two years old, his temples silvered above the unadorned slate-gray tunic of the Imperial Staff, the ivory cursor of his slide-rule still protruding half an inch from his breast pocket.

Below them, along the five miles of stepped concrete embankments from the foot of Ancon Hill to the breakwater of Naos Island, one hundred thousand soldiers and civil prefects of the Hundred and Twenty-Four States stood drawn up in silent blocks of blue and gray: regiments of Manchurian and Siberian Riflemen shoulder-to-shoulder with battalions from the Massachusetts and Virginia cantons; graduates of the Berkeley and New Edo examination-sheds in dark alpaca robes with five-digit silver numerals gleaming on their collars; and ten thousand Cantonese and Jamaican canal-masons holding their iron rock-drills at the present like muskets.

The air above the water reached ninety degrees. Not a single mosquito stirred along the concrete banks; off the bay, where the five-thousand-horsepower hydroelectric turbines hummed inside the dam-spillways, the hot breeze carried only the sharp tang of salt brine and the heavy, resinous smoke of aloeswood rising from the bronze braziers at the corners of the Arch.

Dead-slow into the upper chamber between the concrete walls, towed by four noiseless, thirty-ton electric cog-locomotives whose copper contact-shoes hissed blue sparks along the rack-rails on the coping, glided the first vessel to cross the severed spine of the earth.

She was the thirty-thousand-ton dreadnought battleship *Elias Thorne*. The third flagship of the name had been launched from the slips of Potrero Point six months before, driven by Parsons steam-turbines burning refined Sumatra oil, and armed with twelve twenty-inch breech-loading rifles in four triple turrets of Krupp cemented steel.

As the monstrous blue steel hull settled into the water of the lock-chamber, the hundred thousand pairs of eyes along the concrete banks looked past the twenty-inch guns to the forward armored barbette, directly ahead of the conning-tower where Rear-Admiral Shimazu Tadao, Candidate Seven-One-Zero-Two of the class of eighty-seven, stood at attention with his hand at his visor. There the ship’s carpenters had bolted a ten-ton throne of cast bronze.

Upon that chair, thirty feet above the scorching steel deckplates and facing straight southward toward the open gate of the Pacific Ocean, rode the founder of the Empire.

Down on the lower steps, the Cantonese coolies dropped to their knees on the concrete and touched their foreheads to the stone as the shadow of the bow fell across them. Five years earlier, when the last whispers of a Republican restoration had flickered in the cellars of Boston and Kyoto, Kaiulani and Marcus Vance had ordered the lead casket in the Monterey Basilica unsealed; the embalmed corpse of the Providentor had been encased in an airtight shell of electro-plated copper and bronze molded directly from his death-mask, dressed in the bronze facsimile of his plain Engineer’s coat with the iron walking-stick welded upright between his knees, and bolted to the prow of the Fleet to inspect his provinces forever.

Behind the dreadnought’s stern, the eighty-foot steel leaves of the upper gate swung silently shut, driven by subterranean hydraulic rams without the clank of a single chain. The water in the thousand-foot granite trough dropped toward the level of the Pacific tide.

Foot by foot, while the green Caribbean water drained through the eighteen-foot culverts beneath their boots with a deep, organ-like roar that vibrated through the marble tribunal, the towering steel superstructure of the *Elias Thorne* sank lower between the walls. At last the bronze head of the dead Caesar, crusted white along the cheekbones with the dried salt-spray of the Atlantic passage from New York and Havana, came level with the stone parapet where Kaiulani and Marcus stood.

Only twenty feet of hot, sunlit air separated the woman on the wall from the metal figure on the turret. The sculptor had copied the pitiless fold of the bronze eyelid directly from the paralyzed left side of his face. A square, blunt thumb lay welded over the head of the iron stick.

Her withered, ivory-ringed hand gripped the scorching marble of the balustrade. Atop the Arch of the Pivot, the hydroelectric sirens sounded the noon hour in a single brass chord that drowned the screaming of the sea-birds all the way to Taboga. *We have brought your ship through the mountain, Elias,* she thought. *From the ice of the Yenisei to the reefs of Melbourne, and from the ruins of the Potomac to the gates of this lock, no king or parliament remains to refuse your clerk’s ink. We have ground the names out of the boys; we have turned the ocean into a cistern; we have bolted the world together so tight that even your corpse can steer it.*

Beside her elbow, General Marcus Vance raised his left wrist. He checked the green radium hands of his chronometer against the drop of the water-gauge on the lock-wall while the lower mitre-gates parted outward toward the blinding blue expanse of Panama Bay. "Eight hours and forty-two minutes from the Toro Point breakwater to the Pacific sill, Your Highness," Marcus said. Beneath a solid canopy of oil-smoke that stretched to the western horizon, the fifty-foot gap between the steel leaves widened upon the waiting double columns of the First and Second Battle Squadrons: forty-eight blue-hulled dreadnoughts and armored cruisers riding the swell. "Twelve minutes faster than the Admiralty tables allowed for a thirty-thousand-ton displacement. The First Atlantic Division will clear the locks by sunset, and by the fifteenth of next month we can transfer sixty-four capital ships from the Yellow Sea to the mouth of the English Channel in twenty-one days without asking permission of the winds." From his belt-pouch he pulled a folded white wireless-telegraph flimsy, received ten minutes earlier from the high-frequency spark-towers on Ancon Hill, and held it out between two gloved fingers. On the coping, the four electric towing-locomotives sounded two short bells and hauled the *Elias Thorne* forward through the open gates into the Pacific. "Before we go down to the state barge to follow the flagship out, Madam," Marcus continued, his gaze fixed straight ahead while the bronze effigy glided past their faces in the glare, "the Prefect of the Seventy-First Canton at Irkutsk wirelessed at eleven that the German and French boundary-commissioners at Omsk have refused to countersign the new tariff-schedule for the Trans-Siberian and Ural potash mines, and the Kaiser in Berlin has ordered three army corps to the Polish border to support the Moscow grain-syndicate. If we divert the third transport-flotilla from Manila to the mouth of the Obi before the spring thaw—" Kaiulani left the wireless slip between his fingers. At the extreme edge of the granite wall, where the hot wind off the Pacific lifted the white braids beneath her black mourning-veil, the bronze back of the Providentor’s chair passed through the shadow of the great Arch and rode out onto the long heave of his own ocean; behind the flagship, the upper lock-gates swung open a second time to receive the bow of the *Kamehameha III*. "Let the Prefect at Irkutsk double the transit-duty on the Ural ore-trains at midnight, Marcus," Kaiulani said.
