She turned from the parapet toward the stone steps where her palanquin-bearers in the blue-and-gold livery of the Chancery stood beside the electric elevator-shaft, her hand raised to shade her dark eyes from the brassy glare of the twentieth-century noon just as the twenty-inch turrets of the battle-fleet outside the islands fired the first salvo of the new hundred-year ledger, "and tell the German Ambassador when he calls at Monterey on Tuesday that the Providentor’s rails cross the mountains and stop where the iron runs out."

# Chapter 18: Golden Afternoon

Yet before the iron ran out, and before the bronze effigy upon the turret of the *Elias Thorne* ever met the tropical spray of the Miraflores locks, there lay that luminous decade of the late seventies and early eighties which the school-primers of our own century still call the Antonine Peace. History hastens to record the cracking of the foundations and passes lightly over the noon-hour when the mortar stood dry. When I returned to San Francisco in the autumn of 1879 from my first post as Junior Assessor of Customs at the Hankow landing, both the mud-spattered military camp that my uncle had described from the fifties and the numbered barracks of the later Regency belonged to other eras. This was the Golden Age of the Protectorate. During that brief equinox between the conquest of the circumference and the calcification of the state, the silver of five continents poured into the Golden Gate faster than the Market Street Mint could stamp it, and the taverns had yet to whisper that the Emperor on Rincon Hill lacked an heir of his body. For ten years following the truce along the Yenisei and the pacification of the Chinese river-ports, the great guns of the fleet fired only at target-hulks off the Farallones. Peace lay over the seventy million square miles of the Great Arena like a warm afternoon. In San Francisco, the marble colonnades of the Imperial Exchange had buried the raw redwood palisades of Clark’s Point; beneath those porticos, merchants in silk kimonos from Osaka, broad-hatted cattle-factors from the Sonora cantons, and pale brokers from the Boston protectorates bought and sold the harvests of half the earth in a polite undertone. A man could board a sleeping-car at the Oakland mole on a Monday morning, eat fresh Columbia salmon chilled in ammonia-ice while his train climbed the Sierra snow-sheds, and step down on the following Saturday onto the granite platform of the Potomac Depot with his passport in his pocket and Pacifica thalers in his purse. Along the terraced hills above the bay, the rough mining-captains who had ridden with Elias Thorne at the Rio Frio or marched with the elder Vance through the red clay of Virginia had built palaces of pale Sierra granite and red Hawaiian koa-wood, with conservatories heated by steam-pipes and lit by the new Swan incandescent lamps. Even in that meridian splendor, with four hundred million thalers in uncoined bullion stacked inside the treasury vaults and the grain-fleets whitening the sea from Melbourne to Sitka, a hollow note sounded beneath the gilt. In the coffee-houses along Montgomery Street, when the four-o’clock chimes rang from the syncretic basilica on Nob Hill and the afternoon editions of the *Gazette* reached the marble tables, the old men left the shipping manifests folded. They turned in silence to the brief, three-line bulletin at the top of the court column: *The Providentor walked for twenty minutes upon the south terrace at noon.* The price of Hankow tea and the obedience of the Satsuma admirals hung together with the peace of the Boston streets upon the pulse of a single sixty-two-year-old chest. They drank their wine fast.

***

Nowhere did that late-afternoon sunlight shine with a more cultivated brilliance than upon the white limestone quadrangles of the Imperial University on the Berkeley slopes across the bay. On a crisp afternoon in May of that same year, 1881, Lady Kaiulani walked down the central aisle of the Grand Exhibition Hall. Her hands rested within the wide sleeves of a gown of deep imperial-blue brocade woven in the looms of Kyoto, and at her throat gleamed the ancient whale-ivory clasp of Oahu. The perpetual black bombazine of her later Regency still lay in the future; at forty-four, her dark hair showed only the first threads of silver above her temples, and with the ghosts of Fort Street still in her eyes, she had set the fierce intelligence of her blood to clothing the iron skeleton of Elias’s empire in marble and paint. Behind her walked the Rector of the University, a former professor of aesthetics from Harvard College named Norton whom the Chancery had brought west after the closing of the Massachusetts schools, alongside Master Kano Hogai, the court painter summoned from Edo to direct the Academy of the Two Shores. "You see, Your Highness, how the students of the fourth year have abandoned both the dry academicism of the European salons and the narrow brush-traditions of the old Tokugawa guilds," Rector Norton said, his thin Bostonian voice trembling with enthusiasm while he gestured toward the forty-foot mural of wet fresco on the eastern wall of the rotunda. Upon the plaster stood a score of young apprentices from California and the Hawaiian valleys and Canton, side by side on bamboo scaffolds, laying gold leaf into the wet lime. The painting depicted the *Apotheosis of the Pacific Pivot*. In the foreground, rendered with the anatomical realism of the Italian Renaissance, bronze-cast figures of American iron-puddlers and Polynesian navigators hauled at the capstans of a colossal dreadnought; behind them, in place of European oil-shadows, the sea and sky opened in the mist-veiled ink-washes and hammered sunset-gold leaf of the classic Kano screens, while above the ship’s funnels the Christian archangels and the wind-gods of Ise rode the same stylized, coiling cloud-bank. Kaiulani stopped before the scaffold. Wet lime and turpentine and ground lapis lazuli had replaced the coal-soot of the dockyards in the hall's cool air. "It has grandeur, Master Kano," Kaiulani said in the courtly Japanese of the Kyoto studios, her gaze on the aged master beside her and the spots of Prussian blue and vermilion tempera across his silk *hakama*. "Yet look at the faces of the foundrymen at the capstan. The boy from Philadelphia who painted that left group has given the Americans the brows of Roman senators, and left the Cantonese stokers in the shadow of the boiler like beasts of burden. Tell him to scrape the plaster before it dries tonight." Master Kano bowed low. "I told the youth this morning, High Commissioner, that in the Pacific style all blood shares the foreground. The line must carry the same weight from the corner of the frame to the center." "More than the line, Master Kano: the memory," Kaiulani said. She stepped closer to the wet wall where a young Hawaiian student from Maui laid strips of crimson and yellow bird-feather patterns into the painted border of the architrave. "For thirty years the Providentor has bound these provinces together with broad-gauge rail and provost-courts. An empire kept only in the tax-ledger and the guardhouse is a prison that men tear down the moment the turnkey nods. If our grandchildren in Boston and Nagasaki are to bleed for this ocean when we are gone, they must look up at the walls of their courts and see a beauty beyond the reach of England or the old Shogunate." She turned toward the center of the hall. There, upon velvet pedestals, stood the sculptors’ scale-models for the new district capitals: railway stations with cast-iron arches curved like the hulls of Samoan war-canoes, and municipal basilicas where earthquake-proof frames of interlocked Japanese cedar held the stained-glass windows of Chartres. "Rector Norton," she said, and as her clear voice echoed through the sunny vault, a class of young cadet-architects in blue wool tunics paused at their drafting-boards to bow, "you will double the bursaries for the School of Imperial Letters and the Conservatory of Music from the Honolulu sugar-fund this autumn. I want the history of the Atlantic Rebellion rewritten in three-part verse for the grammar schools before winter as the Deliverance of the Continent from chaos. Let them sing it to the tune of the island chants and the brass cornets together."

***

While the apprentices at Berkeley laid sunset gold into the wet plaster to make a god of him, the man himself sat forty miles south in the gloom of the Santa Cruz mountains, fighting for breath in the cold resinous dark beneath trees that were already two thousand years old when Julius Caesar crossed the Rubicon. The armored private car on the Monterey spur had stopped at the Felton siding three nights ago without the knowledge of a soul in the city below. To the foreign consuls and the brokers on Montgomery Street, the Providentor remained behind the closed doors of the Rincon Hill Citadel with the Siberian timber-schedules. Inside the five-thousand-acre cordon of the Big Basin reserve, where two battalions of the Life Guard patrolled a triple perimeter of barbed wire through the sword-ferns and every telegraph wire had been barred from the branches, the drop-forges and coal-tar and sea-glare of the coast vanished. Only the redwoods stood around the low, unpainted cedar bungalow. Monstrous fluted columns of dark red bark, twenty feet thick at the butt, rose three hundred feet straight up to shut out the sky and split the noon sun into dusty shafts of twilight. On the wide timber veranda the fifty-five-degree air smelled of damp leaf-mold and cold brook-water and the camphor of fallen needles. Elias sat in an oversized hickory rocking-chair near the rough-barked railing with a gray army blanket from the old Mexican war folded across his knees. Over his corded, weather-scarred neck he wore an open flannel shirt instead of a uniform, and soft elk-skin moccasins gave room to the doughy swelling around his ankle-bones. He was sixty-four that summer. Since the afternoon half a century ago when he had pried the hot iron hinges from his father’s threshold in Kentucky, his hands had never rested empty on his lap until today. Across the unpainted redwood table sat his oldest friend, Brigadier Caleb Vance, past seventy-five now and nearly blind with cataracts in his left eye, his white beard brushing the brass buttons of his faded reserve waistcoat while he pared the rind from a green Pippin apple with a bone-handled pocket-knife. "The doctor from Monterey says if you stay up here in the timber till October and leave the salt-fish and the telegraph-ribbons alone, the water’ll go out of your shins by frost, Elias," Caleb said in a cracked wheeze from campfires gone cold forty years ago. He cut a wedge of white apple on his thumb and held it out on the flat of the blade. "Says a man’s heart is flesh, not Bessemer plate. Even an old mule on the Santa Fe trace had to be turned out to the vega grass once in seven years, or he’d drop in the harness with the blind staggers." Elias left the apple on the blade. Beneath his broad, grey-stubbled chin, a heavy pulse thudded behind his ribs like warm mercury sloshing inside a cracked leather flask. Past the veranda steps, where a clear mountain creek brawled over grey granite boulders between banks of five-finger fern, the sheer cinnamon-colored trunk of a giant *Sequoia* rose ten paces from the porch. "That tree was standing there when the Romans were fighting the Carthaginians, Caleb," Elias said. Without a vaulted ceiling to throw the words back at him, his rough voice dropped almost to a whisper. "The bailiffs left its bark alone, and the clerks kept its board-feet out of their books. When the lightning struck the top out of it five hundred years ago, it grew a new crown out of the side branch without calling a council and kept on standing." Caleb chewed his apple with his back teeth and squinted his one good eye across the porch at the tall, stoop-shouldered figure in the flannel shirt. "You’re talking like an old man, boy. Every pine tree you ever looked at before was measured out in railway ties to the hundred-foot log." "I am sixty-four, Caleb, and when I tried to pull my boot on Tuesday morning at the Citadel, my left fingers failed to close on the strap," Elias said, his gaze on the wide, square-nailed left hand resting on the hickory arm.

of the chair. The skin across his knuckles shone tight as tallow stretched over a bladder, and a slight, regular tremor shook his thumb whenever he took his mind off it. "Marcus died in the snow ten years ago because I drove him till his lungs burst. Now his boy is twenty-three, sitting down at the Monterey Academy with a slide-rule in his pocket and a face like a steel trap, waiting for me to hand him the reins; and down in the city, Schuyler and Takashima have their clerks counting how many drops of foxglove-water the apothecary sends up to my room every week."

"Then hang Schuyler before supper and send the Jap back to his islands in a rowboat," Caleb grunted. He shut his pocket-knife with a sharp *snap* and laid it on the plank table. "You got forty regiments of the old boys’ sons between here and the Sacramento who’d burn the Mint down if you lifted your finger."

"And who runs the Mint the morning after they burn it, you and me with a pair of skinning-knives?" Elias asked. A dry chuckle caught in the fluid at the bottom of his throat and turned into a long, rasping cough; he gripped the rough cedar rail until the gray blanket slipped from his swollen knees onto the floorboards.

Before Caleb could rise from his bench to lift the wool, the screen-door at the end of the veranda creaked. Lady Kaiulani stepped out onto the planks. Having ridden a mule up the mountain bridle-path from the Felton station and left her escort of Hawaiian guardsmen at the lower creek-crossing, she wore a plain riding-habit of dark forest-green wool, her black hair loosened by the pine-boughs and a small wicker basket of fresh figs from the Santa Clara mission orchards hooked over her arm.

"The Brigadier has been giving you salt-meat again, Elias, or you have been trying to walk down to the brook without your stick," she said. She set the basket upon the table, bent down to lift the Mexican blanket, and tucked it back around his thick, cold ankles. Her warm fingers brushed his shin through the elk-skin moccasin. Elias looked down at the crown of her dark head, an old frontier wolf in the green twilight of the redwoods with his grey muzzle hidden in the brush.

"I was telling Caleb that the trees don't care who sits in the Chancery at Monterey," Elias said. His rough hand came down lightly upon her shoulder as she straightened up beside his chair.

Down by the lower creek-crossing, a sudden challenge from the Life Guard pickets echoed through the silent trunks. Iron horseshoes clattered against the granite boulders of the forbidden trail, and young Captain Marcus Vance rode up at a measured trot on a lathered bay mare with his academy tunic buttoned neat to the throat.

"Why are you out of the schoolhouse, boy?" Caleb called down from the porch as his grand-nephew dismounted by the fern-bank and tied his reins to a redwood root.

"The Protector’s vacation ended at noon, Uncle," young Marcus said. He climbed the cedar steps with a rolled linen blueprint under his arm and bowed slightly to Kaiulani. "The Benicia Balloon Works has finished the hydrogen-cells for the first aerial cruiser, and the German and French trade delegates have arrived at the Oakland mole asking for an audience before the autumn tariffs close the Rhine. If the Protector does not show his face on the field tomorrow, Comptroller Schuyler intends to sign the European cotton-quotas himself."

Elias looked from the cold, unblinking youth on the steps to the ancient trees rising into the mist. "Help me up, Caleb," he said, and reached for his stick.

***

Two mornings later, the salt-marsh grass of the Imperial Arsenal at Benicia lay flattened beneath a hot, violent smell of sulphuric acid and scorched castor-oil.

Inside the cavernous, open-ended shed that rose two hundred feet above the Carquinez Strait, a vault of riveted angle-iron large enough to swallow two ships of the line side by side, young General Marcus Vance walked slowly beneath the belly of the *Aeolus*. Above his visored cap hung six hundred feet of yellow rubberized silk stretched drum-tight over an internal skeleton of tubular duralumin and split Tonkin bamboo. Forty hemp mooring-lines anchored the gas-bag to fifty-ton concrete blocks. It pulsed slightly in the draft from the bay like the lung of a sleeping whale.

Suspended thirty feet below the silk envelope by a web of piano-wire rigging hung the gondola: a long, narrow boat-hull of corrugated sheet-aluminum, where a twin-cylinder flash-boiler fired by atomized Borneo benzine drove two four-bladed propellers of laminated ash as tall as windmills.

"The gross lift at sixty degrees Fahrenheit is forty-two tons, General," said Chief Engineer Loewe, a former Prussian balloonist from the siege of Paris whom the Chancery had hired out of a Berlin debtor’s prison three years prior. His linen duster was eaten full of small round holes from the acid-vats where eighty tons of iron shavings were still dissolving in lead-lined troughs to fill the stern ballonet. "With four hundred gallons of benzine in the gravity-tanks and twenty hundredweight of water-ballast, we can carry a crew of twelve, two Maxim machine-guns on swivel-mounts, and forty hundred-pound melinite drop-bombs in the central rack."

Marcus kept his eyes level. He tapped the aluminum skin of the gondola with the knuckle of his gloved forefinger. It gave back a thin, tinny *ping*.

"A Cheyenne dog-soldier on the Powder River or a Kirghiz horseman on the Yenisei can put a .45-caliber lead slug through sixteenth-inch aluminum at four hundred yards, Herr Loewe," Marcus said. His clipped voice echoed against the vast curvature of the gas-bag overhead. "And if a single incendiary bullet from a British Martini-Henry pierces that hydrogen envelope while the craft is hovering below three thousand feet, you have built me a four-hundred-thousand-thaler Roman candle."

"We do not intend to hover below three thousand feet, Excellency," Loewe replied. He wiped his spectacles with an oily rag while two Cantonese mechanics in asbestos aprons climbed into the gondola and lit the pilot-burners under the flash-boiler with a sharp *whuff* of blue vapor. "At five thousand feet, no rifle on earth can touch the envelope, and the wind-drift over the interior plains is steady from the west. Think of the economy, General! Right now, to police the three thousand miles of desert between the Salt Lake and the Obi, you keep eighty regiments of cavalry eating six-thaler oats in mud forts every fifty leagues. With six air-cruisers of the *Aeolus* class moored at Denver, Sitka, and Irkutsk, a single lieutenant with a pair of Zeiss glasses and a wireless-spark key can patrol five hundred square miles of steppe between breakfast and noon."

"And when he sees a band of insurgents tearing up the broad-gauge track, what does he do from five thousand feet, drop a melinite bomb into a prairie five miles wide and hope the horse stands still while the shell falls for eighteen seconds?" asked old Brigadier Caleb Vance, who had ridden out from the Presidio on a quiet mule to inspect his grand-nephew’s new toy and now leaned on his hickory stick near the open shed-doors, spitting tobacco juice into the marsh-reeds.

Young Marcus turned his pale eyes upon the old frontiersman.

"He does not drop bombs on horsemen, Uncle," young Marcus said, and pulled his ivory slide-rule from his breast pocket. "A horseman requires a village to winter in, a corral for his remounts, and a well of sweet water within twenty miles. The air-cruiser leaves the guerrilla to the plains. It follows him at night by the glare of his campfires, marks the map-coordinates of his winter *aoul* or his adobe sanctuary, and drops four hundred pounds of white phosphorus and arsenic canister into his granary and his water-hole while he sleeps."

He stepped up the narrow aluminum ladder into the gondola’s forward control-car, where Major Kuroda was already checking the mercury barometer and the brass speaking-tubes leading to the engine-cage.

"Cast off the bow-lines, Herr Loewe," Marcus ordered. He strapped a leather chin-stay under his cap while the flash-boiler behind him built to six hundred pounds of superheated steam with a high, whistling shriek that sent the marsh-ducks exploding out of the tules along the strait. "We will take her up to four thousand feet over the bay and drop three dummy sand-casks onto the Alcatraz target-raft before the Protector’s barge reaches the Mint slip. I want the old men on Montgomery Street to look up from their ledgers at noon and see that there is no longer a roof over their heads that my guns cannot look through."

***

At that very noon, while the monstrous yellow cigar of the *Aeolus* rose slowly out of the Benicia marshes and turned its twin wooden screws toward the Golden Gate against the upper sea-breeze, Lady Kaiulani stood three stories below the street-level of San Francisco. In the cool, grease-scented gloom of the Imperial Assay and Ration Vaults beneath the Custom House, a clerk weighed a dead man’s thumb on the brass pan.

Before the iron grillwork, a Cantonese coolie-broker trembled as though he would gladly have hacked off his own digit to be out of the cellar. On the scale lay a brass identification-tally, Number Seven-Seven-Four-Two of the Washoe Silver Reserve, stamped with the sun-and-anchor and crusted along its rim with green verdigris from the lime-pits of Virginia City.

"Read the voucher attached to that disk again, Auditor Shen," Kaiulani said.

She wore her dark blue riding-habit from the Santa Cruz mountains, with the skirt pinned up out of the damp sawdust of the vault floor and a single electric hand-lamp held in her gloved fingers to illuminate the open double-entry folio on the stone table. After three days in the clean silence of the redwoods with Elias, the capital’s basement smelled like the bilge of an old slave-ship, thick with wet cement and the rank, sweetish pomade used by the third-grade fiscal clerks while the Hollerith sorting-machines clattered in the next room. It choked the lungs.

Then a thirty-year-old assessor newly promoted from the Hankow customs, Shen adjusted his horn spectacles and held the yellow treasury warrant close to the bulb. "Dated the twelfth of August, Your Highness, and countersigned by Deputy-Comptroller Schuyler the younger," Shen read in his uninflected court English. "'To the Factors of the Six Companies Guild, Sacramento: four hundred and eighty silver thalers, being full settlement of five-year accumulated wages and rice-bounty for Coolie Seven-Seven-Four-Two, discharged in good health upon completion of his Comstock tunnel-indenture.'"

"And now read the burial-register from the Mount Davidson typhus-ward that my Hawaiian provosts seized from the mine-superintendent’s safe on Tuesday," Kaiulani said.

Shen turned the leaf of a smaller, grease-stained book bound in rough calfskin. "'Coolie Seven-Seven-Four-Two, native of Swatow: died of the black lung and spotted fever in Shaft Four, November nineteenth, eighteen-seventy-seven. Buried in Trench C without kin.'"

A thin, whistling sigh escaped the fat Cantonese broker outside the iron bars. He dropped to both knees on the concrete. While his silk skull-cap rolled into the sawdust, he knocked his forehead against the lower rail and clawed at the iron palings with plump hands. "Mercy, High Commissioner!" he babbled in the Kwangtung dialect. "The Guild took none of that silver! When a coolie dies in the deep levels before his third year, the white superintendents and Mr. Schuyler’s audit-clerks leave his number on the Hollerith cards! They keep his brass tag on the hook, draw his four pounds of salt pork and his two silver thalers a day from the Crown Commissariat for the remaining three years, and give our Guild ten percent to sign the discharge-mark with a dead man’s ink-thumb! There are six thousand ghosts drawing rations on the Comstock rolls today, Lady, and ten thousand more on the Puget Sound timber-books! If I had refused to stamp the paper, Mr. Schuyler’s provosts would have revoked my rice-license and sent my sons to the rock-piles!"

Kaiulani gave no answer. Beneath the low brick arch of the vault she straightened her spine, and the electric lamp hung down against her dark blue skirt, throwing their faces into deep upward shadow. Across the water at Berkeley, Rector Norton’s apprentices were painting the Antonine Peace in gold leaf and lapis lazuli. From the deck of a battleship or the window of a Pullman car, Elias’s empire presented a seamless monument of granite and Bessemer steel, yet down in the cellar where the oil met the gears, its own bookkeepers were eating the stone hollow. Because no newspaper dared print a line without the censor’s stamp, and because no workman dared strike a blow without facing Marcus Vance’s Gatling guns, the thirty thousand clerks and Satsuma quartermasters who kept the ledgers had discovered a gold-mine richer than the Klondike: an empire of paper phantoms. Dead coolies ate government beef in Nevada. Phantom regiments of Missouri militia drew Spencer carbines that went over the side of lighters at Manila to the Borneo pirates. Above the basement arches, up in the sunlit halls of the Rincon Hill Citadel, the outer crust of the colossus still shone.

That same afternoon, Elias Thorne returned from the redwoods to take his place in the Hall of the Council. Tall casements in the redwood-vaulted throne room looked straight out through the Golden Gate. Seated upon the raised silver curule chair with his heavy cavalry boots laced tight over his bandaged calves and his broad shoulders squared inside the unadorned navy wool of his Engineer’s tunic, he faced the begging bowls of Europe below the porphyry steps. They had come around the Horn on a leased Hamburg packet because they could no longer afford the coal to steam via Suez: Count von Hatzfeldt from Berlin, Monsieur Challemel-Lacour from the French Republic, Sir Julian Pauncefote of Whitehall. For three days they had waited in the anterooms of the Palace Hotel like provincial tax-collectors while Elias rested his knees among the Santa Cruz ferns; now, as the late sun struck through the western glass and turned the brass fasces behind his head into pillars of sunset gold, the envoys bowed from the waist before the Kentucky squatter’s son.

"The winter harvests in Prussia and the Loire have failed for the second year, Excellency," Count von Hatzfeldt said. His high boots creaked on the koa-wood parquet as he laid a vellum schedule upon the lowest step of the dais. Though he wore the white cuirassier tunic of Bismarck’s Reich, salt-damp tarnished the gold braid at his cuffs, and his voice lacked the iron ring of the seventies. "With the Russian steppes closed by your Siberian truce-lines and the Chicago elevators shipping exclusively to Canton, the price of wheat in Berlin has doubled since August. Furthermore, our electrical works at Siemens and the Krupp rolling-mills at Essen are standing at half-time for want of Malaysian gutta-percha and Peruvian nitrates. The European Concert asks no territorial revision in the Pacific; we ask only that Your Excellency lift the forty-percent differential duty upon non-Confederation hulls at Manila and Guayaquil, and release twenty million bushels of San Joaquin red wheat against sixty-day bills drawn upon the Reichsbank and the Bank of France."

Elias left the vellum on the step. His right hand rested upon the head of his iron walking-stick. Behind his ribs, the heavy, sloshing mercury of his pulse beat a slow measure against his wool vest, while the air in the crowded hall carried the scent of French pomade, damp broadcloth, and the warm gutta-percha insulation drifting up from the cable-vaults below.

"Sixty-day paper drawn on Berlin and Paris," Elias said. Down the length of the silent chamber, past the serpentine pillars where Cornelius Schuyler and Marquis Takashima stood, his low, rough voice carried to the doors. "When my father owed sixty-two dollars on his land in thirty-seven, Count, the bailiffs refused sixty-day paper. They asked for hard coin, and when we had none, they burned the logs."

Sir Julian Pauncefote shifted his weight. His pale English cheeks flushed beneath his gray whiskers. "Surely the Providentor does not compare the sovereign credit of Great Britain, France, and the German Empire to a frontier mortgage. We offer the treasury bills of three hundred million civilized people."

"You offer the promises of three armed camps sitting on a worn-out peninsula," Elias said. He leaned forward half an inch upon his stick and fixed his pale eyes on the Englishman. "You spend forty million pounds a year building fortresses against each other along the Rhine and the Alps, and then come to my wharf with your hats in your hands to ask for bread and copper-insulation on credit. My granaries at Vallejo are full to the rafters, gentlemen, and my nitrate-hulks at Callao are riding deep in the water. You may have twenty million bushels of wheat before the November gales, and ten thousand tons of Sarawak rubber."

Count von Hatzfeldt’s narrow chest eased. "On the security of the Reichsbank notes, Excellency?"

"On the security of your blast-furnaces and your naval slips," Elias said. "I take no European paper. For every bushel of California wheat that enters Hamburg or Havre this winter, your governments will deliver to my agents at Antwerp fifty tons of rolled Bessemer rail-iron at forty percent below the Essen market price, or sign five-year indentures transferring four hundred master optical-grinders and chemical engineers from Jena and Lyons to the polytechnic schools at Berkeley. And as for the differential duty, any European steamer that wishes to load nitrates at Callao or tin at Batavia without paying the sixty-percent foreign impost need only haul down her national rag at the harbor-mouth, register fifty-one percent of her hull with Mr. Schuyler’s maritime board in San Francisco, and carry a Hawaiian port-officer on her bridge. Those are the terms of the trough. You may sign them at the Chancellor’s desk before the five-o’clock gun, or you may go home and explain to your weavers why their bread is made of turnip-meal this Christmas."

He left before they bowed. Driving his right arm straight down upon the iron ferrule of his cane in a rigid movement that hid the drag of his left boot across the velvet carpet from the Europeans, Elias rose from the silver seat, turned his back upon the ambassadors of the Old World, and walked through the bronze doors behind the dais.

# Chapter 19: The Galvanic Throne

Only when Brigadier Caleb Vance bolted the double oak panels of the third-floor bedchamber on the inside did the iron go out of Elias's knees. Windowless on the seaward side to keep out the draft, the small room took its heat from a single porcelain stove burning smokeless anthracite. Against the whitewashed plaster wall stood the narrow gas-pipe camp-cot from Vicksburg, a washstand with a tin basin, and a leather armchair smelling of old horse-sweat and camphor. Elias got three paces past the threshold before his right elbow buckled on the stick.

"Easy, boy," Caleb said. With his gnarled, seventy-five-year-old shoulder, he caught Elias’s two-hundred-pound frame beneath the left armpit and eased him down into the leather chair beside the stove. "You held your breath too long out there in front of the quality. Let me get the knife to these laces."

Elias could not answer him at once. His chin tipped back against the greasy leather headrest, his mouth wide open as he fought to pull air through a windpipe plugged with hot wet wool. Carbolic soap and the dried stramonium-leaves smoldering in the brass saucer on the washstand thickened the air, yet behind those familiar odors rose the sharp stench of scorching copper wire and burned feathers inside the left hemisphere of his own skull.

"The... the German," Elias said. His tongue lay thick and dry as salted boot-leather in his mouth while Caleb knelt on the rug, bending his cataract-clouded eye close to the floor to cut the tight leather thongs of Elias’s boots with a pocket-knife. "Did you see his coat, Caleb? White wool... and brass eagles... and begging for twenty shiploads of flour like a teamster at the fort gate."

"I seen him," Caleb grunted. He stripped the split calfskin off Elias’s swollen, purple-mottled ankle and wrapped the cold flesh in warm flannel from the stove-fender. "They’re all whipped, Elias. The whole kit and boodle of ’em from here to Jerusalem. Now keep your jaw shut and drink this foxglove-water before the Princess comes up from the cellar and skins me alive for letting you stand on the steps."

Caleb rose from his knees and held the small blue glass measure to Elias’s lips. Elias reached up with his left hand to steady the old man’s wrist. The hand stayed down. On his flannel thigh it lay like five pounds of dead salt pork wrapped in yellow hide. In the dim light of the stove-grate, he stared at his own fingers. Just as he had commanded forty Rangers to wheel at the Rio Frio and sixteen battleships to steam past Kanagawa, he commanded the thumb to twitch, and though the nerve sent the spark down the arm, the flesh lay still. At the same instant, the scorching smell of burned feathers flared behind his left eye into a silent, blinding flash of white magnesium light. Without a sound, the porcelain stove and Caleb’s white beard tilted sideways alongside the tin washbasin; the left side of his jaw sagged open, bitter digitalis spilled down the front of his navy tunic, and his throat produced only a thick, wet, bubbling rattle that died on his chin when he tried to call out his friend’s name.

Caleb held the glass fast. For two seconds the old artilleryman stood over the twisted, half-stone mask of the boy he had pulled out of the frozen mule on the Platte fifty years before. Then, silent for a man of seventy-five, Caleb stepped to the chamber door, drew the heavy iron night-bolt across the jamb against the corridor pages, and walked into the adjoining dressing-closet where Lady Kaiulani waited beside the private hydraulic lift from the Assay Vaults.

"Don't call the garrison surgeon, ma'am," Caleb said. He closed the closet door behind him and held up his wet, medicine-stained sleeve in the yellow lamp-light. "His left side’s gone dead as a wedge, and he’s lost his tongue. If Takashima’s orderly out in the passage hears a doctor running up the stairs with a lancet-case, the Japanese cruisers will be clearing for action before the six-o’clock bell."

Kaiulani laid the brass identification-tag of the dead Comstock coolie down upon the dressing-table with a steady hand. For ten years she had awaited this hour on the stair. Now it stood in the room.

"Can he see you with his right eye, Brigadier?" she asked, and stripped the long silver hat-pin from her riding-bonnet.

"Looks right through me like a bored cannon," Caleb said.

"Then he is still on the throne," Kaiulani said. She walked past him into the bedchamber, where the great figure slumped crookedly in the leather chair with his solitary gray eye fixed upon the locked oak door. "Put fresh coals in the grate, Caleb, and go out onto the gallery landing with your pipe. Tell the household chamberlain that the Providentor has ordered a cold supper laid in his study and wishes no disturbance while he drafts the Berlin grain-warrants with me. Nobody enters this wing until my nephew brings the Hawaiian Guard up from the Mint at midnight."

***

An empire wired together with six thousand leagues of copper nerve-fiber cannot have its brain struck half-dead at five o’clock without the twitch reaching the extremities before six. A corridor page from the Osaka delegation saw the European envoys dismissed ten minutes early; a laundry-woman in the basement remarked that no hot water was called for in the third-floor bath; and at a quarter past seven, one of Marquis Takashima’s marine orderlies at the side gate intercepted the apothecary’s boy from the Presidio hospital with two cylinders of compressed oxygen wrapped in an army blanket. By nine o’clock that night, while the city of San Francisco drank its beer in the gas-lit gardens along Market Street and celebrated the humiliation of the German Count, silence held the subterranean War Room forty feet beneath the granite foundations of the Monterey Staff College Annex on Telegraph Hill. Here the concrete shut out the fog and the redwoods. Built to withstand the direct hit of a sixteen-inch naval shell, the vaulted chamber hummed with the low vibration of the rotary ventilation-fans, smelling of damp Portland cement, warm battery acid from the twenty telegraph repeaters clicking in the rear alcove, and the rank, oily leaf of the Manila cheroots that Colonel Armistead chewed unlit in the corner.

Around the massive slate plotting-table in the center of the floor stood five men: young General Marcus Vance, still wearing the oil-spotted khaki tunic in which he had descended from the gondola of the *Aeolus* at sunset; Marquis Takashima in his dark naval cape; Colonel Armistead of the Second Virginia Auxiliary; General Saigo of the Choshu Guard; Major Kuroda. Upon the black slate between them lay the purple-inked mobilization grid of the city of San Francisco and the domestic rail-junctions of the Sacramento Valley.

"The oxygen cylinders went up the private bullion-hoist from the cellar at seven-thirty, General Vance," Marquis Takashima said. Under the green-shaded incandescent bulbs, his narrow bronze face gleamed like old lacquer as his gloved finger tapped the red square marking the Rincon Hill Citadel. "And my personal physician has interviewed the apothecary’s assistant. Three cylinders of pure oxygen and ten grains of strychnine sulfate. A physician does not administer strychnine and oxygen to a man of sixty-four unless cerebral hemorrhage has struck the respiratory center of the brain. Either the Providentor lies dead behind that locked oak door, or he sits a mute paralytic under the thumb of the Hawaiian woman and your dottering uncle."

"Old Caleb Vance has two companies of the Life Guard sitting on the stairs with loaded Spencers, Marquis," Colonel Armistead said. He spat a shred of tobacco leaf onto the concrete floor and leaned his scarred knuckles on the edge of the slate. "I rode up to the south gate at eight to present the evening guard-report in person. Caleb came out to the wicket himself with a Colt forty-five in his waistband. Told me Elias was asleep after the German parley and that any officer who brought an armed file within two hundred yards of the Mason Street wall before morning would be blown out of his saddle. Meanwhile, Comptroller Schuyler has locked himself inside the Bank of California with forty hired Pinkerton riflemen and is burning his private Comstock ledgers in the furnace boiler."

General Saigo of the Choshu division rested his left hand upon the hilt of his saber. Over the Virginian’s shoulder, his dark eyes met young Marcus’s gaze. "If the breath leaves the Providentor’s body before the Sword regulates the succession, General Vance, the Comptroller’s syndicate-clerks and the Hawaiian Princess will proclaim a civilian Regency from the balcony at dawn. Within a week, the

eastern provinces will stop the tribute-trains, and the Diet will vote to cut the naval estimates in half. I have four battalions of the Choshu and Satsuma infantry under arms at the Presidio barracks tonight, and Admiral Takashima’s cruisers have steam up off Goat Island. We require only your counter-signature on the Riot Warrant to occupy the Mint, the Telegraph Exchange, and the Rincon Hill gates before midnight."

Young Marcus Vance kept his eyes on the slate table. Beneath the central lamp, the green light caught the pale, beardless planes of his twenty-three-year-old face and the ivory tip of the slide-rule in his breast pocket. All evening these old warlords, the samurai who remembered the Shogun’s wars and the Virginian who remembered Chancellorsville, had talked of barricades and palace gates as if power were a physical chest of silver to be carried off in an ambulance-wagon.

"You propose to march four Japanese battalions down Market Street at midnight to shoot down Brigadier Caleb’s Missourians at the Palace gate, General Saigo?" Marcus’s level voice cut through the hum of the ventilating-fans.

"To secure the person of the Sovereign from insular usurpers," Takashima said. He stepped closer to the youth’s elbow. "Under a Provisional Military Directorate: yourself as Chief of the Continental Staff, myself as High Admiral of the Ocean, and Mr. Schuyler retained at the Treasury under our audit to keep the New York banks quiet. Once our sentries are inside the bedchamber, whether the old man can speak or not is immaterial; we will issue the proclamations over his stamp."

With two fingers, Marcus picked up a small brass marker representing the experimental air-cruiser *Aeolus*. He set it squarely upon the inked outline of the Citadel conservatory dome.

"If your Choshu infantry fires a single volley at the Life Guard on Mason Street tonight, Marquis," Marcus said, looking from the Japanese admiral to the scarred Virginian beside him, "Colonel Armistead’s four regiments of Atlantic Auxiliaries in Oakland will cross the bay on the ferry-barges by four in the morning to shoot your sailors in the back, and by noon tomorrow half of San Francisco will be in ashes while the British fleet steams out of Esquimalt to retake Puget Sound. My father died in the ice at Baikal. His son will not preside over a Mexican *pronunciamiento* in a street-gutter."

"Then what is your calculation, boy?" Armistead demanded. His hand gripped his belt as the telegraph repeater in the rear alcove clattered with an incoming priority wire from the Citadel. "If we stand on our thumbs till daylight while Kaiulani and Shen lock the doors—"

"We leave the doors alone, Colonel; we take the wires," Marcus said. He turned half a pace toward Major Kuroda as the aide tore the wet blue ribbon from the spool and brought it to the slate table.

Marcus read the cipher once. He laid it face-up beneath the green lamp. Bearing the private seal of Lady Kaiulani from the Assay Vaults, the dispatch warned that she had already placed forty tons of nitro-glycerine under the Market Street bullion-cellars and wired the torpedo-boats at Mare Island to sink any cruiser off Goat Island that moved an anchor-fluke without her counter-sign.

"You see, gentlemen," Marcus said, "the High Commissioner understands engineering better than you do. If we fight her tonight, we inherit a crater. Tomorrow morning, I will walk into the conservatory alone and sign a compact with Her Highness to preserve the Triumvirate for as long as the old man’s chest can be kept moving by oxygen and strychnine: five years, perhaps six, until my polytechnic cadets are old enough to take the ships out of your hands without firing a shot."

***

That secret subterranean compact of eighty-one bought the phantom peace. It stretched the half-paralyzed twilight of Elias Thorne’s reign across the middle eighties like a drumhead tightened to the splitting-point. Yet before the final calcification of the Hundred and Twenty-Four States could be proclaimed over his death-bed, during those last suspended summers of eighty-five and eighty-six when the old Titan still sat propped beside the carp-pool while the world awaited the stroke, Lady Kaiulani made one final, unrecorded effort to discover whether blood might yet spare the Empire the tyranny of the examination-shed.

On a warm afternoon in the late summer of 1886, ten months before the Coral Sea and the final silence at Monterey, she walked alone through the terraced bamboo and cypress alleys of the Palace Gardens on the southern slope of Nob Hill. Behind twenty-foot walls of rusticated Sierra granite patrolled by her silent Oahu riflemen, the roar of the Potrero rolling-mills and the brassy clanging of the cable-cars along California Street dropped to a drowsy, insect-like hum. Crushed lemon-verbena scented the air alongside hot Monterey pine-needles and the salt mist drifting through the red-lacquered torii gates around the lotus ponds. Across the clipped emerald turf of the lower bowling-green, in the shade of a weeping *waringin* tree transplanted from Batavia, sat the three young men whom the court whispers called the Left-Handed Princes.

Elias Thorne remained unmarried. A king who weds a daughter of Boston insults Edo; a conqueror who takes a princess of Satsuma or Oahu to his lawful bed turns his own frontier marshals into rebels. Instead, across forty years of camps and chanceries, the Providentor had left his rough, hawk-nosed stamp upon three women of the three great races he had welded into his realm, and because he regarded human beings as timber to be tested for its grain before being mortised into the state, he had brought the three boys up within the garden walls under the eyes of the Chancery tutors, unacknowledged by statute yet clothed in the purple-bordered tunics of Imperial Wards.

Kaiulani paused beside a carved stone lantern. She tilted her black silk parasol against the glare of the western water.

Silas, born in fifty-nine to a dead widow of the Virginia Auxiliaries during the Denver winter, was twenty-seven now. He had his father’s broad, ox-like shoulders and thick wrists, yet as he lounged in a wicker garden-chair with a silver flask of Monongahela rye uncorked beside his knee and tossed bits of sugared biscuit to the golden carp, his face lacked the freezing Kentucky iron. It was soft and florid, petulant around the mouth. He had spent the morning losing four thousand thalers at the Jockey Club races at Ingleside, and turf-mud still crusted his riding-boots. Ten paces away, kneeling upon a straw *tatami* mat spread over the grass, the second son, Kiyoshi, born to a lady of the Choshu house after the treaty of Shimoda, dismantled the breech-mechanism of a new Sacramento repeating rifle with oiled chamois gloves; his narrow, shaved head bent so low over the steel springs that the sun caught the small, livid scar where a court surgeon had trepanned his skull after a childhood bout of the falling-sickness. Apart by the marble balustrade overlooking the harbor stood the youngest, Kalanimoku. Dressed in white linen flannel, he sketched the distant smoke of an incoming Canton tea-liner in a small calfskin water-color book. He was her own second cousin’s child, born in the year after the Honolulu barricades, a boy of eighteen with Elias’s pale gray eyes set inside the warm bronze skin of an island chief.

"Your Highness walks late in the sun," Silas said. He stayed in his wicker chair as her shadow fell across the turf, though he pushed the silver whiskey-flask behind a flowerpot with the toe of his boot. "Have you come down from the conservatory to tell us whether the old man’s left thumb twitched after dinner, or has young General Vance decided to turn this garden into a balloon-shed?"

"I have come to see how the sons of the house employ their afternoon while the grain-brokers in the city below are betting ten to one that the Providentor will not see September," Kaiulani said. She closed her parasol with a sharp *snap*. "Did you attend the sitting of the Maritime Tariff Committee at noon, Silas, as the Chancellor requested?"

Silas laughed, a thick, wet sound that smelled of sour mash at three paces. He flicked a pebble into the lotus pond. "To sit for four hours between old Schuyler’s nose and Auditor Shen’s abacus, listening to how many barrels of salt-pork go to the Sitka mines? Let the Berkeley examination-clerks count the pork, Aunt. When my father’s breath stops, the First Virginia and the California Lancers won't ask a man how many logarithms he knows before they hoist him onto his saddle. They will look for a white man who carries the Thorne jaw and knows how to spend gold in the canteens."

Beside the mat, Kiyoshi kept his eyes on the disassembled rifle-bolt. His thin fingers twitched with the rhythmic, involuntary tic that preceded his seizures. "The Virginia regiments are garrisoned at Hankow and the Yenisei, Elder Brother," the Choshu youth said in his high, strained English. His thumb clicked the firing-pin three times against the steel sear. "In San Francisco there are only the Satsuma Marine guards and the Academy cadets. When the breath stops, Marquis Takashima will clear the palace with the bayonet, and if a man does not wear the sword-belt of the Western Clans, his throat will be cut before he reaches the stable."

Down by the balustrade, young Kalanimoku closed his water-color pad with a quiet sigh and turned his pale gray eyes, stripped of all their father's pitiless ambition, toward Kaiulani. "Ignore them, Aunt," the boy said in the Hawaiian tongue. "One dreams of a tavern-camp, and the other dreams of a shogun’s slaughterhouse. If the throne is an iron chair where a man must sit with a pistol in his lap and watch his brothers’ cups for arsenic, let General Vance and his slide-rules have it. Give me a schooner and twenty islanders, and let me sail back to Kauai to plant taro in the quiet valleys."

Kaiulani looked across the manicured grass from the drunken roaring-boy of the old frontier to the epileptic fanatic of the barracks, and then to the gentle painter who wanted to go home to a garden paved with coal-dredges twenty years ago. For forty years Elias had felled every tall tree between the Potomac and the Yellow Sea so that none might cast a shadow across his camp-cot. In the shade of that solitary, monolithic oak, only toadstools and weeds had grown. If she crowned Silas at dawn, Takashima’s battleships would shell the Citadel by noon; if she crowned Kiyoshi, the American provinces would rise from Boston to Sacramento; and if she placed the gold collar upon Kalanimoku’s slender neck, young Marcus Vance would have him strangled with a telegraph-wire before the ink dried on the proclamation. No blood remained to hold the circle.

***

Down beyond the twenty-foot granite wall of the garden, in the steep, grid-iron canyons of brick and redwood that tumbled from the skirts of Nob Hill to the oily waters of the bay, the seven hundred thousand souls of the city already smelled the sickness in the upper rooms. To the Chronicler who mingled with the crowds along Kearney and Market streets during those sultry days of late August, when a freakish calm off the Farallones left the coal-soot of the foundries hanging motionless between the cornice-stones like a ceiling of dirty yellow flannel, the public temper soured like milk before a thunderstorm.

For twenty years the people of the capital had lived inside the iron parenthesis of the Providentor’s will. Nobody had seen Elias Thorne walk down the steps of the Chancery since the spring of eighty-four. Every morning the official *Gazette* printed the same three-line formula regarding his afternoon audiences in the conservatory, until the lower wards regarded him as an eternal, subterranean boiler that kept the silver thalers circulating and the grain-elevators full. Now, without a single line appearing in the censored press, the invisible telegraph of the streets—the whispers of laundry-coolies coming down from the Mason Street service-gates, the guarded talk of apothecaries’ clerks over their beer-mugs in the German cellars of Bush Street, the sudden doubling of the Hawaiian sentry-posts around the Sub-Treasury—ran through the tenements from the Mission to the Barbary Coast. *The old man’s tongue is black,* the Irish dock-wallopers muttered. They leaned on their bale-hooks beside the silent hydraulic cranes at the Pacific Mail wharf, where two Satsuma torpedo-boats slipped their moorings off Goat Island with their battle-lanterns hooded in broad daylight. *He’s been dead since the German Count came to town, and the Kanaka witch is keeping him packed in rock-salt up in the glass house while the New York bankers ship all the flour out to Canton!*

By the third morning of the rumor, the terror had translated itself into the price of bread. Although forty million bushels of the summer harvest from the San Joaquin filled the stone granaries at Vallejo and Port Costa, the syndicate grain-jobbers along California Street, taking their secret cues from Cornelius Schuyler’s private discount-desk, had locked their warehouse receipts inside their iron safes and refused to release a single barge-load of red wheat against the standard silver-paper certificates of the Municipal Commissariat until they knew whose signature would stand on the Treasury warrants on Monday morning. Within forty-eight hours, the two-pound loaf of regulation barley-and-wheat bread, fixed by provost-statute at one silver tenth since the year of the Sitka purchase, vanished from the bakers’ counters.

At six o’clock in the evening, the shift-whistles blew at the Potrero Point armor-works and the Union Iron Foundry. Ten thousand soot-streaked puddle-men, Cantonese sandal-makers, and discharged veterans of the eastern campaigns stayed away from their boarding-houses. They packed the cobbled triangle before the closed bronze doors of the Old Mint and the neighboring bakeries along Commercial Street, where wooden shutters had been bolted over the broken glass and armed squads of the Tripartite Municipal Police stood ankle-deep in spilled flour and horse-dung with their repeating carbines held across their chests.

"Four silver tenths for a ten-ounce loaf of sour corn-meal at the Italian’s on Dupont Street!" roared a massive, grey-bearded hammer-man from the Risdon boiler-shops. Standing on the hub of an overturned dray, he waved a hard, mildewed ship’s biscuit above the sea of greasy bowler hats and blue coolie-blouses. "And when I laid down a five-thaler Treasury note with the Protector’s own face on the paper, the shopkeeper spat on the counter and said the bank wouldn't give him sixty cents in copper for it because Elias Thorne is nailed up in a lead box at Monterey and the Japs are going to divide the Mint with the Wall Street sharks tonight!"

"Show us the Old Man!" a woman screamed from the steps of the closed savings-bank opposite. She held an empty flour-sack above her shawl while three hundred voices along the curbstone took up the cry in a ragged, rhythmic chant that echoed off the iron shutters of the counting-houses: *"Show us the Protector! Open the balcony, or we’ll bring the sledges to the gate!"*

***

Up on the third floor of the Citadel, inside the windowless, anthracite-heated bedchamber where the air bit the nostrils with the medicinal stench of spilled strychnine and scorching copper from the galvanic battery-box on the washstand, the roar of the street-mob came up through the stone ventilating-shafts like ice-floes jamming against a bridge-pier. Brigadier Caleb Vance and two tight-lipped naval surgeons finished strapping Elias Thorne’s torso into the hinged whalebone-and-steel orthopedic corset beneath his dark blue Engineer’s tunic. A knife-blade scarcely separated the living sovereign from an iron effigy.

Since the second stroke had taken his left arm and his speech after the German audience forty-eight hours ago, Elias had existed inside a vertical prison. His mind remained as clear and pitiless as the winter sun over the Wind River mountains. Through the haze of the drugs, he calculated the tonnage of the Vallejo wheat-bins to the hundredweight and traced to the penny why Cornelius Schuyler’s brokers had locked the flour-barges to force a Regency crisis before the weekend. Yet when he commanded his vocal cords to form the order that would hang twenty grain-jobbers from the California Street lamp-posts, his ruined throat produced only a dry, hissing click; his left leg and arm hung from his shoulder-socket like four stones of wet clay bolted to a pine post.

"Pull the lower buckle another notch, Doctor," Lady Kaiulani commanded. She stood at the foot of the dressing-chair in her dark blue brocade gown, her face pale and immovable, holding the gold-braided collar of his greatcoat open in her hands. "If his knees bend an inch when the hydraulic platform rolls out onto the stone flags of the balcony, ten thousand men down in the plaza with opera-glasses will see it, and by midnight the Presidio garrison will be marching on the Mint."

The senior surgeon’s fingers were stained yellow with picric acid; if the patient died under his wrench, old Caleb Vance would shoot him before he reached the corridor. He pulled the leather strap across Elias’s lower ribs until the steel stays groaned against the swollen liver. "Highness, the fluid in the pleura is pressing directly upon the aorta," the doctor whispered. He wiped the sweat from his forehead with his cuff and pointed to the two copper electrodes of the portable galvanic battery taped with gutta-percha plaster to the muscles of Elias’s paralyzed left neck and shoulder. "With forty grains of digitalis and a twentieth of a grain of strychnine in his veins, his heart is beating like a trip-hammer against a closed valve. If we lock his spine upright in this iron frame for fifteen minutes in the cold wind off the bay, and pass a galvanic current through the cervical nerves to keep his chin from sagging onto his chest, the blood-pressure in the carotid may rupture the remaining vessel in the brain before the crowd clears the square!"

Elias did not wait for Kaiulani to answer the sawbones. With his live right hand, the broad, scarred hand that had held the squirrel-rifle in Kentucky and the Paterson Colt on the Rio Frio, he reached out from the sleeve of his tunic, seized the surgeon’s linen lapel in a grip that twisted the cloth into a knot, and jerked the man’s face down within six inches of his own. From the right side of Elias’s face, a single wide, water-clear eye blazed out of the grey, half-dead mask. The physician went white to the lips. Elias released the lapel. He struck his own iron-corseted breastbone twice with his right fist, *thud, thud*, a hollow sound like a mallet striking a keg of nails.

"He’s telling you he’d rather burst his skull standing up in the wind than rot in the bedsheets while Schuyler steals his horse," Brigadier Caleb Vance said. His one good eye glinted beneath his white bushy brow as he knelt to lock the hinged steel leg-splints inside the wide tops of Elias’s cavalry boots and pulled the dark blue trouser-cuffs down over the iron joints. "Put the coat on him, Princess, and give me the switch to that spark-box. I walked beside him when we didn't have mule-tallow to grease our moccasins, and by God, I’ll hold his chin up for the last parade."

Five minutes later, at the exact stroke of six upon the bronze bell of the Nob Hill basilica, the tall, twenty-foot French casements of the Western Balcony above the Citadel plaza swung inward. Down in the vast, stepped granite amphitheater below, where fifty thousand mechanics, dock-laborers, and off-duty soldiers stood wedged shoulder-to-shoulder between the thirty-foot bronze statue of the Providentor and the cordons of young Marcus Vance’s Academy cadets, the roaring chant of *"Bread or blood!"* died away into a sudden intake of breath like surf drawing back down a gravel beach before a tidal wave.

Out through the dark arch of the doorway, driven at a slow, stately pace by a noiseless hydraulic worm-gear sliding through a groove in the marble flags, came the Sovereign of the Pacific. He stood upright. Bolted from heel to hip inside the hidden steel stirrups of the sliding platform, his broad shoulders squared by the whalebone stays beneath his plain Engineer’s tunic, Elias Thorne glided straight to the stone balustrade and stopped with his right hand planted squarely upon the coping. To his right stood Lady Kaiulani in the full crimson-and-yellow feather mantle of the island kings; to his left stood young General Marcus Vance and old Caleb, whose gnarled hand inside his coat-pocket gripped the vulcanite rheostat of the galvanic wire

running up beneath the skirt of the Providentor’s greatcoat. Down in the front rank by the fountain, five hundred binocular-lenses and spyglasses clicked up in the red, level rays of the setting sun. For ten seconds, nobody breathed. The wind off the Golden Gate smelled of salt-kelp and foundry-smoke; it whipped Elias’s short-cropped white hair against his temples and flattened the blue wool against his chest. Inside the iron corset, red-hot wires sawed him in half. Every beat of his strychnine-lashed heart drove a blinding crimson stroke behind his eyeballs until the fifty thousand upturned white faces in the plaza ran together into a lake of molten brass; water rose from his lungs into his throat, salt and warm, and if his right knee slackened by the thickness of a sheet of paper against the steel splint, the whole monstrous lie would pitch headfirst over the stone rail into the street. Below the balcony, in the reserved loggia beside the Mint gates, old Cornelius Schuyler half-rose from his carriage-seat. His mouth fell open as he stared up at the erect, broad-shouldered figure towering against the sunset gold. "He is standing on his own boots!" Schuyler whispered to Marquis Takashima. His trembling fingers dropped the key to the Vallejo grain-safes into the straw at his feet. "The apothecary lied to your doctor. He has ten years of iron in him yet!" Up on the balcony, the nerve tired; Elias’s left cheek sagged toward his collar. Caleb Vance turned the brass screw in his pocket half a notch to the right. A scorching bolt of galvanic electricity leaped from the wet battery-sponge into the dead muscles of Elias’s neck. His molars clicked shut, his head jerked upright toward the western sky, and with a wrench of his live right shoulder, he lifted his heavy iron walking-stick three inches off the marble balustrade and brought the ferrule down upon the stone. *Crack.* The sharp, metallic report echoed across the hush of the fifty thousand. For thirty-five years that stick striking a floorboard had been the only constitution the Pacific knew. Through the fiery agony of the current, as fifty thousand throats below erupted in a single roar of *"Thorne! Thorne!"* that shook the glass in the conservatory dome and sent the sea-gulls wheeling in panic out over the dark water of the Gate, Elias turned his head half an inch until his wide, unblinking right eye fixed the loggia where Schuyler sat, raised his right arm to point the iron stick down the slope of California Street toward the locked grain-piers, and held the pose while the red sun touched the horizon and Kaiulani leaned close to his stiffened shoulder to repeat the compact young Marcus Vance had sealed with her in the cellar an hour before.

"Hold the rail for thirty seconds more, Elias," she said against the howling square, her hand steadying the hidden hydraulic lever behind the velvet drape. "Schuyler’s clerks are already running to unlock the Vallejo wheat-barges, and Marquis Takashima has signaled his cruisers to bank their fires. We have bought your empire its six years of breath."

***

Those six years of borrowed twilight, bought by galvanic wire in eighty-one and spent in the long, grinding encirclement of the southern waters, came to their final accounting on a moonless night in late August of 1887, forty-eight hours after the promulgation of the Hundred and Twenty-Four States in the Rotunda.

Inside the Private Library on the third floor of the Rincon Hill Citadel, the Providentor’s own gesture had turned off the electric bulbs. Only a fire of seasoned Sierra pitch-pine and black Nanaimo lump-coal blazed in the deep granite hearth. Its resinous, popping heat filled the book-lined vault with the sound of that first Kentucky autumn fifty years before. The room smelled of scorched calfskin and the sharp camphor-spirit that Brigadier Caleb Vance had rubbed into Elias’s chest before being ordered out.

Elias sat alone before the iron hearth-grate in his rubber-tired koa-wood chair. The brake-levers were locked fast against the floor-tiles. The transient paralysis of eighty-one had yielded in his middle eighties to a slow, suffocating calcification of the pericardium, only to return threefold after the Coral Sea; yet tonight, with sixty grains of strychnine and brandy burning through his arteries for the last time, he had forced his swollen right hand to obey the chisel of his brain. Across his lap, upon the sea-otter fur, lay the brass-bound mahogany chest that had traveled under his bunk from the adobe blockhouse at Clark’s Point to the Forbidden City.

Inside it lay forty years of unvarnished memory: the greasy pocket-ledgers in which he had tallied the stolen DuPont powder on the Llano Estacado; the secret correspondence with Major St. Clair of the Golden Circle before the betrayal of Richmond; the true casualty rolls of the Chilkoot ice-steps before Auditor Shen’s clerks had scrubbed the numbers for the Diet; and the three small, salt-stained notebooks bound in Mexican pigskin wherein, during the long nights off the Peiho bar and the vigil at Sitka, he had written down in his cramped, phonetic frontier hand his private meditations upon the creatures who served him.

He picked up the first pigskin book with his thick, purple-mottled right fingers. Firelight caught the faded brown ink on the flyleaf: *No law holds past the range of the gun that wrote it. If Kaiulani lives ten years after my breath stops, she will turn the Legion into a priesthood of eunuchs; if young Vance gets the seal, he will measure men’s skulls with a caliper until the boiler splits.*

Elias stared at the page with his wide right eye. Down in the subterranean archives beneath the Mint, Rector Norton’s historians and Magistrate Shen’s scribes were already engraving the official steel plates of the *Annals of the Providentor*, recording how an unerring, mathematical vision of oceanic harmony had guided the American Caesar from his fourteenth year as he marched from the Platte to the Yenisei without a doubt in his breast or a blot on his escutcheon.

If he left these pigskin books in the mahogany box, fifty years hence some spectacled clerk from the Berkeley sheds would pry open the brass lock. They would read that the founder of the Grand Confederation had cared nothing for their Three Harmonies; that he had built an empire across half the earth for the same reason he had shot Cortina’s horse between the eyes in the Rio Frio, because he could not endure the sound of another man’s whip cracking over his head. They would see the joints in the armor. Once the provinces read that the god in the bronze coat had been a mortal man who feared the dark water rising in his own ankles, and that human hands had mixed the mortar, they would pick at the stones.

History required an iron die that never varied by the thousandth of an inch.

With the hooked ferrule of his walking-stick, Elias pushed the heavy brass fender aside and wheeled his chair two feet closer to the open grate until the heat of the pitch-pine blistered the dry skin of his cheekbones and smoked the grease on his cavalry boots. He left the pages whole. A single sheet blown up the chimney onto the roofs of Mason Street might buy a printer’s boy a rope. He lifted the entire pigskin volume in his right fist and pitched it straight into the white-hot hollow between two burning logs.

The dry Mexican leather curled backward. It hissed, wept black tallow into the coals, and burst into a tall, yellow-green sheet of flame as the copper-gall ink caught fire.

One after another, while sweat poured down his paralyzed left cheek into his white stubble, Elias fed his life into the stone: first the secret receipt from Governor Pesqueira for the Tucson Springfields, then the original surgeon’s certificate from Shanghai showing that the Master of the Ocean had lain helpless on his back for eleven days while a Polynesian woman forged his cipher, and finally the water-color sketch of the Kauai valley that young Kalanimoku had laid upon his knee the week before the boy died of winter pleurisy at Monterey.

For twenty minutes nothing sounded in the library save the heavy, whistling scrape of Elias’s breath and the roar of the chimney draft sucking forty years of blood and ink up into the San Francisco fog. When he had splintered the last mahogany partition of the box with the butt of his iron stick and laid it upon the grate, he leaned forward and poked the black, fluttering skins of carbonized paper with the ferrule until they dissolved into gray powder among the pine-ash.

Only the bronze statues in the squares and the laws stamped in steel remained of Elias Thorne. He had burned the carpenter out of the house.

As he drew the iron stick back from the grate, the heavy, mercury-filled sack behind his breastbone gave a single, monstrous heave; he had lived with the hot wire in his ribs so long that pain was merely the weight of his coat, and now the piston simply stopped at the top of the stroke. The iron cane slipped from his numb right fingers. It struck the hearth-stones with a loud *clang* that echoed through the oak panels of the door. Above the mantel, the gilded face of the bulkhead clock swam backward into a rushing wall of coal-black smoke that smelled of cured hog-fat, frost-bitten Kentucky clover, and the salt-spray of an unbroken sea.

# Chapter 20: The Bells of Rincon Hill

To the Chronicler who walked homeward through the quiet, fog-drenched streets of the capital at four o’clock on that morning of the twenty-second of August, 1887, or who looked back upon that night thirteen years later from the completed concrete ramparts of the Panama locks, the founder's passing came out of the upper mist like the voice of the bronze ocean itself.

For three hours after midnight, while the physicians and the three Regents stood behind the bolted doors of the third-floor library, the operators held every telegraph wire and submarine cable between the Golden Gate and the outer pickets on the Yenisei and the Coral Sea open on a dead, continuous current, forbidding a single private syllable to pass through the repeaters until the garrisons at Boston, Edo, Peking, and Sydney stood under arms at their magazine gates.

Then, at seventeen minutes past four, while cold sea-smoke over the Marin hills still drowned the stars and the seventy foundry-stacks along the Potrero shore first reddened the low sky for the morning shift, the twelve-ton bell of the Syncretic Cathedral of St. Michael and the Sun Goddess on the crest of Nob Hill gave a single, booming stroke.

Marshal Vance had cast that bell from the bronze twenty-four-pounders captured at Tucson and Vicksburg. The hammer fell upon the lip of the metal. Its deep vibration in the key of C-minor traveled downward through the granite bedrock of the peninsula.

For sixty seconds by the watch, the first stroke hung alone in the wet darkness. It hummed through the iron rails of the cable-car tracks and rattled the loose window-sashes in the brick tenements of the Mission.

Then, before the bronze note had quite died against the water of the bay, the second stroke fell, and as if a single electric key had closed the circuit of the world, the water and the hills answered. Down in the deep channel off Alcatraz and Clark’s Point, the eighteen-inch turret-guns of the *Elias Thorne* and the *Prometheus* fired the minute-salute with blank charges of smokeless powder. Each flat concussion tore the fog-bank into yellow rags and set the ten thousand wooden prayer-gongs in the Japanese and Cantonese barracks along the Embarcadero beating a slow, funereal cadence. From the Presidio batteries and the limestone casemates of Fort Point, from the foundry whistles at Hunters Point and the giant bronze *bonsho* bells of the Buddhist temples on the Berkeley slopes, the clamor rolled together into a continuous ocean of mourning iron.

Along Market and Montgomery streets, municipal engineers pulled the master-switches in the power-stations. Five thousand gas-lamps and carbon-arc globes went out by sectors. Darkness took the marble porticoes of the Exchange and the thirty-foot bronze statue before the Citadel until, ten seconds later, from the decks of the anchored battle-fleet out in the roadstead, twenty vertical beams of white electric searchlight shot straight up into the fog.

The streets remained quiet, nothing like the screaming tumult of the bread-panic of eighty-one. As the windows of the boarding-houses and the palaces on Mason Street slid up in the gloom, seven hundred thousand men and women looked out into the cannon-shaken mist. Along the curb below my lodgings on California Street, a night-shift of Irish track-layers and Shantung street-sweepers who had been re-bolting a frog in the cable-slot laid their iron crowbars down upon the granite sets; without a word from their Hawaiian provost-corporal, the white men took off their greasy bowler hats and the Chinese dropped to their knees in the wet coal-mud toward the dark mass of Rincon Hill.

No man under forty in that street could remember a morning when Elias Thorne had not sat above the city. To the youth who had been numbered in the Berkeley sheds, and to the coolie who carried his brass ration-tag around his neck, the Sierra Nevada itself might have slid into the sea while they slept. The providence that had burned a cabin in Kentucky fifty years ago had completed its arc; the mortal hand was cold, and across twelve thousand miles of wire, from the frozen blockhouses of the Obi to the steaming red ditches of Culebra, eight hundred million souls stood still in the dark.

***

Inside the Hall of the Council on the second floor of the Citadel, the roof groaned before the cathedral bell on Nob Hill had finished its twentieth stroke.

The attendants had left Elias’s body above the embalming-tables in the cellar. He still sat behind the locked doors of the library upstairs, his chin propped on his leather collar and the ashes of his journals cooling in the grate, while down in the vast, redwood-vaulted throne room the lamps burned at full pressure against the gray dawn at the seaward casements. Wet military wool and warm beeswax from the ceremonial tapers lit on either side of the empty silver curule chair fouled the room, cut through by the tang of pistol-oil.

Lady Kaiulani stood upon the third porphyry step of the dais, directly in front of the vacant silver seat. Having laid aside the blue brocade of the court, she wore the high-necked black bombazine that would clothe her until that afternoon of the twentieth century when she stood above the Miraflores locks, the heavy gold collar of the Insular Chancelleries resting around her throat.

Young General Marcus Vance’s Academy cadets had barred the outer plaza gates to the sixty senators of the Diet at four o’clock. Below the dais, across the semicircular floor of the Council Chamber, eighteen men in the mud-spattered, gold-braided uniforms of the High Command and the Fiscal Boards stood in three hostile clusters that refused to mingle across the inlaid brass meridians.

To the left, beneath the marble bust of the elder Marshal Vance, stood Colonel Armistead of the Virginia Auxiliaries and four gray-bearded continental division commanders, their heavy cavalry sabers unhooked from their saddle-chains so that the steel scabbards clinked against their spurs with every shift of their boots. Six post-captains of the Satsuma and Choshu fleets flanked Grand-Admiral Marquis Takashima and General Saigo on the right. Coal-smut from the Goat Island launches stained their white gloves. In the center, behind the green baize table where a steel pin locked the lever of the bronze seal-press of the Realm, stood Cornelius Schuyler and three directors of the Market Street Clearing House, their faces gray and pouchy under the competing glare of the electric bulbs and the wet morning sky.

"The Statute of the Hundred and Twenty-Four States was never enrolled upon the parchment books of the Chancery, Madame!" Colonel Armistead’s voice boomed against the redwood rafters, louder than the distant thud of the Alcatraz salute-guns shaking the window-panes. He stepped across the brass meridian of the Tropic of Cancer and slammed his scarred hand down upon the green baize within six inches of Auditor Shen’s ink-stand. "You and the boy-general bullied a dying man into croaking two words from a balcony while his brain was drowned in apoplexy! By the Military Articles of Sixty-Two, written by the Providentor’s own hand at Sacramento, when the Sovereign dies without a named successor of his loins, the supreme executive authority reverts to the Council of Continental Marshals until the army camps have voted!"

"The Articles of Sixty-Two were written for a frontier province of five million white miners before a single keel of the Battle Fleet was laid at Yokosuka!" General Saigo stepped forward from the Japanese cluster until the gold chrysanthemum upon his cuff brushed the Virginian’s elbow. Behind Saigo, the six Satsuma captains shifted their weight onto their left feet, freeing their sword-hilts. "Who holds the sea-lanes from Melbourne to the Kuriles tonight, Colonel? Your Missouri mule-skinners hold nothing! Seventy percent of the armored tonnage in the Pacific carries the flag of the Western Clans! If there is to be a Lord Protector of the interregnum, he must be named by the Joint Admiralty Board, with Grand-Admiral Takashima as Regent of the Sword!"

"And whose silver pays the coal-bills for your battleships, General Saigo?" Cornelius Schuyler wheezed. His plump hands clutched the edge of the seal-table as if he meant to carry the bronze press out under his coat, his watery eyes darting from the Virginian’s saber to the samurai’s katana. "If you set up a drumhead dictatorship of camp-commanders or Japanese admirals this morning, the Clearing Houses in New York, Frankfurt, and Hong Kong will refuse the autumn treasury warrants before noon! The Regency must be vested in the Fiscal Commission: three civilian syndics with the power of the purse—"

"And young Silas Thorne in the silver chair to give the rabble a name they know!" Armistead wheeled upon the banker, the veins standing out like blue whipcord along his grizzled neck. "My Virginians are at the Presidio gate right now with four batteries of three-inch rifles! Put Elias’s eldest son on the horse before six o’clock, or by God, I’ll march them down Mason Street and clear these counting-house rats out with the bayonet!"

"Bring young Silas out of the garden, Colonel," Marquis Takashima said. His thumb released the brass catch of his scabbard with a sharp *snick*, and Schuyler flinched backward against the table. "My marine gunners at the foot of the hill will blow his head off his shoulders before his boot touches the stirrup.
