If blood is to be the title-deed, my nephew Kiyoshi carries the Providentor’s blood and the Choshu seal!"

Up on the third porphyry step, Lady Kaiulani stood still and silent. With her hands folded beneath the heavy gold links of her collar, she looked down at the eighteen old men snarling across the brass lines of the globe like mastiffs over a butcher’s tub.

*Look at them, Elias,* she thought, turning her mind toward the cold figure sitting upstairs in the dark library. *Your body has been cold for scarce ninety minutes, the cannon are still roaring your name across the water, and already the timber is splitting along the grain. Thirty years of syncretism, thirty years of Three Harmonies and Imperial Anthems, and the instant your thumb is off the lever, the Virginian wants a border-camp and the samurai a shogunate. The banker wants a mortgage-deed.*

She left the gavel untouched on the clerk’s desk. Past the gleaming bald crown of Cornelius Schuyler’s head, past the drawn blades by the door, her gaze rose toward the tall mahogany clock above the northern gallery. It lacked two minutes of five.

General Marcus Vance was absent.

***

Three hundred yards down the northern slope of Rincon Hill, inside the brick-and-iron rotunda of the Central Telegraph and Guard Headquarters that straddled the main cable-conduits between the Citadel and the Mint, hot lubricating oil and the vinegary reek of fifty brass telegraph sounders hammering at full speed filled the room under a low ceiling of structural steel.

General Marcus Vance the younger stood upon the raised iron grating in the center of the floor, directly between the master switchboard of the Continental Trunk Lines and the pneumatic tube-terminal that fed the harbor forts. Leaving mourning crape and gold-braided dress coats to the elders quarreling up in the throne room, he wore his plain, slate-gray Academy field-tunic, with a nickeled nine-shot pistol holstered at his hip and his radium-dialed chronometer strapped outside his left cuff.

All around the circular brick wall, forty twenty-year-old cadet-lieutenants of the Polytechnic Corps, boys with five-digit silver ciphers on their collars and no family names in the peerage book, sat on iron stools before the repeaters. Vulcanite headphones clamped over their cropped skulls, they intercepted every wire passing out of the peninsula.

Major Kuroda tore a yellow manifold-sheet from the local military circuit and stepped up onto the iron grating. "The commander of the Second Virginia Auxiliary at the Presidio has just wired Colonel Armistead’s adjutant at the Mason Street gate, General," he said. "He asks whether the horse-artillery batteries are to limber up for a march on the Sub-Treasury at five-thirty. And a signal-launch from the cruiser *Satsuma* off Goat Island is flashing the Naval Annex by shutter-lamp, requesting Marquis Takashima’s personal warrant to land four hundred marines at the Folsom Street wharf."

Marcus ignored the yellow paper. Before him, bolted to the iron stanchions, hung the great illuminated glass map of the San Francisco peninsula, where tiny red and green electric bulbs marked the position of every street-railway power-house, water-main valve, and Academy cadet-company between the Golden Gate and San Mateo. He kept his pale eyes on the glass.

"My father told me before he went to Lake Baikal that when a horse breaks its leg in the traces, you shoot the horse and lock the wagon-brake before the load goes over the cliff," Marcus said. Above the rattling din of the sounders, his clipped voice carried across the room. He pulled his ivory slide-rule half an inch from his breast pocket, then pushed it back with a dry *click*. "You do not hold a committee meeting with the mules behind it. Colonel Armistead and Marquis Takashima are still living in the year sixty-five, when a city of seven hundred thousand souls could be captured by marching men with flags down the middle of the street."

Behind him stood the master switch-panel, where a Cantonese cadet-engineer rested his rubber-gloved hands upon three heavy copper knife-switches painted red. Marcus turned.

"Cut the commercial and municipal telegraph trunks to Oakland and the Presidio, along with the Sacramento line," Marcus said. "Leave only the underground armored lead to Alcatraz, the Mare Island yard, and the Citadel guard-posts open on my personal cipher. Have the cadets at the Potrero generating-station pull the breakers on the Market and California street-railway lines so no cable-car or electric dray moves between the ferry-slips and the hills; and tell Captain Kalakaua’s detail at the Spring Valley water-gate to drop the iron sluices on the Presidio main. Colonel Armistead’s Virginians may start their march into town this morning by drinking their own horse-troughs dry."

Blue electric arcs spat three times. The copper switches dropped from their jaws, and half the brass sounders along the wall went dead.

At the central transmitting desk, the master-key of the Municipal Provost Network sat under a glass hood. Dismissing the clerk, Marcus laid his square-nailed fingers upon the vulcanite knob and tapped out the rapid military code of the Monterey Staff College, a signal that printed simultaneously upon the ticker-tapes of all forty-two police precincts and harbor batteries and railway depots around the bay:

*PROCLAMATION ONE. BY ORDER OF THE IMPERIAL STAFF AND THE BUREAU OF INTEGRATION. TO ENSURE THE PEACEFUL TRANSITION OF THE REALM AND PREVENT FOREIGN SABOTAGE DURING THE OBSEQUIES OF THE PROVIDENTOR, A STATE OF SIEGE AND MARTIAL LAW IS HEREBY DECLARED THROUGHOUT THE METROPOLITAN PREFECTURE OF SAN FRANCISCO FROM FIVE O’CLOCK THIS MORNING. ALL CIVIL COURTS AND SYNDICATE EXCHANGES AND MUNICIPAL ASSEMBLIES ARE SUSPENDED. ANY ARMED DETACHMENT OF THE AUXILIARY OR CLAN FORCES MOVING FIVE HUNDRED YARDS BEYOND ITS BARRACKS PERIMETER WITHOUT THE COUNTER-STAMP OF THE ACADEMY PROVOST WILL BE ENGAGED IMMEDIATELY WITH HIGH-EXPLOSIVE SHELL BY THE HARBOR FORTIFICATIONS. CITIZENS WILL REMAIN WITHIN THEIR WARDS. THE RATION-DEPOTS WILL OPEN AT EIGHT UNDER CADET GUARD.*

The bulkhead clock clicked onto five. He lifted his finger from the key. Outside in the damp courtyard of the Telegraph Annex, where twenty armored traction-lorries mounted twin water-cooled Maxim guns behind quarter-inch nickel-steel shields, multi-ethnic squads of the First Cadet Brigade sounded their steam-sirens through the lifting fog as the iron gates swung open onto Montgomery Street.

"Take two companies of the Shensi and Samoan cadets up the bullion-hoist to the second-floor corridor of the Citadel, Major Kuroda," Marcus said. He drew on his gray buckskin gloves. Over his knuckles, he smoothed the leather flat. "Wait until I tap the glass of the door before you enter the Throne Room. Let the old men shout themselves hoarse for ten minutes more, since a boiler that has blown off its superfluous steam is much easier to bolt down."

***

Yet while General Vance’s cadets could sever the copper wires of the San Francisco peninsula with three strokes of a rubber-gloved hand and lock seven hundred thousand metropolitan subjects inside their brick wards before breakfast, the Polytechnic Staff remained bound by the physics of distance across an empire spanning one hundred and eighty degrees of longitude.

In the unexpurgated cable-logs of that autumn of 1887, which stay locked inside the lead-lined vaults of the Monterey Chancery where no schoolboy ever sees them, the death of Elias Thorne traveled outward from California like a spark running down a train of damp, imperfectly mixed blasting-powder, sizzling beneath the water for three thousand leagues only to detonate wherever the concrete of the new order had not yet set over the ancient rock.

In the home provinces of the Pacific coast, and across the garrisoned plains of the Atlantic protectorates where two generations of white men had been bled by the Sacramento conscriptions, the populace took the news with the stupor of draft-oxen that keep walking between the ruts after the driver falls from the wagon-box because the iron yoke stays bolted to their necks. Shutters remained up on the counting-houses in Boston and Philadelphia. Indoors, the people waited for the provost’s bread-carts.

Along the outer rim of the circumference, in the newly swallowed continent of the Southern Ocean and down the muddy arteries of the middle Yangtze, the iron hoop snapped before the funeral tapers in San Francisco were half burned down.

Because the nineteenth of August on the Pacific coast was already the afternoon of the twenty-second across the international date-line in Australia, the sun was dropping red and smoky behind the eucalyptus ridges of the Blue Mountains when the submarine cable from Noumea brought the dead current into the repeater-office at Sydney.

For twelve weeks since the May morning when Prince Kalakaua and young Marcus Vance had landed their marines at the Man-o'-War Jetty, the three million Anglo-Saxon colonists of New South Wales and Victoria had lived under the lid of the Eighteen-Inch Gun. Their coastal parliaments stood padlocked. Alongside wool-clips seized against silver-paper receipts of the Market Street Mint, forty thousand Cantonese and Irish railway-navvies under Satsuma infantry cordons tore up the colonial tracks from Parramatta to Melbourne to re-lay the broad six-foot gauge of the Empire. While Admiral Hornby’s British fleet rotted at the bottom of the Coral Sea and the old man on Rincon Hill held the lanyard, the sheep-barons and the gold-miners of the interior chewed their bitterness in silence.

At four-ten in the afternoon, a nineteen-year-old Australian telegraph-clerk in the Bathurst railway-shed, whose father had died aboard the British corvette *Wolverene* in June, took the official Monterey death-cipher passing down the wire toward the garrison headquarters at Ballarat.

He kept the slip from the Japanese provost-captain on the platform. Before the Choshu sentry outside the window could unsling his carbine, the youth cross-plugged the main pastoral trunk-line into the local railway-bell circuit and hammered out five words in plain English Morse to every sheep-station and gold-camp and locomotive-roundhouse across twelve hundred miles of bush from Brisbane to Adelaide:

*THE YANKEE CAESAR IS DEAD.*

Thirty minutes later, while the Satsuma colonel commanding the Ballarat mining-district was still decoding his cipher from Sydney, the steam-whistles of the Eureka Deep-Lead Gold Pits blew the old colonial assembly-call in three short shrieks repeated over and over against the darkening winter sky.

Down in the timbered galleries eight hundred feet beneath the red gravel of Ballarat, four thousand Cornish, Irish, and native-born Australian sinkers dropped their pneumatic drills into the sump-water. Sledges broke open the company powder-magazines. With canvas sacks of Nobel’s blasting-gelatine and coiled safety-fuse slung over their flannel shirts, the miners rode up the cages and swarmed out of the shaft-heads into the frosty dusk just as the six-o’clock bullion-train for Melbourne was taking water at the wooden tank.

"Hold the engine, boys!" roared Timothy Lalor. A one-armed veteran of the old fifty-four stockade whose nephew had been shipped to the Bering tunnel-gangs by Magistrate Shen’s assize the week before, he leaped onto the tender-pile with a lighted miners’ flare in his fist and a stolen Martini-Henry rifle crooked in his stump. Around the red-brick station-house, the fifty Choshu riflemen of the treasure-guard ran out of their guardroom while their brass bugle sounded the alarm and their officer screamed orders in Japanese to unlimber the Maxim gun on the flatcar.

In Java, Dutch soldiers had formed ranks against machine-gun fire. The miners scattered. Behind the forty-foot mounds of white quartz-tailings towering above the railway cutting, two hundred veteran blaster-men lit the thirty-second fuses of their gelatine-cartridges from their hat-lamps and hurled a hail of smoking iron cylinders straight down onto the roofs of the armored bullion-vans.

Nitro-glycerine flame split the earth of Victoria in a rolling yellow-white sheet. The blast twisted the six-foot broad-gauge rails into corkscrews of Bessemer steel, hurled the Maxim flatcar upside down into the slime of the cyanide-vats, and buried the Japanese guard-company beneath four hundred tons of shattered brick and quartz gravel.

Six thousand miles to the northwest, where the hot, yellow flood of the Yangtze-Kiang rolled past the stone bund of the Pacifica Concession at Hankow, that same hour of dawn brought a vaster convulsion.

There, in the Forty-Eighth River Canton, where three million Chinese iron-workers and tea-packers labored beneath the brick chimneys of the Hanyang Arsenal to cast railway-chairs for the Siberian line, the secret lodges of the *White Lotus* and the *Righteous Harmony Fists* had bowed their heads for ten years before the mandate of the Western Emperor until Cantonese river-pilots brought word at midnight that the Dragon Chair across the Eastern Sea was empty.

Daybreak came. Off the Hanyang iron-wharf, while the Imperial Paddle-Monitor *Monocacy* lay moored with her boilers banked and half her mixed crew ashore in the tea-houses, the low roar of three hundred thousand voices rose out of the maze of narrow mud-brick alleys behind the foreign compound. Armed with eight-foot iron pikes forged during the night-shifts at the rolling-mills, they carried red silk banners inscribed with charms against foreign lead alongside ten thousand earthenware jars of kerosene stolen from the Standard-Pacifica godowns.

Up on the granite steps of the Customs Inspectorate overlooking the bund, Junior Prefect Hoshino, Candidate One-One-Zero-Eight of the Berkeley class of eighty-four, stood in his black alpaca gown beside a detachment of forty Hawaiian and Californian provost-guards. The red glare of the burning tax-sheds along the riverfront glinted off his horn-rimmed spectacles as a solid, mile-wide wall of blue-bloused iron-puddlers and boatmen surged across the bridge of boats and swung their foundry-sledges against the iron palings of the Concession gate.

"Open the magazine-locks on the three-pounder Hotchkiss guns, Sergeant!" Hoshino shouted in English. His high, scholarly voice cracked for the first time since he had left the examination-cells, and a paving-stone thrown from the front rank of the mob shattered the glass lamp-globe above his head. Splinters showered his shoulders. "Where is the steam-launch from the *Monocacy*? Why doesn't the monitor open fire with shrapnel down the avenue?"

Slipping in the blood of two slain customs-clerks on the lower step while he jammed a brass clip of smokeless cartridges into the receiver of his rifle, the forty-year-old Californian provost-sergeant, a grizzled veteran of the Canton river-patrols, pointed a shaking thumb out toward the yellow river-mist.

Out in the middle of the stream, the *Monocacy*’s turrets remained still, pointed away from the shore. From her quarterdeck rose the sharp, crackling rattle of small-arms fire and the flash of cutlasses. Having taken two contradictory rumors off the telegraph-barge, one that Marquis Takashima had seized the throne in San Francisco and the other that the Virginia regiments had proclaimed Silas Thorne, the American engine-room artificers and the Satsuma deck-guards aboard the monitor had turned their revolvers upon each other across the open engine-hatches. Upstream, forty Cantonese fire-junks, chained together in pairs and piled to the mastheads with blazing pitch-barrels and oil-soaked cotton-bales, drifted straight down the five-knot current toward the monitor’s unprotected wooden sponsons.

"The fleet’s fighting itself in the river, Prefect!" the sergeant yelled. Behind him, the Concession’s main iron gates gave way with an ear-splitting crash under the blows of a six-ton cast-iron girder swung by fifty Hanyang foundrymen. "And there’s forty thousand of ’em coming through the courtyard with kerosene-pots! Get out of that clerk’s dress and get behind the parapet before—"

A hundred jars of burning Borneo naphtha arched over the shattered iron palings at once. A roaring cataract of liquid fire swallowed the white granite steps of the Customs House, taking the Berkeley graduate, his slide-rule, and his forty provosts before the first fire-junk struck the *Monocacy*’s side.

***

In San Francisco, no word of the burning of Hankow or the dynamiting of the Ballarat rails escaped the concrete basement of the Telegraph Annex. On the afternoon of the twenty-fifth of August, as the gun-carriage bearing the soldered lead casket of Elias Thorne rolled down the steep granite pitch of Rincon Hill toward the Monterey funeral-train waiting at the Townsend Street depot, the capital of the Great Arena lay wrapped in a silence more terrifying than artillery.

This hush bore no resemblance to the brass-throated October reviews or the devout quiet that the later school-books described when the bronze effigy had been bolted to the battleship turret at the turn of the century. From the roof of the Mint, the Chronicler looked down upon a city locked in rigor mortis.

Behind the triple cordons of young Marcus Vance’s Polytechnic Cadets, who lined Market Street at two-pace intervals with fixed bayonets and their backs turned outward toward the tenements rather than the coffin, half a million citizens stood behind shuttered windows and barred shop-doors. The grey August fog blew cold through the Gate. It smelled of wet crape and unburned coal-dust from the banked factory chimneys, mingling with the heavy, suffocating clouds of Hawaiian sandalwood and Japanese aloes that poured from the bronze thuribles carried by sixty priests of the Syncretic Basilica.

Twelve black Clydesdale stallions from the Oregon artillery-depots, draped to the fetlocks in purple velvet housings embroidered with the golden sun-and-anchor, drew the six-ton caisson of an eighteen-inch coastal cannon. Upon the iron cradle where the barrel belonged rested the long, narrow box of Sierra granite and sheet-lead. Only the faded blue wool of Elias’s old Mexican War Engineer’s coat and the iron walking-stick tied across the lid with white silk cord covered the metal.

Three paces behind the rear axle walked Lady Kaiulani.

She walked alone upon the fifty-foot breadth of the granite sets. Her long train of dull black mourning bombazine whispered over the wet stones; the whale-ivory clasp of Oahu pressed cold against her throat. Behind her, separated by a file of twenty armed Oahu guardsmen so that they could neither whisper to one another nor gesture to the rooftops, walked the nominal regents and marshals of the broken house: old Brigadier Caleb Vance leaning heavily upon the arm of his grand-nephew Marcus; Cornelius Schuyler, his face the color of lard beneath his tall silk hat; Marquis Takashima in full Satsuma armor beneath a black naval cloak; and behind them, the three Left-Handed Princes, with Silas sweating sour whiskey through his black gloves, Kiyoshi staring at the back of Takashima’s neck, and young Kalanimoku looking up at the grey gulls circling above the cornice-stones.

With every slow, measured *clomp* of the twelve iron-shod horses, the emptiness opened beneath Kaiulani's slippers.

For twenty-five years she had hated the man in the lead box with the dry, undying passion of a princess whose islands had been turned into a coaling-hulk; and for twenty years she had governed beside him because his terrible, scarred right hand was the only bolt holding three hundred million human beings from tearing one another’s throats out in the dark. He had built an arch of unmortared basalt blocks that stood solely because his own two-hundred-pound carcass was wedged into the keystone.

Now the keystone was six feet of cold tallow and strychnine rolling down the hill toward a vault in Monterey. Along the five-mile avenue, past the white, hungry faces of the unpaid foundrymen pressed against the upper garret-panes of the Mission, past the yellow-braided Virginia cavalrymen sitting their horses at the cross-streets with their carbines unslung and their eyes fixed hatred-wide upon the Japanese marine detachments opposite, and down to the lowered cranes along the Embarcadero where forty grain-ships waited for a clearance-stamp that no foreign consul would honor, the vacuum rushed in.

A gust of salt wind off the bay caught the corner of the dead man’s blue coat on the caisson ahead of her. The empty left sleeve flapped once against the lead and fell back lifeless.

Beside her right shoulder, old Caleb Vance stumbled on a slick cable-rail. His cataract-blinded eye wept in the cold wind as he spoke under his breath to the box on the gun-carriage: *"You left the gate unlatched, Elias. We’re eighty miles from the fort, and the wolves are in the horses."*

Young Marcus Vance ignored his great-uncle. Beneath his visored cap, his pale, unblinking eyes stayed fixed upon the signal-mast atop the Goat Island naval depot two miles out in the bay, where a small string of red and yellow bunting had just broken out against the fog in a fleet-cipher missing from the Monterey Polytechnic code-book.

***

Before the casket reached the turntable of the Townsend Street station, while the priests of the Basilica still chanted the *De Profundis* beside the smoking sandalwood braziers on the platform, the polite mask of the funeral procession dissolved behind the closed bronze doors of the Capitol Rotunda on Rincon Hill.

Marcus Vance had left the mourners before the train. Turning his horse out of the cortege at the corner of Third Street as soon as the Goat Island flags broke the mist, he had ridden back up the empty, cadet-lined hill at a hard gallop while his bay's iron shoes struck red sparks from the granite sets and Major Kuroda clattered behind him with six mounted telegraph-orderlies.

Marcus walked into the lower Rotunda. His grey field-tunic was damp with sea-fog, and his left hand rested upon the unbuttoned leather flap of his nine-shot pistol holster. The eighteen marshals and syndicate-directors of the morning had grown to forty.

The great circular chamber beneath the bronze relief-map smelled of wet boots and hot tallow. The guns were already loaded outside. Marquis Takashima had skipped the ride to the depot; he stood beside the porphyry table in the center of the floor, surrounded by thirty younger divisional commanders of the Japanese-Pacific Fleet and the Continental Choshu Brigades. Foremost among them stood General Kaito of the Third Amur and Insular Division, a forty-year-old graduate of the Yedo artillery schools who had lost two fingers of his left hand at the storming of Vladivostok and wore across his chest the pure white silk sash of the League of the Rising Sun.

On the opposite side of the brass meridian, hemmed into the alcove beneath the telegraph gallery by twelve of Kaito’s marine-guards with fixed bayonets, stood Colonel Armistead and Auditor Shen.

"You have left the funeral before the earth is over your master, General Vance," Kaito said as Marcus’s spurs rang across the marble flags toward the center table. Kaito refused to salute the twenty-three-year-old Chief of Staff. He stood with his booted legs planted wide across the inlaid brass line of the Equator, his right thumb hooked into his sword-belt, a wet blue cable-flimsy from Yokohama held in his maimed left hand. "Perhaps your schoolboys in the Telegraph Annex forgot to deliver the two-o’clock relay from Nagasaki and Hankow."

Marcus stopped four paces from the porphyry table. Behind him, Major Kuroda and the six Polytechnic cadets halted in a neat, silent file inside the doorway, their magazine-carbines held port across their chests.

"The Hankow repeater went dead at six this morning, General Kaito," Marcus said. His clipped, level voice dropped into the high vault without an echo. "And the commercial cable from Nagasaki was ordered closed by the Bureau of Integration at five. By what authority have your marine signalmen opened the Goat Island relay during a state of siege?"

Kaito gave a short, barking laugh. Behind him, six Choshu colonels shifted their hands to their scabbards. He tossed the blue cable-ribbon onto the porphyry table beside the locked bronze seal-press.

"By the authority of sixty-four armored ships of the line and a hundred and twenty thousand bayonets of the Japanese-Pacific Division who do not take their orders from a boy’s slide-rule or a Hawaiian woman’s ink-pot!" Kaito said, his voice rising until it rang off the thirty-foot bronze plates of Elias Thorne’s map on the wall above them. "Hankow is in ashes, General Vance! The Chinese iron-guilds have burned the *Monocacy* at her moorings and butchered your Berkeley examination-clerks on the steps of the Custom House because your American artificers shot our Satsuma deck-officers in the back! At Ballarat, the white miners have blown up the broad-gauge track with dynamite and hung the Choshu garrison from the water-tanks! And ten minutes ago, the Imperial Council at Kyoto cabled Marquis Takashima that if the Statute of the Hundred and Twenty-Four States is enforced to dissolve the domains of Satsuma and Choshu into numbered coolie-cantons, the Japanese homeland withdraws from the Treaty of Edo at sunset!"

Over in the alcove, Colonel Armistead strained forward against the crossed bayonets of Kaito’s marines, his scarred face purple above his gray beard. "Let ’em withdraw to hell, Marcus! Give my Virginians the word to open the Presidio magazines, and we’ll drive every yellow-belly on this coast into the surf before the moon rises!"

Marcus ignored Armistead and the Nagasaki cable on the stone. His pale eyes remained fixed upon the white silk sash across Kaito’s breast. Like a surveyor setting a stake, he measured the distance between the general’s fourth brass button and the door.

"The Tenno at Kyoto signed away his foreign war-powers in sixty-eight, General Kaito," Marcus said softly. "And there is no Japanese-Pacific Division on the muster-rolls of this morning. There are only the Seventh, Twelfth, and Nineteenth Imperial Brigades, whose coal is in my bunkers at Mare Island and whose ammunition-lighters are under the guns of Alcatraz. You are twenty minutes away from mutiny."

"Mutiny against whom, boy?" Kaito stepped across the brass meridian. Wet wool and clove-oil filled Marcus’s nostrils. "Against a dead frontier bandit in a lead box? Elias Thorne conquered this ocean with our ships and our blood while you were sucking milk in a Sacramento nursery! Now that his heart has stopped, do you think the samurai who took Peking and sank the British at the Coral Sea are going to stand in iron cubicles at Berkeley to be numbered like cattle by a Polynesian widow and a twenty-three-year-old schoolmaster?"

Kaito’s right hand dropped from his belt and struck the hilt of his two-handed *katana*. Six inches of mirror-bright steel slid from the scabbard.

"The Regency of the clerks is ended, Vance! Marquis Takashima boarded the flagship *Yamato* off Goat Island twenty minutes ago. My four regiments of the First Insular Division have seized the Folsom Street wharves and the Mint bullion-vaults, and our twelve-inch turrets in the stream are trained upon this dome! Sign the warrant restoring the Asian Prefectures and the Fleet Admiralty to the Western Clans before the five-o’clock bell, or when I walk down those steps and hoist the red lantern on the plaza flagpole, the *Yamato* will drop ten hundredweight of shimose shell straight through that glass roof onto your head!"

Marcus’s hand stayed on his holster-flap. From his cuff, he pulled his radium-dialed chronometer half an inch to check the sweeping second-hand.

"It is four-fifty-two, General Kaito," Marcus said. "If Marquis Takashima boarded the *Yamato* at four-thirty, he has had twenty-two minutes to raise steam in cold boilers against a four-knot ebb tide, while my cadet-crews aboard the *Elias Thorne* and the *Prometheus* have been lying off Clark’s Point with superheated oil-burners at three hundred pounds pressure since midnight. Keep your red lantern in your pocket. Major Kuroda—shoot this man."

# Chapter 21: The Time of Troubles

Born in the shadow of Kumamoto Castle, taken from his clan at twelve by the Triennial Assessors, and marked upon his collar only by the silver cipher *Zero-Four-One-Nine* of the Monterey Polytechnic, Kuroda did not blink.

Before General Kaito’s blade could clear the scabbard, Kuroda’s nine-shot automatic pistol barked three times from the hip—*crack-crack-crack*. Smokeless nitro-powder slapped the Rotunda with a sharp chemical sting. Two brass buttons and a spray of dark arterial blood blew out the back of Kaito’s white silk sash.

Kaito pitched forward onto his knees across the brass line of the Equator. His forehead struck the inlaid copper outline of the Galapagos Islands with a dull *thud* as the thirty Japanese officers and the twelve marine guardsmen in the alcove erupted into a screaming tangle of drawn sabers and leveled rifles.

"Drop the bronze shutters!" Marcus vaulted backward over the porphyry table. As a ragged volley from the Choshu marines shattered the marble bust of his father behind him and sent white stone chips whistling past his ear, he kicked the heavy oak council-board onto its side.

Up in the iron gallery surrounding the dome, twenty Polytechnic cadets from Pennsylvania and Oahu had lain flat behind the balustrade since four o’clock. They rolled two water-cooled Maxim guns to the rail. Their thumbs pressed the brass firing-levers.

For forty seconds, flashing muzzle-blast and ricocheting lead filled the iron cauldron of the Rotunda. Beneath the thirty-foot bronze gaze of the world Elias Thorne had bolted together, while the six-hundred-round-a-minute belts scythed straight down through Satsuma silk and Virginia broadcloth alike in the gold-braided cluster around the table, Colonel Armistead seized a fallen marine’s carbine in the smoke to shoot his way out the eastern door toward the Presidio horses and took three .30-caliber nickel-jacketed bullets through his gray beard before his boot touched the threshold.

Marcus left the floor uncleared. Behind him, Kuroda’s cadets fired downward through the yellow cordite haze into the writhing heap of plumed hats and blood-soaked sashes around the seal-press, while Marcus sprinted through the narrow armored passage behind the dais, threw open the iron casement of the seaward observation-tower, and stepped out onto the wind-swept granite parapet seventy feet above the bay.

Below him, the rising sunset wind tore the fog apart. Across three miles of white-capped water, the heart of the Empire split in two.

Eight hundred yards off Goat Island lay the ten-thousand-ton armored cruiser *Yamato*, with the gold chrysanthemum of Satsuma newly hoisted to her maintruck above the torn blue-and-gold ensign of Pacifica. Marquis Takashima had not waited for Kaito’s red lantern. At the first muffled rattle of the Maxim guns inside the Citadel dome, the *Yamato*'s forward eleven-inch turret swung shoreward and spat a blinding, orange-black billow of shimose high-explosive.

The eight-hundred-pound shell screamed directly over the roofs of the Embarcadero coffee-warehouses. It detonated squarely against the granite plinth of Elias Thorne’s thirty-foot bronze statue in the plaza below Marcus’s boots.

Glass shattered for six blocks down Market Street. Sheared at the knees, the cast-bronze legs of the American Caesar gave way; the thirty-ton metal giant tilted slowly forward through the boiling yellow smoke and crashed face-down across the cable-car tracks, where its iron walking-stick snapped in half against the cobbles.

"Signal the *Elias Thorne* and the Alcatraz disappearing-carriages!" Marcus shouted into the brass speaking-tube bolted to the parapet wall. Hot wind whipped granite dust from the shattered monument across his bloodless cheeks, while five more Japanese cruisers in the middle anchorage slipped their cables to open fire with their secondary batteries upon the Folsom Street barracks, and half a mile to the north the eighteen-inch turrets of his own cadet-manned flagship swung their fifty-foot barrels down to point-blank depression against their sister ships. "Do not waste armor-piercing shell on their waterlines. The channel is too shallow, and their hulls will block the grain-slips if they sink in the fairway! Load cast picric-acid high-capacity and fire into their upper bridges and boiler-uptakes at sixteen hundred yards! And tell Captain Kalakaua at the Mare Island torpedo-station to release the Brennan wire-guided mines into the ebb-tide!"

He ignored the acknowledgment bell from the casemate below. Across the water, the first two-thousand-pound broadside from the *Elias Thorne* erupted with a concussion that tore the speaking-tube out of its mortar and rained burning splinters of the *Yamato*’s fore-bridge across the ferry-slips.

***

Two thousand one hundred miles to the southwest, beyond the oil-smoke of the burning San Francisco wharves and under unstained trade-wind clouds, the dispatch-cruiser *Liliuokalani* steamed through the narrow coral jaws of the Honolulu channel at daybreak on the fourth of September, her white hull blistered to the waterline by six days of forced-draft steaming at twenty-two knots.

Up on the flying bridge stood Lady Kaiulani. Behind the splinter-shield, her hands gripped the salt-crusted brass rail while the red sun rose over the volcanic crater of Diamond Head.

The funeral train had gone down to Monterey without her. When the first eleven-inch shell from the *Yamato* brought the bronze Caesar crashing into the Market Street cobbles and set the Virginia cavalry galloping down from the Presidio to loot the Sub-Treasury, the truth had been plain: the machine she and young Marcus had perfected in the examination-sheds was too brittle to survive its own first turn of the wheel. Marcus would fight for the continental rail-heads with his numbered boys until every furnace from Sacramento to the Ohio was cold slag. Takashima would burn the dockyards to keep his ships. Someone had to cut the cable before the fire ran down the wire to the islands and dragged the whole Pacific into the dark.

At the foot of the Fort Street mole, where Elias’s marines had landed in the rain twenty-eight years before, four thousand men of the First Insular Guard and two hundred Cantonese and Portuguese sugar-factors waited beneath the royal palms with their faces turned toward the cruiser’s signal-yard.

The gangplank was still unlashed. Stepping onto the coral quay in her salt-stiffened black bombazine, with young Kalanimoku carrying the iron strongbox of the Oahu Chancery seals behind her and Colonel Kalakaua’s riflemen forming a hollow square around her skirts, Kaiulani walked straight to the stone base of the Harbor Telegraph House.

Inside the open door, the brass siphon-recorders of the San Francisco and Manila submarine cables chattered. One key hammered out General Vance’s peremptory conscription-warrants for ten thousand island laborers; the other screamed Admiral Takashima’s orders to the Pearl River coaling-hulks to seize the Honolulu dry-docks in the name of the Western Clans.

"Bring the cold-chisel and the sledge from the quartermaster’s dray, Colonel," Kaiulani said. Her voice rose clear above the surf booming on the outer reef, though the gray ash of four sleepless nights rimmed her dark eyes.

Two Hawaiian pioneers in blue wool tunics stepped forward to the heavy lead-sheathed trunk-cables where they rose out of the coral sea-wall into the gutta-percha junction-box.

"Your Highness," stammered Director Damon of the Bishop Sugar Syndicate. As the blacksmith set the steel edge of the chisel against the San Francisco line, Damon pushed his white linen helmet through the cordon of rifle-butts. "If you sever the Monterey wire and refuse the fleet requisitions, both Vance and Takashima will declare Oahu in rebellion! Half our autumn sugar-crop is sitting on the wharves waiting for the Oakland steamers, and we have only six weeks of California flour in the komisariat vaults! How can four islands stand alone between two hundred warships?"

"By ceasing to be their coal-bin, Mr. Damon," Kaiulani answered. From her sleeve she took a folded parchment written in the old Hawaiian and English of her brother’s court, and handed it to the herald beside the flag-staff. "For thirty years we gave the Providentor our harbor and our sons because his iron kept the peace of the sea. Now the carpenter is dead, and his apprentices are burning down the workshop with their own kerosene. Strike the iron, Corporal."

The twelve-pound sledge fell twice—*clang, clang*. It sheared through copper core and gutta-percha insulation alike. Blue sparks showered the stone, and the San Francisco sounder died mid-syllable.

"Raise the old ensign of the Eight Stripes over the battery at Punchbowl," Kaiulani commanded as the herald nailed the *Proclamation of the Insular Sanctuary* to the teak door of the Custom House. "From this hour, the Hawaiian Archipelago and the Polynesian Reefs are an inviolable Neutral Zone, closed to every warship carrying a gun larger than a six-pounder salute-piece. Any disabled vessel from California or Japan that enters Pearl Lochs to escape the storm will have its breech-blocks dropped into thirty fathoms of water and its crew interned in the taro-valleys until peace is signed. Close the sugar-mills, Mr. Damon, and turn the cane-fields back to sweet-potatoes and upland rice before the rain tonight. We are going to lock the garden gate."

***

It was well for those small islands that the Princess severed the copper nerve when she did; for across the continental immensity of the American and Asian provinces, the autumn of 1887 and the bitter winter of eighty-eight brought down upon three hundred million souls that catastrophic paralysis which our surviving parish-registers call the *Time of Troubles*.

To the Chronicler who had marveled only six years earlier at the clockwork majesty of the Great Arena, when a bushel of San Joaquin wheat or a pig of Hankow iron moved five thousand miles by broad-gauge rail and turbine-steamer without varying a tenth of a silver thaler in price, the speed with which the nineteenth-century civilization rotted back into the twelfth was the most terrible lesson of the Pivot.

Elias Thorne and Lady Kaiulani had constructed their state upon a single, pitiless principle: no canton could feed or arm itself without the counter-stamp of Monterey. To prevent rebellion, the Seventy-Second Agricultural Prefecture in the Mississippi valley had been forbidden to build iron-forges or textile-looms. It shipped its raw corn and hogs west to the Rocky Mountain depots in exchange for Lowell cottons and Osaka hardware. The mining-towns of the Sierra and the Urals grew not a blade of cabbage; they lived entirely upon canned Columbia salmon and Australian mutton brought up the mountain grades every forty-eight hours by the commissariat trains, while from Boston to Irkutsk, where not a local bank held five thousand dollars in hard specie, every wage-bill cleared by telegraph through the central Hollerith ledgers beneath the San Francisco Mint.

On the twenty-sixth of August, the battle in the Golden Gate burned the Mint cable-terminal to the water’s edge. Within three days, three rival Regents—General Vance at Sacramento, young Silas Thorne among the Virginia cavalry at Denver, and Admiral Takashima aboard his battered fleet off Santa Barbara—simultaneously declared one another’s treasury-notes to be treasonable waste-paper. The circulation of the human body stopped between sunrise and sunset.

Along six thousand miles of broad-gauge track from the Missouri to the Amur, the paper warrants in the freight-conductors' pouches would no longer buy a cord of wood or a tank of water at the way-stations. Within a week, dead iron choked the great transcontinental arteries. At the Ogden and Cheyenne junctions, where the engineers had uncoupled their locomotives and ridden off with stolen coal-tenders to join the local militia-bands, forty miles of double-track siding stood solid with stalled refrigerator-cars in which ten thousand tons of dressed Chicago beef and California fruit rotted into black, buzzing slime under the September sun. Nothing moved.

In the factory-cantons of Massachusetts and the iron-valleys of Pennsylvania, two million mechanics lived from Saturday ration-card to Saturday ration-card. Silence fell over the railway-whistles. Famine followed at once. By October, along the old turnpikes between Philadelphia and Pittsburg, the blue coats of the Tripartite Police had vanished; during the first week of the frost, the starving iron-puddlers had hung the Berkeley prefects, boys born three thousand miles away who spoke the local dialect like foreigners, from their own telegraph-poles. Every county line had become a bristling palisade of felled poles and overturned street-cars, behind which former colonels of the Atlantic Auxiliaries or self-appointed committee-chairmen levied thirty-percent toll in salt pork and rifle-cartridges upon every farm-wagon that tried to pass from one township to the next.

On the high plains of the Humboldt and the Platte, where the golden spikes of the Protector’s first rail had been driven thirty years before, the Cantonese and Irish section-gangs found themselves abandoned without pay or flour three hundred miles from the nearest orchard. They tore up the eighty-pound Bessemer rails to forge pikes and butcher-knives over fires built from the redwood sleepers. Down from the reservation hills for the first time in a generation rode the Paiute and Cheyenne horse-tribes to graze their ponies across the unguarded ruins of the telegraph-stations, fighting pitched battles across the alkali valleys against bands of three hundred men in tattered Imperial slate-gray and buffalo-hides who rolled behind crude armored traction-engines and burned the lonely ranch-houses for a sack of seed-corn.

Elias Thorne had ground the nations into dust too fine to cohere again. Across the continent lay ten thousand starving parishes. Each sat in the cold dark beside a dead locomotive and waited for a train from the coast.

***

By the nineteenth of November, the only army east of the Pacific surf that still kept the six-foot gauge open and the five-digit ciphers upon its collars was the First Polytechnic Corps of General Marcus Vance. At four o’clock that afternoon, three miles below the granite summit of the Donner Pass in the high Sierra Nevada, the snow buried his slide-rules six inches deep an hour.

Marcus stood beside the cab of the armored rotary snow-plow *Polyphemus* at the mouth of Snow-Shed Fourteen. Frozen sleet stiffened his slate-gray greatcoat like sheet-iron, and the green radium dial of his wrist-chronometer glowed dimly through the driving white twilight. At seven thousand feet, the air stood at twelve degrees above zero; wet wood-smoke and scorched cylinder-oil mixed with the raw, butcher-shop stench of the forty artillery mules that his Cantonese pioneers had just shot and gutted in the ditch behind the tender to feed the boiler-fires with their fat.

Three months of mathematical war had pared the twenty-three-year-old Marshal’s cheeks down to the tight, grey bone of his dead father’s skull. He had burned Takashima’s cruisers out of San Francisco bay in September. Yet a fleet without Nagasaki coal-colliers and a capital without San Joaquin grain-barges proved a steel trap that starved its own garrison. When Silas Thorne—proclaimed *Protector of the Free States* by seventy thousand mutinous Virginia, Missouri, and Australian veterans at Salt Lake—had shut the eastern portals of the Sierra tunnels in October and cut the Sacramento aqueducts, Marcus had marched his twelve thousand Polytechnic cadets and his six remaining batteries of eighteen-pounder Krupp field-guns up the icy granite gorge of the Truckee to blow the eastern door open before winter locked him against the coast.

He had calculated the coal-tonnage to the pound. He had calculated the ballistic tables for seven thousand feet of altitude. Only one variable had escaped the ledger: a boy who has spent three years in an iron examination-cell at Berkeley does not shoot as straight when his toes are black with frostbite and the timber roof above his head is raining burning pitch.

"The rotary-blades are jammed solid in the cut ahead, General!" Major Kuroda stumbled back down the six-foot ties out of the blinding smoke of Snow-Shed Fourteen. His left sleeve was burned to the elbow, and frozen blood smeared his horn-rimmed spectacles. "Silas Thorne’s Cornish miners dropped the granite roof of the tunnel, chained three loaded coal-gondolas across the grade, and poured ten thousand gallons of Washoe rock-oil down the timbers before they lit the fuse! The shed is a furnace for half a mile, and the heat is melting the snow-pack on the upper ledges directly over our ammunition-cars!"

Marcus stayed clear of the locomotive tender's shelter. With two frost-blistered fingers, he pulled his ivory slide-rule from his stiffened breast pocket. Though a spent .45-70 slug at the Cisco switch two hours before had cracked the celluloid cursor across the logarithmic scale, he pushed the slide to the mark.

"If the shed timbers are burning at twelve hundred degrees, the draft through the eastern portal will burn the pine arches out in thirty-eight minutes," Marcus said. His clipped voice was flat and breathless in the thin mountain air. High among the invisible granite crags above the tree-line, Silas’s three-inch mountain-howitzers boomed a heavy *crump*, and a fresh shower of pine-boughs and ice-shrapnel rattled off the steel roof of the plow. "Unlimber the two six-inch siege-mortars on the flatcars, Major, and elevate to sixty-five degrees against the north ridge. Have the Third Shensi and Pennsylvania Cadet Battalions fix bayonets and go up the granite chute to the left of the shed in open skirmish-order. Once they clear the rifle-pits above the portal—"

"General, the Third Battalion cannot climb the chute." Kuroda clapped his hand to the ice-crusted frame of the locomotive. Thirty feet overhead in the swirling snow-fog, a four-pound shrapnel shell burst; three lead balls drove with a sharp *whack-whack-whack* through the wooden cab behind them and spilled the dead fireman out across the coal-apron. "Four hundred of the southern and Cantonese boys sat down in the snow by the water-tank ten minutes ago and took their boots off. Their feet are frozen to the ankle-bones, and we haven't issued a hot ration since the Emigrant Gap depot burned on Tuesday! And the aerial cruiser *Aeolus*—"

Kuroda pointed a trembling, soot-blackened finger upward toward the narrow rift between the granite walls where the storm-wind howled down from the summit at fifty miles an hour.

Two thousand feet above the pass, the snow-clouds tore open. For five seconds, the monstrous yellow silk belly of the dirigible *Aeolus*, which Marcus had ordered up from Benicia at dawn to drop white phosphorus upon Silas’s hidden howitzer-batteries, pitched wildly nose-down like a harpooned whale in the freezing downdraft. Sierra sleet had frozen her twin wooden propellers solid in their bearings. Marcus raised his chin. A gust off Donner Peak caught the six-hundred-foot hydrogen bag broadside, tore the aluminum gondola clean out of its piano-wire rigging, and slammed the silk envelope against the jagged granite teeth of the Palisades.

A silent, dirty-orange mushroom of burning hydrogen blossomed against the snow-field. It lit the canyon walls for three miles around.

Up along the blasted granite benches on both sides of the railway cut, where Elias Thorne’s Chinese coolies had chipped the grade out of the living rock with hand-drills twenty-five years before, stood six thousand men of the old frontier legions. Here were the sons of the Rio Frio Rangers and the Cornish blaster-men of the Comstock beside the bearded veterans of the Baikal sledges, wrapped in buffalo-coats and stolen grey army blankets as they rolled hundred-pound kegs of black blasting-powder with lighted fuses straight over the granite lip onto the roofs of his stalled troop-trains.

"Get the locomotive reversed, boy!" roared a cracked, furious voice from the open door of the staff-car behind the tender.

Old Brigadier Caleb Vance, seventy-six years old and blind in one eye, stood upon the icy iron steps of the platform with his white beard blowing across his shoulder and an archaic single-shot Springfield musket braced against his hip. He had refused to stay behind in the Sacramento hospital when the column marched. Now the first powder-keg bounced down the granite talus, blew the wheels out from under the third cadet-coach in a geyser of red fire and mangled seventeen-year-old limbs, and the old man reached out to catch his grand-nephew by the collar of his slate-gray coat.

"You’re in a box-canyon with the snow sliding, Marcus!" Caleb yelled over the screaming of the wounded cadets in the ditch and the roar of the burning snow-shed ahead. "Your little schoolboys don't know how to fight in the brush when the track’s gone! Uncouple the engine from the flatcars and run her backward down the grade to Auburn before Silas drops the whole mountain behind your tail!"

Marcus wrenched his collar out of the old man’s grasp. His pale cheek twitched once as a second avalanche of rock and powder-smoke buried the mortar-flatcar fifty yards down the line and cut his column in half. In his breast pocket, his fingers closed around the broken ivory slide-rule.

"The track is the Empire, Uncle!" Marcus shouted back. He drew his nickeled nine-shot pistol from its holster as a hundred bearded Missouri riflemen in captured blue coats slid down the snowy embankment through the pine-smoke with clubbed carbines and roared Silas Thorne’s name. "If we abandon the six-inch guns on this grade, we have no siege-train left between here and the bay! Major Kuroda, form the headquarters company across the tender-apron! Fire by volleys at fifty yards—"

Before Kuroda could raise his whistle to his frost-split lips, the granite cliff three hundred feet above Snow-Shed Fourteen gave a deep, subterranean groan under the heat of the burning oil-cars below as the foot of the overhanging glacier melted. Five thousand tons of blue ice and burning timber sheared away from the mountain wall at once. The mass plunged toward the track with a roar that drowned the musketry, and Caleb Vance threw his heavy, seventy-six-year-old body squarely against Marcus’s chest to drive the young general backward over the iron coal-gate of the reversing tender. The world went white. Beneath the falling peak, the coupling-pins sheared like icicles; the solitary locomotive hurtled backward down the five-percent grade into the Sacramento fog, while old Caleb Vance’s body remained behind under forty feet of Sierra drift.

***

The exhaustion of that winter brought the three wolves of the broken house to the coral reef of Oahu in the spring, after Marcus Vance’s frostbitten remnant had limped back into the cold foundries of Oakland without a single siege-gun, Silas Thorne’s frontier regiments had starved behind the snow-blocked tunnels of Nevada, and Marquis Takashima’s cruisers had lain anchored off Santa Barbara with empty coal-bunkers and foul bottoms.

Only the dry coal-heaps and unburned rice-granaries behind the mine-fields of Pearl Lochs could have drawn them there, into the newly christened neutral sanctuary that the islanders called *Thalassia*, the sole full storehouse left between the Rocky Mountains and the Yellow Sea.

On the twelfth of April, in an open-sided pavilion of spliced bamboo and dark Hawaiian koa-wood erected upon the neutral spit of Sand Island, where six-foot Marquesan spear-men searched every officer to the skin for derringers before he stepped off his gig, Lady Kaiulani sat alone at the head of a semicircular table of polished basalt. The trade-wind off the outer rollers smelled of wet coral and crushed plumeria blossoms, mixed with clean, stinging salt spray.

Before her sat the three men who had spent seven months tearing Elias Thorne’s coat into rags: General Marcus Vance, his left arm still in a black silk sling from the Donner avalanche and his slate-gray tunic threadbare at the cuffs; Silas Thorne, bloated with dropsical whiskey in a tarnished gold-laced coat of the Virginia Auxiliaries over muddy cavalry boots; and Grand-Admiral Marquis Takashima, gaunt and yellow-cheeked from three months of scurvy rations aboard the *Yamato*.

"You have six days of Welsh steam-coal left in your bunkers at San Pedro, Marquis," Kaiulani said. Her voice barely rose above the hiss of the surf along the reef as she laid three identical sheets of Oahu mulberry-parchment upon the dark stone. "And you, Silas, have forty thousand Missourians at Carson City eating boiled mule-hide because the Cantonese railway-masons have blown up the Humboldt bridges behind you; while General Vance is minting iron ration-tokens in San Francisco that the fishermen at the wharf refuse to take for a basket of smelts. You have proved that none of you is tall enough to wear the dead man’s boots alone."

Silas struck the basalt table with his bandaged fist. The ink-horns rattled. "Give me ten thousand tons of Honolulu sugar-silver and open the Sacramento wire, Aunt, and I’ll hang every Berkeley clerk between the Sierra and the Gate before June! I am Elias Thorne’s blood!"

"You are a tavern-captain whose own regiments sold your artillery-horses to the Mormons last Tuesday for three hundred sacks of corn-meal," Kaiulani replied without looking at him, her dark, severe eyes passing from Takashima’s sunken temples to the broken ivory slide-rule still pinned inside Marcus Vance’s breast pocket. "Neither blood nor logarithms will put this ceiling back up alone. If you leave this island tonight without signing the Truce of Thalassia, I will open the Pearl Lochs coal-docks tomorrow morning to whichever one of you brings me the heads of the other two, or, if you prefer to die together, I will wire the British Viceroy at Calcutta that the Pacific Fleet has no powder for its twelve-inch guns."

Takashima’s dry lips parted over his blackened teeth. "And what is the price of the coal, Your Highness?"

"A tripod of iron," Kaiulani said. From her black bombazine sleeve she drew the whale-ivory seal of Oahu and set it between the ink-pots. "Silas returns to Denver as Hereditary Marshal of the Interior Cantons, with ten million silver thalers a year from the Mint to keep his horsemen drunk and off the tracks. Marquis Takashima retains the High Admiralty of the Western Waters, provided every battleship carries a Polytechnic engineer at the throttles and clears its customs through Monterey. And General Vance remains Chancellor of the Gauge in San Francisco, under my Regency, until we have rebuilt the ditch at Panama and welded the hoop so tight that it will take twenty years of peace before your grandsons are rich enough to finish this war."

***

To the Chronicler who writes these closing pages in the autumn of 1915, at the library windows of the Berkeley Polytechnic above a bay that has known twenty-seven years of armed, sleepless convalescence since that morning on Sand Island, Lady Kaiulani’s tripod shows in every smoke-stack along the shore.

Through the twenty-six years of her Sole Regency, while workmen poured the canal at Panama in concrete and the bronze corpse of the Founder rode the turrets of the fleet to keep the provinces in awe, the truce of Thalassia held the hundred and twenty-four states together like a splint of iron wire bound around a fractured thigh-bone. The wild beasts of the first succession died off in their cages. Silas Thorne drowned in his own dropsy and sour mash at the Denver palace in ninety-nine; old Marquis Takashima went to his ancestors before the Miraflores locks opened; and by the spring of the last year, only the aged Princess and the gray-haired, fifty-six-year-old Marshal Marcus Vance remained alive of those who had stood within earshot when Elias Thorne’s stick struck the floorboards.

A splint remains mere wire. By the summer of 1914, when the eighty-year-old Regent’s breath began failing in the Honolulu trade-winds, the Great Arena had grown too heavy to be governed by a dead man’s bronze statue and a college of unnamed clerks. Three hundred and eighty million souls of the third generation had arrived, men and women who had never seen the frontier or the shoguns, who spoke the clipped, hybrid court-pidgin of the examination-sheds and demanded a living magistrate upon the dais.

At the Grand Conclave of May, 1914, held upon the artificial granite island of the Miraflores Lock-Spillway at Panama rather than in the blood-stained Rotunda of San Francisco or the bamboo pavilions of Oahu, while the Atlantic and Pacific squadrons lay moored gun-wale to gun-wale in the fresh water of the continent’s spine, the *Settlement of the New Century* was sealed.

That noon was blistering. Before the assembled Prefects of the Hundred and Twenty-Four States and the gray-templed Polytechnic Admirals, Lady Kaiulani walked for the last time to the stone parapet beneath the Arch of the Pivot with her hand on the steel arm of Field-Marshal Marcus Vance. At dawn that morning, by her final warrant, the copper-plated corpse of Elias Thorne had been unbolted from the barbette of the flagship dreadnought and lowered with twenty tons of pig-lead into the four-thousand-fathom abyss of the Marianas Trench, where no rebel could ever melt him down and no clerk could use his dead thumb for a stamp.

In his stead, she led forward two twenty-four-year-old youths in the plain slate-gray wool of the Imperial Service: Prince Kalanimoku the younger, the son of her gentle cousin who had died in the Monterey pleurisy, carrying in his veins the mingled blood of the Kentucky Protector and the ancient kings of Maui, and beside him as Imperial Consort, the Lady Chiyo, grand-niece of Marquis Takashima and First Wrangler of the Kyoto Mathematical Synod.

Thus was established the *Syncretic Dynasty of the House of Thorne-Kamehameha*, under the perpetual constitutional guardianship of the Polytechnic Staff. The Caesar of the frontier had gone into the deep water. In his place sat a bronze-skinned, gray-eyed Sacred Emperor who reigned from the coral palaces of Thalassia like the heaven-descended sovereigns of the East, signing no death-warrants and touching no tax-rolls, while in the concrete vaults of Monterey, Marshal Vance’s ten thousand numbered prefects worked the Hollerith engines that moved the grain and the coal.

What had begun in the mud of the Rio Frio as the personal raid of an American border-captain had hardened, sixty years later, into an immortal, self-winding priesthood of bronze and steam.

# Chapter 22: The Treaty of Rangoon

Because an engine that cannot break inward must grind outward until it consumes the last unnumbered acre of the globe, the new dynasty was scarcely six months upon the lotus-throne of Thalassia before the long-delayed reckoning with the fragments of the Old World sounded across the western straits.

For forty years since the disaster in the Coral Sea and the closing of the Suez approaches by the Pacifica tariff-leagues, the remnants of the British Empire had crouched behind the basalt bastions of Singapore and the Himalayan passes like an aged lion driven into its last thorny brake. Stripped of Canada and shut out of the Yangtze and the Australian downs, the House of Windsor and the remnant of the London Parliament had transferred their ragged exchequer and surviving dreadnoughts, along with two million conscripted English and Sepoy riflemen, to the peninsula of Hindostan, where they proclaimed at Delhi the *Imperial Federation of the Indian Ocean*, the last autonomous fortress of the Atlantic race upon the earth.

In the autumn of 1914, the British Viceroy at Calcutta refused to admit the Monterey census-assessors into the jute-mills of Bengal and mined the Straits of Malacca against the Sumatra oil-tankers. Down in the cellar of Rincon Hill, the great brass telegraph-keys sent no stuttering ultimatums as they had in the days of the Tsar.

Field-Marshal Marcus Vance, fifty-seven years old now and cold as the Sierra glacier that had killed his uncle, walked to the illuminated glass wall-map of the hemisphere, pulled his cracked ivory slide-rule from his tunic pocket, and moved four brass markers three inches to the west.

To the Chronicler who accompanied the headquarters staff aboard the eighty-thousand-ton super-dreadnought *Pacifica* as the Combined Fleets forced the Nicobar channel in the red monsoon dawn of November, the *Great Indian War* bore no resemblance to the desperate, smoky brawls of Vicksburg or Vladivostok. A continental trip-hammer struck a wall of dry brick.

Over the churning, slate-green rollers of the Bay of Bengal came a floating industrial city twenty miles wide: forty turbine-driven dreadnoughts burning refined Borneo petroleum, flanked by twelve flat-decked *aeroplane-tenders* from whose five-hundred-foot timber flight-strips rose swarms of twin-engined Curtiss-Nakajima biplanes armed with two-hundred-pound picric-acid torpedoes, while five thousand feet above the mastheads rode the twelve rigid duralumin air-cruisers of the *Aeolus III* class, their wireless-antennas blue with sparks against the monsoon clouds as they corrected the fall of the twenty-inch shells by trigonometry from thirty miles out at sea.

At six o’clock on the morning of the fourteenth of November, off the sand-heads of the Hooghly estuary below Calcutta, the last battle-fleet of the Atlantic world steamed out between the mine-fields to die in deep water: twenty-two coal-burning British battleships of the *King Edward* and *Viceroy* classes, their black smoke-columns trailing low across the rain-squalls and the White Ensign of St. George nailed to their mainmasts.

Up on the armored signal-bridge of the *Pacifica*, three stories above the triple twenty-inch turrets where the hydraulic rammers were already seating the two-ton armor-piercing projectiles into the breeches with a greased, pneumatic hiss, Fleet-General Kuroda the younger held the deck; the fifty-seven-year-old Chancellor of the Gauge, Field-Marshal Marcus Vance, had surrendered his baton to the third generation that autumn, leaving his thirty-year-old former Chief of Operations, Candidate Zero-Zero-One-Four of the class of nineteen-six, in supreme command.

Through the three-inch Zeiss slit of the conning-tower, a row of tiny gray smudges marked the distant British line nineteen miles to the northwest, where the muddy brown outflow of the sacred Ganges stained the green ocean water like a widening pool of rust.

"The flagship *New Delhi* has just hoisted the old Nelson signal at the fore, General," the flag-lieutenant reported. Born in the Massachusetts cantons, the boy wore the cipher *Eight-Eight-One-Two* on his collar and kept his eye pressed to the stereoscopic range-finder while the plot-table ticks clicked off the decreasing yards in red electric numerals along the bulkhead. "And their coastal batteries at Diamond Harbor and Saugor Island are opening fire with thirteen-inch cordite at extreme elevation. The shells are falling four thousand yards short in the outer channel."

Young Kuroda ignored the armored slit. Inside the conning-tower, warm transformer-oil and electric sparks mingled with the sweet scent of the Honolulu sandalwood paper upon which the morning dispatches from the Sacred Emperor Kalanimoku were printed. In his right hand, Kuroda held the standard-issue duralumin circular calculator of the Monterey Staff; its geared rings resolved wind-drift, barometric density, and the Coriolis rotation of the earth without the need for a human thumb to slide an ivory stick.

"They are burning Cardiff and Bengal lump-coal in hand-stoked Scotch boilers, Lieutenant," Kuroda said, his voice dry and quiet as the hum of the gyro-compass between his boots while the first British salvo threw up four harmless white water-spouts two miles ahead of his bow. "After forty minutes at twenty knots against the monsoon swell, their stokers will be fainting on the floor-plates and their speed will drop to sixteen. We will stay outside the range of their thirteen-inch guns and deny their newspapers a Trafalgar."

He turned the knurled brass dial of the ballistic computer two clicks to the left. From the receiver housing, the wireless telemetry ribbon unspooled from the air-cruiser hovering above the Hooghly mud-banks.

"Alter course four points to port and hold the range at twenty-six thousand yards," Kuroda ordered. He laid his gloved finger upon the brass firing-circuit of the master director-tower as the sixty twenty-inch rifles of the First Squadron rose in unison against the wet gray sky of Bengal, their muzzles elevated toward the invisible shoreline where three hundred years of European dominion waited behind the mud-forts.

***

Seven thousand eight hundred miles to the east, where the November afternoon was already sinking into the cold salt fog of the Golden Gate, the salvo that broke the spine of the *New Delhi* registered only as a tiny, silent jump of a siphon-needle upon a glass drum.

Inside the high, glass-walled solarium atop the retired officers' pavilion at the Presidio, a quiet house of unpainted redwood and Sierra stone overlooking the same mile-wide strait where Elias Thorne had watched the *Oregon* steam in sixty-four years before, Field-Marshal Marcus Vance sat alone beside an unlit anthracite grate.

He was fifty-seven years old. Though the rheumatic frost of the Donner avalanche had stiffened his left knee until he walked with a steel brace inside his trouser-leg, and the hair above his temples had turned as white as the salt-crust on the Farallones, he wore the plain dark alpaca coat of a retired polytechnic assessor; when the Synod of Prefects had voted him the Gold Baton of Emeritus Guardian in October and promoted young Kuroda to the supreme command of the Western Expedition, Marcus had folded his slate-gray tunic into a camphor-chest.

Before his knees stood a small mahogany receiver-table connected by a courtesy wire to the Telegraph Annex on Rincon Hill. Every three minutes, the automatic printer beside his elbow gave a soft, oiled *whir* and spat out four inches of perforated yellow tape.

Marcus read the holes in the paper without a codebook. Across his grey wool thigh lay the cracked ivory slide-rule that had stopped the .45-70 slug at Cisco switch during the winter of the Troubles.

*16:12 GMT,* the holes said. *SQUADRON ONE. ELEVATION FOURTEEN DEGREES. CONSUMPTION OF PICRIC-ACID SHELL, TWELVE HUNDRED TONS. BRITISH UNITS SUNK OR BURNING ON SAGAR BAR: SIXTEEN. OWN CASUALTIES: ONE CURTISS TORPEDO-PLANE LOST TO ENGINE FAILURE.*

Marcus picked up the ivory rule between his stiff, square-nailed fingers and pushed the cracked celluloid cursor half an inch along the wood. He looked up from the yellow paper to the wide plate-glass window.

Down below the bluff, across the dark green heave of the bay, the three-tiered granite embankments of San Francisco were lighting their five o’clock carbon-arcs against the dusk. A ten-thousand-ton automated grain-collier from the Sacramento delta slid silently beneath the hydraulic gantry-cranes at the Mint slip, while up on the Berkeley slopes the white marble quadrangles of the Examination Sheds glowed like a row of lighted factory furnaces.

For forty years he had worked to purge the army of his father’s bloody frontier charges and old Caleb’s whiskey-soaked camps, replacing the saber and the family name with the logarithm and the five-digit collar cipher. He had designed the examination cubicles and calculated the ration-tables. Under his curriculum, young Kuroda and ten thousand boys like him had learned to treat the burning of a city or the sinking of a fleet purely as the balancing of an equation in coal and nitrogen.

The equation was complete.

In the concrete vaults of Monterey, his portrait hung in the mathematics hall alongside Elias Thorne’s iron walking-stick. Yet when he had gone down to the Admiralty wharf in October to argue that the Empire’s natural circumference stopped at the Straits of Malacca, demonstrating on paper that three hundred million starving Bengali peasants and two thousand miles of Indian railway on a five-foot-six gauge would overstrain the silver reserves of the Market Street Mint by fourteen percent, the young prefects of the class of nineteen-ten had listened to him with the same polite, stone-faced patience that he had shown to Cornelius Schuyler and Marquis Takashima at the iron turnstile twenty-seven years ago.

*The turbines at Balboa and the blast-furnaces at Hanyang are producing a twenty-percent surplus of steel plate and picric acid, Marshal,* Candidate Zero-Zero-One-Four had answered him, his finger resting on a duralumin calculator unmarred by any bullet-crack. *An industrial machine that fails to expand its market-radius by four percent per annum chokes upon its own pig-iron. We invade Hindostan to absorb the surplus output of the Osaka rolling-mills.*

The ticker-machine beside Marcus’s elbow whirred again.

*16:20 GMT. DIAMOND HARBOR FORTS SILENCED BY AERIAL PHOSPHORUS. VICEROY AT CALCUTTA REQUESTS FORTY-EIGHT HOUR ARMISTICE TO EVACUATE EUROPEAN WOMEN. FLEET-GENERAL KURODA REPLIES: THE TIDE SERVES AT SIX. UNCONDITIONAL CAPITULATION OF THE PENINSULA OR THE DREADNOUGHTS ENTER THE RIVER.*

Marcus looked down at the cracked ivory stick in his lap. His father had ridden a lathered horse into the red mud of Vicksburg to make a king, and he himself had frozen his toes in the Sierra snow to turn that king into a machine; now the machine was rolling westward across the warm oceans of the earth under its own steam.

A quiet tap sounded at the glass door of the solarium. An orderly, a seventeen-year-old boy from the Amur Cossack cantons wearing the blue brassard of the hospital service, stepped inside with a steaming porcelain mug upon a tin tray.

"Your five-o’clock beef-tea, Marshal," the boy said in the flat, accentless English of the primary sheds. He set the mug down directly atop the uncoiling yellow tape from the Bay of Bengal without a glance at the holes. "The surgeon says the damp fog is bad for your knee-joint if you sit by the glass after sunset. Shall I draw the blackout curtains?"

Marcus slid the broken ivory rule back into his buttonless alpaca breast pocket.

"Draw them, Corporal," Marcus said.

***

Three weeks later, on the morning of the sixth of December, the northeast monsoon blew clear and hot down the muddy yellow reaches of the Irrawaddy River. The wind carried the smell of charred teakwood and stagnant paddy-slime, thick with the sweetish smoke of the Rangoon oil-refineries that the retiring British garrison had tried in vain to burn before the Choshu marine-brigades landed at Syriam.

High above the brown water, upon the vast, brick-paved terrace of the Shwedagon Pagoda, where the three-hundred-foot bell-shaped stupa of solid gilded masonry blazed against the tropical sky in a glare of Sunset Gold that outshone the domes of San Francisco, a pavilion of imperial-blue silk stood between the plaster statues of the guardian *chinthe* lions.

Lady Kaiulani had been carried up the four hundred stone steps from the cantonment road. She was eighty years old that winter. Her bones were as light and dry as the bamboo ribs of a fan, and the tropic heat that had once been the breath of her Honolulu youth now pressed upon her shrunken chest like a hot iron weight. Four six-foot guardsmen of the Oahu Household bore her up the southern stairway in an open palanquin of black-lacquered koa-wood, her tiny figure upright among the velvet cushions in her unchanging gown of severe black bombazine, the ancient whale-ivory *lei niho palaoa* resting against the withered parchment of her throat.

The bearers set the poles down upon the scorching red brick of the platform. Beneath her white braids, Kaiulani turned her sunken, obsidian-dark eyes past the golden lotus-spire toward the city below.

Across the miles of green palm-groves and flooded rice-delta, the Union Jack had vanished from the earth. Over the teak-wharves of the Irrawaddy Flotilla Company, the red-brick barracks of the cantonment, and the high iron roofs of the Burmah Oil tanks, ten thousand banners of Imperial Blue and Gold snapped in the wind, while out in the main stream lay the gray, triple-turreted bulk of the cruiser *Kamehameha IV*, her twenty-inch guns trained steadily upon the gilded roofs of the Viceregal residency.

Inside the open silk pavilion, waiting on the shady side of a thirty-ton bronze temple-bell that the Burmese kings had cast a century before, stood a delegation of five men in stained white tropical drill and tarnished gold lace: Lord Hardinge of Penshurst, the last British Viceroy of India; General Sir Beauchamp Duff, Commander-in-Chief of the shattered Bengal Army; and behind them, three silk-turbaned native princes, the Nizam of Hyderabad, the Maharaja of Gwalior, and the Gaekwar of Baroda, whom Fleet-General Kuroda’s air-cruisers had brought down from Delhi under polite escort the night before.

Kaiulani remained in her palanquin chair. The bearers stepped back three paces and grounded their magazine-rifles on the brick; beside her right elbow, across the broad teakwood table, Fleet-General Kuroda unrolled a six-foot linen map of the Indian subcontinent and weighted its four corners with brass fuse-caps from the twenty-inch shells that had sunk the *New Delhi*.

"Your Highness has brought us to a temple of idols to sign away the inheritance of Queen Victoria," Lord Hardinge said. His voice shook with the quinine-ague. Where a splinter had struck his launch at Diamond Harbor, his white linen cuff hung frayed, and as he stood beneath the muzzles of the foreign cannon—the first of his race to sign a treaty under such terms since Yorktown—he kept his eyes averted from the three Indian princes behind his shoulder. "In November you promised at Singapore that if the Home Fleet ceased fire in the Hooghly, the sovereignty of the Crown over the interior provinces west of the Ganges would be respected under a commercial customs-union."

"In November, My Lord, your sappers had not yet blown up the broad-gauge tunnels in the Khyber Pass or invited the Russian remnants at Tashkent to occupy the Punjab," Kaiulani said. Fifty years had stripped away the clear contralto that once charmed the Mexican governors at Monterey. Her voice came now as a dry, musical whisper, like wind through dead palm-fronds, yet every syllable cut through the hum of the temple flies. "When a house-holder sets fire to his own thatch to spite the bailiff, the municipality does not leave him in possession of the kitchen. General Kuroda, read the lines of the Partition."

Kuroda ignored the Englishman and tapped the linen map with the tip of his steel dividers.

"From the first of January, nineteen-fifteen, the corporate entity known as the British Indian Empire ceases to exist," Kuroda read in his flat, Polytechnic cadence. "The littoral provinces of Burma, Bengal, Madras, and Ceylon are incorporated directly into the Grand Confederation as the One Hundred and Twenty-Fifth through One Hundred and Thirtieth Maritime Cantons, under the civil code of Monterey and the six-foot railway gauge. The interior plateau of the Deccan and the Rajput states," he continued, inclining his cropped head half an inch toward the three silent maharajas in their jewel-crusted turbans, "are constituted as the Autonomous Princely Protectorate of Hindostan, answering directly to the Insular Chancery at Thalassia, with native garrisons officered by graduates of the New Edo and Berkeley academies."

Lord Hardinge’s gaunt face went the color of wet chalk under his sun-burn. "And the British Crown? The two hundred thousand Englishmen and women in the civil service and the hill-stations? The tea-planters of Assam, the regimental depots at Meerut and Bombay?"

"The port of Bombay and a ten-mile radius around the Malabar cotton-mills will remain a Free Leasehold Factory of the London Exchequer for twenty years, to liquidate the sterling debt owed to the Market Street Mint," Kaiulani said. Her tiny, blue-veined hand rested upon the whale-ivory clasp at her throat while overhead, low across the golden spire of the pagoda, three Curtiss-Nakajima biplanes droned past and beat the hot incense-smoke down into the pavilion with their twin propellers. "Your soldiers will lay down their Lee-Enfield rifles at the Calcutta docks before the winter solstice and embark upon the Pacific Mail colliers for Southampton at our expense. As for your civil magistrates, My Lord, any young Englishman under the age of twenty-two who wishes to remain in Asia may present himself at the Rangoon examination-sheds on Monday morning, shave his head, and sit for the third-class polytechnic logarithm paper alongside the sons of his Bengali sweepers."

Behind the Viceroy, the Nizam of Hyderabad stepped forward across the carpet. He bowed low until his emerald-plumed turban touched the shadow of the koa-wood palanquin.

"And the salt-tax of the English, Great Lady?" the Nizam asked in careful French.

"Abolished at noon, Highness," Kaiulani answered. She turned her dark eyes upon the Indian prince with the cold, maternal smile that had once locked Don Rafael Núñez into the Panama saloon-car. "You will pay no tribute to London again. You will merely send ten thousand of your Rajput horsemen each spring to patrol the Ural timber-lines for General Kuroda, and buy your locomotives from the Osaka works. Give the Viceroy the pen, General; the sun is rising on the brick, and I wish to be aboard the steamer before the noon heat."

***

Seven days later I stood upon the stone *ghats* of Benares. Below me in the sacred mud of the Ganges, a battalion of Cantonese and Californian railway-surveyors drove their red-and-white leveling-stakes while a squad of Choshu military police superintended the stacking of ten thousand surrendered British Martini-Henry and Lee-Enfield rifles upon the temple steps. The scene required neither commentary nor tears.

In the history of mortal empires, there is always an afternoon when the tide reaches its highest watermark upon the sea-wall, pauses in the sun, and retreats toward the mud-flats. For the race of the Atlantic islands, those bold, red-coated shipbuilders who had sailed out of the Thames and the Bristol Channel three centuries before to girdle the globe with their counting-houses and their steam-engines, that afternoon fell on the thirteenth of December, 1914, along the broad, corpse-strewn flood of the Mother River.
