The London newspapers did not print the *Treaty of Rangoon* until the following month. Off Aden, the Pacifica cable-ships had dredged up and cut the submarine cables through the Red Sea; yet along the twelve hundred miles of the Grand Trunk Road from Delhi to the sea, iron rails and telegraph wire already carried the terms.

All morning, under a pale, dusty winter sky heavy with the smoke of burning cow-dung, crushed marigolds from the Hindu shrines, and the sharp coal-tar of the Monterey disinfectant-carts, the last regiments of the British Raj marched down the stone steps to the river-barges.

By the fourth article of Fleet-General Kuroda’s military convention, the armory smiths at the Allahabad arsenal had already soldered the regimental standards of the Black Watch, the Coldstream Detachments, and the Bengal Lancers inside leaden cylinders to be shipped eastward as curiosities for the Rotunda museum in San Francisco. No brass bands played *The British Grenadiers*. No silk colors flew above the mist. In silence, four thousand sun-blackened Yorkshiremen and Scots in faded khaki drill—the grandsons of the men who had blown open the Kashmir Gate in fifty-seven and held the bloody ridge above Delhi—filed down the ancient stairs between twin ranks of twenty-year-old Imperial Cadets wearing the unadorned slate-gray wool and five-digit silver collar-ciphers of the Great Arena.

At the foot of the Manikarnika Ghat, the sandalwood funeral pyres of the Brahmans smoked beside the oily brown water. I paused behind the shoulder of Prefect-Assessor Shen the younger—son of that Auditor Shen who had weighed the dead coolie’s brass thumb in the San Francisco cellar thirty-three years ago—while he sat before a folding camp-table of stamped duralumin and checked the British embarkation-rolls against a portable Hollerith card-punch.

"Eight hundred and forty-two rank-and-file of the Second Battalion, West Riding Regiment, Citizen-Prefect," reported an English major with an empty left sleeve pinned across his tunic. He halted before the table and laid his rusted Webley service revolver upon the aluminum sheet beside Shen’s brass ink-pot. Coal-smoke from the burned cantonments at Cawnpore had left the officer's eyes bloodshot; out in the middle of the river, past the Chinese magistrate’s horn-rimmed spectacles, a colossal floating steam-hammer towed by an Osaka tug drove creosoted Oregon pilings straight through the sacred bathing-pools to carry the new six-foot-gauge railway bridge. "We have left two hundred men down with the enteric fever in the garrison hospital at Lucknow. By the terms of Lord Hardinge’s capitulation on the pagoda steps, they are to receive full quinine rations and homeward passage aboard the January hospital-transport."

Prefect Shen kept his eyes on his perforated manila cards. With two fingers, he lifted the Englishman’s revolver by the trigger-guard and dropped it into a tarred wicker basket filled with broken Wilkinson sabers and brass crown-badges that two Hawaiian orderlies carried down to the ballast-lighters. He stamped a violet serial numeral across the major’s parchment clearance-sheet.

"The military hospital at Lucknow was reclassified at six this morning as District Quarantine Station Four-Zero-Nine, Major," Shen said in his smooth, accentless Berkeley English. As the next file of disarmed Highlanders stepped onto the gangplank of the waiting stern-wheeler, his right palm depressed the steel lever of the card-punch with a sharp *clack*. "Your sick will be processed according to the Pacifica Sanitary Code. Those whose temperatures return to the normal curve before the fifteenth of January will be embarked on the colliers at Calcutta; those whose fevers prove chronic will be assigned third-class clerical duty in the Assam tea-cantons to defray the cost of their municipal quinine. Step down to the lower deck, please, and instruct your sergeants not to throw their empty biscuit-tins over the rail; the channel is being dredged to sixteen feet for the Hanyang ore-barges."

The one-armed major stood still upon the slimy stone step. High above the river, from the topmost balcony of the great Mosque of Aurangzeb, while the hot winter wind lifted the skirt of his torn khaki coat, a signal-squad of the Choshu Corps unrolled a thirty-foot banner of Imperial Blue and Sunset Gold across the ancient red sandstone.

***

While the British soldiers filed onto the river-lighters at Benares, Lady Kaiulani remained at Rangoon for three days to settle the colony's accounts before the monsoon broke.

She avoided the scorching bricks of the pagoda. On the afternoon of the sixteenth of December, she sat within the high, teak-paneled counting-room of the former Jardine-Matheson Godown No. 1 along the Strand Road, a cavernous vault of dark Burmese timber whose iron-barred windows looked out upon the forest of hydraulic dock-cranes and the gray, armored flanks of the transport-fleet. The room was cool and dim. Raw Patna opium-chests and dried Pekoe tea-brick scented the timbered dark, cut through by the biting naphtha that the sanitation gangs sprayed across the wharf-timbers outside to kill the plague-fleas.

Before her table of polished camphor-wood stood four men in tropical broadcloth and silk robes: Sir Catchick Paul Chater, senior partner of the Hong Kong and Calcutta opium-syndicates; Mr. David Sassoon the younger of the Bombay exchanges; and two corpulent Marwari silver-bankers from the Burrabazar whose fathers had financed the East India Company’s regiments a century before. Inside their immaculate trousers, their knees trembled.

"The political sovereignty of the peninsula does not concern our houses, Your Imperial Highness," Sir Paul Chater said. Beside Kaiulani’s foot, nested in the green velvet of an open iron strongbox, lay the new bronze Revenue Seals of the One Hundred and Twenty-Six Maritime Cantons, and Chater kept his pale, heavy-lidded eyes fixed upon them. "Whether the customs-guard at the Hooghly wears a red coat or a slate-gray tunic, the eighty thousand chests of Bengal and Malwa opium now lying in the Ghazipur maturing-sheds represent twelve million pounds sterling in private commercial paper, hypothecated to the London and Bombay discount-banks. And the Assam tea-clip for the coming spring is already contracted in advance to the Mincing Lane brokers at fourpence the pound. We ask only that the Regency validate our existing export-warrants under the commercial clauses of the Treaty of Rangoon."

Kaiulani did not answer him at once. Inside the rustling black bombazine, her eighty-year-old frame sat deep within the high-backed chair of carved teak; from the sample-tray on the desk she lifted a fist-sized ball of gummy Behar opium, rolled the dark mass between her withered, ivory-ringed fingers, and left the four millionaires before the table holding their breath like schoolboys under a switch.

"For seventy years, gentlemen," Kaiulani said, while outside the window the Osaka steam-winches clanked and hissed under their loads of rice-sacks, "you and the English factors at Canton poisoned the rivers of China with this black mud so that your banks in London might buy Indian cotton and pay the dividends of Whitehall. When Elias Thorne took the Yangtze valleys into his protection in seventy-four, your gunboats stood behind the Singapore straits and smuggled forty thousand chests a year through the Hainan junks to rot the brains of our iron-workers at Hanyang."

Mr. Sassoon took a hasty step forward. His manicured hands fluttered above his white waistcoat. "The trade was licensed by Royal Charter, Madam! If the Ghazipur opium-factories are closed without compensation, forty thousand poppy-cultivators in Behar will default on their land-rents before March, and every bank from Bombay to Singapore will suspend specie payments!"

"The factories at Ghazipur will not be closed, Mr. Sassoon," Kaiulani said. She dropped the black ball of gum back into the brass scale-pan with a dull thud. "An empire of four hundred million labourers requires three hundred tons of morphia and laudanum a year for its field-hospitals and its veterinary depots. From noon today, however, every poppy-field in the Ganges valley and every tea-garden from Darjeeling to the Brahmaputra becomes an exclusive Crown Monopoly of the Bureau of Integration."

At a brief gesture from her left hand, a twenty-two-year-old Polytechnic fiscal prefect stepped from the door and laid four printed indentures across the camphor-wood.

"The word *private* is struck from the commercial dictionary of the Indian Ocean," she said. Her obsidian eyes moved across their grey, slack-jawed faces. "At six o’clock tonight, my Hawaiian provosts will burn sixty thousand chests of your smoking-opium in the lime-kilns at Kidderpore so that no Cantonese furnace-man ever sucks a pipe of English poison again. The remaining twenty thousand chests will be refined into surgical alkaloids at the Monterey laboratories under military seal. Of the Assam and Ceylon tea-harvests, not a single leaf will sail for the Thames in a European bottom. The entire crop is requisitioned in perpetuity by the San Francisco Commissariat at a fixed assessment of two silver tenths the pound, payable in forty-year canal-script."

"Two tenths in paper!" Sir Paul Chater said. His fingers hooked into his silk cravat. "That is twenty percent below the cost of the coolie-hire on the hills! You are confiscating the capital of the City of London by a stroke of the pen!"

"Fleet-General Kuroda confiscated your capital with twenty-inch picric-acid shells off Sagar Island three weeks ago, Sir Paul; I am merely giving you a receipt for the ashes," Kaiulani said. She reached for the whale-ivory seal at her wrist. "If you and your partners sign the transfer-deeds before the four-o’clock gun, you will be retained as salaried factors of the Seventh Tea and Chemical Trust at three thousand thalers a year, with permission to reside in your Calcutta villas under cadet supervision. If you prefer to plead the law of Mincing Lane, the convict-transport *Michigan* is coaling at the jetty to take four hundred railway-masons to the northern Ural mines at daybreak, and Auditor Shen informs me that the winter gang-rolls are still four names short."

***

With the Red Sea cables severed, that news traveled slowly around the tempestuous winter swells of the Cape of Good Hope aboard overcrowded, coal-starved hospital-colliers that limped into Southampton Water in February of 1915, bringing the final iron curtain of the *Long Mourning* down upon the island of Great Britain.

To the Chronicler who traveled to England the following spring as an attaché of the Pacifica Debt-Liquidation Commission, neither the grass-grown quays of Carthage nor the shrunk brick villages huddled inside the shell of Diocletian’s palace offered a spectacle more solemn or instructive than the twilight of the Atlantic metropolis.

London had suffered no sack. No shell from Kuroda’s dreadnoughts had ever fallen upon the chalk cliffs of Kent. Yet as our turbine-packet steamed up the yellow reaches of the lower river past Gravesend and the Isle of Dogs, the unscratched stone walls of the city stood around a metropolis that had died of an embolus in its distant arteries.

Thirty years before, the forest of masts and red-and-black funnels had stood so thick for two miles along the West India and Tilbury Docks that a man might walk across the river on the decks of the tea-clippers and the Australian wool-fleets; now the grey granite basins lay as empty and still as highland tarns. Four hundred rust-streaked tramp-steamers, stripped of their brass fittings to pay the harbour-dues, rotted four-abreast against decaying timber jetties with seagulls nesting in their cold smokestacks. In the freezing drizzle, the hydraulic cranes stood locked at forty-five degrees, red with flaking iron-oxide. Only the stenciled white padlock of the *San Francisco Receivership Board* marked the bolted iron shutters along the brick vaults of the spice- and tea-warehouses.

With the gold of the Rand cut off by the Pacifica cruisers at Delagoa Bay, and the cotton of the Mississippi, the wool of Melbourne, and the tea of Assam clearing exclusively in silver thalers through the counting-houses of Market Street and Osaka, the pound sterling, for two hundred years the measure of human labor from Archangel to Valparaiso, fell in six weeks to the value of provincial waste-paper.

On a raw, sleet-swept Tuesday noon in March, I walked up Threadneedle Street toward the Bank of England. The old aroma of roasting coffee-beans and sea-coal that my father had remembered from before the fall of the East was gone. Boiled turnip-tops and wet shoddy wool soured the air instead, rising from fifty thousand idle dock-laborers and discharged clerks who stood in silent, four-deep queues along the granite curb in threadbare black frock-coats and battered top-hats before the municipal soup-booths that the Pacifica Quaker Relief Mission had set up beneath the portico of the Royal Exchange.

Inside the great domed rotunda of the Stock Exchange, where once the roar of the jobbers had shaken the plaster whenever a gun was fired on the Indus, forty old men in black mourning-armbands sat around a single coke-brazier and traded fractional parcels of Welsh coal-scrip and Irish potato-warrants in whispers so low that the drip of the London rain through the unmended skylight sounded like a drum-roll on the flagstones.

Westminster’s streets remained quiet. The fierce, hot blood of the island had drained away into the mud of the Hooghly and the prison-hulks of the Coral Sea, or had emigrated ten years ago on the steerage-packets to seek a five-digit collar-number in the foundries of Seattle and Nagasaki. Widows and grey-haired pensioners remained behind with silent children in wooden clogs, walking beneath the soot-blackened monuments of Nelson and Wellington like fifth-century Britons wandering among the cold hypocausts of Londinium after the eagles had gone back to Rome.

History had turned its back upon the cold gray ditch of the Atlantic.

# Chapter 23: The Crystal Bowl of Thalassia

And where the light had gone, the stone followed.

San Francisco had been the forge where Elias Thorne hammered the red-hot links of the circumference together, and Monterey had been the subterranean vault where Marcus Vance’s clerks counted the rivets; yet neither the fog-swept peninsula of California nor the earthquake-shaken islands of Japan could remain forever the ceremonial heart of an ocean that now reached from the gateway of the Red Sea to the locks of Panama. A ring of ten thousand leagues required an axle in the middle of the water.

By the third year after the Settlement of 1914, the sleepy Polynesia of the old songs and the fortified coaling-station where Lady Kaiulani cut the telegraph cables during the Time of Troubles had vanished behind the blue volcanic peaks of Oahu. At daybreak, the traveler aboard a turbine-liner looks instead upon *Thalassia*, the City of the Pivot, the marble navel of the twentieth-century earth.

Where the shallow coral flats and the green taro-marshes of Waikiki and Pearl Lochs once drowsed beneath the kiawe trees, sixty thousand Cantonese stone-masons and Samoan diver-gangs now worked beside Italian concrete-pourers to rear a geometric Venice of white Sierra granite and green Japanese bronze that stretched for twelve unbroken miles of black volcanic basalt from the fortress-crater of Diamond Head to the naval slips of Waipahu.

No coal-smoke is permitted to stain the trade-wind clouds above the Sacred Emperor’s water. Thirty miles away, on the windward cliffs of Molokai and the boiling lava-slopes of Hawaii, four hundred thousand horsepower of geothermal steam-turbines and ocean-wave dynamos send their high-tension current beneath the channel through lead-armored conduits; as our vessel glides between the twin hundred-foot bronze lighthouses of the Honolulu Passage, the city rises out of the peacock-blue rollers without a single chimney-stack, humming with unseen transformers and smelling of salt spray and the ten thousand acres of white ginger and sandalwood terraced into the Punchbowl hills.

On the morning of the eighteenth of October, 1916, I stood beside the aging Field-Marshal Marcus Vance upon the high, unfinished basalt causeway of the *Via Triumphalis*, the two-hundred-foot ceremonial mole that runs straight across the dredged lagoon of Kalihi toward the artificial island where the Imperial Palace of the Double Horizon rises forty courses above the tide.

Below our boots, from electric gantry-cranes that spanned the canal-basins like bridges of silver lace, massive twenty-ton blocks of red Rajasthan sandstone—quarried from the demolished forts of the Mogul emperors at Agra and brought eastward as ballast in the returning tea-fleets—descended into the wet Portland cement alongside columns of Californian porphyry and beams of copper-sheathed Taiwanese camphor-wood.

"They are laying the stones of Delhi into the sea-wall at twelve hundred thalers the cubic yard, Citizen-Historian," Marcus Vance said. He leaned his weight upon his steel-braced left leg while the warm, scented trade-wind lifted the thin white hair beneath his plain alpaca cap. Summoned from his Presidio solarium on the autumn steamer by Lady Kaiulani’s final call, he turned a gaunt face, yellow as old parchment against the blinding white glare of the coral dust, toward the swinging electric cranes and measured their arc with his pale eyes. "With the concrete poured into that single bastion to carry the Sacred Emperor’s lotus-pavilion, I could have lined forty miles of the Baikal tunnel or built three dreadnoughts of the *Pacifica* class."

Before I could answer the old Marshal, iron-shod bearer-poles clacked along the marble paving behind us, and the black-lacquered koa-wood palanquin of the Queen-Mother Kaiulani halted at the edge of the mortar-trough.

At eighty-two, she sat small and shrunken beneath her black bombazine and white veil, like a royal mummy brought up from the burial-caves of Kona to inspect the living. When the twenty-six-year-old Sacred Emperor Kalanimoku, tall and bronze-skinned in his ceremonial mantle of yellow *mamo* feathers and silver Polytechnic braid, stepped down from his electric launch to assist her, she waved his young hand aside. She leaned over the side of her chair toward Marcus.

"You are still counting the coal-tons, Marcus, when the winter is over," Kaiulani said. Past the swinging block of red Indian stone, out at the center of the lagoon where four hundred graduates of the Kyoto and Berkeley academies were raising the bronze scaffolding of the Great Gnomon, the zero-meridian obelisk from which all time and longitude upon the planet were henceforth to be reckoned, she pointed her tiny, claw-like fingers. "Elias built the walls of the barn with iron because the wolves were in the timber; you and I kept the roof up with numbers because the mortar was still wet. Look at my grandson’s eyes."

Marcus turned his head half an inch toward the young Emperor. Ten paces away beside his Japanese consort, Kalanimoku stood pointing out the curve of the Samoan-arched senate-house to a group of white-robed Bengali and Virginian prefects while a flight of silver-winged patrol-hydroplanes banked overhead in the sun.

"He has Elias’s eyes, Madam," Marcus said. By forty years’ habit, his hand slipped toward his breast pocket, over the cracked ivory slide-rule hidden beneath the cloth. "And he has never heard a shot fired in anger or seen a man die of the black vomit in a ditch. Within fifty years, these boys in their feather cloaks will forget that the ocean has teeth."

"That is why we are building the walls twenty feet thick out of the stones of the kings we broke, Marshal," Kaiulani answered. Above us, the giant electric crane gave two sharp warning bells and lowered the twenty-ton block of Agra sandstone down toward the bed of gray California lime while her dark eyes closed for an instant against the salt dazzle of the lagoon. "When the boys grow soft in the sun, the sheer weight of the arch will hold them in their chairs whether they have iron in their spines or not. Now come out of the wind, Marcus. The glass is glazed in the upper dome, and I will not have the first parliament of the ocean wait while two ghosts argue over the price of cement."

***

Two hours later, the noon sun stood directly above the bronze tip of the Great Gnomon. Along the reef, the geothermal sirens sounded the meridian chord as the bearers carried her palanquin up the spiral ramp into the Whispering Gallery of the Crystal Palace.

From her cushioned seat behind the pierced screen of gilded Japanese cedar, eighty feet above the inlaid basalt floor, Lady Kaiulani looked down through the blue-tinted prism of the dome upon the finished harvest of her eighty years.

Open to the element that had given it birth, the chamber had no stone walls. Sixteen monumental ribs of cast Pittsburgh duralumin, curved in the high parabola of a Samoan council-house, supported a vault of three-inch Jena glass that rose two hundred feet into the tropical sky, while forty noiseless water-curtains of chilled mountain rain sheeted down the exterior panes and turned the equatorial glare into a submarine twilight of Imperial Blue and pale emerald.

Below her, ranged in five concentric amphitheaters of red Hawaiian koa-wood around the central porphyry rostrum, sat the six hundred Conscript Fathers of the First Pan-Pacific Senate.

Theirs were seats owed to the provincial rolls rather than the brawling ballot-boxes Elias Thorne had burned at Sacramento in fifty-four or the mud-stained camp-commanders who had drawn their sabers around his coffin on Rincon Hill. Each of the Hundred and Thirty Cantons, from the fog-bound timber-wards of Massachusetts and the sheep-downs of Victoria to the steaming jute-deltas of Bengal and the copper-mines of the Amur, had sent up four representatives: two Elder Assessors elected for life by the provincial chambers of commerce and agriculture, and two Senior Prefects of the First Class who had stood for thirty years without a blot upon the Hollerith ledgers of the Bureau of Integration.

Upward on the conditioned draft drifted the fragrance of burning Mysore sandalwood and fresh white ginger-blossoms to meet the faint, omnipresent tang of the high-voltage transformers. Kaiulani rested her chin upon her withered, ivory-ringed fingers. Below lay the floor.

*Here is the cage I promised myself on the morning the* Oregon *broke the reef,* she thought. Down on the rostrum, while Elias’s rough iron stick lay four miles deep in the Marianas mud, the Grand Herald of the Chancery struck the floor three times with a ceremonial rod of braided whalebone and Damascus steel; her old pulse beat with a slow, thin flutter against her black bombazine ribs. *For sixty years we have ruled this basin by the telegraph-warrant and the provost’s carbine, and the first time the hand on the wire went cold, the continent tore itself open from Ballarat to the Donner snow-sheds. No bayonet can hold four hundred million men forever. If the House of Thorne-Kamehameha is to outlast my breath, the provinces must have a temple where their grey-beards can bring their petitions and count the silver in the daylight, believing the law is their own work.*

Down in the third tier of the southern arc sat the Senior Senator for the Eighty-Second Canton, a broad-shouldered, white-bearded pastoralist from Melbourne named MacArthur, whose father had lost an arm fighting Prince Kalakaua’s marines at Sydney Heads in eighty-seven, yet who now wore the blue silk sash of the Imperial Wool Board over his grey colonial broadcloth. He rose in his place. The Herald called the first order of the Ways and Means.

"If it please the Throne and the Conscript Prefects," MacArthur said, his deep, gravelly bush-voice amplified without distortion by the parabolic bronze acoustic-shells built into the duralumin ribs above the dais. "Before the Senate ratifies the quinquennial grain-and-coal assessment for the Ural railway extensions, the delegates of the six Australian and New Zealand cantons lay upon the table a Bill of Right regarding the local appointment of harbor-magistrates. For twenty-nine years since the Pacification, every customs-assessor at Melbourne and Auckland has been sent out from the Berkeley or New Edo sheds without asking the warranty of our provincial guild-councils. Now that the British flag is down at Calcutta and the peace of the ocean is perpetual, we ask that the Constitutional Statute of Nineteen-Sixteen be amended: namely, that no fiscal levy exceeding ten million silver thalers shall pass into law without a two-thirds division of this floor, and that the local guilds shall submit three names from their own blood for every vacant prefecture!"

Along the upper benches of the American and Cantonese tiers, a low murmur ran through the koa-wood stalls. Two merchants from the Shanghai tea-syndicate and a grey-haired iron-master from the Pittsburg valley leaned forward, and their hands rose toward the brass voting-levers on their desks.

Behind the cedar lattice in the gallery, Kaiulani’s shrunken fingers tightened upon the arm of her palanquin. *Let them debate it.* Across the gulf sat young Emperor Kalanimoku in the imperial tribune opposite, beneath his canopy of yellow *mamo* feathers, and she looked straight at him. *Give them the harbor-clerks in Melbourne, Kalanimoku. Let the old sheep-man go home to Victoria and tell his sons that his voice moved the needle in Thalassia. Augustus bound the Roman provinces when the legions grew tired by letting the conquered wear the toga and vote the salt-tax.*

***

Four benches below the Queen-Mother’s screen, in the gallery reserved for the Historiographers of the Academy, the rising of the Australian senator beneath that soaring canopy of glass and duralumin looked for five minutes like the very consummation of human history.

Before a single vote had been recorded upon the electric tally-boards, the building itself spoke a language beyond the vocabulary of Pericles or the builders of the Forbidden City.

Our scholars in the Berkeley aesthetics schools have called this the *Thalassian Style*, that late, ripe blossom of Imperial Syncretism which reached its perfection between the opening of the Panama Locks and the partition of India. In the early decades of the Protectorate, when Elias Thorne was still alive to growl at architects’ bills, the fusion of the shores had been an awkward, military marriage of convenience: an American brick custom-house with a tiled Chinese roof nailed over the rafters, or a Christian garrison-chapel with a wooden Shinto *torii* standing before the porch like a captured trophy.

Here in the Senate House of Thalassia, the seams had vanished into the metal.

Around the vast, sun-filtered rotunda, East and West, island and continent, had fused into a single cast. Cast from Pennsylvania and Hanyang steel, the sixteen colossal ribs of the vault followed in their structural cross-bracing the intricate, earthquake-defying *kigumi* joinery of the Nara temples without a single visible rivet-head, while their bases rested upon octagonal plinths of black Oahu basalt carved with the spiral *koru* reliefs of the Maori navigation-schools. Above the main rostrum, in the place of the painted canvas of kings or battles that would have hung in a European parliament, rose a forty-foot mosaic executed in crushed Mexican turquoise and mother-of-pearl from the Arafura Sea with sunset-gold leaf. In place of Christ or Amaterasu or George Washington blazed the *Sacred Compass of the Pivot*: a golden sun rising out of the centre of the Pacific water while the four winds, wearing the bronze faces of the Polynesian, the Mongol, the Anglo-Saxon, and the Hindoo, poured the rivers of the four continents into a single crystal bowl.

Upon the koa-wood benches below, the dress and speech of the six hundred men showed the old world’s coins melted down in Elias’s crucible.

MacArthur had spoken in English. The nasal colonial dialect his grandfather had brought out from Yorkshire had given way to sentences measured by the crisp, mathematical syntax of the Monterey primers, and when he spoke of the customs-levy, he used without embarrassment the Sino-Japanese fiscal terms, *lijin* and *koku-unit* alongside *kapu-warrant*, that had been the legal tender of the sea for forty years. Across his grey broadcloth chest, the Australian wore a collar of woven Samoan hibiscus-fiber dyed Imperial Blue and fastened with a clasp of Klondike gold; beside him, the Senior Prefect from the Kyoto silk-wards wore Boston-cut trousers of dark navy wool beneath a short, stiff *haori* jacket embroidered with the five-digit silver cipher of the Polytechnic Corps.

They breathed an artifact of the unified globe, an atmosphere chilled by ammonia-compressors forged in Osaka and scented with the bruised sandalwood of conquered Mysore above the steady sixty-cycle hum of the Molokai lava-turbines.

From the doorway where a young cadet stood looking down, the long tragedy of the human races was over: the frontiersman’s rifle and the samurai’s sword had been beaten into a mighty, translucent greenhouse wherein all the tribes of the Great Arena might sit in eternal, well-ventilated harmony to regulate the price of rice and copper.

Up behind the gilded cedar screen of the Whispering Gallery sat an eighty-two-year-old woman who had seen the foundation-trenches dug in blood, ignoring the turquoise mosaic on the wall.

***

Lady Kaiulani looked at her grandson’s right hand.

Across the rotunda, beneath the flaring crimson-and-yellow feather canopy of the Imperial Tribune, the twenty-six-year-old Sacred Emperor Kalanimoku had not inclined his head in the prescribed constitutional nod to admit the Australian senator’s bill to the floor.

He sat straight upon the curule chair of cast bronze and whale-ivory. His broad, island-born shoulders bore the heavy mantle of *mamo* feathers that three generations of Hawaiian bird-catchers had died in the mountain rain to gather for her dead brother’s line. Beside him sat his consort, the Lady Chiyo of Kyoto, her face painted white and still as a porcelain Noh mask, her small hands hidden within silver-brocade sleeves; two steps below the feather footstool stood Fleet-General Kuroda the younger, his thumb resting upon the duralumin hilt of his staff-sword.

When Senator MacArthur finished speaking and sat down upon the Melbourne bench, a hush fell over the six hundred stalls. Under the *Organic Charter of the Senate*, drafted by Kaiulani and Rector Norton’s clerks during the winter after Rangoon, the Chancellor of the Floor should now have called upon the Fiscal Assessor of the Treasury to reply with the balance-sheets, leaving the Sacred Emperor above the battle like the sun above the clouds.

Instead, Kalanimoku lifted his right hand from the ivory armrest.

No iron walking-stick leaned at his knee. He held a slender, twelve-inch baton of polished duralumin wired directly to the electric annunciator-board above the rostrum. From beneath the feather canopy, where Elias Thorne’s unblinking Kentucky eyes sat like two chips of glacier-ice inside the warm brown velvet of a Polynesian face, he looked down across the blue twilight at the white-bearded Australian. The young man did not smile.

He pressed the button in the butt of his baton once.

A sharp, metallic *clack* echoed through the glass vault like the cocking of a giant rifle. Above the rostrum, the great red semaphore-arm dropped across Senator MacArthur’s canton-number and cut the current to the acoustic microphones on the southern benches.

Kalanimoku did not wait for the Herald. Rising to his full six feet two inches as the sunset gold of his cloak spilled over the porphyry steps, he spoke into the golden amplifier at his breast. In secret before the phonograph-cylinders in the Monterey archives, forsaking both the high chanting cadence of the island chiefs and the dry academic Latinity of the Berkeley sheds, he had practiced until he caught the exact, gravelly, short-breathed bark of the grandfather he had never seen.

"The Eighty-Second Canton is four thousand tons in arrears upon its autumn tallow-and-mutton delivery to the Manila fleet-freezers," Kalanimoku said. The amplified iron of his twenty-six-year-old voice rolled down from the sixteen bronze horns in the ceiling until the chilled water-curtains on the glass panes trembled. "When my grandfather took Sydney into the peace of the Ocean, he did not ask the sheep-graziers of Victoria whom he should send to weigh their wool. He sent men with numbers on their collars who could not be bribed with colonial claret."

Down on the southern tier, old MacArthur half-rose from his koa-wood desk. His weathered face flushed dark crimson above his blue sash. "Majesty! By the Charter of the Settlement of Nineteen-Fourteen, a Bill of Right presented by six cantons cannot be struck from the order-book by the Chair without a division of the Conscript Fathers!"

Up behind the cedar screen, Kaiulani leaned forward so sharply that the whale-ivory clasp at her throat struck the lattice with a dry *tap*. Beside her palanquin, old Field-Marshal Marcus Vance stood still. Leaning on his steel leg-brace in the shadow of the curtain, he kept his pale eyes on the four galleries above the entrance-doors, where eighty young cadets of the Palace Guard in the new gold-and-crimson shoulder-cords of the *Emperor’s Own Household Regiment* had stepped up to the brass rails with their hands on their pistol-holsters.

"Look at the floor, Madam," Marcus said under his breath, so low that only Kaiulani heard him above the hum of the air-ducts.

Kaiulani looked down at the five concentric rings of koa-wood desks.

The two Shanghai tea-merchants and the Pittsburg iron-master had raised their hands to second MacArthur’s motion three minutes before. Now their hands stayed clear of the voting-levers. Upward from the tall figure in the yellow feather cloak to the four machine-gun apertures concealed behind the bronze wind-gods of the mosaic, and then sideways toward Fleet-General Kuroda’s cropped head below the dais, their gaze traveled before their hands dropped back into their laps.

Across the central aisle, Prefect-Senator Shen the third, grandson of the old auditor and representative of the First Metropolitan Canton of San Francisco, rose in his black alpaca robe and bowed until his forehead touched the brass rail of his desk.

"The First Canton moves that the petition of the Australian delegates be referred without debate to the Imperial Household Chancellery for ten-year archival review," young Shen said in an oiled, faultless voice, "and that this Senate proceed immediately to ratify by acclamation the Sacred Emperor’s warrant for the construction of the four new dreadnoughts of the *Kalanimoku* class at Yokosuka, together with a special benevolence of forty million silver thalers to be placed at His Majesty’s personal disposal for the fortification of the Persian Gulf."

"Second the motion!" barked thirty voices at once from the military benches of Satsuma and Choshu and California, where sat the men whose sons held commissions in Kuroda’s new Western Fleets and whose canton-assessments had been quietly halved by the Palace Secretariat the night before.

Kalanimoku did not ask for the nays. With a downward sweep of his duralumin baton, he closed the master-circuit on his armrest. Around the circular wall, while the twenty-four lamps of the Australian and New England benches remained dark, five hundred and eighty green electric bulbs flashed on beside the canton-numbers.

"The benevolence is voted without division," Kalanimoku said. He sat back down upon the bronze curule chair and pulled the yellow feather cloak across his knees with the exact, heavy-shouldered movement that Elias Thorne had used when wrapping his Mexican blanket around his swollen ankles in the redwoods thirty-five years ago. "Let the Melbourne delegates take notice: the Senate is assembled to register the harmony of the circumference. We do not haggle over the gauge of the track. The Chancellery will appoint the Sydney harbor-masters at six."

Behind the cedar screen in the Whispering Gallery, the scents of mountain rain and white ginger vanished under the stench of cold mutton-tallow and burned stramonium, thick with the damp, airless concrete of a tomb.

Four miles deep in the Marianas Trench she had buried Elias Thorne’s copper-plated corpse so that no man could rule by his dead bones; she had mixed the blood of Oahu and Kyoto with his frontier clay to soften the iron, and in the middle of the warm sea she had built a palace of crystal and called six hundred elders from the four corners of the earth to make a law that would not need a tyrant.

Out of the womb of her own gentle cousin’s son, backed by the logarithm-wheels of the third generation, the Kentucky wolf had climbed back onto the chair in a cloak of island feathers.

These six hundred men in their silk sashes and alpaca robes were a chorus of frightened clerks hired to clap their hands in unison whenever the great bronze machine in the center of the ocean required another forty million thalers of coal and blood to grind its way from the Persian Gulf to the Cape of Good Hope.

"Take me down from this bird-cage, Marcus," Kaiulani whispered. As the six hundred senators below rose to their feet to chant the three-part Polynesian-Latin hymn of the *Pax Pacifica* and the great pipe-organ in the dome thundered out the brassy chords of the Imperial Anthem, her tiny, eighty-two-year-old hand reached blindly through the cedar gloom and caught the sleeve of the retired Marshal’s plain alpaca coat.

Marcus Vance laid his square, age-spotted fingers over her cold knuckles upon the palanquin rail. He did not signal the Hawaiian bearers to lift the poles.

"There is nowhere left to go down to, Your Highness," the old general said. Through the diamond-shaped openings of the lattice he looked down at the tall, gray-eyed youth on the throne, who was already leaning over the side of the dais while the Senate sang to trace with Fleet-General Kuroda’s steel dividers the red line of the Suez and Cape railway concessions across the map of Africa. "The land is only the wharf now, and the wharf belongs to the water."

***

The literal truth of the old Marshal’s words lay three miles westward from the crystal dome of the Senate that same afternoon, along the broad basalt causeway of the *Via Triumphalis*, in the inner basins of the Pearl Lochs Imperial Dockyard.

In the ancient empires of the continent, in the Rome of the Antonines or the China of the Ming, the ultimate measure of sovereignty had been the road and the wall: the paved military highway down which the foot-soldier marched with his pike, and the masonry rampart behind which the tax-collector sat safe from the nomads of the steppe. Even in the first generation of our own Protectorate, when Elias Thorne and the elder Vance were spiking the six-foot gauge across the alkali deserts of Nevada and the frozen birch-forests of the Yenisei, the sea had been treated as a salt ditch to be bridged by steam-packets so that one railway terminal might feed another.

Here at Thalassia, in the autumn of 1916, the element had swallowed the road.

Upon the upper observation gallery of Dry-Dock Number Four, a cyclopean trough of poured California concrete fifteen hundred feet long and two hundred feet deep hewn straight out of the ancient coral limestone of Waipahu, the land beneath my boots was a fragile, temporary raft moored beside the real architecture of the state.

Below me, riding in forty feet of oiled, emerald-green harbor water along the three-mile curve of the Battleship Quay, lay the First Battle Division of the *Thorne*-class super-dreadnoughts: the *Providentor*, the *Golden Gate*, the *Sakurajima*, and the newly commissioned flagship *Thalassia*.

They bore no more resemblance to the low, monitor-hulled ironclads that had battered the forts of Vladivostok than a cathedral bears to a frontier blockhouse. Sixty-four thousand tons of Krupp cemented nickel-steel went into each of those four hulls. They were painted a dark Imperial Blue that turned almost black in the shadow of the cranes, with a gilded bronze sun-and-anchor thirty feet wide bolted across the flared clipper bow. They carried no coal-bunkers; deep beneath their triple-layered torpedo-blisters, twelve high-pressure Yarrow boilers fired by atomized Borneo and Persian petroleum fed ninety thousand horsepower to four geared Parsons steam-turbines, driving that mountain of armor through a typhoon swell at twenty-eight knots for twelve thousand miles without once dropping anchor at a shore depot.

Along the eight-hundred-foot flush deck of the *Thalassia*, tiered four high fore and aft of the massive tripod lattice-masts, sat the true legislators of the Hundred and Thirty Cantons: sixteen twenty-two-inch breech-loading rifles housed in four quadruple turrets of eighteen-inch hardened steel.

The four-o’clock dockyard bell sounded across the lagoon. Inside the flagship’s barbettes, the hydraulic testing-pumps began their afternoon calibration. Without a single sailor appearing upon the scorching teak planks of the deck, each weighing three thousand tons like an entire regiment of artillery with its horses and caissons, the four forward turrets swung forty-five degrees to port with a low, greased, subterranean hum that vibrated through the basalt quay wall, while the sixty-foot steel barrels elevated in unison toward the western clouds.

The green volcanic peaks of the Koolau range rose only five miles behind the machine-shops, yet the trade-wind across the basin carried only the hot, greasy breath of refined fuel-oil and the metallic bite of red-lead paint baking on five-inch deck-plate. Blue sparks crackled from the two-hundred-ton electric gantry-cranes. Back and forth along the coping they rolled like iron spiders, and into the armored bowels of the fleet they lowered thirty-ton crates of frozen Melbourne mutton and Hanyang cordite.

A shore garrison could mutiny, as Colonel Armistead’s Virginians had done in eighty-seven; a railway track could be torn up in a night by three hundred starving miners with crowbars and blasting-gelatine. A sixty-four-thousand-ton floating fortress stood entirely apart from the land: its freshwater condensers distilled five hundred tons of drinking water a day from the brine, its refrigerating-vaults held six months of meat, and its twenty-two-inch guns could drop a three-thousand-pound high-capacity picric shell onto a city hall twenty-four miles inland from the five-fathom line. It required neither the love nor the consent of the earth.

The continent had shrunk to a quarry for ore and a plantation for oil. Upon sixty feet of salt water floated the throne of humanity, where the five-digit ciphers in the conning-tower could starve any displeasing province from Boston to Calcutta back into the twelfth century or blow its stones into red brick-dust before the local militia could march within sight of the surf.

***

Late that night, when the electric gantry-cranes down at the Waipahu basins had finally ceased their clanking and only the green and red riding-lights of the sixty-four-thousand-ton dreadnoughts glimmered across the five miles of dark water like a second, geometric constellation fallen into the lagoon, Lady Kaiulani sat alone upon the high seaward balcony of the Coral Pavilion.

She had dismissed her Oahu tire-women and forbidden even old Marcus Vance to follow her through the sliding doors of Hawaiian koa-wood. At eighty-two the blood in her veins ran so thin and slow that even the warm October trade-wind of her childhood chilled her like the draft from the Donner snow-sheds; wrapped to the chin in a heavy mantle of black silk and gray sea-otter fur, she rested her withered hands upon the broad volcanic basalt of the parapet. She looked up at the sky.

Above the black, saw-toothed silhouette of the Waianae mountains, where no electric arc-lamp had yet been bolted to the rock, hung the ancient stars of the Polynesian navigators: *Hokulea*, the Star of Gladness, and the long, tilting diamond of the Southern Cross dipping low toward the Line.

Sixty years ago, before the *Oregon* had ever stained the reef with coal-soot, her grandfather’s canoe-steersmen had read those fires without a sextant or a logarithm table. By the warmth of the current against their dip-nets and the angle of the constellations above the masthead, they had guided their double-hulled koa dugouts across two thousand miles of empty blue swell from Tahiti to Hawaii. The ocean had possessed a rim then. A chief sailed until he found an island where the taro grew sweet in the black mud and the reef kept the sharks from the bathing-pool; and there he drove his ridge-pole into the earth and called his boundaries good.

Now Kaiulani lowered her gaze half an inch from the Southern Cross. Three miles out in the roadstead, mounted upon the fore-top of the super-dreadnought *Providentor*, two vertical beams of ten-million-candlepower carbon searchlight swept slowly across the underside of the trade-wind clouds and wiped the ancient stars out of the heavens in a white, chalky glare. Atop the Great Gnomon, the high-frequency spark-transmitters crackled with a continuous, violet hiss to relay the midnight tallies from the newly conquered customs-sheds of Madras and Colombo.

*Will it ever be enough for them, Elias?* she asked the dark water. Her small, shrunken chin sank down upon the whale-ivory hook at her throat while the night breeze rose over the bruised night-blooming jasmine in the palace courts below, carrying the faint, greasy tang of hot Borneo bunker-oil from the fleet.

The wind died against the stone. That very afternoon in the crystal dome, her grandson Kalanimoku had struck the Melbourne petition from the table, and Fleet-General Kuroda’s steel dividers had walked across the map from the mouths of the Indus toward the red sands of Aden and the silver mines of the Transvaal.

When Elias Thorne had ridden into Sacramento in fifty-two, he had sworn that the Sierra Nevada was wall enough to keep his house safe from the eastern bailiffs. Then the wall had required the sea-coast to feed the forts; and the sea-coast had required the islands to coal the cruisers; and the islands had required the rivers of China and the sheep-downs of Australia to pay the interest on the ironworks; and the ironworks had required the three hundred million souls of India to consume the surplus steel of the rolling-mills.

Now the circumference stood at the Bab-el-Mandeb and the Ural crests, and already the young men with the five-digit silver numerals on their collars were complaining in the Chancellery corridors that the German tariffs on the Rhine and the petty wars of the French generals along the Seine were disturbing the price of Pacifica nitrates at Antwerp.

An empire built upon the steam-piston and the clearing-house had no skin to hold it in. Where a living tree stops growing when its crown reaches the light of the forest, this monster of cast bronze and numbered clerks could keep its balance only by falling forward into the next continent. Tomorrow Kalanimoku and Kuroda would take the Suez ditch and the gold-reefs of Africa to protect the Indian tea-ships. Ten years hence, when her bones were dust in the Kona caves, they would steam through the Pillars of Hercules to turn the Mediterranean into a numbered barge-canal, grinding London and Berlin and Paris into the same grey, sanitary mortar as Hankow and Boston until no unnumbered village or unmeasured bushel of wheat remained between the rising and the setting of the sun. Only its own iron bowels would be left for the machine to eat.

A cold spasm of coughing shook her tiny frame beneath the sea-otter fur. The silver bell on the table behind her remained untouched. With her hands gripping the rough basalt of the rail until her ivory rings clicked against the stone, the last Queen of the Islands stared out into the blinding white sweep of the battleship searchlights across the empty sky where the stars had been.

# Chapter 24: The Atlantic Kiln

Yet if the aged Queen-Mother upon her Hawaiian terrace trembled before the specter of an infinite, all-devouring order, the Chronicler who crossed the Atlantic protectorates three months later with Emperor Kalanimoku’s Third Diplomatic Mission in the winter of 1917 to inspect the defaulted European grain-mortgages soon encountered, at the opposite end of history’s balance-beam, a spectacle far more hideous.

Over sixty years the Pacific basin had consolidated into a single, blinding sun of regulated bronze and hydroelectric power, while the old peninsula of Western Europe—stripped of its oceanic colonies and cut off from the rubber of Malaya and the oil of Sumatra, along with the silver of the Americas—had gone mad where it had not simply rotted like the widow-like docks of London.

On the continent across the Channel, the starvation of the body had bred the delirium of the brain.

On the afternoon of the nineteenth of January, 1917, hauled from the Pacifica leasehold-wharf at Havre behind an old, coal-burning French locomotive whose leaky brass flues showered the frosty Normandy hedgerows with cinders, our armored sleeping-car rolled into the Gare Saint-Lazare in Paris. We stepped down into the sour stench of a nineteenth-century siege. Horse-dung, wet charcoal-smoke, and unwashed sheepskin fouled the air.

No sixty-cycle electric turbines hummed beneath these streets. Because the German Syndicates had seized the Saar coal-fields during the Tariff War of nineteen-twelve, and the British colliers could no longer spare a ton of Cardiff steam-coal across the water, the great boulevards that Baron Haussmann had carved through the stone of Paris sixty years ago lay in a perpetual, freezing twilight. Stripped of their mantles, the bronze gas-standards along the Rue de Rivoli stood dark. At every third cross-street, squads of frostbitten boys in tall, brass-fronted shakoes and sky-blue greatcoats tended open iron braziers of smoking peat and split boulevard-chestnuts.

Our carriage rattled over the broken wood-paving of the Place de la Concorde under an escort of twelve cuirassiers whose horses showed every rib beneath their tarnished steel breastplates. Beyond the sheer poverty of the streets, these starving Europeans had summoned frantic, theatrical ghosts out of their grandfathers’ closets to warm their hands.

The Third Republic had perished five winters ago in the bread-riots following the collapse of the Suez Canal shares. Now the *Fourth Plebiscitary Empire* reigned over a shrunken, bankrupt France whose southern departments around Marseilles and Lyons had already seceded under an autonomous *Commune of the Rhone* financed by smuggled Pacifica silver; at its head stood Marshal-Protector Jean-Baptiste Victor, a former colonial brigadier from Algiers who had married a grand-niece of the house of Murat and styled himself *Regent of the Eagle*.

Every crumbling limestone facade along the Rue Royale, where the plate-glass windows of the dead luxury-shops were boarded up with rough deal planks, was plastered ten feet high with wet, screaming lithographs in red, white, and blue ink: the hooves of a white Marengo charger trampled the spiked helmet of the German Kaiser and the golden sun-and-anchor of Pacifica above the legend: *YEAR V OF THE NATIONAL REVANCHE—IRON FOR BREAD, BLOOD FOR GLORY!*

"You see, Citizen-Historian, what happens to a house when the roof-beam is sawed through and the tenants are left to stew in their own sour wine," said Prefect-Legate Shen the third. Opposite me upon the faded crimson velvet cushions of our hired landau he sat with a fur muff drawn up to his chin, his horn-rimmed spectacles misted by the raw Seine fog. Outside the cracked window-glass, three hundred French conscripts—boys of sixteen and grey-beards of fifty wearing the red trousers of eighteen-seventy and carrying obsolete single-shot Gras rifles with twenty-inch triangular bayonets—tramped through the slush behind the din of twenty brass drums and brazen bugles. "They have no Borneo benzine for an aeroplane; their treasury-francs sell at forty-two to the silver thaler in the Zurich alleys; and yet they spend their last three hundred tons of foundry-brass casting eagles for their hats and marching up and down the cobbles to keep from freezing."

Before I could reply, our carriage swung through the gilded iron gates of the Cour du Carrousel at the Tuileries, rebuilt in cheap, flaking stucco over the burned stones of seventy-one, and pulled up before the Grand Staircase.

Inside the Salle des Maréchaux, where the cold draft from the river rattled the painted canvas ceilings and the only heat came from four huge porcelain stoves stuffed with green poplar logs that wept black creosote down the marble pilasters, the court of the new Bonaparte stood assembled to receive the creditors of the earth.

Two hundred of them packed the space between the peeling gold caryatids: marshals in high jackboots and white buckskin breeches stained with stable-mud; frantic-eyed journalists and poets of the *Ligue de la Patrie* wearing tri-color sashes over their frayed evening-coats; and bony-shouldered duchesses of the Faubourg whose diamonds had long since gone into the vaults of the Market Street Mint, leaving only paste tiaras and dyed ostrich-plumes trembling above their rouged, hungry cheeks. At the head of the room, upon a gilded pine platform draped in crimson cotton velvet, stood Marshal-Protector Victor himself. He was a short, bull-necked man of sixty with waxed mustaches dyed jet-black. Enameled tin crosses of the Legion of Honor covered his chest from collarbone to belt, and while his left hand rested upon the guard of a curved Mameluke saber, his right remained thrust inside the breast of his green general’s coat in slavish imitation of the Corsican.

"The Legate of the Pacifica Chancellery will approach the Eagle!" bawled the Grand Chamberlain. He struck the parquet with an ebony staff tipped with a gilded lead bird.

Prefect Shen kept his fur gloves on. Neither did he bow from the waist as the European ambassadors had bowed before Elias Thorne on Rincon Hill thirty-six years ago. Across the cold floor in his plain, high-collared tunic of dark slate-gray wool, with the silver cipher *Zero-One-Zero-Two* gleaming at his throat, Shen walked at his unhurried Berkeley pace, halted six paces from the pine dais, and drew a single folded sheet of blue Monterey bond from his leather portfolio.

"To the Provisional Magistrate of the Seine Municipalities," Shen said in his flat, nasal French. Every imperial title was omitted. Around the porcelain stoves a furious hissing ran through the crowd of plumed marshals, and above his gold collar, Protector Victor’s fleshy jowls turned the color of raw beef-liver. "The Bureau of Integration at Thalassia acknowledges receipt of your December memorandum requesting a further moratorium upon the eighty million silver thalers advanced by the Osaka and San Francisco syndicates during the famine of nineteen-fourteen, together with your application for the purchase of four hundred thousand barrels of California mess-pork and twenty thousand tons of Chile saltpeter against ten-year bonds of the French Customs."

Protector Victor took half a step forward to the edge of the pine platform. His hand came out of his waistcoat and slapped the hilt of his curved saber with a loud metallic *clack*.

"France does not beg for pork like a coolie canton, Monsieur l'Assesseur!" Victor roared. He threw his head back toward the gallery of journalists behind the pillars so they might catch the full Napoleonic thunder of his voice. "The sword of Austerlitz and Jena holds the balance of the Rhine! If the German Emperor marches into Belgium this spring to seize the Antwerp docks, who stands between your merchant-hulks and the Prussian artillery? Five hundred thousand French bayonets! We offer the Grand Confederation an alliance of equals, the Grand Army of the Continent and the Fleet of the Ocean, provided the nitrate-ships unload at Brest before the first of March without prior hypothecation of our state railways!"

Behind his spectacles, Shen never blinked. He turned the blue sheet over between his gloved fingers.

"The Bureau of Integration has no interest in whether the German customs-guards or your own occupy the mud-flats of Belgium, Magistrate," Shen said. Two young Polytechnic naval lieutenants behind me stepped forward with a brass tripod-case as his quiet voice cut across the theatrical echo of the vault. "And a bayonet is worth precisely four cents in scrap-steel at the Hanyang furnaces. As for your state railways from Havre to Dijon, they were forfeited to the Market Street Clearing House at midnight on the first of January for non-payment of the rolling-stock annuities. If a single barrel of Chile saltpeter is unloaded at Brest before our receivers take possession of the roundhouses, the cruiser squadron at Cherbourg will shell the custom-house into the harbor."

***

While Prefect Shen was locking the bailiff’s padlock upon the rusted gates of Paris, a far more dangerous chemistry was brewing five hundred miles to the east, in the soot-darkened winter twilight of Berlin.

Against the prayers of her physicians, who warned her that the frost of the North German plain would stop an eighty-two-year-old heart that had beaten all its life among the hibiscus and the redwoods, the Queen-Mother Kaiulani had come across the continent from Genoa in the heated observation-car of the Imperial Chancery train. Her own secret agents in the Warsaw and Moscow telegraph-sheds had brought the warning. Stripped of their oceans by Elias Thorne’s iron ring, the two wounded giants of the Eurasian heartland had finally turned back to back in the snow.

On the afternoon of the twenty-fourth of January, inside the gloomy, brown-varnished Congress Hall of the Reichskanzlei on the Wilhelmstrasse, the air smelled of wet military broadcloth and synthetic coal-tar benzine, thick with the coarse Makhorka tobacco of the Omsk steppes.

Kaiulani sat in her wheeled koa-wood chair beside the roaring porcelain stove. Wrapped to her white braids in double cloaks of sea-otter fur, her tiny obsidian eyes studied the two men across the green baize table who held three hundred million white peasants under their boots: Chancellor von Bethmann’s successor, Field-Marshal von Mackensen of the German Syndicates, with the black-and-silver skull busby of the Death’s Head Hussars resting upon his bony knee; and beside him, buttoned to the chin in a long, grease-stained Cossack caftan of grey camel’s-hair, Generalissimo Brusilov of the Directory of All the Russias, that grim military dictatorship risen from the ashes of the eighty-seven revolution after Elias Thorne locked the Siberian gates at the Obi.

"Your Imperial Highness has traveled six thousand leagues through the winter to offer us the crumbs from your grandson’s table," Marshal von Mackensen said. His gloved finger pushed Kaiulani’s draft treaty—an offer of a twenty-percent reduction on Malaysian rubber duties and five million bushels of Manchurian soy-beans—back across the green baize. "For thirty years, ever since the old bandit in San Francisco cut Russia off from the Pacific and closed the China seas to German keels, you have treated the two greatest military empires of the white race like bankrupt tenants in an alley. Our Krupp furnaces at Essen have iron ore, Madam, and General Brusilov’s Directory from Moscow to the Urals has twelve million marching men who do not need a five-digit collar-tag to carry a rifle."

"And you have neither copper for your shell-casings nor nitrates for your smokeless powder, Marshal," Kaiulani said in her thin, musical whisper. She left the rejected parchment untouched on the cloth. Under the sea-otter fur, her withered fingers gripped the whale-ivory hook at her throat; it was a powder-magazine in which two blind men struck flints over an open keg. "Because your banks cannot pay silver in Market Street, you have signed the Pact of Breslau with the Moscow Directory to pool your coal and your conscripts. You think that by marching west across the Rhine this spring to plunder the French railways and seize the Antwerp docks, you will break out of the box Elias Thorne built around you."

Generalissimo Brusilov leaned his broad, bearded face toward the lamp. Across his cheekbone, the old shrapnel-scar from the Yenisei winter campaign gleamed white. "When a wolf is walled up in a stone cellar, High Commissioner, he does not ask the mason’s permission before he eats the sheep in the next stall. You took the Amur and the Baikal mines from us when the Tsar fell; you took the oceans from the Germans. Europe is all that is left on the board. If Thalassia wishes peace on the Atlantic seaboard, lift the blockade on the Silesian munition-trusts and return the Vladivostok railway to Moscow before the thaw!"

"Return a single verst of the Siberian gauge, General, and Fleet-General Kuroda’s thirty air-cruisers at Irkutsk will turn every timber-town between the Obi and the Volga into a pillar of white phosphorus before Easter," Kaiulani said. Her small chin rose an inch from the fur collar. "I did not come to Berlin in my winding-sheet to bargain away the Providentor’s border-stones. I came to tell you what will happen if your Prussian divisions cross the Meuse to strangle this pantomime Bonaparte in Paris. You will not win a six-week promenade as Bismarck did in seventy. You have no Peruvian saltpeter; you are making your nitric acid out of the air with coal-furnaces that eat half your harvest-labor. Within six months, you and the French will be bleeding each other to death in flooded ditches from the North Sea to the Alps, and when both your armies have eaten their horses, my grandson’s young prefects at Monterey will come through the Suez canal with sixty-four-thousand-ton dreadnoughts and turn Berlin and Moscow into numbered cantons like Calcutta!"

Mackensen rose stiffly to his feet. He lifted his black hussar busby from his knee while Brusilov’s heavy boot-spurs clinked together behind the table.

"Then let your grandson’s clerks bring their slide-rules to the Rhine, Madam," the Prussian said. He bowed from the neck as two giant Pomeranian grenadiers threw open the double doors at the end of the hall. "It is better to die in the iron than to rot in a coolie-shed paying sixty-percent tribute on a pound of Java coffee. The mobilization telemetry for the Western Army Group was transmitted to Cologne twenty minutes before your train crossed the Spree."

***

To the Chronicler who fled westward out of Germany aboard the last diplomatic special permitted to pass the frontier bridge at Herbesthal on the night of the third of February, 1917, the bursting of the European dam bore no likeness to the mathematical slaughter we had witnessed from the conning-tower of the *Pacifica* in the Bay of Bengal.

In the Great Arena, war had become a branch of municipal engineering, a silent, twenty-mile-distant accounting of oil-pressure and gyroscopic angles conducted by beardless youths who smelled of soap and cordite. Here in the narrow, over-populated cockpit of the old continent, where three hundred million starving, pride-maddened Europeans had been penned behind Elias Thorne’s tariff-walls for half a century without an outlet to the sea, war returned as a mediaeval plague armed with the cast-offs of the machine age.

At four o’clock on the freezing, sleet-lashed morning of the fourth of February, our train was shunted onto a high stone viaduct overlooking the gorge of the Meuse three miles below Liège, while the Belgian customs-guards tore up the track ahead of us with crowbars.

Down in the pitch-black valley below our carriage windows, the air smelled of wet coal-slag and burning beet-sugar factories, fouled by the rank, ammoniacal reek of forty thousand Russian and Prussian draft-horses churning the frozen turnip-fields into mud. Darkness hid the clouds where no searchlights swept from sixty-four-thousand-ton ships and no duralumin air-cruisers hovered at five thousand feet to correct the fire by wireless.

Instead, across five miles of river-mist, the night split open with the low, continuous, red-orange sheet-lightning of three thousand short-range Krupp and Putilov field-howitzers firing black-powder and cheap, smoky ammonal shells hub-to-hub from the apple-orchards.

Through my field-glasses, by the blinding magnesium flare of the parachute-rockets that the Belgian fortress-gunners were firing from the concrete cupolas of Fort Barchon, the first waves of the German-Russian *Sturm-Korps* went down to the riverbank.

They did not advance in open skirmish-lines like our Polytechnic cadets in the Sierra. Driven forward by the famine in their bellies and the revolvers of their syndicate-officers behind them, sixty thousand grey-coated Brandenburgers and sheepskin-clad Don infantrymen charged shoulder-to-shoulder in dense, nineteenth-century phalanxes across the pontoon-bridges, singing old Lutheran hymns and Tsar’s marches while the French divisions of Marshal-Protector Victor, who had marched north from Sedan three days earlier in their bright red trousers and tarnished brass cuirasses, met them on the western dike with fixed twenty-inch bayonets and hand-cranked Mitrailleuse batteries.

When the two walls of starving men collided in the red mud between the burning farmhouses, the artillery on both ridges kept firing; the Prussian and French batteries simply lowered their sights and pumped shrapnel straight into the screaming, locked mass of their own infantry.

In twenty minutes, the ice-choked channel of the Meuse below our viaduct was jammed from bank to bank with a solid, undulating weir of sky-blue coats and grey sheepskins wedged among disemboweled artillery-mules, over whose backs the second reserve regiments of Moscow and Lyons were already scrambling with clubbed rifles and butcher-knives.

"Close the mahogany shutter, Citizen-Historian," Prefect-Legate Shen said behind me in the warm, electrically lit saloon-car. He remained in his leather armchair, entering the morning depreciation of the Paris-Orleans railway shares into his pocket ledger with a gold-nibbed fountain pen. "There is no military instruction to be derived from watching paupers beat each other to death with iron bars in a ditch. The old man in San Francisco pulled the linch-pin out of their wagon forty years ago when he turned the trade-routes into the Pacific; now the wheels have come off on the hill, and the load is going into the ravine. Let us hope the engine-driver clears the Calais switch before noon, or we shall miss the *Empress of Oahu* at Southampton."

***

Yet when our fast turbine-liner steamed through the Golden Gate twenty-two days later, on the first morning of March, the smoke of the burning Meuse had traveled faster through the submarine cables than our propellers could cut the water.

For the first time since the funeral of Elias Thorne in eighty-seven, the Imperial Court had left the warm coral lagoons of Thalassia to sit in the cold stone fortress of the continental forge.

Up on the crest of Rincon Hill, above a San Francisco where every dry-dock at Hunters Point and every blast-furnace along the Potrero shore roared day and night under a low ceiling of greasy black oil-smoke, the great bronze doors of the Council Chamber stood bolted against the spring rain. Inside the redwood-vaulted hall, the old silver curule chair had given way to a raised metallic tribune wired directly to the subterranean telegraph-vaults below, where the twenty-six-year-old Sacred Emperor Kalanimoku stood without his yellow *mamo* feathers.

He wore the dark blue, double-breasted coat of an Admiral of the Ocean. His broad brown hands were planted flat upon the illuminated glass chart of the North Atlantic bolted over the old porphyry steps. Around him stood the young wolf-pack of the third generation: Fleet-General Kuroda with his duralumin calculator gleaming at his belt, Prefect-Chancellor Shen, and twelve thirty-year-old Polytechnic Marshals of the Aerial and Submarine Boards whose silver five-digit collar-ciphers caught the cold gray light from the seaward casements.

Only two figures in the room belonged to the century that had built the walls: old Field-Marshal Marcus Vance, sitting stiff-legged upon a camp-stool by the dead hearth with his hands folded over his cane; and in the center of the brass meridian lines, wheeled straight up to the edge of the glass map in her black koa-wood chair, the Queen-Mother Kaiulani.

She had survived the Atlantic gale and the snowy crossing of the Rockies on five grains of digitalis a day; her face beneath her black bombazine hood was the color of wood-ash, and her breathing sounded like dry leaves scraping across a gravestone, yet her small, shrunken hand struck the brass rim of the Atlantic chart with a force that made the red glass markers along the English Channel rattle.

"Twelve armored divisions of the First and Fourth Continental Armies, and thirty dreadnoughts of the *Thorne* and *Kalanimoku* classes to assemble at Halifax and the Azores by the fifteenth of April!" Kaiulani’s dry, whistling contralto cut through the hum of the chart-transformers as she read the mobilization warrant lying beneath her grandson’s palm. "Have the fumes of the Osaka furnaces rotted the brains in your skulls? Why are there Pacifica transport-markers laid down upon the ports of Brest and Antwerp?"

Fleet-General Kuroda met the gaze of the eighty-two-year-old woman who had signed his father’s commission. He tapped the red-lit cluster of bulbs marking the mouth of the Scheldt with his steel dividers.

"On Tuesday morning, Your Imperial Highness, Field-Marshal von Mackensen’s Russo-German spearheads broke the French line at Namur and entered Brussels," Kuroda said in his flat, uninflected Monterey voice. "Marshal-Protector Victor is surrounded in the Lille fortresses with the remnant of the French army, and the German vanguard is four leagues from the Antwerp quays. Within ten days, the Berlin-Moscow Directory will hold every deep-water slip and coal-mine from the Baltic to the Bay of Biscay. Our clearing-houses in San Francisco and Canton hold four hundred and eighty million silver thalers in defaulted French and Belgian railway-mortgages, and thirty percent of our surplus nitrate and copper exports depend upon the Rotterdam barge-traffic. If we allow Mackensen and Brusilov to weld the European continent into a single autarkic fortress, the Atlantic market is closed to our factories forever."

"Then let the Atlantic market sink into the mud where Elias Thorne left it!" Kaiulani cried. She leaned forward in her wheeled chair until her whale-ivory clasp swung clear of her shrunken breast, her obsidian eyes fixed past Kuroda upon the cold, pale-gray stare of her grandson Kalanimoku. "Listen to me, boy! I sat beside your grandfather on this very floor when the German Count and the Englishman came begging for twenty shiploads of California flour! Do you know why Elias tore up the tracks in Pennsylvania and turned his back on New York? Because he knew that the Atlantic is a tar-pit! For three hundred years the white tribes of that peninsula have done nothing but cut one another’s throats over five acres of turnip-mud along the Rhine!"

Kalanimoku held his grandmother’s stare; his heavy, square-hewn jaw, the legacy of the Kentucky squatter’s son looking strange and terrifying beneath the smooth bronze skin of a Maui king, set hard against his gold-braided collar.

"When my grandfather sat in this room, Grandmother, a steamer took nineteen days to cross from Yokohama, and an army fought with horses and black powder," the young Emperor said, his practiced, gravelly bark making old Marcus Vance’s white eyebrows twitch beside the hearth. "Today, if von Mackensen puts German submarines into the Brest pens and Russian conscripts into the Essen rolling-mills, within five years their long-range dirigibles will be dropping picric-acid shells onto the locks at Panama and the oil-wells at Baku! There is no longer room upon this planet for two balance-sheets. Either Thalassia audits the books of Berlin before harvest, or our sons will be fighting the Europeans along the Mississippi and the Indus!"

"You are marching not to protect Panama, Kalanimoku, but because you have built leviathan hammers at Waipahu and your clerks cannot bear to see an unflattened nail on the other side of the earth!" Kaiulani’s voice cracked into a harsh, tearing cough that stained her black lace handkerchief with a bright fleck of scarlet. She crushed the linen in her fist before the chamberlains could step forward. Her trembling right index finger pointed down at the inlaid brass circle of the Pacific Ocean beneath her wheels. "Look at the floor under your boots! From the ice of the Bering Bridge to the reefs of Tasmania, from the temples of Benares to the locks of Darien, you hold four hundred and fifty million human beings in the palm of your hand! You have the rice, the gold, the oil, and the iron of three-quarters of the globe! If you send two million of our boys across the Atlantic ditch to police the ruins of Paris and Moscow, you will never bring the legions home again! The pivot will slip from the sea back to the land, and this empire will bleed its heart out in the snows of Poland just as Bonaparte did!"

Across the hearth, old Field-Marshal Marcus Vance slowly raised his white head from his cane.

"Her Highness’s logistics are correct, Majesty," the fifty-nine-year-old Marshal said quietly, his voice like two dry stones rubbed together in the silence of the vault. "To maintain forty divisions across three thousand miles of Atlantic water against twelve million Russian and German rifles will consume eighty thousand tons of Borneo fuel-oil and four million silver thalers a day. Within eighteen months, you will have to double the rice-tax in Hankow and re-introduce the blood-conscription in the American cantons. The boiler is not riveted for that pressure."

Young Emperor Kalanimoku looked slowly from the broken old general by the cold fireplace to the dying eighty-two-year-old woman in her chair. He said nothing. He turned his head toward Fleet-General Kuroda and Prefect Shen.

"The Marshal Emeritus and the Queen-Mother are tired after their voyage from Europe," Kalanimoku said, his hand descending toward the heavy bronze seal-press on the glass table while outside in the rain-swept plaza of Rincon Hill the steam-whistles of the Potrero troop-trains blew the assembly-call, "and they are thinking of an ocean that still had two shores. Chancellor Shen, prepare the Imperial Warrant for the Armed Neutrality Escort. Fleet-General Kuroda will assume command of the vanguard at Gibraltar on the first of May, and he will hold the Rock and the Channel approaches until both European wolves have bled themselves white enough to beg for our bailiffs."

***

To the Chronicler who went back across the Atlantic that May aboard the supply-colliers of Kuroda’s vanguard, as the gray, turbine-driven mountains of the Pacifica fleet dropped their anchors across the mouth of the Tagus and the Strait of Gibraltar like turnkeys locking the iron grate of a madhouse, the wisdom of the young Emperor’s delay soon manifested itself in a horror that neither Thucydides nor the prophets of Israel had ever been required to set down in ink.

For Kuroda did not land a single marine upon the beaches of France or Flanders that summer. Anchored six miles off the chalk cliffs of Dover and the sand-bars of the Scheldt, with their twenty-two-inch rifles trained indifferently upon the shore and their wireless masts intercepting every frantic cipher from Berlin and Paris to Whitehall, the squadrons of the Great Arena simply kept the ring while the tribes of the Atlantic tore their own ancestral house down upon their heads.

It was in the first week of June, 1917, after Marshal-Protector Victor’s desperate counter-offensive along the Somme had shattered against the Russo-German barbed wire and the starving British Cabinet in Westminster had secretly leased the Harwich coaling-slips to the Prussian torpedo-flotillas in exchange for ten shiploads of Pomeranian rye, that the dying Bonapartist regime in Paris struck its last, blind blow across the ditch.

I stood at midnight on the sixth of June upon the roof-leads of the Pacifica Debt-Receivership House at Greenwich, four miles down the river from St. Paul’s, where our numbered Cantonese and Virginian clerks were cataloguing the impounded bullion-books of the Royal Naval College by the light of portable storage-batteries. The moonless night was warm and stiflingly still. Down in the dark, unlighted bend of the Pool of London, where no coal-fire had burned since the winter defaults, the smells of low-tide mud and rotting wharf-pilings mingled with the sour turnip-gruel of three million sleeping paupers between the brick warehouses.

At twelve minutes past midnight, the silence above the Surrey hills broke. In place of the clean, high-pitched hum of our Osaka turbine-planes came the heavy lawn-mower throb of two hundred low-compression Renault and Gnome petroleum-engines burning crude shale-naphtha.

Out of the low cloud-bank over Croydon, flying at barely nine hundred feet above the chimney-pots because their warped wooden propellers could lift their loads no higher, came the last reserves of the *Flotte Aérienne de la Revanche*: forty lumbering, canvas-covered Voisin triplanes and twelve sausage-shaped, non-rigid hydrogen dirigibles painted dead coal-black with lamp-soot.

The Parliament embankments stood stripped of anti-aircraft batteries. The British twelve-pounders had been shipped to the Bengal front three years ago and now sat as rusting trophies in the parks of Monterey. Only a single ragged volley of Lee-Enfield rifle-fire crackled up from the veteran watchmen at the Tower of London. Then, with a nineteen-year-old tubercular count from Lyons chained to the steering-wheel—as we learned afterward from the wreckage—the lead French dirigible dropped its nose to five hundred feet above the timber-yards of Southwark and pulled the brass trip-cord of its ballast-racks.

The French arsenals at St. Etienne had run out of copper driving-bands and picric acid in April, leaving them without high-explosive steel shells. Five thousand forty-gallon iron drums tumbled from the racks instead. They held a thick, syrupy mixture of boiled Gascon pine-turpentine, white phosphorus, and raw Baku petroleum residue hoarded since the tariff blockade.
