The first hundred drums struck the dry, tarred deal roofs of the Bermondsey tea-wharves and the medieval timber-framed tenements along Thames Street simultaneously.

A hollow, drumming roar like giant hailstones smashing through rotten slate echoed across the Pool. Three seconds later, across a mile-wide front along the wharves, a curtain of blinding greenish-white phosphorus flame leaped two hundred feet straight into the air and turned the lead dome of St. Paul’s across the water into a globe of blood-red copper.

The heat-draft from the river struck our faces four miles away at Greenwich like the opening of an iron-foundry door. In the lenses of my binoculars, a stray Maxim bullet from the Victoria dock-guard pierced the second French airship directly through its hydrogen-valve.

The two-hundred-foot envelope split from bow to rudder in a rolling, saffron-colored thunderbolt. Two tons of flaming rubberized silk and melting aluminum girders rained straight down onto the crowded shingle roofs of Cheapside and Threadneedle Street.

Within forty minutes, the fire-storm had created its own hurricane. The Wapping hydraulic pumping-stations lacked their brass pistons, stripped out months before to pay the autumn rice-warrants. In the streets below, while a sixty-mile-an-hour gale of superheated air sucked the flames through the narrow lanes from the Bank of England to the Fleet Ditch, the bucket-brigades of old men and women stood in the boiling white smoke with empty wooden pails.

The oak belfries of St. Mary-le-Bow and St. Bride’s caught fire. Swinging wildly in the hurricane draft without a human hand on the ropes, the bells of both churches rang out until the ancient bronze melted in its cages and poured down through the burning rafters like white-hot syrup. Five hundred thousand screaming, half-naked shadows tumbled down onto the muddy foreshore of Queenhithe and Blackfriars. They drove horses, hand-carts, and hospital-stretchers into the oily river. Above their heads, the stone arches of London Bridge disappeared behind a solid cataract of burning turpentine that floated across the surface of the Thames from bank to bank.

Beside me on the Greenwich roof, Junior Prefect Adams, Candidate Three-Three-Zero-Nine of the Seattle class, kept his eye to the brass theodolite, plotting the bearing of the fallen French airship.

"The Royal Exchange roof has just collapsed into the bullion-vaults, Citizen-Historian," the boy said. He wiped a flake of greasy black Thames soot from his celluloid collar while the roar of the dying metropolis four miles upstream shook the lead plates beneath our soles. "That will save our engineering gangs three weeks of demolition-dynamite when the foreclosure warrant takes effect in July. If the wind holds from the south-southeast until daybreak, the entire commercial parish from the Tower to the Temple will be cleared to the Roman brick."

***

Nine thousand miles away from that pitch-black cauldron on the Thames, the June morning broke over the coral lagoons of Thalassia in a haze of pale pearl and Sunset Gold so pure that the distant smoke of the inter-island fruit-steamers looked like strokes of a sable brush across Chinese silk.

Lady Kaiulani had left the Whispering Gallery of the Senate for good. During the three months since her return from San Francisco, her small body had shrunk until she weighed scarcely more than a ten-year-old child; the dropsy had risen above her knees, and the physicians had confined her wheels to the tiled, shady veranda of the Queen’s Marine Audit Pavilion. Built of white coral stone and dark koa-wood directly atop the sea-wall at the entrance to the Waipahu commercial basin, the low, open-sided loggia caught the trade-wind coming in clean and damp over the breakers.

Her body was anchored to the stone like a barnacle. Beneath her white linen sun-veil, her dark, sunken eyes held their terrible focus. Across her knees, upon a light board of polished cedar, lay the daily clearing-sheets of the Neutrality Syndicate, printed in violet ink upon thin rice-paper.

Fifty yards below her veranda balustrade, incoming and outgoing merchant hulls packed the deep-water channel of the Pearl Lochs commercial canal. Their screws churned the green harbor water into a permanent creamy lather of propeller-wash, raising the smells of warm coconut-oil and wet hemp mingled with the sharp tang of fresh red-lead paint.

Two electric harbor-tugs towed a ten-thousand-ton Swedish-flagged tramp-steamer slowly past the customs-buoy. Her rusty iron plates wore the broad white vertical stripes of the *International Relief Commission*, freshly painted, though her waterline sat four feet below the Plimsoll mark with the weight of the Hanyang pig-iron and Sacramento nitro-cellulose in her holds. Scarcely a cable’s length astern of her followed a Dutch four-masted auxiliary bark out of Rotterdam. Her deck-winches clanked rhythmically as the Cantonese stevedores hoisted crates of seized French gallery-paintings, Sèvres porcelain, and stripped church-bell bronze out of her hatches onto the Mint lighters.

"Read me the Lisbon and Gothenburg transfer-totals again, Malia," Kaiulani whispered. Her thin, blue-veined hand lay motionless beside the untouched cup of papaya-broth on her tray. Her niece, a forty-year-old woman in the severe gray linen dress of the Insular Secretariat, turned the ledger-page against the breeze.

"For the week ending June the ninth, Aunt," Malia read in her low, clear Hawaiian voice, "the Neutrality Clearing Board at the Azores delivered to the Swedish intermediaries at Gothenburg forty-two thousand tons of refined Chilean nitrates, eighteen thousand barrels of Borneo lubricating-oil, and four hundred thousand obsolete model-ninety-eight Sacramento magazine-rifles, against payment of sixty-four million gold marks drawn upon the collateral of the Krupp and Siemens machine-tool patents and the freehold deeds of the Westphalian coal-seams."

"And the Spanish frontier account at San Sebastian?" Kaiulani asked. Below the seawall, the Swedish steamer dipped her patched blue-and-yellow ensign to the bronze statue of the Providentor on the canal-head.

"Delivered to the agents of Marshal-Protector Victor via the Pyrenees narrow-gauge," Malia continued, her finger sliding down the violet column, "thirty thousand tons of Manchurian soy-meal, twelve thousand cases of Monterey picric-acid boosters, and six hundred reconditioned Curtiss rotary-engines, against the mortgage of the Lyons silk-looms and the final surrender of the Madagascar and West African harbour-leases. The net specie balance accruing to the Thalassia Treasury for the seven days, after deducting the coal-charges of Fleet-General Kuroda’s blockade squadrons at Gibraltar, stands at nineteen million, four hundred thousand silver thalers."

Kaiulani closed her eyes against the blinding dazzle of the sun on the water.

Across the lagoon, the electric gantry-cranes hummed a deep note as they swung another twenty-ton load of Sacramento guncotton down into the belly of a neutral Norwegian hull. *Nineteen million thalers a week,* she thought. *In San Francisco three months ago, I wept blood into my handkerchief to keep Kalanimoku from sending our boys to die in the mud of the Meuse. I thought I was saving the Pacific from the furnace.*

She opened her eyes. Down on the rice-paper, the neat violet figures lay cleaner and infinitely more lethal than the sixty-four-thousand-ton dreadnoughts lying off Dover.

Kalanimoku and young Chancellor Shen had spared every cadet from landing in France. By locking the gates of the ocean at Gibraltar and opening a pawnbroker’s wicket in the Azores, the priesthood of the slide-rule had found how to conquer Europe without firing a single Pacifica rifle.

Whenever the Russo-German divisions pushed too close to the Channel ports, Shen’s agents at San Sebastian released ten thousand tons of Californian smokeless powder to the French at three hundred percent interest so that Marshal Victor’s conscripts might blow another fifty thousand Brandenburgers into the mud. The moment the French bugles sounded too loud along the Somme, the Swedish steamers unloaded forty shiploads of Hanyang shell-steel and Montana copper at Gothenburg to keep Field-Marshal von Mackensen’s howitzers barking until autumn.

They tended the war like a pair of Cantonese lime-burners feeding wet brushwood and coal-slack into a kiln. A turn of the telegraph-key adjusted the draft so that the fire burned on until every ounce of gold and every title-deed, along with every factory-lathe and every twenty-year-old boy between the Atlantic surf and the Ural mountains, had been rendered down into grey ash and mortgaged paper in the vaults of Market Street.

"Look at the Dutch ship at the third slip, Malia," Kaiulani said. Her withered chin trembled slightly as the electric crane hoisted a massive, eight-foot bronze altar-cross and four bundled tapestries from the Cathedral of Rheims out of the Hollander’s fore-hold in a cargo-net and swung them over the concrete coping toward the disinfection-sheds. "When Elias took the silver out of the Comstock, he left the rock in the mountain. My grandson is buying the skin off their dead children’s backs with our spoiled warehouse-powder, and calling it the Peace of the Pivot."

# Chapter 25: The Brussels Liquidation

By the winter of 1918, the kiln was cold.

The European Civil War ended without a Waterloo, and without even such a formal, sword-surrendering ceremony as we had witnessed upon the sun-baked bricks of the Shwedagon Pagoda four years earlier. The fire on the continent simply went out for want of timber to burn.

After the typhus and the black influenza of the second winter had carried off four million half-starved soldiers in the flooded trenches along the Rhine, and the great peasant mutinies of March had hung Generalissimo Brusilov from the Kremlin wall and driven Marshal-Protector Victor to blow his own brains out in a cellar at Tours, neither a government in Berlin nor an army in France retained the strength to lift a rifle.

On the tenth of May, 1918, Fleet-General Kuroda’s white-painted hospital-cruisers and engineering-transports steamed up the Scheldt into the blackened, silent basins of Antwerp. The coastal batteries stood silent beneath the sun-and-anchor flag. Along five miles of ruined stone quays, where two hundred thousand emaciated Belgian, French, and German deserters in rotting rags of sky-blue and field-gray had thrown their rifles into the canal, the survivors knelt side by side on the cobbles in the spring drizzle and held out rusty tin pannikins toward the steam-winches as our Cantonese quartermasters lowered the first nets of California salt-pork and San Joaquin barley-biscuit.

Four months later, the Chronicler sat in the newly whitewashed hall of the old Reichstag in Berlin. Prefect-Chancellor Shen and the twenty-eight-year-old Sacred Emperor Kalanimoku were promulgating the *Organic Act of the European Protectorate* before the assembled municipal receivers of the Western Peninsula. The chamber had the quiet, antiseptic finality of an operating amphitheater after the amputation is done.

All traces of the old monarchies and republics had gone into the dust-bins with the broken plaster of the victory columns. Outside in the Tiergarten, where the bronze statues of the Hohenzollerns and Bismarck had already been unbolted from their red granite pedestals and loaded onto flatcars for the Hanyang scrap-furnaces, gangs of former Prussian guardsmen and French cuirassiers in identical, unbadged overalls of coarse gray Canton denim widened the Charlottenburg railway embankment from the old European four-foot-eight gauge to the six-foot Imperial standard. Samoan and Californian provost-corporals kept watch.

Inside, carbolic whitewash and fresh Oregon pine-varnish stung the nostrils, sharp above the hot insulation of the sixty-cycle transformers that our Osaka engineers had installed in the cellar to replace the burned-out German dynamos.

The floor held neither kings nor parliaments. Ranged upon twelve rows of plain, numbered iron benches sat the newly appointed *Syndics of the Fourteen European Cantons*: sixty gaunt, hollow-cheeked former civil-servants, railway-directors, and municipal engineers from London, Paris, Berlin, Vienna, and Warsaw. Each wore a dark gray alpaca coat with a brass six-digit debtor-cipher pinned to his left lapel.

"Under Article Seven of the Brussels Liquidation Accord," Prefect-Chancellor Shen read from the steel podium. His horn-rimmed spectacles flashed in the white electric glare of the skylight, and his flat, unhurried voice echoed across the silent benches. "The historical boundaries and customs-barriers of the kingdoms and republics heretofore known as Great Britain, France, Germany, Italy, Austria, and Western Russia are abolished in perpetuity. From the first of October, nineteen-eighteen, the peninsula west of the Vistula and the Dnieper is constituted as the Autonomous Fiscal Territory of the *European Confederation*, divided into fourteen numbered industrial and agricultural cantons under the supreme supervision of the High Commissioner at Antwerp."

Down in the second row sat the Syndic for the Third Rhine Canton, a former director of the Essen steel-works named Hugenberg. His left cheek still bore a purple carbuncle from the winter turnip-scurvy. Slowly, he raised a trembling hand that held a printed balance-sheet.

"Citizen-Chancellor," the German said in thick, hesitant English. He rose half out of his iron seat; by the wall, two Polytechnic cadets shifted their hands to their pistol-belts. "By the schedule attached to Article Nine, eighty percent of the coal and pig-iron output of the Ruhr and Silesian basins is hypothecated for ninety-nine years to the Market Street Mint to service the Neutrality War-Loans, while our universities at Jena, Göttingen, and Paris are forbidden to maintain laboratories of chemistry or ballistics above the third primary grade. If our young men are excluded from the Monterey and New Edo polytechnic examinations, and our blast-furnaces work only for export to Osaka, by what trade are the two hundred million inhabitants of these fourteen cantons to purchase their winter wheat?"

Up on the dais, beneath the newly erected bronze relief of the *Sacred Compass*, Emperor Kalanimoku left his electric baton untouched. His heavy, bronze-skinned hands rested upon his knees inside his dark blue Admiral’s coat. Past the German’s bald head, his cold, pale-gray eyes stared as if out over four thousand miles of empty salt water.

Prefect Shen answered without lifting his gaze from the parchment.

"The demographic census completed by Assessor Adams in August indicates that the urban population of the European peninsula exceeds the agricultural carrying-capacity of its soil by sixty-two million souls, Citizen-Syndic," Shen said. The parchment rustled dryly under his fingers. Outside in the Friedrichstrasse, the deep, brassy hoot of a broad-gauge Baldwin locomotive announced the departure of the noon labor-train for the Siberian timber-camps. "To relieve your municipalities of that burden, the Bureau of Integration has authorized a permanent annual draft of four million unmarried European males and females between the ages of sixteen and twenty-six to be transported via the Suez and Panama liners to the rubber-plantations of Borneo, the guano-beds of Peru, and the new irrigation-trenches of the Australian interior. Those who remain behind in the fourteen cantons will find ample subsistence in maintaining the tourist-monuments of Rome and Paris for our vacationing prefects, and weaving flax-linen for the Commissariat. Citizen Hugenberg, you may sit down; the High Commissioner’s train for Geneva leaves at four, and we have still to sign the indenture for the removal of the Louvre and Vatican collections to the museum at Thalassia."

The German sank back onto the iron bench. He buried his grey face in his hands. From my historiographer’s desk, I looked toward the tall window behind the dais, where through the rain-streaked glass a squad of Cantonese and Hawaiian riggers hoisted the thirty-foot banner of Imperial Blue and Sunset Gold to the top of the Brandenburg Gate; the long, bloody river of human history, begun three thousand years ago when the Greeks sailed out of Aulis toward the East, had run backward into the great ocean and frozen into a single, shoreless sheet of blue ice.

"Hand me the crimson sealing-wax, Citizen-Historian," Prefect Shen said. He turned half a pace from the podium to hold his brass stamp over the alcohol-lamp on my table, his cold, spectacled eyes meeting mine across the tiny blue flame. "The local syndics have accepted the liquidation schedules. All that remains is for the Queen-Mother’s train to meet the Atlantic Expeditionary transports at the Swiss lakes so her hand may close the ledger."

***

Seven days later, the October wind off the snow-fields of Mont Blanc swept the grey, choppy waters of Lake Leman. It carried the raw, sulfurous stench of Welsh slack-coal and the metallic pounding of ten thousand Cantonese railway-navvies re-laying the Geneva marshaling-yards to the six-foot Imperial gauge.

Inside the glass-walled conservatory of the Hôtel Beau-Rivage, where sixty years before the idle dukes of the old continent had sipped their mineral waters before Elias Thorne’s tariffs broke their banks, Lady Kaiulani sat before a long table of polished Swiss walnut. She was eighty-four years old this autumn. The Atlantic crossing from Halifax aboard the rolling flagship of the Expeditionary Force, followed by the jolting military train up from the ruined docks of Marseilles, had drained the last drop of warmth from her shrunken limbs. In her heavy gown of dark mourning silk, with a cape of Russian sable drawn tight around her narrow shoulders and the ancient carved tooth of the Oahu chiefs resting cold against her collarbone, she resembled an obsidian idol carried in the baggage-train of her grandson’s legions.

Outside on the stone quay, the Atlantic deployment ground on. Forty steam-traction lorries of Fleet-General Kuroda’s Gibraltar Vanguard rumbled past the iron palings; their solid rubber tires crushed the frozen dahlia-beds while squads of Samoan and Californian military police unloaded crates of Hollerith sorting-machines and spools of copper field-wire into the requisitioned casino.

Before her table stood the last titular magistrates of the Western world: a trembling sub-deacon of the Roman Curia in a mud-stained soutane; a former federal councillor of the Swiss cantons with a piece of hempen twine in place of his gold watch-chain; and General von Seeckt of the dissolved German Quartermaster Staff, his left arm strapped in a pasteboard splint.

"The military railway from Marseilles to Basel passed the load-test at six this morning, Your Imperial Highness," Fleet-General Kuroda said. He stepped in from the terrace with the lake-sleet melting upon the dark blue shoulders of his boat-cloak, and laid a heavy parchment folio bound in grey vulcanized gutta-percha directly across the walnut table. "The first six-foot-gauge grain-trains from the Genoa grain-elevators are already unloading San Joaquin barley at Zurich, and our garrison gunboats have been lowered by crane into the lake. The delegates have examined the *Geneva Accord*."

Kaiulani kept her gaze lowered. Her dark, sunken eyes remained fixed upon the parchment title-page, where the scraper had erased the double-headed eagles of Austria and Russia and the lilies of France to make room for the single, geometric Sun-and-Anchor of the Pivot.

*So it is finished, Elias.* The cold draft from the terrace made the dry skin of her knuckles ache as her hand reached toward the gold fountain-pen in the stand. *Sixty-five years ago you sat in a leaky adobe hut at Clark’s Point with a stolen map of the Sacramento river on your knee and told Caleb Vance that the East was a dead tree waiting for the axe. You died in your iron corset before you could cross the Mississippi, and I buried you under four miles of salt water so your shadow would not swallow the sun. Yet your dead hand has reached across two oceans and locked the doors of Charlemagne’s house.*

"Does the Chancery of Thalassia guarantee the municipal salt-ration if we sign away the customs of the Rhine and the Danube?" General von Seeckt asked hoarsely. His solitary hand twitched toward his empty belt.

"The Bureau of Integration guarantees three hundred grams of barley-meal and twenty grams of cured pork per diem to every registered laborer who presents his brass thumb-tag at the cantonment wicket," Kaiulani said, her dry, papery whisper barely clearing the rim of her sable collar. She did not wait for the German to bow. She pressed the gold nib to the gutta-percha vellum and traced the single, spiky Hawaiian word, *Kaiulani R.*, beneath the seal of the Protectorate.

***

That November, the Chronicler traveled southward from Geneva by the newly widened military track through the Mont Cenis tunnel, embarking at Genoa aboard the dispatch-cruiser *Manila* to inspect the winter moorings of the Gibraltar Vanguard. The transformation of the ancient world’s cradle surpassed all the marvels of the Indian war.

For three millennia, the inland sea that washes the marbles of Athens and the basalt moles of Ostia had been the private lake of the Caucasian race. Upon these blue, tideless waters the triremes of Themistocles had broken the Persian king; across these swells the legions of Scipio had carried the bronze wolf to Carthage, and the galleys of Venice and Don John had locked their oars against the Turk. To the European mind, the Mediterranean was the very *Mare Nostrum*, the warm hearth-fire around which all philosophy, law, and dominion had been warmed while the outer oceans lay in darkness.

Now, on a clear, sharp morning in late November, 1918, I stood upon the armored bridge-wing of the *Manila* as our squadron steamed at fourteen knots through the narrow Strait of Messina between Sicily and the toe of the Italian boot.

Hot Borneo fuel-oil and stinging salt spray blew across the deck, sharp with the chemical tang of the picric-acid smoke-floats that our torpedo-destroyers were dropping along the five-fathom line to calibrate the coast-defense range-finders.

Ahead of our clipper bow, riding in single-line-ahead formation across the exact channel where Ulysses had steered between Scylla and Charybdis, steamed the Second Battle Squadron of the Pacific Fleet: the *Kamehameha*, the *Satsuma*, the *San Joaquin*, and the *Monterey*. Their towering, pagoda-like tripod masts and dark Imperial Blue hulls cast shadows half a mile long across the wine-dark water. From their maintrucks snapped the Golden Sun, while upon their broad teak quarterdecks, companies of Japanese and Hawaiian marines in slate-gray wool performed morning bayonet-drill to the brassy, syncopated blare of the Imperial Anthem.

Every European warship between the Pillars of Hercules and the mouth of the Nile had been swept from the sea. At the foot of the white limestone cliffs of Taormina, beneath the broken brick arches of the Greco-Roman theater where Aeschylus had once been recited to the colonists of Syracuse, two hulking, rust-streaked Italian dreadnoughts, the *Dante Alighieri* and the *Conte di Cavour*, lay beached upon the shingle with their twelve-inch turrets cut open by oxy-acetylene torches. Four hundred Cantonese scrap-cutters swarmed over their decks like blue ants. They loaded the Krupp armor-plate into Osaka ore-barges to be shipped back through the Suez ditch and melted down into railway-chairs for the Manchurian branch-lines.

"The semaphore station atop Mount Etna reports the grain-convoy from Alexandria has cleared the Malta channel, Citizen-Historian," said Commander Hirose at my elbow. He lowered his Zeiss binoculars and glanced down at the duralumin gyro-repeater beside the binnacle. Born in the Nagasaki naval wards and educated at the Berkeley sheds, the thirty-two-year-old captain looked up at the snow-streaked volcanic cone of Sicily with the mild, detached curiosity of a botanist examining a pressed fern. "Have you been ashore at Naples yet? The Prefect of the Seventh Italian Canton has cleared the beggars out of the Pompeii excavations and laid an electric tramway from the quay to the forum. Our stokers go up in parties of fifty on Sundays to photograph one another beside the plaster casts."

Beyond the swinging twenty-two-inch muzzles of our forward turret rose the ancient Calabrian hills, where a giant whitewashed cipher, *CANTON XI : SECTOR 4*, had been painted in fifty-foot numerals across the granite cliff below a ruined Norman watchtower.

The wheel of providence had completed its revolution. The barbarians of the outer water, those children of the Polynesian coral-reefs and the Californian gold-gulches and the Japanese fishing-villages that neither Caesar nor Alexander had ever dreamed existed beyond the rim of the flat earth, now kept the peace of the Roman sea with turbine-driven iron; meanwhile, the descendants of the senators and the doges stood bareheaded on the seawall to sell a basket of oranges for a copper token stamped in San Francisco.

***

Yet the earth is older than the slide-rule; when an empire bolts the doors of the world so tight that not a single rifle can be lifted against its prefects from the Vistula to the Sacramento, nature herself reaches into the mud for a weapon impervious to eighteen inches of Krupp steel.

In the middle of January, 1919, six weeks after the hospital-liner *Solace* brought the Queen-Mother Kaiulani home from Marseilles through the Suez locks to the wheeled chair upon the seaward veranda of the Coral Pavilion she would never leave again, the first queer, unindexed numbers appeared upon the perforated manila cards of the Bureau of Integration at Thalassia.

The trade-wind had died completely away on that sultry, overcast afternoon. The peacock-blue water of the Pearl Lochs lagoon lay as flat and oily as a sheet of warm lead, and the heavy, sickening perfume of over-ripe night-jasmine and hot transformer oil from the Molokai stations filled the open-sided loggia where Kaiulani rested among her linen pillows. On the bamboo veranda table, the portable Hollerith tabulator that Prefect-Chancellor Shen had set up gave its slow, rhythmic *whir-click, whir-click*.

At eighty-four, the white pearly cataract of the islands clouded her sight, turning the distant hulls of the super-dreadnoughts out in the Waipahu roadstead into grey ghosts floating in milk, yet her hearing remained as sharp as a night-heron’s.

"Why has the sorting-needle stopped on the Antwerp and Genoa cards, Shen?" Kaiulani asked. Her thin, dark fingers rested upon the curved bone hook at her breast while the machine gave three sharp rejection-bells, and beside the Chancellor, a young Cantonese clerk pulled a handful of red-bordered mortality slips from the brass hopper. "You told the Emperor at noon that the winter wheat-ration had been distributed without a single bread-riot in the fourteen European cantons."

Prefect-Chancellor Shen paused. He took off his horn-rimmed spectacles and wiped the equatorial sweat from the bridge of his nose with a silk handkerchief; then he held three of the red-punched cards up to the grey light filtering through the palm-fronds.

"There are no riots, Your Imperial Highness," Shen said. For the first time since Kaiulani had known his father’s house, a tiny, hairline crack of uncertainty broke the smooth Berkeley voice. "A starving man with a turnip in his belly does not throw paving-stones at a Maxim gun. This is the weekly sanitary telemetry from the embarkation-barracks at Antwerp, Brest, and Odessa, where the first draft of four hundred thousand European labor-conscripts is being held for the Borneo and Peruvian transports."

"Have they brought the lice-typhus out of the Russian trenches again?" Kaiulani said, her eyelids drooping in the stifling heat. "Tell Fleet-General Kuroda’s surgeons to double the cresol-baths at the pier-heads."

"This is the Rhine-mud fever, Madam," said a rougher, older voice from the shadow of the koa-wood pillars behind her chair. Old Field-Marshal Marcus Vance stepped slowly out onto the tiles. He leaned heavily upon his rubber-tipped cane while his steel leg-brace creaked at the knee. In his square, liver-spotted hand he held a long blue submarine-cable flimsy that had come in ten minutes before through the private military conduit from Monterey, bypassing Shen’s commercial sorting-frames entirely. "Cresol does not kill this, Princess," Marcus said. He hobbled to the edge of the veranda table and laid the wet blue paper directly over Shen’s perforated cards. "Read her the post-mortem dispatch from Chief Surgeon Takagi at the Gibraltar coal-hulks, Chancellor, and then read her the morning report from the Vallejo grain-docks in San Francisco Bay." Kaiulani turned her clouded eyes toward the old general’s grey, gaunt face. "Vallejo? What has Vallejo to do with the Belgian labor-draft?" Shen looked down at the blue military wire, his thin lips pressed white at the corners. "On the twenty-eighth of December, Your Highness, the returning empty munition-collier *Suisun*, which had discharged nitrate cargo at Rotterdam and taken on two thousand German and French railway-conscripts for the Panama canal-locks, put into Gibraltar with three hundred men dead in the steerage holds. Starvation and trench-typhus spared them; a faster contagion took them in the dark. According to Surgeon Takagi’s autopsy, the lungs fill with black, frothy blood within twelve hours of the first shivering-fit; the skin turns the color of wet slate—" "They call it the *Rhine-Mud Grippe* in the Antwerp alleys," Marcus Vance cut in, his pale eyes fixed grimly upon the distant, smoke-wrapped funnel of a ten-thousand-ton transport rounding the quarantine-buoy off Diamond Head with its yellow jack flying at the fore. "It bred in the flooded shell-craters along the Meuse last autumn, where half a million unburied horses and men were rotting in the chemical sludge of our own picric-acid shells. As long as the Europeans were locked behind their trenches, it stayed in the mud. Then we knocked the walls down in May. We marched four million conscripts onto the broad-gauge trains and packed them into the twenty-eight-knot turbine liners that Elias and I built to bring the world inside a fourteen-day circle." Marcus lifted his cane two inches off the tiles and pointed the rubber ferrule straight at the yellow-flagged steamer dropping anchor in the outer roadstead. "That is the fast troop-transport *Great Republic*, nine days out from Panama via San Francisco," the old Marshal said. Down at the naval landing-slip below the pavilion, the brass alarm-bell of the Quarantine Launch clanged across the still, sultry water, while four marine orderlies in white carbolic-masks ran up the basalt steps toward the terrace with a red dispatch-case between them. "She touched at Vallejo on Tuesday to coal, and by Friday noon four hundred examination-clerks in the Berkeley sheds and half the stokers on the *Thalassia* were spitting black blood into their hammocks. Chancellor Shen, leave that telegraph key alone until the surgeon tells us whether the quarantine line at Gibraltar has held or if the Atlantic Vanguard has already carried the rot into the Danube basins."

***

It had not held. Yet in the strange, merciless arithmetic of the Bureau of Integration, the pestilence that the Fast-Transports carried out of the Meuse craters became, within ninety days of its outbreak, the very mortar with which the Chancellery sealed the cellar doors of Central Europe.

To the Chronicler who entered Vienna in the late March of 1919, riding in the disinfecting-van of the Tenth Sanitary Train after the newly laid six-foot tracks had pierced the Semmering Pass from Trieste, the old seat of the Hapsburg Caesars offered a lesson in imperial geometry that neither sword nor shell could have cut so deep. Where the Russo-German batteries had left the outer Ringstrasse standing, the black grippe had emptied the inner courtyards like a scythe.

Forty white-painted steam-lorries of the *Imperial Pacific Relief Commission* formed our entire vanguard into the Austrian capital, rolling in without brass bands or lowered bayonets. Their boilers burned clean Borneo oil that smelled of hot paraffin and scorched insulation against the sour, fetid miasma of unburied dead and boiled cabbage beneath the chestnut trees of the Prater. Across the broad, cracked flagstones of the Heldenplatz, directly between the bronze hooves of Prince Eugene’s charger and the shuttered, mortar-chipped windows of the Hofburg, our Cantonese and Californian engineer-companies had erected six long rows of galvanized-iron triage sheds and twenty high-pressure field autoclaves.

"Keep the queue inside the whitewashed ropes, Sergeant, and do not permit the former municipal magistrates to enter the soup-line ahead of the tramway-stokers," ordered Senior Sanitary Prefect Watanabe. He stood beside me upon the granite plinth of the Empress Maria Theresa’s monument, a clipboard of stamped aluminum in his gloved hand and a gauze pad soaked in eucalyptus-camphor tied across his mouth and nose.

Below our boots, stretching for half a mile down the Mariahilferstrasse in the raw spring sleet, stood thirty thousand citizens of the Ninth Danubian Canton. Former colonels of the Imperial-Royal Uhlans stood wrapped in ragged, lice-ridden horse-blankets beside hollow-eyed university professors hugging empty leather briefcases to their ribs, while pale, barefoot girls shivered in the faded silk ball-gowns of nineteen-thirteen. Nobody shouted. Nobody cursed the blue-and-gold Sun banner snapping from the dome of the Kunsthistorisches Museum. When a man has buried three children in the frozen garden-mould behind his tenement and feels the first hot, dry tickle of the Rhine-mud fever in his own windpipe, the pride of a thousand years of Christendom melts away before the smell of boiling mutton-tallow and synthetic quinine.

Shivering families reached the duralumin turnstile at the head of the shed with their bowls and papers ready for the Hawaiian hospital-orderlies. Before a ladle of San Joaquin barley-gruel or a five-grain tablet of Osaka coal-tar febrifuge crossed the counter, the householder had to lay his old Austrian parish-papers, land-deeds, and guild-certificates into the iron hopper of a portable furnace beside the cauldron; in return, our blacksmith-corporals handed him a square brass ration-plate stamped with a six-digit canton numeral and riveted a lead wire permanently around his left wrist.

"You observe the economy of the transaction, Citizen-Historian," Prefect Watanabe said through his camphor-mask. In the lenses of his spectacles, where three centuries of Hapsburg feudal charters and municipal franchises curled into black ash inside the paper-furnace to heat the carbolic vats, a bright orange flare jumped. "In Poland last autumn, General Kuroda’s regiments expended four hundred rounds of machine-gun ammunition for every village we cleared for the gauge-widening. Here, a pound of compressed salt-pork and two pennies’ worth of carbolic soap buy us the freehold of the Danube without exploding a single cap. A man conquered by a bayonet remembers his grievance when his ribs heal; a man who has sold his father’s name at a turnstile for a tin of hot broth and a clean shirt is a numbered clerk for life."

Down at the third wicket, an aged Austrian archduke hesitated for three seconds, his collar-less linen shirt flapping beneath a moth-eaten fur pelisse while the Samoan corporal took his parchment patent of nobility with a pair of iron tongs and held the cold brass wrist-shackle open over the anvil.

"Next in the file!" the corporal barked in the flat, clipped pidgin of the Monterey depots. He tapped the iron rivet-hammer once against the block; without lifting his eyes to the bronze eagles on the palace roof above him, the last cousin of Charles the Fifth thrust his wasted white wrist into the ring.

***

By the autumn of that same year, the brass wrist-rings of the Relief Commission had locked the last starving parish between the Baltic and the Adriatic; yet in the high, glass-roofed Chart-Vault of the Imperial Palace at Thalassia, five thousand leagues away from the Vienna soup-booths, the sheer tonnage of the ledger was breaking the tables.

On an afternoon in late October, 1919, Lady Kaiulani sat in her wheeled koa-wood chair at the center of the great circular floor. Court silks had hung untouched in her wardrobes since spring. A plain, heavy wrapper of dark gray Oahu wool covered her shoulders, and below her white hair, cropped short like a dying soldier’s to save her tire-women the labor of the comb, the ancient carved whale-tooth hung loose upon a neck no thicker than a child’s wrist.

All around her, the marble rotunda that she and Marcus Vance had designed five years ago to hold the quiet, clockwork balance of the Pacific basin had become a roaring, suffocating factory of unindexed paper. Gone was the cool submarine twilight of the dome. To feed the eighty supplementary Hollerith tabulators and high-speed pneumatic sorting-frames that Chancellor Shen had bolted across the mosaic floor, four temporary copper power-cables had been dragged in through the shattered lower panes of the stained glass; they filled the vault with the blinding blue flash of overloaded mercury-rectifiers and the smell of scorching gutta-percha insulation, while ten million manila cards rattled like an unending hail-storm through the brass needles.

"The repeater-cable at Aden has been jammed for nineteen hours with the quarantine tallies from the Third Rhine and Eleventh Danubian Cantons, Your Imperial Highness!" shouted Junior Assessor Adams. His linen shirt was soaked through with sweat and machine-oil as he elbowed his way through a knee-deep drift of unfiled yellow telegraph-tape that had spilled out of the pneumatic chutes from the Monterey Annex. "Until the Vienna and Warsaw mortality-deductions are cleared off the main wire, I cannot transmit the October rice-warrants to the Hankow granaries! Thirty grain-hulks are lying idle in the Yangtze with their steam up because the Canton prefects have no cipher-authority to open the sluices!"

"Then clear the Hankow warrants over the Siberian land-line through Irkutsk!" snapped Prefect-Chancellor Shen from the raised steel podium. His horn-rimmed spectacles slid down his sweat-greased nose while three Cantonese mechanics with iron wrenches worked beneath his feet to unjam a smoking sorting-wheel that had chewed a bundle of Bengal salt-cards into pulp.

"The Irkutsk trunk-wire was cut sixty miles west of Omsk on Tuesday by forty thousand escaped European labor-conscripts who seized a broad-gauge timber-train when their guard-battalion came down with the black grippe!" Adams yelled back over the clatter of the bells. "And the High Commissioner at Antwerp wires that unless four hundred thousand tons of Argentine beef and Sacramento flour are diverted from the Osaka foundry-allocations before the November frost, the Ruhr coal-miners will abandon the pumps and let the Westphalian shafts flood to the collar!"

In the center of the floor, Kaiulani kept her voice low. The iron din of the tabulators swallowed any sound six feet away. With her rubber-tipped ebony cane, she reached out and hooked the hem of old Field-Marshal Marcus Vance’s alpaca coat where he leaned against a marble pillar beside her wheels.

"Look at Shen’s hands, Marcus," she whispered, and lifted her chin toward the steel podium.

Up above the sea of overflowing wicker baskets stood the grandson of Elias Thorne’s imperturbable Chinese auditor, the man who had smiled when Paris starved and never blinked when London burned. He struck the brass housing of the master-telegraph printer with his fist. Carbon-smut blackened his slate-gray cuffs, and against the roar of the seventy ventilators his mouth worked without a sound.

"We built a heart to pump the blood of one ocean, Marcus," Kaiulani said. She closed her cataract-clouded eyes against the warm, greasy draft of burned lubricating-oil blowing from the overloaded Molokai transformers. "Now Kalanimoku has spliced the veins of three hundred million dead-weight Europeans and two hundred million Hindoos into the same brass pipe, and the valves are bursting in the cellar. It takes eleven days for a famine-report from the Vistula to pass through the sorting-frames at Monterey, and while the needle is hunting for the card in this room, the rice rots on the Hankow wharves and the mutineers tear up the Siberian sleepers."

Marcus Vance looked down at the mile of tangled yellow paper coiling around the wheels of her chair like dead kelp on a beach after a typhoon.

"Elias told me once at the Panama cut that an engineer can build a bridge across any river in the world, provided he doesn't make the span so wide that the iron breaks under its own weight before a single train crosses it," the old Marshal said. His stiff knee popped as he kicked a jammed bundle of Antwerp debtor-cards out of the path of her wheels. "We have no reserve battalions left in California, Princess. Every boy from the class of nineteen-eighteen who survived the winter grippe in the Berkeley sheds has been shipped out to police the Rhine soup-kitchens or guard the Suez oil-docks. This morning, Emperor Kalanimoku signed the field-orders for Fleet-General Kuroda to march six divisions from the Indus up into the Hindu Kush to close the last hole in the fence."

# Chapter 26: Khyber

That hole in the fence was the Kingdom of Kabul.

To the Chronicler who stands today, in this bitter December of 1919, beside the frozen wreck of an Osaka armored traction-engine three miles below the summit of the Jagdalak Pass, while the snow-wind off the sixteen-thousand-foot peaks of the Hindu Kush screams through the empty eye-sockets of our unburied draught-mules, the folly of that final campaign requires no logarithmic demonstration.

Upon the illuminated glass charts in the Palace of Thalassia, the mountain massif between the Indus and the Oxus had looked to young Emperor Kalanimoku and his Polytechnic staff like a mere thumb-smudge of unnumbered gray paper: an intolerable gap of four hundred miles where the six-foot Imperial gauge from Peshawar failed to meet the Russian broad-gauge military line coming down from Tashkent and Samarkand. *"An empire that leaves an unbolted door between its Indian jute-cantons and its Siberian timber-wards invites every bandit in Asia to cut the wire,"* Fleet-General Kuroda had written in his September memorandum from Delhi. On the first of October, with sixty thousand men of the Combined Pacific Corps—veteran Satsuma infantry and Californian railway-pioneers alongside newly conscripted Bavarian and Yorkshire debtor-battalions—he had marched up the dry, slate-walled furnace of the Khyber Pass behind forty steam-tractors pulling six-inch Krupp mountain-howitzers and ten thousand tons of creosoted Oregon pine sleepers.

For three weeks, so long as the column remained within the range of the flat-trajectory naval guns mounted upon our armored broad-gauge trains at Jamrud, the machine had rolled forward with the old, effortless grandeur of the Great Arena.

Then the six-foot track ended against the vertical black granite of the Kabul Gorge, and the winter came down out of Tartary.

Eight hundred miles of dry stone separated these crags from any sea that could float a dreadnought. At ten thousand feet the thin, dry air refused to lift our twin-engined Curtiss-Nakajima biplanes with a hundred-pound picric bomb over the passes; when the great rigid duralumin air-cruiser *Sakurajima II* was ordered up from Karachi to spot the tribal rifle-sangars among the crags, a ninety-mile-an-hour freezing gale above Jelalabad ripped her envelope open from nose to tail and pitched the hull into a ravine, where the Ghilzai herdsmen hacked her aluminum girders into horse-shoes before the staff-cars could reach the smoke.

At four o’clock on this afternoon of the eighteenth of December, the thermometer on the dashboard of Fleet-General Kuroda’s command-lorry stands at fourteen degrees below zero. The Borneo petroleum in the fuel-tanks of our forty traction-engines has frozen into a thick, yellow jelly that will not pass the brass injectors. Frost has split the water-jackets of the Maxim guns. Along five miles of narrow, ice-glazed mule-track winding between the two-thousand-foot limestone precipices of the Kurd-Kabul defile, the rear-guard of the Grand Confederation is dying in the snow.

"Break up the pine railway-sleepers from the third flat-sled and pile them under the crank-case of the tractor, Captain!" Fleet-General Kuroda shouts. A frost-bitten rasp has replaced the quiet Monterey baritone that once sank the British fleet at the Hooghly, and he stands knee-deep in the blood-stained drift beside the stalled ammunition-train. Frozen mule-slobber and black oil-soot stiffen his slate-gray greatcoat. In his frost-blackened right hand, the duralumin circular calculator is useless; no wireless telemetry reaches this granite trough, and the enemy above us has no railway-bridges to shell.

Eight hundred feet overhead, invisible behind the grey limestone boulders that crown the knife-edged ridges on either side of the gorge, four thousand Afridi and Ghilzai tribesmen crouch in the wind. None of them has ever seen a steamship or worn a brass ration-tag upon his wrist; subsisting for a month on a handful of parched barley and raw mutton-fat tucked inside their greasy sheepskin *postins*, they fire down into the packed, dark-blue mass of our stalled column with long-barreled, home-forged jezails and stolen Lee-Enfield rifles left behind from the old British wars.

*Crack. Whir-r-r. Thud.*

Fired from a cliff a quarter of a mile away, a heavy, soft-lead slug strikes the frozen iron boiler-plate of the traction-engine behind Kuroda’s shoulder, flattens into a jagged star the size of a silver thaler, and ricochets sideways through the throat of Junior Prefect Adams, who has come out from Thalassia with the November audit-rolls. He pitches face-first into the snow across a pile of unlaid eighty-pound Bessemer rails. Beneath his forehead, his horn-rimmed spectacles snap in two; his purple blood freezes into red ice before it can soak through the manila cards spilling from his haversack.

"The Bavarian debtor-company at the rear-guard cairn has thrown down its carbines, General!" screams Colonel Kalakaua the younger. Thirty years old, an Oahu graduate whose brown Polynesian cheeks are grey and peeling with high-altitude frostbite, he stumbles down the icy boulders from the tail of the column; his left hand clutches a jagged, nine-inch Afghan *choora* knife-wound in his ribs, and his dark wool tunic steams in the zero air. "The tribesmen came straight down the dry watercourse on the flank with their long knives before the artillery could unlimber, while our boys were trying to thaw the grease in their rifle-bolts over burning telegraph-poles! They’ve hamstrung the mule-teams on the howitzer-sleds, and they’re cutting the brass number-tags off our wounded while they’re still breathing!"

Kuroda ignores the dead assessor at his boots. With his stiff, fingerless left glove he draws his nine-shot automatic pistol and steps up onto the frozen iron draw-bar of the stalled tractor. His cropped head is bare to the whistling sleet. A second volley of jezail-balls spanks off the rock wall above us and showers his shoulders with granite splinters.

"Turn the two remaining three-inch mountain-guns around on the sled-runners and fire canister straight back down the defile through the Bavarian company!" Kuroda roars against the howling wind of the pass. Two hundred yards up the narrow gut, where a thousand bearded hillmen leap from boulder to boulder like mountain-goats with their three-foot curved blades flashing dull red in the twilight, a writhing tangle of grey sheepskins and slate-blue coats chokes the trail; Kuroda points his pistol barrel toward the melee, but a three-hundred-pound boulder levered from the upper ledge crashes squarely upon the tractor's frozen steam-dome and crushes him into the iron before his thumb can press the trigger.

***

Command of the bleeding column passed in that instant of escaping steam and shattered cast-iron to Brigadier Marcus Vance the third, grand-nephew of the lame Marshal in the Presidio solarium, and first in the class of nineteen-twelve at the Thalassia Staff College.

Twenty-eight years old, the third Marcus was a stranger to the smell of burning pine-tar in a snow-shed or the sight of an artillery mule gutted for its tallow. He had earned his silver collar-numerals in the air-conditioned glass vaults of Oahu with a celebrated thesis upon *The Trigonometric Optimization of Coal-Collier Turnaround in the Coral Sea*. Now he scrambled out of the overturned staff-lorry. Fur-lined gauntlets smeared with Kuroda’s brains and his gold-rimmed pince-nez dangling by its silk ribbon against his cheek, he stared up at the darkening limestone walls of the defile like a clerk whose counting-house roof has suddenly caved in.

"Form the hollow square by cantons!" young Marcus screamed. His voice pitched up into a thin, reedy falsetto while he fumbled inside his velvet-lined map-case for the printed *Manual of Mountain Pacification* that the Monterey presses had issued at Peshawar. "Where is the wireless operator? Signal the air-cruiser station at Jelalabad to lay a curtain of white phosphorus along grid-sector nineteen! Why aren't the Bavarian companies dressing their ranks by the telegraph poles?"

"There are no telegraph poles left standing for forty miles to the east, Brigadier!" barked Sergeant-Major O’Higgins. A sixty-year-old grey-bearded survivor of the elder Vance’s Donner Pass rear-guard who had left his ear behind in the Sierra snow thirty-two years ago, O’Higgins grabbed the young general by his gold-braided shoulder-strap and dragged him bodily behind the dead carcass of a frozen camel just as a volley of hammered iron nails and telegraph-wire slugs tore through the canvas hood of the lorry. "The hillmen chopped the cedar posts down on Tuesday to roast their mutton, and the wireless dynamo is at the bottom of the Kabul River with its wheels in the air! Put that paper book back in your pocket, boy, or by God none of us will ever see the Indus again!"

Marcus tore his arm free from the old Irishman’s grip. Terror and the zero wind blotched his soft, indoor cheeks purple and white. Down in the trough of the trail, five hundred Satsuma and Californian cadets huddled in a frozen, sheep-like herd around the stalled baggage-wagons; because their Polytechnic drill-regulations forbade independent volley-fire without range-finder elevation from a section-officer, and the Afridi marksmen had systematically shot every youth carrying a brass sextant or a pair of Zeiss binoculars through the forehead during the first hour of the march, not a rifle answered the flashes on the ridge.

"I am the senior surviving graduate of the First Class!" Marcus shouted. With fingers so numb he dropped the weapon twice into the bloody slush before his thumb found the safety-catch, he pulled a silver-plated revolver from his patent-leather holster. "By General Order Four-Zero-Two, no rolling-stock or Hollerith ledger-chests may be abandoned to an unnumbered population! Uncouple the surviving mules from the hospital ambulances and hitch them to the two treasury-vans! If we leave the November tax-rolls of the Punjab in the snow, the Audit Board at Monterey will strike my cipher from the peerage!"

"The Audit Board isn't up on that ridge with a three-foot *khyber* knife, you little counting-house fool!" O’Higgins roared back. He swung the butt of his heavy magazine-carbine to smash the padlock off an ammunition-limber and tossed double handfuls of loose brass cartridges to the shivering Cantonese pioneers in the ditch. "Your grandfather left six-inch Krupp mortars in the Donner drift to save his men's skins, and his uncle rode a raw-boned mule through the Comanche fires with nothing in his saddle-bags but parched corn! If you hitch the ambulance-mules to those paper-wagons, four hundred frost-bitten boys will have their throats slit before the moon rises!"

"Insubordination under fire!" Marcus shrieked—Wait. Turbaned shadows were pouring down the shale-slides fifty yards away with the terrible, ululating war-cry of the hills, yet he leveled his silver pistol straight at the chest of the sixty-year-old sergeant-major. "Hitch the mules to the audit-vans, Sergeant-Major, or I’ll have you shot against the wheel! The records of the Hundred and Twenty-Eighth Canton must reach the Peshawar wire before—"

He never finished the regulation. From the overhanging crag directly above the stalled treasury-van, an eighty-year-old Ghilzai grandfather in a greased wolf-skin coat spared his lead bullets and tipped a forty-pound fire-pot of blazing pine-resin and camel-dung over the lip of the rock.

The clay jar burst squarely atop the varnished roof of the audit-wagon. Liquid fire showered young Marcus Vance’s slate-gray shoulders, and as ten thousand perforated manila census-cards roared up into the freezing night like a chimney-flue, the hillmen came in among the baggage-train by that bright orange light with the steel.

***

Twelve hundred miles west of that burning wagon in the Kabul gorge, the winter wind off the Elburz mountains rattled the loose, diamond-paned casements of the Golestan Palace in Tehran. A fine, gritty dust of dried salt-marsh and pulverized brick blew across the faded Shiraz carpets of the Hall of Mirrors.

Lady Kaiulani’s wheeled chair stood empty. Because the jolting forty-hour journey up from the British-built railhead at Basra in an unheated military ambulance-van had inflamed the pleurisy in her eighty-four-year-old lungs, she could breathe only when propped upright at a forty-five-degree angle upon a camp-bed of folded grey army blankets set directly before the smoking charcoal brazier.

She had left the mourning silk of the Oahu court and the sable cape of Geneva in her trunks. Buttoned over her shrunken, fever-racked chest was old Field-Marshal Marcus Vance’s spare field-greatcoat of coarse Californian wool, which smelled of camphor and stale tobacco; the dying general had taken it off his own shoulders at the Suez landing-slip when the cable arrived that his grand-nephew had lost forty thousand men and all the siege-trains in the snows between Jelalabad and Jamrud.

Across the brazier reclined Ahmad Shah Qajar, the twenty-two-year-old King of Kings of Persia. The fat, sulky youth sat cross-legged in a tall black astrakhan cap with an uncut three-carat diamond pinned to the front, upon a divan of tattered crimson brocade from which the gold thread had been picked out during the famine of nineteen-sixteen to buy Russian kerosene; four grey-bearded Mujtahids of the Shi’a clergy flanked him alongside the Warlord of the Bakhtiari horse-tribes, whose bandoliers of British .303 cartridges clinked against his silver-mounted dagger every time he scratched his lice.

"At Calcutta five winters ago, Great Lady, your Fleet-General Kuroda told the Nizam of Hyderabad that the Pacific Ocean needed no allies who rode horses," the Bakhtiari khan said in guttural, camp-fire Hindustani. He spat a husk of roasted pumpkin-seed straight into the charcoal embers between Kaiulani’s small, wool-stockinged feet. "Now Fleet-General Kuroda’s skull is nailed to the gate-post of the Bala Hissar in Kabul, and the Turkoman raiders from Merv have cut your broad-gauge track at Kushka and burned sixty of your oil-cars on the Oxus bank. Why does the grandmother of the Sacred Sun come coughing through the mud of Mesopotamia with ten mules of silver thalers at her tail, instead of sending the flying iron ships to blow the mountains flat?"

Grey charcoal-ash clung to Kaiulani's chin. Beneath her cropped white hair, her cataract-milky eyes stared through the faceted glass reflections of the walls, back across sixty-seven years of water and iron to the afternoon when Elias Thorne had ridden into Monterey with four batteries of brass twelve-pounders and dictated the law of the hemisphere to governors who crawled on their knees for a railway-station.

The Empire had been young then. A single regiment of boys with repeaters could buy a kingdom for a handful of telegraph-wire. Now the iron hoop was stretched around twenty-five thousand miles of earth, while the German and Russian debtor-cantons took three hundred thousand bayonets to hold down, the black grippe rotted the examination-sheds at Berkeley, and here, in a freezing mud-walled room at the back of Asia, the last Regent of the Pivot had to beg a twenty-two-year-old mountain thief to guard her flank.

"The flying ships stay on the ground when the ice is on the wings, Sardar," Kaiulani whispered. Every breath rasped in her throat like a rusty saw drawn through wet koa-wood, while beside her camp-bed Junior Prefect Hoshino the younger, whose father had burned in the naphtha on the Hankow steps thirty-two years before, held an open tin of warm Californian condensed milk that she could no longer swallow. "And my grandson has no desire to waste the boys of Oahu and Satsuma hunting goats among the rocks of Herat. Take the iron boxes off the pack-frames, Hoshino."

Four Hawaiian marine-guards stepped forward. The last survivors of her personal household company, with their blue tunics patched at the elbows with grey canvas and their boots tied together with copper telegraph-wire, they pried open three unpainted pine chests with their bayonets; a dull, heavy cascade of minted San Francisco silver thalers and five hundred new, grease-packed Sacramento magazine-carbines spilled across the worn wool of the carpet.

"The Shah-in-Shah may keep his unshaven head and stay out of the examination-cubicles," Kaiulani said. Her thin, bluish lips curled in that cold Polynesian smile that had once bought the kings of Peru and Siam. "Keep your astrakhan caps; keep your mullahs and your customs-houses at Bushire. The Chancery of Thalassia repeals the Mesopotamian Tariff-Ordinance of nineteen-fifteen. Provided your tribesmen ride east to the Hari Rud river before Tuesday and cut the throat of every Afghan or Turkoman rebel who tries to cross the desert toward our oil-pipes at Basra, we will pay your Bakhtiari and Qashqai horsemen four million silver thalers a year out of the Abadan petroleum-royalties, and deliver twenty thousand magazine-rifles with five hundred rounds apiece at the Bandar Abbas wharf before the spring equinox."

Over his bolster leaned young Ahmad Shah, digging pudgy fingers into the silver coins like a child in a sand-heap. The old Bakhtiari khan left the money untouched. He lifted one of the new Sacramento carbines, worked the bolt twice with an oily *snick-snack*, and looked down at the dying woman in the soldier’s coat.

"Four million thalers is the price of the spring grass, Lady," the khan said. He rested the hot muzzle of the American carbine across his knee. "In the autumn, when the snow closes the Russian tracks again and your sick boys in the Basra hospital die of the marsh-ague, the price of the winter guard will be eight million, plus the four twelve-pounder mountain-guns from your escort train."

Kaiulani closed her cloudy eyes. Her head sank back into the rough wool of Marcus Vance’s collar.

*Give them the guns.* Outside the tent flap, before the parchment even bore a seal, the Persian khan’s spurs jingled while his men dragged the silver-chests through the doorway. *That was how the Caesars at Ravenna paid the Goths when the legions forgot how to march in the snow. This year we buy them off with silver and carbines; next year Kalanimoku will make this horse-thief a Patrician of the Senate; and ten winters from now, when the Molokai turbines lose their pressure, they will ride down to the sea and stable their mares in the marble baths of Thalassia.*

***

Yet even the Bakhtiari horsemen whom the dying Queen-Mother hired with her silver patrolled only the flat salt-deserts along the Persian border. None dared ride ten leagues eastward into the jagged black teeth of the Hindu Kush, where the spring thaw of 1920 uncovered what our Monterey war-bulletins called the *Pacification of the One Hundred and Thirty-First Canton*, and what the soldiers in the armored blockhouses called the *Hidden War*.

At the fortified railhead of Peshawar through that burning May, third-generation Polytechnic engineers attempted to repair by pure horse-power the prestige that young Brigadier Vance had left burning in the Kurd-Kabul snow. There the struggle bared our history's sharpest contradiction: the world’s mightiest industrial machine stood impotent before an enemy who possessed nothing worth bombarding.

In the Great Indian War, and again in the liquidation of Europe, the victory of the Pacific had been swift and mathematically certain because the English, the French, and the Germans lived inside the same nineteenth-century house of iron and paper as ourselves. When Fleet-General Kuroda dropped a two-thousand-pound picric shell into a railway junction at Calcutta or cut the telegraph-trunk outside Brussels, three million urban mechanics starved within forty-eight hours and came out with their hands up to beg for a brass wrist-tag.

Between the Indus and the Oxus lay a labyrinth of dry limestone canyons and twenty-thousand-foot glaciers without a nerve-center to sever. Kabul itself was only a sprawling mud-brick village whose bazaar burned to the ground on Monday and rose again out of river-clay on Thursday. The mountains held no banks to foreclose or factory-chimneys to range upon with our stereoscopic sights; they kept no parish registers in which to punch a Hollerith card.

Stung by the loss of Kuroda’s column, Emperor Kalanimoku ordered the Osaka and Pittsburg arsenals in March to send out the First Heavy Land-Flotilla: sixty forty-ton *Leviathan*-class steam-tanks, each plated in two inches of cemented nickel-steel, propelled by twin kerosene-fired flash-boilers on broad caterpillar-treads, and mounting a six-pounder Hotchkiss cannon and four water-cooled Maxim guns in revolving sponsons. The young prefects at Thalassia reckoned that the mountain passes would be swept clean of bandits at a fuel-expenditure of twelve gallons to the linear mile.

On the twelfth of May,forty miles north of the ruined Kabul cantonment, twelve of those rumbling, oil-belching iron tortoises crawled at four miles an hour up the dry boulder-bed of the Panjshir valley, and I rode behind the vanguard of the Seventh Land-Flotilla in the armored observation-tender.

The heat inside the steel hull reached a hundred and thirty degrees Fahrenheit. Vaporized kerosene, hot brass, scorching asbestos boiler-lagging, and the sour sweat of eight half-naked Cantonese and Californian mechanic-gunners thickened the cabin air as they sat upon the iron floor-plates and pressed their faces to the narrow prismatic periscopes while the sixty-horsepower steam-cylinders hammered like trip-hammers between their knees.

Outside in the white glare of the noon sun, the valley lay as empty and silent as a crater of the moon. Not a single turbaned head showed above the grey stone *sangars* on the ridges. Three days before, the inhabitants had abandoned the terraced mulberry-orchards and flat-roofed mud villages along the stream, carrying off every grain of barley and driving their sheep up into the twelve-thousand-foot snow-fields where no forty-ton machine could climb.

"Seven miles from the entrance of the gorge, Citizen-Historian, and we haven't seen a target worth a six-pounder shell," shouted Tank-Commander Lieutenant Sato, Candidate Zero-Nine-Two-Two of the class of nineteen-seventeen. He wiped the black cylinder-grease from his chin and leaned down from the forward turret-basket to tap the brass steam-gauge. "The tribesmen took one look at the two-inch Krupp plate at Charikar last week and ran for the Pamirs! Once our pioneer gangs lay the six-foot sleepers through this cut tomorrow, we can run the armored trains straight through to the Oxus!"

His fingers had scarcely left the gauge when the lead forty-ton *Leviathan*, lumbering fifty yards ahead of our bow across a narrow, dry gravel-fan where a mountain torrent came down from the limestone cliffs, pitched its iron snout forty-five degrees downward into the earth. Timber collapsed beneath it with a dull, hollow *boom*.

No mine had exploded; the electric induction-sweepers mounted on the front horns of the tank would have detected five pounds of iron casing three feet under the stones. Four hundred Tajik and Ghilzai women and children had worked by night with wooden shovels and goat-skin baskets, wearing not a single scrap of metal on their bodies, until they had dug a twenty-foot pit across the torrent-bed, roofed it over with split juniper-poles and river-shingle to match the dry wash, and lined the bottom with ten tons of loose, greasy soapstone boulders.

The forty-ton iron monster crashed through the juniper roof. Against the soapstone, its left caterpillar-track sheared its bronze drive-pins. The flash-boiler pipe snapped at the flange, and three-hundred-degree superheated steam filled the sealed steel hull, parboiling the eight numbered cadets inside like lobsters in a pot before a single hatch could be unbolted.

Before our second tank could reverse its steam-valves in the narrow defile, the sun-baked cliff-face sixty feet above our roofs broke open.

Not a rifle cracked against our two-inch armor. From behind a hundred grey boulders along the mountain wall, three hundred ragged men in earth-colored wool leaped straight down onto the flat steel decks of the stalled machines where our gun-sponsons could not elevate to reach them.

In the three-inch glass block of my periscope, a barefoot sixteen-year-old boy with a tangled black beard and a tattered blue turban landed like a mountain-cat atop the ventilator-grating of Lieutenant Sato’s turret. He carried a heavy iron shepherd’s crowbar in his left hand, and in his right a greasy goatskin bag filled with ten pounds of fine, dry quartz-sand and powdered sheep-dung.

"Traverse the dorsal Maxim! Clear the roof!" Sato screamed. He slammed the iron lever of the steam-siren while two more hillmen jammed their iron crowbars straight between the teeth of our rear drive-sprockets; with a screech of stripping steel gears, the caterpillar-treads locked solid.

Up on the roof, the barefoot boy did not wait for the machine-gun turret to turn. Bracing his heel against the hot chimney-cowl, he poured the entire goatskin of dry quartz-sand and dung straight down the air-intake funnel of the forced-draft blower. The high-speed fan sucked the grit into the main engine-bearings, seizing the pistons in a blinding cloud of black, oily smoke that filled our cabin to the roof, while a second hillman stuffed a burning rag soaked in stolen kerosene down the periscope-shaft and crowbars pried at the red-hot bolts of the forward hatch.

Then the third observation-tender’s external shrapnel-howitzer fired a canister round directly across our buckled deck-plates. The blast swept both the tribesmen and our own brass periscope-hoods into the gravel, and my driver uncoupled the armored trailer to drag our crippled hull backward down the dry wash toward Charikar.

***

Eleven forty-ton *Leviathans* stayed behind smoking in the Panjshir stones that afternoon, at a cost to the San Francisco Treasury of four million silver thalers; by the time the cable-summary of that week’s wastage passed through the submarine repeaters to the middle of the Pacific, the price of ten pounds of Afghan quartz-sand was shaking the marble floor of the Crystal Palace.

In June the hospital-cruiser *Oahu* had brought Lady Kaiulani back from the Persian Gulf with oxygen-cylinders strapped beside her berth by the naval surgeons. On the nineteenth of July, 1920, ignoring the frantic protests of her niece Malia, she ordered her bearers to bypass the screened privacy of the Whispering Gallery and carry her koa-wood chair straight out onto the lower porphyry rostrum of the Pan-Pacific Senate, directly beneath the empty bronze curule chair of her grandson.

The dais stood empty of Emperor Kalanimoku. Three miles away in the fortified Naval Chart-Room at Waipahu, he had secluded himself from the provincial assessors until the Osaka arsenals completed the eighty new *Titan*-class mountain-tanks he had requisitioned over the Treasury’s veto. Down in the five concentric rings of koa-wood stalls, the docile chorus of nineteen-sixteen had vanished.

Because the geothermal conduits from Molokai had been diverted since April to power the twin-shift electrolytic aluminum furnaces at Pearl Lochs, no chilled mountain water-curtains sheeted down the outer Jena glass of the dome; the equatorial noon beat straight through the dry panes, heating the vast greenhouse to ninety-six degrees. Stagnant air held the sour reek of six hundred sweating wool robes and overheated transformer-varnish, thick with the stench of bruised, rotting ginger-garlands wilting around the bronze pillars.

The *Pax Pacifica* went unchanted. Leaving their green acclamation-levers untouched, five hundred and forty senators stood at once, waving long, violet-inked strips of canton clearing-house paper and shouting in English, Cantonese, and Japanese across the marble gulf at Prefect-Chancellor Shen.

"Fourteen percent discount upon the silver canal-scrip in the Shanghai rice-alleys since Tuesday!" roared Senior Senator Wu of the Forty-Sixth Yangtze Canton. Unlike the rebellious colonial sheep-farmer old MacArthur, who had died in the Melbourne grippe-wards the winter before, Wu was a life-long graduate of the First Class whose collar bore the silver numerals of the Hankow Iron Trust; he stepped out into the central aisle and shook a fistful of depreciated Market Street Treasury notes straight toward the steel podium. "For eight months you have requisitioned every ton of Hanyang pig-iron and every barrel of Borneo fuel-oil to build forty-ton steam-coffins that the hill-bandits in Kabul crack open with ten-cent crowbars! Our river-barges from Ichang to Nanking are tied up to the mud-banks for want of kerosene, our foundry-puddlers are being paid in unstamped paper that will not buy three ounces of salt-fish, and this morning the Chancery Assessors demand another ninety million silver thalers for a third winter mobilization on the Indus!"

"And the California orchards are rotting on the boughs!" shouted Assessor Miller of the Third Sacramento Canton from the upper tier. He slammed the lid of his koa-wood desk so hard the brass ink-horn leaped from its socket and rolled down the steps. "You took forty thousand of our Mexican and Cantonese harvest-hands in March to lay six-foot sleepers through the Khyber snow, and fewer than five hundred have come back with their toes on their boots! The San Joaquin grain-syndicates will not honor another War-Benevolence warrant while the gold reserve in the Rincon Hill vaults sits below twenty percent!"

Up on the porphyry rostrum, Prefect-Chancellor Shen gripped the edges of the steel lectern. Sweat fogged his spectacles. Behind his head, as canton after canton broke the circuit, the electric tally-board flashed a stuttering blizzard of red refusal-bulbs.

"Conscript Fathers!" Shen’s amplified voice cracked across the vault in a harsh metallic feedback screech. "By the Constitutional Statute of Nineteen-Fourteen, military appropriations certified under the Sacred Emperor’s war-seal are exempt from provincial audit! If the Hankow and Sacramento chambers suspend the July silver-remittance, the Bureau of Integration will close the telegraph-clearing houses at six o’clock!"

"Close them and see who starves first, clerk!" bellowed thirty voices from the Satsuma and Osaka shipping-benches, where the great syndicate-factors who had grown fat on the looting of London now had their own turbine-liners rusting empty at the buoys.

In her low chair beside the porphyry steps, eighty-five-year-old Lady Kaiulani lifted her right hand from the grey wool lap-robe. Her fingers were too weak for the heavy duralumin baton. With only a light, hollow bamboo fan-stick in her palm, she struck the bronze rim of the rostrum gong once; that thin, dry *ting* barely reached the first row of benches before her niece Malia threw the master-switch of the dais microphones, and the amplification horns in the roof caught the dying Queen’s breath.

"Be silent," Kaiulani said.

In the upper gallery, young officers of the Household Guards stood with their hands off their holsters, glancing at one another as the roar of the six hundred stalls died away under the rattle of that ancient throat falling from the sixteen bronze horns like the voice of the dead century speaking out of the Marianas mud.

"You shout at Chancellor Shen because your paper thalers have lost fourteen cents on the dollar in the Shanghai alleys," Kaiulani said. Her cataract-white eyes stared straight out into the shimmering, uncooled heat of the dome, while a drop of sweat trickled down her shrunken brown temple to catch against the ancient carved bone hook at her neck. "Did you think, when you clapped your hands three summers ago to buy the cathedrals of France and the iron-works of the Ruhr with spoiled guncotton, that the wheel only turns one way? You wanted an empire without a rim. You voted the ships to break Calcutta, and you voted the conscription-trains to empty Vienna. You sat in these koa-wood chairs and cheered when my grandson told you that the world was a single ledger."

She leaned an inch forward against the leather strap that held her upright in the chair. Her small, crooked fingers pointed down at the pile of rejected violet warrants on the floor.

"Now you have reached the rock where there is nothing left to steal," she said, the breath whistling through the fluid in her chest. "A forty-ton steam-tank costs sixty thousand silver thalers at the Osaka dock, and a boy in a sheepskin coat destroys it with a handful of sand that costs him nothing. Shouting at the clerk will not balance this book. Either you vote the ninety million thalers today and eat barley-husks in San Francisco until the snow melts on the Hindu Kush, or you tell my grandson to pull up the six-foot rails and admit to four hundred million debtors from Antwerp to Benares that the Pacific gun can be stopped."

***

The ninety million thalers went unvoted.

When the division-bell rang at four o’clock through the stifling, ninety-eight-degree twilight of the Crystal Palace, three hundred and ninety-two red bulbs burned upon the basalt wall against two hundred and eight green; for the first time since Elias Thorne had bolted the eighteen-inch cannon to the Fort Point casemate sixty-six years before, the treasury of the Great Arena refused the warrant of the camp.

Five weeks later, on the sultry, dust-choked morning of the twenty-eighth of August, 1920, I stood as Chronicler upon the stone parapet of the Jamrud Fort at the eastern mouth of the Khyber Pass, where the consequence of those three hundred and ninety-two red electric lamps unrolled across the baked gravel plain of Peshawar like a funeral cortege that had lost its coffin.

Drafted by Prefect-Chancellor Shen himself in the cool language of the Berkeley engineering primers, the official bulletin pasted that morning upon the lime-washed boards of the Hundred and Thirty Cantons announced a *Rectification of the Trans-Indus Metering Perimeter*: having completed the punitive topographical survey of the Kabul basin, the Seventh and Ninth Imperial Corps were retiring to the permanent broad-gauge terminal along the right bank of the Indus to economize winter fuel-allocations.

Outside the Jamrud cantonment, forty thousand dark-skinned Punjabi and Rajput peasants lined the dry irrigation-ditches behind the leveled bayonets of our Choshu provost-cordons. They stood in dead silence. Without English or a slide-rule, every villager along those ditches understood what was coming down out of the narrow red jaws of the hills.

For sixty-eight years, the law of the Pivot had rested upon a single, unanswerable demonstration: where the six-foot track was laid down, it remained. Kingdoms might burn or plagues empty the tenements, and three hundred thousand men might die in the snow, yet the broad Bessemer rail crept forward like the basalt lava of Hawaii and turned everything behind its sleepers into numbered stone.

Now, out of the shimmering, hundred-and-ten-degree heat-haze of the Khyber defile, the last armored flatcar-train of the Western Frontier backed down the two-percent grade toward the Indus at three miles an hour.

The train was eating its own road.

Behind the blackened, dented steel skirt of the locomotive, whose cab-plates were starred by ten thousand soft-lead jezail slugs and whose water-tender leaked a rust-colored stream of boiling radiator-scum across the ties, rolled four heavy crane-cars manned by soot-blackened Californian and Cantonese pioneer-gangs. Yard by yard the train crept backward. Over the tail-board dropped the iron claws of the steam-grapples; they wrenched the eighty-pound Bessemer rails loose from the creosoted Oregon pine sleepers with a high screech of drawn spikes and swung the thirty-foot steel bars up onto the flatcars like a defeated giant gathering up his broken spears.

Behind the crane-train marched the remnant of the Ninth Polytechnic Division.

On the marble quays of Messina, brass bands had played the Imperial Anthem while rigid duralumin air-cruisers hovered overhead to cast the shadow of the Sun-and-Anchor across the dust; here, only the boots scraped the gravel. In ragged columns of fours, their slate-gray wool tunics stiff with dried salt-sweat and gray mountain lice, their boots bound up with strips of raw sheepskin, and the silver numerals torn from half their collars so the Afridi knife-men would not single them out as officers in the night, sixteen thousand frost-scarred, dysentery-hollowed boys from Seattle and Kyoto and Canton limped out of the pass. They dragged their six-pounder Hotchkiss guns behind them on hand-ropes. At Landi Kotal, we had blown up the last of the traction-engines with our own dynamite to keep their bronze bearings out of the tribesmen’s forges.

Five hundred yards behind our rear-most pioneer-squad, three hundred Afridi and Shinwari horsemen walked their mounts down the middle of the torn-up roadbed before the dust of the departing flatcars had even settled upon the crushed ballast-stone.

Every carbine stayed slung.
