High in their wooden saddles, with our captured model-ninety-eight Sacramento magazine-carbines across their greasy sheepskin shoulders and necklaces of brass Imperial ration-tags clinking around their stallions’ throats, they halted at the exact whitewashed stone cairn that marked the old British boundary-line, dismounted in the hot sun, and pried the remaining Oregon pine sleepers out of the gravel with iron bars to build a bonfire for their noon tea.

Beside me on the Jamrud parapet stood Senior Engineer-Prefect Sato, the older brother of that Lieutenant Sato who had been pulled half-blinded out of the Panjshir tank in May. His hands gripped the scorching sandstone battlement. Leaving his Zeiss binoculars untouched against his chest while the tribesmen burned the ninety-cent sleepers out on the plain, he kept his gaze fixed downward upon the inner courtyard of the fort.

There, in the shadow of the commissariat grain-sheds, a company of our own Autonomous Rajput Lancers—men whose fathers had bowed to the ground before Lady Kaiulani on the Shwedagon steps six winters ago—sat their horses with grounded lances. Their tunics were buttoned to the chin in strict Monterey regulation. As the last crane-car pulled the final pair of six-foot rails through the iron gates of the perimeter and the Cantonese blacksmiths swung the barriers shut, the Rajput subadar turned his head and looked up at the pillar of black pine-smoke rising from the abandoned track half a mile away.

He spat a red stream of betel-juice squarely onto the stone threshold of the Pacifica telegraph-office.

"They have seen the iron go backward, Citizen-Historian," Prefect Sato said at my shoulder. His fingers trembled so hard upon the sandstone that the duralumin circular calculator slipped from his belt-loop and struck the parapet flags with a tinny ring. "For sixty years we held three hundred million of them with ten thousand clerks because they believed our gauge was a law of nature, like the monsoon or the tide. Now a thousand barefoot goat-herds with iron crowbars have pried up the track in broad daylight, and before the moon is full tonight, every bazaar from Calcutta to the Amur will know that the circumference has a crack."

# Chapter 27: The Audit of the Red Needle

The bazaar-rumor traveled by the very copper wires that Elias Thorne had strung across the world to bind his provinces together, reaching the frozen birch-forests of the Sixty-Fourth Siberian Canton before the first September snow-squall blew down from the Sea of Okhotsk.

Ordered northward from Peshawar that autumn via the Tashkent-Irkutsk military junction to accompany the Special Audit Commission investigating why the August deliveries of Lake Baikal copper-matte and Lena pit-props had fallen forty percent below the Hollerith projections, I crossed the Roof of Asia as if passing through the chambers of an enormous iron clock whose mainspring was uncoiling in the dark.

Ever since the Brussels Liquidation Accord of nineteen-eighteen, the sub-arctic wilderness stretching from the Yenisei River to the Stanovoy Mountains had been the subterranean ash-pit of the Great Arena. Into those three thousand miles of larch-swamp and open-cut copper-shale, Prefect-Chancellor Shen’s demographic tabulators had poured four million unassimilated European war-debtors. Former Prussian artillerymen, French mechanics from the ruined Saint-Étienne arsenals, Yorkshire coal-hewers, and Russian veterans of Generalissimo Brusilov’s dissolved regiments wore the riveted lead-and-brass shackle of the Relief Commission upon their left wrists; at fourteen degrees below zero, they dug ore and felled railway-timbers to pay the interest on their burned cities.

So long as the armoured broad-gauge trains rolled punctually every forty-eight hours out of the Vladivostok and Hanyang depots with the winter tallow-tubs and the fresh relief-battalions of Satsuma and Californian cadets, the four million wrist-tags had swung their picks in silence.

Then came the summer of the Afghan drain. The Senate’s treasury-veto held the coal-colliers in port, and the War Office stripped half the Siberian garrison-companies from the timber-stockades to hold the Indus line.

On the night of the fourteenth of October, 1920, our three-car armoured audit-train lay stalled on a high wooden trestle-siding at Mining-Sector Nine. Eighty miles north of the Chita junction yawned the *Krasny-Yar* copper-and-shale pit, where sixty thousand German, Russian, and Polish debtor-masons worked in three eight-hour shifts beneath the glare of overhead carbon-arcs to feed the Osaka smelting-furnaces. Outside our double-glazed observation windows, the windless air sat at twenty-two degrees below zero. From the brick roasting-kilns at the bottom of the two-mile-wide terraced canyon, yellow sulfur smoke rose straight toward the green curtains of the northern aurora in solid pillars that stank of scorched iron-pyrites and boiled horse-tallow, thick with the reek of frozen human night-soil. Inside the steam-heated saloon-car, Senior Auditor Hoshino had come up from the Persian Gulf after leaving the dying Queen-Mother at Oahu; behind his spectacles, his brow furrowed over a green-baize table covered with unpunched manila cards while he tapped the dead brass key of the portable field-telegraph.

"The repeater at Nerchinsk has not answered the nine-o’clock parity-check, Citizen-Historian," Hoshino said. His breath frosted inside the car as the locomotive boiler-pressure dropped for lack of dry birch-cordwood. "And the pit-superintendent here has delivered only fourteen gondolas of crushed matte since noon instead of forty. Look down at the third gallery: why have they shut off the pneumatic rock-drills before the ten-o’clock bell?"

I wiped the rime from the inner pane with my fur gauntlet. Five hundred feet below our trestle, the open-cut abyss glared white and violet.

The rhythmic *chug-chug-chug* of the three hundred Ingersoll-Osaka steam-drills that usually shook the permafrost night and day had stopped dead. Along the twenty-foot-wide granite ledges of the lower galleries, where the narrow-gauge ore-tubs ran on iron rails toward the central hoisting-shaft, twenty thousand men in padded grey canvas coats and frozen bast-shoes stood motionless in the snow. Four-pound sledges and six-foot steel crowbars rested across their shoulders like pikes. Up on the timber guard-towers at the four corners of the pit, solitary Choshu and Hawaiian sentries leaned over the pine rails; kept on double-watch for three months without relief, the nineteen-year-old boys wrapped their hands in greasy rags around the frozen water-jackets of their Maxim guns and shouted down through tin megaphones into the yellow sulfur-fog.

"Shift Three to the rock-face!" bawled the megaphone from Tower Two. The thin, cracked voice of the Oahu corporal echoed across the canyon. "Clear the ore-switches on Gallery Four, or the night-gruel ration is forfeited!"

Down on the bottom step of Gallery Four, beside the red-hot cast-iron brazier where the drill-bits were tempered, a tall, gaunt man in the tattered, sleeveless coat of a former Prussian pioneer-major stepped out of the ranks.

In the circular lenses of my field-glasses, he held his left arm straight out over the white-hot coals of the forge and laid the lead-and-brass debtor-shackle on his wrist squarely across the iron anvil beside the fire. A bearded Russian forge-striker swung a ten-pound smith’s hammer in one heavy blow. The Monterey rivet sheared in two. Raising his bleeding wrist into the violet glare of the carbon-arcs, the Prussian flung the stamped brass number-plate straight into the melting-pot.

"The Khyber track is up, brothers!" Across the frozen stone amphitheater, repeated at once in Russian and Polish and English by fifty voice-leaders along the galleries, the German’s baritone roar rolled from terrace to terrace. "The hillmen have burned the tanks at Kabul, and there hasn't been a troop-train through Irkutsk since the September frost! There are sixty thousand of us in the ditch, and eighty sick boys on the wall with frozen water-guns!"

Up in Tower Two, the nineteen-year-old Oahu corporal slammed the brass thumb-piece of his Maxim gun forward.

A dull metallic snap echoed across the rim.

The firing-pin fell upon a chamber locked solid with twenty-degree grease and frozen condensation. Every cartridge stayed cold. Before the boy could draw his cleaning-rod or unbuckle his nine-shot pistol from beneath his sheepskin coat, forty Russian and Yorkshire quarry-blasters on the ledge directly beneath the tower-stilts swung two hundred-pound wooden boxes of thawing nitro-glycerine against the frozen larch-wood pilings and touched their red-hot drill-irons to the grease-paper.

The northern wall of the canyon vanished. A sky-high geyser of yellow flame and splintered timber blew Tower Two and its Maxim gun three hundred feet into the air across the pit, while the severed main high-tension copper power-line from the Chita dynamos spat ten-thousand-volt blue sparks across the ledges and dropped the entire two-mile gorge into blackness. Only the forge-braziers burned red at the bottom as sixty thousand iron-shod boots roared straight up the timbered haulage-ramps toward our railway-siding.

"Reverse the locomotive! Cut the audit-vans loose from the coal-tender!" Auditor Hoshino screamed. He leaped from the green-baize table as the nitro-glycerine blast wave shattered every double-paned window in our saloon-car and showered his unpunched Hollerith cards with jagged needles of frozen glass. Tearing open the iron door to the forward platform while his horn-rimmed spectacles flew off into the dark, he hammered with both fists against the armored bulkhead of the engine-cab. "Engineer! Open the throttle for the Chita main-line before they reach the trestle switches!"

Ahead of us in the freezing dark, the cab-door of the six-foot-gauge Baldwin locomotive stayed shut. From the footplate where our two deportee firemen, a former locomotive-artificer from Lyons and a boilermaker from Essen, had shoveled birch-logs since sunset, an iron coal-pick struck flesh with a heavy *thud*. The body of our Californian cadet-engineer rolled down the icy iron steps onto the snow-bank beside the track. Leaning out of the cab window with a stolen service-revolver in his soot-blackened fist, the tall French fireman fired twice into Hoshino’s chest and toppled the Senior Auditor backward over the coupling-chains just as my clerk dragged me out the rear vestibule door into the sub-zero scrub-pine.

***

Four hundred miles west of that slaughtered audit-train, where the black, unfreezing rapids of the Angara River boiled out of the ice-crust of Lake Baikal, Brigadier Marcus Vance the Third kept his gold-rimmed pince-nez well out of reach of any deportee’s coal-pick.

Five thousand feet above the snow-buried stockades of the Irkutsk Timber-Canton, he stood inside the electrically heated aluminum control-gondola of the rigid dirigible *Vengeance of Oahu*.

Across his soft cheeks, the scars of the Kurd-Kabul defile remained raw and purple where burning pine-resin from an Afghan fire-pot had splashed him before Sergeant-Major O’Higgins dragged him onto a pack-mule. His left ear-lobe was gone, taken off by a surgeon’s shears at Peshawar to stop the gangrene. Inside his wired silk flying-gloves, his hands twitched with a perpetual tremor whenever a gust of wind off the Stanovoy peaks made the duralumin deck-plates creak beneath his boots. Yet he kept his peerage. Because Emperor Kalanimoku dared not admit to the rebellious Senate that a Vance had lost forty thousand men to barefoot goat-herds, an aero-transport had carried the young brigadier northward across the Gobi to command the Aerial Suppression Flotilla of the Baikal Sector.

"The rebel column from the Chita copper-pits has broken into the central marshaling-yards at Innokentyevskaya, Brigadier," Flight-Captain Noguchi said. Set into the glass floor between their feet, the stereoscopic drift-sight cast a pale green glow upward across his face. "They have six captured broad-gauge locomotives under steam and are mounting the depot's two-inch Hotchkiss field-pieces onto flatcars. Our surviving garrison—three hundred Californian and Cantonese railway-guards—is barricaded inside the brick grain-elevator by the river, with forty thousand Prussian and Russian quarry-men piling oil-soaked sleepers against the walls."

Marcus kept his gaze averted from the glass floor-plate; tiny dark figures swarming over a stalled train in the snow always prickled the burnt skin on his neck with cold sweat. He studied the polished brass pressure-gauges of the chemical ballast-tanks lining the bulkhead. Around the *Vengeance of Oahu*, arranged in a tight twelve-point diamond across the starlit Siberian night, rode the eleven sister-ships of the Third Aerial Division: six-hundred-foot cigars of duralumin lattice and silver-doped silk whose forty-eight Maybach-Osaka petroleum engines hummed in a deep, synchronized drone that shook dry frost crystals from the birch-forests a mile below.

"What is the barometric temperature on the river-ice, Captain?" Marcus fingered the silver collar-numerals at his throat, his voice high and tight.

"Twenty-six degrees below zero, sir, with a four-knot thermal inversion trapping the coal-smoke at three hundred feet above the roofs," Noguchi said, looking up from the brass eyepiece.

"Then the liquid phosgene will settle into the cellars and the railway-cuts like water in a trough," Marcus said. A small, wet smile twitched at the corner of his scarred lip. In the Hindu Kush, the hillmen had hidden under fifty feet of overhanging limestone beyond the reach of any bomb while the gale tore his airships to rags, whereas here on the flat, frozen plain of the Angara, sixty thousand escaped European debtors and their families crowded inside two square miles of wooden barracks and brick marshaling-sheds without a single anti-aircraft piece larger than an infantry rifle.

"Captain Noguchi, what is the replacement book-value of the Innokentyevskaya grain-elevator and the three hundred garrison-guards inside it?" Marcus pulled his new duralumin circular calculator from his fur-lined breast pocket.

Noguchi blinked behind his fur-trimmed goggles. "The grain-elevator holds forty thousand bushels of Manchurian barley, Brigadier, and the three hundred boys of the Seventy-First Guard are Berkeley third-year—"

"If the Chita mutineers seize the Baikal tunnel-mouths tomorrow morning, the demolition of the masonry arches will cost the Monterey Treasury fourteen million silver thalers and sever the Ural copper-supply for six months," Marcus interrupted. His trembling thumb spun the logarithmic disc. "Three hundred third-class cadets and a brick granary represent less than half of one percent of the canton's capital valuation. Low-altitude drops with picric-acid shells invite a rifle-volley into our hydrogen cells. Signal the flotilla to open the main ballast-valves simultaneously."

"All twelve ships, sir?" Noguchi’s gloved hand stopped half an inch above the brass telegraph-handle. "We are carrying eighty tons of pressurized chlorine-phosgene mixture and four thousand white-phosphorus incendiary cylinders! With this thermal inversion, the gas-cloud will drift straight across the municipal timber-workers' settlement and the hospital-stockade on the east bank. Twelve thousand women and typhus-convalescents are in those sheds who haven't joined the Chita column!"

"An unnumbered debtor who watches a mutiny from a window without lifting a shovel for the Emperor is a mutineer on half-ration, Captain!" Marcus shrieked. His voice broke into the same reedy falsetto that had echoed through the Kurd-Kabul gorge before the fire-pot fell, and his palm slapped the pistol-holster at his hip. "Open the valves across the entire grid-square, or I will log your cipher for court-martial before we touch the Vladivostok mooring-mast! Drop the phosphorus first to set the outer stockades burning and drive them inward toward the railway-cut, then dump the phosgene tanks into the middle of the funnel!"

A Vance with a cheek twitching like a galvanized frog’s invited no second argument. Noguchi pulled the red master-lever three notches back against the brass quadrant.

Beneath the belly of the *Vengeance of Oahu*, the pneumatic bomb-bay doors parted with a greasy hiss of compressed air. A cold Siberian draft smelling of pine-needles and wood-smoke rushed up into the cabin as twelve hundred fluted iron cylinders tumbled out of the squadron's racks. Long, white-hot ribbons of igniting phosphorus trailed behind them toward the yellow camp-fires of the railway yard.

Marcus stepped to the edge of the glass floor-panel and looked down between his boots.

A mile below, the wooden roofs of the hospital-sheds, the tarred timber stockades, and the stalled freight-cars erupted simultaneously into a geometric square of blinding, greenish-white fire that lit up the snow-plain for ten leagues around. In the high-powered Zeiss lenses of the drift-sight, the dark, ant-like multitudes of the Chita rebels swarmed inward. Women dragged blankets from the burning barracks while three hundred Californian cadets waved blue-and-gold signal-flags from the roof of the central grain-elevator, all of them running toward the only unburned ground in the canton: the deep, sunken granite trench of the six-foot railway cut.

Then the second flight of airships passed over the fire-ring. Their crews opened the two-inch brass stop-cocks of the chemical ballast-tanks.

A thick, heavy rain of pale yellow liquid fell in silence. The instant that deluge struck the heat of the burning sleepers, it flashed into a dense, rolling fog of greenish-gray vapor five hundred yards wide and forty feet deep. Too heavy to rise through the freezing air, the cloud of phosgene and chlorine slid down the terraced snow-banks into the sunken railway-cut like liquid lead.

Within four minutes, the waving blue-and-gold flag atop the grain-elevator dropped over the parapet. Down in the trench between the six-foot Bessemer rails, the sixty thousand dark specks ceased to run. Across the two-mile basin, while hydrochloric acid dissolved their lungs and set them clawing at their own throats, they collapsed in long, wind-rowed heaps against the locked wheels of the locomotives until the yellow fog covered the cut like a dirty sheep-fleece. Only the flames of the burning hospital moved upon the snow.

"Log the expenditure at seventy-two tons of chemical ordnance and four hundred gallons of Borneo benzine, Captain," Marcus Vance the third said. He turned from the glass pane and drew his silk glove across his scarred cheek to wipe away the sweat. "And wire the Chancellery at Thalassia that the Baikal sector has balanced its labor-rolls for the winter at zero cost in rolling-stock."

***

On the morning of the twenty-fourth of October, after the wind had blown the yellow vapor down the Angara, that telegram and four photographic glass-plates taken at dawn from the reconnaissance-basket of the *Vengeance of Oahu* were laid upon the porphyry table of the Privy Cabinet at Thalassia. Outside the palace windows, the trade-wind blew soft and warm through the blooming hibiscus. The sixty-cycle transformers in the basement hummed their steady, sunlit chord.

Lady Kaiulani left the stereoscope untouched. Holding the four-by-five negative up against the blinding tropical glare of the veranda archway, she peered through the milky white veil of her cataracts at the black geometry of the six-foot railway cut. Packed between the iron rails for two miles, the twisted shapes of the women from the timber-sheds and the boys in the slate-gray coats of Berkeley lay frozen solid into a single grey pavement, over which the pioneer-sleds were already laying new pine sleepers without digging graves.

Across the porphyry table, the twenty-eight-year-old Sacred Emperor Kalanimoku stood in his white linen Admiral’s undress. A silver pencil rested between his strong brown fingers as he initialed the promotion-warrant advancing Brigadier Marcus Vance the third to Marshal of the Northern Marches.

"With the Chita and Irkutsk pits cleared of the European strikers, we can bring eighty thousand fresh Cantonese and Javanese contract-coolies up the Amur line before the spring thaw," Kalanimoku said. His voice rang with the hard, gravelly frontier cadence learned from the wax cylinders, and he handed the wet sheet to Prefect-Chancellor Shen. "Tell Marshal Vance to leave the corpses frozen in the ballast along the sidings until April; when the new gangs step off the box-cars, forty thousand white debtors under the ties will save us two battalions of provost-guards."

Kaiulani lowered the glass photographic plate toward the table. Six inches above the polished stone, she opened her fingers. It broke in two with a sharp, musical splintering of glass right across the Emperor’s signature.

Kalanimoku stopped his hand. He looked down at his grandmother. For the first time in three years, she had refused her wheeled chair; flanked on her left by her niece Malia and on her right by old, lame Field-Marshal Marcus Vance, whose face had gone the color of wet salt-cod above the photograph of his grand-nephew’s handiwork, the eighty-five-year-old woman stood upright upon her two swollen, dropsical feet. She wore a plain, coarse *holoku* of unbleached native tapa-bark, such as the fish-wives of Molokai wore when they went down into the salt-pans.

"Three hundred of those bodies in the ditch are your own cadets of the Seventy-First California Guard, Kalanimoku," Kaiulani whispered. Her thin, rough breath cut through the quiet hum of the ceiling-fans. "Boys who passed the Monterey examination-sheds with your name stamped on their primers, gassed like wharf-rats in a grain-bin because young Vance was afraid to come down below five thousand feet and soil his gloves."

"They were an acceptable structural loss to save the Baikal tunnel-arches, Grandmother," Kalanimoku answered. Those pale gray eyes, the dead Protector's eyes, were cold inside his smooth Polynesian face. "When my grandfather burned the cholera-ships at Panama, he never asked whether the carpenters on the deck were from Kentucky or Canton. He counted the days to the opening of the locks."

"Your grandfather was a border-butcher who fought men with rifles in their hands so that this ocean might have a roof over its head!" Kaiulani’s cry brought the four Samoan guardsmen outside the veranda doors stiffly to attention. "I stood beside Elias Thorne for thirty years while we hammered the iron together, and I lied to my own dead brother’s ghost and told myself that the blood we spilled at Hankow and the Sacramento was the price of the peace! I cut the wire at Honolulu; I drowned Elias’s body in the deep water; I put the feathers of Kamehameha upon your shoulders and built you a house of glass so that you might rule like a father over living men!"

Her shrunken brown hands wrenched upward to her withered throat. Seizing the ancient braided hair-cord of the *lei niho palaoa*, the sacred curved hook of whale-tooth that had been the Regent’s seal of the Insular Chancery since the morning of the Sand Island truce, she tore the cord in two and flung the heavy ivory pendant squarely across the broken glass negative at Kalanimoku’s knuckles.

"Take back your bone, grandson of the mainland!" she gasped. Dark blood flecked her bluish lips, and she leaned her feather-light weight against old Marcus Vance’s trembling arm. "You are no chief of Maui, and this is no city of peace! You have turned the Great Arena into an iron slaughter-house where children with numbers on their necks pour poison from the clouds upon women in their beds to save four cents on a ton of copper! Strike my name from the Regency rolls, Chancellor Shen! I will die on clean rock instead of under a roof held up by frozen corpses. Take me out to the leper-spit at Kalaupapa tonight, Malia, where the sea is clean and the rocks are bare of telegraph-wire!"

***

They carried the old Queen out of the palace at sunset aboard a coast-guard steam-launch. Retired Field-Marshal Marcus Vance sat silent and uncovered upon a coil of tarred hemp at her feet, leaving the twenty-eight-year-old Emperor alone beneath the sixty-cycle lights of the Chart-Room; yet before her boat had even crossed the Molokai channel, the poison-cloud of Irkutsk was already raining back down in blood six thousand miles to the southwest.

That November, after the Singapore submarine cable went dead on the twelfth of the month, I was hurried southward from Vladivostok aboard the fast turbine-cruiser *Sendai*, transferred in mid-winter from the frozen birch-forests of the Baikal to the steaming, ninety-degree rubber-jungles of the One Hundred and Fourteenth Malayan Canton. The Siberian contagion had leaped from the snow to the equator in a fortnight.

For forty years, the great tropical plantation-belt of the Confederation—the tin-mines of Perak, the gutta-percha forests of Borneo, the petroleum-wells of Sumatra, and the endless, terraced rubber-estates of Mindanao and Cochin-China—had been the quietest, most profitable cellar of the Empire. Beneath a perpetual green twilight of banyan and teak where no dreadnought could steam and no air-cruiser could pierce the hundred-foot canopy, three million indentured coolies from Madras, Java, and Canton had been joined since nineteen-eighteen by eight hundred thousand deported French, Belgian, and Ukrainian labor-conscripts. They bled the white latex from the trees. They pumped the crude naphtha into the coastal pipe-lines.

Word of the Innokentyevskaya gas-massacre soon reached the Singapore and Batavia docks. While the censored Monterey bulletins reported an accidental explosion in a chemical magazine, the Ukrainian and Cantonese stokers of the returning ore-colliers who had smelled the burned flesh on the Vladivostok wind carried the truth word-for-word to the wharves, and the four hundred thousand European deportees in the Malayan jungle abandoned their barracks before chlorine could strangle them in their sleep.

The quarry-men at Chita had died in an open railway-cut under the dirigibles; the deportees of Malaya took to the trees.

On the afternoon of the twenty-eighth of November, 1920, I stood inside the sandbagged redoubt of Pumping-Station Six. Forty miles up the muddy Pahang River in the interior of the Malay Peninsula, the thirty-inch steel petroleum conduit from the central storage-tanks crossed the jungle gorge beside the narrow-gauge rubber-tramway.

Beneath the corrugated-iron roof of the blockhouse, the shade temperature stood at a hundred and four degrees. The air was foul with rotting bamboo-leaves, stagnant river-slime, boiling crude petroleum, and the sharp, sweetish citronella-grease smeared over our faces to keep the malarial mosquitoes out of our eyes. Thirty yards beyond the barbed wire, the hundred-foot wall of the Pahang rain-forest rose in a curtain of dripping green lianas and giant tree-ferns, loud with the drone of cicadas and the rhythmic, hollow *tok-tok-tok* of wooden slit-drums beaten miles away in the hills.

"Four days since the repair-train left Kuala Lipis, Citizen-Historian, and the down-grade is still clear of smoke," said Captain Takahashi of the Nineteenth Satsuma Provosts. He wiped the greenish sweat from the breech-block of his hot Maxim gun with an oily rag while his forty surviving cadets, half of them shaking with the tertian ague under their sodden slate-gray tunics, peered through the steel loop-holes into the green gloom. "Yesterday the air-cruiser *Kagoshima* came over the canopy at two thousand feet and dropped sixty tons of phosgene-cylinders along the river-trail where the telegraph-poles were cut. Every rebel escaped. The triple-tier banyan leaves caught half the drums before they hit the mud, and the tropical updraft dissipated the gas in ten minutes. It poisoned three miles of river-fish and blinded our own Malay trackers in the launches!"

Down at the base of the timber trestle below the blockhouse, where the thirty-inch oil-pipe emerged from the dense brake of giant bamboo, cold steel struck iron. The ring echoed through the afternoon stillness.

Out of the dripping green fern-roots, smeared from head to foot with grey river-clay until their naked skins vanished against the bark of the mangrove-trunks, wriggled two hundred men side by side: former French machine-fitters from the Creusot works with their brass debtor-tags filed off their wrists, bearded Cossack sappers from the Don, and sinewy Dyak and Moro wood-cutters carrying four-foot *parang* machetes between their teeth and heavy cast-iron pipe-wrenches stolen from our own tool-sheds.

"Depress the muzzle! Fire into the bamboo roots at thirty yards!" Takahashi yelled. His thumbs jammed the brass triggers of the Maxim forward. The gun hammered. A stream of .303 bullets ripped through the wet fern-fronds and splintered the green bamboo stems into white pulp.

The clay-smeared figures stayed low in the scrub. Twenty Ukrainian riflemen lay flat in the mud behind the iron pipe-flanges and returned a slow sniper-fire with captured Sacramento carbines; a heavy soft-nosed slug tore straight through the two-inch vision-slit beside my ear, took off the top of Takahashi’s skull, and drenched my notebook in hot blood and brains. Underneath the curving belly of the thirty-inch petroleum main, three French mechanics crawled where our machine-gun bullets only ricocheted off the half-inch steel.

They had built half the high-pressure boilers in Europe before the tariff-wars broke them. Fitting their four-foot iron spanners to the main expansion-collar of the pipeline, the three Frenchmen threw their weight together upon the levers until the twelve rusted Monterey bolts sheared open, and a solid, roaring jet of black Sumatra crude oil, pumped at two hundred pounds of pressure to the square inch from the coastal tanks, fountained straight out across the muddy ditch and down the slope toward the trench surrounding our sandbags.

"Cut the main pump-valve inside the engine-house!" screamed young Lieutenant Miller. The nineteen-year-old boy from the Oakland sheds had dragged Takahashi’s headless body away from the Maxim tripod and was jabbing at a jammed canvas belt with his bayonet. Black, stinking raw naphtha and petroleum flooded knee-deep through the barbed-wire entanglements and soaked into the dry palm-thatch of our ammunition-bunker. "If they drop a match into the ditch, the whole gorge will go up like a lamp-wick! Corporal, get the wireless key working—"

Out at the edge of the bamboo brake, a tall, bare-chested Belgian artilleryman with a six-digit debtor-scar burned across his forearm stood up for a single second in the open mud. Around his head he whirled a homemade sling of braided rattan holding a blazing ball of dry coconut-husk soaked in rubber-latex. As Lieutenant Miller wrenched the iron door of the pump-house open to reach the steam-cock, the flaming ball arched high over the barbed wire and struck the oil-slicked sandbags with a wet, muffled *whump* that turned the entire Pahang gorge into a roaring funnel of orange flame. With four scorched survivors, I bolted headlong down the muddy river-bank toward our armored steam-launch while the ammunition-bunker behind us blew its corrugated iron roof straight through the banyan canopy.

***

Six hundred miles across the Gulf of Siam from that burning pipeline, Marshal Marcus Vance the third stood knee-deep in the warm, leech-infested bilge-water of the flat-bottomed river monitor *Tonkin*, his gold-rimmed pince-nez so crusted with dead gnats and yellow marsh-sweat that the pressure-dials on the forward bulkhead blurred before him.

When the rubber-estates of Cochin-China and the rice-canals of Mytho had risen in December behind a hundred thousand runaway Annamite canal-diggers and deported Belgian mechanics, Emperor Kalanimoku had ordered the victor of Irkutsk south to repeat his chemical miracle in the tropics. Marcus had brought six rigid airships down from Vladivostok. Within three weeks, the ninety-percent equatorial humidity had rotted the doped silk of their gas-cells until the hydrogen leaked through the seams like water through a sieve, and the monsoon lightning over Cambodia had burned two of the silver giants out of the clouds before they could drop a single canister.

Now the Marshal of the Northern Marches was down in the mud.

All around the shallow-draft iron hull of the *Tonkin*, for fifty square leagues between the Bassac and the Vaico branches of the great river, stretched a flat, steaming expanse of twelve-foot elephant-grass and flooded rice-paddies that smelled of putrefying catfish, warm human ordure, and the sulfurous coal-smoke of his own stalled boilers.

"Why have the paddle-wheels stopped turning, Captain?" Marcus shouted. His high, reedy voice cracked as he slapped the blistered grey skin of his neck where a malaria-mosquito had bitten through his wet silk scarf. His left hand twitched against the butt of his silver-plated pistol; the purple resin-scars from the Afghan pass itched in the hundred-degree steam of the delta. "If we do not clear the Vinh-Long canal-lock before dusk, the night-mists will blind the searchlights! Give the engines full steam and ram the barrier!"

Down in the open iron engine-pit amidships, Lieutenant-Commander Brooks, his uniform tunic stripped off over ribs raw with prickly-heat sores, wiped his greasy forearm across his brow and pointed with a monkey-wrench toward the stern wheel-housing.

"There is no barrier to ram, Marshal," Brooks said, his voice flat after forty days without sleep onshore. "The Annamites and the French deportees left the stone-junks out of the channel this time. They floated three miles of twisted wire-rope and green water-hyacinth down the current while we were shelling the empty bamboo village on the left bank. The cables have wound themselves six inches thick around the main paddle-shaft, and the hyacinth-roots have choked the condenser intakes until the vacuum-gauge is at zero. If I open the throttle another notch, the cylinder-heads will blow out."

"Then send the Cantonese pioneer-squad over the side with axes and diving-helmets to hack the wire off the shaft!" Marcus screamed. He stepped up onto the hot iron grating above the boilers. His scarred cheek jerked like a frog's leg. "We have twelve tons of chlorine-shells in the forward magazine! Clear the paddles and fire gas at zero elevation into the mangrove screen on both banks!"

"We put six boys over the side with axes at the noon bend, sir," Brooks answered. A hollow *plop* sounded from the green wall of nipa-palms forty yards away, and a four-foot bamboo blow-dart tipped with rotting buffalo-liver stuck quivering into the wooden chart-table between them; Brooks did not flinch. "The rebels have staked sharpened iron harrow-teeth and poisoned bamboo spikes across the mud-bottom under the hyacinths, and their frog-men swim underneath the hull with hand-augers to pull our diver-hoses loose. You can fire all twelve tons of chlorine into those mangroves if you please, Marshal, and the afternoon sea-breeze will blow the gas straight back over our own deck in five minutes, while the rebels are already three miles away in the swamp-canals poling their flat-punts where a ten-inch shell only throws up ten thalers' worth of warm mud."

Marcus stared out through the armored gun-port at the shimmering wall of green reeds. Nothing moved. From somewhere deep inside that miles-wide vegetable sponge came the rhythmic *clink-clink-clink* of an iron hammer striking a stolen railway-plate, the signal-telegraph of an army that needed neither coal nor Monterey logarithms while the iron ships rusted to the bottom of the ditch.

"Fire the six-pounders into the reeds anyway!" Marcus shrieked. His trembling boots slipped on the wet slime of the deck as he dragged at the breech-lever of the nearest sponson-gun himself. "Fire by the clock every thirty seconds! I will not report another negative tally to the Palace!"

***

I returned to Thalassia in the spring of 1921, limping ashore at the Waipahu quay with my left arm still bandaged from the Pahang oil-fire. The reports that Marshal Vance was firing sixty-thaler shells into empty mud-banks to manufacture casualty-lists for the telegraph caused me no surprise whatever.

By that April, the capital had ceased to trust its own numbers. The terror that had begun in the snows of Kabul and the swamps of the Mekong had crawled inside the crystal dome.

As my electric cab rolled along the *Via Triumphalis* toward the Chancellery, the sun still shone in Sunset Gold upon the twenty-ton blocks of red Agra sandstone, yet pedestrians hurried past in a silent, sidelong crouch. The great geothermal fountains in the Piazza of the Pivot stood dry. Their high-tension power had been diverted to feed the six rings of electrified barbed wire and the forty searchlight-towers that now separated the Sacred Emperor’s artificial island from the municipal wards of Honolulu.

In the first generation of the Empire, when Elias Thorne had suspected a general or a silver-syndicate of treason, he had sent a company of cavalry in broad daylight to hang the offender from a telegraph-pole, and the streets had gone back to their business. Now, because the third generation had been taught from the cradle that the Polytechnic machine was mathematically infallible, the simultaneous collapse of the Siberian copper-output and the Malayan oil-lines alongside the European tax-remittances left the mandarins with a single hypothesis: that an unseen conspiracy of saboteurs was falsifying the equations inside the Bureau of Integration itself.

The people in the street called it the *Audit of the Red Needle*; history will know it as the *Great Purge*.

When I entered the subterranean sorting-vaults beneath the Palace of the Double Horizon at ten o’clock that morning to deposit my Malayan field-diaries, the corridors smelled of scorched paper and the raw, vinegary reek of the photographic developing-acid that the new *Board of Internal Verification* was using to check the thumb-prints upon forty million civil-service dossiers.

Down the center of the main marble corridor, where five years earlier the young graduates of Berkeley and Kyoto had walked like kings, stood a double file of Samoan and Choshu Household Provosts wearing the black-and-crimson brassards of the Palace Secret Police. Every twenty minutes, the heavy bronze elevator-doors at the end of the hall slid open with a greased sigh. Four guards marched out between them leading a Senior Prefect of the First or Second Class, grey-templed men who had spent thirty years calculating the grain-allocations of Canton or the customs-tariffs of Melbourne, with their silver identification-ciphers ripped from their collars and their thumbs locked together behind their backs in steel thumb-screws.

"Step aside to the wall, Citizen-Historian, and present your travel-warrant to the perforator," ordered a twenty-year-old Inspector of the Verification Board. He barred my path before the archive-turnstile while his partner, a boy from the Nagasaki wards, held a magnifying-glass over the violet serial-stamp on my wrist.

Inside the glass-walled office of the Chief of the Chancellery, the steel podium stood empty.

Prefect-Chancellor Shen the third, the grandson of Elias Thorne’s auditor, knelt upon the mosaic floor in his shirt-sleeves with his horn-rimmed spectacles mended across the bridge by a strip of adhesive tape and his hair hanging in damp grey strings over his forehead, feeding bundles of old nineteen-eighteen European debt-ledgers into a portable brick incinerator mortared directly into the base of the Great Gnomon.

"Shen!" I stepped past the unguarded inner glass door while the Samoan sentries in the corridor dragged a screaming hydraulic-engineer from the Panama locks down the stairs toward the harbor-hulks. "What are you burning? Those are the Brussels master-schedules!"

Shen looked up over his shoulder. His face had shrunk to the yellow-gray parchment of a consumptive, and beneath the damp grey strings of his hair, his fingers trembled so violently around the brass poker that the iron tip rattled against the brick mortar.

"The Emperor signed Warrant Nine-Zero-Zero at midnight, Historian." Shen's gaze darted toward the ceiling-ventilators where the Palace Secret Police had wired carbon listening-microphones inside the bronze wind-gods. "The spring rice-fleet from Saigon arrived at Manila yesterday with sixty percent of its holds empty because the Mekong barges were burned at Mytho, and the Ruhr coal-syndics have suspended the April tribute. His Majesty refuses to hear that the peasants are in the jungle! He says that the fuel-oil and the rice are still in the warehouses, and that the Senior Assessors of the First Class have entered a treasonous league with the European debtors to shift the decimal-points on the clearing-sheets!"

With a jerky heave of his arm, Shen shoved a three-hundred-page bound volume of the Siberian census into the white-hot coke of the furnace.

"They took Rector Norton’s successor out of the Berkeley mathematics hall on Tuesday and drowned him in the bay with an iron weight tied to his neck because the winter birth-rate in the Ohio cantons fell twelve percent below the curve!" Orange glare from the burning paper glinted across Shen's cracked lenses while down the marble corridor outside my door, the heavy, regular tramp of eight iron-shod boots rang out against the stone. "And ten minutes ago, the Verification Board found a three-million-thaler discrepancy in my father’s nineteen-fourteen Rangoon opium-balance! If you have a single notebook in your satchel that says the Pahang pipeline is broken, throw it into the fire before the Samoan corporal reaches the glass, or by noon tomorrow you and I will be chained to an oar-bench in the Peruvian guano-pits!"

# Chapter 28: The Steel Revolution

I slipped out before the Samoan corporal reached the glass. Through the pneumatic-tube service-tunnel behind the Molokai transformer-banks, while Shen’s voice rose in a thin scream of loyalty before his arresters, I fled to the docks and boarded a returning mutton-collier for the southern hemisphere that same night. Three weeks later our rusty hull raised the heads of Port Phillip Bay. In the Eighty-Second Australian Canton, the dying brain at Thalassia had installed a colder substitute for the human hands it no longer trusted.

As the Great Purge emptied the examination-sheds of Berkeley and Kyoto, and the Hidden Wars in the Malayan jungles and the Siberian snow-drifts swallowed ten thousand young engineers a month, the remaining syndicate-lords who fed the fleet had reached the final conclusion of Marcus Vance’s philosophy: if a man with a number on his collar could still catch the black grippe, strike for four ounces of salt-fish, or throw a coconut-fireball into an oil-ditch, then flesh itself was a flaw in the iron.

Historians in the provinces have called this last convulsion the *Steel Revolution*.

On a freezing, rain-lashed afternoon in June, 1921, I walked up the long basalt wharf of Williamstown on the outskirts of Melbourne. Two miles of curving dock lay empty of stevedores or tally-clerks. Six stories above the oily gray swells of the bay, where the wool-clippers had once berthed four abreast under forests of pine spars, stood the newly completed *Automated Imperial Wool-and-Ordnance Complex Number Four*, a windowless, mile-long fortress of poured grey concrete and corrugated duralumin that hummed with a sixty-cycle roar like a hive of iron hornets.

Along the coping of the quay, forty giant gantry-cranes unloaded raw copper-ingots and bales of Riverina fleece from a line of crewless, gyro-steered steel barges. No glass cabins hung upon the crane-legs for a human operator. Guided by overhead copper trolley-wires and five-inch strips of perforated brass tape that unreeled continuously inside cast-iron control-pillars along the rail, the mechanical claws dropped straight down into the hatches with an unvarying *clank-whir-shunt*, gripped four-ton loads of greasy wool, and swung them directly into the open jaws of the electric scouring-vats faster than any human wrist could turn.

Where, then, were the two hundred thousand Yorkshiremen and Cantonese mechanics who had filled the Melbourne wards when old Senator MacArthur rose in the Crystal Palace five years before?

Half a mile inland from the humming concrete wall of the automated foundry, across a waste of cold coal-slag and flooded clay-pits encircled by a double fence of ten-thousand-volt barbed wire and twin-turreted Maxim blockhouses, they stood in the winter mud of the Yarra flats.

Eighty thousand of them huddled beneath torn tarpaulins and rusted sheets of flattened kerosene-tins. Their fathers had sheared the sheep of Victoria or puddled the steel of Ballarat; now their grey canton-coats hung in rags from their starved shoulders, and their left wrists still bore the riveted brass ration-shackles that no longer opened a turnstile at the factory gates.

I stood beside the armored gate-house of the foundry wire with Chief Mechanical Prefect Ozawa, a twenty-four-year-old graduate of the Osaka Cybernetic Institute whose left arm had been replaced at the elbow by a jointed steel prosthetic hook after the Chita explosion. Outside in the sleet, four hundred gaunt, barefoot foundry-smiths pressed against the outer wooden palings and held up cold iron hammers and empty tin pannikins toward the twenty-foot-high intake-flues where hot tallow-steam from the automated mutton-canneries vented into the sky.

"Open the third-shift wickets, Prefect!" Below the windowless wall and the relentless *thump-thump-thump* of its crewless steam-hammers, a grey-bearded giant in a leather apron shouted through the sleet, his chest still bearing the bronze medal of the nineteen-fourteen Panama Concrete Gang. "Our women haven't seen a pound of barley-meal since you locked the manual lathes in May! Put a hundred men back on the shell-presses at half-ration, or by God we’ll bring the timber-jacks down from the bush and pry the concrete off your dynamos with our bare hands!"

Prefect Ozawa ignored the medal on the old man’s leather apron. With his steel hook, he turned the brass rheostat upon the gate-post and raised the current in the upper insulators until the rain-drops sizzling along the barbed wire gave off a sharp smell of burnt air.

"A human lathe-turner consumes three thousand calories of wheat and mutton per diem, requires eight hours of sleep in twenty-four, and introduces a four-percent variance in the driving-bands of a twenty-two-inch shell whenever his child dies of the winter grippe, Citizen-Historian," Ozawa said in his flat Osaka English. Down at the southern corner of the slag-heap, pine-timber splintered with a roaring crash through the rain where two thousand shearers and dock-men swung a forty-foot telegraph-pole like a battering-ram straight against the main power-conduit pylon.

"Whereas the Babbage-Nakajima tape-loom behind this wall," Ozawa said, while his hand dropped toward the red brass trip-lever of the gate-house steam-mortars and the great iron pylon at the corner of the fence buckled inward in a thirty-foot fountain of blue high-tension sparks and screaming men, "requires only two gallons of mineral oil a week, never petitions the Senate for salt, and cannot remember the name of its father."

He pulled the brass lever back against the stop.

Compressed steam coughed from the blockhouse roof. The four short-barreled mortars lobbed their canisters of liquid lime and shrapnel straight into the tangled mass of men around the fallen pylon. Leaving the gray mud of the Yarra to turn red under the rain, I walked away from the humming concrete wall and the citizen the Empire had sought since Elias Thorne rode into Sacramento: a wheel that spun in the dark without a mouth.

***

Yet if the iron wheel in Melbourne needed no bread, it drank the blood of the islands like water.

Exiled by her own choice from the leper-spit of Molokai after Emperor Kalanimoku’s naval engineers seized the Kalaupapa cliffs in July to mount long-range acoustic hydrophones, eighty-six-year-old Lady Kaiulani had been carried sixty miles northwest across the channel to the last unfortified corner of the archipelago: the deep, red-walled canyon of Waimea on the island of Kauai.

Here, in her childhood, the world had smelled of wet mountain fern and crushed *maile* leaves under the cold spray of the Waialeale cataracts tumbling four thousand feet from the clouds to feed the ancient stone-walled taro-patches of the valley floor. Now, on a stifling afternoon in August, 1921, as she sat propped upon a mat of woven pandanus beneath the thatched eaves of an old priest’s grass-house above the river-bend, the wind coming up from the coast carried the stench of blistered copper and dead fish.

Her milky, cataract-clouded eyes were blind, yet the ruin her grandson’s syndicates had wrought upon the Garden Isle reached her on every breeze. Three miles down the gorge, where the sacred river met the sea at Koloa, the Bureau of Ordnance had erected the *Seventh Electrolytic Nitrate and Bauxite Works*, a sprawling, treeless scar of corrugated iron sheds and open-cut red-mud leaching vats that drew its power from a concrete dam thrown straight across the mouth of the high mountain waterfalls.

The river below her bamboo rail had gone silent among the boulders. Diverted through four-foot cast-iron penstocks to spin the Pelton wheels of the chemical vats, the ancient stream had shrunk to a stagnant, ankle-deep trickle of warm, rust-colored sludge that steamed with sulphuric acid and yellow picric run-off.

"Are the mullet-ponds at Lawai still breathing, Malia?" Kaiulani’s tiny, shrunken head rested back against the rough cedar post while her niece knelt beside her and wiped the yellow chemical dust from the old Queen’s lips with a damp rag of native tapa-bark.

Malia looked down the valley toward the coast. A greasy bank of coal-black and saffron smoke from the bauxite roasting-kilns hung low over the dead palms like a bruised thunderhead and blotted out the sunset gold of the western water.

"The seawall at Lawai broke on Tuesday, Aunt," Malia said. "The dredging-barges were blasting the coral reef with dynamite to deepen the channel for the Osaka acid-tankers, and when the tide came in through the gap, it carried the yellow tailings from the copper-wash straight into the royal fish-ponds. Forty thousand silver mullet floated belly-up against the lava stones this morning, and the taro-terraces from here to Hanapepe are burned down to the gray clay. The roots turn to black slime in the women’s hands before they can pull them from the mud."

Down on the narrow gravel path below the grass-house, a file of thirty old Hawaiian fishermen and their wives, the last villagers who had escaped the draft for the Koloa leaching-sheds, shuffled past in silence. Their hands were empty of throw-nets or carved wooden calabashes. With rusted five-gallon kerosene-tins balanced on shoulder-poles, they climbed four miles up into the high, dry rocks above the dam to dip muddy rainwater out of the goat-wallows because the wells in the valley burned the skin off a child’s throat.

Kaiulani had left her ivory rings behind on the palace floor; her withered brown hands closed slowly over the dry pandanus reeds of her mat.

"When Captain Cook’s iron nails first came to Kealakekua, my great-grandfather’s priests said the gods had sent us a harder stone for our adzes," she said. Her breath whistled in the sulfurous heat while the distant, regular *boom-crump* of the reef-blasting charges shook dead yellow fern-fronds down upon her white hair. "We thought we could take the white man’s steam-engine and the Chinaman’s abacus and wear them like a feather cloak over our own skin. Look at the mountain, Malia. We have eaten the reef to build the ships, and boiled the river to fill the shells, and now the island itself is dying of the iron before I can get into the ground."

***

To the Chronicler who crossed the turbulent autumn swells of the North Pacific six weeks later, fleeing northward from the burning wool-sheds of Melbourne aboard an automated grain-hulk whose gyro-compass brought us through the Golden Gate without a single sailor touching the wheel, the death of the earth that the old Queen mourned on Kauai had already produced its monstrous birth at the center of the web.

I stepped ashore at the Market Street Ferry-Slips in San Francisco on the twelfth of October, 1921. The old brick metropolis where Elias Thorne had hammered his empire together lay half-abandoned under a perpetual, choking fog of unrefined Mexican bunker-oil and nitric-acid vapor.

Neither Senior Assessors nor syndicate-directors walked the cracked asphalt of Montgomery Street or climbed the steep cobbles of Rincon Hill anymore. Since the great bread-and-typhus riots of the previous winter, when sixty thousand unemployed foundry-hands from the automated Potrero works had tried to storm the Mint vaults with crowbars and been mowed down by the crewless Maxim-towers along the Embarcadero, the hereditary caste of the *Imperial Citizens* had severed their last gangplank to the soil.

Half a mile out in the deep, racing tide-way between Alcatraz Island and the Marin headlands, moored to the bedrock by sixteen-inch chains of vanadium steel, floated the three linked pontoons of *New Thalassia-in-the-Bay*, the first of the mobile, self-contained Sanctuary-Arks that the Osaka and Hunters Point slips had launched for the families of the First Class.

Through my field-glasses from the rusted iron rail of the Telegraph Hill ruins, that floating island of three hundred acres rose out of the gray, oil-scummed water of the harbor like a wedding-cake of white porcelain and triple-glazed crystal.

Encircled by a forty-foot outer breakwater of sloped Krupp armor-plate, upon whose coping automated torpedo-tubes and rapid-fire pom-pom guns tracked every fishing-skiff or drift-log that came within a thousand yards, the upper decks of the Ark escaped the coal-soot of the shore and the sweat of the cantons. Submerged tidal-turbines and oil-reactors powered the whole floating city. It carried forty-foot terraced gardens of imported Kyoto cherry-trees and Oahu hibiscus heated by artificial quartz-suns; its air passed through water-curtains scented with sandalwood; and along its marble promenades strolled the three thousand surviving shareholders of the Great Arena.

The plain dark wool of the old Polytechnic examination-sheds had vanished from their backs. Dressed in flowing, syncretic robes of imperial-blue Lyons silk and golden Vicuña fleece, the grandsons of Elias Thorne’s rough Missouri pioneers and Marquis Takashima’s samurai drank iced champagne from the mortgaged vineyards of Rheims while the sixty-piece orchestra of Vienna played upon a bandstand of solid Burmese teak.

"They haven't set a boot on the California shore since the April quarantine, Citizen-Historian," said my guide, a one-legged former telegraph-clerk named Higgins who lived by boiling salt out of the bay-mud in a ruined tin-cannery beneath the cliff. He spat down into the greasy black water at the foot of the Meiggs Wharf, where the bloated carcass of a horse floated among the empty ration-tins. "Their meat comes straight up from the New Zealand freezer-ships by electric crane on the seaward side; their sons are examined for the peerage by wireless inside the glass dome; and when they want to move the price of copper in Chile or turn the steam-mortars onto a strike-camp in Seattle, they don't even have to look through a spy-glass at the smoke. They just press a pearl button on their dinner-tables, and the tape-machines down in the Hunters Point basement punch the warrant."

As the sun sank behind the Golden Gate and stained the toxic yellow smog over the Oakland mud-flats a lurid blood-and-brass, the ten-thousand-candlepower pleasure-lanterns along the upper terraces of the Ark flashed on all at once, throwing a golden carpet across the oily tide toward the dark wharves where half a million unnumbered men sat in the cold without a match to light a pipe.

***

Three thousand miles from the lighted decks of the San Francisco Ark, the night-wind off the Kauai channel drove an unnumbered skiff through the dynamited gap in the Koloa reef.

At two hours past midnight on the third of November, the mountain dogs in the mud lane below Lady Kaiulani’s grass-house gave a low, uncertain growl at the smell of salt water and wet canvas, quite unlike the frantic, yapping alarm they raised whenever the Choshu tax-patrols marched up the valley in their iron-shod boots.

Inside the dark hut, a single stone saucer of burning kukui-nut oil sat upon the floor-mats. Eighty-six-year-old Kaiulani was already awake. At her age, sleep came only in ten-minute shreds between the spasms of fluid in her lungs; propped against her cedar post in her coarse bark-cloth wrapper, she lay under the distant, unending *thump-hiss* of the bauxite-stampers down at the dam.

The woven reed screen at the doorway parted without a sound. Malia sprang up from her pallet with an iron fish-spear in her hand, then froze as two figures slipped out of the sulfurous mist under the eaves.

Old Kahuku came first, a seventy-year-old one-eyed canoe-steersman from Niihau whose grandsons had all died in the Bengal landing-craft seven years before. Behind him stood a young man of no more than twenty-three, dripping wet to the waist from the surf, dressed in the greasy, unbadged blue denim trousers of an engine-room stoker and a torn Chinese quilted jacket.

The youth stepped into the red circle of the kukui-nut lamp and dropped upon one knee on the pandanus mat. Even through the milky veil of her cataracts, the mingled blood of the old earth showed plain in his frame. Above the torn sleeve of his jacket, where a machine-belt had ripped the cloth away from his bare left forearm, a livid white scar marked the bone where a six-digit Monterey brass ration-shackle had been pried off with a cold chisel, while the red lamplight caught the high, broad cheekbones and copper skin of an Oahu boatman beneath the narrow, heavy-lidded eyes of a Cantonese furnace-man.

"Who brings the grease of a warship into a dying woman’s house?" Kaiulani whispered. Her thin, claw-like hand rested motionless upon the reed mat.

"My name is nothing, Great Grandmother of the Islands," the young man said. Leaving behind the clipped, mathematical English of the Berkeley primers and the old missionary Hawaiian, he spoke the rough, rhythmic *Creole of the Lower Decks*, that bastard tongue of Cantonese, English, Tagalog, and Polynesian which four generations of stokers and coolies had hammered out in the bilges of the Pacifica fleet. "In the Osaka rolling-mills they stamped me *Seven-Seven-Four-Zero-Two*. Down in the coal-bunkers of the flagship *Thalassia*, where the boys from the three shores pass the shovel in the dark, they call me *Keawe*."

"If you are off the *Thalassia*, you have swum from the Pearl Lochs roadstead with the provost-launches behind you," Malia said. She lowered her spear-point to his throat. "Why have you come to Waimea? The Queen has no gold left to buy you a passage to Mexico, and her name has been struck from the Chancery seals."

"We do not want gold, Lady, and we are not sailing to Mexico," young Keawe answered. He held his throat steady against the iron barb at his windpipe, his dark eyes fixed through the dimness on Kaiulani’s blind face. "The automated tape-ships have locked the grain-silos at Vallejo, and the Emperor on his floating pontoon in San Francisco has signed the winter order to clear the manual stokers out of the Battle Fleet and replace our watches with gyro-feeders from the Nagasaki yards. Forty thousand of us, from the Hawaiian gunners and Cantonese oil-tenders to the Californian machinists and the Russian debtor-gangs at the Waipahu dry-docks, have our fingers on the main Kingston sea-valves and the magazine-flooding cocks of every dreadnought between Diamond Head and the Golden Gate."

Kaiulani’s old heart gave a single leap against her shrunken ribs, like a dying bird striking the bars of its cage.

"You are going to sink the fleet at its moorings," she said.

"Turn the twenty-two-inch turrets inward upon the Crystal Palace and the San Francisco pontoons when the noon meridian-siren blows on the day of the Jubilee, Great Mother!" Leaning forward across the mat, Keawe reached inside his oil-stained shirt and drew out a six-inch strip of stiff crimson silk upon which someone had clumsily stenciled in white deck-paint the ancient, pre-Imperial emblem of the crossed Hawaiian canoe-paddles and the broken iron chain. "The Russian and German quarry-men in Siberia rose for their dead kings, and the airships strangled them with yellow fog. The hillmen in Kabul fought for their mullahs, and the steam-tanks burned their orchards. Our boys in the boiler-rooms have no kings and no mullahs; half of us don't know what island our mothers came from! The older petty-officers on the *Sakurajima* are afraid to turn the turret-keys unless there is a righteous law behind the gun. They remember that your hand signed the truce with the old Protector before the clerks took the sea. Put your thumb-mark in kukui-soot upon this silk, Queen Kaiulani, and give the word of Kamehameha’s blood that the throne in the lagoon is forfeit, and before the sun goes down on the Exhibition we will blow the glass dome and the counting-machines into the coral!"

Outside in the dark gorge, the wind shifted from the sea. Half a mile below the hut, an armored railway-motorcar screeched on its brakes along the narrow-gauge ore-track at the foot of the bluff.

Kaiulani kept her head turned from the window. With her trembling, blind right hand, she reached out through the red lamplight and touched the ragged white scar on the young stoker’s forearm where the brass collar of Elias Thorne’s machine had eaten into his flesh.

"And when you have blown the Crystal Palace into the lagoon, boy," the aged woman whispered, while her fingers slid down from his scarred wrist to dip the tip of her thumb into the black grease around the rim of the stone oil-lamp and the heavy *tramp-tramp* of twenty Choshu provost-boots mounted the gravel grade through the dead taro-patches, "who will feed the four hundred million mouths when the ships stop running?"

"The earth will feed them, Mother, when the iron is off its chest!" Keawe said. He snatched the crimson rag back into his shirt as the black print of her thumb touched the weave; and before Malia could blow out the saucer-flame, he and old Kahuku had dived headlong through the rear thatch into the sulfur-steaming cane-brake just as the rifle-butts of the patrol crashed against the cedar door-post.

***

Keawe’s conspiracy failed that Friday. A terrified Cantonese turret-oiler aboard the *Golden Gate*, whose brother lay hostage in the Nagasaki examination-wards, sold the plot at the eleventh hour; before a single twenty-two-inch barrel could traverse toward the shore, the provosts drowned the manual stokers' mutiny in the bilges. Nine years passed. While the gangrenous rot of the outer cantons ate inward from the Vistula and the Indus toward the sea, the priesthood of the Pivot kept its balance by replacing every mutinous human nerve with a strip of perforated brass tape.

An empire that loses the consent of the living doubles the theater of its bronze, and when I returned to Thalassia in October of 1930 for the opening of the *Centennial Exhibition of the Circumference*, the Pearl Lochs causeway resembled a paralytic giant painting his cheeks with vermilion over the mortification of his limbs.

The proclamation of the thirty-eight-year-old Sacred Emperor Kalanimoku invited the Hundred and Thirty Cantons to celebrate the first century since Elias Thorne’s birth, hailing the Steel Revolution that had liberated humanity from the curse of Adam. Half the chairs in the Pan-Pacific amphitheater stood empty. The trans-Siberian land-line ended now at a fortified trench outside Chita; scuttled hulks of Egyptian grain-rebels choked the Suez canal-locks; and across the Bay of Bengal, no steamer dared sail without a four-destroyer convoy to beat off the Tamil pirate-junks.

Within the six-mile electrified perimeter of the artificial lagoon, the display glared like noon sun off a sheet of tin.

Along the *Via Triumphalis*, where vibrations from the subterranean bauxite-stampers had cracked and spalled the twenty-ton blocks of red Agra sandstone, the Bureau of Public Harmony had erected the *Avenue of the Hundred Automaton-Tributes*. The marble curb stood empty of living soldiers. Four miles inland, the remaining Choshu and Samoan flesh-and-blood regiments held the barbed-wire stockades around the Waipahu coolie-compounds, where two hundred thousand idle dock-hands were dying of the red beri-beri. Along the canal stood eighty colossal, thirty-foot effigies of cast Pittsburgh aluminum and polished Osaka brass representing the pacified races of the earth—the Hindoo, the Prussian, the Maori, the Californian—wired to the high-tension Molokai conduits so that as the Emperor’s gilded electric barge glided past, the metal giants bowed from the waist in sixty-cycle unison while their internal steam-calliopes blasted the syncopated chords of the Imperial Anthem through clouds of synthetic Mysore sandalwood spray.

At the head of the lagoon, four hundred feet above the dwarfed dome of the old Senate House, stood the centerpiece of the Exhibition: the *Pylon of Perpetual Equilibrium*.

Cast from the melted bronze cannon of the European protectorates and the stripped copper roofing of the Westminster Parliament, this ten-thousand-horsepower Babbage-Nakajima Difference Engine carried forty-foot illuminated glass dials across its exterior faces. The master-pendulum swung. Every ten seconds, as the weight crossed the gilded sun-and-anchor at the apex, the giant hands jumped forward with a hydraulic *thwack* that shook the dead mullet-float in the harbor and registered the theoretical tonnage of coal, rice, copper, and human blood-tax existing at that moment between Antwerp and Valparaiso.

"Observe the third dial on the western face, Citizen-Historian," said Junior Minister Sato. He was the last surviving brother of that family of engineers, and as we stood upon the crimson-carpeted reviewing-barge beside the canal, his left cheek twitched beneath the heavy white lead-powder that the court nobles wore to mimic the porcelain masks of the Kyoto consort. "The Silesian coal-reserve registers four million tons above the autumn requirement, and the Bengal jute-index stands at par."

I kept my field-glasses to my eyes. Past the gilded shoulder of the thirty-foot aluminum Prussian automaton on the quay, straight out through the Honolulu Passage, two hospital-cruisers returning from the Mindanao rubber-war limped inside the reef; native naphtha-rafts had blackened their armored sides, and their scuppers ran red into the peacock-blue swell.

Polish insurgents had flooded the Silesian mines three winters ago. Not a single bale of Bengal jute had cleared the Hooghly since March, and while everyone beneath the silk awning of that barge knew the truth, the engineers in the Pylon basement had disconnected the broken submarine cables from the differential gears and coupled the four-hundred-foot brass hands directly to a closed-loop governor-wheel spinning in the dark.

"It is a masterpiece of providence, Minister," I said, and bowed low. Out onto the proscenium of his barge stepped the Sacred Emperor Kalanimoku, corpulent and heavy-jowled at thirty-eight, his yellow feather mantle stiffer now with woven gold wire and bulletproof duralumin scales than with the plumage of dead mountain birds, raising his baton to salute the bowing iron statues that could not shoot back.

***

Across the Kauai channel, in the high red gorge of Waimea where the trade-wind no longer cleared the yellow sulphuric mist from the canyon walls, the steam-calliopes of the Jubilee never reached Lady Kaiulani.

She was ninety-five years old. The old island priests called that age *ka wa maloo*, the season of the dry bone, when the spirit has walked halfway down the cliff at Polihale to leap into the dark water and left the husk upon the mat to wait for the tide. Five years had left her blind and stone-deaf to a man's voice; yet through the sole of the bare, withered foot resting against the cedar center-post of her grass-house, the unending sixty-cycle tremor of the Koloa bauxite-stampers three miles down the dry river-bed shook the volcanic bedrock day and night like a fever-pulse.

On the afternoon of the twentieth of October, Malia—grey-haired at fifty now, her linen skirt pinned up over her knees and her arms stained red to the elbows from digging wild fern-roots in the high goat-pastures—entered the hut and laid a heavy piece of rusted iron across the pandanus mat between her aunt’s knees.

Kaiulani’s small, translucent hands, light as two dried breadfruit leaves, crept across the reeds until her fingertips touched the cold metal.

A four-foot bar of rough, hand-puddled California wrought-iron lay across the weave, pitted with seventy winters of mountain rust and worlds removed from the smooth duralumin castings of the automated Osaka presses; a square iron spike remained wedged through the flange, and along the web rose the faint, chisel-stamped letters *S. P. & M. R. R. — 1861* like a scar.

"Where did you dig this bone up, child?" Kaiulani whispered. Her voice came so thin and dry that Malia laid her ear down beside the old Queen’s cracked lips to catch the Hawaiian words.

"The washout above the Koloa dam broke the old missionary bridle-path this morning, Aunt," Malia shouted back. She pressed her mouth against the hollow of Kaiulani’s temple so the vibration of her jaw carried through the bone. "It uncovered the ballast of the first sugar-tramway that the Protector’s engineers sent over from Monterey in the year of your brother’s marriage! The Choshu scrap-patrols are coming up the gorge with sledges to break the old rails up for the electric furnace!"

Kaiulani held fast to the rusted bar. Sitting in the yellow chemical gloom, she drew her thumb back and forth across those rough, uneven hammer-marks that a sweating Irish or Cantonese blacksmith had beaten into the red-hot iron at Sacramento seventy years ago, when Abraham Lincoln still lived beyond the snows and Elias Thorne was a bearded forty-year-old wolf in a mud-splashed linen duster.

In the milky dark of her blindness, the fat, painted boy Kalanimoku beneath his bulletproof feathers on the lagoon and the windowless concrete walls of the Melbourne tape-looms vanished.

Elias Thorne stood upon the windy bluff at Fort Point in the autumn of fifty-four. Salt fog dripped from his square jaw, and his short, thick fingers wrapped around a hickory walking-stick as he pointed out across the empty Golden Gate.

*"A man who builds a fence across his pasture isn't trying to own the stars, Princess."* That dead, gravelly voice growled inside her skull, clearer than the roar of the bauxite-mills. *"He’s just keeping the wolves out of the calves so his boys can eat their beef in the lamp-light without asking a banker in New York for the salt."*

A dry, soundless laugh shook her tiny chest beneath the tapa-bark.

Elias had been a tyrant. Across the Pacific basin he had burned the ballot-boxes and hung the strike-leaders from the snow-sheds, and after drowning the Yangtze forts in naphtha, he had struck every blow of his terrible hammer for the living flesh before his eyes and the sweat in his nostrils. He had loved the roar of twenty thousand bearded track-layers drinking whiskey around a desert bonfire; he had known the name of every locomotive-driver on the Truckee grade; he had wanted an ocean of strong, meat-eating men who could hold a rifle and look their captain in the face.

If Elias Thorne rose today out of the four-mile mud of the Marianas Trench to walk the streets of Thalassia—if he saw his great-grandsons hiding behind forty-foot walls of floating Krupp steel on San Francisco Bay, painting their faces white and pressing pearl buttons to turn steam-mortars onto starving boilermakers while eighty-foot brass dolls bowed by electricity along a dead lagoon—he would leave his crown in the dirt.

He would call for Caleb Vance’s old twelve-pounder mountain-howitzers and blow the Crystal Palace and his own bastard dynasty straight into the reef before he let a punch-card rule a man.

"Leave the iron on the mat, Malia," Kaiulani whispered. She curled her shrunken fingers tight around the rusted 1861 flange as if it were the only warm thing left in the world. "Do not give it to the furnace. When the stokers come back through the reef, they will need a crowbar that was made by a man’s hand."

# Chapter 29: The Season of the Red Terror

Three thousand miles away, eighty feet beneath the rotting wharves and vitrified brick cellars of San Francisco where the airships hunting the sunlit mountain passes could never reach them, the stokers were already forging that crowbar.

On the night of the nineteenth of November, 1930, after I bribed the automated turnstile-guards at the Ferry-Slips with three tins of stolen naval morphia and followed the one-legged salt-boiler Higgins down into the subterranean labyrinth of the old Potrero and Mission wards, the underworld of the abandoned continental capital opened before me like the catacombs of Nero.

Above our heads, on the rain-swept surface of Market Street, only the four-wheeled, gyro-balanced *Pacification Automaton-Patrols* moved. Those squat, crewless beetles of riveted nickel-steel rolled up and down the six-foot tramway tracks on solid rubber tires, while their selenium light-cells scanned the boarded-up shop-fronts and their twin Maxim muzzles traversed toward any stray dog or starving child that broke the searchlight beams after curfew.

Down here, in the five miles of abandoned six-foot freight-tunnels and flooded storm-sewers and old Comstock bullion-vaults that the elder Vance had honeycomb-blasted out of the Franciscan sandstone sixty years ago before the Court moved to the bay-pontoons, four hundred thousand human beings lived like termites inside the foundations of the throne.

The air pressed down hot and thick. It reeked of wet sandstone, fermenting rice-mash, human sweat, and cheap joss-smoke cut by the acrid tang of stolen nitric acid. Every fifty yards along the dripping brick arch of the old Southern Pacific freight-subway, where the rusted rails had been pried up to forge pike-heads and cold chisels, small iron dishes of rendered sewer-rat fat burned with a smoky yellow flame before shrines hacked straight into the rock.

These niches owed nothing to the state *Shinto-Christian* syncretism that the Polytechnic chaplains preached in the cantonments.

In the first generation of the Protectorate, when Elias Thorne had crushed the European internationals and burned the printing-presses of the eastern socialists, the Chancellery had congratulated itself on burying the specter of *Communism* forever beneath the prosperity of the Great Arena. The clerks had miscalculated. Lock ten million Cantonese iron-puddlers, Russian deportees, Californian ditch-diggers, and Japanese stokers into the same dark cellar, strip the names off their collars, and their ghosts will marry in the dark.

As Higgins and I limped round the bend of the flooded Howard Street siphon, the low, rhythmic drone of two thousand voices chanting in the *Creole of the Lower Decks* rolled down the tunnel like the hum of a giant dynamo, and we stepped out into the *Cathedral of the Unnumbered*: the subterranean brick cavern of the old Mission Street Gasometer.

Around the circular iron catwalks and down upon the dry sludge-floor stood three thousand gaunt figures in rags. White-bearded American machinists held up hands mangled by the Babbage-looms; runaway Polish and German debtor-youths bore the livid white scars of chiseled ration-rings upon their left wrists; barefoot Cantonese women from the closed Potrero canneries carried sleeping infants in slings of burlap.

In the center of the floor, raised upon an altar of stacked, unexploded twenty-two-inch naval shells smuggled out of the Hunters Point magazines, stood the icon of the new faith.

Some nameless foundry-sculptor had hammered the six-foot figure out of scrap-copper and boiler-plate: a three-faced, six-armed bodhisattva sitting cross-legged upon a broken gear-wheel. The center face was the bearded, ferocious visage of the old German prophet Karl Marx, cast like a wrathful Buddhist guardian-king with a third eye of red signal-glass blazing in his forehead; the left face was the compassionate, weeping countenance of Kwannon, Goddess of Mercy of the Chinese seas; and the right was the scarred Polynesian mask of Maui-the-Snarer. In his six copper hands he held a pair of five-foot iron bolt-cutters, a coal-heaver’s shovel, and a stick of mining-dynamite.

Before this trinity stood a man in the oil-stained blue denim of a fleet-stoker. He was forty years old now, his hair streaked with iron-gray, his left forearm bearing the deep, jagged trough of the Monterey shackle-scar, and over his heart he had pinned a six-inch strip of faded crimson silk stamped with a black thumb-print in kukui-soot.

It was Keawe.

"The Great Mother on Kauai is dead!" Unamplified by any bronze horn, Keawe’s voice carried through the hush of the three thousand outcasts to the highest iron gallery of the gasometer vault. "They threw her bones into the salt-ditch at Koloa on Tuesday without a chant or a feather, because she spat upon the Emperor’s brass doll! And tonight, brothers of the shovel, the seven-digit lords out on the San Francisco pontoons are drinking wine under their quartz-lamps while the gyro-tenders load the winter phosgene-drums onto the *Thalassia* to gas the Melbourne camps!"

From three thousand throats rose a single, low, vibrating growl, the deep, chest-rattling *Haka* of the ocean-floors:

*"Huli ka lima! Break the wheel! One blood, no number!"*

"For eighty years," Keawe cried, and snatched a heavy iron spanner from the altar of shells to raise it toward the dripping brick vault overhead, where the automated patrol-beetles ground along the Market Street rails directly above our skulls, "the bearded prophet of the West told our fathers that the iron belonged to the hands that hammered it! And for eighty years the Merciful Mother of the East promised that when the measure of the clerks’ wickedness was full, the Pure Land would rise out of the mud!
