They thought they could get away from us by cutting the gangplanks and floating out onto the bay on chains of vanadium steel! They forgot who forged the chains, and they forgot who walks along the bottom of the water!"

He leaped down from the shell-altar onto the top of a riveted iron air-lock bolted directly over the mouth of the old municipal main-sewer outfall: the twelve-foot cast-iron pipe that ran straight out under the bay mud for three-quarters of a mile to discharge directly beneath the central buoyancy-pontoons of *New Thalassia-in-the-Bay*.

Around the base of the air-lock stood forty men in patched brass-and-canvas Siebe-Gorman diving-suits stolen from the Mare Island salvage-sheds, their heavy lead-soled boots already strapped to their feet, while upon their backs, in place of air-cylinders, Cantonese women were lashing waterproof gutta-percha knapsacks packed solid with four hundred pounds apiece of ninety-percent nitro-gelatine and clocked magnesium-fuses.

"Brother Ivan of the Baikal pits! Brother Chen of Hanyang! Brother Miller of the Sacramento shops!" Keawe shouted. His scarred hand grasped the brass rim of the first diver’s copper helmet as two mechanics stepped forward with iron wrenches to bolt the faceplate home. "You will not come back through this pipe! When you walk out through the silt onto the bedrock under the Emperor’s garden-pontoon, there will be no air-hose behind you, only twenty minutes of compressed oxygen in your dress and the sixteen-inch anchor-chains of the Ark above your heads! Do you take the Pure Land tonight?"

Inside the open copper collar of the diving-suit, the gaunt, one-eyed Russian deportee smiled, leaned forward to kiss the red glass eye upon the forehead of the copper Marx-Bodhisattva, and spat once upon the iron floor.

"Screw the glass down, Comrade Keawe," the Russian said. He raised his two lead-weighted hands in the sign of the broken chain as the Cantonese girls swung the heavy bronze helmet over his head and the wrenches squealed against the brass studs, while at the rear of the cavern a violent hammering of iron crowbars against the upper sewer-manhole announced that the surface patrol-beetles had detected the heat-plume from our tallow-lamps and were unbolting the street-grating.

***

Flesh and bone, not an unmanned patrol-beetle, dropped through the shattered brickwork of the Mission Street siphon three seconds later.

A thirty-pound breaching-charge of guncotton blew the rusted cast-iron manhole cover straight down into the sludge-floor with a deafening yellow flash that extinguished half the rat-fat lamps in the vault; and out of the choking fog of pulverized mortar and nitric acid tumbled forty Choshu and Californian assault-provosts in gas-masks, their short-barreled automatic carbines already spitting orange flame into the packed tiers of the iron catwalks.

Behind their leveled bayonets, lowering himself gingerly down the iron ladder rungs with his silver-plated revolver drawn in his right hand and a silk handkerchief soaked in cologne pressed tight against his nostrils with his left, came Marshal Marcus Vance the third.

Ten years of counter-insurgency in the jungles and the cellars had turned the thirty-eight-year-old victor of Irkutsk into a stooped, prematurely aged phantom. The purple pine-resin burn from the Hindu Kush still pulled the left corner of his mouth upward in a permanent, wet sneer; his hair beneath his peaked service-cap was as white as salted lard; and as his boots splashed into the warm, ankle-deep filth of the gasometer floor, he squinted hard through his gold-rimmed pince-nez into the drifting cordite smoke.

"Seal the outfall sluice-gate before they flood the lock!" Marcus screamed. His high, reedy falsetto cracked against the brick vault as the three thousand unarmed machinists and cannery-women surged backward against the slime-coated walls, trampling one another in the dark while the provosts’ carbines hammered at point-blank range into the press. "Don't shoot the men in the diving-dresses, shoot the mechanics at the air-lock wheel! If a single four-hundred-pound sack of gelatine gets into the bay-pipe, the Emperor will have our skins nailed to the dry-dock!"

Up on the riveted iron lip of the sewer-lock, Keawe had already thrown his entire weight upon the four-spoked brass flooding-valve to let the bay tide rush in and sweep the first six helmeted divers down the cast-iron tube; but before the rusted screw could turn a quarter-inch, three heavy .45-caliber slugs from the lead Choshu sergeant’s carbine tore through the calves of the stoker’s legs.

Keawe pitched sideways off the iron drum into the black silt. His fingers still clawed for a dropped wrench as two provosts leaped over his body and jammed an iron crowbar through the spokes of the air-lock wheel.

"Hold your fire on the center platform!" Marcus shouted. He shoved past a bleeding Cantonese girl who was trying to drag a dead infant out from under the boots of the squad. Holstering his unfired pistol, he stepped up onto the stacked twenty-two-inch naval shells at the base of the six-armed copper idol, his scarred cheek jerking rapidly as he looked down at the twelve men in Siebe-Gorman canvas suits who stood immobilized by their own eighty-pound lead boots around the sealed hatch.

"Unscrew their helmets!" Marcus ordered. He pointed with his cologne-soaked handkerchief at the nearest diver, whose heavy bronze faceplate was already fogging on the inside from the rapid breath of a man whose oxygen-valve remained shut. "Don't cut the gelatine-sacks off their backs yet. I want the Verification Board photographers to take their faces while the fuses are still wired to their belts! Let us see what breed of wharf-rat thinks he can swim under the First Class!"

Two Californian corporals stepped forward. After fitting their T-wrenches to the brass neck-studs of the lead diver, the one-eyed Russian from the Baikal pits, they wrenched the sixty-pound copper dome off his shoulders. Unblinking in the glare of the electric torches, the deportee spat a mouthful of bloody phlegm straight onto the shiny patent-leather toe of Marcus’s boot.

"Take the next three off!" Marcus snarled. He stepped back half a pace and kicked the Russian in the groin with his heel as the wrenches squealed down the line of canvas figures.

The second helmet came off: a sixty-year-old Sacramento boilermaker with the bridge of his nose eaten away by the mercury-fumes.

The third helmet came off: a boy of seventeen from the Macao rope-walks, his eyes rolling white in terror.

Then the corporals lifted the bronze dome from the fourth diver in the file, the man who had been standing with his lead-weighted gauntlet resting directly upon the electric detonator-plunger of the air-lock chamber, and the high, triumphant sneer froze upon Marcus Vance’s scarred face.

Inside the patched canvas collar stood a twenty-six-year-old officer, clean-shaven, his hair cropped in the severe quarter-inch brush of the Monterey Staff Academy. Around his neck, tucked neatly inside the rubberized waterproof flange to keep the chafing off his skin, gleamed the high collar of an Imperial Naval Lieutenant’s service tunic; and pinned squarely above the breast-pocket, directly beneath the canvas harness of the four-hundred-pound nitro-gelatine pack, shone the golden winged-torpedo of the *New Thalassia* Submarine Guard.

"Lieutenant-Assessor... Hoshino?" Marcus stammered. His gold pince-nez slipped down his sweat-greased nose to dangle by its black silk ribbon against his chin while he stared into the calm, heavy-lidded Japanese eyes of his own third-tier ordnance-aide: the grandson of the old Hankow auditor, a youth who had stood behind Emperor Kalanimoku’s chair on the flagship barge forty-eight hours before.

"Open the sixth and seventh helmets, Marshal," young Lieutenant Hoshino said in the crisp English of the First Class examination-halls. Down on the wet bricks at his feet, the wounded Keawe raised his bloody head and laughed aloud through his broken teeth. "You will find Captain Miller of the Alcatraz Torpedo-Battery in the sixth suit, and Senior Navigator Kuroda, nephew of the late Fleet-General, in the seventh. And before you reach for your whistle to call the surface-launch, sir, you should know that the four Choshu corporals holding the carbines behind your shoulder took the red thumb-print on Tuesday night."

Marcus whirled upon the stacked naval shells. His right hand dived blindly for his patent-leather holster. Before his fingers touched the flap, across the damp stone arch where the tallow-lamps sputtered in the draft from the bay, the lead Choshu sergeant raised the butt of his automatic carbine and smashed the iron heel-plate squarely across the bridge of the Marshal’s nose. Marcus went flat on his back among the lamps. The mutinous guards swung their muzzles around and cut down the two Californian wrench-men in a single burst that echoed down the dark sewer-pipe toward the water.

***

Three months later, after a loyal reinforcement company of automated flame-tanks had broken through the Howard Street brick-wall, burned the gasometer to black clinker, and dragged the bleeding, half-strangled Marshal out from under a pile of dead divers, the truth reached this Chronicler: the grandsons of the Polytechnic peerage were strapping nitro-gelatine to their own backs.

An empire is like one of those giant hydraulic presses from my youth at the Hanyang ironworks: so long as the cast-iron cylinder remains sound, it can crush ten thousand tons of cold stone into dust; yet let a single hairline flaw appear inside the metal of the piston itself, and the very pressure of its own steam will blow the machine through the roof.

During the winter of 1930 and the spring of 1931, that flaw ran crack by crack around the entire twenty-five-thousand-mile rim of the basin. Crack by crack, it spread. In the First generation, a strike in the coal-pits of Nanaimo or the rolling-mills of Pittsburg had been a local ulcer, easily lanced by a regiment of cavalry while the rest of the ocean kept the forges hot. Now the *Steel Revolution* had welded the Hundred and Thirty Cantons into a single clockwork animal whose heart beat at Oahu and whose lungs breathed the oil of Sumatra, while its stomach digested the iron-ore and fleece of Australia.

When the disciples of the three-faced Marx-Bodhisattva failed to blow the San Francisco pontoons into the Golden Gate from below, they wasted no more gelatine upon eighteen-inch Krupp armor.

They went south to the place where the iron came out of the ground.

On the morning of the fourteenth of May, 1931, I stood upon the high basalt bluff overlooking the *Port Kembla and Newcastle Imperial Steel-Corridor*. Along that sixty-mile strip of blackened coast south of Sydney in the Eighty-Second Canton, twelve million tons of red Australian hematite and Southern Alps coking-coal were smelted every year in automated, tape-driven blast-furnaces to feed the shipyards of Yokosuka and the Pearl Lochs, alongside the slips at Hunters Point.

For twenty years, a solid ceiling of blood-orange flame and greasy coal-black soot had poured across the Tasman Sea from those eighty four-hundred-foot Bessemer-Nakajima converter-chimneys, day and night, fifty-two weeks in the year, while the subterranean *thud-clank-hiss* of the crewless rolling-mills shook the eucalyptus forests ten miles inland.

This morning, the sky above Port Kembla was as blue and quiet as on the day Captain Cook’s bark first raised the heads of Botany Bay.

The eighty chimneys stood cold. Down on the three-mile concrete ore-wharf, where six forty-thousand-ton gyro-steered colliers from the Osaka yards lay dead in the green swell, the automated unloading-claws hung forty feet above the hatches like the legs of dead iron spiders.

The outer wire was intact. In the Yarra and Newcastle mud-camps, eighty thousand starving, locked-out boilermakers and shearers had stayed back from the Maxim towers. At midnight on the tenth of May, inside the windowless concrete walls, the four hundred elite *Cybernetic Maintenance-Prefects*—young graduates of the Kyoto and Melbourne polytechnics who wore the golden gear-wheel on their collars and had secretly swallowed the soot-stained rice-wafer of the *Cathedral of the Unnumbered* in the subterranean tram-tunnels—had walked down the central aisle of the tape-looms with pockets full of thermite-grenades and cold chisels.

The switches stayed untouched.

Wait until a four-hundred-ton blast-furnace is filled to the throat with molten white-hot pig-iron and slag at three thousand degrees Fahrenheit, and then cut the high-tension power-cables from the Snowy River hydro-dams and blow the auxiliary steam-blowers off their beds with thermite.

Within six hours, as the temperature inside the eighty giant brick-and-steel towers dropped below the melting-point, sixty thousand tons of liquid iron congealed inside the hearths and tuyeres and tapping-spouts into solid, immovable mountains of cold grey steel. Foundry-men call it a *frozen salamander*.

"You cannot drill it out with diamond-bits, Citizen-Historian, and if you put five hundred pounds of dynamite under the hearth, you will only blow the furnace-shell into the harbor," said Chief Assessor MacArthur. A distant, pale-faced nephew of the old senator, he stood beside me on the bluff with an unlighted pipe between his teeth and his field-glasses trained on the concrete fortress below, where ten thousand unarmed strikers from the bush-camps sat cross-legged upon the railway tracks, chanting the slow, three-note mantra of the *Kwannon-of-the-Shovel*. "To get a single pound of ship-plate out of Port Kembla again, the Chancellery will have to tear all eighty furnaces down to the bedrock with hand-picks and rebuild the fire-brick from the foundation. And there isn't a ton of spare structural steel between here and the Yangtze to build the scaffolding."

I lowered my glasses. Far to the north, the blue plains of the Pacific glittered in the sun.

Before the iron in the Newcastle hearths had even grown cold to the touch, the paralysis leaped across the submarine cables like mortification up a severed limb: at Yokosuka, the gantry-cranes stopped riveting the hull of the new super-dreadnought *Kalanimoku II* for want of Australian nickel-plate; at Vallejo, the automated tin-canneries shut down their stamping-presses, leaving forty thousand carcasses of Californian beef to rot on the sidings while the garrison-troops in Vienna and Warsaw went on quarter-rations; and down in the deep-water channel of Sydney Harbor, three leagues north of where we stood, the sixty-foot dark-blue turrets of the Pacific Battle Fleet swung their twenty-two-inch rifles toward the silent brick chimneys of the shore.

***

Marshal Marcus Vance the third stood upon the open flying-bridge of the armored cruiser *Monterey*, anchored four hundred yards off the Circular Quay in the heart of Sydney Cove. A heavy steel splint was strapped across his broken nose. He had his fur-lined greatcoat buttoned to the chin against the sharp May wind off the Southern Ocean.

Since the night in the San Francisco sewer when his own third-tier ordnance-lieutenant had tried to blow him into the bay mud, the Marshal had abandoned his locked cabin; he had his camp-cot pitched directly inside the armored conning-tower between two mute, deaf Samoan bodyguards whose tongues had been cut out in childhood by the Palace surgeons so they could never repeat a password in the dark.

He leaned his gloved knuckles upon the wet teak rail of the bridge-wing. Through his new, heavy-framed spectacles, the semi-circular amphitheater of the Sydney docks rose in tiers of grey stone.

George Street was clear of barricades, and the roofs of the wool-warehouses showed only bare slate. From the water’s edge at Bennelong Point all the way back up the sandstone slope to the gates of the Botanical Gardens, a hundred and twenty thousand men, women, and children sat shoulder-to-shoulder upon the cold granite paving-stones in silence.

In the front ranks, dangling their bare feet over the timber string-pieces of the ferry-wharves not fifty yards from the *Monterey’s* bow-casemates, sat the four hundred young Cybernetic Maintenance-Prefects who had frozen the Port Kembla furnaces; they still wore their dark-blue Polytechnic tunics, though the silver identification-numbers had been ripped from their collars and piled in a neat pyramid upon the capstan-head beside them. Behind them sat eighty thousand grizzled Australian sheep-shearers and Yorkshire foundry-hands beside Cantonese track-layers. They linked their arms through ragged sleeves. They kept their eyes fixed upon the gaping black muzzles of the cruiser’s eight-inch secondary battery.

Along the broad macadam roadway of the quay, standing at regulation parade-rest with a double belt of three-hundred-round Maxim cartridge-boxes at their feet and twenty rapid-fire pom-pom guns unlimbered on the cobbles, waited the three thousand flesh-and-blood infantrymen of the *Fourteenth Californian and Satsuma Pacification Regiment*, the last reliable mainland brigade that Marcus had brought south from the Golden Gate.

"The noon meridian-chronometer has ten seconds to run, Marshal," said Captain Noguchi at his elbow. He held a brass megaphone in one hand and a pocket-watch in the other, speaking quietly enough that the Hawaiian quartermaster at the wheel could not hear the tremor in his throat. "They have not touched the coal-lighters, sir, and the furnace-engineers have made no move to return to the Port Kembla trains. If you fire the eight-inch ship-guns at four hundred yards into that granite slope, the ricochets will cut down our own regiment on the quay wall."

"I am not going to waste naval picric-acid on sheep-clippers when I have three thousand rifles on the pavement!" Marcus said. The steel nasal-splint gave his high, reedy voice a metallic whistle like a leaking steam-pipe. Stepping out to the tip of the starboard bridge-wing, he snatched the brass megaphone from Noguchi’s fingers and pointed it straight down across the narrow strip of green harbor water at the mounted figure of Colonel Kalakaua, brother to the officer who had died in the Khyber snows, sitting his bay charger behind the center company of the Californian line.

"Colonel Kalakaua!" Marcus’s amplified shriek echoed off the stone facades of the custom-house and rolled back across the bay. "The Emperor’s grace has expired! Load with flat-nosed riot-ball! Dress your front rank at thirty paces from the wharf-edge, aim straight into their chests, and clear the stone to the warehouse doors! Give the word to the Maxim sections. *Fire!*"

Down on the granite quay, Colonel Kalakaua drew his nickel-plated regulation saber from its scabbard and raised it straight toward the pale autumn sun.

"Fourteenth Regiment!" the Hawaiian colonel’s deep baritone rang out across the water. Among the hundred and twenty thousand sitting men and women on the stones, every head stayed upright, while from the wharves rose a low, rhythmic murmur like the surf before a typhoon: that same three-note chant of the *Pure Land* from the black sewer under Market Street. "Load—*lock!* Present—*arms!*"

Drilled for four years on the Monterey asphalt, the fifteen hundred Californian and Satsuma riflemen of the standing rank brought their model-twenty-four magazine-rifles up to their shoulders; fifteen hundred steel bolts slid home with a single, oiled *snick*; and along the line of the twenty Maxim tripods, the gunners laid their thumbs against the brass firing-pieces.

"At the front rank of the mutineers, zero elevation, *Fire!*" Kalakaua shouted. He slashed his saber downward toward the cobbles.

The line stood still.

The three thousand muzzles stayed cold and silent on the quay.

At the exact instant the colonel’s blade touched his stirrup-iron, the twenty-year-old Californian corporal at the right-flank guide of Company A—a tall, freckle-faced boy from the Fresno irrigation-wards whose grandfather had ridden with Caleb Vance at the Truckee River—slowly lowered his rifle from his shoulder, flicked open the breech-bolt so the live brass cartridge spun onto the stones, and drove his bayonet point-first between two granite paving-blocks. The steel stood upright by itself.

With both hands at his throat, the boy tore the stitched linen strip bearing his six-digit Monterey birth-cipher off his tunic collar. He tossed it onto the pile of silver badges on the ferry-capstan and sat down cross-legged on the cold stone beside a one-armed Australian boilermaker.

*Tink—clink—tink—clatter.*

Down the three-quarter-mile curve of the Sydney waterfront, three thousand magazine-rifles came down from three thousand shoulders like a line of falling dominoes. Three thousand steel bolts clicked open. Unfired brass cartridges rained bright and golden across the granite cobbles. In the trace, Colonel Kalakaua wheeled his horse around, his dark Polynesian face grey, and raised his revolver to shoot the Fresno corporal through the back of the head; before his finger could take up the slack, four Choshu machine-gunners behind the nearest Maxim tripod stood up, caught their colonel by his gold-braided belt, and dragged him out of the saddle onto the pavement. Up on the bridge of the *Monterey*, Marshal Marcus Vance dropped his brass megaphone over the rail. He lunged backward into the armored conning-tower and clawed at the quartermaster's tunic. "Turn the main turrets on the regiment!" he screamed. "Open the sea-valves of the magazine! Noguchi, why isn't the forward turret turning?"

***

The turret stayed dead in its ring. At four o’clock that morning, the cruiser’s own warrant-machinists had packed the hydraulic return-pipes in the lower handling-room with shaved emery-stone.

When the *Monterey* limped back into the Pearl Lochs roadstead nineteen days later, steered from the auxiliary hand-wheel on the after-deck by a skeleton watch of terrified Staff Academy instructors after the entire stoker-division had jumped overboard into the Sydney whale-boats, I stood upon the fortified mole at Waipahu and saw the Great Strike for what it was: a curtain-raiser. Bayonets had turned to soft lead in the Emperor’s hand. The disciples of the three-faced idol no longer needed to sit upon railway tracks; they came inside the wire with the knife and the glass ampoule.

The Chancellery bulletins called that summer of 1931 the *Season of the Red Terror*, though the old Russian nihilists had worked with noisy bombs and this slaughter moved through the marble corridors of Thalassia as silently as a diving-bell sinking through dark water.

Every chamber between the Diamond Head batteries and the artificial reefs stood open to them. Because the automated Babbage-Nakajima looms required human hands to oil their cams and replace their blown mercury-tubes, the assassin was already inside the fortress before the steel shutters were bolted down at sunset. He was the quiet Cantonese pantry-boy who had served the Senior Assessor’s papaya for twelve years; he was the Nagasaki torpedo-artificer who checked the pressure-gauges on the palace air-pumps; he was the third-class Californian cipher-clerk who carried the morning clearing-slips into the subterranean vault.

On the twelfth of July, watch-officers found Senior Minister Sato—the last surviving brother of that illustrious engineering house, who had stood beside me at the Exhibition barge only nine months before—sitting upright in his air-conditioned glass cubicle beneath the Great Gnomon. Someone had poured two drams of anhydrous hydrocyanic acid into the sandalwood water-pan of his desk-ventilator. His white-leaded face had turned the color of an eggplant, his tongue bitten through.

Four nights later, the Chief Justice of the Maritime Debt Court stepped into his private electric elevator at the top of the Coral Pavilion. Above the grease-box, a jeweler’s hack-saw had cut nine-tenths through the two-inch vanadium hoisting-cable; at the sixth floor the steel parted, and the bronze cage dropped two hundred feet down the shaft into the basement sump like a plumb-lead.

By the first week of August, the Imperial peerage had left the mosaic floors above ground.

Summoned on the night of the fourteenth of August down into the *Third Sub-Basal Command Bunker* forty feet beneath the coral bedrock of the lagoon, I found the seat of oceanic providence reduced to the flooded bilge of a sinking ironclad. Above us, the high rotunda of the Crystal Palace stood empty, its stained-glass maps dark and its ferns dead for want of water; down here in the low-ceilinged, steel-ribbed tunnel where the main submarine telegraph-trunks came up out of the ocean floor, triple-charcoal filters pumped the air down with a slow, wet wheeze at every stroke of the piston.

Wet Portland cement and sour carbolic fouled the passage, thick with the rank tallow of emergency candles burning beside the electric lamps lest the dynamo-tenders at Molokai cut the current. Every thirty yards along the dripping five-foot corridor, heavily armed naval cadets of the First Class—boys whose fathers owned ten thousand acres of San Joaquin wheat—stood back-to-back behind sandbags of crushed coral. Their fingers shook on the triggers of short-barreled trench-shotguns. They ignored the outer seaward hatches to keep their sights trained on the brass food-lifts and the four-inch ventilation-pipes in the ceiling.

"Do not touch the tin water-dipper by the filter-butt, Citizen-Historian," Junior Assessor MacArthur whispered. He met me at the third armored bulkhead, a drawn revolver in his hand and four days’ growth of red stubble on his hollow cheeks. "The relief-watch found two grains of soluble barium-salts in the ice-chest at noon, and the chief cook hung himself with his own apron-string in the scullery before the Verification Board could put the hot irons to his feet. Keep your hands outside your coat-pockets when you pass the Samoan. The Marshal has not slept since Tuesday."

***

Inside the innermost iron casemate, a windowless twelve-by-twelve box of two-inch Krupp plate originally forged to house the master-gyroscope of the Pearl Lochs harbor-mines, Marshal Marcus Vance the third sat upon an upturned ammunition-crate with his back wedged tight into the ninety-degree angle of the steel walls.

That corner had no ventilation-grating behind his head and no rivet-seam wide enough to pass a needle. The surgeons had taken the steel splint off his broken nose; the flattened bridge twisted sideways across his scarred left cheek like a lump of purple putty. Spilled beef-tea that he had been afraid to drink stained the front of his unbuttoned Marshal’s tunic. Across his knees lay a cocked, double-barreled ten-gauge riot-gun loaded with buckshot.

Two paces in front of his boots stood his mute Samoan bodyguards, Tui and Mano, motionless as twin statues of oiled bronze beneath the naked carbon-bulb swinging from the sweating ceiling-plate.

Six feet four inches tall, bare-armed to the shoulder where the tattooed bands of the Pago-Pago guard encircled their biceps, they kept their broad backs turned toward their master and their faces toward the bolted iron door, five-foot steel boarding-pikes held slantwise across their chests. Four years earlier, Palace surgeons had cut the tongues from their mouths and punctured their eardrums with silver needles so no rebel preacher could corrupt them with the Creole of the Lower Decks. In all the bunker, Marcus Vance dared close his eyes within reach of those two mutilated giants alone.

*Tick—tock—tick—tock—shunt.*

On the steel bulkhead beside the Marshal’s ear, the brass second-hand of the naval master-chronometer jerked around the dial toward two o’clock in the morning. Every sixty seconds, as the minute-hand touched the top of the circle, the pneumatic pressure-valve in the air-pipe overhead gave a long, wet sigh, answered thirty feet away by the dull *thud-thud* of harbor water slapping the outer submarine caisson.

MacArthur slid the viewing-slot back and let me step over the high iron coaming. Marcus ignored me. Behind thick lenses, his bloodshot eyes stayed fixed on the sweating, naked shoulder-blades of the two mutes.

*One minute past two.*

Directly above the carbon-bulb, a drop of warm condensation gathered on a rusted rivet, hung for five seconds in the yellow glare, and fell with a sharp *spat* onto the hot glass globe.

Marcus’s right thumb twitched against the shotgun hammer. His tongue swelled dry as boiler-scale behind his teeth. For thirty-eight hours, ever since Captain Noguchi had dropped dead across the chart-table at Waipahu after licking the gummed edge of an official Monterey telegraph-envelope, he had refused solid food, and tonight even the air from the brass nozzle above the door smelled faintly, sickeningly sweet, like the sewer-rat tallow that had burned before the copper idol in the Mission Street gasometer.

"Why is the left-hand Samoan shifting his weight onto his right heel, MacArthur?" Marcus’s voice whistled through his ruined nose, loud and ragged in the twelve-foot iron box.

MacArthur stopped half a pace inside the door. His hand tightened on his pistol-butt as he looked at the broad, scarred back of the giant Tui. "The deck-plates are greasy from the bilge-seep, Marshal. They have been standing on watch since the six-o’clock bell."

"They stood fourteen hours on the *Monterey* without moving an ankle!" Marcus said. He drew his boots two inches tighter under the ammunition-box and raised the twin muzzles of the ten-gauge until they pointed squarely between the lower ribs of the two guardsmen. *Two minutes past two.* The chronometer escapement clicked like a beetle in a coffin. "Look at the sweat on the back of Tui’s neck! The air-pump is set at sixty-eight degrees. Why is a boy from the islands sweating in a cold room unless his blood is up? Turn him around! Take the boarding-pike out of his hands and look inside his mouth!"

"Inside his mouth, sir?" Stepping sideways along the steel wall to stay clear of the shotgun’s arc, MacArthur kept his eyes on the pikes. "The surgeon cut his tongue out at the root in twenty-seven. I signed the hospital-voucher myself."

"They don't need a tongue to take the soot-mark!" Marcus shrieked. His scarred cheek jerked so hard that his heavy spectacles slipped crookedly across his broken nose; the cramped steel cabin swam out of focus into a double-blur of yellow light and bronze skin. "In the San Francisco pipe, Hoshino said they were passing the wafer in the water-ration! Pull his left wrist back. Let me see if there is a kukui-oil smudge between his thumb and his forefinger!"

Ruptured eardrums kept the two mutes from hearing a word of that high, whistling scream, yet as MacArthur reached out with his left hand to tap Tui upon the tattooed muscle of his shoulder, the vibration of the Marshal’s voice through the iron floor-plates—or the shadow of the Assessor’s arm against the swinging bulb—gave them the signal.

Tui did not wait for the tap.

At four minutes and twelve seconds past two by the bulkhead clock, the two deaf-and-dumb giants moved as if their tendons were wired to the same sixty-cycle cam.

Keeping his back to the Marshal, the right-hand guard Mano drove the heavy iron butt-ferrule of his boarding-pike straight backward behind his hip. The iron caught Junior Assessor MacArthur squarely in the pit of the stomach. He doubled over voiceless into the corner by the door as his revolver spun across the wet steel plates.

In the same half-second, Tui pivoted on the ball of his bare left foot.

Marcus Vance pulled both triggers of the ten-gauge shotgun at once.

The double-charged roar of smokeless powder inside the sealed twelve-foot iron box blew out the carbon-bulb in an orange flash and choked the casemate with white sulfur-smoke that split our eardrums. Because the Marshal’s crooked spectacles had thrown his sight three inches high in his panic, the double load of buckshot tore through the fleshy top of Tui’s left shoulder. Hot lead spattered across the two-inch Krupp armor-plate behind him.

Before the half-blinded Marshal could drop the empty gun and claw at his holster, the six-foot-four Samoan stepped straight through the burning powder-smoke with his left arm hanging in red rags.

The boarding-pike was too long to swing in the cramped box. Tui dropped the wood. Reaching down through the dark with his uninjured right hand, he caught the grandson of Caleb Vance’s brother by his windpipe and his broken nose, lifting the hundred-and-thirty-pound Marshal clean off the ammunition-crate until his patent-leather boots kicked eighteen inches above the floor.

Through the acrid, ringing blackness, by the red glow of the emergency tallow-wick smoldering in the corner, the mute giant opened his mouth as he slammed the back of Marcus Vance’s skull four times against the projecting two-inch iron corner-bolts of the gyroscope-mount. Pinned to the raw stump of the Samoan’s severed tongue by a brass safety-pin driven straight through the living gristle gleamed a one-inch square of crimson silk.

# Chapter 30: The Restorer

After the last Vance had been carried feet-first out of the Pearl Lochs bunker with his skull crushed like a dropped seagull’s egg, the Chronicler left Thalassia without waiting to see whether Emperor Kalanimoku would replace his bodyguards with clockwork dolls. A historian who wishes to record the death of an empire must follow the blood back to the heart. In the autumn of 1931, the heart of the Great Arena had abandoned the coral lagoons of Oahu and the white porcelain decks of the floating Arks.

It had returned, in the delirium of its final fever, to the cold brick ruins of the shore where the first hammer had been lifted.

Our coal-starved mail-steamer crept through the fog of the Golden Gate on the afternoon of the third of November. Between Alcatraz and the Marin cliffs, the three hundred acres of *New Thalassia-in-the-Bay* listed six degrees to larboard. During the October tides, after the Snowy River power-strike shut down the automated cathodic rust-preventers, salt water had eaten through two of the sixteen-inch vanadium anchor-chains on the southern face; three thousand silk-robed shareholders now sat marooned atop the rotting pontoons, their opera-glasses trained on the new fire rising from the abandoned streets of San Francisco.

For ten years, the mainland wards from the Embarcadero to the Twin Peaks had been left to the subterranean mole-people of Keawe’s cult and the rolling Maxim-beetles of the Chancellery. Now, along the steep, grass-grown cobbles of Montgomery Street toward the shell-pocked ruins of the old Mint, the crewless patrol-cars lay on their backs in the gutters like dead iron turtles. Sledgehammers had smashed out their selenium eyes.

Above the avenue, the rusted gas-standards bore a new flag.

From every crumbling brick cornice and every burned-out window-frame hung thirty-foot vertical pennants of raw, unbleached Californian canvas, dyed crimson with red-lead ship’s paint and stenciled in coal-tar with a single angular black emblem: the crossed *Broad-Gauge Spike and Cavalry Saber* of 1852.

Up the center of the torn-up tramway tracks, tramping four abreast with a heavy, flat-footed frontier swagger to the crash of forty skin-drums and brass field-bugles, came a column of five thousand young men.

Their necks were bare of numbers or collars. Dressed in sleeveless shirts of red Californian flannel and high-laced logger’s boots, with black leather gauntlets reaching to their elbows, they wore the exact theatrical costume of the *Vigilance Pioneers* who had burned the Sacramento legislature for Elias Thorne seventy-nine years before. Here marched the starving, unindexed sons of the middle wards: displaced third-tier tally-clerks whose fathers Shen had purged, unemployed locomotive-firemen from the closed Oakland roundhouses, alongside the feral, sun-browned grandsons of San Joaquin wheat-foremen whose harvests had rotted on the sidings while the court at Oahu painted its cheeks with white lead.

At the head of the column, astride a raw-boned sorrel stallion whose iron shoes struck sparks from the granite cobbles, rode a man of thirty-two with his head bare to the cold November mist.

"Take off your hat when the *Iron Blood* passes, grandfather, or the boys with the pick-handles will take it off along with your ears," said an old, toothless typesetter beside me on the cracked curb. He pulled his greasy cap to his chest as the horsemen drew level with the ruined façade of the Bank of California.

I looked up into the rider’s face. My hand shook upon my notebook.

Whether he had any true drop of the Protector’s blood in his veins, no parish register in California could prove; the Verification Board swore before its dissolution that he was the bastard son of a Eureka sawmill-boss and a stage-actress from the Nevada silver-towns. Yet nature, in her most malicious mood, had given *Julian Thorne* the unmistakable mask of the bronze statues that stood upon every breakwater from Valparaiso to Vladivostok: the heavy, square-hewn jaw, the short iron-gray brush of beard trimmed close to the chin, the hawk-bridge of the nose, and those pale, unblinking eyes that looked through a crowd of men as if they were standing timber waiting for the saw.

Over his red flannel shirt he wore an old, mud-splashed linen duster copied stitch for stitch from the glass reliquary in the Monterey Museum. Strapped across his pommel was a heavy, octagonal-barreled 1851 Colt dragoon revolver.

Sixty thousand red-shirted men and women stood packed shoulder-to-shoulder across the plaza beneath a forest of smoking pitch-pine torches. At the broad, broken granite steps of the Old Mint, Julian Thorne ignored the footpath.

He drove his iron spurs into the sorrel’s flanks. Hooves scattered the broken glass of the doors as he rode the horse straight up the twenty marble steps until the beast stood snorting and rearing between the Doric pillars above the crowd.

"Men of the First Shore!" Julian Thorne’s voice rolled out across the twilight plaza in a harsh, chest-rasping bark that he had practiced for ten years in the timber-camps until every syllable sounded like two mill-stones grinding dry corn. "This morning, out on that floating whore-house in the bay, the painted half-breed who calls himself the Sacred Emperor sent a wireless message to the Fort Point batteries! He ordered the coastal guns to turn their muzzles inward and shell the Mission wards unless we hand over the Vallejo flour-mills to his Cantonese clerks before sundown!"

A roar like the breaking of an ocean reef went up from the sixty thousand red shirts below the steps. Five thousand iron pick-handles and stolen magazine-rifles flashed upward into the red glare of the pitch-torches.

Leaning forward over the sorrel’s wet neck, his thick, bare forearm corded with muscle, Thorne pointed a short hickory walking-stick straight out through the fog toward the listing white pontoons in the harbor.

"Seventy-nine winters ago," Thorne bellowed, the veins in his bull-neck swelling above his unbuttoned flannel collar, "my great-grandfather rode down from the Donner snow-sheds with four hundred white-handed pioneers and built an empire of iron and beef! He didn't build it for a pack of tea-drinking eunuchs on a coral reef to trade away by punch-card! And he didn't build it for a rabble of sewer-rats down in the gas-pipes to divide up with the Chinamen and the Russians before their four-armed brass monkey! The rotting body at Oahu is dead, brothers! Tonight the blood goes back into the iron! Colonel Miller, bring the three six-inch siege-howitzers up to the Telegraph Hill parapet and load with solid armor-piercing shot!"

***

The report of Keawe’s November stoker-preaching had been premature, a rumor floated down the Waimea gorge by Malia herself to fool the Koloa tax-assessors into striking the blind nonagenarian from the salt-rolls. Three thousand miles across the grey autumn rollers, the image of that rearing sorrel horse traveled faster than submarine paper.

It arrived through the ether. Across the curving glass bull’s-eye of the *Baird-Nakajima Tele-Vision Receiver*—which the mutinous garrison-mechanics at the Koloa bauxite-dam had dragged up the mountain bridle-path on a mule-sled and wired directly into the high-tension penstock cable outside Lady Kaiulani’s hut—thirty-line neon-red bars flickered.

Inside the grass-house, the smell of wet pandanus and yellow river-sludge gave way to the hot, oily stink of the spinning Nipkow scanning-disc. Ninety-six-year-old Kaiulani sat propped within two inches of the thick convex lens. To a normal eye, the four-inch screen showed only a jerky, blood-colored phantom of a bearded face and a waving hickory stick swimming through a blizzard of diagonal static-snow; to the blind woman, whose ruined retinas had long since lost the soft daylight of the valley, the pulsing glare of the neon-tube pierced the white opacity of her lenses like a red-hot needle.

Ears were unnecessary. To make the old Queen understand why the bauxite-stampers down at the river had stopped their tremor at noon, the rebellious Hawaiian line-men had bolted a copper bone-conduction vibrator directly to the cedar center-post against which her bare, shrunken skull rested.

*"—tear the silk off their backs and put the pick-axe back into their soft hands!"*

Hammering straight through the mastoid bone of her jaw, the voice vibrated in the hollow, toothless cavern of her mouth in a harsh, metallic travesty of the dead Protector’s gravel.

"Look at him, Aunt," Malia cried. She knelt beside the humming mahogany cabinet with her hands clasped together over her stained linen skirt, her fifty-year-old face lit crimson by the spinning holes of the brass disc. "The soldiers at the Koloa dam have thrown their Choshu officers into the leaching-vats and pinned red flannel to their hats! They say he has sunk the San Francisco pontoons with three shots from the hill, and that the fleet at Pearl Lochs has hoisted the Spike-and-Saber! He is going to burn the counting-machines, Aunt! He is going to give the land back to the living!"

Kaiulani did not answer. Upon the rusted 1861 iron rail across her knees, her translucent, leaf-light fingers trembled with the mechanical shudder of the cedar post.

Through the burning red bars of the glass lens, the square-jawed head turned in profile, and the linen duster flapped in the artificial wind of the scanning-beam.

*That is not Elias.* Cold nausea rose in the old woman’s dry throat while the bone-vibrator rattled her skull with the roar of sixty thousand Californian throats. *When Elias rode into Monterey, he wore a linen duster because the dust of the San Joaquin lay two inches thick on his shoulders, and he carried a dragoon pistol because Caleb Vance’s enemies were shooting at him from the chaparral. This play-actor in the red lamp-light has bought his mud from a theater-wardrobe in Sacramento.*

Elias had built the machine because the wilderness was too wide for a horse; now the machine had eaten the wilderness and gone mad in the dark, leaving the terrified grandchildren to dress up in their dead grandfather’s clothes and trust a flannel shirt and a hickory stick to charm the rust out of eighty frozen blast-furnaces.

"Pull the copper wire out of the wall, Malia," Kaiulani whispered. On the screen, the phantom raised a heavy cavalry saber and kissed the flat of the blade; the old woman turned her blind, red-lit face away from the spinning glass bull’s-eye. "That is no man on the horse. That is only the smell of the grave coming back up through the floor-boards."

***

Yet a corpse that walks by electricity moves faster than a living army. To the Chronicler who returned to Thalassia aboard the flagship of the *First Restoration Vanguard* on the nineteenth of November, 1931, the fall of the Polynesian dynasty lacked both the tragic dignity of King Kalakaua’s surrender at Sand Island and the fiery grandeur of the London raid.

Not a single twenty-two-inch shell crossed the reef. When Julian Thorne’s six requisitioned turbine-transports steamed straight through the Honolulu Passage at dawn, their hulls painted a glaring, rust-red lead from waterline to funnel-top and their bridges manned by red-shirted Californian river-pilots alongside defecting third-tier naval lieutenants, the colossal coastal batteries at Diamond Head and Barber’s Point remained as silent as the coral rock.

Three days earlier, the terrified maintenance-clerks in the casemates had watched the San Francisco pontoons burn on the Tele-Vision screens, disconnected their own automated fire-control computers, and stitched squares of red tradesman’s flannel over the silver numerals on their collars.

By ten o’clock that morning, I stood once more beneath the vast, unwashed Jena glass dome of the Pan-Pacific Senate.

The rotunda stifled at ninety-four degrees. Uncollected stable-manure and raw methylated spirits fouled the air, for Julian Thorne had brought two hundred rough-shod Californian stock-horses ashore from the cattle-decks and quartered them directly among the dead tree-ferns of the botanical floor. Around the five concentric tiers of the amphitheater, the surviving senators of the inner cantons—white-leaded Osaka shipping-peers and plump Cantonese rice-syndics beside trembling Berkeley assessors—sat frozen in their stalls with hastily torn strips of red silk curtain-cord tied around their left biceps to save their throats from the three thousand logger-booted *Vigilance Pioneers* leaning on iron pick-handles along the marble aisles.

Up on the central porphyry rostrum, the Sacred Emperor Kalanimoku stood stripped of his yellow *mamo* feathers.

In a sweat-stained white linen undershirt, his corpulent belly sagging over his belt and his dark Polynesian cheeks grey beneath the smeared remnants of his court powder, the grandson of Kaiulani sagged between two six-foot Eureka timber-fellers who held him upright by the elbows. The bulletproof metal scales of his royal mantle lay heaped at the foot of the steps. There, a pioneer blacksmith was already breaking them up with a sledgehammer to shoe the cavalry mounts.

Julian Thorne spurned the bronze curule chair as well. He planted one mud-caked logger’s boot squarely upon the edge of the porphyry table and threw back his mud-splashed linen duster to expose the twin 1851 Colt revolvers at his hips, while at the base of the Great Gnomon three technicians from the Monterey Signal Corps worked with soldering-irons to wire up a massive, four-sided bank of neon Tele-Vision cameras and carbon-arc floodlights.

"Are the San Francisco and Yokohama relay-towers locked onto the wave-length?" Thorne barked. Ignoring the trembling Emperor beside him, he squinted into the blinding white glare of the carbon-arcs while a former stage-manager from the Sacramento Opera House dabbed grey grease-paint onto the bridge of the Restorer’s nose to sharpen his profile for the thirty-line scanning-beam.

"The west-coast and insular receivers are synchronizing now, Citizen-Restorer," the signal-captain answered. He dropped his soldering-iron as the two-foot brass Nipkow discs inside the camera-boxes whined up to their eighteen-hundred-revolution pitch. "You have forty million eyes on the glass."

Thorne spat a chew of coarse Virginia plug tobacco squarely onto the inlaid brass map of the North Atlantic at his feet. He wiped his iron-gray beard with the back of his leather gauntlet and stepped into the focal circle of the lenses.

Leaving the parchment scroll untouched, he seized the trembling, half-fainting Kalanimoku by the scruff of his linen collar, dragged him two paces forward into the white-hot light of the carbon-arcs, and forced the Emperor’s heavy jaw down upon the steel anvil of the broken Hollerith master-tabulator.

"Look into the glass, brothers of the Pacific!" Thorne’s gravelly, theatrical roar thundered into the suspended microphones and echoed back from the cracked sandstone colonnades outside, where wire-ropes had dragged the eighty aluminum automatons down into the canal. "Look at the soft, painted slug that has been eating your beef and selling your birthright to the Chinamen and the machines while you starved in the mud! Sixty years ago, when the old Protector took his eyes off the wheel, the Honolulu women crept into his bedroom and stole the ring off his dead finger! Today, the pioneer takes back the forge!"

Thorne’s right hand snatched up a four-pound track-layer’s spiking-maul beside the anvil. Because the stage-manager had warned him that blood on the lens would blur the neon transmission, he spared Kalanimoku’s skull; instead, he brought the iron head crashing down upon the bronze Seal of the Double Horizon resting beside the Emperor’s ear. The die split in two. Kalanimoku’s knees buckled, and his bladder emptied down his white trousers onto the marble steps.

"By the authority of the First Shore and the Vigilance Committee of Nineteen-Thirty-One," Thorne bellowed, his boot planted atop the shattered bronze seal and the spiking-maul raised toward the whining red eye of the camera, "I declare the Polynesian Regency and the Bureau of Integration abolished forever! There are no more numbers, and there are no more peers! From this noon, I assume the office of *Lord-Restorer of the Grand Confederation*—and by God, before the winter snow closes the Sierra passes, every man with white blood in his veins will have four pounds of beef in his pot and two Chinamen to carry his shovel!"

***

Across the Kauai channel, the noon sun had not yet burned the yellow copper-fog out of the Waimea canyon when the first motor-launch of the *Insular Restoration Guard* came roaring up the shallow, sludge-choked mouth of the river at Koloa.

The launch spared them the four-mile march up the mountain path that the Choshu patrols had endured. Towed behind the red-painted bow upon a flat-bottomed timber scow rode two four-wheeled *Dodge-Sacramento Field Lorries*, each armed with twin air-cooled Browning machine-guns and packed with twenty young men in sleeveless red flannel shirts—half of them Californian mechanics from the Pearl Lochs repair-yards, the rest mixed-blood Portuguese and Hawaiian plantation-overseers from the Waipahu sugar-mills who had bleached their hair with lime-water and bound red rags around their arms to prove they belonged to the *First Shore*.

Up in the grass-house above the dry waterfall, the copper bone-vibrator on the cedar post had gone dead ten minutes after noon, when the operators at Koloa shut off the penstock dynamos to join the looting of the Cantonese company-stores.

For the first time in eleven years, the volcanic bedrock of the island beneath Kaiulani’s bare feet lay completely still.

The subterranean fever-pulse of the bauxite-stampers had ceased. In the sudden stillness of the gorge, the ghost of the old Waimea river seemed to trickle once more through the dry fern-roots outside the door. "They are coming up the missionary road in the gasoline-wagons, Aunt," Malia said. She no longer shouted into the hollow of Kaiulani’s temple, only knelt on the pandanus mat and pressed her forehead against her aunt’s shrunken, bark-wrapped knee, her hands resting beside the four-foot bar of rusted 1861 railroad iron. Through the open doorway, the stench of burning thatch and raw kerosene drifted up from the lower village, mingled with the flat, sharp pop-pop-pop of pistol-shots where the crimson-clad overseers were settling thirty years of wage-scores with the Cantonese tally-clerks. Low-gear pinions ground; crushed red lava-stone showered the slope as the lead Dodge lorry burst through the dry banana-brake below the terrace, pulverized the ancient stone salt-pans beneath its solid rubber tires, and skidded to a halt ten paces from the grass-house porch. Four men in sleeveless scarlet wool and high logger’s boots jumped down over the tail-board. At their head walked a twenty-five-year-old youth named Cazneau, the grandson of an American customs-collector at Hilo and a Maui woman, who had smeared grey wood-ash across his brown cheekbones to pale his skin and strapped a rusted cavalry saber over his canvas riding-coat. In place of a perforated manila warrant, he carried a five-gallon tin of rock-oil and a portable battery-operated megaphone. "Come out of the straw, old spider!" Cazneau shouted. He kicked the woven reed screen from the doorway with the toe of his boot and blinked into the dim, kukui-scented gloom of the hut while two Californian machinists behind him leveled their short-barreled riot-guns at Malia’s chest. "By Order Number One of the Lord-Restorer, all pensioners of the Honolulu blood are summoned to the Koloa wharf for public audit! Where is the gold bullion-chest that you and the lame general brought back from the Geneva banks in eighteen?" Malia rose in front of the cedar post. Her grey hair fell loose over her red-stained arms as she bent down and lifted the heavy, four-foot bar of rusted 1861 Sacramento wrought-iron in both hands. "She cannot hear your horn, half-breed," Malia said in Hawaiian, her gaze fixed on the streak of grey wood-ash running down Cazneau’s sweating brown neck, "and the only iron left in this house is the rail your grandfather’s master laid down before you were born." "Speak English when you answer a Restoration Officer, you kanaka bitch, or I’ll have the skin off your back!" Cazneau snarled. Dark purple flushed his face beneath the ash; stepping across the threshold, he swung the heavy iron nozzle of his battery-megaphone straight against the side of Malia’s jaw, knocked her sideways across the pandanus mat, and dropped his left hand to seize the collar of ninety-six-year-old Kaiulani’s bark-cloth wrapper. He dragged the feather-light, blind bundle of bone and dry skin straight out across the threshold into the blinding yellow sulfur-haze and tossed her onto the tail-board of the Dodge lorry like a sack of spoiled copra. Behind him, his two machinists splashed the five gallons of rock-oil over the dry pandanus thatch of the priest’s house and dropped a wax vesta into the doorway.

***

Julian Thorne’s theatrical instinct was too shrewd to give the islands a martyr at the Koloa wharf while the stokers in the Battle Fleet still held their hammers behind their backs. He spared the rope. Upon the rock of Sand Island, where her brother had signed away the crown sixty years before, his guards locked the old Queen inside the abandoned stone quarantine-lazaretto while the Lord-Restorer searched the horizon for an enemy his pioneers could shoot.

A usurper who rides to power upon a stallion in an age of dead dynamos cannot feed his horsemen on stage-paint. Forty days passed after the November coup. The four pounds of beef that Julian had promised to every white throat in California shrank to four ounces of salted horse-marrow. At Port Kembla, eighty frozen blast-furnaces stood as cold monuments of grey slag; beside Lake Baikal, the self-governing Soviet of the Unnumbered cut the Siberian trunk-line permanently, and the Cantonese rice-junks ceased to cross the bar at Macao when red-shirted customs-collectors offered unbacked Restoration scrip for the grain.

To keep five hundred thousand logger-booted Vigilance Pioneers from turning their stolen rifles upon the Sacramento Opera House, Julian Thorne invented a wilderness.

In the January of 1932, when I sailed southward from San Diego aboard the requisitioned cattle-liner *Sierra* alongside what the Restorer’s neon bulletins styled the *Grand Expedition of the Austral Frontier*, our armada wallowed across the warm equatorial swells toward Peru as a spectral parody of Elias Thorne’s early vigor. One afternoon's cannonade had sufficed in 1868. With three fast cruisers dispatched to Callao, the first Protector had locked the guano-islands straight into the Market Street ledger. Now Julian scraped together thirty rust-streaked, coal-burning transport-hulks whose gyro-pilots had been smashed with sledges to give employment to human steersmen, and into their holds he crowded ninety thousand hungry, scarlet-shirted youths from the Oregon timber-camps and the Los Angeles oil-slums upon the promise that the high valleys of the Andes burst with unmined Inca silver and unnumbered Indian cattle.

"Look at the smoke from the third transport’s funnel, Citizen-Historian," said my cabin-mate, a sixty-year-old retired hydrographer named Kemp whom the Pioneers had dragged out of the Monterey almshouse after purging every navigator who could read a logarithmic table. Our squadron rolled through the Humboldt Current off Guayaquil. Over the blistered iron taffrail Kemp leaned, his trembling finger aimed at the ragged, yellow-brown smudge of lignite dust that trailed from the *Comstock’s* stacks. "They are burning green redwood sleepers and soft Coos Bay peat under high-pressure Yarrow boilers because the Sumatra oil-tankers haven't touched at San Pedro since October. Half those boys on the fore-deck are carrying single-shot Springfield trap-door rifles they pried out of the Presidio war-memorials, and they think they are going to march up to Cuzco and carve out ten-thousand-acre ranchos like Cortés."

On the twelfth of February, when our thirty transports dropped their rusted anchors into the brown, lifeless rollers off the roadstead of Callao, the shingle held neither plumed Inca kings with baskets of virgin gold nor a rebellious Spanish general to cross swords with the Restorer’s vanguard.

The Empire’s own corpse rotted in the sun.

For sixty-four years, the Hundred and Ninth Peruvian Canton had functioned as a thoroughly digested bowel of the Grand Confederation. Ten winters ago its guano-beds on the Chincha rocks had been scraped down to bare white granite; at Cerro de Pasco, automated Osaka leaching-vats had pumped the copper-veins dry, leaving three million Quechua and mestizo inhabitants wearing the same six-digit brass ration-shackles on their left wrists as the coal-hewers of the Ruhr.

Not a shot came from the shore. Below the rusted iron skeleton of the Callao nitrate-piers, while buglers blew the old cavalry charge of the Truckee River and boys in heavy logger’s boots leaped waist-deep into the warm, sewage-fouled foam with their hickory sticks held high, the first flat-bottomed landing-barges of the Californian Pioneers grounded in the greasy surf.

Along the cracked concrete coping of the seawall, beneath a faded banner of Imperial Blue and Sunset Gold that nobody had hauled down since November, stood four thousand emaciated Peruvian dock-coolies and twenty aged Cantonese tally-clerks from the local Bureau of Integration.

"Where are the rebel barricades?" shouted Vanguard-Colonel Miller. He waded ashore with a drawn 1851 dragoon pistol in each hand. Equatorial sweat darkened his heavy wool shirt while he glared up at the silent, hollow-cheeked crowd on the quay. "Where is the Peruvian gold-reserve? By order of the Lord-Restorer Julian Thorne, this coast is annexed to the First Shore as Pioneer Settlement-Land! Bring out your municipal syndics to surrender the keys of the Lima mint!"

At the head of the seawall steps, where the Senior Canton-Assessor—a seventy-year-old Chinese graduate of the class of eighty-four whose left eye had gone blind with the trachoma of the nitrate-flats—stood with fingernails grown two inches long over his empty ledger-board, the old clerk bowed from the waist.

"There has been no silver in the Lima mint since Chancellor Shen transferred the bullion-reserve to the San Francisco pontoons in nineteen-twenty-two, Honorable Pioneer," the clerk answered in crisp, archaic Monterey English. He held out a rusted iron key ring hung with three brass padlock-keys and a dead Hollerith sorting-needle. "And the automated copper-smelters at Oroya stopped turning in June when the Melbourne dynamo-parts failed to arrive. If your soldiers have brought the winter barley-ration from the San Joaquin, my four hundred thousand registered laborers will gladly paint the Spike-and-Saber upon the customs-house; if you have brought no barley, Honorable Colonel, there is nothing left in this province to eat except the mules beneath your wagons."

***

Before March was out, they ate the mules. When the wireless dispatch arrived from Callao to report that ninety thousand pioneers sat in the dry white dust of the Rimac valley, dying of Verruga fever and shooting one another over the last barrels of salted Californian horse-beef across a frontier his own dead grandfather had stripped to the bone fifty years earlier, Julian Thorne retreated into the subterranean Chart-Vault of the Palace at Thalassia and bolted the bronze doors against his buglers.

Four drunken Eureka timber-guards dragged me out of my quarters in the Old Archives on the night of the nineteenth of April, 1932. Because the Restorer had driven the last Polytechnic cartographers to the sugar-ditches and needed an old man who could read the Latin ciphers on the nineteenth-century globes, they hauled me down into that vast circular basement where Kaiulani and Marcus Vance had once weighed the tides of the earth, a chamber now reduced to a bear-pit in a ruined theater.

Pioneers' sledges had smashed the eighty pneumatic sorting-machines into twisted heaps of brass and cast-iron. Their shattered frames lay kicked into the corners to clear space for forty open whiskey-barrels and a smoky brick barbecue-pit where half an Oahu wild bullock charred over burning cabinet-mahogany. Scorched beef-fat, sour Kentucky mash, stale horse-liniment, and the acrid metallic tang of the single surviving Molokai power-cable that fed the great illuminated glass map of the world in the central mosaic floor thickened the suffocating air.

Julian Thorne paced alone upon the thirty-foot glass continents.

His logger’s boots were off. In filthy grey wool socks, with his canvas riding-coat stained down the front by tobacco-spit and spilled bourbon while two heavy dragoon revolvers banged against his naked thighs beneath an unbuttoned flannel shirt, he walked around and around the glowing glass circle of the Pacific Ocean, one fist closed around the handle of a five-pound iron track-spiking maul.

"Come out onto the water, Historian!" Julian barked as the timber-guards shoved me across the threshold. Five months of screaming into neon microphones had stripped the theatrical Sacramento boom from his throat and left it raw and ragged; beneath the grey stage-paint flaking in the creases of his square jaw, his bloodshot pale eyes held the sleepless terror of an actor who hears the audience tearing up the benches in the dark. "You wrote the books for the old wolf! You were with Kuroda when he took the Indian rivers, and you were at Berlin when the Chinaman locked up the Germans! Bring your lantern over here to the glass and show me where they hid the uncut timber!"

Half the subterranean electric bulbs beneath the Mariana Trench had burned out. Across that cold glass crust of the North Pacific, over black blind patches in the sea-lanes, I limped until I reached the glowing red outline of the American continent.

"What timber does Your Excellency seek?" I asked.

"The frontier, damn your spectacles!" Julian roared. Down came the iron spiking-maul against the thick plate-glass of the Peruvian coast. A star-shaped crack leaped from Lima to the Galapagos. "An empire has to march, old man! Elias Thorne told Caleb Vance at the Sacramento river that the day the wagons stop rolling into new grass, the boys in the camp will cut their captains’ throats! I sent ninety thousand red-shirts to Peru, and there’s nothing there but rusted Osaka tin-cans and Chinamen with numbers on their wrists! Where did the old Protector leave an unplowed valley where a white pioneer can plant a flag and take a chest of gold with a rifle?"

He dropped to his knees upon the glowing glass dome of the world. Like a blind crab hunting for a crack in a porcelain bowl, his broad, grease-stained hands crawled across the illuminated continents.

"What about the African interior?" Julian muttered, and stabbed his stubby forefinger down upon the green glass of the Congo basin. "The Belgian and French leases that Kaiulani took at Geneva!"

"The Bureau of Integration stripped the rubber-vines to the roots in twenty-four, Citizen-Restorer," I answered, my gaze on his sweating iron-gray crown, "and when the automated river-dredges poisoned the Lake Chad fisheries with mercury-sludge in twenty-eight, the surviving tribes burned the railhead at Matadi and died of the Belgian grippe. There is not a pound of ivory or an unmortgaged acre between Cairo and the Cape."

"Then the Russian steppes beyond the Urals!" Across the cracked glass of the Indian Ocean he scrambled backward on his knees while his revolver-butts clanked against the Himalaya peaks. "The wheat-lands of the Ukraine!"

"Fourteen numbered cantons, Excellency," I said, "plowed by crewless steam-tractors until the topsoil blew into the Black Sea during the drought of twenty-nine, and now held by two million armed Prussian and Russian deportees who shoot every man wearing a collar at five hundred yards."

Julian stilled his hands upon the glass. Under the single flickering arc-lamp of the vault, he raised his square, painted face and looked around the thirty-foot circle at his knees.

From the ice-floes of the Bering Strait to the basalt cliffs of Tasmania, and from the ruined brick wharves of the Thames to the dry salt-pans of the Rimac, every river, mountain-pass, coal-seam, and island upon the terrestrial globe lay ruled off in indelible black one-degree squares, each stamped with a three-digit canton cipher and crossed by the red spider-web of the submarine cables.

For ten thousand years, whenever a Caesar or a Khan exhausted the soil of his own valley, a dark, unmapped margin had waited beyond the rim of the parchment with barbarian blood and uncut forests. Now Elias Thorne’s steamships and Marcus Vance’s broad-gauge rails had closed the circle of the earth at the meridian. The world had no outside left.

No land remained to march across; no foreigner remained to rob; the pioneer had ridden all the way around the ball of the earth and come up behind his own back door.

"He didn't leave me an inch," Julian whispered. The five-pound spiking-maul slipped from his slack fingers and rolled across the glass of the Coral Sea with a hollow groan. "The old bastard ate the whole plate himself, and left me locked in the cellar with the bones."

# Chapter 31: A Graveyard of Dreams

Above our heads, the cellar door was already splintering under the axe.

When I climbed the dark spiral service-staircase out of the Chart-Vault at dawn on the twentieth of April, I left the Lord-Restorer sitting alone on the cracked glass of the North Pacific with a dipper of raw bourbon in his fist, bypassed my sleeping-cell, and walked straight across the weed-choked marble courtyard of the Palace toward the low octagonal basalt tower of the *Imperial Historiographer’s Archive*, where the seventy-eight bound folio volumes of this *Chronicle of the Grand Confederation* stood ranged upon their iron shelves.

Over the eastern rim of the Oahu craters, the sun climbed as a dull, copper-red ball swimming through a mile-high curtain of greasy black bunker-smoke, sixty years removed from the clear pearly Sunset Gold I had seen from the deck of Marquis Takashima’s flagship when the world was young.

The *Cult of the Unnumbered* and the starving Pioneer regiments had finally met in the middle of the lagoon.

Out in the Waipahu roadstead, the last four operational dreadnoughts of the Battle Fleet (*Elias Thorne*, *Sakurajima*, *Kamehameha*, and *California*) had hauled down both the Golden Sun and the red Spike-and-Saber. During the night, young Keawe’s surviving submarine-mechanics had swum out from the Koloa reefs with cold chisels and red silk rags; they had fraternized with the starving Oregon boys whom Julian had left unpaid on the gun-decks; and at five o’clock this morning, they had welded the three-faced copper idol of the *Marx-Bodhisattva* directly to the jack-staff of the flagship and turned sixteen twenty-two-inch naval rifles point-blank upon the artificial island of Thalassia.

*Boom. Whir-r-r-r. CRUMP.*

Fired without range-finder computers by a manual gun-crew sighting along the open barrel, the first two-thousand-pound armor-piercing shell from the *Elias Thorne* missed the Senate House entirely and struck the four-hundred-foot *Pylon of Perpetual Equilibrium* squarely in the belly at the third glass dial.

At my long cedar table beside the tall lancet window of the Archive tower, I dipped my steel nib into the last bottle of gall-ink while the ten-thousand-horsepower Babbage-Nakajima Difference Engine, that great bronze brain forged from the melted cannon of Europe, split open from top to bottom in a blinding fountain of yellow picric-flame. Ten tons of spinning brass cog-wheels, escapement-springs, and shattered glass numerals showered the marble canal and the dead aluminum automatons.

"Citizen-Historian!" cried my young Cantonese amanuensis, Dao. The last clerk who had not fled to the hills burst through the iron door of the turret with his arms full of the early Monterey campaign-rolls, his face white with plaster-dust while three hundred yards away a second twenty-two-inch shell obliterated the grand colonnade of the Bureau of Integration and sent a seismic shudder through the coral bedrock that toppled the bronze bust of the First Protector off its bracket beside my desk. "The mutineers from the Waipahu coolie-pens have broken through the electrified wire with stolen steam-tractors, and Julian’s timber-guards are setting fire to the oil-tanks on the causeway before they run! The harbor-launches at the south slip are leaving for the Kauai hills. If we do not go now, they will burn the books with the palace!"

I stayed in my chair. At eighty-two years of age, a man who has walked from the burning wharves of Hankow to the frozen corpses of the Khyber Pass has had enough of the outer air; and my master Thucydides held fast to his stylus when the Spartan flutes played along the Long Walls of the Piraeus.

"Lay the eighteen-fifty-two Sacramento rolls upon the lower shelf, Dao, and bolt the iron window-shutters on the seaward side so the shell-splinters do not tear the vellum," I said. My hand moved steadily across the heavy linen page while outside in the Piazza of the Pivot the chest-rattling roar of a hundred thousand voices chanting the *Haka of the Shovel* mingled with the crackle of burning sandalwood beams and the frantic, unattended clangor of the Palace alarm-bells. "A stone wall that has been built with blood must come down in fire; that is the law of providence, which neither the slide-rule nor the rifle has ever repealed. Yet if we leave the sentence unfinished, the children who dig in these ashes a hundred winters from now will think that the giants who bridged the ocean were only devils in the dark, and nobody will remember that for sixty years the ships ran on time and the sea was one."

Across the narrow courtyard, the great stained-glass dome of the Pan-Pacific Senate bulged outward from the heat of the burning cedar stalls within, and with a long, chiming crash like all the ice in the Bering Sea breaking up in the spring, the crystal maps of the two hemispheres rained down in ten million colored shards upon the empty porphyry throne.

The heavy bronze handle of the Archive door rattled from the outside. Someone hammered against the oak panels with the iron butt of a carbine, while the smell of raw kerosene and wet salt-mud seeped in beneath the sill.

"Take the copper cylinder with the final chapters down the dry-well shaft, boy," I said. I kept my eyes on the wet black line of the ink as the upper hinge of the door gave way with a screech of torn iron and a tall figure in the oil-stained blue denim of a fleet-stoker stood upon the threshold with a smoking crowbar in his scarred left hand.

Keawe had come. The left leg of his trousers was stiff with dried blood from the San Francisco sewer-locks, and he leaned heavily upon the shoulder of a barefoot Oregon timber-boy who carried a flaring kerosene torch.

The stoker held his iron bar at his side. Past the spilled ink-horn on my table, straight through the unshuttered eastern lancet window, he looked toward the center of the Piazza of the Pivot.

"Save your kerosene for the ledger-vaults downstairs, brother," Keawe said in the rough Creole of the bunkers. He caught the Oregon youth by his wrist before he could toss his pitch-brand into the racks of the Early Protectorate. "That old man is only writing down the burial-service. Look out the window, grandfather, if you want to put the last line in your book. The boys from the dry-docks have got the wire-hawsers around your master's neck."

I laid my steel pen down upon the blotting-paper. Stiffly, I rose from my cedar chair and limped to the narrow stone embrasure beside the stoker's shoulder.

Down in the vast circular plaza below the ruined Senate House, where dead cavalry horses, smashed brass sorting-frames, and the stripped, bleeding corpses of Julian Thorne’s timber-guards choked the dry basins of the geothermal fountains, twenty thousand men and women of every race between the Sacramento and the Yangtze had swarmed around the hundred-foot red granite pedestal of the *Colossus of the Meridian*.

There stood the supreme monument of the First Dynasty: the seventy-ton bronze effigy of Elias Thorne that old Marcus Vance had cast from the melted cannon of the federal batteries at Fort Point in eighteen-seventy-six. Forty feet high in his heavy frontier riding-coat, with his right hand resting upon the bronze lever of a railway-switch and his square, bearded face turned forever toward the sunset over the Asian sea, the American Caesar had looked down upon three generations of kings and auditors as if the granite beneath his boots were part of the earth's own crust.

Now, six captured military traction-engines from the Waipahu causeway had been backed up to the steps of the pedestal, their armored boilers painted over with the white three-faced emblem of the Marx-Bodhisattva and their safety-valves screaming at two hundred pounds of steam. Forty naked Cantonese and Hawaiian shipyard-riggers had climbed the bronze folds of the Protector's coat like gulls upon a sea-stack. Twice around the thick bronze bull-neck and the outstretched arm, they looped four-inch braided steel towing-cables.

"Take the slack out of the hawser!" roared a voice through a salvaged naval megaphone from the roof of the lead tractor; and across the smoky, fire-lit square, a hundred thousand throats took up the working-chant of the Honolulu pile-drivers:

*"Huki! Ho! Huki! Ho!"*

The twelve broad iron drive-wheels of the six steam-tractors bit into the cracked marble paving-flags and spun in a shower of white sparks and black Borneo oil-smoke. Out of the crowd, the four-inch steel cables snapped taut like harp-strings; their deep subterranean bass note vibrated through the basalt walls of my tower.

For ten seconds, the seventy tons of Fort Point bronze held still against six hundred horsepower of steam, anchored five feet down into the red Agra granite by the two-inch iron bolts that Vance's masons had leaded into the stone.

Then, from the base of the statue's heels, a puff of pulverized grey mortar-dust jetted out into the morning smoke. Above the roar of the burning oil-tanks, a sharp pistol-crack echoed as the eastern anchor-rods sheared through the stone.

Slowly, like a forest redwood leaning from the saw, the forty-foot bronze giant tilted forward over the edge of his granite cliff. For a single breath, silhouetted against the mile-high pillar of black petroleum smoke rising from the Waipahu docks, Elias Thorne strode out into the air to walk upon the waters he had conquered.

Then the center of gravity passed the plinth.

He fell. Crashing headlong from a height of a hundred feet onto the broken porphyry steps of the Via Triumphalis, the statue struck with a hollow *BO-O-O-M* of fractured bell-metal that shook the island like an earthquake. Cast nine inches thick from the brass twelve-pounders of the Missouri frontier, the great bronze head broke clean off at the collar-bone upon impact, bounded twice down the marble terrace like a child's bowling-ball, and rolled to a stop in the muddy gutter of the canal, where it lay turned straight up toward the red sky with one cheek crushed flat and its empty bronze eyes filling with the black, oily water of the broken sewers.

"He is down, Citizen-Historian," Dao said behind me. He clutched the eight sealed copper cylinders of our manuscript against his ink-stained tunic while a thousand barefoot coolies and red-shirted Oregon deserters leaped atop the fallen bronze torso with sixteen-pound sledges to beat an iron tattoo upon the hollow ribs of the Protector, and down in the basement of the Archive the dry cedar beams of the lower library crackled as the fire from the Chancellery roof-timbers leaped the alley. "The staircase is filling with smoke! If we do not go down the well-shaft to the canal-gate now, the lead on the roof will melt over our heads!"

***

I turned from my table and the seventy-eight bound folio volumes lining the upper shelves, where the parchment spines were already curling in the orange heat-draft rushing up the stairwell.

From the desk I took only my pocket-compass, the small leather satchel holding the rough notes of this final morning, and the brass astrolabe Marquis Takashima had given me on the deck of the *Kuroshio* fifty-eight years ago; then I followed Dao and the silent Keawe behind the hanging of the eastern alcove, where an iron ladder descended forty feet through the living coral rock to the subterranean tide-culvert that drained the palace moat into the outer Honolulu Passage.

"Why do you help us carry the dead skin of the clerks to the water, stoker?" I asked between my teeth. My eighty-two-year-old knees trembled upon the rusted iron rungs in the pitch dark, while above our heads the floor of the Archive tower gave way with a thunderous roar of falling masonry and ten thousand burning vellum rolls snowed down the upper mouth of the shaft in a whirlpool of red sparks.

Below me in the wet gloom, where the green sea-water slapped waist-deep against the barnacled stone blocks of the culvert, Keawe waited until Dao had lashed the eight watertight copper cylinders into the bilge of a twenty-foot native outrigger canoe hidden inside the grating.

"Because a man who doesn't know what burned him will stick his hand back into the fire when the iron cools, grandfather," the scarred machinist answered.
