With his crowbar he shoved the heavy iron portcullis-grate upward until three feet of clearance opened above the oily swell of the canal. "Go out through the south coral-cut toward Molokai before the magazine on the *California* catches fire. The Oregon boys on the fore-deck are drunk on the Admiral's rum, and they're firing the secondary batteries at everything that floats."

He stayed on the stone ledge. Turning his back upon the daylight at the mouth of the tunnel, the forty-year-old stoker limped back up the dark stone steps toward the roaring furnace of the Piazza to find his hammer, while Dao and I lay flat on our bellies among the copper cylinders and pushed the low koa-wood dugout beneath the iron teeth of the grate out into the open lagoon.

To the Chronicler who had last crossed that harbor six months before amidst the gilded electric barges and bowing aluminum colossi of the Centennial Exhibition, the water of the Pearl Lochs had become the river Phlegethon, rolling in waves of liquid fire toward the reef.

The great forty-thousand-barrel naval petroleum tanks along the Waipahu causeway had ruptured from the concussion of the *Elias Thorne's* twenty-two-inch shells. A flood of unrefined Sumatra naphtha poured across the surface of the incoming tide. For two square miles between the artificial island and the outer quarantine-spit, the sea itself burned with a fifty-foot wall of roaring, orange-and-soot-black flame that licked the blistering armor-plate of the moored dreadnoughts and filled the air with a heat so fierce that the skin peeled from my knuckles on the steering-paddle.

Everywhere through the yellow sulfur-fog, the floating wreckage of seventy years of oceanic supremacy drifted past our scorched outrigger-float.

Here bobbed the bloated, parboiled carcasses of Julian Thorne's Californian cavalry-horses, tangled in miles of snapped copper submarine-cable; there floated half a mahogany cabinet from the Bureau of Integration, surrounded by a million sodden, water-logged manila census-cards that covered the oily swells like a scum of dead yellow scales; and fifty yards to larboard drifted an overturned life-raft from the hospital-hulks upon which three white-leaded Osaka court-peers in scorched Lyons silk fought with bare teeth and fingernails over a single pair of splintered pine oars.

"Paddle hard for the Sand Island channel, Dao!" I coughed through the blinding grease-smoke. Low over the ruined customs-wharf burst a stray six-inch shrapnel-shell from the mutinous cruiser *Monterey*, and a hail of lead balls whistled across the water ten oars'-lengths behind our stern, severing the red-painted tow-rope of a sinking pioneer motor-launch.

Dao said nothing. His young shoulders hunched double over the forward paddle and blood trickled from his nostrils in the scorching sulfur-fumes as our narrow hull shot through the last sixty-yard gap between two advancing tongues of burning oil, riding out at last upon the deep, clean cobalt heave of the open Pacific.

***

Two miles outside the foaming white line of the coral breakers, where the trade-wind off the eastern ocean blew the furnace-smoke back against the dark green wall of the Koolau mountains, Dao drew his dripping paddle inboard across the gunwales and let the canoe rise and fall upon the long, unhurried rollers.

I turned myself painfully around in the stern-sheets, rested my chin upon the warm copper cylinders that held the only surviving memory of the Great Arena, and looked back across the water at the city that had called itself the Navel of the World.

From the basalt cliffs of Diamond Head to the distant red-earth cane-fields of Ewa, the entire southern horizon formed a single, unbroken volcanic crater of flame and Sunset Gold smoke that blotted out the noon sun and turned the tropical sea around our outrigger to the color of clotted blood.

At the center of the lagoon, the cracked sandstone ziggurats of Thalassia were already vanishing behind the collapsing iron ribs of the Senate dome. Across two miles of wind came the continuous, subterranean rumble of the Molokai high-tension transformers exploding one after another in the flooded basement vaults as the sea-water rushed in through the broken sluices. The iron heart of the century was bursting inside its ribs.

Then, out in the middle of the burning oil-slick of the roadstead, the fire reached the forward picric-acid magazines of the flagship *Elias Thorne*.

First came a sudden, silent lifting of the whole eighty-five-thousand-ton super-dreadnought thirty feet clear out of the lagoon, until her red-leaded keel and her four giant bronze propellers stood plain against the smoke. A second later, the sky split open.

A column of blinding, violet-white flame and pulverized Krupp steel, half a mile wide at the base and crowned with the spinning, three-hundred-ton wreck of her forward twenty-two-inch turret, shot five thousand feet straight up into the equatorial clouds; and when the shock-wave struck our canoe ten seconds later, flattening the ocean rollers into white foam and tearing the pandanus matting from our outrigger-boom, the spot where the flagship of the Pivot had ridden was only a boiling, empty whirlpool of steam into which the burning oil-scum rushed from all four quarters.

"The ships are gone, Master," Dao said. His young face was grey and salt-crusted as he stared back at the black rain of falling armor-bolts hissing into the swell a mile inshore, while from the low stone quarantine-spit of Sand Island a single, thin plume of white wood-smoke rose where the freed prisoners had broken down the lazaretto doors. "The furnaces are cold in Melbourne, the wires are cut at the Baikal, and there is not a keel left afloat between here and the Golden Gate that can carry a hundred tons of coal. What will become of the islands now?"

I looked down at the eight sealed copper cylinders between my knees, and then out across the vast, sparkling desert of the western sea, that four-thousand-league wilderness of salt and wind over which, for a brief watch in the night of time, one man’s iron will had thrown a bridge of steam and numbers.

Already, a hundred yards ahead of our bow, a school of flying-fish broke the clean blue mirror of the swell. They skimmed across the wave-crests without a shadow of smoke to darken their silver wings, just as they had leaped before the prows of Kamehameha’s war-canoes and Magellan’s rotting caravels.

"The rust will eat the tracks on the Khyber grade before the third winter is out, Dao," I said. I dipped my steering-paddle once more into the warm current that set toward the high, cloud-wrapped cliffs of Kauai. "In fifty years the banyan-roots in Malaya will pry the concrete off the oil-wells until the grandchildren of the stokers think the forty-ton tanks in the jungle were built by the gods before the flood. Yet listen to the water under the plank, boy: the tide never asks whether the flagship is on top of the wave or at the bottom of the coral. Pull for the west channel while the trade-wind holds."

***

We steered clear of the poisoned mouth of the Waimea, where the yellow acid-sludge from the broken Koloa vats still stained the surf a furlong from the beach. Instead, riding the strong northerly set of the Kauai channel through two nights of clean, starlit squalls, we brought our scorched outrigger through a narrow gap in the black basalt needles of the Na Pali coast, that precipitous, roadless wilderness of the northern shore where three-thousand-foot fluted cliffs of dark green lava drop straight into the thunder of the Pacific rollers, and where no surveyor’s chain or telegraph-insulator had ever climbed the goat-ledges.

Here, four hundred feet above the booming white surf of the Kalalau beach, in a dry, wind-scoured cavern of porous volcanic stone where the ancient canoe-makers of the island had once hidden their adzes, I have set up my last table.

Seven months have passed since the smoke cleared from the Oahu horizon. Down on the narrow crescent of black sand below my ledge, young Dao and forty runaway survivors from the Koloa leaching-sheds—Cantonese mechanics who have forgotten the cipher on their wrists, alongside Hawaiian fishermen whose fathers died at Rangoon and three deserted Oregon timber-boys from Julian Thorne’s vanguard—have cleared the wild guava-scrub from the ancient stone-walled terraces along the stream and planted the green shoots of the winter taro.

Steam-plows and silver thalers are gone from their hands; to dig the irrigation-ditches, they use heavy mattocks forged over a charcoal driftwood fire from the rusted, hand-puddled 1861 iron rail that we found lying beside the dead body of the woman Malia in the ashes of the Waimea hut.

As I sit this afternoon of November at the mouth of the stone cave, with a plank of drift-cedar balanced across two empty naval powder-kegs for my desk, the trade-wind carries the scent of wet salt spray and crushed mountain fern, mingled with the wood-smoke of the evening cooking-fires rising toward the clouds, washed clean at last of burning Borneo bunker-oil and the synthetic Mysore sandalwood that the court-peers sprayed upon the dead lagoon.

Beside my ink-horn lies the tarnished brass astrolabe that Marquis Takashima placed in my hands when we steamed out of Yokohama harbor fifty-eight years ago to divide the hemisphere with the American Caesar. Its vernier-scale is green with verdigris; its sighting-vanes are bent from the fall of the Archive roof; yet when I lift my eyes from the brass circle to the unbroken blue arch of the ocean stretching four thousand miles northward toward the Aleutians, I need no logarithmic table to read the sum of our century.

The snows of the Hindu Kush and the subterranean gasometers of San Francisco, where the priests of the three-faced idol brewed their poisons, produced only the final convulsions of the fever that destroyed the Grand Confederation of Pacifica. The fatal rot was born on that triumphant morning in the eighteen-fifties when Elias Thorne stood upon the windy casemate at Fort Point and believed that because a man could bolt an eighteen-inch cannon to the rock and string a copper wire across the Sierra, he had conquered geography itself.

History is a living body of flesh and soil. It keeps its natural stature and its appointed season, refusing to be bolted together like an iron bridge extended forever across the abyss by doubling the thickness of the girders. So long as the Protectorate remained an ocean of fierce men who traded the timber of Oregon for the silk of Canton across an open sea, the grandeur of the design matched the strength of the human wrist. Every power that rises by the perfection of its instruments falls slave to the tool it has forged.

Elias Thorne built railways to set the frontier free from the eastern bankers. His successors turned the entire terrestrial globe into a single, airless counting-house to feed those tracks. They mistook order for life itself. Once they boiled the rivers of Kauai into nitric acid and locked four hundred million Europeans and Asians into numbered wrist-shackles, they sought to replace the human heart with a strip of perforated brass tape, blind to the certainty that the earth would rise to cast the iron off its chest.

The American Caesar wanted a pedestal beyond the reach of the mob. Tonight he lies at the bottom of the Mariana Trench in four miles of freezing slime, while his seventy-ton bronze head houses the crabs of the Pearl Lochs, and from Peru to the Golden Gate, the horizon stands empty of a single steamer’s smoke-plume.

Down on the black beach below my cave, the ancient sun of the earth—far older than the gilded emblem stitched upon the Chancellery banners—sinks into the western water and washes the crests of the long Pacific rollers in Imperial Blue and Sunset Gold before the tropical night rushes up from the equator.

Up the steep basalt goat-path from the taro-patches climbs Dao. She carries a wooden calabash of baked fish and fresh stream-water for my supper, alongside a soldering-iron heated in a pot of charcoal embers to seal the eighth and last of the copper cylinders.

The tallow-wick in my stone saucer gutters in the rising sea-breeze; gray twilight creeps from the cave walls over the cedar plank, leaving only half an inch of white rag-paper at the bottom of the seventy-ninth roll before the steel nib of my pen wears down to the wood.

My scarred left hand holds the parchment steady against the salt-damp of the wind. I dip the point one last time into the dregs of the gall-ink and write the final line for whatever eyes may pry open this copper tube when the jungles have grown back over the ruins of Thalassia:

*And so the Pacific, like the Atlantic before it, became a graveyard of dreams.*
